en: Homage to Mañjunātha, to Śrī Kālacakra, whose nature is emptiness and compassion;
who is the single embodiment of knowledge and the object of knowledge, wherein the arising and destruction of the three realms of existence do not exist.

I, who am free from the pleasures of laughter and so forth, prostrate to that very non-dual [reality]: the Blessed Lady Prajñā, who possesses both form and formlessness; embraced by her, the Father is free from arising and decay, possesses immutable bliss, is endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*), and perceives the three times. He is the omniscient one of all Buddhas, the Blessed One, the Supreme Ādibuddha. I prostrate to the Buddha seated upon the lion throne, honored by the three worlds, the reality that has reached beyond existence through the divisions of the body, the unity of knowledge and the object of knowledge, the commitment (*samaya*) of the supreme Victor, the bodhicitta for the sake of sentient beings, and the vajra-word of the Victor. I prostrate to that very non-dual [reality].
Having prostrated to the Vajrayoga, which is pure, single, and of sixteen aspects, and to Kālacakra, who has twelve aspects through his limbs;

Having prostrated to that Primordial Buddha—the omniscient one, the body of gnosis, the coemergent Lord of Victors, the Dharma-body, as well as the Enjoyment-body and the Emanation-body whose form is like the sun with eyes as broad as lotus petals; who is the pure yoga through the liberations that have transcended existence and non-existence, and who is the non-duality of wisdom and means, praised by humans, gods, and demons— [The verse continues: The *bindu* is the supreme, stainless, and unchanging *bindu*, the great bliss, the *bindu* of the Victor, the *bindu* of the Sugata. It is the *bindu* of the *dharmadhātu*, the *bindu* of the *nirmāṇa*, and likewise the *bindu* of the *sambhoga*. It is the *bindu* of the *svabhāva*, the *bindu* of the *jñāna*, and the *bindu* of the *kāya*. It is the *bindu* of the *mantra*, the *bindu* of the *mudrā*, and the *bindu* of the *samaya*. It is the *bindu* of the *prajñā*, the *bindu* of the *upāya*, and the *bindu* of the *advaya*. It is the *bindu* of the *śūnyatā*, the *bindu* of the *karuṇā*, and the *bindu* of the *advaya*. It is the *bindu* of the *vimala*, the *bindu* of the *amala*, and the *bindu* of the *anāsrava*. It is the *bindu* of the *anutpāda*, the *bindu* of the *anirodha*, and the *bindu* of the *anālaya*. It is the *bindu* of the *anābhāsa*, the *bindu* of the *anirbhāsa*, and the *bindu* of the *anābhāsa-anirbhāsa*. It is the *bindu* of the *anādi*, the *bindu* of the *ananta*, and the *bindu* of the *anādi-ananta*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvadharma*, the *bindu* of the *sarvajña*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvākārajña*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvasattva*, the *bindu* of the *sarvabuddha*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvayogin*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvakāla*, the *bindu* of the *sarvadeśa*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvakāla-sarvadeśa*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvabodhi*, the *bindu* of the *sarvamukti*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvabodhi-sarvamukti*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvārtha*, the *bindu* of the *sarvasiddhi*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvārtha-sarvasiddhi*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvakāma*, the *bindu* of the *sarvarasa*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvakāma-sarvarasa*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvagandha*, the *bindu* of the *sarvasparśa*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvagandha-sarvasparśa*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvaśabda*, the *bindu* of the *sarvarūpa*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvaśabda-sarvarūpa*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvamantra*, the *bindu* of the *sarvamudrā*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvamantra-sarvamudrā*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvayoga*, the *bindu* of the *sarvatantra*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvayoga-sarvatantra*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvadevatā*, the *bindu* of the *sarvavidyā*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvadevatā-sarvavidyā*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvakula*, the *bindu* of the *sarvamaṇḍala*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvakula-sarvamaṇḍala*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvabīja*, the *bindu* of the *sarvākṣara*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvabīja-sarvākṣara*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvapuṇya*, the *bindu* of the *sarvajñāna*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvapuṇya-sarvajñāna*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvadāna*, the *bindu* of the *sarvaśīla*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvadāna-sarvaśīla*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvakṣānti*, the *bindu* of the *sarvavīrya*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvakṣānti-sarvavīrya*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvadhyāna*, the *bindu* of the *sarvaprajñā*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvadhyāna-sarvaprajñā*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvopāya*, the *bindu* of the *sarvapraṇidhāna*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvopāya-sarvapraṇidhāna*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvabalā*, the *bindu* of the *sarvājñāna*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvabala-sarvājñāna*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvavimokṣa*, the *bindu* of the *sarvābhisambodhi*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvavimokṣa-sarvābhisambodhi*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvadharmadhātu*, the *bindu* of the *sarvajñānakāya*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvadharmadhātu-sarvajñānakāya*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvatathāgata*, the *bindu* of the *sarvabuddha*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvatathāgata-sarvabuddha*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvabodhisattva*, the *bindu* of the *sarvapratyekabuddha*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvabodhisattva-sarvapratyekabuddha*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvaśrāvaka*, the *bindu* of the *sarvadeva*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvaśrāvaka-sarvadeva*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvanara*, the *bindu* of the *sarvasura*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvanara-sarvasura*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvamanuṣya*, the *bindu* of the *sarvāsura*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvamanuṣya-sarvāsura*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvagati*, the *bindu* of the *sarvabhava*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvagati-sarvabhava*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvaduḥkha*, the *bindu* of the *sarvasukha*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvaduḥkha-sarvasukha*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvānanda*, the *bindu* of the *sarvamahāsukha*, and the *bindu* of the *sarvānanda-sarvamahāsukha*. It is the *bindu* of the *sarvaprakṛti*, the *bindu* of the *sarvaviś
The imperishable, pure gnosis, completely purified by the knowledge of emptiness;
the non-dual mind, whose nature is the Dharma, completely purified by the knowledge of the signless.
The mantra is the inexhaustible sound, pure through the knowledge of speech unconditioned by volition;
likewise, it is indeed stainless, pure through the knowledge of non-conditioning.
Oṃ, homage to Mañjunātha!

O, for the sake of truth: in the Vimalaprabhā, yoga consists of wisdom and means; it is the attainment of the miraculous power of the body of form, [namely] Vajrasattva, Mahāsattva, Bodhisattva, and Tathāgata.
Having prostrated to that Bodhicitta— the Samayasattva who is the all-pervading Lord, the exhaustion of both existence and non-existence, without beginning or end, and peaceful— I pay homage.
The single yoga-vow of the emanation body, speech, mind, and gnosis of the world-system;
the single yoga-vow of the enjoyment body, speech, mind, and gnosis.
The singular yoga-vow of the glorious Dharmakāya, Vāk, Citta, and Jñāna; the singular yoga-vow of the Sahajakāya, Vāk, Citta, and Jñāna.

It is not waking, dreaming, or deep sleep, nor is it the fourth state; it is not the pleasure born of two sense organs, nor is it knowledge, mind, speech, or body—yet it abides within these four states.
Abandoning the action-seal (karmamudrā) and devoid of the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā), that which is born from the great seal (mahāmudrā) is the innate (sahaja); it is not with another.

Having prostrated to that syllable *Evaṃ*, the yoga consisting of wisdom and means— the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), the immutable bliss beyond the cultivation of conceptual construction, free from the forms of subject and object and devoid of the chatter of mental fabrication, having the appearance of a city of Gandharvas and the nature of a reflected image— [I pay homage].
Having prostrated to that Mahāmudrā, who transcends the nature of atoms, whose form is like a reflected image, and who is endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
Having prostrated before that Mother of the Universe, the mother of all Buddhas, who is free from arising and ceasing, and the conduct of Samantabhadra;
Having prostrated to that Kālacakra, the body arisen from syllables, which is devoid of the vowels, consonants, the *samāpatti*, the *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* syllables, and so forth;
The omniscient one, known as the Body of Gnosis, the all-pervading Lord with a body like the sun and eyes as broad as lotus petals— that is the reality in its sixteenfold division.
Having bowed to the Buddha, who consists of the four bodies and is seated upon the vajra lion-throne, and who was formerly entreated by Sucandra after being praised by gods and asuras;
In this verse, "the non-exhaustion of existence is *acitta*," and in those verses where it says "*saṃvara*," [it refers to] the section on the instruction for the discipline of the true path:

the yoga of the single unity of pure gnosis; the speech as the yoga of the *saṃbhogakāya*, honored by the three worlds; the excellent commitment (*samaya*) of the Victors as the yoga of the single unity of mind and phenomena; and the yoga of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Vajrasattva, having prostrated to the fourfold Vajrayoga.

Having bowed my head to that Lord who is non-dual in knowledge and the object of knowledge, who has transcended the power of worldly existence, whose nature is wisdom and skillful means, the single state [of union] placed upon the *vajramaṇi*—the dust and the sun—and the second state placed upon the *uṣṇīṣa*—the semen and the moon; which is eternal, indivisible, inseparable, desired, and honored by the three worlds; and having saluted him as the son of men, gods, and demons: [The following verse follows: Oṃ, homage to the venerable Vajrasattva, the essence of all Buddhas, the embodiment of the five families, the lord of the three realms, the one who has attained the supreme state of the non-duality of wisdom and skillful means. May he, the protector of beings, grant his grace so that this [tantra] may flourish for the benefit of all sentient beings. Thus, having prostrated with my head to the Lord who is worshipped by the three worlds, who is the desired [goal], indivisible and eternally indestructible, and who is the single state [of union] consisting of wisdom and skillful means—namely, the first [state] placed upon the *vajramaṇi* (the dust and the sun) and the second [state] placed upon the *uṣṇīṣa* (the semen and the moon)—who has transcended the power of worldly existence (*bhava-vibhava*), and who is the non-dual of knowledge and the knowable; [I shall now explain this].

Having bowed my head to the Lord of the gods, whose foot—placed upon the wind, fire, water, earth, the circle of Mount Meru, the lotus, the moon, and the sun, and finally upon the head of Īśvara and Māra—is together with the state of the Mother of the World; |||

Desiring to speak of that Yoga—the supreme bliss of the syllables—which has been practiced, taught, and chanted by all the infinite Sugatas as the Vajrayoga, [I, though] dull-witted, shall do so within the Kālacakra, accompanied by Bodhisattvas who are holders of the excellent thunderbolt and knowers of mantras. Does not the lord of birds travel swiftly through the sky, while other birds do not?
In that body wherein the Lord of Jinas has proclaimed the entire universe as manifest, together with the mantras, the *ali*, the *bindu*, and the *dharas*—
having entered that great ocean to float therein, I shall reach the further shore if there is the power of the Jina.
That which was previously prophesied by the One Endowed with the Ten Powers as a short tantra from the *Paramādibuddha* spoken by the Lord of Secrets—
that *Kālacakra-laghutantra*, the entirety of the sages, has been proclaimed here in the *Kalāpa* by Mañjuśrī.
The commentary written by Sucandra, which indicates the meaning of all vehicles, was sixty thousand [verses] long; that was obtained by me from Puṇḍarīka.
The twelve-thousand-verse text of the *Laghutantra*, which follows the *Mūlatantra* and elucidates the vajra-words, is now being written.

Having heard this tantra and received the supreme consecration according to the procedure taught by the Victor, the yogi— having mastered the entire King of Short Tantras and being established on the path of gnosis—
renounces pride, manifold enjoyments, and power, offers his mind to the Guru for the sake of Buddhahood, and, practicing for the benefit of others, listens to the commentary of the Lord.

He who, though established in the glorious Vajrayāna, lacks supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), yet composes a commentary while possessing a heart of various scriptures and the essence of Dharma, and endowed with the excellence of scholarship—he, like a reckless blind man [touching] an elephant, would destroy that very Tantra of his own. For this [Tantra] stands ever as the enemy of Māra’s kinsman, intended for the conquest of Māra’s Tantras.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, one who is conceited due to his scholarship, whose nature is ignorance regarding the words of the Lord of Jinas, and who is perpetually blind, enters hell after composing a commentary on the Supreme Vehicle (Agrayāna), having caused others who are blind to fall there as well.

With a mind drawn toward the pleasure of women on the unwholesome path of regret, killing living beings, and so forth, he is deprived of the bliss of glorious Wisdom (*Prajñā*); struck down by the state of the Vajra, he is overwhelmed by external enjoyments.

Those who have been prophesied by the Teacher in the Vajrayāna, which bestows the bliss of the Lord of Jinas—all those commentators and compilers of the *saṅgīti*, holders of the supreme *vajra* like myself—they proclaim the power of the Buddha in this world for the sake of maturing gods, *nāgas*, and humans. "We are those Lords of Jinas who possess the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*); our words are not false"—thus do the Bodhisattvas of the world-systems proclaim.
Indeed, in the future time, will not the various views of the Buddhists— always dedicated to treatises such as *Tarka* and the like—
become false due to the influence of their attachment to logic? Therefore,

I write this commentary (*ṭīkā*) which crushes the defect of the evil intellects of those very [Buddhists] who, though dedicated to logic and so forth, provide misleading instructions regarding the path to the desired goal.

In the ocean of existence within the glorious Vajrayāna, may this commentary always serve as the helmsman—[an ocean] whose infinite waters are passion; which is infested with crocodiles such as hatred devoid of discernment; which abounds in the waves of delusion; whose coastal shores are the greed for wealth and status resulting from coming and going; and which possesses the fierce roar of the submarine fire-vortex of karmic actions such as regret, killing, and the like.

That Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) of the Vajra-holder is the leader who swiftly traverses the path of the great ones by means of the wind-cloth of wisdom for those seeking the shore of Nirvāṇa; she is the destroyer of the hosts of Māras and afflictions, the bestower of sovereignty over the three worlds, and the inner guide who reveals everything. She alone bestows the bliss of omniscience, has as her object the abandonment of the obscurations of the aggregates and so forth, and is like a lamp that has been lit.

He who abandons her and would serve that woman of crooked heart who is greedy for wealth, or who serves her with a mind conceptualized by her, is led to rebirth and death by that intellect imagined by her.
Evil arises from the destruction of passion (*rāga*), for hatred (*dveṣa*) is born therefrom; from hatred comes delusion (*moha*), and from that, the mind’s swoon due to the falling of its own vajra.

[In another chapter: The instruction on the restriction of the true path: When the mind engages entirely with sense objects such as improper food and drink, it is thereby mocked, its happiness destroyed, and it wanders through six births after six births.

For those seeking the path of the Omniscient One, the investigation of words and non-words is not of great importance; for the Great Ones always proceed upon the path even through various local dialects.

The language of the Omniscient One is supreme, conforming to the inclinations of sentient beings, whereas other grammars composed by gods and serpents are intended for those who seek disputation over words and the like.
A yogi grasps even the meaning from a corrupt word, and a yogi grasps it from a regional dialect; for swans drink the milk that is mixed in the water only after extracting it.
Regarding the subject of ultimate reality, the great ones never rely on the literal letter;
once the meaning is understood through local designations, what is the use of the words of the scriptures?
That alone is true knowledge which possesses words free from corrupt forms;
for the Omniscient One, there is no speech that is merely local in this world.
The supreme syllable is the fourth, the gnosis of wisdom; that alone belongs to the Buddhas. Furthermore, that which is likewise described by the Victor as his own Mahāmudrā is this very same thing.

For one whose white [garment] leaks through attachment to wisdom, by what means can there be an increase in happiness? When the bud falls through contact with spring, by what means can the mango fruit remain?
He who has not attained the Imperishable, being miserable, seeks perishable pleasure;
like every thirsty lion, he does not seek the water that lies upon the earth.

The great fool desires even unattained worldly pleasure, which is impermanent and subject to decay; the wise man, however, having attained the bliss of sovereignty, renounces it for the sake of liberation.
Sometimes during the rainy season, the lion, who is the consumer of deer, delights in celestial pleasures; meanwhile, the pigeon constantly subsists on grains of stone.
But for both, there is no supreme bliss simultaneously and eternally, just as it does not exist due to the emission of semen;
likewise, it is absent for the ascetic and the lustful, and for those in sleep and waking, because of its perishability.
Immediately thereafter:
the etymology of *apaśabdaśabdāḥ* as "the words 'incorrect word' (*apaśabda*) and 'word' (*śabda*)" must be made in accordance with the Tibetan [translation].
By this, the meaning becomes clear: that there is not the same cognition for both the term *apaśabda* and the term *śabda*.
The meaning is that sound does not take anything as its object;
although the reading in manuscript *ka* is "sound, sounds," it is as follows:

just so, once seen, he perishes; like one bitten by a snake while asleep, he does not live because of the absence of the gathering of the vital breath (*śukta*). This is from the *Vimalaprabhā*, in the section on the World-Sphere (*lokadhātu*).

Just as that which has fallen from the womb of a virtuous woman is purified by asceticism, so too that which has fallen from the womb of a wicked woman becomes pure through penance, just as bark-garments and silken cloths are cleansed when scorched by fire.
Just as that [is purified], so too is the true mind of men purified by wisdom and knowledge.
Just as mercury, upon contact with fire, flees and does not remain stationary, so too semen, through contact with this female organ, is constantly moved by her even without skillful means,
being set in motion by the power of medicinal herbs and the like, just as it is when in contact with fire.
Just as that [fire], even when situated within wood, is not seen through methods of cutting or splitting, yet is seen when in contact with wisdom through the application of pure intelligence;
so it is.
Just as the reflection of the moon situated within a jar is not seen when the jar is churned, so too the appearance of the mind is not perceived through the methods of conceptual meditation;
yet it is perceived right there through the singular union of *lalanā* and *rasanā*.
One who lacks the path does not attain that reality which was proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
The generation stage, which has sixteen and fourfold divisions according to various conceptual paths and so forth, has been explained; however,
the yoga of the completion stage is the reality, for the realization of reality is nothing other than that.

By means of this path— consisting of breath control characterized by smoke and other signs, the flow through the central channel, the vow of the Vidyā, and the descent of the vajra, which is the upward-moving semen— the yogi attains the bliss of all the Buddhas.
The innate (*sahaja*) state, designated as the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), belongs to all the female messengers (*dūtī*).

Due to conceptualizations of form and so forth, and through the practice of meditating on the maṇḍala circle and other such things, there has been a corruption of the reading among those with divergent understandings; therefore, the reading is provided here as it occurs in this chapter, according to what is possible.
This instruction on the rules for the true path: this jewel of the excellent path has been given to another, a heedless being.

The jewel of the excellent path is carried away by the thieves of evil sense-objects for one who has entered the forest of his own home; and it is carried away by the thieves of doubt, remorse, sleep, laziness, and restlessness for one who has entered the dense thicket of wicked companions—
namely, killing, false speech, taking what is not given, adultery, and harsh and malicious speech.

By thieves consisting of divisive speech, covetousness, ill-will, wrong views, and false conduct; by major sins, minor sins, murder, malice, and addiction to the senses—by these five groups of five thieves, the jewel is constantly stolen.
Even from one who is vigorous, it is stolen by those many thieves through excessive food, drink, and various enjoyments. It is not stolen from one who has fallen into the stupor of negligence;
for the examiner himself would certainly not show [the jewel] to another common person in order to have it identified.

It becomes of great value; it does not release that jewel from its speech. From those experts in fine jewels who cause the examination of the great jewel to be performed, one's own jewel is indeed to be recognized by their pure words.
Māra creates obstacles by assuming the forms of fully enlightened Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,

as well as fathers, mothers, daughters, sisters, sons, brothers, beloved wives, and so forth; therefore, disciples must diligently keep the jewel of the excellent path bestowed by the true guru strictly concealed, having abandoned the household— which is like a family of thieves.
The path of the hero's conduct (*vīrakrama*) and the path of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*) are not for liberation;
it is the single path of perfect purity (*suviśuddhakrama*) that has been shown by the Buddha for liberation.
Those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) are not included therein because of their bliss.

In the sense of consecration (*sekārtha*), the Lord of Jinas [teaches] in the tantra consisting of wisdom and method the "Heroic Progress" (*vīrakrama*); this is not external, for it is said to be the destruction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the body.
Self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is the vision of the three realms within emptiness.

In this essence-less saṃsāra, Buddhahood is the fruit resulting from its exhaustion; therefore, for men, it arises through the destruction of saṃsāra, like a ripe plantain fruit arising through the destruction of the plantain tree. In the *Vimalaprabhā*, those beings who are like scorpions and crabs [to it] are its destroyers. *Note on variants:* - *kha. ṭu ṅa. ḍu, bho. ṭu* (referring to specific manuscript readings). - *kha. upapāpaka*; *ka. upapāpaka*. - *kha. vahi*; *ka. vadbhi*. - *ka. jñātram*. - *ṅa. mahārthaṃ*. - *ga. ṅa. vākyam*. - *gha. caurai ṛkṣakuṭumbaṃ*. - *kha. 0na*. - *vimalaprabhāyāṃ vṛścika kulīrasattvā yasyāḥ syuste vināśinastasyāḥ*.

Thus, that mind of union is perishable; yet, it is the non-dual, immovable, and unblinded [reality] of illusion, the desired supreme syllable, the knowledge that is neither existence nor non-existence within great passion, the essence, and Samantabhadra.
The passionless one, the great passion, the innate, the glorious holder of the drops of bodhicitta,
the glorious Kālacakra-vajra, the yoga whose nature is wisdom and means,
the embodiment of compassion and emptiness— Kāla is that which has the form of relative truth (saṃvṛti).
It is called the wheel of emptiness; Kālacakra is considered non-dual.
For the sake of swiftly attaining his glory, whatever yogi constantly and perpetually meditates upon the feet of the Yoginī, for him there shall be the destruction of all obstacles.

Enemies, lions, lordly elephants, sacrificial fires, serpents, thieves, and those bound by nooses; agitated oceans, flesh-eating demons (*piśācas*), diseases that cause fear of death, Indra’s portents, poverty, separation from one's wife, fear of an agitated king, the fall of a thunderbolt, and the loss of wealth—all these clearly go to destruction for him who remembers the feet of the Yoginīs. Even when being struck in battle by enemies on elephants and chariots, with their bodies fully armored, holding spears, discuses, swords, bows, and arrows, amidst a multitude of excellent men...

Having conquered all those enemies—who grant death, possess fierce forms, and have gone in every direction and intermediate quarter—with his own weapons, he who remembers the lion’s roar of the Yoginīs obtains fame for victory on all sides. That lion—whose face is utterly distorted, who is terrifying with sharp fangs, who lashes his tail, whose curved claws are firm, who has dug into the temples of rutting elephants, who is enraged, whose eyes are like the rising sun, whose mane flows, and who desires to kill—[is no match for him]. For him who remembers the feet of the Yoginīs, which remove fear, [the lion] flees far away.

Blue-hued, with tawny eyes, his pair of temples overflowing with abundant rut-fluid, uprooting and crushing various excellent trees while thundering like a cloud—that preeminent lord of elephants who, breaking the bond at the tips of his tusks, protects the feet of the *yoginīs* from fear—by remembering him, one is released from the body’s passion (*rāga*).

Śakra said: The fire that spreads in every direction and intermediate quarter with flickering flames, a great darkness of smoke over all, consuming villages, groves, and food-stores; emitting sparks like falling meteors, causing the fear of death for sentient beings at all times, and reaching every direction—that fire becomes cool for one who remembers the feet of the Yoginīs, which remove all fear.

Enraged, resembling black collyrium in hue, with a crooked gait and a slender body, accompanied by fierce hissing sounds, crooked-eyed, double-tongued, causing fear of death, possessing the speed of the wind, and violent— the Lord of Serpents,
who has arrived with a cruel gaze, displaying his expanded hoods and biting— perishes for that person who remembers the feet of the Yoginīs which remove all fear.

In the forest, bandits with evil intent—holding bows in their palms, with arrows drawn to their ears, blocking the path of the true way, and wandering in every direction with spears, discuses, and swords in hand—have arrived with fierce eyes to plunder the best of travelers; yet for him who remembers the feet of the Yoginīs, which remove all fear, they vanish far away.

Afflicted by hunger, his pair of lotus-feet bound with many snares and filled with chains, his tongue, throat, and lips parched, and his body withered due to the lack of pure water— yet even he who, while being guarded day and night by the guards at the command of his master’s anger, remembers the feet of the Yoginīs which remove all fear, attains liberation from this state.

He who remembers the feet of the Yoginīs, which remove all fear—even when embarked upon a sea-vessel tossed by endless, violent winds, whirled in eddies by swarms of sea-monsters and fish, obstructed by wicked ocean-pirates, and assailed from all sides by a constant rain of great fires from discharged oil—shall reach the further shore.

With hands like *kattikā* knives and *śukti* shells, uttering *phetkāra* cries and terrifying roars, their mouths blazing with fire, the Vetālas—cruel-minded, flesh-eaters, afflicted by hunger, delighting in human blood, emaciated, and naked—stand stationed within the circle of the ten directions to terrify; yet they provide protection for one who remembers the feet of the Yoginīs, which remove all fear.

One whose fingertips have perished, who daily loses his nose, lips, and ears, from whose pus-soaked wounds much matter flows repeatedly, whose limbs, feet, and hands are crooked—such a person, abandoned by his circle of kinsmen like a corpse due to the power of a foul stench, becomes free from diseases and gains beautiful feet if he remembers the Yoginīs.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "With blazing worlds, sharp fangs, and the faces of hooded serpents, lions, tigers, and elephants; with hands holding wheels, swords, discs, tridents, hooks, and vajras—all the messengers of the lords of the gods threaten the practitioner who is intent solely on meditation for enlightenment and established in supreme bliss. Yet they meet their destruction before him, he upon whose mind the feet of the Yoginīs rest."

In the rainy season, he carries a burden even from the forest to the city on a path filled with mud; in the winter, he travels through snowy regions without clothing; and in the summer, he journeys to another land along a waterless desert path, scorched by the sun's rays and full of danger—yet the poor man who endures these sufferings becomes free from desire for those who meditate upon his auspicious feet.

A pungent odor emanates from their armpits, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and body; they are perpetually unfortunate, deprived of sexual pleasure due to separation from all women, and always harbor hatred toward women by the power of inauspicious results. However, for those who meditate upon the Yoginīs—who bestow the boon of beauty, form, and happiness—all good fortune, complexion, and beauty shall belong to them.

The lord of men, agitated by treachery and single-mindedly intent on total destruction like the Yama of the dissolution, dispatched his army—which struck fear of death even among his own servants—yet he too becomes pacified toward those [servants] through gifts of honor and respect; for he is the granter of boons to the yoginīs who meditate with a tranquil mind upon the feet of the Lord of the Three Worlds.

For those who [otherwise] experience the fall of the thunderbolt from the sky anywhere at all, and who constantly undergo death, fainting, and detachment through association with women throughout various births and lifetimes—for them, even that [thunderbolt] becomes pacified and reaches its end; they are not born again, provided they are yoginīs meditating upon the divine abode of the Vajra, O Śrī Karma-jñāta.

For those who, through detachment from attachment to women, experience the destruction of all worldly aims day and night, that [destruction] arises again and again through many future births due to a mind clung to latent impressions (*vāsanā*). However, for the wise yoginīs who meditate upon that which is worshipped and praised by the supreme Victors—the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) that is the peerless state—every aim becomes indestructible.

The Yoginīs—Piṅgalā, Iḍā, and Avadhūtī—traverse the three paths of the sun, moon, and Rāhu. Between those two is the Gnosis-body (jñānakāya), where existence and non-existence have perished. Those two possess equal movement and gait; that one is the Imperishable, the state of innate bliss (sahajasukha). Whoever meditates upon that, for him the fruit described here will quickly arise in this very life, removing all fear.

The abode of the glorious Yoginīs is the House of the Vajra-Jewel; for the sake of entering it, the path free from afflictions and with Māra destroyed has been declared here by me, preceded by a hymn as spoken by the Jina. This is the instruction on the rules of the true path in this chapter. For those whose path is lost, who have always gone into the darkness of falsehood and the company of Māra, let them come not far from here to the House of the Vajra-Jewel through the path attained by men, [the teacher] whose body possesses the thirty-two marks, the Guru of this world.

Established upon the wheel of Dharma, his lotus feet kissed by the mass of rays from the crest-jewels of the crowns of the gods, showing the true path like the sun that destroys all darkness, he who has meditated through the paths of smoke and so forth upon the state of innate bliss shall become Kālacakra.

I, impelled by the wisdom of that [Buddha], shall always write this commentary through his grace, for he is the Śrī Śākyasiṃha—the sun of perfect knowledge who stands at the glorious Wheel of Dharma for the three worlds; whose lotus feet are resonantly praised by the crowns of the lords of gods, nāgas, and asuras; and who is the fierce slayer of the beasts of Māra and the afflictions.
From the letter *ka* comes the peace in the cause; from the letter *la*, there is indeed dissolution (*laya*) here.
From the letter *ca* comes the steadying of the flickering mind, and from the letter *ṛ* comes the knowledge of imperishable bliss as the means through the sequential binding.
The nature of compassion;
the wheel of the world, which is the form of the knowable, is the glorious Prajñā, whose essence is emptiness.
The designation of this Śrī Kālacakra, this vajra-yoga which is established in every respect within the two truths, shall be its expressive term.
In this tantra, a commentary is being written by me, the Lord of the World, who has been prophesied by the Sugata and indeed impelled by Mañjuśrī.
This illuminator of secrets in the tantra is beneficial for the ignorant, the learned, and the foolish;
like a mother to her sons, it is for the happiness of all embodied beings.
Because by means of this [treatise] yogins find the true path of Vajrasattva,
therefore this commentary, the *Vimalaprabhā*, is being written swiftly.

Thus ends the first chapter, the instruction on the rules for the supreme tutelary deity, which destroys all obstacles and māras, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghu-kālacakra-tantra-rāja* following the root tantra.
(0 Mahoddeśa) | This is the summary of the teaching of the Tantra in the *Vimalaprabhā*.
First, the construction of the world-system (*lokadhātu*) is explained; afterwards, the purpose, the purpose of the purpose, and so forth, are set forth in the *Laghu-tantra*.

In this regard, first of all, having thoroughly considered the subject matter, the expression, the relationship, the purpose, and the ultimate purpose, [this work] bestows the fruit of Buddhahood in this very life according to the inclination of the minds of those to be trained.

In the abode of great bliss, within the supreme primordial Buddha’s Great Vajra-Dhātu Maṇḍala, seated upon the vajra lion-throne, surrounded by a host of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, wrathful kings, gods, nāgas, deities, and goddesses, with his lotus feet worshipped by the inhabitants of the three realms, the sovereign of the single wheel of the world-systems, the Supreme Primordial Buddha, the Blessed Śrī Kālacakra, who is free from obstruction, was requested by Sucandra.

The *Paramādibuddha*, consisting of twelve thousand [verses], the lineage-less *Kālacakra*, the king of tantras, is embraced by the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, which serves as the witness to the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of Vajradhara; it is the witness to the vajra-words in all tantras, having opened the jewel-casket of the Buddhas. It rests upon the mundane and supramundane truths, is purified by the four enlightenments and the four vajras, and expresses the subject matter consisting of the four bodies, the six families, the twelve truths, the sixteen realities, the sixteen emptinesses, and the sixteen compassions. It reveals the ten mundane and eleven supramundane initiations, and elucidates the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*), and the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), both mundane and supramundane. Comprising five chapters on the world-system, the internal, the initiation, the means of achievement (*sādhana*), and gnosis—or alternatively, comprising five sections—it was taught for the sake of all beings, beginning with humans, attaining the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.

Therefore, there was the prophecy of the Tathāgata for Mañjuśrī regarding the compilation of this *Laghutantra*: for the sake of converting the Brahmin sages in a future time; for the sake of my own composition of a commentary; for the sake of teaching the tantra to others such as Yamāntaka and the rest; and so that all sentient beings dwelling in the sixty million villages of the realm of Sambhala and elsewhere may attain the path.

In this context, the world-system is preceded by an aggregation of atoms; sentient beings are preceded by the world-system; worldly and supramundane consecration is preceded by sentient beings; the accumulation of merit, the cultivation of the maṇḍala circle, and the accomplishment of worldly siddhis up to the Akaniṣṭha realm are preceded by consecration; and the accomplishment of the Great Wisdom Seal (mahājñānamudrā)—which transcends the aggregation of atoms, is devoid of the conceptual cultivation of maṇḍalas and the like, and is achieved through the power of the latencies of emptiness, compassion, the conventional, and the objectless from previous births, along with the accumulations of merit and wisdom—is preceded by worldly siddhis.
Therefore, first is the *Lokadhātu-kalpa*, then the *Adhyātma-kalpa*, then the *Abhiṣeka-kalpa*, then the *Laukikasiddhisādhana-kalpa*, and then the *Paramākṣarajñānasādhana-kalpa*.
Thus, according to this sequence, the King of Tantras consists of five *kalpas* or five chapters (*paṭalas*).
Subsequently, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is the Vajrayoga consisting of Wisdom and Means—the *Ādibuddha*, the *Niranvaya*, the Blessed One Kālacakra.
And it exists by way of the nature of these five chapters:
the chapter on the world-system;

First, the chapter on the world-system (*lokadhātupaṭala*) is established as having the nature of the Teacher, beginning with the words "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*); it is established as having the nature of the indication of the location; it is established as having the nature of the perfection of the great assembly; it is established as having the nature of the requester; it is established as having the nature of the inquiry into the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the designation (*abhidhāna*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the ultimate purpose (*prayojanaprayojana*) of the Vajrayoga; it is established as having the nature of the request for the initiation into the mandala and the arising of the universe from the five-syllable Great Emptiness (*pañcākṣaramahāśūnya*); it is established as having the nature of the Teacher’s reply; it is established as having the nature of the collection on the arising of the world-system, mantras, planets, constellations, sentient beings, life-force, and so forth; it is established as having the nature of the number of the mandalas of wind and the other elements, the oceans, islands, and mountains; it is established as having the nature of the prophecy concerning Mañjuśrī; it is established as having the nature of the thirty-one states of existence (*bhava*); it is established as having the nature of the arising of the Great Universal Monarch (*mahācakravartin*); it is established as having the nature of the measurement of days and the very subtle breaths (*śvāsa*) and so forth; it is established as having the nature of the astronomical calculations (*jyotirgaṇita*) that constitute the established doctrine (*siddhānta*); it is established as having the nature of the movement of the planets and the rising of the constellations from the breaths of the central channel (*madhyamanāḍī*); it is established as having the nature of the twelve-fold zodiac signs and the terrestrial globe; it is established as having the nature of the *svarodaya* (astrology) and so forth; it is established as having the nature of the strength of the earth and Rāhu and the other [planets]; it is established as having the nature of the machines for breaking and protecting fortresses; it is established as having the nature of the wandering of the Universal Monarch through the twelve divisions of the earth; it is established as having the nature of uprooting the religion of the Mlecchas and establishing the Buddha-dharma; it is established as having the nature of bestowing the mundane and supramundane paths of accomplishment (*siddhi*) upon all sentient beings; it is established as having the nature of the Teacher being positioned behind and in front of Mañjuśrī and Lokeśvara; and it is established as having the nature of the maximum lifespan of humans, from the Great Universal Monarch down to Kalkin.
Thus, in the chapter on the world-systems.

Then, within the chapter on the internal self (*adhyātmapaṭala*), *rajas* (the menstrual blood) exists first as the nature of the conception and retention of the embryo; it exists as the nature of the union of the white element (*śukla*), the substrate consciousness (*layavijñāna*), and gnosis (*jñāna*); it exists as the nature of the production of the embryo month by month; it exists as the nature of the ten stages beginning with the fish; it exists as the nature of the four bodies (*kāya*) and the four purities; it exists as the nature of the production of the embryo through the four types of awakening (*sambodhi*). It exists as the nature of the twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths (*śvāsa*), each [breath] corresponding to the thousands of channels, the three hundred and sixty joints, the six elements (*dhātu*), the six tastes, the six sense faculties, the six objects, the six organs of action and their objects, the six consciousnesses, the six formative forces (*saṃskāra*), the six feelings (*vedanā*), the six perceptions (*saṃjñā*), the six forms (*rūpa*), the six cognitions (*jñāna*), the six wheels (*cakra*), and the six mandalas. It exists as the nature of the flow of the five aggregates (*skandha*) and the five elements (*dhātu*) through the petals of the navel-lotus and the two nostrils via the left and right mandalas; it exists as the nature of the emergence of the entire tantra through the central channel (*madhyamā*); it exists as the nature of the vital winds (*prāṇa*, etc.); it exists as the nature of the arising of the symbols of the deities from the elements; it exists as the nature of the signs of death (*ariṣṭa*) of the moon, sun, and fire; it exists as the nature of birth in the six realms of rebirth (*gati*) as the ripening of karma; and it exists as the nature of the seizing, moving, and cutting of the channels (*nāḍikā*) and so forth.

Thus, in the chapter on the Inner [Science], he abides by way of having the nature of deceiving death and untimely demise through the bliss of entering the middle way and so forth; he abides by way of having the nature of accomplishing external worldly activities; he abides by way of having the nature of examining all philosophical systems and inference; and he abides by way of having the nature of establishing the Dharma according to the inclinations of various sentient beings.

Then, in the *Abhiṣeka-paṭala*, there occurs a recurrence of the following passage: "It exists as the nature of the examination of the guru first; it exists as the nature of the summary of the examination of superior, inferior, and middling disciples; it exists as the nature of the characteristics of the ground and so forth, divided by direction such as the village, for the sake of accomplishing the expansion of activities (*karmaprasara*); and it exists as the nature of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the materials for the fire offering (*homadravya*), the rosary beads (*akṣa*), the thread (*sūtra*), the seat (*āsana*), the ritual stake (*kīlaka*), the water-jar (*kalaśa*), the powder-line (*rajaḥsūtra*), the placement of the machine (*yantranyāsa*), and the glorious prophecy (*śrīvyākaraṇa*). Indeed, that [passage] does not exist in the Tibetan [translation].

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, he abides by way of the nature of the characteristics of the world-system (*lokadhātu*); he abides by way of the nature of the thorough knowledge of the ten principles (*tattva*) through the drawing of the mandala for the acquisition of the stages (*bhūmi*); he abides by way of the nature of bestowing mundane and supramundane consecrations (*abhiṣeka*); he abides by way of the nature of all foundations and meditative absorptions (*samādhi*); he abides by way of the nature of the gathering, the pledge (*samaya*), and the worship in the wheel of the pledge (*samayacakra*); he abides by way of the nature of the thirty-six family goddesses, their mudrās, gazes, signs, pledges, conventions, castes, and so forth; he abides by way of the nature of the dismissal of the mandala circle; he abides by way of the nature of the worship and dismissal of the dust-circle assembly (*rajo-gaṇacakra*) in great rivers and so on, or in one’s own respective home; and he abides by way of the nature of satisfying the glorious Guru with all kinds of gifts.
Thus, in the Chapter on Consecration.

Then, in the chapter on the means of achievement (*sādhana-paṭala*), he first abides by way of the nature of the radiation of Tathāgatas through the rays of light from the seed-syllable upon the moon at his heart, beginning with the protection wheel (*rakṣā-cakra*) and the purification of the face; he abides by way of the nature of the unsurpassed offerings, the confession of sins, the rejoicing in merit, the taking of the three refuges, the self-dedication, the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), the reliance upon the path, and the focus on emptiness (*śūnyatā*); he abides by way of the nature of the means of achievement such as the King of Mandalas (*maṇḍala-rājāgrī*), the Supreme King of Rituals (*karma-rājāgrī*), the yoga of the drop (*bindu-yoga*), and the subtle yoga (*sūkṣma-yoga*) according to the stage of generation (*utpatti-krama*); he abides by way of the nature of the means of achieving external worldly accomplishments (*laukika-siddhi*); he abides by way of the nature of the means of achievement such as the knowledge of the secret reality of the Vedānta and sacrifices, the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅga-yoga*), and so forth; he abides by way of the nature of the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*) through generosity and other virtues; and he abides by way of the nature of the cultivation of the mind, both perceptible and imperceptible.
Thus, in the chapter on the means of accomplishment.

Then, in the *Jñānapaṭala*, [the Lord] abides as the nature of the maṇḍala of the purification of the elements (dhātu), such as the bones of the body; he abides as the nature of the deities of the six families of body, speech, and mind; he abides as the nature of the six mantra-families beginning with A and Ka; he abides as the nature of the thirty-six tantras of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*); he abides as the nature of the emanation of the Great Sovereign of the Six Wheels (*ṣaṭcakravartin*) permeated by the great vows (*mahāsaṃvara*) of wisdom, means, action, and yoga; he abides as the nature of the means for accomplishing the gnosis of the supreme immutable Great Seal (*paramākṣaramahāmudrā*) through the fourth consecration; he abides as the nature of the emanation of the gnosis-maṇḍala; he abides as the nature of the practice for serving the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); he abides as the nature of the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which is the essence of all aspects of gnosis and the knowable; he abides as the nature of the examination of all activities of body, speech, and mind; he abides as the nature of the teaching of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma; he abides as the nature of the withdrawal of the Buddha-fields; he abides as the nature of dwelling together with Bodhisattvas and Mahāsattvas, equal in number to the atoms of Mount Sumeru within the realm of space; he abides as the nature of the arising of Buddha-fields; he abides as the nature of the adamantine empowerment (*vajrādhiṣṭhāna*) in the Buddha-field; and [he abides] by virtue of the inclinations of beings with various dispositions.
He abides as having the nature of teaching the Dharma;
he abides as having the nature of accomplishing physical attainments such as the elixirs and alchemy;
and he abides as having the nature of performing the welfare of all sentient beings through supreme unchanging bliss.
He abides by way of the nature of the collection of dharmas, the collection of numbers, and the collection of designations;
he abides by way of the nature of the five syllables, the six syllables, the great emptiness, the bindu-emptiness, and praise.
Thus, in the Chapter on Gnosis.

[In this] chapter: The Summary of the Teaching of the Tantra. Therefore, the Blessed One Kālacakra, who exists as the nature of these five chapters according to the sequence mentioned above, is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) here.
The collection of chapters that establishes him is the title of the *Tantrarāja* (the King of Tantras), which is the expression (*abhidhāna*).
Between these two—the subject matter and the expression—there is a relationship characterized by the signifier and the signified (*vācya-vācaka*).

The Blessed One Kālacakra is the signified (*vācya*), abiding as the nature of the five chapters; the signifier (*vācaka*) is the expression (*abhidhāna*) consisting of the five chapters. Furthermore, the Blessed One Ādibuddha is the signified, and the expression Ādibuddha is the signifier; such is the characteristic of the signified and the signifier.
This is the relationship between the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the expression (*abhidhāna*).
Therefore, the purpose (*prayojana*) of entering the mandala by means of bestowing the worldly consecrations (*laukikābhiṣeka*) is the accomplishment of the accumulation of merit (*puṇyasambhāra*);

and the purpose of bestowing the supramundane consecrations (*lokottarābhiṣeka*)—the fourth [consecration] of great wisdom—for the sake of attaining the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrāsiddhi*) free from all traces, is the accomplishment of the accumulations of merit and gnosis (*puṇyajñānasambhāra*). This is the purpose of the purpose.

Having thoroughly observed these very characteristics of the subject matter, [the teaching is given] according to the intention of the minds of those to be trained who are devoid of restrictive rules (*niyama*).

The "restrictive rule" refers to the vow of the Śrāvaka vehicle, which is a restraint consisting of the renunciation of the five objects of sensual enjoyment; those who are "devoid of restrictive rules" are those who lack that. Their "intention of their own minds" is the desire for the enjoyment of the five objects of sensual pleasure, as well as the desire for great bliss through the two sexual organs—this is the "intention of their own minds" for those devoid of restrictive rules.
By means of this intention of their own minds, it bestows the fruit of Buddhahood in this very life.
In this birth—that is, in a human birth—the King of Tantras bestows the fruit of Buddhahood, but not in births within the five destinies such as those of the gods and so forth. Why is that?
Because they are born in non-karma-bhūmi regions.
Thus, there is the Lord’s rule that even for gods and others, it will bestow the fruit of Buddhahood upon obtaining a human birth in this world.
"By means of the two accumulations of merit and wisdom, [one becomes] a Great Being, a bull among men, consisting of the six elements;

it cannot be otherwise. It is the fixed rule of the Tathāgata that in this human birth, even for one who has committed evil deeds, the fruit of Buddhahood will be bestowed through this mantra vehicle. As it was said by the Blessed Buddha in this mantra vehicle: 'Outcastes, bamboo-workers, and others who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution...'"
"In this very life, those who practice the conduct of mantra shall become Buddhas"—
this word of the Blessed One is true.

In this life, whatever fierce karma—such as the five crimes of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*)—was previously committed, that is destroyed in this Mantra Vehicle by means of the samādhi of the immutable bliss of Mahāmudrā. To prevent the entry of other adventitious unwholesome states, one places the door-panels of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), such as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, upon the gates through which the four Māras and obstacles enter the abode of the Vajra-Dharmodaya. Having accomplished Vajrasattva therein together with Mahāmudrā, even those who have committed the five crimes of immediate retribution become attainers of the fruit of Buddhahood in this very life; such is the rule of the Tathāgata. However, it is not the consensus of the Tathāgata that those who, having entered the Mantra Vehicle, continue to commit fierce karma such as the five crimes of immediate retribution, will nevertheless become attainers of the fruit of Buddhahood in this life.

In this regard, regarding all three vehicles, there is the word of the Blessed One: "It is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end. According to this statement of the Blessed One, it is not the rule of the Tathāgata that those who have entered the Mantra Vehicle become attainers of the fruit of Buddhahood even while performing sinful actions. Now, here in this Mantra Vehicle, the Blessed One has spoken of the consumption of meat by yogins; that very act always occurs through the taking of life.
Sometimes destruction occurs through the taking of life even when there is no eater and no killer;
therefore, the act of taking life would belong to both the eater and the killer.
In this regard, it is the command of the Tathāgata that a practitioner must perform the four equalities daily;

that is true. For that reason, the taking of life occurs through that which possesses a causal sign (*nimitta-sāvadya*). Therefore, for that reason, the Blessed One has declared that for yogins, that which is without a causal sign (*animitta*) and blameless (*niravadya*), such as cow-meat and the like, is edible.

In this world, whatever is inedible and unsaleable for people in a given region—such as cow-meat and so forth—if it has died by its own karma, been killed in battle, killed by evil deeds, or killed by its own fault (such as a thief), all of that is edible for yogins.

The Tathāgata has said: "Meat that is not purchased with wealth, nor killed for sacrificial rites such as those for one’s father and so forth, and which is done with a specific motive—that meat is to be eaten. Thus the Tathāgata has spoken. Now, regarding that which must be performed four times every day: it should be done with the five blameless items, such as cow-milk and so forth, and the five [substances] beginning with Vairocana, in the form of mustard-seed-sized pills for the purpose of daily commitment-observance (*samaya-sevā*). Alcohol and women are always blameless; they are taught for the sake of meditative cultivation according to the principle of non-attachment.

In the *Mūlatantra* as well, the Blessed One said: "If a being who is innocent is killed by those who are difficult to tame and commit evil deeds for the sake of the gods, for fear, for the sake of pleasing [deities], for the sake of attaining supernatural powers (*siddhi*), or for sale—that meat of his is faulty; it is not desired when purchased and eaten."
Indeed, that which is not obtained through sacrifice, is not fallen [from a pure source], and is blameless in the bowl is excellent;
it is better for one person to eat the flesh of many living beings than for one human being to eat the flesh of many living beings.
One who is engaged in yoga should eat that which is blameless with a mind free from conceptual construction, having truly generated compassion; for indeed,
food and drink are always intended for the destruction of the seizing spirits of the [eighteen] families.
"Attainment of the unwholesome has been proclaimed by Vajrin, the seer of reality.
Thus,
according to the sequence stated, this King of Tantras bestows the fruit of Buddhahood even upon those who are devoid of restrictive observances.

Buddhahood consists of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the majestic qualities such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Because it bestows these, it is the "Bestower of the Fruit of Buddhahood.

The Abode of Great Bliss (*mahāsukhāvāsa*) is the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) characterized by space, unmixed, the source of the Dharma, transcending worldly analogies, and universally auspicious; this is the Abode of Great Bliss.

In the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu of the Paramādibuddha, which is without parts, in which knowledge and the object of knowledge have become one in a single fusion, which is indivisible and impenetrable, characterized by the realm of all aspects, and equal to a mirror-image or a prognostic reflection— in that Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu,
[the Lord] seated upon the vajra-siṃhāsana, which consists of the maṇḍalas of moon, sun, and fire, is indivisible and impenetrable.

The letter *e* is the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), the vajra-lion throne; he dwells upon that, therefore he is the Vajra-lion. "Go-kvādikam" means "cow-pen and so forth" (*gokulādikaṃ*). However, this being is everywhere struck down; his vital essence (*sattva*) has been destroyed.

In the great mandala of Sanandhātu, *sana* is *Kul La sana*; it is situated in *sana*. The syllable *vaṃ* consists of the nature of body, speech, mind, and gnosis; by means of that [syllable], he is seated upon the vajra lion-throne.
"Surrounded by a host of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Wrathful Kings, gods, nāgas, male deities, and female deities":

the Buddhas are Akṣobhya and others; the Bodhisattvas are Samantabhadra and others; the Wrathful Kings are Uṣṇīṣa and others; the gods are Īśvara and others; the nāgas are Ananta and others; the female deities are Vajradhātvīśvarī and others, Dharmadhātviśvarī and others, Atinīlā and others, Carcikā and others, Gaurī and others, Śvānāsyā and others. The collection of these is a "host" (*gaṇa*); surrounded by that is "surrounded by a host of male and female deities. By that [phrase], it means "surrounded by a host of male and female deities."
"By him whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the three realms" means:

the three realms are the realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*), form (*rūpadhātu*), and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*); he is one whose lotus-feet are worshipped by those [realms], thus he is "the one whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the three realms. By that term, "by him whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the three realms," it is meant "by the universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the three realms."

He for whom the wheel of Dharma turns simultaneously throughout the three realms is the Universal Monarch (cakravartin) of the three realms; by that Universal Monarch of the three realms—that is, by the Paramādibuddha.

The Paramādibuddha is characterized by the perfect awakening through the net of illusion consisting of five aspects in a single moment and twenty aspects, which is immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*) and supreme. Because he is the primordial Buddha (*ādi-buddha*) who is supreme, he is the Paramādibuddha; [the phrase] "by that Paramādibuddha" refers to him.
"By the one without continuity" (*niranvayena*):

"continuity" (*anvaya*) refers to the phenomenon (*dharma*) consisting of wisdom and skillful means, characterized by the grasped and the grasper; that continuity which has been discarded is "without continuity," and thus it is said "by that one without continuity," namely, the Blessed One Kālacakra.

*Kāla* is the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*), the protector of great bliss (*mahāsukha*); he whose body is the wheel (*cakra*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, which has been uprooted and rendered free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇa*) by that [Kāla], is *Kālacakra*. Furthermore, by each individual syllable: the letter *ka* signifies the peace of the cause; from the letter *la*, dissolution (*laya*) occurs here; from the letter *ca*, the wandering mind is restrained; and from the letter *ṛ*, there is the binding of the sequence.

The sequence of descent (*rātkrama*) is the emission of the drops (*bindu*) of the body and so forth; its binding through innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*), known as Kālacakra.

He is "Blessed" (*bhaga*) because he shatters the Māras and the afflictions (*kleśa*); "Blessed" (*bhaga*) refers to the collection of qualities such as omniscience and sovereignty; he who possesses that *bhaga* is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*).
By that Blessed Kālacakra, [it is said] "requested by Sucandra.

He is "Sucandra" because he is both auspicious (*śobhana*) and the moon (*candra*); he has become the listener for all Tathāgatas; he is the Stainless Light of the Vajra-moon (*vajrendu-vimalaprabha*); and because he compiles the Dharmas spoken by the Tathāgatas in the various languages of all sentient beings, he has become the ear for all Tathāgatas.
*Guhyādhipati*:

"Secret" (*guhya*) refers to the Vajrayāna, which is superior to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; he is the *adhipati* (lord) as the compiler (*saṅgītikāraka*) of that [Vajrayāna], hence *guhyādhipati*. Furthermore, according to external worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), by the word "secret" (*guhya*) they mean the *yakṣas*; he is their *adhipati*, hence *guhyakādhipati*, the resident of Aḍakavatī.

Externally, by the word *aḍaka* is meant a multitude of corpses whose life-force has perished; that which possesses this is the cremation ground called *Aḍakavatī*. In that place dwell great yakṣas who harass sentient beings and create manifold obstacles. He is their slayer, a dweller of *Aḍakavatī*, like a lord of deer in a forest; thus he is the Great Yakṣa Lord dwelling in *Aḍakavatī*.

Internally, "Aḍaka" refers to the cessation of twenty-one thousand six hundred and thirty-six inhalations and exhalations; because this [cessation] exists in her, she is the stage *Dharmameghā* (Cloud of Dharma). The resident of that [stage] is the dweller of Aḍakavatī, the Lord of Yakṣas who slays the yakṣas of the afflictions of Māra and the obscurations to the knowable.
Through the lion’s roar of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, he sets forth the Dharma for all sentient beings in their respective languages. By means of that emanated body, he is Vajrapāṇi.
Requested by King Sucandra; [the commentary on] the Uṣṇīṣa and Carcikā sections of the Khasarpaṇa.
The secret word "Vajrendra" is spoken of [in relation] to the yakṣīs.
O King, requested by Sucandra; thus,
in the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is called the "Twelve-Thousand-Line [Commentary] on the World-Sphere."

The collection of three hundred and eighty-four thousand syllables consists of thirty-two-syllable *anuṣṭubh* verses; it is called the "Twelve Thousand" (*dvādaśasāhasrikam*) because it is the *Paramādibuddha*. It is the *Paramādibuddha* because it expresses the subject matter (*abhidheya*), and because it exists as the very nature of the expression (*abhidhāna*) of that subject matter. Thus, it is the *Kālacakra*, the *Paramādibuddha*; and it is the *Abhidhāna* (the expression) because it expresses the subject matter *Kālacakra*. It is "without lineage" (*niranvaya*) because it expresses a subject matter that is without lineage. Here, "lineage" (*anvaya*) refers to the side of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the side of method (*upāya*). That lineage, consisting of distinct sides, is discarded; therefore, that Tantra is "without lineage. It is called "non-dual" by the Victor (*Jina*) because it is a Yoga Tantra whose essence is wisdom and method. In this Royal Tantra (*tantrarāja*), which has as its subject matter the essence of wisdom and method, if there were a division between the sides of wisdom and method, there would be an absence of the subject matter that is the essence of wisdom and method. From the absence of the subject matter that is the essence of wisdom and method, there would be an absence of non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). From the absence of non-dual gnosis, there would also be an absence of Buddhahood. And from the absence of Buddhahood, there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, here, without the relationship between the expression and the expressed, the non-dual yoga whose essence is wisdom and method—characterized by the signified and the signifier—would not exist in the Yoga Tantra named *Upāya*. Furthermore, the word "yoga" does not denote only the meaning of method, nor does the word "yoga" denote only the meaning of wisdom; rather, the word "yoga" denotes the meaning of both wisdom and method. Thus it has been said: "Yoga does not occur through the body of method alone, nor through wisdom alone; the union (*samāpatti*) of wisdom and method is called 'yoga' by the Tathāgatas."

Therefore, in whichever tantra the subject matter consists of both wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*), that tantra is, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), neither a wisdom-tantra nor a method-tantra. According to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛtyā*), however, the categories of wisdom and method are taught by the Tathāgata through the distinctions of the ten cognitions and so forth, and through the purification of the elements (*dhātu*) and aggregates (*skandha*), in accordance with the inclinations of beings of inferior capacity. Thus, even regarding what is called a "Yoginī-tantra," here in this yoga, one who possesses discipline (*śīla*) is a "yogī," and likewise a female practitioner is a "yoginī. Consequently, there exists both Yoga-tantra and Yoginī-tantra, due to their mutual relativity. Therefore, the tantra whose essence is wisdom and method—the Kālacakra, which is without partiality—is, from the perspective of ultimate truth, embraced by the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, which serves as a witness to the Gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) of Vajradhara.

Because it is designated as the *Ādibuddha* (Primordial Buddha), just as the *Nāmasaṅgīti* has been spoken, will be spoken, and is being spoken by the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present, so too is the *Ādibuddha*. Here, the word "primordial" (*ādi*) signifies that which is without beginning or end; it was taught, will be taught, and is being taught by the Primordial Buddha in beginningless time—not by Śākyamuni alone, nor even by the Tathāgata Dīpaṅkara. Regarding this, Vajrapāṇi said: "That which was spoken by the Buddhas of the past, and which the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the future and the present will speak—the *Māyājāla*, the Great Tantra—which is also [spoken] again and again in this [tantra] by the holders of mantras, the Great Vajradharas, who are joyful and delighted."
It is fully proclaimed.

Thus, [the phrase] "thirty-two syllables per *anuṣṭubh* pāda" does not appear in manuscript Gha; in manuscript A, [the word] "of Brahmanhood" (*brahmatvasya*) is missing; in manuscript Gha, "in the *Anopāyatantra*" is missing. [The text continues: "O King Sucandra, at his request, [this is] the *Paramādibuddha*; O, it consists of twelve thousand [verses]; it is a collection of three hundred and eighty-four thousand syllables; because there are thirty-two syllables per *anuṣṭubh* pāda, it is called the 'Twelve Thousand' (*dvādaśasāhasrika*); it is without lineage (*niranvaya*). This is the summary of the teaching of the Tantra in the Abhiniṣpatti chapter. Therefore, from this statement of the request for the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, it is established that the Mantrayāna was taught by all the Tathāgatas.

Regarding the statement that "in this assembly, amidst Dīpaṅkara and Śākyamuni, the Mantra Vehicle was not taught by any Tathāgata," this means that at that time and on that occasion—that is, during the period of teaching the Dharma in the Noble Land (Āryaviṣaya)—it was not taught to the assembly of the Noble Land because of the disposition of beings who were unfit due to their pride in the four castes. It does not mean, however, that it was not taught at other times, in other lands, or to other assemblies of world-systems. Therefore, according to the word of the Tathāgata, all Tathāgatas are teachers of the three vehicles; otherwise, there would be a lack of omniscience due to not teaching the Vajrayāna. Thus, all Tathāgatas are teachers of the three vehicles and teachers of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*), in accordance with the dispositions of sentient beings.
Therefore, because it is embraced by the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, which serves as the witness to the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of Vajradhara, it is the witness to the vajra-words in all the kings of tantras.

In this Vajrayāna, by the power of the dispositions of sentient beings, the *vajrapada* is concealed in all the *tantrarājas*. According to the words of the Tathāgata, "The fourth is that again, likewise," the fourth is not the third; because of the statement "the fourth" and the statement "that again, likewise," the *prajñājñāna* is itself the fourth. Therefore, according to the word of the Bhagavān, the *vajrapada* is concealed in all the *tantrarājas* and does not appear openly; it is to be understood through the sequence of the lineage of gurus. According to the words of the Tathāgata, "A *tantra* is to be understood by means of another *tantra*," here in the Mantranaya the *vajrapada* is twofold: one is by worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*), and the second is from the ultimate point of view (*paramārtha*). Of these two, the *vajrapada* by worldly convention bestows the accomplishments of the *samaya* in rites such as slaying, while the *vajrapada* by ultimate truth is the fourth, "that again, likewise," which bestows the fruit of the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. For this very reason, in this *Ādibuddha*, the *vajrapada* is revealed by the Bhagavān through summary, detailed explanation, and further sub-explanation. For the sake of its realization, the path of the signs beginning with smoke—the meditation on Mahāmudrā—is revealed: "Having made the mind one-pointed in emptiness, one should examine for one day. From this word of the Bhagavān, in the *Paramādibuddha*, the *vajrapada*—the path of meditation on Mahāmudrā consisting of smoke and so forth—is revealed; it has not come through the sequence of the lineage of gurus, nor is it an empowerment by the command of a guru. There is proof for this path: "One who is worthy should examine for one day," according to the word of the Bhagavān. Here, no other means of mantra-realization is to be examined by a yogin in a single day, apart from the signs beginning with smoke. The sign is also threefold: the initial sign, the middle sign, and the final sign. The initial sign is the path of smoke and so forth, and the attainment of the protection of the manifestation of the universe through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*). The middle sign is the attainment of the first stage (*bhūmi*) through eighteen hundred moments of supreme immutability (*paramākṣara-kṣaṇa*), the perception of unseen objects through the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), and the attainment of worldly accomplishments. The final sign is Buddhahood, the state of a Vajradhara, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā through the attainment of the twelve stages and ten stages via twenty-one thousand six hundred and sixty moments of supreme immutability. This *vajrapada* and so forth, preceded by the signs, was taught openly by the Bhagavān in the *tantrarāja* *Paramādibuddha*. Therefore, among all the *tantrarājas*, this *tantra* is the witness to the *vajrapada*; it was not taught for those who seek it in other *tantras*. (Note: Regarding the variants in the Tibetan text: *sahasra* is absent in the Ka manuscript; *tantrāntareṇa* is rendered as *rgyud gSan Dag Gis*; *adhiṣṭhitaṃ* as *byin gyis brlabs pa*; *akṣarakṣaṇa* as *skad cig ma*; *adṛṣṭārtha* as *ma mthoṅ ba'i don*; *antanimittaṃ* as *mtha'i mtshan ma*.)

"Opening the jewel-casket of the Buddha": the "Buddha-jewel" is the supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*); the "casket" is the "vajra-jewel" and the "lotus. That which opens this very casket of the Buddha-jewel by means of this king of tantras is called "opening the jewel-casket of the Buddha. Regarding "based upon the mundane and supramundane truths": the mundane truth consists of the cultivation of conceptualizations of the maṇḍala-circle and the accomplishment of mundane siddhis through the generation stage (*utpattikrama*). The supramundane truth consists of the accomplishment of the siddhi of Mahāmudrā through the completion stage (*utpannakrama*), by means of the signs such as smoke and so forth, with a non-conceptual mind. The completion stage is the innate (*sahaja*), non-conceptual state, possessing all aspects, yet devoid of the mental construction of faces, arms, colors, and shapes.

"Based on these two truths" means based on the mundane and supramundane truths; "because of seeing the two paths" refers to the four types of perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*). "Purified by the four vajras" refers to: the perfect awakening in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodhi*), the fivefold perfect awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*), the twentyfold perfect awakening (*viṃśatyākārābhisambodhi*), and the perfect awakening through the net of illusion (*māyājālābhisambodhi*). It is completely purified by these; that is, it is purified by the four perfect awakenings through the process of birth from the womb (*garbhajotpattikrama*) and the process of generating the images of smoke and so forth (*dhūmādibimbotpannakrama*). Thus, it is completely purified by the four perfect awakenings.

It is the elucidation of the path to the accomplishment of the four bodies (*catuḥkāya*), the six families (*ṣaṭkula*), the twelve truths (*dvādaśasatya*), the sixteen realities (*ṣoḍaśatattva*), the sixteen emptinesses (*ṣoḍaśaśūnyatā*), the sixteen compassions (*ṣoḍaśakaruṇā*), and the mundane and supramundane empowerments (*laukikalokottarābhiṣeka*), as well as the actions (*karman*) and the great seal of gnosis (*jñānamahāmudrā*).

Regarding the four bodies— pure (*śuddha*), dharma (*dharma*), enjoyment (*sambhoga*), and emanation (*nirmāṇa*)— they are characterized by the states of the fourth state (*turya*), deep sleep (*suṣupti*), dream (*svapna*), and waking (*jāgrat*) of the one born from the womb (*garbhaja*).

And these are the six families of the Buddhas, which are unobscured (*nirāvaraṇa*). Thus, syllabic bliss is the gnosis element (*jñānadhātu*); consciousness is the space element; formations are the wind element; feeling is the fire element; perception is the water element; and form is the earth element. These are obscured for those born from a womb, but they are unobscured for the Buddhas.

The twelve truths are ignorance, mental formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death. These twelve truths are with obscuration for those born from a womb, but without obscuration for Buddhas.

Due to the flow of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) through the divisions of the twelve transits (*saṃkrānti*), they are with obscuration for those born from a womb, but without obscuration for Buddhas, because of the cessation of the twelve links.

The sixteen principles (*tattva*) are as follows: the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), emanation speech (*nirmāṇavāk*), emanation mind (*nirmāṇacitta*), and emanation gnosis (*nirmāṇajñāna*); the enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*), enjoyment speech (*sambhogavāk*), enjoyment mind (*sambhogacitta*), and enjoyment gnosis (*sambhogajñāna*); the dharma body (*dharmakāya*), dharma speech (*dharmavāk*), dharma mind (*dharmacitta*), and dharma gnosis (*dharmajñāna*); and the innate body (*sahajakāya*), innate speech (*sahajavāk*), innate mind (*sahajacitta*), and innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*). These sixteen principles are divided according to the [joy] of bliss (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*parama*), cessation (*virama*), and the innate (*sahaja*). For those born from a womb, they are with obscurations because of the emission of sixteen half-and-quarter drops (*bindu*); for the Buddhas, they are without obscurations because of the retention of sixteen half-and-quarter drops.
The sixteenfold emptiness is the dark fortnight, the sun, and wisdom; the sixteenfold compassion is—
The white fortnight, the moon, and skillful means are the three divisions of emptiness: namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), and ultimate emptiness (*paramārthaśūnyatā*).
Among these, emptiness is the emptiness of the five aggregates; it corresponds to the five lunar dates beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight.
Great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) is the emptiness of the five elements (*pañcadhātu*), which are the five lunar days beginning with the sixth;
ultimate emptiness (*paramārthaśūnyatā*) is the emptiness of the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*), which are the five lunar days beginning with the eleventh.
Thus, the fifteen lunar days constitute the fifteen types of emptiness, extending up to the new moon (*amā*).
The sixteenth day, which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in all its aspects, occurs between the entry into the first day of the waxing moon (*amānta-śukla-pratipat*) and the following [day].

Likewise, compassion (*karuṇā*) is threefold: that which has sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambanī*), that which has phenomena as its object (*dharmālambanī*), and that which is without an object (*anālambanī*).
Among these, that which has sentient beings as its object consists of the five lunar days beginning with the first day of the waxing moon.
The five lunar days beginning with the sixth are "with support" (*dharmāvalambinī*);

the five lunar days beginning with the eleventh are "without support" (*anāvalambinī*). Up until the full moon—within the interval between the entry of the first day of the dark fortnight at the end of the full moon and its conclusion—the sixteenth is *karuṇā*.

The state of being without duality or plurality is the subject matter, consisting of the sixteen emptinesses and the sixteen compassions; its designator is "the worldly and supramundane consecrations.
