Regarding these, first, the worldly ones are: water, crown, ribbon, vajra-bell, great vow, name, permission, vase, secret, wisdom, and gnosis.

For those born from a womb, there are ten initiations according to worldly convention, consisting of the purification of body, speech, mind, gnosis, the elements, aggregates, sense-bases, the action-faculties, and so forth;

the eleventh is supramundane. Regarding the fourth [point], it is likewise established as such by rule: Mahāmudrā, characterized by the supreme unchanging gnosis, is the mouth of the Guru, which purifies through the removal of obscurations of body, speech, and so forth; thus, there is the accomplishment of Karmamudrā, Jñānamudrā, and Mahāmudrā.
The action-seal (karmamudrā) possesses breasts and hair;
the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā) is imagined by one's own mind;
the great seal (mahāmudrā) is free from conceptual construction and has the nature of a reflected image (pratisenā).

The accomplishment (*siddhi*) of these is threefold: the accomplishment of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), which belongs to the desire realm; the accomplishment of the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*), which belongs to the form realm and is characterized by the nature of existence within the form-existence (*rūpabhava*); and the accomplishment of the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), which is devoid of both existence and non-existence and is endowed with the excellence of all aspects. This *Paramādibuddha*, which elucidates the mundane and supramundane paths of these four bodies and so forth, consists of five chapters—on the world-system, the internal, consecration, means of achievement, and gnosis—or alternatively, five sections; it was taught for the sake of attaining perfect buddhahood by all beings, beginning with humans.
"In the correct manner" (*samiti*) means not in the manner of the concealed *vajrapada*;

therefore, from the *Paramādibuddha*, there is the prophecy of Mañjuśrī by the Tathāgata for the purpose of compiling the *Laghutantra*, as well as my own commentary (*ṭīkā*), and the teaching of the tantra to Yamāntaka and others.

Furthermore, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, for the sake of training the Brahmin sages in a future time, and so that all sentient beings dwelling in the sixty million villages beginning with the realm of Sambhala may attain the path of the Mahāyāna.

Therefore, from this *Paramādibuddha* in twelve thousand [verses], Mañjuśrī was prophesied by the Tathāgata for the purpose of compiling the *Laghu-tantra*. Furthermore, in a future time, for the sake of converting three hundred and fifty million Brahmin seers residing in the village of Kalāpa, I, Lokeśvara, have also been prophesied to compose a commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Laghu-tantra*. Moreover, twenty-three other Bodhisattva Wrathful Kings (*krodharāja*) have been prophesied to teach the *Laghu-tantra* through their emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to all sentient beings residing in ninety-six million villages, so that they may attain the path of the Mahāyāna.

The "Mahāyāna path" refers, O Mañjuśrī, to the initiation of the vase, the secret, the wisdom, and the gnosis within the Vajra family. For the sake of attaining that—meaning for the sake of attaining the Great Vajrayāna path—one becomes of a single *kalka* among all castes (*varṇa*) by virtue of these initiations of the vase, the secret, the wisdom, and the gnosis.
One who possesses that *kalka* is a *kalkī*; his lineage is the *kalki-gotra*.
"From the consecration of the Vajra family for all mantra-practitioners"—this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Thus, Mañjuśrī, this Yaśas Kalkī has been prophesied; in the lineage of this Yaśas, I, Lokeśvara, am prophesied as the second Kalkī.

Thus, according to the sequence, there are the ten wrathful kings beginning with Yamāntaka and the thirteen bodhisattvas beginning with Kṣitigarbha; these thirteen bodhisattvas are prophesied to appear in the intervals between the wrathful kings beginning with Yamāntaka. In their emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), they are kings residing in ninety-six million villages, who propagate the Dharma of the Tathāgata for all sentient beings, destroy the wicked teachings of barbarians and others, possess the thirty-two marks of a great man, and are fully endowed with the qualities of sovereignty such as the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).

Henceforth, from the *Ādibuddha*, [the topics of] Mañjuśrī’s prophecy for the purpose of compiling the *Laghu-tantra*, my own composition of the commentary (*ṭīkā*), and the teaching of the Dharma by Yamāntaka and others are presented.

Thus ends the second chapter, concerning the Lord’s exposition of the tantra after having examined the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the expression (*abhidhāna*), the relationship (*sambandha*), and the purpose (*prayojana*) and the purpose of the purpose (*prayojanaprayojana*), within the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghu-kālacakra-tantra-rāja* following the *Mūla-tantra*. 2.

The summary of the connection between the Teacher, the requester, and the Root Tantra and the Condensed Tantra for those who practice the purpose [of the teaching]. Now, furthermore, the connection between the Teacher and the requester is stated here;
it may happen that someone has not heard the commentary on the preceding and subsequent tantras and might speak [as follows]:

Indeed, here in the Vajrayāna, it is well known that the great Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the great Yakṣas and resident of Aḍakavatī, was the requester of the Tathāgata and the compiler of the teachings. How then can King Sucandra—the son born from the womb of Queen Vijayā and the ruler of the village of Kalāpa in the land of Sambhala—be the requester? It is not heard in some other tantras, nor has he been prophesied [therein]. Is there not a contradiction regarding the relationship between the teacher and the requester? To this, it is said:
For here, as for what some must say—that in the Mantra system there is no requester of the Tathāgata born from the womb—that is not so; it has been established.
Because of the statement "from the subject matter" (*abhidheyāt*) here in the manuscript, it has been placed at the end;
even in the oral recitation (*bho pāṭhe*), the sentence is complete.

Śaka: It is not in the manuscript; nevertheless, O sir, since there is an introduction concerning the teacher, the requester, and the relationship between the root tantra and the condensed tantra at the beginning, why is it so?

Since even the Blessed One was born from a womb, if in this system of Mantra one born from a womb were not the requester of the Tathāgata nor the compiler of the teachings, then Śākyamuni—the omniscient teacher born from the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā in the womb of King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan—would not exist; for he was born from a womb.

Now, there is a statement by someone [to the effect] that "first he performed the defeat of Māra, then he generated the awakening (bodhi), and thereafter he became the omniscient teacher of Dharma; after he had passed into parinirvāṇa, there was no further descent into a womb. Because of this statement, there is a supreme contradiction, since that which is not established for oneself cannot establish it for another. Furthermore, since there is no state of being old at the very beginning here, who could perform the defeat of Māra? [The opponent claims: "Among gods, asuras, and humans, he is the first to attain perfect awakening..."
Nor does he do so [gradually], because of the absence of all obscurations;
nor does he do so simultaneously, for in the very moment that Māra exists, Buddhahood would not exist, since the mind would still possess obscurations;
and in the very moment that Buddhahood exists, Māra does not exist, because the mind is free from obscurations.

Furthermore, in this land of action (*karmabhūmi*), apart from the Blessed One, no other born from a woman’s womb possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), the thirty-two circles of the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft, or the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Therefore, what is called "Māra" is the mind of transmigrating beings (*saṃsāra-citta*), which is stained by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-mala*); whereas what is called "Buddhahood" (*buddhatva*) is the mind free from the habitual tendencies of saṃsāra.
And thus the Blessed One said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "There is that mind which is mindless" (*asti tac cittaṃ yac cittam-acittam*). (Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p.)
That very [mind] is naturally luminous when free from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of saṃsāra; therefore, Māra is the stained mind, while the Buddha is the stainless mind.
Here, the defeat of Māra by the Buddha externally is, for sentient beings, a manifestation of their own minds like a dream.
In ultimate reality, this is the heart of the Tathāgata, which shall be explained in detail in the fifth chapter.
In this saṃsāra, the entry of beings into the state of the noble Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is ineffable for those who wander in cyclic existence.

It was said by the messengers of Yama and King Yama at the time of entering hell for the sake of sentient beings: "We bow down to those Buddhas who, though liberated from the bonds of existence, take up existence for the sake of sentient beings; who, out of compassion, do not abandon the fruit of their actions even when the time [for liberation] has come, being the ones who convey the message of the meaning of emptiness; whose mental impurities have been burnt away by the fire of right perception, who are always moistened with perfect compassion, and who delight in the welfare of beings while acting beyond the reach of discursive thought. Thus it is said.

Therefore, regarding the welfare of sentient beings, it is impossible for ordinary people to speculate that the entry into a womb or the descent into hell by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is anything other than such.

Even a single Bodhisattva—who has emerged through the ten perfections, is a master of the ten stages, and has attained the ten masteries—teaches the Dharma of a Bodhisattva to those beings who are to be trained by a Bodhisattva by means of numerous emanation bodies throughout the great trichiliocosm; yet that Great Bodhisattva does not become many.

Thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One—having fulfilled the equipment of merit and wisdom through the power of his former vows, and being endowed with all the qualities of sovereignty such as the fearlessnesses—resides in the Buddha-field. In the thousands of great thousandfold world-systems, being requested by infinite and boundless beings through infinite and boundless voices and various invocations, he teaches the mundane and supramundane Dharma in the language of the Omniscient One, which proceeds according to the sounds of all sentient beings, by means of infinite and boundless works of illusory emanations that are unobstructed. It is not the case that there are many omniscient ones.

Just as a certain illusory person might manifest many illusory forms, and by means of those manifested forms uproots trees and even shakes the peaks of mountains— [in this regard], O Mahādeva, regarding the attainment of Buddhahood,
it is not found in the book titled *Mahāsāhasra*.
Sahadeva, O Great God, I am.
By virtue of the nature of Buddhahood; there is no "kha na sa."

Just as Viṣṇu, like Devadatta and others, binds beings for the sake of their welfare, yet that illusory person is not manifold; so too, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas act for the benefit of sentient beings within the three realms by means of illusory emanation bodies (*māyā-nirmāṇakāya*).

Therefore, for the sake of teaching the mundane and supramundane Dharma to all sentient beings, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was previously the master of the twelve stages, the holder of the Great Māyā, the learned one, the great illusionist and master of *indrajāla*. He was born from the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā in the Śākya clan of King Śuddhodana in the noble land of Lumbinī as Prince Siddhārtha;
and likewise, in the land of Sambhala, in the village of Kalāpa, he was born from the womb of Queen Vijayā of Sūryaprabha as Vajrapāṇi, the master of the ten stages, known as Sucandra.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, was born in the Buddha-field for the purpose of teaching the mundane and supramundane Dharma; he has directly realized the twelve stages (*bhūmi*).

To the north of the Śītā River, for the sake of those to be trained by Sucandra who dwell in ninety-six million villages, King Sucandra became a Bodhisattva, Vajrapāṇi, so that they might attain the path of the Perfectly Awakened One through the *Paramādibuddha-tantrarāja*.

The relationship between these two—the Buddha as teacher and the Bodhisattva as requester—is established through their emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) or enjoyment bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*), without contradiction regarding their prior or subsequent states.
By that emanated body, Vajrapāṇi, for the sake of accomplishing the mundane and supramundane siddhis of all sentient beings, King Sucandra requested the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata, having perceived the imminent readiness and the purity of mind of those dwelling in the ninety-six million villages in regions such as Śambhala, north of the Śītā River, taught the *Paramādibuddha* in twelve thousand verses, which reveals the vajra-word while being free from the concealment of the vajra-word.

From this king of tantras consisting of twelve thousand verses, for the purpose of composing a concise tantra and for the teaching of the Root King of Tantras, the Tathāgata—having seen the ripening of one hundred and fifty million Brahmin seers (*brahmarṣi*) in the future time, as well as those dwelling in ninety-six million villages—prophesied Mañjuśrī with the consecration of the Vajra family as "Yaśaḥ Kalkī" for the sake of unifying all castes into a single mass (*ekakalka*).
Furthermore, I, Puṇḍarīka, the author of the commentary, was prophesied as the second Kalkī;
therefore, after me, Yamāntaka and the others were prophesied.
Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "Six hundred years from the first year, for the sake of maturing the sages, Mañjughoṣa shall become the king Yaśas in the land called Sambhala;
his great queen will be Tārā, and their son will be Lokeśvara, the holder of the lotus."

O Sucandra, in your lineage there shall be an eloquent one born of the Śākya clan; by him, belonging to the Vajra family, [shall come] Yaśas, O Lord, a performer of drama. He is a Kalkin through the single essence of the four castes, but not a Kalkin through the Brahmin caste. Thus was this teaching of the Dharma heard by me from this sage;
it is not a doctrine heard from another, nor is he "the Omniscient One" in that sense. In such various ways, one should perform the teaching of the Dharma.
The yogi diligently grasps the Dharma through both correct words and corrupt words;

since [the meaning] is obtained through the word of the region (*deśa-śabda*) on the path, what is the use there of the word of the scripture (*śāstra-śabda*)? And because it is found in the Tibetan [translation], "in the meaning" (*arthe*) alone is correct. [End of] Chapter: The Summary of the Connection between the Teacher, the Petitioner, and the Root Tantra and the Condensed Tantra.

Just as various names for a single jewel are proclaimed separately on the earth according to different regions, yet there is no actual difference in the jewel itself, so too it is with my pure Dharma through the various compilers of the teachings.
Due to the diverse dispositions of sentient beings, various distinct designations have been proclaimed;

therefore, it is my view that this *Śrītantra*, consisting of one hundred and thirty verses in the *Sragdharā* meter, contains a concise yet essential meaning regarding the "Omniscient One" and so forth.
The King of Speakers will teach this [tantra], complete in five chapters; he is the compiler and the commentator, the bearer of the white lotus,
who reveals the path of the Buddha to the lineages of sages and others within this tantra.
Candra, Sureśvara, Tejī, Somadatta, Sureśvara, Viśvamūrti, Sureśāna, Yaśas, Puṇḍarīka, and Kramāt-sūryaprabha— these were the kings; Vighnaśakra was created as the last.
Vajrapāṇi, you Sucandra, Kṣitigarbha, Yamāntaka,
Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhī, Jambhaka, Mānaka, Khagarbha, and Mañjughoṣa are the Lords of the World in their respective order.

From these ten noble wrathful ones (krodha), there will arise thirteen other Bodhisattvas within that lineage (gotra) of Kalkin, in succession: Yaśas, Kalkin, and the lineage [of Kalkin], followed by Puṇḍarīka.
Bhadrakalkī is the third, and Vijaya is the fourth;
Sumindra and Raktapāṇi, and Viṣṇugupta is the seventh; Arkakīrti and Subhadra, Samudravijaya and Aja; Kalkī is the twelfth; Sūrya, Viśvarūpa, Śaśiprabha, Ananta, Mahīpāla, Śrīpāla, and Harivikrama.
Mahābala, Aniruddha, Narasiṃha, Maheśvara,
Puṇḍarīka, King Mahīprabha, and Vighnāri— these are the emanations of the Victorious One (Vimalaprabhā). Then, Anantavijaya, Kalkī Yaśas, and Kalkī follow thereafter.
His son will be the great wheel-turner, Raudrakalkī,
who puts an end to the dharma of the Mlecchas; he will be eloquent and, through supreme meditative absorption,
will become the eloquent teacher of Sūryaratha and others.

Sucandra, you are the compiler of the Root Tantra; you alone are the commentator here, the ripener of sentient beings. In the Abridged Tantra, you are Mañjughoṣa, and the holder of the lotus (Avalokiteśvara) himself is the commentator.
Thus,

because the Tathāgata prophesied that the wheel-turning monarchs of the world-system were the teachers of the mantra, and by virtue of that decree of the Tathāgata, King Sucandra had the twelve-thousand-verse Root Tantra King and its sixty-thousand-verse commentary written in books using the various languages of the regions such as Sambhala, and then revealed them to the inhabitants of the ninety-six million villages.
Those beings who were devoted to this very [teaching] heard it, recited it, and retained it in their own minds, and they also revealed it extensively to others.

Therefore, in the second year after the time of the Tantra's teaching, having displayed the miraculous power of the maṇḍala-circle, he departed from that very place with his emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and returned there with his enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*). For the sake of the accomplishment of sentient beings, Sureśvara then taught the Tantra for a hundred years; likewise did Tejina, Somadatta, Sureśvara, Viśvamūrti, and Sureśāna.

Within the womb of Viśvamātādevī, Mañjuśrī Yaśorāja was born as the emanation-body (*nirmitakāya*) of this Lord of Gods, Khagarbha. On that lion-throne of a Bodhisattva, he taught the Dharma for a hundred years.

Then, when those hundred years were complete, through the power of the Tathāgata’s prophecy and empowerment, and seeing that the time had come to ripen the sages, King Yaśas—knowing through the power of his five super-knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) that they had attained the true path and desiring to bestow the ascetic discipline (*niyama*) upon them—issued an invitation to all.

To the south of Kalāpa village is the Malaya Garden, twelve yojanas in length and equal in size to Kalāpa village. To its east is Lake Upamānasa, twelve yojanas in length; to the west is Lake Puṇḍarīka, of the same dimensions. Between these two lies the Malaya Garden.

In the midst of the Malayavana grove, King Sucandra constructed the maṇḍala-circle of the Blessed One Kālacakra, consisting of deities and goddesses fashioned from the five precious gems; it was square, measuring four hundred cubits in extent. On the outside, the Body Maṇḍala was square, with four gates, four archways, and adorned with eight cremation grounds, and it was encircled by five walls.

On the exterior, it was adorned with the four circles of earth and the other elements, as well as a garland of vajras; from the outer edge of the vajra-garland, it measured eight hundred cubits in length.
In the center, measuring half the size of the body-maṇḍala, is the speech-maṇḍala, which is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways, and surrounded by five walls.

Measuring half the size of the speech-maṇḍala is the mind-maṇḍala, which is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways, and surrounded by three walls. Half of that [size] is the wisdom-wheel (*jñānacakra*), beautified by sixteen pillars.
With half of this [measurement], there is an eight-petalled lotus; the pericarp is one-third of the lotus.

In this manner, the maṇḍalas of body, speech, and mind are complete with all characteristics, adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, provided with jeweled bands, altars, and *vakulikā* railings, and resplendent with mirrors, crescent moons, and bells.

In this maṇḍala-house consisting of the three spheres, on the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, King Yaśas gave a decree to the three and a half crores of Brahma-ṛṣis headed by Sūryaratha: "O Brahma-ṛṣis, Sūryaratha and the rest, listen! My word brings about the prosperity of omniscience.
On the full moon day of Caitra, I shall bestow upon you a charter for those of you who observe the rules of the Vedas and Smṛtis;
therefore, having set aside those Brāhmaṇas of noble lineage from various other regions, you must present them to me."

When all of them were examined through that statement and their various regional practices, they were found to be mutually contradictory; they had all fallen away due to the eating of the flesh of goats and buffaloes by the devotees of the Kāpālikas, the drinking of intoxicants, the taking of [prohibited] mothers and other [women], and their local customs.

Having seen such contradictions among them, King Yaśas said: "I must enter here into this mandala-house of the Blessed One Kālacakra, and I shall bestow upon you both the worldly and the supramundane consecrations."

Furthermore, by my command, you must partake in food and drink together with my family, and establish a matrimonial alliance. If you do not carry out my command, then abandoning our ninety-six million villages, you may go wherever it pleases you; otherwise, when eight hundred years have passed, your sons, grandsons, and descendants will adopt the Mleccha religion and propagate the teaching of that religion throughout the ninety-six great regions, such as Sambhala and others.

Having slain an animal at the neck with a knife while reciting the mantra "mlecchadevatāviṣavitvā" (vismillāha), they will then eat the meat of those animals killed with their own deity-mantras; they will declare the meat of animals killed by their own [prescribed] rites to be non-forbidden food. That too shall be your authority, because of the Smṛti statement: "Animals were created for the sake of sacrifice. Thus, there is no difference between the religion of the Mlecchas and the Vedic religion in terms of the taking of life.

Therefore, in your lineage, sons, grandsons, and others—having witnessed the prowess of those Mlecchas, or seeing the incarnation of the god Māra in battle—when eight hundred years have passed in the future, they will become Mlecchas.

Once those Mlecchas have arisen, even all the four castes and so forth residing in the ninety-six crores of villages will become Mlecchas, according to the words of the Brahmanical Ṛṣis: "The path is that by which the great men have gone."

In this regard, even in the Mleccha-dharma and the Vedic dharma, the taking of life must be performed for the sake of the deities and ancestors; and likewise in the Kṣatriya-dharma, because of the Brāhmaṇa’s statement: "Having gratified the ancestors and the gods, one who eats meat does not partake in fault. Similarly: "I see no fault therein for one who is wicked to act toward the wicked. (*Note:
In manuscript Gha, the reading "ninety" (navati) frequently occurs in place of "ninety-six" (ṣaṇṇavati).*)
"In this way, having taken the Vedic dharma as their authority, they will embrace the dharma of the Mlecchas.
For that reason, I have given you this injunction so that the dharma of the Mlecchas does not enter [this land] in the future; therefore, you must carry out my command."

When these words had been spoken by Yaśas, together with the royal command and the accompanying order for punishment, the *brahmarṣis* spoke to Sūryaratha as if lightning were striking their heads: "O Sūryaratha, inform King Yaśas: 'We shall not abandon the Vedic dharma of our caste and proceed to follow the religious practices of the consecrated Vajra lineage;
therefore, at your command, we shall go to the excellent land of the Āryas, to the region south of the Himavat and north of the Śītā river, within the island of Laṅkā.'"

By the word of those brahmin seers, Sūryaratha addresses you, O King of Men: "O Great King of Kings, Supreme Lord, you who are fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics, the ornament of the Śākya clan, O Most Compassionate One, show compassion toward us who are engaged in virtuous deeds! Furthermore, we must certainly carry out your command; otherwise, we shall not proceed with the consecration of the Vajra family."
"By your command, we shall go to the noble land situated to the south of the Śītā River, on the Himavat mountains, in the midst of the island of Laṅkā.

Then, at the words of Sūryaratha, King Yaśas said: "May you depart quickly from the region of Sambhala, so that all sentient beings dwelling in the ninety-six million villages north of the Śītā River may abandon the unwholesome paths of action, such as taking life, and become attainers of the path of perfect knowledge through the empowerment of the Blessed Kālacakra."
By the command of King Yaśas, all these brahmin seers departed from Kalāpa village; on the tenth day, they entered the interior of the forest.

When they had entered the midst of the forest, King Yaśas, by means of his power of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), came to know that because these brahmin seers (*brahma-ṛṣi*) had gone to the Noble Land (*āryaviṣaya*), all the beings dwelling in the ninety-six million villages would develop hostile thoughts. For this reason—that the path of right knowledge taught in the Vajrayāna would not exist here—these seers, out of fear of King Śrī-Yaśas, abandoned their own abodes and, taking their families and belongings with them, departed for the Noble Land.

Thinking that "all [people] desire liberation," the people, including the Kṣatriyas and others, will become unfortunate, as they lack the capacity for the profound and vast Dharma due to their unworthy minds.
Thus, having understood the intentions within the minds of all people, Yaśonarendra entered the samādhi named "Deluding the Families of All Viṣṇus, Brahmās, and Rudras."

Through that meditative concentration and by the power of the deities' empowerment, all those sages became deluded in that very forest; they were bound by the inhabitants of the forest, including the *sara* and others, and brought back once again to the great maṇḍala house. Having been cast at the feet of Yaśonarendra, they regained their senses and beheld Yaśonarendra.

Seeing that very same maṇḍala-palace in the Malaya garden, they were filled with wonder and spoke these words: "Aha! This is a great marvel! While we were unaware, by whom have we been brought from the Great Forest to this great maṇḍala-palace? Having heard these words of the Brahman sages, Sāgaramati, who had manifested a created body as the minister of King Yaśas, said: "O Sūryaratha and you other Brahman sages, do not be filled with wonder."

This King Yaśorāja, who appeared in another continent, was not some mere local person; rather, he was a certain great bodhisattva who, seeking to favor you, came into being through the empowerment of the Buddha. Therefore, having gone for refuge at his feet, make your request for the path that accomplishes mundane and supramundane siddhis, as well as for the empowerment, within this *Ādibuddha-tantrarāja*.

Then, by virtue of those words of Sāgaramati and through the empowerment of the Buddha, the Brahmin seers Sūryaratha and the others were awakened and spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent, Sāgaramati! Since our minds have been awakened by your speech, you should now go for refuge to the Three Jewels and make a request for the empowerments and the path for accomplishing mundane and supramundane siddhis in the *Kālacakra-tantrarāja*, so that all sentient beings may attain perfect buddhahood in this very life."

Having spoken thus, those sages addressed King Sūryaratha in the Brahma-family: "O Sūryaratha, your heart grasps the meaning of all mundane and supramundane treatises, beginning with the Vedas, as if they were a single volume; therefore, at our request, extend an invitation to King Yaśas. We too, having first gone for refuge to the Maṇḍala, shall all offer our invitation."

Then, at the word of that Brahma-rishi, Sūryaratha fashioned a mandala with flowers made of jewels and gold, and having cast a handful of jewel-flowers at the feet of King Yaśonarendra, he prostrated at the feet of Yaśas together with the Brahma-rishis—his two knees touching the ground and his two hands placed upon his head—and resting his right knee on the earth with his palms joined at his forehead, he requested King Yaśonarendra: "May the Blessed One teach the *Ādibuddha*, the King of Tantras, in which even those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution are prophesied for Buddhahood in this very life; in which they are gathered by the Blessed Vajradhara through supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*) and prophesied as attainers of Mahāmudrā."

"This *Ādibuddha* consisting of six and twelve thousand [verses], which was taught by the Tathāgata to King Sucandra—let that very same *Ādibuddha* be condensed into a short text as the *Alpa-tantrarāja* (Short King of Tantras) and taught to the Brahmā-sages for their instruction. Then, having heard this request from Sūryaratha, and by the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment and through the force of the resolute faith of the Brahmā-sages, he taught the *Tantrarāja* in the *Sragdharā* meter, acting as the author of the concise compendium and summarizing the teachings of the Omniscient One and others.

And for the sake of destroying the attachment to beautiful words among those who speak only of such words, [the author], relying on the principle that the meaning is the refuge (*arthaśaraṇatā*), employs here and there an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) where there should be a correct one; in some places there is a breach of the pause (*yati*) in a metrical foot; in some places a word lacking an inflection; in some places the elision of a vowel or a consonant; in some places a long vowel becomes short, and a short vowel becomes long; in some cases the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative, and the genitive in the sense of the dative; in some instances the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs where the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is expected, and the active voice where the middle voice is expected; in some cases the plural is used for the singular, and the singular for the plural; the neuter gender for the masculine, and the masculine for the neuter; in some cases the dental *ś* is used where the palatal or retroflex is required, the dental or palatal where the retroflex is required, and the palatal or retroflex where the dental is required—other such instances are likewise to be followed by the teacher who instructs according to the system (*tantra*).

Likewise, the Blessed One said in the Root Tantra: "Sucandra, that which is the most cherished object among all Buddhas must always be given by the gurus to their disciples—namely, wife, daughter, and son. [The element] smell exists in earth; form in water; taste in fire; touch in wind; and sound in the imperishable (*akṣara*), which is the great principle of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Having worshipped with incense, perfumes, lamps, food, drink, clothing, and so forth, the good son offers the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) to the guru. *In the Vimalaprabhā [commentary], it is stated:* "In the sky, [one worships] with incense, perfumes, and lamps, as well as with food, drink, clothing, and the like."
"World-systems" (*lokadhātu*) and other such terms, as well as others not explicitly mentioned, are to be understood by the yogi from the recitations of the scriptures (*āgama*).

Thus, even in this commentary, I have written while relying on taking the meaning as the refuge (*arthaśaraṇatā*), for the sake of destroying the pride of those who take fine words (*suśabda*) as the primary concern.

Now, by whatever means the destruction of the pride of fine words regarding family-mantras (*kulavidyā*) occurs, by that very means—relying on taking the meaning as the refuge—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach the Dharma for the sake of liberation, using the local dialects of various lands and the linguistic conventions of various grammatical treatises.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghu-kālacakra-tantra-rāja* following the *Mūla-tantra*, this is the third chapter: the teaching on the relationship between the *Mūla-tantra* and the *Laghu-tantra* concerning the teacher, the time, and the petitioner. [The fourth chapter] is the teaching on the means of accomplishment regarding the teacher and the petitioner. Now, I shall expand upon the *Laghu-tantra-rāja* by means of the relationship between the teacher, the petitioner, and others, beginning with Śrī-narendra-sūryaratha, who was emanated by Mañjuśrī.

Here, in this most glorious Kālacakra maṇḍala palace, at the conclusion of the eastern gate, in the great jewel pavilion, Yaśonarendra—seated upon a great jewel lion-throne, his lotus feet honored by millions upon millions of village lords who were born into the lineages of the ninety-six great royal families of gods, asuras, and nāgas, and who were bound with crowns of great jewels; he who is the embodiment of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas and was entreated by Sūryaratha—spoke thus to Sūryaratha: "Excellent, excellent, Sūryaratha! Since you have exerted yourself to hear from me the true essence of the Supreme Primordial Buddha Tantra King (*paramādibuddhatantrarāja*) for the sake of all beings, beginning with the lineage of Brahmin seers, so that they may attain the path to perfect enlightenment, it is well for you."

I shall teach all of this Kālacakra Vajrayoga—the essence of the supreme *Paramādibuddha-tantrarāja* which accomplishes both mundane and supramundane attainments—of which you have asked. As the compiler (*saṅgītikāraka*), you too should listen with a one-pointed mind. By the power of the previous prophecy and the empowerment of the Tathāgata, I [Yaśas] am extracting from the Great King of Tantras this Yoga, the essence of the Minor King of Tantras, consisting of Wisdom and Means, through a compilation in verse. This is done by means of the relationship between the Perfectly Awakened One as the teacher and Sucandra as the requester, for the sake of King Yaśas.

Then the Blessed Mañjuśrī, the emanation-body Yaśonarendra, spoke the first chapter on the compendium of the teacher and so forth, as prophesied by the Tathāgata from the Paramādibuddha: "Having bowed his head to the Omniscient One, the Body of Gnosis, whose form is like the sun, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, who is seated upon a lion throne, and who is saluted by the best of gods—King Sucandra, placing his cupped hands (palms together) upon his head, shall ask concerning the Yoga in the Śrī Kālacakra for the sake of the liberation of men during the time of the Kali Yuga.
From this point, the manuscript is fragmentary.

[The mudrā is always [present]; it does not exist in the manuscript. In this *paṭala*, titled "The Summary of the Realization of the Teacher, the Requester, and so forth," the Blessed One sang this initial verse in order to summarize the Teacher and the others within this King of Tantras.

Here, the "Teacher and others" refers to: the Teacher (*deśaka*), the place (*sthāna*), the great assembly (*mahāparṣad*), the requester (*adhyeṣaka*), the teaching of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*), and the purpose, the purpose of the purpose, and the ultimate purpose (*prayojana-prayojana-prayojana*).
Regarding these, first, the inclusion of the Teacher is accomplished by the Blessed One through these twenty-three syllables: "sarvajñaṃ jñānakāyaṃ dinakaravapuṣaṃ padmapatrāyatākṣaṃ buddham.
The inclusion of the location is accomplished by these five syllables: "siṃhāsanastham. The inclusion of the great assembly is accomplished by these seven syllables: "suravaranamitam."
Having bowed with his head and placed his cupped lotus-hands upon his crown, King Sucandra made this request in twenty-eight syllables; thus, the summary of the requester is established.
With these fourteen syllables—"the yoga in the Śrī Kālacakra at the time of the Kali age"—the summary of the teaching of the Dharma is established.

"Of men for the sake of liberation"—by these seven syllables, there is a summary of the purpose, the purpose of the purpose, and the purpose of the purpose of the purpose. Thus, in this sequence, by these eighty-four syllables, there is a summary of the teacher, the location, the great assembly, the requester, and the purpose, the purpose of the purpose, and the purpose of the purpose of the teaching of the Dharma. This was extracted from the Root King of Tantras by the Blessed Mañjuśrī, who was prophesied by the Tathāgata.

Regarding the statement "Dhara has been prophesied by the Tathāgata," one might ask: since in all the *tantrarājas* the Blessed Lord Vajradhara’s dwelling place is indicated by the Tathāgata through the formula "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth, how is it that this *tantrarāja* was taught by the Blessed Buddha without the "Thus have I heard" formula and the like, beginning instead with "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*)?

Because there is no mention of the place where [the Buddha] dwelt in the opening formula beginning with "Thus by me" (*evaṃ mayā*), it might be argued that this King of Tantras was not taught by the Blessed Buddha; however, such a statement will not belong to anyone here who relies on names and words as a refuge. Therefore, it is said: regarding what must be stated here—that in the future time, foolish people relying on names and words as a refuge will [claim] for all the Kings of Tantras the mention of the dwelling place of the Blessed Vajradhara in the form "Thus by me heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*) and so forth—this is not so. Why? Because the Teacher of the Dharma relied upon the refuge of the meaning (*arthaśaraṇatā*), and because the compilers (*saṅgītikāra*) also performed the compilation in various local languages.

In this regard, if the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma were produced through the localized effort of the throat, palate, and so forth, by means of refined Sanskrit speech such as "Thus have I heard," then even over many periods of time, the Tathāgata would be unable to teach the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma, nor could the compiler record them, because of the limitation of using only one localized form of refined speech.

In this regard, because there would be no infinite emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), one who teaches the Dharma simultaneously through the voices of infinite and infinite sentient beings across infinite and infinite world-realms would not exist; and due to the absence of the teaching of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*), he would not be omniscient (*sarvajña*). But it is not so. Here, the Buddha is immeasurable, the Dharma is immeasurable, and the Saṅgha is immeasurable. Therefore, according to the word of the Tathāgata, there is not just one omniscient teacher, nor is there just one omniscient language that conveys meaning through the voices of all sentient beings, nor is there just one description of the places where he dwelt.
The community of Śrāvakas is not the sole requester of the Tathāgata.

Here, by virtue of the diverse inclinations (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings, there are many omniscient ones, many languages of the omniscient one, many places of residence, many requesters, and many teachings of the Dharma.

Therefore, the teaching of all the tantras is not [expressed] by the Tathāgata through a single divine language—such as "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*)—produced by the palate, throat, and other articulatory organs.

In this regard, first of all, in the Śrāvaka system, there is the teaching of the Dharma in the Magadha language at the beginning of the Three Piṭakas, as follows: "Thus indeed (Itipi) that Blessed One is a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed one," and so forth; likewise, there is the teaching of the Dharma in the Koṭigrāma language in the region of Campaka north of the Śītā River, as follows:
"Akarṣu, ṣaka, gagalku, jirāmaka, vijirikā, dudurūpaka," and so forth, up to khuṣṇuka.
O Palku,
O Bho!
Jigamaka Vijiriṭaku. Dadarūpaka (Arā tvakhaṣṭaka; Bho. Bho. 0ṭuku). Khaṣṇu Ke Gaganaka. In the *Vimalaprabhā* [on the *Lokadhātu*], regarding the teaching of the Dharma:

likewise, in the most delightful region to the north of Rukma, the teaching of the Dharma was given in the language of Koṭigrāma; namely, the teaching of the Dharma by means of such names as Akamayasatre (Da), Baladatta Viraṭa, Manika, Akuṭa, Varadatta, Jigita (Ti) Varadatta, and so forth.

Thus, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the three vehicles pertains to many locations; it is not necessarily expressed solely in the Sanskrit language with the formula "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth.

Now, even among the *tantrarāja*s written in Sanskrit by the compilers (*saṅgītikāraka*), in some the location where [the Buddha] dwelt is indicated by the formula "Thus have I heard" and so forth, while in others it is not.

First, the indication of the dwelling place by the formula "Thus have I heard" and so forth occurs in many *tantrarāja*s, such as the *Śrīsamāja* in twenty-five thousand lines and the *Māyājāla* in sixteen thousand lines; however, in some it does not exist.

First, in the *Paramādibuddha* consisting of twelve thousand [verses], in the *Yogānuviddha* consisting of thirty-six thousand [verses], and in the *Mahālakṣābhidhāna*; likewise in many other *Tantrarājas*; similarly in the *Mūlatantrarājas* and also in the minor tantras (*laghutantras*) extracted from them—in some cases the teaching begins with "Thus by me," while in others it does not.
In this *Śrīsamāja*, the Blessed One said: "Thus have I heard at one time: the Blessed One was dwelling within the wombs (*bhaga*) of the vajra-wives of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.
This is the indication of the place of dwelling. Likewise, in the *Māyājāla*, the indication of the place of dwelling begins with "Thus have I heard" and continues up to "was dwelling."
Thus, in other Root Tantras and King of Abbreviated Tantras as well, there is an instruction on the places of residence.
Here, in the *Paramādibuddha*, the Blessed One said: "The glorious Buddha, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, is seated upon the lion throne."

The Omniscient One is the Body of Gnosis (*jñānakāya*), whose nature is the passion of body, speech, and mind; through the passion of body, speech, and mind, he is the imperishable solar form. Vajrasattva is the presiding deity within the mandala of body, speech, and mind. He is the indestructible Vajrayoga, Kālacakra, the immutable bliss. The Buddha without beginning or end is the Primordial Buddha (*Ādibuddha*), who is without lineage.
He is the Vajra-auspiciousness in every respect, the universal vow in every respect; he possesses the meaning of reality in twelve aspects and upholds the truth in sixteen aspects.
The description of the place of residence (*vijahārasthāna*) in the *Paramādibuddha* begins with: "(Śrīkālacakragarbha-nāma-tantra, Bhā-ka; Paṅkti-bī)," and so forth.

Likewise, in the *Yogānuviddha* consisting of thirty-six thousand [verses], the Blessed One said: "The one supreme deity, abiding in the form of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) within the vajra-lotus of the ḍākinīs, is established within the nature of the three realms of existence. Thus, the description of the place of residence is given in the *Yogānuviddha*.
Furthermore, in the *Lakṣābhidhāna*, the Blessed One said: "Akamapasat" (Bho. *rukamasyo*; Akamayasat; Kha. *baladdatta*; Bho. *jigiti*).

*The Great King of Ritual Manuals named the Guhyasamāja, the Secret of Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas.* — [Chapter on] the Teacher, the Petitioner, and the Means of Achievement: "In the secret [reality], the Being who abides within the self of all beings and all female messengers, consisting of all female messengers, is Vajrasattva, the Great Bliss."
(With these words, the description of the places where he dwelt is given;

and that is to be understood from the oral instructions of the Guru. Likewise, regarding the requester in the *Śrīsamāja*: "Then Vajrapāṇi, being empowered by the Blessed One Vajradhara, spoke thus: 'May the Blessed One teach the Great King of Tantras, the unsurpassed among all tantras—the *Śrīsamāja* of all Buddhas, which is the designation of all Buddhas.'"
Thus [ends the section]. By such means, there is the entreaty of Vajrapāṇi. Likewise, in the *Māyājāla*, Vajrapāṇi is well known as the petitioner; so it is in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*.

Here, however, the *Paramādibuddha* is the petitioner; having been urged by the Blessed One for the sake of destroying the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings, he says: "Having worshipped the two lotus-feet of the Teacher with the yoga of body, speech, and mind, and with jewel-flowers, and again with a handful of flowers in his joined palms..."
Then, with his head and both knees touching the ground, he placed his right knee firmly upon the earth and prostrated himself at the circle of his birth.
Placing his palms together at his forehead, the King made this request: "O Teacher, please teach the entirety of the unsurpassed tantra of all systems."
The primordial Buddha, who is always characterized by the mass of all accomplishments, is the yoga in this Śrī Kālacakra, endowed with the *ālī* and *kālī*.
The reality realized in a single moment, bearing the four drops, is divided and distinguished by the four moments through sixteen divisions.
Emptiness, gnosis, and the drop (bindu), the supreme and great Vajradhara; the five-syllabled great emptiness and the six-syllabled emptiness of the drop.
One should perceive the Buddha, the gods, and the asuras within one's own body and in others; likewise, one should perceive the Puruṣa and the Prakṛtis—thus, the supreme twenty-five principles.
Whatever measure exists within the body, which is the cause of the origin of the three worlds, and all the enjoyments of the gods, asuras, and others—all this is clearly [manifested] therein.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, such is the request of King Sucandra in the *Paramādibuddha*.
Likewise, in the *Yogānuviddha*, Viśvarūpiṇī said: "Having bowed to the illustrious Viśvarūpiṇī, she asks Vajrabhairava: 'What is the *Yogānuviddha* Tantra? Is Vajrasattva the supreme bliss?'"
Such is the request regarding the yoga-pervaded [tantra].
Likewise, in the *Lakṣābhidhāna*, Vajravārāhī said: "Having prostrated to Heruka, who is the essence of the three worlds, O Vajrasattva, what is the *Lakṣābhidhāna* Tantra, the supreme bliss?"
Thus, the request [for teaching] is set forth in the *Lakṣābhidhāna*.
In this way, the request by the yogin should be understood in other royal tantras as well.

Therefore, because the Blessed One is the teacher of infinite dharmas, the Buddhists should not state that the indication of the place of residence [where the teaching occurred] in all the royal tantras begins with the words "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*).
By this limited Sanskrit speech, even the Buddha becomes limited, were it not for the omniscient language which possesses the nature of the cries of all sentient beings.

Here, having observed the pride of the learned non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) who advocate for [Sanskrit] sound in the noble land of India, there arose the intention of the Buddhist-minded of dull intellect: "Just as Brahmā, Hari, Hara, and others are the desired deities of the Brāhmaṇas, Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas, and so forth, and they are speakers of Sanskrit, so too our own desired deities—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—must be speakers of Sanskrit."
In this regard, it is not by means of this limited, conditioned language that the compilers of the Dharma become preachers of the Dharma through the voices of all sentient beings;

for without the speech of the omniscient ones, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would be bound to the birth-status of gods and thus limited. Therefore, [the Buddha's speech] is not limited to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, because he teaches the Dharma through the various voices of all sentient beings.

In this Mantra system, a single designation is not the [ultimate] entity; for even a single entity has multiple designations, and because of this multiplicity of designations, no single designation can be primary, since it serves to indicate the entity as being of the nature of all designations.

Just as among the terms *strī*, *nārī*, *yuvatī*, and so forth, no single term "woman" (*strī*) would be primary because they all equally convey the state of possessing breasts and hips; likewise, among the terms *ekāra*, *rahasya*, *padma*, *dharmodaya*, *khadhātu*, *mahāsukhāvāsa*, *siṃhāsana*, *bhaga*, and *guhya*, no single term "the letter *e*" (*ekāra*) is primary, because they all equally convey emptiness in all its aspects.

Likewise, among the designations of the syllable *vaṃ*, great bliss (*mahāsukha*), great passion (*mahārāga*), the innate (*sahaja*), the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*), the drop (*bindu*), reality (*tattva*), primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), and the purified mind (*viśuddhacitta*), no single designation such as *vaṃ* is preeminent, because all of them establish the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), the innate joy (*sahajānanda*), and immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*).

In this way, the syllables *e* and *vaṃ* represent emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects (*sarvākāravaropetā śūnyatā*) and the non-dual bodhicitta of compassion that is non-referential toward all phenomena (*sarvadharmanirālambakaruṇā*), as they establish their essential nature (*bhāva*).

The syllable *Evaṃ*, Vajrasattva, Bodhicitta, Kālacakra, Ādibuddha, Yoga consisting of wisdom and means, the nature of the knowable and knowledge, non-dual, without beginning or end, peaceful, Saṃāja, Saṃvara—through such various names, the non-dual yoga consisting of wisdom and means, which is without succession, is to be understood by the yogin.

In this regard, the syllable *E* and the syllable *Vaṃ*, which were taught by the Blessed One at the beginning of the *Samāja* and other *Tantrarāja*s in the form of an etymological definition (*nirukti*), were likewise written by the compiler at the beginning of the tantra for the sake of maturing the gods through their divine language. Therefore, the elision of these two syllables at the beginning of the *Samāja* and other *Tantrarāja*s is not intended;
for it is not the case that the Blessed One taught these two syllables with his palate and so forth, nor did the compiler write them down without having heard them.

Therefore, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of these two syllables is stated: the preceding *a* is the space-element (*khadhātu*), the secret lotus; from that, the *visarga* is the sun (*sūrya*), the passion (*rajas*); then the *a* is consciousness (*vijñāna*) presided over by bliss, [the nature of] Rāhu; then the *anusvāra* is the moon (*candra*), the semen (*śukra*).
Between these two *a*s—the space-element and the consciousness of Rāhu—the *visarga* (the sun) and the passion (*rajas*) undergo the change to *i*.

Then, when the *visarga* (the sun) and the passion (*rajas*) have undergone the change to *u*, there is an absence of *guṇa* in ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*); due to the absence of *guṇa*, there occurs the substitution (*yaṇādeśa*).

The letter *vaṃ* is formed by the coexistence of the subsequent vowel *i* with the Rāhu-consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the *anusvāra* is the conjunction with the Moon-semen (*candra-śuka*). Thus, the letter *vaṃ* is produced. Likewise, the preceding vowel *a* is the space-element (*khadhātu*) or the secret lotus; this *a*, ending in the locative case, becomes strengthened (*guṇībhavati*) by the subsequent vowel *i*. Thus, the letter *e* arises. Within this *e*, which is the space-element as the support (*ādhāra*), the letter *vaṃ* is to be understood as the supported (*ādheya*). This consists of the Visarga-form, the *anusvāra*, the Sun, Rāhu, the Moon, the *rajas*, the *ālayavijñāna*, and the semen-nature; it is to be understood in the center, externally, in the body, and in the supreme (*para*).
In this Root Tantra, the Blessed One said: "Within the letter *e* is the letter *vaṃ*, the abode of the bliss of all Buddhas;
in the expanse of space (*khadhātu*), this Vajrasattva exists through the union of body, speech, and mind.
Body is the drop (*bindu*), the moon, and the semen; speech is emission (*visarga*), the passion (*rajas*), and the sun."
These modes of mind are said to be established within the single realm;

through the union of body, speech, and mind, they abide as the maṇḍala of body, speech, and mind, and through passion for body, speech, and mind, they reside within the nature of the three realms of existence.

For this reason, for the sake of maturing the gods and for the attainment of perfect buddhahood, the Tathāgata has spoken in the *Samāja* and other sovereign tantras (*tantrarāja*) regarding the description of the place where he dwelt by means of the phrase "Thus have I heard" and so forth.

By this designation "thus," whatever reality was taught in the *Śrīsamāja* and other works, that very same reality was taught by the Tathāgata in the sovereign tantra known as the *Lakṣābhidhāna* and others by means of the phrase "the secret" and so forth. And that [reality] is to be understood through the instructions of the guru, via the various tantras and through the various types of intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).

Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the *Mūlatantra*: "The *tantra* characterized by the six points consists of intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*), as well as literal speech (*ruta*), and neither [of these], nor that which is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), nor that which is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Therefore, according to the word of the Blessed One, no single designation alone should be considered primary.
In this Mantra system, the Blessed One has taught three kinds of conviction (*pratyaya*): first, conviction in the tantra; then, conviction in the guru; and then, conviction in oneself.

Through these three convictions, the path of the perfectly enlightened one (*samyaksambuddha*) becomes completely pure. Otherwise, the path that is taught by a guru in the absence of these three convictions does not bestow the fruit of perfect enlightenment upon the disciple. Due to the disciple’s dullness of faith, it results only in a worldly fruit by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

In this other tantra, the Blessed One has made this declaration: "Having rendered the mind free from conceptual construction, one should examine the sign for one day. If—[the portion beginning with] "yadi" is missing in manuscript *ṅa*—according to the procedure taught in the *Vimalaprabhā* regarding the world-system and the method stated in the tantra, the conviction of the disciple does not arise through the instruction of the Guru, then the word of the Blessed One would be false.

Now, if the guru does not become the bestower of the path to the disciple according to the procedure taught in the *Gurutantra*, then the promise of the Blessed One does not become false; for it is due to the guru’s lack of knowledge of the path and because he teaches a cultivation of a perverted and impure path.
In this regard, one should not examine another for even a single day as a means for accomplishing the maṇḍala circle, setting aside the signs such as smoke, according to the word of the Blessed One.

In this King of Tantras consisting of three families (*trikula*), the subject matter (*abhidheya*) consists of body, speech, and mind, and thus has three faces. In that which consists of four families (*catuḥkula*), the subject matter consists of body, speech, mind, and gnosis (*jñāna*), and thus has four faces. When combined with the single family of gnosis, the tantra becomes four families in nature, and the subject matter likewise becomes five families in nature. Together with the single essence (*svabhāva*), it becomes six families in nature.

Here, in this tantra consisting of four families, the subject matter consists of four families—the union of the sun, moon, Rāhu, and fire; and of *rajas*, semen (*śukra*), mind (*citta*), and gnosis (*jñāna*)—as a single yoga.

In this *Nāmasaṅgīti*, the Vajrayoga has been clearly proclaimed by the Tathāgata through three verses beginning with the thirty-third in the Praise of Discriminating Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*); namely: "The Great Light of the Vajra-Sun, the Vajra-Moon of stainless radiance;
the Great Passion beginning with dispassion, blazing with light of universal color; seated in the vajra-posture of the Perfect Buddha, upholder of the Dharma of the Buddha’s proclamation."
The glorious one born from the lotus of the Buddha, the bearer of the treasury of omniscient wisdom,
the king who holds the universal illusion, the great master of the Buddha-vidyās,
the adamantine sharpness, the great sword, the utterly pure, the supreme syllable.

Thus, from these words of the Blessed One (*Nāmasaṃgīti*, 8.33, 34, 35), the subject matter consists of the four families; the Blessed Kālacakra is the essence of Vajrasattva, characterized by the establishment of the pure Dharma-mantras.
Likewise, he consists of five families through the division of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*).

Likewise, the Blessed One said in the *Māyājāla*: “The five-faced one, with five topknots, adorned with a crest of five locks of hair, bearer of the great vows, wearing a girdle of muñja grass, a celibate student, the supreme observer of vows” (*Nāmasaṃgīti* 8.17, 18). In this way, by means of the division of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*), he is to be designated as consisting of six families (*ṣaṭkula*); yet, by means of the division of his faces, he is also said to consist of a hundred families (*śatakula*). This is stated together with the final quarter-verse of the *Viśuddhadharmadhātu-stotra* and the first verse of the *Ādarśajñāna-stava*, as follows: kha...
Gha, by means of the single intrinsic nature,
Kha.
Vajrendu; Ka Vajñendra Kha.
In the manuscript, the word "anā" is not present; nor is the ṅa-cakra.
[In the manuscript designated as Gha, a transposition of the sequence has occurred on folios 39–40.
Chapter [X]: The Summary of the Means for Accomplishing the Teacher and the Supplicant; the Terrifying Vajrabhairava.
The King of Wrath, six-faced, formidable, six-eyed, six-armed, and powerful;
a skeleton terrifying with fangs, possessing hundreds of faces like the Halāhala poison.

Therefore, according to the words of the Blessed One, it should be understood that in various tantras and other scriptures, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is three-faced, four-faced, five-faced, six-faced, or hundred-faced.

Thus, the very place which the Blessed One designated by the syllable *e* in the *Samāja* and other texts is the same place designated by terms such as "secret" (*rahasya*) in the *Lakṣābhidhāna* and other works. Furthermore, that which was expressed by the syllable *vaṃ* is expressed by the term "great bliss" (*mahāsukha*) as Vajrasattva.

In this manner, according to the sequence thus stated, within the *Paramādibuddha*—which consists of four families and also consists of six families—the subject matter is both that which consists of four families and that which consists of six families.

This is indicated by the Blessed One through twenty-three syllables beginning with "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*). It is the Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*), the Vajra of Bodhicitta, inseparable from emptiness and compassion.
Here, by the term "lion-throne" (*siṃhāsana*), the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) in all its forms is meant; he who is situated upon that lion-throne is "seated on the lion-throne."
"Buddha" refers to Vajrasattva;
"Yoga" refers to the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*); and "Supreme Immutable" (*paramākṣara*) refers to this very Yoga.

This is celebrated in fourteen verses within the *Vajradhātumaṇḍalastava* of the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, beginning with: "Thus, for example: The Blessed Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, born from the syllable A..."
The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, the supreme syllable,
the great vital breath, indeed unarisen, devoid of verbal expression,
the foremost cause of all designations, and the brilliant light of all speech.
The Lord is the supreme among great vidyās; the Guru is the supreme among great mantras; he is established in the system of the Mahāyāna; he is the supreme of the Mahāyāna system.
Up to the verse ending with *nā0 sa0 5.14*,
this subject matter has been celebrated in all other tantras according to the dispositions of middling and superior beings;
likewise, by means of these fourteen syllables beginning with "emptiness" (*śūnya*) and "gnosis" (*jñāna*), the subject matter consists of the six families (*ṣaṭkula*).

That very same [mantra] is called the *Saṅgīti*, as it is also stated in the second verse of the *Kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñānastava* within the *Saṅgīti*: "The progenitor of the meaning of all mantras, the great bindu, the syllableless,
the five-syllabled, the great void, the bindu-less, and the six-syllabled."
( Nāmasaṃgīti 10.2) Gha. 90 Compassionate in nature; Ka. Chariot.

Therefore, because it is taught through infinite designations as the "Teacher of Dharma" (*dharmadeśaka*), the King of Tantras taught by the Tathāgata—beginning with the words "Thus have I heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*)—is indeed the teaching of the Tathāgata. It must not be asserted by Buddhists that what is taught by means of [terms such as] "the Secret" (*rahasya*) and so forth, or "the Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*) and so forth, is not the teaching of the Tathāgata; for by finding fault with one's own tenets (*svasiddhānta*) or the tenets of others (*parasiddhānta*), the sixth root downfall (*mūlāpatti*) occurs.
Therefore, having understood the connection between the preceding and following parts within other tantras, their virtues and faults must be discerned.

Otherwise, due to the grasping of the fault of the unseen (*adṛṣṭadoṣa*), there is a falling into the Avīci hell for those wicked non-Aryans who have strayed from the heart of the Tathāgata, who are attached to the enjoyment of sense objects and faculties, and who engage in false speech;

such is the sequence stated according to the reasoning of the supreme scripture, which is consistent from beginning to end. Thus, by means of the words "Omniscient One" and so forth, the Blessed One has taught the *Paramādibuddha*, the King of Tantras.

Now, one might think that this is a redundant statement: "Is it not the case that he who is omniscient is precisely the Buddha, the Blessed One, because these two designations refer to a single entity? This may be someone's intention here as to why the Blessed One is called "Buddha" again;
therefore, it is said: In this context, it is true that the statement "he who is omniscient is the Buddha, the Blessed One" holds;
however, others such as Hari, Hara, and so forth are also imagined by the ignorant to be omniscient.
In order to refute their [claim] regarding omniscience, it is stated here that "the Buddha, the Blessed One, is omniscient," and not anyone else;
for among Hari, Hara, and others, there is no one who is omniscient within the three realms and who teaches all phenomena through the languages of all sentient beings.
Why, then, is it said that among them there is no one who is omniscient and a teacher of all phenomena through the languages of all sentient beings?

In this context, because the classes of gods such as Hari, Hara, and others have arisen within the saṃsāra of the six realms of existence, whereas the Blessed Buddha stands at the far limit beyond saṃsāra, it was stated by the Tathāgata here in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, in the thirteenth verse of the *Suviśuddhadharmadhātustava*: "Standing at the far limit beyond saṃsāra, having accomplished what was to be done, standing on firm ground,
established in the knowledge of absolute liberation, he is the one who rends [ignorance] with the weapon of wisdom."
Thus, since the Buddha, the Blessed One, is omniscient, is it not the case that the term "Buddha" is not redundant?
For surely he who is omniscient is himself the *jñānakāya* (the embodiment of gnosis); for what purpose, then, is the term "embodiment of gnosis" used again for the Blessed One?
That which is stated here—that he who is omniscient is alone the *jñānakāya* (embodiment of wisdom)—is indeed true.

However, there are also other Buddhas, namely the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; in order to exclude them from being considered *samyaksambuddhas* (perfectly enlightened ones), the Blessed One has used the repetitive expression "the omniscient one, the *jñānakāya*, the perfectly enlightened Blessed One is the *jñānakāya*" to establish that the *jñānakāya* is exclusively the *samyaksambuddha*.

Regarding the statement that "among these Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, no one has become a Samyaksambuddha endowed with the body of gnosis (jñānakāya)," why is it said here that "no one among the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas has become a Samyaksambuddha"?

It is because the Śrāvakas and Buddhas [Pratyekabuddhas] abide in a nirvāṇa with remainder (sopadhi-nirvāṇa), whereas the Samyaksambuddha is completely liberated from all remainders (sarvopadhi-vinirmukta).

And likewise, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, in the eleventh verse of the *Prajñājñāna-stava*: "Completely liberated from all limiting adjuncts, well-established in the path of space, bearing the great wish-fulfilling gem, the all-pervading Lord, the supreme among all jewels."

[In this] chapter, regarding the summary of the means for the Teacher and the Supplicant: "Therefore, the Omniscient One, the Gnosis Body, the Perfectly Awakened Lord is the Gnosis Body"—this repetition of the word by the Lord may lead some to ask: "Is it not the case that he who is the Gnosis Body is himself the Sun-like Body because he destroys the darkness of ignorance; for what purpose, then, did the Lord repeat the words 'Sun-like Body'? To this, it is said: Herein, this statement is true—that he who is the Gnosis Body is indeed the Sun-like Body, because he destroys the darkness of ignorance.

What then? There are also other Buddhists who are proponents of Consciousness-only (*vijñānavādin*); in order to refute their doctrine that consciousness is the ultimate nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is the repeated statement: "The Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*) is the Body of Gnosis (*jñānakāya*), whose form is like the sun, and who has transcended the nature of consciousness.

Why is it said here, "His form is like the sun," and why is it stated, "Among these proponents of Consciousness-only, there was no Perfectly Awakened One who was the Body of Gnosis with a form like the sun"?

In this context, because the proponents of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*) abide in the nature of consciousness (*vijñānadharma*), whereas the Perfectly Awakened One has transcended the nature of consciousness;

thus it was said by the Tathāgata in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, in the praise of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), in the thirty-third verse: "Transcending the nature of consciousness, bearing the form of non-dual gnosis, free from conceptual construction, effortless, and bearing the body of the Buddhas of the three times."
Thus,
for this reason, the Blessed One’s repeated statement that the *jñānakāya* is the Perfectly Awakened One whose body is like the sun is [justified].

Now, one might object: "That which is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) in the Tantra is the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*), which is formless; whereas he who has eyes as broad as lotus petals is possessed of form. For what purpose, then, would there be any intention here for the Blessed One’s statement, 'one whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals'? To this it is replied: Indeed, that which foolish people might say—that the subject matter of the Tantra is one possessed of form with eyes as broad as lotus petals—is not so. Here, by the word "lotus" (*padma*) in its definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) is expressed. Within that lotus, in the space-element, sentient beings abide with the nature of the hundred families (*śatakula*) being long like the petals of a lotus; thus, "lotus petals" refers to them as far as their limit. He whose hundred eyes are broad is "one whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals."

This was spoken here by the Blessed One in the sixth verse of the *Ādarśajñānastava* within the *Nāmasaṅgīti*; namely: "Vajra-flame-terrible-eyed, Vajra-flame-haired, Vajra-penetration, Great-penetration, hundred-eyed, Vajra-eye."
Therefore, according to the word of the Blessed One, Padmapatrākṣa—the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One—is devoid of form.

That Buddha is seated upon a lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*); the lion-throne is the space-element (*khadhātu*). Alternatively, the lion-throne consists of the mandalas of the moon, sun, and fire; he who is situated upon that is "seated on the lion-throne.
Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the Root Tantra: "In the secret place, in the space-element, or in the womb (*bhaga*), in the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), or in the lotus..."

Seated upon the lion throne, the Vajra-holder has been described by me in other tantras under the names Vimalaprabhā, Vaṃ-vajrī, Vajrasattva, Vajrabhairava, Īśvara, Heruka, Kālacakra, Ādibuddha, and so forth.

The All-Knowing One, the Vajra-Holder, the Teacher, the Buddha, seated upon the lion throne, has described by me— through various perceptions of objects— the locus as having the characteristic of a support, and that which is supported, according to the diverse inclinations of sentient beings.
The teacher of Kālacakra, requested by you, Sucandra— therefore,

the omniscient Buddha, the Blessed One, the teacher of mundane and supramundane dharmas, the instructor of gods, asuras, and humans, the supremely compassionate one who is affectionate without cause, and liberated from all obscurations; for this reason, even for Hari, Hara, and others, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is the teacher and the omniscient one.

There is no other who, within the triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems, can simultaneously teach the mundane and supramundane Dharma to infinite and boundless sentient beings through infinite and boundless modes of speech;
why?
Because [such a person] has arisen within a limited, single divine birth, and because they employ only a limited, single refined (saṃskṛta) language.

It is not observed here in this mortal world that their omniscient speech teaches the mundane and supramundane Dharma to sentient beings of various inclinations through their respective individual languages; rather, all the Siddhāntas, Purāṇas, and Dharmas taught by them in the Sanskrit language are seen to be merely regional, as are the four Vedas, which are studied only by Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
Why is this so? Because [the Vedas] are derived from the study of the Brahma and Kṣatriya Vedas.
In this world, the study of the Vedas must be performed by Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, and not by Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and so forth;

likewise, the teachings on the Gītā, the Siddhāntas, the Purāṇas, and the Dharma are to be heard from the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa by the four castes—Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—and the taking of renunciation (pravrajyā) is not for fishermen and the like.
Therefore, because they are taught through statements that exclude certain groups from the Dharma, such Dharmas are merely regional and do not benefit all sentient beings.

In this mortal world, because they are unable to teach the mundane and supramundane Dharma to beings of diverse inclinations through various sounds using a limited Sanskrit language, they therefore impose prohibitions upon the *viṭas*, *śūdras*, and others. Their intention—held by those overcome by false pride—is that in this world, those born of inferior lineages such as *viṭas* and *śūdras* must not study the Vedas nor take up the staff of renunciation (*pravrajyā-daṇḍa*), based on the claim: "A single word, well-employed, is a cow of plenty in heaven. This is so because there is no language spoken by an Omniscient One [among them].

If, in this mortal world, all men—including Śūdras and others—were to become knowers of the Vedas, the Gītā, the Siddhāntas, and the treatises on logic (tarka), then who would show respect to the Brāhmaṇas? For there would be no distinction among them, as all householders attached to the enjoyments of worldly existence would possess an equal understanding of knowledge, dharma, and wisdom, lacking any superior quality.

Having understood this, wicked sages greedy for wealth wrote down religious texts such as the *Gītā*, *Siddhāntas*, and *Purāṇas* in the Sanskrit language in books, while establishing the rule that the Vedas must be studied through oral recitation; this created great delusion among the ignorant. This is the underlying intention behind the teachings of those who are not omniscient: that in former times the religious systems of the Vedas, *Gītā*, *Siddhāntas*, and *Purāṇas* did not exist in written form but resided in the mouths of ascetics (*yatīs*), and subsequently, due to the influence of the age of the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya-kāla*), they became subject to appropriation [and corruption].

The teachings of those who are not omniscient, the instructions of those who are not omniscient, and the presentations of the means for the teacher and the requester have been written in books by ascetics due to their lack of wisdom.

Herein, the partial teaching of the Dharma by Hari, Hara, and others is not to be approved by Buddhists, for it is devoid of compassion for all sentient beings, it bestows the suffering of saṃsāra, it produces false egoism, and it is characterized by pride in the doctrine of caste.

In this realm, those dharmas which were taught by the Omniscient One in the language of the Omniscient, recorded in books by the compilers in various languages of sentient beings—those which expound worldly matters such as the Vedas and so forth, those which expound the meaning of the three vehicles, and those taught according to both conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—are heard and studied for the sake of all sentient beings. Sentient beings who are devoted to them hear, read, recite, preserve, and extensively proclaim to others these eighty-four thousand aggregates of dharma (*dharmaskandha*) taught by the Omniscient One, which expound both worldly and supramundane meanings. Having honored them with various flowers, various perfumes, various incenses, various powders, various garments, various bells, various banners, various yak-tail whisks, various parasols, various canopies, various pearl necklaces, various jewels, various lamps, and various precious ornaments, they prostrate before them with the five limbs.

Thus, these teachings taught by the Omniscient One are for the benefit of others; by the power of one's own resolute conviction, they serve to benefit others. They were neither enjoined nor prohibited by the Tathāgata on account of anyone’s birth or lack of birth. Therefore, even today they have not vanished;
let them remain thus for the time being, even in other regions.

In this noble land where the Tathāgata attained perfect awakening, once the Blessed One had entered parinirvāṇa, the compilers recorded the three vehicles in written form according to the Tathāgata’s own injunctions: the Tripitaka in the Māgadha language; the Sūtrāntas in the Sindhu language; the Pāramitānaya and Mantranaya in the Sanskrit language; and the Tantras and Sub-tantras in Sanskrit, Prākṛt, Apabhraṃśa, and the unrefined languages of the Śavaras and other mlecchas. In this manner, the Dharma taught by the Omniscient One was committed to writing by the compilers.

The Three Vehicles have been written by you in the Voṭa region in the Voṭa language; in China, in the Chinese language; in Greater China, in the Mahācīna language; in the Pārasika country, in the Pārasika language; to the north of the Śītā River, in the language of the Campaka region, the Vānara region, and the region called Suvarṇa; likewise, to the north of the Nīla River, in the language of the Ruhaya region and the Surasmā region—in this manner, they have been written in the ninety-six regional languages throughout the ninety-six regions consisting of tens of millions upon tens of millions of villages.

Thus, in the twelve sections of the heavens, the mortal realm, and the subterranean worlds, the three vehicles were recorded through the various cries of diverse beings by various compilers: the Śrāvaka vehicle by the Śrāvakas, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle by the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Mahāyāna of Perfections as well as the Mantra Mahāyāna—consisting of both cause and fruit—by various compilers for the sake of training sentient beings.

"When examined through this reasoning based on the scriptures written by various compilers in various regional languages, the Blessed Buddha alone is the omniscient one who teaches the Dharma in an omniscient language; it is no other, such as Hari, Hara, and so forth."

Now, if among Hari, Hara, and others there is anyone who is fully endowed with these qualities, he too is to be saluted, worshipped, and honored by us—this is the case in every respect. In this text, regarding worldly matters, the reading "nānā-daśaḥ" (of various kinds) is an additional one; let the very beautiful [qualities] remain; intending to say "books have been written," the usage "written in books" is employed. In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "The devotion of the virtuous is toward qualities, not toward the Buddha, nor toward Īśvara and others;
that devotion which is directed even toward those devoid of qualities is inert and born of inauspicious karma."

Dharmas that benefit sentient beings, even when taught by commoners, are dear to me; whereas those that harm sentient beings, even when taught by the wise, are not dear to me. Even a mother in this world is like a rākṣasī if she intends to devour her own son.
