How can there be compassion for others in one who has no pity for her own offspring? Since the killing of father and mother is declared a dharma caused by sacrifices and the like by Brahmins intent on their own self-interest, what need is there to speak of [the treatment of] others?

Thus, [regarding the world-system]: from this [it is established that] the omniscient Buddha, the Blessed One, who is compassionate toward all sentient beings, is the omniscient teacher of the Dharma through all sounds; likewise, Sucandra, Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the ten stages, is renowned in the *Paramādibuddha* as the requester and the compiler.

This concludes the fourth chapter, the summary of the means for achieving the Teacher and the Requester of the King of Tantras, beginning with the words "Omniscient," etc., in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Mūla-tantra*.
The summary of the collection of the place and so forth. Now, the summary of the Vajrayoga is stated: "Yoga is the glorious Kālacakra," and so on.

Here, in the Mantra system, relying upon the mundane and supramundane truths, the Blessed Buddha has taught the meaning in two ways within the tantras and other scriptures: one is by way of worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), and the second is from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Among these, that which is taught by way of worldly convention is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*); that which is [taught] from the perspective of ultimate reality is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
These two points must be understood by disciples through the instruction of the Guru.
Thus, in all other tantras, the subject matter is twofold: one is according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), and the second is from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

That which exists according to worldly convention is characterized by color, arms, emblems, and physical form; that which exists according to ultimate truth is devoid of color, arms, emblems, and physical form.

Of these two, that which is taught according to worldly convention (*loka-saṃvṛti*) is a phenomenon imagined by one's own mind for the sake of accomplishing mundane attainments (*laukika-siddhi*) within the external and internal, and it bestows the fruit of mundane attainment. That which is taught according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is devoid of phenomena imagined by one's own mind for the sake of accomplishing the supramundane Mahāmudrā attainment endowed with all excellent aspects; it is a direct manifestation of one's own mind appearing in the sky for yogins, like a prognostic image (*pratisenā*) in a mirror for a young girl, and it bestows the desired fruit, which is the fruit of immutable bliss—the gnosis-mind (*jñāna-citta*).

The unity of these two minds is the Dharma consisting of wisdom and means; it is the single cause, described as fourfold: the Svābhāvika, the Susambhoga, the Nairmāṇika, and likewise the Dharmakāya together with its activity.

Thus, that very Blessed One, characterized as the fruit in the Mantra system, is called *sahajānanda* (innate bliss) and the *sahajakāya* (innate body). Devoid of subject and object, transcending the nature of consciousness, and non-abiding in either cyclic existence (*bhava*) or nirvāṇa, he is the assembly (*samāja*) of the Buddhas and the enclosure (*saṃvara*) of the Goddesses.
By means of this Gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*), there is innate homogeneity (*samarasatva*); such is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Herein, this vajra-yoga is without succession, free from the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, transcending worldly analogies, abandoned by the notions of "is" and "is not," unconstructed by one’s own mind like the reflection in a maiden’s mirror, directly perceived, the object of realization in all its aspects, arisen from space, Samantabhadra, present in all sense faculties, abiding within the self of all sentient beings, innate bliss, devoid of causes and examples.
Because of the difference in properties regarding its existence, non-existence, and oneness, there is an example for yogins to destroy the grasping of all positions;

just as in a worldly example: due to its difference in properties from a jar, a sky-flower does not exist because of its total non-existence; likewise, due to its difference in properties from a sky-flower, a jar exists because of its total existence.

Thus, because of the mutual dissimilarity between these two, there is indeed an illustration: "In this way, due to its dissimilarity with annihilation, existence exists in all its aspects; due to its dissimilarity with existence, annihilation does not exist in the absence of all things. By the word "annihilation," nirvāṇa is meant as that which has the characteristic of non-existence.

Likewise, the world perceives that there is no identity between these two—the jar and the sky-flower—due to their dissimilarity. According to worldly convention (*loka-saṃvṛti*), there is no identity between this jar and this sky-flower because they are mutually contradictory:
that which is existent cannot be non-existent, and that which is non-existent cannot be existent, by virtue of their respective natures as being and non-being.

For that by which the mind has the characteristic of existence, it does not have the characteristic of non-existence; and for that by which the mind has the characteristic of non-existence, it does not have the characteristic of existence, due to contradiction.

Furthermore, in this context, the form of the image consisting of emptiness and compassion—the pure mind comparable to a young girl’s reflection—possesses no characteristic of form, because atoms do not exist; nor does it possess the characteristic of non-form, because it exists within emptiness.

Therefore, conventional reality has the nature of emptiness, and emptiness has the nature of conventional reality. Because it transcends worldly analogies, that mind exists which is a mind that is no-mind, free from the characteristics of the phenomena of permanence and annihilation, and inseparable from emptiness and compassion.

Because of the difference between the two minds from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is said in the words of the Tathāgata: "The non-dual Vajrayoga is that which transcends existence and non-existence, and is the exhaustion of being and non-being," because it is without any [substantial] continuity.
Regarding this, the Blessed One says in the Root Tantra: "The Svabhāvakāya is present in the self-nature of all."
In terms of all existence,
the sky-flower and [the mind] are of one flavor by their very nature;
in this manuscript, the word "citta" does not appear here.

Between "Viśvasya" and "Bimbasya Viśuddhacitta," a certain two-syllable word is seen in all the manuscripts, which is indeed indistinct— * *Note: The asterisk indicates that the original text contains an unclear or illegible term.*
Furthermore, the portion marked by square brackets does not exist in the two manuscripts.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "The Vajrayoga is great bliss; it transcends existence and non-existence, is the exhaustion of being and non-being, is non-dual, is emptiness inseparable from compassion, and has transcended the nature of atoms. It is devoid of empty phenomena, is liberated from eternalism and nihilism, and is the lineage-less Vajrayoga. Thus, in other tantras, the Tathāgata has declared that Vajrayoga is the bestower of the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā.

This pure Vajrayoga, having attained perfect awakening in a single instant, is of great purpose, the supreme immutable, and innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). It does not abide in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), nor does it abide in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), nor does it abide in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). It does not abide in the nirvāṇa of desire, nor does it abide in the nirvāṇa of form, nor does it abide in the nirvāṇa of the formless, because it is non-abiding in both existence and nirvāṇa. It does not abide in both together, because they are mutually contradictory;
there is no unity between existence and nirvāṇa, just as there is none between shadow and sunlight.

Just as fire does not reside in the fire-drill wood (*nāraṇī*), nor does it reside in the fire-stick (*araṇi*), nor does it reside in the exertion of a person’s hands; in the same way, the Vajrayoga is to be understood by the yogin everywhere—in the external, the internal, and the supreme.
Here, that which is called "enlightenment in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodhi*) is the moment of supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*) great bliss;
this one who is enlightened in a single moment becomes the manifestor of all moments until the end of the count of breaths.
Then, at that moment, he became fully awakened as a Samyaksambuddha.

Here, in that moment of fullness (*pūrṇakṣaṇa*) in which all Tathāgatas have attained perfect awakening, from that moment there is neither arising, nor staying, nor ceasing of all phenomena, because they are without continuity (*niranvayatvāt*).
In the moment in which the arising of phenomena occurs, in that very moment there is no staying or ceasing.
In this context, at the very moment when there is stability (*sthiti*), at that moment there is neither destruction (*bhaṅga*) nor arising (*utpāda*).
And at the very moment when there is the destruction of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), at that moment there is neither arising nor stability.

Thus, in this sequential manner, for all phenomena, there would be no simultaneous occurrence of the moment of arising, the moment of stability, and the moment of destruction; nor is it possible for them to occur simultaneously, for while all phenomena exist at one time, the moments of their arising, stability, and destruction cannot be identical.

Now, as for the claim that from the moment of arising comes the moment of duration, from the moment of duration comes the moment of destruction, and from the moment of destruction comes the moment of arising—
this very thing is not tenable by ultimate reasoning. Here, a subsequent moment does not arise from a preceding moment that has not ceased, nor does it arise from one that has already ceased.

Just as a sprout does not arise from a destroyed seed, nor does it arise from a non-destroyed seed, so too, due to the absence of ultimate existence (*paramārthasattā*), there is no single moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), because of the contradiction between the one and the many.

Thus, regarding the statement that "one who is awakened in a single moment is the manifestor of all moments": first, being awakened in the moment of supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*), one becomes the manifestor of twenty-one thousand six hundred moments of supreme unchanging bliss;

beyond that, the absence of all moments, devoid of both the one and the many, is the supreme non-dual yoga (*paramādvayayoga*) of the Buddhas, which is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because existence is devoid of existence.

As long as there is worldly existence, so long is there an investigation into the one and the many, because phenomena are but the manifestations of momentary consciousness (*citta*). When consciousness is said to be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)—being free from momentary phenomena—then the "position" (*pakṣa*) of being without intrinsic nature was taught by the Blessed One as being "without position. For a "position" is indeed an entity (*bhāva*) or a non-entity (*abhāva*); it is existence and non-existence, being and non-being, oneness and multiplicity, permanence and annihilation, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, form and formlessness, sound and silence, the momentary and the non-momentary, passion and the absence of passion, hatred and the absence of hatred. [In the] southwest...
In the *Mahāsukha* manuscript,
the text from "apūrṇakṣaṇe" up to "yasmin" is not present among the manuscripts.
In this chapter, the summary of the teacher and so forth: [the positions] such as "delusion" and "non-delusion" exist because they are mutually relative.
Free from such positions, the non-abiding *nirvāṇa* of the Buddhas is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
This gnosis, which is devoid of being one or many and free from moments (*kṣaṇa*), is called "reality" (*tattva*) by the Victors.
That very [reality] appears in four ways to sentient beings by the power of the inclinations of their own minds, and it is sixteen-fold;
it is fourfold through the divisions of *ānanda*, *parama*, *virama*, and *sahaja*.
From that [arise]: bodily bliss (*kāyānanda*), vocal bliss (*vāgānanda*), mental bliss (*cittānanda*), and gnosis-bliss (*jñānānanda*).
Thus there is the supreme bliss of body, supreme bliss of speech, supreme bliss of mind, and supreme bliss of gnosis;
likewise, the bliss of cessation of body, bliss of cessation of speech, bliss of cessation of mind, and bliss of cessation of gnosis;
likewise, the innate bliss of body, innate bliss of speech, innate bliss of mind, and innate bliss of gnosis.
When the yogi knows reality in these sixteen aspects, he is called by the Blessed One "one who knows the sixteen-aspected reality.
That very reality is called the Sahajakāya;
from that, the Dharmakāya; from that, the Saṃbhogakāya; and from that, the Nirmāṇakāya.

Thus, there are the innate speech, innate mind, and innate gnosis; the dharma-speech, dharma-mind, and dharma-gnosis; the enjoyment-speech, enjoyment-mind, and enjoyment-gnosis; and the emanation-speech, emanation-mind, and emanation-gnosis. Due to the mental inclinations of sentient beings, reality appears in sixteen aspects. This very [reality] is the innate body (*sahajakāya*), purified by the liberation of emptiness, the gnosis-vajra, the omniscient one, whose nature is wisdom and means—the pure yoga.
That very *dharmakāya*, the vajra of mind purified by the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokṣa*), is called the *jñānakāya*, the yoga of phenomena (*dharmayoga*) consisting of wisdom and means;

that very same [body] is the *sambhogakāya*, the vajra of speech purified by the wishless liberation (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*), having the form of the sun, the yoga of mantra (*mantrayoga*) consisting of wisdom and means;

and that very same [body] is the *nirmāṇakāya*, the vajra of body purified by the unconditioned liberation (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣa*), with eyes as broad as lotus petals, the yoga of form (*saṃsthānayoga*) consisting of wisdom and means.
Thus, Vajrapāṇi asked the Buddha regarding this fourfold Vajrayoga:

the Wisdom-Vajra, purified by the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*), which consists of wisdom and means and is the Innate Body (*sahaja-kāya*); the Mind-Vajra, purified by the liberation of the signless (*animitta-vimokṣa*), which consists of wisdom and means and is the Dharma Body (*dharma-kāya*); and the Knowledge-Body (*jñāna-kāya*), which has attained the knowledge of the aspects of the path, because it abides in supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣara-sukha*) due to its all-seeing nature. Thus he is the All-Knowing One who has attained omniscience.

The Speech-Vajra, purified by the wishless liberation (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*), consists of wisdom and skillful means; it is the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) that has attained the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*), for it possesses a body like the sun and simultaneously teaches the mundane and supramundane Dharma through the voices of infinite, infinite sentient beings—thus it is purified by the wishless liberation. The Body-Vajra, purified by the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokṣa*), consists of wisdom and skillful means; it is the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) that has attained the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), with eyes as broad as lotus petals, for it simultaneously manifests a display of bodies in all their aspects through the miraculous power of infinite, infinite emanation bodies—thus it is purified by the signless liberation. In this way, the Wisdom-Vajra, awakened in a single instant, perceives all objects of knowledge.

The one perfectly awakened through five aspects is the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*), the supreme unchanging bliss; the one perfectly awakened through twenty aspects is the Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*), whose reality has twelve aspects, teaching the Dharma through the voices of all sentient beings; the one perfectly awakened through the Net of Illusion (*māyājāla*) is the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), who knows the reality of sixteen aspects and whose body is emanated through infinite nets of illusion.

Herein, the fourfold Mind-Vajra is purified and possesses the characteristics of the four bodies (*catuḥkāya*): the mind that is the non-existence of the fourth mind, which consists of the two organs defiled by the stain of irresistible passion—this is the yoga of the nature of phenomena (*dharmātmayoga*). (This is the yoga of the nature of phenomena.)
(The mind of the fourth state is the mind of non-existence.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said that the Svābhāvikakāya is omniscient;
thus, the mind of non-existence belonging to the mind of deep sleep overcome by darkness is the Dharmakāya, which is the Jñānakāya.
Thus:
the mind that is the absence of the dream-mind, consisting of the existence and non-existence produced by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is the *saṃbhogakāya*, whose body is like the sun.
The mind that is the absence of the waking-mind, consisting of the perceptions of various conceptualized phenomena, is the *nirmāṇakāya*, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals.
This Vajrayoga is to be explained in detail in the *Jñānapaṭala* (Knowledge Chapter), whereas in this *Lokadhātupaṭala* (World-Sphere Chapter) it has been presented merely by way of summary.
Thus, one should inquire about the yoga consisting of the nature of gnosis, mind, speech, and body in the *Śrī Kālacakra*, the King of Tantras.
In what kind [of tantra]?
"At the time of the Kali age.
What is the meaning of "kali" in the phrase "at the time of the Kali age"? It is the consonant *ka*; that is, the series of consonants beginning with the letter *ka*.
The letter *ka* is the mouth of all consonants because it is indicated at the beginning, or it should be understood as such due to its nature as *rajas*.
Likewise, its *samaya* (convention) is called the *svaramelāpaka* (the meeting of notes).
Herein, what is the *ko'li*? *k, kh, g, gh, ṅ; c, ch, j, jh, ñ; ṭ, ṭh, ḍ, ḍh, ṇ; p, ph, b, bh, m; t, th, d, dh, n; ś, ṣ, s, *ka*—this is the *ko'li*, the series of consonants.

Herein, the *asamaya* (non-convention) is: *a, ā, i, ī, ṛ, ṝ, u, ū, ḷ, ḹ, aṃ, aḥ; a, ā, e, ai, ar, ār, o, au, al, āl, aṃ, aḥ; ha, hā, ya, yā, ra, rā, va, vā, la, lā, ha, haḥ*. This is the *asamaya-svaramelāpaka*.

"At this time" means the time of the Kali age; at that time of the Kali age, in the *Kālacakra*—designated as the *Yogatantro* consisting of primordial Wisdom and Means (*prajñopāya*), the *Ādibuddha*, which is without parts—in that *Ādibuddha* where the subject matter, the *Vajrayoga* known as *Kālacakra*, exists as the very nature of the tantra, Sucandra asks. This is the summary of the teaching of the Dharma.
Now, the summary of the purpose, the purpose of the purpose, and the ultimate purpose is stated: "for the sake of the liberation of men."

For the sake of liberation, the primary purpose for human beings is first of all to act for the benefit of sentient beings through entry into the maṇḍala and so forth; the purpose [of that] is the accomplishment of worldly siddhis by means of the accumulation of merit and the power of meditating on the form of the maṇḍala-circle, as well as by the power of meditating on the empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) through the sequence of hero-steps (vīrakrama) and the sequence of empowerment. Thus, it is the "purpose of the purpose," meaning the purpose of the purpose itself in its successive stages.

In this realm of space, by means of the non-conceptual mind, through signs such as smoke and so forth, by meditating upon the Mahāmudrā in its universal form of all aspects, and by the means of achieving supreme unchanging bliss, one attains Buddhahood and Vajrasattva through the two accumulations of merit and wisdom. Thus, for beings in this very life, this is the summary of the purpose and the purpose of the purpose. This Yoga of the Paramādibuddha was taught by the Buddhas of the past, is being taught by those of the present, and will be taught by those of the future.

By means of the past, present, and future times; by means of the past, present, and future moments; and by means of infinite, infinite Tathāgatas for the sake of the buddhahood of infinite, infinite sentient beings in infinite, infinite Buddha-fields—this has been taught, is being taught, and will be taught to the assemblies. Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Summary of the Teacher and Other Elements, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Mūla-tantra*. [End of] the reading.

In the *Dvādaśasāhasrikā*, there is an additional reading: [Xxx x Homila Paṭala] "The Summary of the Maṇḍala Initiation and Other Topics" (6). The Summary of the Maṇḍala Initiation and Other Topics: Now, having been requested by Sūryaratha, the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī—who is the emanation-body Yaśo Narendra—spoke with a second verse regarding the request of Sucandra as prophesied by the Tathāgata from the *Paramādibuddha*: "Explain correctly this void (*śūnya*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and the drop (*bindu*); the Holder of the Supreme Vajra; the Buddhas, gods, and asuras; the external and internal body; the Supreme Self (*puruṣa*) consisting of twenty-five principles within the nature of things; the measurement of the universe; the construction of the three worlds; and that which bestows enjoyment upon gods and asuras. Explain also the maṇḍala and the initiation of the Teacher of the thirty-three gods and of men. Regarding the purpose of this request here: the Blessed One spoke of the "Great Void of Five Syllables," the "Void of the Drop," and the six syllables for the sake of summarizing the six families (*ṣaṭkula*) and so forth. I shall now explain this with the words beginning "the void" (*śūnyam*).

Here, first, by means of the procedure of the request (*adhyeṣaṇā*), the secret meaning of the Tantra has been revealed so that it may become easy to understand for those of dull intellect when it is explained below; therefore, it must be stated briefly at the beginning of this commentary.

Here, through designations such as "void" (*śūnya*) and so forth, entities that have not been seen and those that have been seen are revealed—those which are beyond the range of each individual sense faculty and those which are within the range of each individual sense faculty.
In every case, whether an entity exists or does not exist, linguistic convention is preceded by a designation, just as in the cases of a "sky-flower" and a "jar."

In this context, non-existence designated by the term "sky-flower" does not become existence, and likewise, existence designated by the term "pot" does not become non-existence; such is what is meant by "spoken according to its own designation.

Thus, those entities (bhāva) which were taught by the Tathāgata in various tantras and other scriptures through designations of treatises, designations of locations, designations of mantra-syllables, and designations of individual syllables, and which were recorded by the compilers—these all must be understood by yogins according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and not the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
In this regard, there are various designations even for a single non-entity or entity.

Therefore, yogis should not engage in conceptualization regarding the designations of even a single entity that has been described through various names; for they must rely on the reality itself, which has been well-examined like gold and taught by a true guru.

Here, this great person (*mahāpuruṣapudgala*) consisting of the six elements is comprised by the designations "void" (*śūnya*) and so forth, by means of these fourteen syllables: "void," "knowledge" (*jñāna*), "drop" (*bindu*), and "holder of the excellent vajra. They are as follows: the aggregate of knowledge, the aggregate of consciousness, the element of knowledge, the space element, mind, ear, sound, the dharma-element, the divine faculty, the bhaga, the emission of urine, and the emission of semen. The state of being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*), the state of having a single flavor (*samarasatva*), and the state of being unified into one (*ekalolībhūtatva*) of these is called "void"; it is not a total non-existence, because it is to be personally realized (*svasaṃvedya*) by the yogi. That very [state] is called the "unstruck" (*anāhata*) by the Victors.

The sign of this Unstruck (*anāhata*) is a mere line in the shape of a knife-blade located in the middle between the left, right, front, and back; it is the first syllable, the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*), and is unutterable.
Then there is "Knowledge" (*jñāna*); here, the letter *ca* is indicated for the purpose of conjunction, because it conveys the sense of a collective union.
By this designation "Knowledge," the third void is to be understood; namely: the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*), the eye, taste, the hand, and movement.

The state of being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*) of these [elements], their state of equal flavor (*samarasatva*), and their state of having become a single unity is gnosis; it is the third syllable, the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*). Its symbolic sign (*saṃjñācihna*) consists of two dots (*bindu*) to the right of the central unstruck sign (*anāhataciṅha*), which are not to be vocalized. [This concludes] the verse on the request. In manuscript *ka*, the phrase "by means of the designations of each single syllable" does not appear.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated: "By this designation, 'the drop' (*bindu*), the fourth void is to be understood from the preceding word 'and' (*ca*); namely: the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the water element (*toyadhātu*), the tongue, form (*rūpa*), the foot, and grasping (*ādāna*).

The state of being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*) of these, their state of having a single flavor (*samarasatva*), and their state of being unified into one (*ekalolībhūtatva*), is the 'drop'—the great void of the fourth syllable."
Its identifying mark is a single, unpronounced *bindu* to the left of the central mark.
Regarding the term "wielder of the excellent vajra" (*varakuliśadhara*): it is a singular compound formed from the two words "excellent" (*vara*) and "vajra-wielder" (*kuliśadhara*).
Due to the preceding word "ca" (and), these three should be designated as "voids.

By the first "excellent designation" (*varasaṃjñā*), the second void is explained, namely: the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), the wind element (*vāyudhātu*), olfactory contact (*ghrāṇasaṃsparśa*), the faculty of speech (*vāgindriya*), and the excretion of feces (*viṭsrāva*).

The state of being unobscured (*nirāvaraṇatā*) regarding these, their state of having a single flavor (*samarasatva*), and their state of being unified into one (*ekalolībhūtatva*) is the "excellent"; this is the second syllable-void.
Its symbolic sign (*saṃjñācihna*) is a mere line in the shape of a staff to the east of the sign of the Unstruck (*anāhata*), which is unutterable.

By the designation of the second excellence (*vara*), the fifth void is described; namely: the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), odor (*gandha*), the anus (*pāyu*), and speech (*ālāpa*).

The excellence of these is their state of being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*), their single flavor (*samarasatva*), and their state of being merged into one (*ekalolībhūtatva*); this is the five-syllable void.
Its symbolic sign (*saṃjñācihna*) is to the west of the sign of the Unstruck (*anāhata*), in the form of a plow, and it is unutterable (*anuccārya*).

Thus, according to the sequence described, through the five [vowels] having become one in a single mass, the five-syllabled Great Void, the syllable *vaṃ*, Vajrasattva, is called the Great Bliss Vajra.
Here, the five syllables are the names of the vowels and are unutterable; namely: in the center is the void of the letter *a*, in the shape of a curved knife (*karttikā*).
In the south is the void of the letter Ṛ with two dots;
in the north is the void of the letter Ū with one dot;
in the east is the void of the letter Ī in the form of a staff.
In the west is the syllable *lṛ*, which is empty and has the form of a plowshare (*halākṛti*).
In this way, the modifications consisting of the long vowels, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and *yaṇ*-substitutions are to be understood.

Thus, the syllable *vaṃ* consists of five phonemes; it is the Great Emptiness, whose nature is non-referential compassion, transcending the reality of atoms, resembling a reflected image (*pratisenā*), and accessible only to yogins.
Herein are the vowels for the aggregates of gnosis, consciousness, and so forth; namely: the aggregate of gnosis is *aṃ*;
the aggregate of consciousness is *a*;
the element of gnosis is *aḥ*.
The element of space is *ā*;
the faculty of mind is *aṃ*;
the ear is *a*.
Śabda is Aḥ;
Dharmadhātu is Ā; Bhaga is Ha.
Incontinence of urine is *haḥ*. The divine faculty is *haṃ*. Emission of semen is *hā*.
These, being unstruck in the center and free from obscuration, are to be understood by the sign of the symbol known as the shape of a sword (kattikākāra).
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is *i*;
the wind element (vāyudhātu) is *ī*.
The olfactory faculty is *e*;
touch is *ai*;
the vocal faculty is *ya*.
"Viṭsrāva" refers to that which flows out.
These [elements] previously mentioned should be understood as having the form of a staff (*daṇḍākāra*) when unobstructed. This concludes the section on the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
The fire element is ṛ; the eye faculty is ar; the taste [faculty] is ār.
The hand-faculty is *ra*; movement is *rā*. These are to be understood by the sign of two unobscured drops (*bindu*) on the right side.
The aggregate of perception is *u*;
the water element is *ū*;
the faculty of the tongue is *o*.
The sense-object of form is *au*;
the foot-faculty or the hand is *va*.
These are to be understood as unobscured, located to the north of the central sign by means of the drop-mark (*bindu*).
The aggregate of form is *lṛ*;
the earth element is *lū*;
the body faculty is *al*.
The object-field of odor is *āl*;
the faculty of the anus is *la*;
speech is *lā*.
These [syllables] in the west are to be understood as being without obstructions (nirāvaraṇa) by means of the mark in the shape of a plow (halākṛti).

These are the thirty-six divisions consisting of the modifications of vowels, qualities (guṇa), increases (vṛddhi), and the substitution of *yaṇ*. Wherein the aggregates (*skandha*) are separately divided into thirty-six types, there, in the place of the aggregates, the six tastes (*rasa*) are taken: sour, astringent, bitter, pungent, sweet, and saline. The syllable *kha* is zero; *sanu* is zero.
Ka. The agent. Bho. *Reg bya* (spa). Ka.
