and the six tastes are *a*, *i*, *ṛ*, *u*, *lṛ*.
The remainder is according to the method already explained;
this very Great Void of five syllables, consisting of thirty-six aspects, is called the "Vajra" by the Victors (Jinas). One who holds that is the "Vajradhara."

The drop (*bindu*) is emptiness; the six-syllable *ekāra* is the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), whose form is the emptiness of all aspects. That is to say: the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*), the ear, the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and the emission of semen from the female organ (*bhaga*).

The unobscured emptiness (*nirāvaraṇaśūnyatā*) of these is in all its aspects for one who does not rely on the middle; above this is its symbolic sign, the consonant *ka* belonging to the *ka*-group, which, without being vocalized, is first the "emptiness of the drop" (*binduśūnya*),
[representing] the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
The wind element, the nose, touch, speech, and the discharge of feces.

The unobscured emptiness of these [elements] is the prior sign of the sign of all aspects; and preceding this is the conceptual sign consisting of the *ca*-group, namely the consonant *ca*, which, when not pronounced, is the second "emptiness of the bindu"—
this is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
The fire element,
the eye, taste, and the movement of the hand.
The unobscured emptiness of these is of all forms; it is on the right of the right-hand symbol.

Its symbolic sign consists of the *ṭa*-group (*ṭavarga*); it is the unaspirated consonant *ṭa*, the third [vowel], which is the emptiness of the bindu—this is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
The water element, the tongue, visible form, and the foot are the sense of appropriation.
The all-aspected emptiness free from obscuration of these [elements], located to the north of the northern sign,
has as its conceptual sign the letter *pa*, which constitutes the *pa*-group; it is unutterable and is the fourth, the emptiness of the bindu— this is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The earth element, the body faculty, odors, and the anus are the [first] group.

The emptiness free from obscuration of these is of all aspects; it is located behind the last symbol, and its symbolic sign consists of the *tavarga*, namely the consonant *ta*, which is unpronounceable— the fifth, the emptiness of the bindu— this is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
The element of gnosis,
mind, sound, the divine faculty, and the emission of urine—
the emptiness of these, free from obscuration, is the all-aspected [emptiness] located below the central unstruck symbol.

Its symbolic sign consists of the class of *sa*, namely the consonant *sa*, which is unpronounceable, the sixth, and the void-point (*binduśūnya*). Thus, the six-syllabled *dharmodaya* consisting of the void-point is the bearer of the vajra, the letter *e*; it is emptiness with an object, having the nature of a magical reflection (*pratisenā*).
Here, the consonants represent the aggregates, elements, and so forth: *k, kh, g, gh, ṅ; c, ch, j, jh, ñ; ṭ, ṭh, ḍ, ḍh, ṇ; p, ph, b, bh, m; t, th, d, dh, n; s, ṣ, ś, ka, ha, ya, va, la, kṣ*.
Furthermore, it should be understood that among these vowels and consonants, there is a division into aggregates, elements, and so forth, based on the distinction between short and long [vowels].

By way of bodily division, the aggregates (*skandha*) and faculties (*indriya*) are phenomena with short vowels and consonants; the elements (*dhātu*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are phenomena with long vowels and consonants. Through the division of the transformations of the elements, there are thirty-six elements: the six aggregates, through the division of the six faculties and so forth, become thirty-six aggregates; namely—the six tastes, the six elements, the six faculties, the six objects, the six action-faculties (*karmendriya*), and the six objects of the action-faculties—these being the transformations of the six taste-elements;
and the six consciousnesses, such as auditory-consciousness and the rest.

Thus, the six formations (*saṃskāra*), the six sensations (*vedanā*), the six perceptions (*saṃjñā*), the six aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*), and the six aggregates of gnosis (*jñānaskandha*)—these transformations of the aggregates are to be explained in detail as they will be stated later; here they are merely indicated by way of enumeration.

In this context, the group of vowels consisting of five syllables, which is the great void (*mahāśūnya*) and the semen (*śukra*), is called the Moon (*candra*); the group of consonants consisting of six syllables, which is the void of the drop (*binduśūnya*) and the passion (*rajas*), is called the Sun (*sūrya*).
In this context, semen (*śukra*) is the moon and the syllable *vaṃ*, while passion (*rajas*) is the sun and the syllable *e*. The union of these two—the vajra and the lotus—is Vajrasattva.
Thus, "vajra" refers to supreme bliss, gnosis, and semen.
*Sattva*—[this term is not in manuscript *ka*;
in manuscript *bho.* it appears after ‘*sa*’; in manuscript *kha* the word ‘*jñāna*’ is absent]. The reflection of Prajñā in all her aspects is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), the Sun.
The reality (*tattva*) which is empowered by both primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), being unobscured and unified into a single essence, acts for the benefit of the world.
This very single yoga of body, speech, mind, and gnosis is the cause of the four faces:
gnosis is the western face, yellow; consciousness is the eastern face, black; the moon is the body-face, white in the north; and the sun is the speech-face, red in the south.
Of these two, the moon and the sun, the six elements of each are to be understood according to the distinction between the secondary and the primary.

And these are the components of earth, water, fire, air, taste, and great taste; among these in semen, three are manifest (udbhūta) and three are unmanifest (anudbhūta)— namely, the water element, the air element, and the taste element— these elements are manifest in semen.
The designation "space element" refers to the taste element; thus, within the passion (rajas), three elements are manifest and three are unmanifest:
the earth element, the fire element, and the great taste element—these elements are manifest within the passion.
In this context, the designation "element of gnosis" (jñānadhātu) refers to the great flavor (mahārasa); thus, the remaining [elements] are not manifest in the semen and the menses.
In this way, for those born from a womb, the three elements of the moon and sun become the body, speech, and mind respectively.
The elements of the moon are the body, speech, and mind of skillful means (*upāya*);
the elements of the sun are the body, speech, and mind of wisdom (*prajñā*), because they arise from the causes of semen and blood.
These elements are the six families of the six sense faculties and so forth.
Thus, the families of body, speech, and mind, together with the family of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), become four families;

the three bodies become four bodies; and the three states become four states. Likewise, the five element-families (*dhātu-kula*) together with the gnosis-element (*jñāna-dhātu*) become six families; similarly, the five aggregate-families (*skandha-kula*) together with the gnosis-aggregate (*jñāna-skandha*) become six families for those born from a womb.
For a girl, [this is realized] at twelve years, and for a man, at sixteen years; until the time of a girl’s menses, the three families or five families should be understood [to apply].
Up until the time of the emission of the semen of the person, the three families or five families are to be known;
at the time of the arising of the gnosis-element (jñānadhātu), for both [man and woman], there are four families; until death, there are six families.
Thus, the Blessed One said in the Root Tantra: "The three families, the five families, and indeed the hundred families are one in their essential nature."
Thus,
now those of noble lineage are described as "Buddhas" and so forth;
here, "Buddhas" refers to the six aggregates, such as primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the rest.

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "gods and asuras," the six [faculties] beginning with the mental faculty (*manas*) and the sense faculties (*indriya*) are included; thus there are the six elements (*dhātu*), the six objects (*viṣaya*),
likewise the six wrathful deities (*krodha*), and the six action faculties (*karmendriya*).
The six wrathful goddesses are the activities of the six organs of action; the twelve deities at the joints of the hands and feet will be described later.
Thus, there are eight yoginīs beginning with Śvacikā; the asuras are the serpent kings; and the goddesses begin with Śvānāsyā.

Now, for the purpose of introducing [the teaching] to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the primordial nature and the person (*prakṛti-puruṣa*) are explained; thus the Blessed One said in another tantra: “Mahāmāyā is the great and fierce one who effects the destruction of all beings; she herself is the creator, she herself is the destroyer, she herself is the king, and she herself is the sovereign.”

Thus it is false; from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no agent or experiencer, nor do other dharmas imagined by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) exist, such as *prakṛti* (primordial nature) and *puruṣa* (the self).
For the non-Buddhists, *prakṛti* consists of twenty-four principles, while the *puruṣa* is the twenty-fifth.
In that regard, the root nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), which is unchanging,

is the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*) and the progenitor of sentient beings; and the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) refers to the seven [principles] beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), which are both natures and transformations (*prakṛtivikṛti*).
Earth, water, fire, air, mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness— these sixteen are the transformations (vikāras).
They consist of the five sense organs, the five objects of the senses, the five organs of action, and the divine organ (the mind).
There are twenty-four primary natures (*prakṛti*); the *puruṣa* is neither a primary nature nor a transformation (*vikṛti*).
Here, because the *puruṣa* is all-pervasive, it is neither a primary nature nor a transformation; it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, it is established that [the reality] consists of twenty-five principles, both externally in the body and in the supreme [state].
Externally, however, there are the five elements, Rāhu, the Sun, and the Moon—these eight are the *prakṛti* (primordial nature).
The five planets beginning with Mars, the five sense organs, the five objects of the senses, and the six tastes of earth and the other elements—these sixteen are the *vikāra* (evolutes).
Furthermore, some maintain that the six classes of living beings (*jīvakāya*), beginning with the sense organs, constitute [the constituents].
Thus, the measurement of the universe within the body is to be explained in the chapter on the inner self (*adhyātmapaṭala*) as "the construction of the three worlds.
Here, "the three worlds" refers externally to the *lokadhātu* (the world-realm).
The rule of action is that the construction of that body within the self shall be explained according to the sequence to be described;
as for the phrase "the enjoyment of gods and asuras," here the enjoyment of the gods occurs by day, while the enjoyment of the asuras occurs by night.
Likewise, explain correctly the northern course and the southern course, as well as the maṇḍala and the initiation of the Teacher of Gods and Men;
here, according to worldly truth, describe the dust maṇḍala by means of the casting of lines and colored powders.

Furthermore, according to ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it is free from the casting of lines and the scattering of powder; it is devoid of the mental cultivation of conceptualizations regarding deities with color, arms, and shape; and in every aspect, it is like a reflection in a mirror within the expanse of space.

Likewise, there are the seven worldly initiations—water, crown, ribbon, vajra-bell, great vow, name, and authorization—and likewise the higher ones: the vase, secret, and wisdom-knowledge initiations. The eleventh is the supramundane initiation, which is the fourth [in the sequence]. Explain all of this correctly; for what reason?

In this noble land, in the future time, there will be Vajrācāryas who are plunderers of wealth; for the sake of material gain, they will go to the houses of wealthy men who are conceited about their riches and sell the Dharma;
out of greed for wealth, they will bestow supramundane consecrations upon those who are unworthy.
First they will become servants to kings and others, and later they will become gurus;
yet even for other fortunate-minded individuals who are devoid of wealth but have abandoned the ten unwholesome paths of action, they will not grant the supramundane consecration,
but will instead produce affliction in them.
Driven by material gain, they will proclaim the Vajra-word to wicked beings;

others, likewise ignorant of the Vajra-word, will engage in mutual disputes out of pride in their own scholarship, and even without understanding the meaning of the Tantra, they will compose commentaries on the Tantra.
The beings belonging to the host of Māra, acting as teachers for sentient beings, will teach the vajra-word perversely;
they will reveal to those of childish intellect the Buddha-knowledge as the bliss born of the two organs.

They will claim that the third is the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*) and that the fourth is that very same thing, asserting that the third knowledge is the Buddha-knowledge because it was spoken by the Blessed One through the non-differentiation of cause and fruit—this being the meaning of the word "thus" (*tathā*).

Thus, having seen that in the future time corrupt teachers will prevail, the Blessed Buddha did not reveal the fourth initiation of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*) in any of the other tantras. This is because, in the noble land [of India], people will become teachers of the Vajrayāna based on their pride as scholars after merely looking at books, even without having received the initiation.

Therefore, in all the *laghutantras* and *mūlatantras*, the fourth wisdom-knowledge—the cultivation of Mahāmudrā and the path of smoke and so forth—is kept strictly secret; it is only in some *mūlatantras* that it is made manifest.

Furthermore, here in this *Paramādibuddha*, both in the *Mūlatantra* and the *Laghutantra*, the fourth [empowerment], the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), as well as the cultivation of Mahāmudrā and the path beginning with smoke (*dhūmādimārga*), are not explicitly manifest because they have not been transmitted through the lineage of the Vajrācāryas; whereas the means for achieving external accomplishments through mantra-deities, the *Vīrakrama*, and the *Svādhiṣṭhānakrama* have indeed come down through the lineage of the Gurus.

"Regarding the phrase 'not yet come': this sequence of purification, which bestows the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, is clearly set forth in writing in the *Paramādibuddha*. Having understood the mental inclinations of fortunate beings to the north of the Śītā River, it was taught by the Blessed One and written down in a book by Vajrapāṇi, taking the *Nāmasaṅgīti* as the authoritative standard so that beings might become free from doubt. Therefore, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the entire Mantra system of the Mantrayāna was indicated by the Blessed One to Vajrapāṇi within the *Nāmasaṅgīti*."

Therefore, those who do not know the Paramādibuddha do not know the Nāmasaṅgīti; those who do not know the Nāmasaṅgīti do not know the wisdom-body (jñānakāya) of Vajradhara; those who do not know the wisdom-body of Vajradhara do not know the Mantrayāna; and those who do not know the Mantrayāna are all transmigrators, devoid of the path of the Blessed Vajrasattva.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, the summary of the mandala initiation and so forth, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Mūla-tantra*. 6. *Paramādya-a*.

(7) Summary of the Compendium of World Systems (ka) Summary of the Response: Now, the response of the Blessed One from the *Paramādibuddha* has been compiled by Mañjuśrī, the compiler, in the third verse. That very [response] I shall expand upon, beginning with "I am pleased," etc.: "I am pleased with you, O Sucandra, by the excellent gods, humans, rākṣasas, daityas, and nāgas; this which was asked by you is known by the supreme family of sages who are free from passion."

O Lord of Men, listen as I explain the entire yoga—from Nirvāṇa down to the Earth, together with the movement of the stages—within the center of the body, as well as the maṇḍala and the consecration. || 3 ||
"I am pleased with you, Sucandra"—this is the address; "O Sucandra, I am pleased with you.
Why? Because:
"Since this *Kālacakra-yoga* which you have asked about has not been known by the most excellent gods, humans, and others, I am therefore pleased.

Here, "the most excellent gods" refers to those from the Cāturmahārājakāyikas up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanopagas; "humans" refers to the Cakravartins and so forth; "rākṣasas" refers to the Nairṛtas and so forth; "daityas" refers to the Aparājitas and so forth; "nāgas" refers to Ananta and so forth; "those free from passion" refers to Ārya Ānanda and so forth; and "supreme ṛṣis" refers to Nārada and so forth.
By these lineages—the most excellent gods, humans, and others—this *Kālacakra-yoga*, beginning with Nirvāṇa and ending with the Earth, has not been known.

Nirvāṇa is the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*) which is the beginning; at the end is the earth (*dharā-pṛthivī*); and since they are not explicitly mentioned in the middle, there are the elements of space, wind, fire, and water.
These elements, beginning with space, are the pervaded (*vyāpya*), while the element of gnosis alone is the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
Thus, the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is *yoga*. Accordingly, the Blessed One said: "Earth, water, fire, wind, and the element of space."
"Consciousness is called the six elements; it is the Great Being, the individual (pudgala).
[End of section] In the chapter on the *ga* syllable, the summary of the world-system (*lokadhātu-saṃgraha-uddeśa*) states that "it is accompanied by the movement of the words.
The word is twofold, consisting of *āli* and *kāli*.

The movement of those two is the movement of the speech-sounds (*padagati*); it is the articulation of vowels and consonants in the places of the throat, palate, head, lips, and teeth. Accompanied by that movement is "utterance" (*pravyāhāra*), which refers to the convention of mantra.
Here, the convention is twofold: first, the convention of mantra, and second, the convention of suchness (*tathatā*).
Among these, the convention of mantra is utterance, which is worldly; the convention of suchness is ultimate, being devoid of vocal expression.

Where there is a convention for verbal expression, there the designations of mantras such as *oṃ*, *āḥ*, and *hūṃ* are used. Where there is a convention for suchness (*tathatā*), there [it is said]: "The letter *A* is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are unarisen from the beginning.
Thus, in the *Māyājāla* in sixteen thousand [stanzas], the Blessed One said: "For example, the Blessed One, the Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, is born from the letter *A*.

The letter *A* is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, the supreme syllable. It is indeed the Great Breath, the unarisen, the foremost cause of all verbal expression, yet devoid of the utterance of speech."
"The radiance of all speech.
Furthermore, in that same *Samādhijālapaṭala* (*Nāmasaṃgīti*, 5.1): "The syllable-less source of mantra, the three great mantra families;
the five-syllabled, the great void, the void of the bindu, the six-syllabled."
Thus, as stated in the *Nāmasaṃgīti* (10.11, 2), suchness (*tathatā*) is the ultimate convention taught by the Blessed One in the Mantra Vehicle;
likewise, nirvāṇa, the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*), and the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) are not uttered, nor do they possess the characteristics of articulated vowels and consonants.

Thus, the Blessed One has taught the characteristic of vocal expression as the symbolic convention of mantra, beginning with the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*). Herein: *a*, *ku*, *ha*, and the visarga (*visarjanīya*) are gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*); *i*, *cu*, *ya*, and *śa* are palatals (*tālavya*); *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣa* are retroflexes (*mūrtya*); *u*, *pu*, and the labial spirant (*upadhmānīya*) are labials (*oṣṭhya*); *ḷ*, *tu*, *la*, and *sa* are dentals (*dantya*). In this way, there are those produced from two places, three places, four places, and five places. It should be understood that these are mantras and peak-mantras (*kūṭamantra*), by means of the symbolic convention of vocalized mantras (*pravyāhāramantrasaṃketa*).

And all those [conventional signs] consist of designations (*saṃjñā*) that serve to indicate conceptual entities for the sake of achieving worldly accomplishments; however, that which is the conventional symbol of suchness (*tathatā-saṃketaka*), devoid of verbal expression, the ultimate *mahāmudrā*, free from the accomplishments of the *karmamudrā* and *jñānamudrā*, has been taught by the Blessed One in all the kings of tantras for the sake of achieving accomplishment.

"O Lord of Men, listen as I explain this entire yoga within the body; I shall describe the mandala and the consecration according to the sequence to be taught, for the sake of all beings attaining the state free from obscuration"—this is the summary of the Blessed One’s reply.

(kha) Summary of the Compendium of World Systems: Now, I shall explain the compendium of the world systems of the Blessed One, as taught by Mañjuśrī, the compiler, through the fourth verse of the *Paramādibuddha*, beginning with "From time, in the voids..."—from time, in the voids, arise wind, fire, water, the continents, mountains, oceans, the constellations, the moon, sun, stars, planets, sages, and nāgas.

And having become gods in the Vimalaprabhā world-system, they are born in four ways among the animal realm on the various surfaces of the earth, as humans, and as hell-beings within the void, like salt in water; and those born from eggs are within the egg. || 4 ||

In this context of the Mantra system, the Blessed One has stated that the practitioner (mantrin) who has emerged from the three vehicles and is established in the fruit of the single vehicle is one who understands the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) of the three vehicles. However, he who does not understand it becomes lost to the path of omniscience in the course of time.

Not understanding the various forms of intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*) within the Mantra vehicle, he commits acts such as taking life and consumes the property of monasteries and temples. By adhering to the positions of eternalism and nihilism, and being attached to the enjoyment of external objects, he goes to hell after having mocked the Three Jewels under the pretext of being a teacher (*ācārya*).
In this regard, four types of elders are to be propitiated by sentient beings for the sake of both the next world and this world.

Among these, the one advanced in knowledge (*jñānavṛddha*)—a Vajrācārya who has attained the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), reached the stage of *muditā*, and is either a monk or a householder—is to be honored; as the Blessed One has stated, he is equal to ten monks. In his absence, the one advanced in austerity (*tapovṛddha*)—one who wears the saffron robes—is to be saluted. By the number of years since donning the saffron robes, among those wearing saffron robes, and by the consecration of a mantra-practitioner, the householder teacher is always to be venerated because of his advancement in austerity, whereas householders lack the superknowledges.
One who is advanced in learning, wise, venerable, an illuminator of the teaching, and a subduer of adversaries and those belonging to the host of Māra—
such persons are to be propitiated by sentient beings for the sake of the next world;
whereas a king who is advanced in wealth is to be propitiated by those seeking enjoyments in this world.
Thus, four types of elders are to be honored by sentient beings.

Therefore, one who knows the three vehicles is an elder by virtue of asceticism (*tapovṛddha*). For a householder, there is no authority over the *prātimokṣa* or the study of the scriptures within the Śrāvaka vehicle until he becomes an ascetic;
therefore, a householder does not become an elder.
Furthermore, it has been stated by the Blessed One in no sūtra that householders who lack the life of renunciation may enjoy monasteries and hermitages without the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).

Therefore, for the sake of fully understanding the three vehicles (*yāna*), one must first rely on the Vaibhāṣika system: there exists a world-system (*lokadhātu*) consisting of an aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*), and likewise there exists a person (*pudgala*).

This is because of the Blessed One’s words: "The person is the bearer of the burden; I declare it to be neither eternal nor non-eternal. Thus, the arising and cessation of the world-system are to be understood.
There is the period of dissolution (*saṃvarta*) and the period of evolution (*vivartakāla*).

Therefore, by virtue of the time of evolution following that dissolution, [the elements] are "in the voids"—meaning, according to worldly convention, they are not within the range of the sense organs such as the eye; existing in the form of atoms, they are the substances of earth, water, fire, air, and space, possessing natures of five, four, three, two, and one quality respectively.
The sixth quality is the *dharmadhātu*, which is all-pervasive; thus, within those empty atoms, by the power of the time of origination, there arises what is called "wind.
Among those atoms, first of all, the atoms of wind become mutually adhered.

Therefore, because of that conjunction, or because of its lightness and mobility, it is called "wind" (*vāyu*). Likewise, when fire-atoms are embraced [by wind], they are called "lightning-fire" (*vidyudagni*) due to their conjunction with wind.
Similarly, when water-atoms are embraced [by wind], they are called "rain-water" (*vṛṣṭijala*) due to their conjunction with wind and fire.
In this way, the earth atoms, when closely joined, manifest the "Indra's bow" (rainbow) in the sky; thus it is called "Dharā" (the Earth).
The taste atoms are all-pervasive.
Likewise, within the five voids, wind, fire, water, and earth come into being through the power of the winds of support, churning, and structural formation.
Regarding "islands, mountains, and oceans":
there are seven islands, seven mountains, and seven oceans.
In the ten directions; O Bhikṣus, Bgu and Mñam-par-ska. Kha. The Elder Kāyadhārī.
O, the one who carries the burden by depending [on others] is I;
O, attachment is I. 0. Wind, space, and the primary elements are I.
For it is thus:

In the chapter on the summary of the world-system (*lokadhātu-saṃgraha-uddeśa*): "The constellations, moon, sun, clusters of stars, planets, and sages"—the constellations are twenty-seven; those associated with them are infinite.
[The sun and moon] have the form of Indra’s mandala; likewise, the clusters of stars have the form of stars; [and] Mars and the others [are as described].
The seven seers are the stars;
the gods are the nāgas;
and the deities are those belonging to the Four Great Kings and so forth. The spirits (bhūtas) are the unconquerable pretas and so forth; the nāgas are Ananta and so forth.
The animal realm (*tiryagyoni*) is fourfold:

those born from eggs, such as *garuḍas* and others, have wind as their source; those born from a womb, such as lordly elephants and others, have fire as their source; those born from moisture, such as insects, moths, worms, and others, have water as their source; and those born spontaneously, such as trees and others, have earth as their source.
Likewise, the great spontaneously born have taste as their source.
The scriptural reading is *vividhamahitale*.

"Vividhamahī" (the manifold earth) is a compound meaning that which is both manifold (*vividhā*) and the earth (*mahī*). Its surface (*talam*), consisting of the nature of the seven continents and the nature of the twelve regions, is the "manifold-earth-surface" (*vividhamahitala*), which is the realm of the *nāgas* and the realm of the seven hells. In that [surface], there are humans on the manifold earth, and in the surface—the hell—there are the denizens of hell (*nārakas*).
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Thus, [the text says] they are produced like salt in the midst of water within the void, and like eggs in the midst of an egg; this is the illustration here: salt for the production of stationary beings (*sthāvara*), and an egg for the production of moving beings (*jaṅgama*). The word "ca" indicates conjunction, meaning that just as the water-molecules of salt attain the state of solid salt through contact with heat, so too do Meru and the other mountains arise as stationary beings.
Just as the atoms of semen and fluid within the egg attain the state of being limbs such as the face and body, so too should mobile beings be understood.
The detailed arising of this world-system is to be explained in the fifth chapter;
thus concludes the summary of the collection of world-systems.

The Summary of the Vajra Body. Now, I shall expand upon this fifth chapter, the *Vajrakāyasaṃgrahavṛtta*, which was taught by Mañjuśrī according to the previous sequence, beginning with the words "In the body," and so forth: "In the body, in gnosis, in space, in wind, fire, water, and earth; in their union, in divine vision, and in emanation—within the tenfold world thus described as the Vajra Body, O Lord of Men, birth occurs from the womb of mantra, and liberation likewise occurs right here. He who understands this correctly does not become a bound beast (paśu); his mind is liberated from conceptual construction. // 5 //
"Body" (kāya) is the moon, unobscured; "knowledge" (jñāna) is the sun, unobscured;
"space" (ambaram) is the element of space, unobscured.
Likewise, the wind element, the fire element, the water element, and the earth element—these fivefold constituents are "stable."
The element of the immobile is unobscured,
and the element of the mobile— consisting of the six elements— is the unobscured *pudgala*-element;
this pertains to both divine vision and creation.

And that creation is both divine and invisible; within that divine and invisible creation, in the formless existence (*arūpabhava*) consisting of mere consciousness and ego—namely the fourfold [realms] such as the Sphere of Infinite Space—and likewise in the tenfold worlds beginning with the body, which are described by the Tathāgatas as the support of vajra-wisdom, there occurs birth in the vajra-body from the mantra-source, such as the *bindu* and so forth, O King; herein lies the mantra-source.

From the moon comes the *bindu*, from the sun the *visarga*, from the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) the letter *a*, and from the wind element (*vāyudhātu*) the letters *ka* and *kha*. In manuscript *kha*, the reading here is "other tantras related to that" (*tatsambandhānyatantrāṇi*); however, according to the Tibetan [translation], the reading "innumerable [tantras] connected to that" (*tatsambaddhānyanantāni*) appears to be correct. In manuscript *kha*, [the term] *mantrayāna* [is used].

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the world-realms (*lokadhātu*): the seed-syllable of the fire element (*tejodhātu*) is *ṛ*; of the water element (*udakadhātu*), *u*; of the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), *la*; of the stationary element (*sthāvaradhātu*), the semi-vowel *ma*; of the moving element (*jaṅgamadhātu*), the semi-vowel *kṣa*; and of the formless element (*arūpadhātu*), the semi-vowel *ha*. One should place these mantra-syllables in counter-clockwise order. Then, the upward movement of the subsequent semi-vowel over the preceding semi-vowel occurs; for the vowels beginning with *ḷ*, there is the substitution of *yaṇ* according to the rule *iko yaṇaci*;
at the end, there is conjunction with the vowel *a*, followed by the *visarga*, the half-moon-shaped *bindu*, the circular *jñāna-bindu*, and the flame-shaped *śikhā*.

The source of mantras refers to those mantras characterized by the increase of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth; for example: *ha kṣa mū la u ṛ i aḥ*. The body of the world-system (*lokadhātukāya*) is the vajra-body.
Within the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), there is the syllable *ya*, which is the mandala of wind;
above that is the syllable *ra*, which is the mandala of fire.
Above that is the syllable VA, the water mandala;
above that is the syllable LA, the earth mandala;
and above that is the syllable MA, Mount Meru, which has five aspects.
Above that is the letter *kṣa*, representing the mobile body under the designation of a lotus;
above that is the formless body, the *visarga* from the letter *ha*, which is the sun.
The moon, the drop (bindu),
the resonance (nāda), and the single-pronged vajra symbol—
thus the vajra-body, the world-realm (lokadhātu) in the form of a maṇḍala, is to be described by means of what is about to be said.
Thus, liberation occurs right here for those who possess the mantra of *sambhūti*; furthermore, at the time of reabsorption (*saṃhāra*), liberation—which is dissolution—occurs right here.
He who knows this correctly [attains it].
Thus, by this stated sequence, whoever knows the vajra-body as being without obscuration does not become a beast; a "beast" is one who lacks knowledge.
"Free from mental conceptualization" (*cittasaṃkalpamukta*) means that conceptualization is the nature of imagining a maṇḍala; being free from that is "free from mental conceptualization.

The summary of these ten aspects was spoken by the Tathāgata in the *Suviśuddhadharmadhātustava*: namely— "The Lord of Sages has ten aspects, seeks ten goals, possesses the ten powers, and is all-pervading."

He who accomplishes the welfare of the entire world without exception, the Great One who masters the ten aspects; whose self is beginningless and free from conceptual proliferation, whose self is pure, and whose nature is suchness (*tathatā*);
who speaks what is real, who acts according to his word, and whose speech is never otherwise; non-dual and a proponent of non-duality, established at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
who utters the lion’s roar of selflessness and strikes terror into the deer-like followers of false paths. Thus ends the summary of the Vajra Body.

In the *Kṣamāvalaya-vakapaṭala*, the section on the summary of the world-system (*lokadhātusaṃgrahoddeśa*), specifically the sixth chapter, the summary of the origin of Rāhu and the other [planets], I shall now expand upon it, beginning with the verse starting "On the left side" (*vāmāṅge*). On the left side is the white radiance, the digit of nectar for the world; on the right is the red-colored Rāhu. Kālāgni, Candra, and Ravi; Śaśitanaya, Bhauma, Śukra, Guru, and Ketu; Mandu, Vṛṣṭi, Pavija, and Śikhiga—these seven pairs exist in the world as radiant entities. However, there is one pair devoid of darkness at the end of darkness. 6. On the left side is the white radiance, the digit of nectar for the world; on the right is the red-colored Rāhu. Kālāgni, Candra, and Ravi; Śaśitanaya, Bhauma, Śukra, Guru, and Ketu;
Mandu, Vṛṣṭi, Pavija, and Śikhiga—these seven pairs exist in the world as radiant entities. However, there is one pair devoid of darkness at the end of darkness.

"In the left limb, white radiance" means that in the left limb, within the previously mentioned *anāhata* [cakra] situated in the center and marked by the sign of the half-vajra, there is a single drop (*bindu*); and that white radiance is a white ray of gnosis, which is the very digit of the nectar of the world (*jagadamṛtakalā*). That same [digit], on the right, is red in color.
To the right of that Unstruck (anāhata) is the red radiance known as the sign of emission (visarga), which is the ray of red gnosis;
outside of those two, on the left and the right respectively, there are Rāhu and Kālāgni,
and then the Moon and the Sun.
In this way, Mercury, Mars, Venus, Jupiter, Ketu, Saturn,
and the pair consisting of rain and lightning (or the lord of rain and fire/flames)— these seven pairs existing in the world, within the world-system,
are for the purpose of that regulation.
In these [directions], the mantra-syllables are, respectively, for the left and the right:
*aṃ aḥ*, *u ṛ*, *ū ṛ*, *o ar*, *au ār*, *va ra*, *vā rā*. These seven groups are the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) of the seven days.
Thus, there is one pair free from darkness, with darkness at the end.

Free from darkness (tamas), having the form of white and red rays of knowledge, it is the limb of the Unstruck (anāhata) on the left and right; there is nothing else. On the back is the yellow Tārā, whose ground is the rainbow of the gods; she is fourfold and divided into two. The vital breath (prāṇa) is the single wind that becomes tenfold at the head and in the impurity (mala).

In the east, in the middle, is the seed-syllable above the Vajra, accompanied by a multitude of qualities, situated below its own power (śakti). Knowledge is everywhere empty, joined with the state of Śiva, and liberated from all phenomenal existents (bhāva). || 7 ||
"And yellow on the back"—by the word "and" (ca), the meaning is that there is a yellow ray of gnosis (*jñānaraśmi*).
On the back of the *anāhata* [cakra], there is a sign known as the shape of a plow (*halākṛti*); outside of that is the form [of the deity] with yellow radiance in the west;
then the subtle star (*sūkṣmatārā*), the great star (*bṛhattārā*), and likewise the rainbow (*suradhanuḥ*).
The earth is of two kinds, consisting of clay and stone;
likewise, that yellow radiance is fourfold, and [the breath] becomes twofold.
There is a single wind called *prāṇa* which becomes tenfold—at the head, at the base, and in the front.

Above that Unstruck Sound (*anāhata*) is a dark blue ray; externally, it is the prāṇa-vāyu, born from the seed-syllable of emptiness (*śūnya*). Below is a blue ray; externally, it is the apāna-vāyu, produced from the seed-syllable of gnosis (*jñāna*). To the east is a black ray; externally, it is the vāyu named samāna.
From there come udāna, vyāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya—these are the ten winds (*daśavāyu*).
Below and above these is one pair; to the east and west are seven pairs of wind and earth. Dhanañjaya is neuter because he does not abandon the dead body.
In these [sections], according to the Vimalaprabhā, are the mantra-syllables of the world-system (*lokadhātu*). Above and below—
Ha, hā, and then, according to their respective order:
a, ā, i, ḷ; ī, la; e, al; ai, āl; ya, la, yā, lā; and kṣa—these are the seven pairs.
East and west,
above and below, one pair at the end of darkness.

The seven pairs are the presiding deities of the seven days; according to the division of the four twilights, they are: *a* at midnight on Sunday, *a* at the eastern rising, and *a:* at the southern rising.
In the western rising: Ā; in the northern rising: AṂ;
in the lunar [quarter]: I, Ṛ, Ḷ, U.
In Maṅgala: ī, ṛ, lṛ, ū;
in Budha: e, ar, al, o;
in Bṛhaspati: ai, ār, āl, au.
Ya-ra-la-va for Venus, and yā-rā-lā-vā for Saturn; these are the sandhyā-bījas for the seven days of the week in their respective order.

"Vajra above the seed-syllable in the center" means that in the middle of the seed-syllables of the upper, lower, eastern, southern, western, and northern directions, there is an unstruck (*anāhata*) vajra in the form of a chisel; the anusvāra, which is the seed-syllable above it, is situated upon its left side, and below it resides one's own Śakti, accompanied by a multitude of qualities.
The power (*śakti*) of that *anusvāra* is the *visarga*;

its qualities (*guṇa*) are the red rays (*rakta-raśmi*). That power, accompanied by those qualities—a multitude of qualities—is situated below the *anusvāra*, having the form of a half-moon (*ardhacandra*).

"Her own power abides"— this is the mark of the preceding and following [syllables] because it is not explicitly stated that [the power] is in the foot or the head of the *anāhata* [mantra]. Thus, the five-syllabled *vaṃ* is for the sphere of Vajrasattva, while the syllable *haṃ* is for the practice of Vajrānaṅga.

Outside of that, the six-syllable [seed] which is the void of the bindu is called the support (*ādhāra*); in the case of the syllable *vaṃ* or the syllable *haṃ*, the syllable *kṣa* is the womb (*yoni*), as well as the vajra and the lotus.
Knowledge (*jñāna*) is everywhere void;
by the word "knowledge," the visarga is meant. Above the unstruck sound (*anāhata*), it has the form of a half-moon and exists everywhere within every external letter.
"Void everywhere" refers to the *bindu*;

"accompanied by the state of Śiva" means liberated from all states of being—that is, the unstruck (*anāhata*) Śiva. His "state" (*pada*) is the mark of the preceding and following [syllables]. Accompanied by that, Śiva is liberated from all states of being. That very [Śiva] is "everywhere," in everything—whether in the external phonemes (*varṇa*), qualities (*dharma*), feet, or head—and in wind and earth respectively.
Above the head is the *kalā*, above the *kalā* is the *bindu*, and above the *bindu* is the *nāda* known as *anāhata*.
These are its mantra-syllables: *e~ va~ śa~ ha~ a~ a~:*; *ā~ a~ i~ ī ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ u~ ū e~ aiṃ ara~ āi~ a ā au~ ha~ hā~ ya~ yā~ ra~ rā~ va~ vā~ la~ lā~ kṣa*.
Thus, it should be understood that among all mantra-words, the five-syllabled Great Void (*mahāśūnya*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) within those to be pervaded (*vyāpya*).

In this *Māyājāla*, the King of Enumerative Tantras, it was said by the Blessed One: “Likewise, the King who holds the universal illusion (*viśvamāyādharo rājā*), the great Buddha-Vidyādhara, the adamantine sharpness, the great sword, the utterly pure, the supreme syllable; partless, all-pervading, omnipresent, subtle, the seed-syllable, untainted, stainless, free from dust, immaculate, with faults expelled, and free from disease. Thus ends the summary of the arising of Rāhu and the others.

Thus ends the summary of the world-system (*lokadhātu-saṃgraha*). Now, the summary of the universal mantra beginning with the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*): "The first thirty vowels," and so forth. The first thirty vowels, joined with *ha*, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, and *la*, move through the groups of consonants starting with *ka* along with their measures (*mātrā*) for the days of the lunar fortnight (*kalā*). The Sun moves through these for a measure of zero, six, and fire (thirty). The consonants starting with *ha* are the measures and the channels (*nāḍī*); they are the gods, humans, and serpents, as well as the elements (*bhūtayoni*) and the mantras. Thus, when joined with the group starting with *ka*, there indeed occurs the birth of a king from the three elements in this threefold manner. (8)
The first thirty vowels, joined with *ha*, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, and *la*, belong to the moon.

Those beginning with *a*—namely *i*, *u*, and so forth—are the "first" ones; when joined with *ha*, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, and *la*, they become thirty through the distinctions of short and long, as well as the *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and *yaṇ*-substitutions.
These are the "moons," which serve as the cause for the increase and decrease of the lunar digits (*kalā*).

The five divisions beginning with *pratipad* are threefold; they are threefold according to the division of *nandā* and so forth: threefold is *nandā*, threefold is *bhadrā*, threefold is *jayā*, threefold is *riktā*, and threefold is *pūrṇā*.

These fifteen digits of increase (*vṛddhikalā*) in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) are further divided by the qualities of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*, and by the degrees of weak, medium, and intense.
Established here as threefold by way of the nature of the elements beginning with space:

the first is *a*, the second is *i*, the third is *ṝ*, the fourth is *u*, and the fifth is *la*. These are Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā, corresponding respectively to the elements of space, wind, fire, water, and earth. Among these, the first is the "soft" (*mṛdu*) measure for the removal of darkness;
thereafter follows the second stage, which is a differentiation of qualities (*guṇabheda*).
The sixth is *a*, the seventh is *e*, the eighth is *ar*, the ninth is *o*, and the tenth is *al*.
[These correspond to] Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā; and the elements—space, wind, fire, water, and earth.
Darkness (*tamas*) is the opening; it is the first soft measure (*mṛdumātrā*) of the first stage (*pūrvakāṇḍa*), while that which is its middle measure (*madhyamātrā*) has become manifest (*bhūtā*).
The *udghāṭana* alone is considered mild;

therefore, in the third section (*kāṇḍa*), the *yaṇ*-substitutions beginning with *ha* are as follows: the eleventh is *ha*, the twelfth is *ya*, the thirteenth is *ra*, the fourteenth is *va*, and the full moon (*pūrṇamāsī*) is *la*.

Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Ākāśa, Vāyu, Tejas, Udaka, and Pṛthivī are the elements (*dhātu*). [The breaths] are *satva*, *udghāṭana*, *mṛdumātrā*, *rajomātrā*, and *madhyamā*; in the first section (*kāṇḍa*), they are *adhimātrā*, *riktā*, *pūrṇā*, *bha*, *tamaḥ*. This is its fivefold division.

On the eleventh day, by the differentiation of the quality of *sattva*, the digit of the first lunar day (*pratipat-kalā*) is "excessive" (*adhimātra*) and is called "the girl" (*bālā*); on the twelfth day, it is "the maiden" (*kumārī*); on the thirteenth day, "the young woman" (*yuvatī*); on the fourteenth day, "the aged woman" (*vṛddhā*); and on the fifteenth day, it has reached full maturity.
Thus, the digit of the first lunar day, having matured on the fifteenth day, is designated as "full" (*pūrṇā*).
In this manner, the increase of the lunar digits in the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*) is divided into fifteen distinct stages.

At the end of that [sixteenth digit], at the beginning of the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapratipad*), the time of entry into darkness is called the sixteenth digit (*ṣoḍaśī kalā*). At its end, upon the digit of the first day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapratipat*), there occurs an entry into darkness on the first day of the dark fortnight, and the second digit of the bright fortnight becomes fully ripened. Then, on the second day, the second digit also enters into darkness; the third digit becomes fully ripened, and in this way, on the third day of the dark fortnight, it too enters into darkness.
In this manner, from the fourth day until the fifteenth digit (*kalā*) has fully matured, they enter into darkness.
Then, at the end of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), at the juncture when the first digit begins to rise—in the portion marking the emergence of the sixteenth part—there occurs the entry of Rāhu.

Thus, the lunar eclipse is of two kinds: on the full moon, Rāhu swallows [the moon] up to the end of the full digit; on the new moon, it is Rāhu that swallows [it] beginning from the rise of the first digit.
In this context, during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), there is an entry into darkness (*tamas*) by way of the process of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*) starting from earth and the other elements.
Subsequently, there is the dissolution of those [elements] arisen in the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).

On the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapratipad*), the earth-element enters into the darkness of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*); it becomes veiled by darkness. On the second day, the portion of the air-element (*vāyukalā*) becomes veiled by the darkness of water. On the third day, the portion of the fire-element (*vahnikalā*) becomes veiled by the darkness of fire. On the fourth day, the portion of the water-element (*udakakalā*) becomes veiled by the darkness of air. On the fifth day, the portion of the earth-element (*pṛthivīkalā*) becomes veiled by the darkness of the space-element.
Thus, in the first stage (*kāṇḍa*), the entry into darkness is mild;
then, in the second stage as well, the act of covering with darkness occurs according to the stated sequence,
wherein in that second stage the darkness is of a mild degree, whereas in the preceding stage it was of a middling degree.

Thus, in the third *kāṇḍa* as well, the activity of veiling by *tamas* is of mild intensity (*mṛdu-mātrā*) in that *kāṇḍa*; it is of medium intensity (*madhya-mātrā*) in the second *kāṇḍa*; and in the third [section], it is of intense intensity (*adhimātrā*).
In that regard—
The fivefold division of *mātrā* is as follows:

on the eleventh day, it is *bāla*; through the division of intense (*adhimātra*) *tamas*, on the twelfth day it is *kumāra*; on the thirteenth day, *yuvan*; on the fourteenth day, *vṛddha*; and on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), it becomes fully matured (*paripakva*).
Thus, in the second *kāṇḍa* [the divisions] are of medium *mātrā*, and in the third *kāṇḍa*, they are of mild (*mṛdu*) *tamas*.
Then, with the arrival of the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*), there occurs the departure of the earth element characterized by darkness;

on the second day, that of the water element; on the third, that of the fire element; on the fourth, that of the wind element; and on the fifth, that of the space element. Thus, the first digit (*kalā*) is the soft measure (*mṛdu-mātrā*): the earth becomes full and ripened on the second [day], increased on the third, youthful on the fourth, a maiden on the fifth, and an infant on the sixth; from the sixth onwards, they remain set in decline.

Thus, in the stage of the soft digit (*mṛdukāṇḍakalā*) and during the soft ripening (*mṛdupāka*), there would be no entry into darkness; for as long as [the digit] has not reached the third stage of intense ripening (*adhimātrapāka*) within the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
Of these fifteen digits each, those that have set on the sixteenth day rise again, while those that have risen on the sixteenth day set.
In this way, the lunar digits are the thirty vowels at the beginning; these are the names of the digits, and they are white until they enter into darkness.
The Kṛṣṇā [vowels] are the designations for the ritual service;
their vowels are the mantra-words for the Śukla and Kṛṣṇa [fortnights], beginning with the Pratipad: aṃ, iṃ, ṝ, uṃ, laṃ, aṃ, eṃ, ar, o, aḥ, haiṃ, yaṃ, raṃ, vaṃ, laṃ.
155. *lāḥ*, *vāḥ*, *rāḥ*, *yāḥ*, *hāḥ*, *ālḥ*, *auḥ*, *ārḥ*, *aiḥ*, *āḥ*, *luḥ*, *ūḥ*, *ṛḥ*, *īḥ*, *āḥ* 156.
Thus, in the bright fortnight, the moon is adorned with the nasal bindu and consists of fifteen digits; in the dark fortnight, the sun is adorned with the visarga and obscures those fifteen digits.
The moon is short (hrasva) and the sun is long (dīrgha).
In this way, the moon possesses the qualities [of the vowels], and the sun is increase; as before,
the sun moves through the classes beginning with *ka*, each consisting of five measures, by means of the measures of zero, six, and three.
Here, "ka-series" (kakārādayo vargāḥ) refers to those series whose first letter is *ka*;

"series" (*varga*) means a collection of five syllables, which is recited according to the divisions of the five elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*) and earth (*pṛthivī*). The "collection of vowels" (*svarasamūha*) is recited at all times according to the divisions beginning with space.
In this regard, the *pratyāhāra* serves as the indicator that in every enumeration of consonants (*vyañjana*),
the thirty pure consonants beginning with *ya* are here [treated] as modifications of vowels (*svaravikāra*),
whereas elsewhere they are included within the enumeration of consonants beginning with *ka*.
They are recited in the section on the initial vowels (*ādisvarakāṇḍa*); namely: a, i, ṛ, u, ḷ, k, a, e, ar, o, al, ca, ha, ya, ra, va, laḍ.
Then: ṅa ña ṇa ma na na gha jha ḍha bha dhadha ga ja ḍa ba dada.

Kha cha ṭha pha tha ṭha ka ca ṭa pa ta t ka śa ṣa ya ka; in this chapter, the summary of the world-system (*lokadhātusaṃgrahoddeśaḥ*) is [indicated] by the reading ending in the nominative case (*sasiti prathamāntapāṭhāt*).
The letters beginning with *ya* do not exist within the groups beginning with *ka*, because through *saṃprasāraṇa* they possess the nature of vowels;

therefore, the six groups (*varga*) consisting of consonants beginning with *ka*—namely *ka, ca, ṭa, pa, ta,* and *sa*—have the nature of the elements of space, wind, fire, water, earth, and consciousness, due to their being articulated from the throat, palate, head, teeth, and lips respectively.
Thus, the sixth [group] consists of five elements when articulated individually.

Those groups beginning with *ka* and the others consist of equal measures (*mātrā*). The vowels beginning with *a* are five short and five long; these ten combined constitute the [first] ten measures.

At the end of the short vowels, the *anusvāra* constitutes the sixth measure; at the end of the long vowels, the *visarga* constitutes the sixth measure. These are to be pronounced through the union of consonants and vowels.
"Endowed with those measures, he moves with equal measures"—the Sun moves for a duration of zero, six, and fire (360) measures; that is, for three hundred and sixty measures.
By those measures of zero, six, and fire, which constitute twelve months, the two solstices (ayana) occur.
In each solstice, whether southern or northern, there are one hundred and eighty days.

At the beginning of Karkaṭaka and so forth during the southern solstice, the Sun moves for six months through the six groups of consonants (*ṣaḍvarga*) accompanied by the six short vowels, according to the order of creation starting from space (*ākāśa*), distinguished by the transition (*saṃkrānti*) and the month. Then, during the northern solstice, it moves for six months through the six groups of consonants accompanied by the long vowels, according to the order starting from earth (*pṛthivī*).
Where it moves accompanied by short vowels, there is an increase in the night; where it moves accompanied by long vowels, there is an increase in the day.
Here, the moon is the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) and the sun is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa);
a single consonant is the moon.
The sun is joined with two consonants,
and Rāhu is joined with three consonants;
likewise, the short vowel is the moon, the long is the sun, and the prolated (pluta) is Rāhu— this applies everywhere.
Thus, because Rāhu has eclipsed [the sun], darkness is threefold, consisting of the mild, the moderate, and the intense.

Here, on the day of the Cancer transit (*karkaṭa-saṃkrānti*), by means of the division of creation (*sṛṣṭi-bheda*), the Sun moves through the letter *ṅa* of the *ka*-group accompanied by the vowel *a*; on the second day, *ṅi*; on the third, *ṅ*; on the fourth, *ṅa*; on the fifth, *ṅga*; and on the sixth, *ṅa*.
Proceeding thus from the seventh day until the end of the twelfth day, he moves through the letter *gha*, just as he moved through the letter *ṅa*.
In this way, for eighteen days he moves through the letter *ga* with its prosodic measure (*mātrā*); until twenty-four days he moves through the letter *kha*;
and thus for thirty days he moves through the letter *ka* with its prosodic measure; on the day of emptiness (*śūnyadina*), he moves through the Unstruck (*anāhata*) sound somewhere.
Thus, during the thirty days of the month of the Leo transit, he moves through the letters beginning with *bha* together with their vowels;

during the days of the Virgo transit, he moves through the letters beginning with *ṇa* together with their vowels; and during the days of the Libra transit, he moves through the letters beginning with *ma* together with their vowels.
During the days of the transit of Scorpio, he moves through the consonants beginning with *na* together with their vowel measures;
during the days of the transit of Sagittarius, he moves through the consonants beginning with *ka* together with their vowel measures.

Thus, in the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), during the days of the six months, he moves through the six groups of consonants together with their vowel measures, numbering one hundred and eighty, by means of the nature of the moon and according to the differentiation of the increase of the night.

Thereafter, the divisions of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) are described in reverse order, beginning with the letter *sa*, according to the divisions of days and months of the transits (*saṃkrānti*) starting from Capricorn (*makara*). The Sun moves through the six groups (*ṣaḍvarga*) along with their vowel measures (*mātrā*); that is, he moves through the groups accompanied by long vowel measures according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). Here, on the day of the transit of Capricorn, he moves through *ssā* with its measure; on the second day, *ssla*; on the third, *ssū*; on the fourth, *ssū*; on the fifth, *ssī*; and on the sixth, *ssā*.

Thus, in another six days— [namely] *āḥ*, *ya*, *ā*, *gra*, *yo*, *yā*— and likewise *ṣa*, *tathā*, *śa*, and *evaṃ śrī śrī*— in the *Vimalaprabhā* [on the chapter on the World System], it is said that during the three days of the Makara-saṃkrānti, the *savarga* (the group of consonants) moves together with its vowels (*samātraṃ*).

Thus, by means of the days of the transits of Aquarius (Kumbha), Pisces (Mīna), Aries (Meṣa), Taurus (Vṛṣabha), and Gemini (Mithuna), the *tavarga*, *pavarga*, *ṭavarga*, *cavarga*, and *kavarga* each move for a period of one month, totaling one hundred and eighty days; this constitutes the increase of the day until the transit of Cancer.
During this increase of the day, the Sun should be understood as being of the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).

Herein are the syllables representing the nature of the increase of night and day; namely: In Cancer (*karkaṭa*), the increase is: *ṅa ṅi ṅṝ ṅu ṅlṝ ṅaṃ*, *gha ghi ghṝ ghṝ ghlu ghaṃ*, *ga gi gṝ gu glṝ gaṃ*, *kha khi khṝ khu khlu khaṃ*, *ka ki kṝ ku klṝ kaṃ*.

ḍḍa ḍḍī ḍḍā, ḍhāḥ ḍhala ccāḥ cclū ccū ccū ccī ccā, chchāḥ chchlū chchū chchū chchī chchā, jjāḥ jjlū jjū jjū jjī jjā, jhjhāḥ jhjhla ijhū jhjhū ijhī jhjhā, ññāḥ kkū kkī kkā, khkhāḥ khkhkṣa lṛ ña ña ñī ñña—this is the vowel-increment (*vṛddhi*) in Taurus (*vṛṣa*).

Up until six months there is increase, and at the end there is decrease; thus, in the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), the consonant joined with a short vowel is characterized by both as the moon. In the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), the two consonants joined with a long vowel become characterized by both as the sun.
A single consonant joined with a long vowel becomes the nature of the Moon and Sun;
likewise, two consonants joined with a short vowel become the nature of the Sun and Moon.
Thus, by the distinction of vowels and consonants, the Moon is twofold and the Sun is twofold.
Likewise, the consonant should be understood as being joined with *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; thus,
by means of the division of the solstices (*ayana*), there is another division of measures (*mātrā*) based on the difference in the movement of the sun.

The sixty-one-fold division [of the winds] resulting from the flow of the five maṇḍalas beginning with space is to be explained in the section to be discussed hereafter; its summary was stated by the Blessed One in the *Māyājāla*, the King of Tantras, within the *Pratyavekṣaṇā-stava*: "He who is the great mind of all Buddhas, who moves through the minds of all Buddhas, who is the great body of all Buddhas, and who is the Sarasvatī (speech) of all Buddhas—he is the Vajra-Sun of great light, possessing the stainless radiance of the Vajra-Moon."

"Great passion beginning with dispassion, with a brilliant radiance of all colors"—thus [it is said]. Dispassion occurs on the fifth, tenth, and full moon days of the bright fortnight; passion occurs on the fifth, tenth, and new moon days of the dark fortnight.

Between these two, at the end of the three full moons and at the conclusion of the *virāma*, there is the great void (*mahāśūnya*), the five-syllabled yoga that has become a single fusion, the heart of the Tathāgatas.
Therefore, the moon, which is the great mind of all Buddhas, is the great void at the end of the sixteen digits;

the sun, which is the movement of the minds of all Buddhas, is darkness at the junction of the rising of the first digit at the end of the new moon; and at the end of the sixteen [digits], it is the six-syllabled [yoga] consisting of the void of the *bindu*.
Thus, the great body of all Buddhas is the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*), the Sarasvatī of all Buddhas is the Bindu-Void;

the Vajra-Sun is the Great Light, the Bindu-Void, the six-syllabled [mantra]; the Vajra-Moon is the stainless light, the five-syllabled Great Void. This Dharma of Wisdom and Means shall be explained in detail below.
The syllable-less is the source of mantra, the three great mantra families, as will be explained in detail.
Now, the nadīs of day and night for each day are being described;
"hādyāmātrāśca nāḍyaḥ" means those which begin with *ha* (hādya) and are also measures (mātrā), thus "hādyāmātrāḥ."

By virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), these consonants together with the twelve vowels constitute sixty measures (*mātrā*). Among them, those joined with short measures (*hrasva-mātrā*) from midday until midnight consist of thirty measures during the increase of the night;
those joined with long measures (*dīrgha-mātrā*) from midnight until midday consist of thirty [measures] during the increase of the day.
In this manner, the increase of night and day should be understood to occur every single day.

Here, the mantra-syllables follow the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) during the increase of night, and the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) during the increase of day. They are as follows: *ha hi hṛ hu haḷ haṃ*, *yayi yṛ yu yuḷ yaṃ*, *ra ri ṝ ru ḷ raṃ*, *va vi vṛ vu vūla vaṃ*, *lali lu lu lulu laṃ*. Thus, night is [the wisdom] through the differentiation of the state of wisdom (*prajñā*), while means (*upāya*) is through the differentiation of the body (*kāya*).

llāḥ llḹ llū llu llī llā, vvāḥ vvlu vvū vva vvī vvā, ru rū ra rūrā, yyāḥ yyūla yyū yya yyī yyā, hhā hla ha hhha ha hī hai, hā—thus during the day; [this is] the means (*upāya*) through the differentiation of existence (*bhāva*) and the differentiation of the body (*kāya*).
Wisdom (*prajñā*) arises from the state of wisdom, and semen is the moon, which is wisdom; it is the limb produced from the body of the means (*upāya*).

In manuscript Kha, there is here: *cāḥ ccū ccū cclū ccī ccā!* Candrakalā says: "O friend! In the Vimalaprabhā, [regarding the world-system and reality], it is said that because it arises from the nature of means (*upāya*), *rajas* (the menstrual flow) is the sun and the means;
and because it arises from the body of wisdom (*prajñā*), it is wisdom."
"In this way, it should be understood everywhere.

Now, the mantras of the threefold world of the stationary and the moving are stated: "The mantras are the gods, humans, hooded serpents (phaṇins), and the source of beings (bhūtayoni). Here, "gods" refers to those of the desire, form, and formless realms.
The Asuras dwelling therein, as well as the well-known humans and serpents such as Ananta and others,
and the fourfold source of beings previously mentioned.
All immobile sources of birth, such as Mount Meru, trees, and so forth, are mantras; they are designated by the name "mantra.
In this regard, whatever the name of anything within the triple world may be, that very name serves as the convention for its accomplishment.

The first letter becomes the seed-syllable of knowledge (*jñānabīja*), and the entire name becomes the recitation mantra (*jāpamantra*) for the accomplishment of the welfare of the world. Infinite mantras are to be understood through the distinction of the names of infinite sentient beings.

Just as a calculation is made from the first letter of a name for the sake of determining auspicious or inauspicious results, so too [the result] is determined by all the letters of the name, starting from the short vowel (*hrasva*) downwards.

Likewise, through the first syllable and the universal noun (sarvanāman), there is the accomplishment of the activity of the reciter of the meditation (*bhāvanājāpaka*). There is no delusion regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), for the power of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs is inconceivable; it arises from the transformation of one's own mind.

Thus, in the sequence beginning with *ka*—that is, in the initial collection of vowels beginning with *a* joined with the consonants beginning with *ka*—there indeed occurs the addressing of kings, as well as their origin. In this manner, according to the stated order, [this applies] to the three realms: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

Thus ends the summary of the collection of all mantras, beginning with Candrakalā. (c) Now I shall explain the ninth chapter, the description of the birthplaces of the vowels, starting with the words "the birthplace," which summarizes the origin and other attributes of the vowels: The birthplace of the vowels associated with *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and *ya*—when joined with the consonants beginning with *ka*—is as follows: [the vowels] born from *ka* and so forth are located in the throat, the upper part of the palate, the space (*kha*), wind, fire, and water; in the lips and teeth, which correspond to earth and water respectively; in the crown wheel (*uṣṇīṣacakra*) for the first vowel; in the heart, the neck, and the head; and in the navel wheel and the secret place. They are associated with the universal [deities], the black one, the red one, those resembling the moon and gold, and the deities of the elements such as the shoulders.
Haḥ is the birthplace of the vowels joined with ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and pa, beginning with ka. Here, the vowels previously mentioned are the five starting with 'a': a, i, ṛ, u, and ḷ.
The birthplace of these [letters] is fivefold, according to their respective order.

Of what kind are they? They are "joined with *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*," meaning joined with the groups beginning with *ka* and so forth, respectively. Wherever "beginning with *ka*" (*kādi*) is written, or where the seed-syllable *ka* is written, there an empty space is seen; O [Bhagavān].
In the manuscript (pāṭhe), "aka" is seen; [it is] the letter *ka* in sequence:
*dha*, *e*, *ta*, *pa*, *ṭa*, *la*. [End of] the chapter on the summary of the mental world-system (*lokadhātumānasaṃgrahoddeśa*). Not so.

Regarding the phrase "joined with each letter beginning with *ka*" (*kādi pratyekākṣarayojitānām*), this refers to those joined with *ka*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and so forth; by the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*), it includes those accompanied by *ha*, *ya*, *va*, *ra*, and *la*. Thus he said: "The vowels (*a*), *ku* (the velars), and the visarga are produced in the throat (*kaṇṭhya*); *i*, *cu* (the palatals), *ya*, and *śa* are produced in the palate (*tālavya*); *ṛ*, *ṭu* (the retroflexes), *ra*, and *ṣa* are produced in the root of the tongue (*mūrdhanya*); *u*, *pu* (the labials), and the *upadhmānīya* are produced in the lips (*oṣṭhya*); *lu*, *tu* (the dentals), and *la*, *sa* are produced in the teeth (*dantya*). The place of birth (*janmasthāna*) is the throat, the upper part of the palate, the hollow (*kha*), the wind (*pavana*), and the fire-born (*havija*) [fire-place] locations.

On the lips and teeth are the birthplaces of water and earth; "birth" refers to the birth of the letters *ka* and so forth, according to their respective order. Thus, the comprehension of the meaning of the words uttered in those locations occurs. Here, in the phrase "comprehension of the meaning of the words," the birthplace should be understood as being for the purpose of the ritual procedure of mantra recitation (*mantrajāpa*).

Furthermore, for the purpose of the place of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it is described according to the divisions of the wheels (*cakra*) within the body: first in the crown wheel (*uṣṇīṣacakra*), then in the heart, the throat, the head, and finally in the navel wheel, in sequence.

Regarding the phrase "of the first," this refers to the vowels beginning with *a*; they are to be understood as the birth-places [of the consonants] according to their respective order, based on the classification of the elements starting with space (*ākāśa*), for the purpose of meditating upon the wheels (*cakra*) such as the *uṣṇīṣa* and so forth, in their respective order.
Here, in the *uṣṇīṣa* wheel, the sounds *a*, *ku*, *ha*, and the *visarjanīya* are to be meditated upon;

*i*, *cu*, *ya*, and *śa* in the *hu* wheel; *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣa* in the throat wheel (*kaṇṭhacakra*); *u*, *pu*, and the *upadhmānīya* in the forehead wheel (*lalāṭacakra*); and *lṛ*, *tu*, *la*, and *sa* in the navel wheel (*nābhicakra*) are to be meditated upon.

The multicolored [wheel] is at the crown wheel (*uṣṇīṣacakra*), the green at the heart wheel, the red at the throat wheel, the moon-colored at the forehead wheel, and the gold-like at the navel wheel;
these correspond respectively to the deities of the aggregates and elements, such as consciousness and the space element at the crown wheel, and the formations and wind element at the heart wheel.

Thus, feeling (*vedanā*) is in the throat-cakra, presided over by the fire element (*tejodhātu*) and so forth; perception (*saṃjñā*) is in the forehead, presided over by the water element (*udakadhātu*) and so forth; and form (*rūpa*) is in the navel-cakra, presided over by the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*) and so forth. It should be understood that the ritual placement of limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and so forth regarding the deities of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, will be explained below.
This is the instruction on the birthplaces of the vowels.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Summary of the World System (*lokadhātusaṃgraha*), in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Śrī Kālacakra Tantra-rāja*, extracted from the *Śrī Paramādibuddha*. 7.
(8) The Summary of the Measurement of the World-Sphere: Now, the measurement of the world-sphere was spoken by the Blessed One according to the inclinations of sentient beings;

it was compiled by Mañjuśrī, the compiler, from the *Paramādibuddha* in verses beginning with the tenth. I shall now expand upon that very [teaching], starting with "up to the wind [at the base] and ending at the limit of Meru."

From the wind-circle to the limit of Meru, including the hells and the city of the serpent-king, there are two hundred thousand *yojanas*. The measure from Meru to the abode of the host of planets is one hundred thousand;

the neck is fifty thousand, and the mouth, the immovable pole-star region, is likewise twenty-five thousand. Beyond that is a single void, devoid of the three worlds, without qualities, and lacking all principles (*tattva*).
In the manuscripts Kha and Ṅa, the word "kiṃbhūte" (in what state? is added here; in the Bhoṭa manuscript it says "Ji Tar Gyur Pa Se Na" (if it is asked, "how does it become?"). Kha: 0thaṃ.

This section is absent in the Kha and Ṅa manuscripts. Ka: "In the moon of the heart. *Vimalaprabhā*: From the wind at the end of the world-system up to the boundary of Meru, the city of the hell-beings and the nāgas measures two hundred thousand yojanas. Here, according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), the measurement of the world-system appears as it is taught for beings and so forth, by way of the various inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings.
From the perspective of ultimate truth, measurement by means of scales and measures is not possible for the world-system, due to the power of the merit and demerit of sentient beings.

In this regard, in whatever cave measuring five cubits a Bodhisattva free from passion dwells, by the power of his merit and knowledge and through the force of his supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) together with his army enters that cave; yet it is not expanded by anyone, nor does any crowding occur for the universal monarch and his army once they have entered that cave. In the same way, the measurement of the world-system (*lokadhātu*) is to be understood from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

In this context, whatever is the measure of the world-system (*lokadhātu*) is as it is in the body, according to the statement: "As it is externally, so it is in the body" (*Kālacakratantra*). Because of the statement: "The measure of the world-system is for the sake of the world-system mandala; the measure of the body-system is for the sake of the body mandala; thus it is called the 'body mandala'. Just as externally Mount Meru is one hundred thousand *yojanas* in height by worldly measurement, so too the skeleton of the body is one cubit (*hasta*) in height; by that measure of a cubit, the body is four cubits.

The world-system consists of four hundred thousand [yojanas], with Mount Meru measuring one hundred thousand yojanas; otherwise, it would not be the case that "as it is externally, so it is within the body," because of the disparity.

Thus, let the measurement of the world-system be as it may according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*); there would be no contradiction of the Blessed One’s thesis here, such as [the arguments] beginning with "because of burning and cutting" (cf.
*Tattvasaṅgraha*). Furthermore, the thesis pertains to the sphere of the accumulations of merit and wisdom.

Since there are various opinions regarding the measurement of the world-system (*lokadhātu*) according to the intent of the Vedic Siddhāntas— which falsely claim that a single Brahmāṇḍa measures ten million *yojanas*—

the measurement of the world-system has been established here through the logic of the planetary mathematics, the zodiacal spheres, and the celestial bodies, in order to mature the Sun, the Chariot, and so forth, and for the purpose of destroying that [Vedic] notion of the Brahmāṇḍa’s size. Therefore, one should not fall into error here by looking at the Buddhist Kośa (*Abhidharmakośa* or *Kośakāra*).

If it is asked how it is that the Blessed One stated the measurement of the world-system (*lokadhātu*) to be more than three million six hundred thousand [yojanas], while elsewhere it is said to be four hundred thousand yojanas—such that someone might think, "Does the Blessed One here speak falsely?"—that statement should not be taken literally by the wise. It is rather according to the inclinations of sentient beings (*sattvāśaya*).
Thus it has been said: "Sentient beings have diverse inclinations and perceive various systems of tenets."
They have embarked upon various paths and are conceited with the pride of knowledge.
As long as their own and others' established doctrines are not demonstrated through reasoning,
even proud men who claim omniscience fall under their sway.

Untruth [is that which arises] from benefiting sentient beings; truth is the cause for the accumulation of merit, whereas [certain forms of] truth result in rebirth in the Avīci hell and other such states.
Those who did not give shelter in their homes see a mountain as hungry ghosts;
the evildoers see their own dwelling as a mountain in the shape of the point of a needle.
The perfected ones see the earth as entirely firm, even where there are fissures; having attained mastery over the netherworld, they go to the cities of the apsarases.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has spoken of the measure of the world-realms as it appears to sentient beings through the power of their own mental impressions (*vāsanā*).
No Tathāgata, having perceived a world-realm through attachment, speaks of the measure of a thing in the form of subject and object.
Having thus fully understood all this, the Blessed One spoke of the measure of the world-realms for the sake of maturing the sages and for the purpose of the body-mandala.
kha. ṅa. of sentient beings;
kha. ṅa. [a distance of] one yojana.
In this [chapter], the summary of the measurement of the world-systems, from the limit of the wind up to the boundary of Meru, [concerns] the mandalas of earth, water, and fire.
Below, the wind-mandala is situated within the space-element.
From that [wind-mandala] down to Meru, there are seven hells, and the eighth is the city of the hooded serpents (phaṇipuram).
The hell-city of the hooded serpents measures two hundred thousand yojanas.
Here, the wind-maṇḍala is fifty thousand [yojanas] in extent.

Within that great, harsh wind and great darkness, there are two hells, each twenty-five thousand yojanas in vertical division from bottom to top; their horizontal measurement is equal to the circumference of the earth-circle.
Likewise, within the fire-maṇḍala there are two hells: one is the Fire Hell, and above it is the Intense Smoke Hell.

Likewise, within the water-sphere (*udakavalaya*), there are two hells: *Paṅkāmbhas*, which is joined with mud and water, and *Vālukāmbhas*, which is joined with sand and water; these are extremely cold. Within the earth-sphere (*pṛthvīvalaya*), there is the hell *Śarkarāmbhas*, measuring twenty-five thousand *yojanas*.
Above that is the city of the Serpents (*phaṇipura*), also measuring twenty-five thousand *yojanas* from bottom to top.
That same measurement is twofold: one half is the world of the Asuras, and the other half is the world of the Nāgas.
Likewise, within the body, from the soles of the feet up to the waist is two cubits (*hasta*).
Having divided those same two cubits into eight parts, the hells, the hoods, and the cities should be understood to exist in each individual part in their respective order.
The measurement of Meru is one hundred thousand [yojanas].
From that terrestrial mandala, the measure from the base of Meru to its summit is one hundred thousand yojanas.
The body [of the system] is one cubit from the waist down to the throat; therein the host of planets revolves.
From that abode of the hosts of planets, twenty-five thousand [yojanas] is the neck of Meru;
in the body, this is six finger-breadths.
From there, fifty [thousand] is the mouth, the face of Meru, extending from the neck to the forehead; in the body, this is twelve finger-breadths.
Therefore, the firm and immovable state is the *uṣṇīṣa*, measuring twenty-five thousand [yojanas].
Within the body, it measures six finger-breadths from the forehead to the location of the crown-lock (*śikhā*).
That is the external void, singular, devoid of the three worlds, without qualities, and free from the [lower] principles (*tattva*).
The external emptiness between the lower wind-mandala and the upper uṣṇīṣa consists of individual atoms in the form of elements, whether material or immaterial; thus, it is empty.
One should understand that space is not all-pervasive by means of this "single emptiness.
