Such is the measurement of the four-lakṣa world-system.
In the body, it is four cubits;

a cubit (*hasta*) consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Now, the horizontal measurement is stated here: from the wind-element boundary up to the limit of the wind, on the stable surface of the earth, there are the continents, mountains, and oceans—four hundred thousand, fifty thousand, and two hundred thousand *yojanas* respectively—and the circle of the fire-mountain (*śikhicala*) is two hundred thousand *yojanas*.

Above the center of Meru, the stellar wheel of the zodiacs revolves day and night; divided into six parts, each measuring two hundred thousand [yojanas], the entire triple world has arisen through the conjunction of time.
From the end of the wind to the limit of the wind, there are four hundred thousand [yojanas] from the wind to the edge of the wind, extending from the eastern wind-circle to the western wind-circle;
likewise from the south to the north.
Upon the stable surface of the earth are the continents, mountains, and oceans.
Then, within the wind-mandala, there is the fire-mandala in the shape of a circle;

likewise, in the middle of the fire-circle is the water-circle, in the middle of the water-circle is the earth-circle, which is that very firm surface of the earth. Upon it are the six continents, the six mountains, and the six oceans.
Together with the seventh water-circle, there are seven oceans; together with the seventh Jambūdvīpa, there are seven continents; and together with the Vajra mountain, there are seven mountains.
Vajraparvata is the submarine fire (*vāḍavāgni*).
The salt ocean (*kṣārasamudra*) is situated below and across the end of the water-ring; the earth, at the edge of the great Jambūdvīpa, is surrounded on all sides and below by the salt ocean.
From the edge of the salt ocean [extends] the salt ocean. Re!
The fourfold [measurement] in the *Vimalaprabhā* regarding the world-system is as follows:
half of four hundred thousand is two hundred thousand.
From the center of Mount Meru, extending to the left and right, it reaches the edge of the encircling salt-water ocean.
Two hundred thousand with the right hand, one hundred thousand with the left, and one hundred thousand with the left again;
thus [he performs it] for the east and west, the northwest and southeast, and the southwest and northeast.
The circle of fire is two hundred thousand *yojanas* in extent.

From that circle of salt water, the circle of fire and wind extends for two hundred thousand *yojanas* to both the right and the left—specifically, one hundred thousand *yojanas* to the right and one hundred thousand *yojanas* to the left—and likewise one hundred thousand *yojanas* to the north; thus it is in all directions.
In the center is Mount Meru, around which the wheel of the zodiac together with the stars revolves day and night above.

What is Meru like in the center? It is that above which the wheel of the zodiac (rāśicakra), possessing twelve spokes and accompanied by the multitude of infinite stars, revolves day and night together with the stars.
In this regard, what kind of verbal logic is this—is there another Meru as well, on account of which such a statement is made?
In this context, even the Mandāra tree is included under the designation "Meru"; therefore, this statement is intended to distinguish it from the Mandāra.
Regarding the phrase "in the sixth part, two hundred thousand":

In this sequence, below, above, east, west, south, and north—in six divisions from the center of the earth-circle—the entire threefold world, comprising the realms of heaven, the mortal world, and the subterranean regions, has arisen through the conjunction of time; it has been produced by the power of the times of dissolution and creation, and through the conjunction of the winds of support, churning, and configuration, for the sake of sentient beings experiencing the fruits of their virtuous and non-virtuous karma.

Now the measurement of the circumference is stated here: the circumference of the world-system, all around, is three times its horizontal extent; the circumference of the earth is three hundred thousand [yojanas], and those of water, fire, and wind follow the sequence of six, nine, and twelve [lakṣas].

O King, when there is one lakṣa of yojanas for the external [circumference] in the abode of the three worlds, that corresponds correctly to one cubit in the body of a human being in the abode of the earth, according to their respective measures.
"The circumference of the horizontal measurement of the world-system is threefold all around.

Here, in this world-system, everywhere the circumference of the horizontal measurement is threefold for all [elements], from Mount Meru up to the wind-circle, including the continents, mountains, oceans, and so forth.
The circumference of the earth is three hundred thousand [yojanas]; the horizontal measurement of the earth’s circle is one hundred thousand, and its circumference is three hundred thousand.
Thus, regarding "the water, fire, and wind":

for the circles of water, fire, and wind, the horizontal measurement from the end of each respective circle to the end of the next is two hundred thousand and three hundred thousand [yojanas] respectively.
The circular measurement follows the sequence of six, nine, and twelve [lakhs].

It should be understood that the water circle is six hundred thousand [yojanas], the fire circle nine hundred thousand, and the wind circle twelve hundred thousand, in sequence. O Lord of Men, that which is one hundred thousand yojanas in the external abode of the three worlds is correctly one cubit in the body, in the abode of the earth's surface, according to their respective measures.

That which is one hundred thousand *yojanas* in the external world-system becomes the measure of a single cubit in one's own body by means of one's own hand, according to the sequence previously described.

Now, the measurement beginning with the atom (*paramāṇu*) is stated by the verse beginning with "by subtle" (*sūkṣmaiḥ*): Eight subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) indeed make one minute atom (*aṇu*); by these [eight] minute atoms, a hair-tip (*bālāgra*); by these [eight] hair-tips, a louse-egg (*rājī*); by [eight] lice-eggs, a nit (*yūkā*); by [eight] nits, a barley-corn (*yava*); by [eight] barley-corns, a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*); by [eight] finger-breadths, a cubit (*hasta*); by two pairs of cubits [i.e., eight], a bow (*dhanus*) here; by two thousand bows, a *krośa*; and by four *krośas*, a *yojana*—by that [unit] is the measurement in heaven, on earth, and in the sky. (13)
In the chapter on the summary of the dimensions of the world-system, it is said: "Indeed, one atom (*aṇu*) consists of eight subtle [particles].
Here, when eight subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) are arranged in a row, they constitute one atom; such is the measurement of an atom.
By these eight atoms of ordinary humans, [one *liksā*] is formed.

The measure of a *rājī* is formed by these eight hair-tips (*vālāgra*) standing in a row. By those [rows] is the measure of a *yūka*; by those [yūkas] is the measure of a *yava*. Eight such *uraga-yavas* constitute one *aṅgula*.
Thus it is said: "by twelve *aṅgulas* [is a span]."

Twelve *arkas* make one *yugma*, and two kinds of *yugmas* make twenty-four; thus, by twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) arranged in a row, the measure of a cubit (*hasta*) is obtained. Four of those make one bow (*dhanus*).
Here, by two thousand bows, a *krośa* is formed; four of those make one *yojana*.

By that *yojana*, there is the measurement of the celestial abodes (*divimāna*) of the gods, the terrestrial abodes (*bhuvimāna*) of humans and others, and the measurement in the sky for the purpose of the revolution of the moon, sun, and so forth.

Now, the thirty-one states of non-form existence (*arūpabhava*) are described: first, the two pairs of *yuga-yugayugala* in the Saudharma Kalpa; then the Brahmaloka-Uttara and the Śrī Kalpa; the Śveta Kalpa from the world of Suvasita; and the eleventh, Kāma. There are four initial forms devoid of the *ha*-pair; sixteen beginning with *ya*; those beginning with *ha* and ending with *la*; and the ten manifest *kāmas*. Each of these consists of a single consonant, [ending] with *ṣa*.

"At first, the Saudharma-kalpa": "At first" means initially; by the word *saudharma*, the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*) is expressed. "Kalpa" refers to that place where gods with a lifespan of a kalpa dwell; thus, the celestial region is called the Saudharma-kalpa. "A pair of pairs of ages."

Two *yugas* constitute a pair, which makes four; the meaning is that the station of the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*) consists of four types, namely: one, two, three, and four great aeons (*mahākalpa*), which is the intended sense of their lifespan. Below the crown of Mount Meru is the station of the hair, which for those who have cultivated it is the fourfold totality of space (*ākāśakṛtsna*).
Likewise, the pair of pairs of *yugas* is the station of the forehead, which for those who have cultivated it is the fourfold totality of wind (*vāyukṛtsna*), lasting for a Brahma-aeon.

Thus, for those who have meditated upon it, the fourfold fire-totality (agni-kṛtsna) consists of two pairs of yugas in the region of the nose, which transcends the world of Brahmā. Likewise, for those who have meditated upon it, the fourfold water-totality (udaka-kṛtsna) consists of two pairs of yugas in the Śrī-kalpa, from below the nose to the chin.
Similarly, for those who have meditated upon it, the fourfold earth-totality (pṛthivī-kṛtsna) consists of two pairs of yugas in the region of the throat, which is the Śveta-kalpa.
Thus, for the sixteen [deities] possessing form, there are sixteen kalpas; starting from sixteen kalpas down to one kalpa, such is their lifespan.

Thereafter, starting from two finger-breadths below the throat down to the limit of the wind-circle below, there are the eleven realms of desire (*kāmabhava*); the realm of desire is said to be the eleventh, beginning from the world of *Suvasita*.
This means that the realm of desire is divided into eleven types, and the first four forms are devoid of the pair of *Ha*.

Here, the seed-syllables of form and the other [sensory objects] are the four vowels beginning with *a*; these are [the sixteen vowels] excluding the two *ha*s. The statement "by means of the six voids" (*ṣaṭśūnyāsaṃkhyā*) refers to the sixteen forms beginning with *ya*.
In this context, those sixteen vowels of which *i* is the first are called the "beginning with *ya*" (*yādi*); thus, they are the sixteen forms beginning with *ya*.

The desires beginning with *ha* and ending with *la* are manifest as tenfold. From the letter *ha* to the letter *la*, these ten modifications of the vowels constitute the tenfold desires beginning with *ha* and ending with *la*. They are manifest (*prakaṭa*)—[the word *vidyamānā* is not present in manuscript *ṅa* or *rāja*; it is absent in manuscript *kha*]; they are stated in the *Vimalaprabhā* in the section on the *Āgama* of the World-Sphere (*Lokadhātu*): "The consonants are one by one, six.
Thus, all the consonants beginning with *ka* are subsumed by way of abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*).
Which single phoneme becomes *ka* and *ṣa*, and the conjunction of *ka* and *ṣa* is the letter *kṣa*?
And that is the eleventh, the existence of desire (*kāmabhava*).

Through the thirty-one existences, the three existences (*tribhava*) would here come to be; due to the division of the elements (*dhātubheda*), there is the division of the three realms (*tridhātubheda*)—this is the meaning of "mo. This should be the triple-vajra (*vajratraya*), and the entirety of the three worlds (*tribhuvana*) through the divisions beginning with *ā* and *ka*.
The hell called Ratnābha consists of gravel and water; the second is Vālukāmbhas, consisting of sand and water; then Paṅkāmbhas, Tīrṇadhūma, Havi, Tamas, and Raurava is the seventh.
"By means of thirty-one existences (*bhava*), the threefold existence (*tribhava*) occurs here.

By these thirty-one existences beginning with the letter *a*, there are the threefold existences: the existence of desire (*kāmabhava*), the existence of form (*rūpabhava*), and the formless existence (*arūpabhava*).

Here, "thirty-one existences" refers to the formless ones and so forth: those who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanopaga*), those who have reached the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatanopaga*), those who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatanopaga*), and those who have reached the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatanopaga*); these are the four formless [existences].

The sixteen levels of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are: the Akaniṣṭhas, Sudarśanas, Atapas, Abṛhas, Bṛhatphalas, Puṇyaprasavas, Anabhras, Śubhakṛtsnas, Apramāṇaśubhas, Parīttaśubhas, Ābhāsvaras, Apramāṇābhas, Parīttābhas, Mahābrahmans, Brahmapurohitas, and Brahmakāyikas—these are the sixteen levels of the form realm. The eleven levels beginning with the Paranirmitavaśavartins are those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Here, the six classes of gods belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*)—namely, the Paranirmitavaśavartins, the Nirmāṇaratis, the Tuṣitas, the Yāmas, the Trāyastriṃśas, and the Cāturmahārājakāyikas—are of inferior eons; their lifespans last for six, five, four, three, two, and one eon respectively.
Herein, the asuras, along with humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings, constitute the five states of existence within the realm of desire.
Thus, there are thirty-one states of existence in total.

The vowels beginning with *a* are the designatory mantras (*saṃjñāmantra*) for formlessness (*arūpa*) and the rest, according to their respective numbers and in the order previously stated. They are as follows: *a, ā, aṃ, aḥ* are the [bases of] the totality of formlessness (*arūpakṛtsna*) and space (*ākāśakṛtsna*); *i, ī, e, ai* are the totality of wind (*vāyukṛtsna*); *ṛ, ṝ, ar, ār* are the totality of fire (*agnikṛtsna*); *u, ū, o, au* are the totality of water (*udakakṛtsna*); *ḷ, ḹ, al, āl* are the totality of earth (*pṛthivīkṛtsna*). Thus, by the power of ethical discipline (*śīlabala*), there are sixteen forms. By the power of meditative concentration (*samādhibala*), the [realms] beginning with Akaniṣṭha arose from the totality of wind and the others.

By the syllables *ha*, *hā*, *ya*, *yā*, *ra*, and *rā*, the six classes of beings belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) came into being: through the power of generosity and the power of mantra-recitation, the Asuras and humans came into being; through the power of wholesome and unwholesome karma, humans came into being; through the syllable *la* and *lā*, animals and hungry ghosts (*preta*) came into being—animals by inferior evil and hungry ghosts by middling evil; and by the syllable *kṣa*, hell-beings (*nāraka*) came into being by supreme evil.

In the first *nāga*-world, by the power of merit, and in the first hell, by the power of evil, there is a lifespan of one *adhamakalpa*; in the second and third hells, a lifespan of a *madhyamakalpa*; in the fourth and fifth hells, a lifespan of an *utkṛṣṭakalpa*; in the sixth and seventh hells, a lifespan of a *mahākalpa*; and in the eighth hell, a lifespan until the dissolution of the world-system (*lokadhātūpasaṃhāra*). Thus, by these thirty-one existences, the meaning is "the three realms" (*tribhava*); the divisions of the realms are thus the "three realms."

This is the triad of vajras, namely body, speech, and mind. "The entirety of the three worlds"—heaven, earth, and the underworld—is to be understood as arising from the divisions of the letters beginning with *ka* and *ā*. Although in the Ka., Kha., Ṅa., and Bho. manuscripts the dental *sa* alone is written here and elsewhere, since the letter *kṣa* is formed through the conjunction of the retroflex *ṣa*, the retroflex has been adopted in place of the dental.
Not present in manuscript Kha;
found in both manuscripts Ka and Kha; [variant] Ka: by the power of... (0vaśena).
kha. 0trama apāyena | ka.
0bhavā | tra [This word is not present in the manuscript] iti bho nāsti paṭale ] The summary of the measure of the world-system.

A *adhamakalpa* (lowest eon) is one *yojana* in length and breadth to traverse; and when that space, filled with fine tips of hair, is emptied by removing a single tip of hair every hundred years, that duration constitutes one day of an *adhamakalpa*. Thirty such days make a month, twelve months a year, and a hundred such years are called a *kalpa*.
Thus, the square of that [unit]—the multiplication of *adhamakalpas*—is a *madhyamakalpa* (middle eon); and the square of a *madhyamakalpa* is an *utkṛṣṭakalpa* (supreme eon).

Thus, by the power of evil, the suffering of beings in the hells and other realms occurs for many incalculable eons; by the power of merit, the happiness of the gods in the heavens and other realms likewise occurs for many incalculable eons.
Now, the designations for the abodes of the *nāgas* and so forth are stated;
regarding these, there is no dispute with the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) or others concerning the names.
Regarding the phrase "the hell Śarkarāmbhas is said to be from Ratnābha":

here, that dwelling in which there is light (*ābhā*) by means of jewels (*ratnaiḥ*) is called Ratnābha; twenty-five thousand *yojanas* below that world of Asuras and Nāgas is the hell Śarkarāmbhas, as stated; the meaning is that it has been described as being from that Ratnābha.

The second is called Bālukāmbhas (Sand-Water), and the third is Paṅkāmbhas (Mud-Water); these two are the cold hells. Then, the fourth is Tota-dhūmra (Smokeless) hell, and the fifth is Havis; these two are the hot hells. Below that is the sixth, Andhatamas (Blinding Darkness), and the seventh is Raurava Mahātamas (Great Darkness); these two are the hells of harsh wind, along with Vajrārcis (Thunderbolt Flame). By the force of the word "and" (ca), the eighth is the ground of Vajrasūcyagra (Diamond-Needle Point), which is eternally ablaze. These are the eight great hells in Pātāla.

The seven oceans are respectively of salt, wine, water, milk, curd, clarified butter, and sweetness; the mountains are Nīla, Abhoga, Mandara, Niṣadha, Maṇikara, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavān. The islands are Candra, which is white in appearance, Varaparama, Kuśa, Krauñca, Raudra, Bhogabhūmi, and Jambū, where humans dwell; the seventh is the land of action (karmabhūmi). // 16 //

"The seven oceans are saline, wine, water, milk, curd, ghee, and sweet; thus, the saline ocean is on the exterior of the terrestrial circle, while the mountains above the earth, beginning with wine and so forth, are seven."—[This means: the mountain Nīlābha [is the first], then Mandara, Niṣadha, Maṇikara, and Droṇa. That region which is one hundred thousand *yojanas* in length and three hundred thousand in circumference, where humans dwell, should be known as the Land of Action (*karmabhūmi*). Regarding the six Lands of Enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*), Jambūdvīpa extends from the shore of the saline ocean, while the remaining [continents] extend from the shores of the oceans of wine and so forth.

Now, O Lord of Men, the four continents within the great Jambūdvīpa are described: in the east it is a semi-circle of wind; in the south, a triangle of fire; in the north, a full moon of water; and in the west, a quarter-moon of earth. In the center of these mandalas is Mount Sumeru, composed of the supreme vajra. The mountains, the nāgas, the planets, the directions, and the surface of the earth consist of thousands of yojanas. //17//
There are no other mandalas; these are the voids.

In the *Vimalaprabhā* [on the world-system], it is said: "First, the wind mandala is circular in the east, having the nature of the eastern wind mandala; it is half-moon shaped. In the south, it has the nature of the fire mandala and is triangular. In the north, it has the nature of the water mandala and is circular, half-moon shaped. In the west, it has the nature of the earth mandala and is square, with three corners [triangular]."

In the center of the mandalas—namely, those of the east, south, west, and north—is Meru, having the nature of the solar (empty) mandala, in the form of a drop (*bindu*), consisting of the supreme vajra. Thus, Meru is in the middle.
The mountains, the *nāgas*, the planets, the directions, and the surface of the earth consist of one thousand *yojanas*.

The measurement in *yojanas* of these four mandalas is, respectively: the surface of the earth (*bhuvitala*) as seven thousand, the mountains (*śailāḥ*) as eight thousand, the planets (*grahāḥ*) as nine thousand, and the directions (*diś*) as ten thousand *yojanas*. This is the measurement for the four continents (*caturdvīpāṇām*) in their respective order. Here, that which is circular in the east and square in the west has the nature of wind and earth from front to back, while on the left and right sides of the body it has the nature of water and fire;
therefore, the characteristic of the four continents is by way of the form of the four mandalas.

Now, the measurement of the extent of Meru and the others is stated: the height of Meru from its base on the surface of the earth is one thousand five hundred and sixteen yojanas; on the excellent surface of the ground, the Cakravāḍa is perfectly [situated] above, with five peaks; on the surface of the earth, there is the Cakravāḍa in every direction, and outside of that are the islands, mountains, oceans, and the fires and winds in all directions. //18//

The extent of Meru from base to summit, reaching as far as its eastern, western, northern, and southern portions, is fifty thousand [yojanas] in width at its foundation on the surface of the earth. The circumference of the Cakravāḍa is sixteen thousand and one thousand [yojanas];
five of its peaks are submerged within the foundation on the surface of the earth. And outside of that, in all directions, are the Cakravāḍas and the islands and mountains.

Outside that Cakravāḍa, within the space of the four peaks at the location of the opening, there are six continents (*dvīpa*), six oceans, and six mountains; among these, Himādri with its peak is the seventh, Jambūdvīpa. Outside of that is the ring of the salt ocean, and on all sides the rings of fire and wind—each of these is one thousand [yojanas]. The six oceans are each less than the moon by one moon (i.e., 43,897); likewise, the continents are one thousand, and the Kulagiri mountains are twenty-five thousand.
Jambūdvīpa is vast, measuring half a hundred thousand [yojanas] across the salt ocean; likewise is the measure of Vahni, Vāyu, and the final one, the supporter of the three worlds.
[47] Each of the six oceans is one thousand minus one moon’s reflection (candracandraka);
that is to say, each individual ocean is one thousand less one hundred and one.
Likewise, there are six continents and six excellent mountain ranges (kulagiri).
Thus, the equal measurement of these eighteen islands, oceans, and mountains is six;

that same [measurement], when divided by eighteen from sixteen thousand due to its subtlety, is the clear [result]: six, two, and eleven. This is the summary of the measurements of the world-system in the eleventh chapter.
The statement "devoid of moon and moonlight" refers to the gross measurement stated in brief here:

at the center of Meru, below the abode of Brahmā, there is one [ring] of the Cakravāḍa extending eight thousand *yojanas* in all directions; outside of nine thousand *yojanas*, up to sixteen thousand *yojanas*, the six continents and so forth are situated.
Therefore, the measurement derived by dividing sixteen thousand by eighteen becomes the precise [measurement].

Outside of that, the vast Jambūdvīpa, measuring twenty-five thousand [yojanas], is ring-shaped in the eight directions from Meru. Outside of that, the measure of the salt-water ocean is half a hundred thousand [yojanas] in all directions;
likewise is the measure of the fire-ring, the wind-ring, and the final one which supports the three worlds.

Thus, from Meru, the abode of Brahmā, the measurement in all directions is two hundred thousand yojanas each. In the body, the earth-ring is half the chest; the water-ring is the upper arm; the fire-ring is the forearm; and the wind-ring extends from the wrist to the end of the hand.

Thus, having described the measurement of the world-system, the locations of the Kālacakra, the gods, the *pīṭhas*, *upapīṭhas*, and so forth, are now stated, beginning with "In the Brahmāṇḍa is the Kālacakra": "In the Brahmāṇḍa is the Kālacakra, praised by hosts of gods together with the Supreme Victor; on Meru is the circle of the gods, and on the surface of the earth is that of the serpents in five colors.

From all directions around the glorious Meru, extending to the edge of fire and wind, lies the entire circle of the earth, comprising all the *pīṭhas*, *upapīṭhas*, *kṣetras*, *chandohas*, *melāpakas*, and the abodes of the cremation grounds. (20)

In the external body, which is the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), there is the Kālacakra at the *uṣṇīṣa*-jewel; that very one is praised together with the best of Jinas and together with all the Buddhas as the *Samāja*, having become unified with the hosts of deities such as the Bodhisattvas and Brahmā.
Thus, on Mount Meru is the circle of the gods (*gīrvāṇacakra*) beginning with Brahmā, while on the surface of the earth is the five-colored circle of the *Nāgas*.
In all directions from Śrī Meru, situated upon the circle of the earth, are all the *pīṭhas* and *upapīṭhas*.

The *pīṭha* is established in the four cardinal directions as the nature of air, fire, water, and earth: Pūrvavideha, Laghujambūdvīpa, Uttarakuru, and Aparagodānīya. The *upapīṭhas* are likewise situated in the four directions by virtue of that same nature, in the intermediate directions of Agni (southeast), Nairṛti (southwest), Īśāna (northeast), and Vāyu (northwest).
Thus, Kṣetra and Upakṣetra are in the eastern half of the ocean;
Chandoha and Upachandoha are in the western half of the ocean;
and Melāpaka and Upamelāpaka are in the half-circle of the fire-girdle.
The half behind the fire is the Veśma and Upaveśma;
the half behind the wind-circle is the Śmaśāna and Upaśmaśāna;
and at the end of the wind-circle are the eight Mahāśmaśānas.
In this way, the twelve stages (*bhūmi*) beginning with the seats (*pīṭha*) are to be understood;
and within the body, the twelve stages correspond to the twelve joints of the hands and feet.

Now, the positions of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) are described: Śakra is in the east, Agni in the southeast; Yama, Dhanada (Kubera), and Varuṇa are in the south, southwest, and west respectively; Vāyu, Yakṣa, and Hara are in the northwest, north, and northeast; and [Īśvara] is in the upper portion, while [Ananta] is below.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and all the guardians of the directions together with their retinues; in their midst is Kālacakra, the progenitor of the best of Jinas, the invincible one with a vajra-body. ||21||

In the east is Śakra; in the east, on the summit of Mount Meru, is Śakra; in the eastern direction is Śakra; in the southeast is Agni; Yama is in the south; Danu is among the Daityas; Varuṇa is in the west; Vāyu is in the northwest; Yakṣa is with Dhanada (Kubera); Hara is in the north; in the upper region is Brahmā; and below is Mahāviṣṇu. [From the *Vimalaprabhā* commentary on the *Lokadhātu* chapter]

All these, Śakra and the others, together with their retinues, are the guardians of their respective directions; among them, Kālacakra—the progenitor of the Jinas, the Unstruck One (*anāhata*), the Vajra-body—is the lord of the guardians of the directions. Thus it is said: Now, the wandering of the Great Wheel-turner (*mahācakravartin*) across the twelve divisions of the earth is described: on the ridges of Meru, he wanders in all directions upon the surface of the earth. He is invincible to the Dānavas; wherever the Dharma has perished, there he goes, and there the Kali Yuga prevails.

Having slain the Mlecchas in battle, he wanders about after establishing them in their own dharma; indeed, the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and the other, the Kali Yuga, proceed again according to the conjunction of time.

On the ridges of Meru, he wanders through the directions for the sake of enjoyment; he is difficult for the Dānavas and Mlecchas to conquer. In whichever region of the earth the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished and their own contrary dharma prevails, upon that ground the Cakrin wanders during the Kali Yuga. This means that in the Kali Yuga, it is precisely he who initiates unrighteousness (*adharma*). That very Kali Yuga, characterized by unrighteousness, proceeds extensively to each and every region where the dharma of the Mlecchas prevails; he goes forth and advances throughout those regions.

Having slain the Mlecchas and the Dānavas and others in battle, he moves about, having established those Mlecchas and others in their own duty (*svadharma*). Indeed, the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and the other, the Kali Yuga, exist here according to the conjunction of time (*kālayoga*);
the meaning is that this present Yuga exists through the conjunction of time, and it is not another [cycle] such as the Mahākṛtayuga and so forth.
This Yuga proceeds by the conjunction of time.

Time is the wheel of the twelve zodiac signs; through its conjunction—that is, the conjunction of time—it proceeds by way of the division of the four *sandhyās*. In whichever region that powerful Wheel enters, there the *Kṛta-yuga* prevails; the *Tretā* is behind the King [of the region], and the *Kali* is in front, while the *Dvāpara* is between the two.
The duration of each of the *yugas* is twenty-one thousand years plus one hundred and sixty; when multiplied by the arrows of the *yugas*, that is one hundred human years. (23)
In whichever region that powerful wheel-turner (*cakravartin*) enters, there the Kṛta Yuga proceeds; the meaning is that the Dharma of the Perfectly Enlightened One (*samyaksambuddha*) proceeds.

Tretā is behind the king; Tretā occurs behind the king, which means there is an absence of one quarter of the Dharma at the end of the Kṛta and an absence of two quarters at the end of the Tretā. Kali also is in front of the king, which means there is an absence of all four quarters of the Dharma at the end of the Kalpa.
And Dvāpara is in the middle of the two.

Between the Kṛta and Tretā [ages] lies Dvāpara, which is characterized by the absence of three quarters of Dharma; thus, the measure of the four ages is twenty-one thousand years plus six hundred and sixty—that is, one thousand six hundred and sixty years. This constitutes the duration of the four ages.
"The measure of each is multiplied by *yuga* and *śara*":
here, *yuga* means four and *śara* means five; thus, multiplied by those forty-five, it is "multiplied by *yuga* and *śara*," meaning that which is a hundred in human years.

Five thousand four hundred years multiplied by one hundred become [five hundred and forty thousand]; thus the measure of each individual *yuga* is equal. This concludes the summary of the measurement of the world-system in the *Havirnīta-paṭala*. Now, the measure of the respective breaths of those born from human wombs and so forth is stated: By twenty-one hundred and six [units]—consisting of subtle breaths (*sūkṣmocchvāsa*), *dhunāḍī*, days, and *yugas*—the measure is established respectively for the minute-bodied beings, humans, spirits (*bhūta*), gods, and asuras.

The Lord of Śakti bears the day of the sun; the possessor of power [endures] for the duration of the Yugas; and in every division of the Khaṇḍa, the Wielder of the Discus proceeds to the state of Śiva, while twelve suns exist within a single day.
Regarding the passage beginning with "subtle exhalation" (*sūkṣmocchvāsa*):

"Subtle" refers to one part of a single human inhalation and exhalation, which consists of twenty-one thousand six hundred [moments]; this is a subtle breath. Six such breaths constitute one *pāṇīpala* for those born as insects and the like. Sixty *pāṇīpalas* make one *ghaṭī*, and sixty *ghaṭīs* make one day. Thus, a "day" for those born as insects and the like is a count of twenty-one thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations. By those exhalations, a day passes for the *bhūtas*; by *dhrus*, a day passes for the *pretas*. "Dhru" means a day.

Thirty times a human breath constitutes a breath for the dark fortnice (kṛṣṇapakṣa), which is the day, and the light fortnight (śuklapakṣa), which is the night; this is the "own day" of the *pretas* and *pitṛs*.

By means of the *nāḍīs*, three hundred and sixty breaths of humans constitute one breath of the gods, which is their day. Twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths of humans constitute one breath of the *asuras*.
A *dhrū* is a year for humans;

a *śakti* is one breath of Śakti. A *śakti* is the lifespan of the Akaniṣṭha class of beings. A *yuga* is a single breath of the Sustainer (*bhartṛ*), which consists of an aggregate of thirty-one thousand six hundred years for humans.
Regarding the "Lord" (*bhartuḥ*), this refers to the class of beings belonging to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñāyatanopaga*).
For those of subtle body, humans, spirits (*bhūta*), gods (*deva*), and asuras, the measure of their respective lives is, in sequence, one thousand four hundred and twenty-six days of the Lord.

Thus, according to the previously stated order, for these beings beginning with those of subtle body, their own respective days amount to twenty-one thousand six hundred. This constitutes a single day of the Lord.

Among these measures, the measure of power (*śaktimāna*)—the measure of the gods of Akaniṣṭha—is borne upon the surface of the earth by the Wheel-turner (*cakrin*). This is the measure of power for the ages (*yuga*); and as the Wheel-turner proceeds from region to region, he goes to the state of Śiva.
Having established the Buddha-dharma in each individual region, he proceeds to the state of Great Bliss, the abode of Great Bliss (*mahāsukhasthāna*).
In this manner, twelve suns [arise] in a single day;

likewise, in each individual segment, there is one universal monarch (*cakravartin*) who propagates the Dharma, such that twelve universal monarchs exist in a single day. Each one passes away in eighteen hundred years of human beings, which correspond to eighteen hundred breaths of power (*śaktiśvāsa*).

Thus, the twelve suns are the suns of Dharma, the initiators of the path of merit and wisdom; externally, in the course of a year, these twelve suns move according to the division of the twelve zodiac signs.

Now, the temporal divisions for each individual day are described according to the divisions of breath for the subtle [sun] and the others: all fortnights, months, seasons, yugas, and ages, as well as the time of fire (the three seasons), the two solstices, and the entire year, O King, are contained within the daily ghaṭikās, lagnas, and pāṇīpala units.

In this manner, these very [elements] move within the bodies of gods, humans, and asuras—those born again and again—in the abode of the three worlds, just as they do within the body on the day of their respective powers. (25)
Regarding the phrase "pakṣāḥ" and so forth:
here, on each individual day, there are twenty-four fortnights (pakṣas) for the [houses] beginning with the Ascendant (tanuja);
these constitute all the months, which are twelve months in total.
The six seasons, the four periods of the yuga,
and the three times known as the fire-time (agnikāla).
"O King, there are two solstices (*ayana*) [which constitute] one year; all this is to be understood according to the division of years.

Likewise, day by day, there are three hundred and sixty days, three hundred and twenty *ghaṭikā*-lagnas, and thirty *pāṇī* (minutes). A month consists of three hundred and twenty breaths (*śvāsa*), and with twelve months, a day-year (*dinavarṣa*) passes.
Sixty-three hundred breaths constitute a season (*ṛtu*), and with six seasons, a day-year passes."
Every five hundred and forty breaths, a yuga passes;
every four yugas, a day passes; and every seven hundred and twenty breaths, one kalpa passes.
Three thousand six hundred breaths constitute a day;
ten thousand eight hundred breaths constitute a solstice (ayana);
and by two solstices, a day and a year are constituted.
Thus, by means of twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths according to their respective measures, a year passes for each day of the [lunar] days (tanujā) and so forth;
likewise, a day-and-night (ahorātra) passes by sixty breaths,
and a year passes by three hundred and sixty such day-and-nights.
With five breaths, one *lagna* passes;
with four hundred and thirty-two *lagnas*, a day passes; with one hundred and twenty *lagnas*, a year passes; and with one breath, one *ghaṭikā* passes.
Sixty breaths constitute one *pāṇīpala*.
One-sixtieth of a breath constitutes one breath.
[One twenty-one thousand one hundred and sixteen-thousandth part of a breath constitutes one breath.]
A day and a year consist of twenty-one thousand six hundred *ghaṭikās*;
a day and a year pass with twelve hundred and ninety-six thousand *pāṇipalas*;
and a day and a year pass with seven hundred and seventy-six thousand seven hundred and seventy *śvāsas*.
Thus, by seventy-seven crores and seventy-six lakhs of breaths, one hundred days (or one hundred years) pass;
this [life span] becomes less or more due to the power of karma.
By the power of yoga for yogins and by the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for ascetics, it becomes increased according to their respective measures.
A single breath lasts for one *ghaṭikā* for sinful beings due to the power of their sin, and thus it becomes deficient;

there is no fixed rule for this according to the reasoning of the supreme scriptures (*paramāgama*). However, it is stated in the Vedas: "Man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred faculties" (*Ai. Br.*).
In this regard, there is this figurative statement: "The maximum lifespan of humans is one hundred years," which refers to the increase in the lifespan of men during the Kṛta Yuga.
Here, according to the definitive meaning (nītārtha), the word "man" (*puruṣa*) denotes each day and each year.

By means of a hundred days or a hundred years, within the internal [self], and again by means of the revolution of another cycle of breaths externally, it is said, "Man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred faculties";
thus, by two hundred days, the four yugas pass within the internal self.

With forty-three hundred and twenty thousand breaths, there are external years; thus, by the revolution of both wheels, for both persons, two months constitute one season. On the left and right, there are ten mandalas, and the flow of the vital breath (prāṇa) constitutes one mandala every four hundred and thirty-two thousand years.

Thus, by five cycles, all the planets enter their respective houses of birth when it is empty; thereafter, through the commencement of another step, it shall be stated as will be explained that "another person has emerged from the middle [channel]. This concludes the eighth chapter, the Summary of the Measurement of the World System, in the *Vimalaprabhā* commentary on the *Śrī Kālacakra Tantra*, the King of Tantras extracted from the *Śrī Paramādibuddha*, consisting of twelve thousand verses. ||8||
This portion, written within a bracket in manuscripts Ka and Kha,
is also absent from the Bhutanese manuscript (Bho.).
In this manuscript, there is an additional reading, "Lo brGyar" (*varṣaśatam*, "a hundred years").

This is found thus in the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*: "Man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a vigor of a hundred [years]... [End of] chapter. The Great Chapter on the Method for Knowing Astrology (9): The Great Chapter on the Method for Knowing Astrology. Now, I shall elaborate upon the birth of Mañjuśrī in the land of Sambhala, the destruction of the astronomical Siddhāntas due to the arising of the Mleccha religion, the commencement of the *Laghukaraṇa*, and the prophecy of the Tathāgata beginning with "from the first year," and so forth.
Six hundred years from the first year, King Yaśas will appear in the place called Sambhala. From that time, for eight hundred years, the Mleccha religion will indeed prevail in the land of Makha.

At that time, O humans, the clear *laghukaraṇa* [simplified astronomical calculation] must be understood on earth; the destruction of the Siddhāntas will occur throughout the entire surface of the world through the conjunction of time (*kālayoga*). || 26 ||
"In six hundred years from the first year, Yaśas, the lord, will appear in the place named Sambhala.
Here, "the first" refers to the year of the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma;
six hundred years from that year, in the region named Sambhala to the north of the Śītā River.

"Yaśas" is the reading found in the scriptures; the meaning is that Mañjuśrī, the Greatly Renowned One, will become manifest and will assume an emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Therefore, "by the nāgas after a hundred years" means after Yaśas has passed away.

Thus it was determined by the Nāgas over eight hundred years that the practice of the Mleccha religion will prevail in the land of Makha. In the southern part of Makha, adorned with ten million villages, the practice of the Asura religion of the Tāyi (Jikā) Mlecchas will prevail.
In that age of the Mlecchas, people on earth should clearly understand that the *laghukaraṇa* [astronomical manual] is to be known by men;
for there is the destruction of the *siddhāntas*.
The *siddhāntas* are the Brahma, Saura, Yavana, and Romaka; the destruction of these four is what constitutes the "destruction of the *siddhāntas*."
Regarding the phrase "on the entire surface of the earth" (*sakalabhuvitala*):
"entire" (*sakala*) refers to where the tenets of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) prevail;
therein, the "entire surface of the earth" (*bhuvitala*) is that which extends from Śītā to the south, and it is upon that surface of the earth.
There will be no destruction of the Buddhist tenets in regions such as Sambhala;
rather, it will come about through the "conjunction of time" (*kālayoga*).

Time refers here to the religion of the barbarians (*mleccha*); the conjunction of the tenets with that [religion] is the "conjunction of time," and from that conjunction of time, [the destruction] will occur.
The term "kālayoge" (in the conjunction of time) is a locative used in the sense of the ablative;

therefore, the statement that "the simplified calculation (*laghukaraṇa*) is clear because of the destruction of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)" is like the proverb of the mother’s sweetmeat. For non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the simplified calculation and so forth are not actually clear in the ultimate sense.
Why?
Regarding the statement "the destruction of the Siddhāntas," which is spoken as a figurative censure:
if the Karaṇa and other systems were indeed accurate, then there would be no destruction of the Siddhāntas, since the planets are established even by means of the Karaṇa.
Furthermore, the correction of the Sun is not observed in other Karaṇas when tested by shadow on the day of the summer solstice.

During the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa), the solar motion is impure without the purification of the shadow; from that impure solar motion, the lunar motion is likewise impure. In this way, even Mars and the other planets, though corrected with respect to the sun, have their motions rendered impure because the solar motion is impure.
Due to the impurity of the planetary motions, the results of the planets in horoscopes and other such works are useless for the followers of the Tīrthikas.

In this Siddhānta, the corrections and additive values for the planets are to be calculated by women and children, so that the planets may be easily understood even by the ignorant and others. Because of this, envy has arisen among the wicked heretics in this Kali age:
"If all women, children, and the like come to know the movement of the planets, who then will show us respect?
Therefore, [they devised] the *kara-varṣātra*...

In this Tibetan translation, four philosophical systems are recorded as: "the proponents of Brahmā-deva, the proponents of Sūrya-deva, the naked ones (Śaivas), and the proponents of Rāhu-deva. [The Tibetan text reads: *gCer Bu Pa* and *sGra Can* (*ka*).
[The Sanskrit] *nivartante* [is rendered as] *bho.* *vartate* (*Sugs Pa*)—[*ka.*] *bhaviṣyat*; [*bho.*] *hByun Bar hGur Ro* (*bhaviṣyati*).
—ka. Nine—ka.

Thus, having reflected, "Having taken away the Siddhāntas from the Vimalaprabhā, we shall compose the Tantras and so forth," the Siddhāntas were made secret, while the composition of the Tantras and so forth was made public.

In the Tantra, there was a multitude of various calculations for days; even in the Karaṇas, an elaborate expansion was made consisting of the fourfold operations of slow and fast motion, by which ignorant people, seeing it to be difficult, fled far away and ceased to practice what is called Jyotiṣa.

Thus, due to the passage of time, the fixed parameters (*dhruvaka*) in the Karaṇas became inaccurate; because of this inaccuracy, the solar longitude was incorrect, and due to the incorrectness of the solar longitude, the longitudes of all the planets became incorrect.

In this context, whatever [astronomical] instruments and such were constructed by wicked people for the sake of deceiving others out of ignorance, precisely that has resulted in their own lack of understanding due to the passage of time, serving only to harm others;
therefore, harming others is everywhere contradictory.
Here, the daily additive increments (bhoga-kṣepaka) of the planets are to be stated as they will be explained later.

Now, first, the simplified calculation (*laghukaraṇa*) is stated: The well-known Mleccha year beginning with the Prabhava cycle is mixed with [the numbers] fire (3), sky (0), and ocean (4). The Mleccha king’s year is diminished by hand (2), serpent (8), and moon (1); the remainder is multiplied by twelve and mixed with the months starting from Caitra. This is multiplied by four and divided by one hundred and thirty; the quotient is added to the top [value], O King, and thus the pure total of months is obtained. || 27 ||
Regarding the statement "mixed in the ocean of nine [and] ten" (*nau khe'bdhau vimiśram*),
the constant (*dhruvaka*) here is not fixed, because in the *Tantrarāja* a new constant is established at the end of each sixty-year cycle.
Thus, in this system, the time of Mañjuśrī becomes the constant in the calculation (*karaṇa*) six hundred years after the time of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the period of the Mlecchas lasts for eight hundred years;
from that period of the Mlecchas, diminished by one hundred and eighty-two, is the period of Aja-Kalkī, by whom Aja the Laghukaraṇa was purified—
that very period becomes the constant (*dhruvaka*) in the Karaṇa reckoning, starting from the year of the Mlecchas.

"Having entered the beginning of the *prabhava* [cycle]" means that those sixty-year cycles of years for which *prabhava* is the first or opening (*mukha*) are called "those beginning with *prabhava*" (*prabhavamukhāḥ*). Within each of these, a mixed period of four hundred and three years is known as the *mleccha* year;
starting from the first year up to the sixtieth year, it remains thus mixed, having entered the beginning of the *prabhava* cycle.
That very year becomes well-known among all other systems of calculation, just like the days of the week beginning with Āditya;

it is mixed into the aggregate of four hundred and three years, and thus the "Mleccha year" becomes well-known. The Mleccha is the incarnation of Rahmaṇa at Madhumatī, the teacher of the Mleccha dharma, and the preceptor and lord of the Mlecchas.

The year of the Mleccha king diminished by one hundred and eighty-two—“diminished by one hundred and eighty-two” (karaphaṇiśaśinonam) means the year of the time of Ajakalkī in the region of Sambhala; that itself is the aggregate of years in the *Laghukaraṇa*.
The remainder, multiplied by twelve:

that same aggregate of years, the remainder after being diminished by one hundred and eighty-two, is multiplied by twelve for the purpose of determining the aggregate of months; thus it becomes the aggregate of months.

"Combined with the months beginning with Caitra" means that very same aggregate of months becomes mixed with the current months starting from Caitra for the sake of the current month; thus it is "multiplied by the lower yuga."
That same sum of months, having placed the sum of months both above and below the heap— having multiplied by the yuga (fourfold) for the purpose of determining the intercalary month—
is divided by zero-fire-moon (130). Here, an intercalary month occurs every thirty-two and a half months of the sun, due to the absence of a solar transit on the new moon day.
By that [method], there would be no quotient; therefore, the heap is multiplied by four to become the quotient-heap.
When the quotient-heap has been multiplied by four, according to the principle that "in the absence of the cause, there is an absence of the effect," the heap to be divided becomes fourfold.
Therefore, the result obtained from dividing the heap by the quotient-heap is the fruit.

That which was obtained [from the previous calculation] has entered the top; that very same accumulated sum of intercalary months (māsapiṇḍa) has entered the heap of months at the head. O Lord of Men, this purified sum of months is for the purpose of calculating the thirty lunar days (tithis) in the current month.

Now, the monthly constant (māsadhruvaka) is stated: The months, situated in three places, are multiplied by ten and three (13); those which remain in the middle heap, the quotient obtained from dividing the root [heap] by six becomes a debt and must be subtracted from the middle heap.

The upper and lower [values] multiplied by thirty and divided by sixty reveal the mixed wealth; that which is obtained is entered at the head, and the remaining day-count is reduced by the best of sages. ||28||
"Months situated in three places, multiplied by hand and fire, are those which stand in the middle heap"— here,

having placed the pure months in three places, those months that stand in the middle heap are multiplied by "hand and fire," meaning they are multiplied by thirty-two, as it says in the root text: "the quotient obtained from division by six."

The quotient obtained by dividing the base heap (mūlarāśi) by six becomes a debt in the middle heap; therefore, it must be subtracted from the middle heap because it is a debt. Since "netratriṃśat" (thirty-two) indicates that this mixed wealth is placed above and below, this constant (dhruvaka) for Mars and the others has arrived as the calculation for setting (astamana). Hence, for the purpose of calculating the rising of the Sun and other planets, there is a credit of two signs added to the top heap.
In the lower heap, thirty ghaṭikās become positive;

therefore, they are mixed with the upper and lower [values] respectively as "two and thirty," i.e., two and thirty. That which is obtained by dividing by sixty is the result; that which is obtained by dividing the original heap of ghaṭikās by sixty becomes the total of the days of the week (vārapiṇḍa).

The remainder of the *ghaṭikā*-total becomes the [remaining] portion for the day (*vārabhoga*). That same amount entered at the top, when divided by sixty, yields the quotient which is added to the total of the days already at the top; this, when reduced by the seven excellent sages—that is, divided by seven—the remainder is the actual day itself. Thus, in the monthly calculation, the day should remain at the top, while the *ghaṭikā*-total is placed below the day.

The sum of the Sun and Moon in two places, increased by five and divided by sixty-seven, should be added to the topmost zodiacal sign; that [sum] is multiplied by the first hand (twenty) and divided by eight and two (ten), yielding the *piṇḍa*.

The middle of the three places is multiplied by eight, and the lower by nine; the quotient obtained from these divisions is increased by two. This is subtracted from the middle place, and further divided by six; however, it is added to the topmost sign after being doubled. || 29 ||
Now the words regarding the weekdays (*vārapada*) are stated: "The same monthly total, mixed with the sun and moon, [is] in two places.
That very monthly total is mixed with the sun and moon and further increased by one hundred and twelve.
The phrase "sun and moon" refers to the *karaṇa* system and not to the *siddhānta*; thus, it exists in two places.
The heap of months is divided by the sun (twelve) and the quotient is divided by one hundred and twenty-six; the result is added as a positive quantity to the top heap,
which is to be added to the top heap for the purpose of two piṇḍas per month.
When the first [period] has elapsed, everything mixed with the *bhūta* (five) should subsequently be given; this is the requirement for the calculation (*karaṇa*),
and the quotient obtained by dividing by the sun’s seasons (*ṛtu*) is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Since one *piṇḍa* becomes additional in the place of the *piṇḍas* after one hundred and twenty-six months due to the movement of the moon, it is said that the *piṇḍa* is divided by eight. Thus, the *piṇḍa* is divided by twenty-eight; because there are twenty-eight divisions for the seven-day week, the quotient obtained by that division constitutes the weekly position (*vārapada*) for each month.
The remainder obtained by dividing the *vāra-ghaṭikā* by six (*ṛtu*) becomes the constituent part of the *piṇḍa*; it should be placed beneath the *piṇḍa*.

Now, the calculation for the solar asterism (*sūrya-nakṣatra*) is stated: "The lords multiplied in the three places"—those purified months are [placed] in the three places: at the top, in the middle, and at the bottom.

Those months which are in the middle are multiplied by the lords (eleven); thus, "multiplied by eleven" refers to the *karaṇa* system, not the *siddhānta*. In the case of a [calculated] decrease (*kṣaya*), the quotient obtained by dividing the lower amount by nine times ten (ninety) is added to two;

that is, the quotient obtained by dividing the lower quantity by forty-nine (nine times five and one less than forty) is added to two—this is the additive (*kṣepaka*) according to the *karaṇa* system.
If [the time] is deficient, it is subtracted from the middle heap; "deficient" means it is a debt (*ṛṇa*). However, even when divided by *ghaṭīs*, it becomes a credit (*dhana*);
that is, the quotient obtained by dividing the middle heap by sixty *ghaṭīs* is added as a credit to the heap at the top, which is the stellar total (*nakṣatrapinda*).

The remaining *ghaṭikās* of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) are divided by sixty; that same [remainder] is the wealth at the top. Having doubled it in the zodiac sign (*rāśi*), it is joined with the *cakṣa* and becomes the divisor, O King. The remainder of the Sun is the enjoyment of the asterism (*ṛkṣa*) and so forth. To the day of the week (*vāra*), one day should be added. Two *ghaṭikās* multiplied by the number of men (sixteen) are in the heap; two below and eighteen *nāḍīs* manifest the wealth. This should be applied to the solar enjoyment; this shall be the fixed [correction] for the month. Furthermore, it is said that this should be applied month after month. (30)
And when divided by twenty-seven,
it becomes the invitation to the king;
the remainder is the sun's enjoyment of the asterism and so forth.
Here, at the top is the aggregate of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-piṇḍa*), and below is the aggregate of the lunar mansion minutes (*ghaṭikā*).
Furthermore, although it has been purified, this impure monthly reckoner (*māsa-dhāvaka*) has been composed for the sake of instructing beginners.
One day (*vāra*) should be added to the day; that is, one day should be added to the place of the days.

"Twice the royal ghaṭīs" means sixteen ghaṭīs (since "nṛpa" signifies sixteen); "twice the royal ghaṭīs" means thirty-two ghaṭīs to be placed in the position of ghaṭikās (where "dehā" refers to the body). "And two in the piṇḍaka below" means that two are to be given in the position of the piṇḍa beneath the ghaṭikās; and "two asterisms" means two in the position of the nakṣatras.

In the place of the *ghaṭikās* of the asterisms, "Rudra" means eleven *nāḍīs* are to be added; this makes it clear that [this] is wealth (positive). In the solar calculation (*sūryabhoga*), the asterism and so forth are to be applied as an addition.
Therefore, it should be a "monthly offering" (*māsaghṛvaka*); even though it has already been described, it is to be given month after month—that is, it is to be given in each individual month.
Thus, the Blessed One prophesied this very "monthly offering" even before it occurred, by virtue of his consideration of the causal conditions.

Now, the calculation by means of the month, lunar day (*tithi*), and so forth is stated: The lunar days (*tithis*) are to be added, subtracted, or added again to the *vāra*, *nāḍī*, and *pada* [of the weekday]; in the *piṇḍa* [total], the divisor is four and one hundred (401). When the result is even or odd, the values to be added or subtracted are as follows: in the case of zero, the value is zero; in the case of three and one hundred (301), it is two; in the case of five and two hundred (520), it is ten; in the case of two and one hundred (210), it is twenty minus one (19); in the case of five and two hundred (520), it is ten; and in the case of eleven and three hundred (311), it is three. [Note: This verse provides a table for calculating the *vāra-pada* based on the *tithi*. The specific values depend on the position of the *tithi* within the cycle of 60.]
"Dates are to be added and subtracted, and again added, in the places of the days, nāḍīs, and pādas.

Here, in the monthly constant (*dhruvaka*), starting from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) of the bright fortnight up to the thirtieth new moon (*amāvāsī*), the dates (*tithi*) are to be added and subtracted; "again added" means they are to be added in the place of the days (*vāra*) for the sake of the daily day-count. They are to be subtracted in the place of the *ghaṭikās* due to the loss of one *ghaṭī* per lunar digit (*kalā*); and they are to be added again in the place of the *piṇḍas* through the purification of the positive and negative movement of the lunar *pādas*.
Regarding the phrase "in the piṇḍa, in the division by four, the items (padārtha) are to be added or subtracted according to whether it is even or odd":
in the place of the piṇḍa, when there is an even division by fourteen (caturdaśa), the item is a credit (dhana); when there is an odd division, the item is a debit (ṛṇa).
Here, in the case of an even division, whether two have passed or four have passed, even if none have passed, it is considered even.
In the uneven division, one has gone and three have gone;
there is no further division beyond that. Above fifty-seven, twenty-seven aggregates together with thirty lunar days do not exist.
Therefore, since four [units] are divided by fourteen parts, it should be understood that objects (*padārtha*) are to be added or subtracted according to those even and odd divisions.

An "object" (*padārtha*) refers to the lunar-day positions (*candracārapada*); in fourteen places, above and below, they are distinguished by the sevenfold rotation of the qualities (*guṇa*) starting with earth, through both direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*viloma*) order.
And those objects are to be added or subtracted.
In zero, zero is pure;
if that which remains as the fourteenth part is zero, then the object itself is also zero—this is the principle that "it is neither to be added nor subtracted.
In the calculation, there are five in the place of the thirty-three (tridaśaśaśi).

When the remainder is seen in the thirteenth position, or in a single position, there are five *ghaṭikās* of either wealth or debt. Likewise, when the remainder is in two positions, or in the twelfth, ten *ghaṭikās* are to be given, according to the increase or decrease of the lunar digits (*candrakalā*). Thus, it is called "the name of the lunar day" (*tithyākhyam*), which is fifteen. In the eleventh, "in fire," that is, in the third, they occur.
In the fourth pada, when ten remain as the remainder of the division, twenty minus one—that is, nineteen—are seen;
in the fifth [pada], thirty-two; in the sixth, twenty-five; and in the seventh, twenty-five. In that [seventh], by the divisions of the sun, the solar [additions] are to be given;

in the odd and even [padas], the days are four, three, two, and one. In the eastern part of the aggregate, and likewise in the other, the portion is four and one; and these are to be added or subtracted according to whether the position is even or odd.

Twenty-two in the fifth interval, nine in the ninth, six in the eighth called *vasu*, and twenty-four *jinās* in the seventh step; when the remainder of the division is seen, twenty-five *ghaṭikās* are to be added if it is even, and subtracted if it is odd.

In that [calculation], by means of the divisions of the sun, the solar positions (*sūryapada*) are produced through the division of the sun during the lunar-day enjoyment (*tithibhoga*); when there is a debt for the sun, there is a debt in that [total], and when there is a credit for the sun, there is a credit in that very [total]—this is the "division of the sun.
Here, the lunar positions (*candrapada*) are five, four, three, two, one, zero, four, three, two, and one, in the eastern and western halves respectively.

"Bhūta" refers to five; "punarbhūta" refers to five below that; "iṣu" refers to five below that; "veda" refers to four below that; "śikhin" refers to three below that; "kara" refers to two below that; and "śaśin" refers to one position below that—thus there are seven positions for the words.
Then, in another seven positions in reverse order, starting from one, there are five words up to the fourteenth position.
Thus, the placement of the lunar positions occurs in fourteen locations by means of one and so forth (*ekādinā*). [In the manuscript Ka: *ekodina*; [in Ga: *ekadināt*.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the aggregate of the world-system (*lokadhātu-piṇḍa*), it is said: "When the years have reached an even or uneven state by dividing by four and one, the days of the week are to be added or subtracted."
In this case as well, when the remainder of fourteen parts is seen to be even, five and so forth are to be added to the days; if it is odd, they are to be subtracted.

When one-fourteenth remains, if one [digit] is seen, five *ghaṭikās* are to be taken; in the second [case], ten together with those situated in the second place; in the third, fifteen together with those situated in the third place; in the fourth, nineteen together with the four situated in the fourth place; in the fifth, twenty-two together with the three situated in the fifth place; in the sixth, twenty-four together with the two situated in the sixth place; and in the seventh, twenty-five together with the one situated in the seventh place. Thereafter, the increase of the lunar steps ceases.

When the eighth [digit] is seen, having first discarded eight places together with the seven preceding ones, the remaining six places—treated as a single unit—are to be added to or subtracted from twenty-four *ghaṭikās*.

In the ninth [place], there are twenty-two *ghaṭikās* for five places; in the tenth, nineteen for four places; in the eleventh, five for three places; in the twelfth, ten for two places; in the thirteenth, five for one place; and in the fourteenth, it is zero: such is the established conclusion of the Siddhānta.

The remainder [of the days] is struck by the seasons (six) and the sun (twelve); the quotient obtained therefrom is likewise added to that same place. The ghaṭīs of the Sun’s position are to be added according to the divisions of the sun (twelve).

That which is multiplied by the lunar days (fifteen) and made precise is indeed a positive value; it should be mixed with one-third of itself. The asterism of the seasons, together with three-quarters, is a negative value for the Sun; one should subtract this from the midst of the motion.

"By the movement of the breath (saccāra), the remainder [is found]; by the sun of seasons (ṛturavi), the quotient and likewise the remainder"—here, "movement of the breath" refers to the components of the aggregate situated below the aggregate; "by the sun of seasons" refers to those remaining after division by the quotient.
Thus, *saccāra*.

In the aggregate (piṇḍa), that which remains as a fourth part is the position of motion (cārapada); above that is the position of movement (sañcārapada). Therein, the hundredth part of the components of the aggregate becomes the position where the planet has entered;
therefore, that [remainder] is to be taken for the purpose of addition or subtraction.

By that same method, the remainder of the aggregate of *piṇḍa* parts is multiplied; then, the quotient obtained by dividing by one hundred and thirty-six should be added in the same manner as everything previously [stated], just like the aggregate of *ghaṭikās* for the preceding quarter.
In that very context, according to the specific divisions of the Sun, the *ravikās* are to be added or subtracted as before; such is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
Now, the daily solar motion is stated: "That which is multiplied by the Vedas and the lunar day is indeed positive; it is mixed with one-third.
This means that the result multiplied by the four Vedas and the lunar day becomes the precise positive value in the place of the *ghaṭikās* (minutes) for the sun.
That [result] multiplied by the lunar day, when mixed with one-third of the lunar day, is to be added as a positive value in the place of the *ghaṭikās*.

"However, one should subtract the asterism of the sun with three quarters [of a lunar mansion] from the middle of the degrees of the sun's revolution"—here, for the purpose of purifying the position of the sun, the sun's natal sign (*janmarāśi*) must be subtracted, by which the daily movement of the sun in terms of days, *ghaṭīs*, *pāṇīs* (minutes), *palas* (seconds), and so forth, is known; otherwise, there is no purification of the sun's position day by day. Therefore, from the movement of the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, six asterisms with three quarters—namely forty-five *ghaṭīs*—are subtracted, whereby the triad of signs beginning with Aries becomes purified.

When Cancer becomes the birth constellation (*janmarāśi*), it is due to the purification of the Sun’s degrees; therefore, one should subtract the constellation together with three quarters from the Sun. In the section on the calculation of luminaries (*jyotirjñānavidhi*), "consumption" (*bhukti*) refers to the duration of the enjoyment of a constellation and so forth. Within that consumption, one should subtract the constellation from the position of the constellation, and subtract the *ghaṭikās* from the position of the *ghaṭikās*.

The remaining work for the slow motion (*mandakārya*) is as follows: having multiplied the degrees by the elapsed time, one obtains *nāḍīs* through the divisor of sixty; the quotient obtained by dividing by eleven hundred and thirty-one, along with its remainder, is to be added to or subtracted from the Sun according to the direction of the solstitial motion (*ayanagati*), and not otherwise, for there is no correction in the Sun [without this]. The time values are six, six, eight, ten, eleven, eleven, eleven, eleven, eleven, ten, eleven, eleven, eleven, eleven, six, and eight.
"Purity occurs daily by virtue of the movement of the [solar] course and not otherwise; it is not by the method stated in the *Karaṇa*.

Here, the method stated in the *Karaṇa* is explained: "In the Sun, Time, and Taste" means that in Cancer, during the first fortnight, there is a debt of "Time," which is three *ghaṭikās*, and "Taste," which is six, during the second fortnight of Cancer.
Thus, in Leo, there are eight and ten; likewise, in Virgo, eleven Hara-s and again eleven Hara-s; then in Libra, eleven Rudra-s and ten (Dik); and thus in Scorpio, eight and six Naga-s. ||34||

At the end of the northern and southern solstices, there is fire and space [respectively], and there is wealth and debt in the north and south; the sun moves for six months through the divisions of the fortnights according to the distinctions of the monthly transits.

O King, having given the lunar days to the sun and multiplied them by six, mixed with the portion of the weekday, and then diminished, they become the moon; this is the conjunction of the mixed sun and moon.

Text: Following the Tibetan reading of the root text, "wealth-debt" (*dhanamṛṇam*) is established. In the *Vimalaprabhā* [Lokadhātu-paṭala], it says: "Then, in Sagittarius (*dhanuṣi*), there is fire—thus three; 'space' (*kham*) means emptiness at the end of the solar transit (*ayana*).
Thus, in Capricorn and so forth, it is "wealth" (*dhanam*) in the context of the *Karaṇa* system, but this is not the intention in the *Siddhānta*.
Everywhere it is thus: the sun moves for six months through the divisions of the fortnights, according to the divisions of the monthly transits (*māsa-saṃkrānti*).

Now the lunar course (*candrabhoga*) is described: "Having added to the sun" means having added the lunar days (*tithi*) to the solar portion. The lunar days multiplied by six (the "lower flavors") are divided by six;
mixed with the solar course—that is, mixed with the minutes and so forth of the solar course—they become diminished. In the place of the minutes, the lunar course occurs;
this is called the "mixed conjunction of sun and moon," meaning the combined course of the sun and moon becomes the conjunction.

[55b] The elapsed lunar days multiplied by twenty-three, with the number of elapsed months subtracted, and the remainder divided by seven; the pure years mixed with eight, multiplied by four hundred, and from which eight is subtracted, divided by three hundred and seventy; [the result] multiplied by zero and six, and divided by thirty-two, gives the weekday and *nāḍīs* and so forth. This constant is added here for the month of the solar ingress (*saṃkrānti*) of the year.

"Multiplied by two, the elapsed lunar days minus one, and divided by seven"—this means that when the elapsed lunar days are multiplied by two (akṣṇā), reduced by one, and the remainder is taken after division by seven, that is the *karaṇa*. The usage [of the other factors] occurs through the passage of the days of the week (*vāra*).
Here, the five components (*pañcāṅga*) are: the day of the week (*vāra*), the lunar day (*tithi*), the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the conjunction (*yoga*), and the *karaṇa*.

Herein, the days of the week (*vāra*) are seven: Āditya (Sunday), Soma (Monday), Maṅgala (Tuesday), Budha (Wednesday), Bṛhaspati (Thursday), Śukra (Friday), and Śani (Saturday). The lunar days (*tithi*) are fifteen, beginning with the first (*pratipad*). The lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) are twenty-seven: Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśirā, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Aśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphālgunī, Uttaraphālgunī, Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā, and Revatī.

Likewise, the *yogas* are twenty-seven: Viṣkambha, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Atigaṇḍa, Sukarmā, Dhṛti, Śūla, Gaṇḍa, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Śaṅku, Vyāghāta, Harṣaṇa, Vajra, Siddhi, Vyatipāta, Varīyān, Parigha, Śiva, Sādhya, Śubha, Śukla, Brahmā, Aindra, and Vaidhṛti. These are the twenty-seven *yogas*.

In the second half of the first day of the bright fortnight, the first *karaṇa* is *vava*; on the second day, in the first and second halves, they are *vālava* and *kaulava*; on the third day, in the first and second halves, they are *taitila* and *garaja*; on the fourth day, in the first and second halves, they are *vaṇija* and *viṣṭi*. Likewise, on the fifth day, they are *vava* and *vālava*; on the sixth day, *kaulava* and *taitila*; on the seventh day, *garaja* and *vaṇija*; and on the eighth day, in the first half, it is *viṣṭi*.

On the eighth day, in the latter half [of the lunar month], it is *vava*; on the ninth day, in the first and second halves, it is *vālava* and *kaulava*; on the tenth day, *taitila* and *garaja*; on the eleventh day, in the first and second halves, it is *vaṇija* and *viṣṭi*. [Note: Beyond this point, the manuscript "ṅa" was not obtained. On the twelfth day, in the first and second halves, it is *vava* and *vālava*; on the thirteenth day, *kaulava* and *taitila*; on the fourteenth day, *garaja* and *vaṇija*; on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), in the first half it is *viṣṭi*, and in the second half it is *vava*.

On the first lunar day of the dark fortnight, in the first and second halves respectively, there are *vālava* and *kaulava*; on the second lunar day, in the first and second halves, there are *tailija* (or *tila*) and *garaja*; and on the third lunar day, in the first and second halves, there are *vaṇija* and *vṛṣṭi*.

Thus, on the fourth [tithi], in the first and second halves, there are Vava and Vālava; on the fifth, in the first and second halves, Kaulava and Taitila; on the sixth, Garaja and Vaṇija; on the seventh, Viṣṭi in the first half and Vava in the second half; on the eighth, in the first and second halves, Vālava and Kaulava; on the ninth, Taitila and Garaja; and on the tenth, in the first and second halves, Vaṇija and Viṣṭi.

Thus, on the eleventh day, [in the first and second halves respectively] there are *vava* and *vālava*; on the twelfth day, *kaulava* and *taitila*; on the thirteenth day, *garaja* and *vaṇija*; and on the fourteenth day, in the first half, *viṣṭi*. This is the sequence of the seven *karaṇas*. Then, on the second half of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, there is *śakuni*; on the first half of the new moon day, *catuṣpada*; and in the second half, *nāga*.
On the first day of the bright fortnight, the first half is Kiṃstughna, while the latter half is Vava;
thus there are eleven Karaṇas—this is the sequence of the five-fold calendar (pañcāṅga).
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and one quarter of Kṛttikā constitute Aries (Meṣa).
In this manner, the twelve zodiac signs beginning with Aries are to be understood through nine new quarters each.
Mars, Venus, Mercury, Moon, Sun, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—these are the respective owners (*kṣetrin*) of the signs starting from Aries.

Now, for the purpose of determining the *rāśis* (zodiac signs) of the non-Buddhist sectarians (*tīrthikas*), the system of assigning syllables to names is explained. Here, because the sages did not fully understand the vowels and consonants of the mandala, they devised this system of assigning syllables to names. It is as follows: *a, i, u, e* correspond to Kṛttikā; *o, vā, vi (vī), va (vū)* to Rohiṇī; *ve, vo, kā, kī* to Mṛgaśirā; *ku (kū), gha, ṅa, cha* to Ārdrā; *ke, ko, hā, hī* to Punarvasu; *hu (hū), he, ho, ḍā* to Puṣya; *ḍi (ḍī), ḍu (ḍḍū), ḍe, ḍo* to Aśleṣā; *ma (m), mi (mī), mu (mū), me* to Maghā; *mo, ṭā, ṭi (ṭī), ṭu (ṭū)* to Pūrvaphālgunī; *ṭe, ṭo, pā, pī* to Uttaraphālgunī; *pu, ṣa, ṇa, ṭha* to Hastā; *pe, por, ari* to Citrā; *rū, re, ro* to Svāti; *ti, tu, te, to* to Viśākhā; *nā, ni, anu* to Anurādhā; *no, yā, yi, yu* to Jyeṣṭhā; *ye, yo, bhā, bhi* to Mūlā; *nu, ne, bhū, dha, pha* to Pūrvāṣāḍhā; in its latter half is Taitila; and in its former half is Kaulava.
In the manuscript, the portion "pūrvāparārddha taitilaṃ garajam" is an addition to the first half; the phrase "pūrvāparārddhe" does not exist in the manuscript,
and here "pūrvāparārddha" has been supplied.
In this manuscript, the term "pūrvāparārddhe" has been applied; that is, the first half [of the lunar day] is assigned to the Vaṇija yoga, and the second half to the Viṣṭi yoga.
In this manuscript, "pūrvāparāddha" has been applied.

Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and one quarter of Kṛttikā constitute the zodiac sign of Aries (*meṣarāśi*). Furthermore, the twelve distinct letters representing the names of the zodiac signs are as follows: *tu, rkān pa gcig* (Vimalaprabhā, Lokadhātu section);

*pūrvāṣāḍhā*, *bhe, bho, jā, ji* (Uttarāṣāḍhā), *ju, je, jo, khā* (Śravaṇā), *khi, khu, khe, kho* (Abhijit), *ga, gi, gu, ge* (Dhaniṣṭhā), *go, sā, si, su* (Śatabhiṣā), *se, so, dā, dī* (Pūrvabhādrapadā), *du, tha, jha, ña* (Uttarabhādrapadā), *de, do, cā, cī* (Revatī), *cu, ce, co, lā* (Aśvinī), *li, lū, le, lo* (Bharaṇī). These are the letters for the twelve zodiac signs.

The intention of the non-Buddhist outsiders—that the multitude of sentient beings is to be known by these syllables, and that through them the results of the auspicious and inauspicious are to be known—is devoid of logic.

In the ultimate sense, the auspicious and inauspicious arise solely through the power of one's own karma. As it has been said: "The day of the week, the lunar date, the asterism, the conjunction, the lunar mansion, and the ascendant—even when these are occupied by malevolent planets—these bring auspiciousness to those who perform meritorious deeds."
For those born at the same moment, the fruits are distinct and not one and the same, due to the experience of their respective individual karmas—
such as in battle, forest fires, or being caught in a fisherman’s net.
Many embodied beings die simultaneously;
through merit come longevity, strength, vigor, supernatural power, and beauty,
while through demerit there is the loss of longevity, vigor, and power— this is the summary of the fivefold effects.

Now, the calculation for the solar transits (saṃkrānti) according to the Karaṇa system is stated: "The years of embodied beings, mixed with the serpents"—thus, the "pure years" (śuddhābda) are the years of the Karaṇa; "mixed with the serpents" means mixed with eight.

"Multiplied by four hundred minus the oceans" means they are multiplied by four hundred. "Subtracted by those mixed with Nāgas" means subtracted—that is, diminished—by the years of the *karaṇa* system mixed with eight [i.e., increased by eight].
"Divided by mountain-moon-fire" means divided by three hundred seventeen; the resulting values are the days of the week (*vāra*).
"Struck by the taste of space" means that the remainder of the division is multiplied by sixty for the sake of *nāḍikās* (ghaṭikās);

[this total] is divided by twenty-seven, resulting in the addition of two to the weekday and thirty to the *nāḍikā* place. This is the constant (*dhruvaka*) here to be added for the purpose of the *karaṇas* beginning with Ārdrā; specifically, two are to be added to the weekday position and thirty to the *ghaṭikā* position. The quotient obtained by dividing by sixty becomes the weekday, and the remainder is the *ghaṭikās* of the weekday. The remainder from the division by seven is the weekday in the solar month of the year at the time of the *saṃkrānti*; such is the rule.
According to the currently prevalent modern astrology: "Jū Je Jo Khā Abhijit Khī Khū Khe Kho Śravaṇa.
