Regarding the matter of *abhijit* here—the final fifteen *ghaṭikās* of the *nakṣatra* Uttarāṣāḍhā, together with the initial four *ghaṭikās* of the *nakṣatra* Śravaṇa; thus, nineteen *ghaṭikās* constitute the measure of the *abhijit* *nakṣatra*.

The nakṣatra Abhijit has the mongoose (nakula) as its source, belongs to the human class, is associated with others, and consists of the final nāḍī; furthermore, because it falls within the zodiacal signs of Dhanus and Makara, it is [also] Bhadrapadā.
In that manuscript, in many places, instead of "Bhādrapadā," there is merely "bhadra" as well as the weekday and lunar day.
In that place, the manuscript was damaged by insects and other such causes.
Regarding the "parts" (bhāgāḥ),
according to the Tibetan tradition, the reading "bhaktā ghaṭikā" is correct; here, the bracketed term *nāḍikā* can more appropriately be rendered as *ghaṭikā*,
[referring to] the fixed values (*dhruvaka*) beginning with Mars and so forth.

In the manuscript, *ga* and *gha* are not present; *abhici* is found in the chapter [on] the Great Chapter on the Method for Knowing the Luminaries (*jyotirjñānavidhimahoddeśa*). Now, the constants (*dhruvaka*) for the twelve-year cycle used as additive values (*kṣepaka*) during the ingress (*saṃkrānti*) of Aries and the other signs are stated: "In the additive values for the days and *nāḍīs* starting from Aries, these twelve are arranged in sequence: moon (1), mountain (7), earth (1), fire (3), qualities (3), arrows (5), moon (1); mountain (7), moon (1) in the third."
The Vedas, fires, the moon, and two eyes; the Vedas and eyes in the sixth; six in the [sixth] day; the moon, arrows, mountains, pairs, and fires; six, the moon, Vedas, mountains, and worlds. || 37 ||
"In the *vāranāḍī* of Aries and the others" means in the place of the weekday (*vāra*) or the place of the *ghaṭikā* (time-unit);
these twelve, arranged in sequence for addition, are "moon-mountain-earth" (*candrādrībhūta*).
"Candra" means one in the place of the weekday (*vāra*); "become mountains" (*adribhūta*) means fifty-seven in the place of *ghaṭikās*.

Here, whichever weekday occurs together with the fixed year (*varṣadhruvaka*) in the place of the weekday, by that weekday the Aries (*meṣa*) transit occurs; and by those *ghaṭikās* which are in the place of *ghaṭikās*, such is the rule of the *karaṇa*.
"Vedāḥ" is in the dual number due to Vedic usage.
Veda (4) in the place of days; guṇa-śara (53) in the place of ghaṭīs for the Taurus transit; śaśin (1) in the place of days;
and śaila-candra (17) in the place of ghaṭīs.
"Third" refers to the Gemini transit; "Veda" means four in the place of the weekday;
"Agnibhūta" means fifty-three in the place of the *ghaṭikās* during the Cancer transit;
and "Candra" means one in the place of the weekday.
"Nayanakara" (eye-maker) refers to twenty-two in the place of *ghaṭikās* during Leo (*siṃhasaṃkrānti*);
"yuga" (age) refers to four in the place of days;
and "vedanetrāṇi" (Vedas-eyes) refers to twenty-four in the place of *ghaṭikās*.
"In the sixth" refers to the transition [of the sun] into Virgo (kanyā-saṃkrānti);
"six days" means sixty; "moon and arrows" means fifty-one in the place of ghaṭikās; and at the transition into Libra (tulā-saṃkrānti), "the moon" means one day.
In the case of the *giri-yuga* [yoga], there are forty-seven at the place of the *ghaṭikās* during the *saṃkrānti* of Scorpio;
"flame" (*śikhī*) means three at the place of the weekday;
and "moon" (*candra*) means sixteen *ghaṭikās* at the place of the *ghaṭikās* during the *saṃkrānti* of Sagittarius.

In the place of the *vāra* (day of the week), there are four; in the place of the *adri-loka* (mountain-worlds), thirty-seven; and in the place of the *ghaṭikā* (hours), six for the Makara-saṃkrānti. For the Sun in the sign of Pisces (*mīna-rāśi*), there are two Vedas and zero-zero, and the value of the term "eye-arrow" (*nayana-śara*). Through the movements of the Sun, there occurs a decrease and increase of day and night over the course of six months.

The [units] smeared by the ocean (4), breaths (2), and fire (3) increase or decrease at every daily interval according to the parts of the solstice (ayanāṅga); there is an increase of night on the left, and of day and night on the right during the day.
In the place of the days, "Veda" (4) and "zero" (0); thus, there are four units in the place of the ghaṭikās. In the Aquarius transit (kumbhasaṃkrānti), "zero" (0) is placed;
therefore, nothing is to be added in the place of the days.

"Nayanaśara" (52) is the term to be placed in the position of the ghaṭikās for the Sun in the sign of Capricorn (*monarāśi*); thus, this transit-consumption (*saṃkrāntibhoga*) is to be known from the *Karaṇa*, whereas in the *Siddhānta* this transit-consumption does not occur. Because [the correction] multiplied by the lunar days (*tithi*) and divided by four is added as a positive value, and mixed with one-third [of that]—by this, the absence of ghaṭikās within the month is established even through detailed exposition, as seen in the meter of the root text: "In the middle of the three places, multiplied by eleven," and "the two Vedas."
Thus,
by this method of restoring what was lost, the solar longitude becomes accurate;
for one year, the daily motion— without the addition of the daily solar disc-motion— remains pure.

Furthermore, at the end of another year, there is a constant term for the next transit (*aparasaṃkrāntidhruvaka*); by means of that, the solar motion (*sūryabhoga*) is purified for each individual year from the month of Caitra until the following Caitra. Therefore, with respect to the subsequent year, one month’s constant term is purified in the calculation (*karaṇa*). Consequently, the daily solar motion becomes impure; every day, by an interval of three breaths, four *pāṇis*, and [four] *palas*, five days become deficient due to the force of the motion, from one northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*) until the next northern transit.

In each month, twenty-five *ghaṭikās* are deficient from the time of one *karaṇa-saṃkrānti* to the next; conversely, in each month, there is an excess of twenty-five *ghaṭikās* up to the end of the year, resulting in an excess of five weekdays. How is this deficiency or excess known? An examination must be performed for ten days at the beginning of the months of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) by means of the shadow of the *saṃku*.
From whichever day the shadow begins to turn back toward the north, that is the day of the sun’s *saṃkrānti* (equinox), with its specific weekday, lunar date (*tithi*), yoga, and *karana*.
On that day, the solar position is twenty in the place of the asterism (*nakṣatra*) and fifteen in the place of the *ghatikās*; this is the fundamental constant (*mūla-dhruvaka*).

In that fixed point (*dhruvaka*), one should add the solar orb obtained per day, and then subtract the solar signs (*ravi-pada*) according to the previously mentioned method; where the solar orbs, days, *ghaṭikās*, *pāṇīpala*s, and the consumption of the breaths and the circle of zodiacal signs are stated in the Root Tantra (*mūla-tantra*). It is as follows: the single year multiplied by zero and three (300) is placed in two positions; the lower one is doubled and multiplied by sixty-five; the quotient is added as a credit to the upper sign (*rāśi*);
the remainder is again multiplied by sixty, and the quotient obtained from that division is placed below it.

Furthermore, O Lord of Men, the remainder [obtained] by dividing [the total] by sixty should again be multiplied by six; the remainder from that, divided by sixty-five, should be placed below that [previous quotient] as the aggregate of breaths (*śvāsapiṇḍa*). Having thus converted days, ghaṭīs, and liptās into breaths, one should again divide [the total] threefold.
One should subtract the mountain-portion (seven) from the lower heap and add it as wealth to the middle heap;
then, having divided by sixty, one should subtract the quotient as a debt from the upper heap;
the remainder here are the days, while the [quotient] are the ghaṭīs, pāṇīs, and palas.
The solar mandala becomes one day through the consumption of the zodiacal signs by the horse-like breath; since that [day] consists of sixty nāḍīs,
it is then [calculated] by the solar mandala's consumption of three hundred and sixty-five [nāḍīs].
Thus,
the nāḍīs obtained by means of the movement of the solar orb per day are further multiplied by sixty to become liptās; when divided by six, they become breaths (śvāsa).
One should apply this correction (bhoga) to the solar asterisms, nāḍīs, and so forth; it should be added daily from the commencement of the solstice until the next solstice occurs.
The Great Chapter on the Method for Knowing the Luminaries: The position of the sun must be purified according to the prescribed rules of calculation;
otherwise, by way of the *karaṇa* system, there is never any purity for the sun.
When this solar longitude is impure, Mars and the other planets, though corrected, do not become true; they are like trees whose roots have perished.
I shall describe the orb of the moon according to its enjoyment of the zodiacal signs;
the channels of the [solar] wheel, along with half a channel, are combined with the monthly enjoyment.

The portion of the moon traversed each day shall be obtained by dividing [the total] by thirty; it consists of minutes and the minutes of the circle of time (nāḍīcakra) through which the moon moves during those days.
That maṇḍala of his consists of ghaṭīs, pāṇīs, palas, and breaths;
the maṇḍala of Rāhu consists of nine hundred and six thousand days.

The well-known mandala of the planets beginning with the auspicious [Sun] is divided by its own respective weekday; when multiplied by one day and divided by the [total] mandala, [the result is the daily portion].
The resulting asterism is obtained; the remainder, multiplied again by sixty, yields the nāḍīs through division by the number of asterisms in a revolution, and likewise the liptās.
O King, by means of the portion of the mandala of the breaths, one should calculate the daily [motion] of the planets;
having made that very [value] the additive, one should correct the planet by means of the planetary movements.

When the planetary longitude is impure, then the lunar digit (kalā) at the time of moonrise is to be known by means of the moon's motion, specifically for that [planet] situated on the line of the solstice (ayanarekhā).
One should subtract the sun from the [longitude of] the node; one should subtract the moon from the sun.
When the result is one unit of arc (kalā), Mars and the other planets should be subtracted from the moon in their respective motions.
Through the entry of Rāhu into the lunar day (tithi), when there is a break in the parvan at every dark and light fortnight, between both lunar days occurs the *vimardana* of the moon and the sun.
"Having thus fully understood everything, one should avoid impurity arising from the Siddhānta’s view of enjoyment and from the calculation of the *laghukaraṇa* and so forth."
Thus,

according to the sequence stated above, the definition of the established tenets (*siddhānta*) as taught in the *Paramādibuddha-tantrarāja* has been clearly elucidated by the *Laghutantrarāja* through the statement, "the destruction of the established tenets.
For what reason is this so?

In this regard, when the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthikas) see the *Laghutantrarāja* and observe the purification of the solar movement (*sūryabhoga*), they will write it into their own systems, thinking, "The purification of the solar movement exists in our system as well. For this reason, it has not been fully elucidated here with reference to the commentary.
Now, the decrease and increase of day and night are stated: for six months there are two, namely decrease and increase, respectively. Decrease and increase occur accordingly.

Regarding day and night—of both the day and the night—by means of the movements of the sun, namely its northern course (*uttaracāra*) and southern course (*dakṣiṇacāra*): "by the movements of the sun" refers to the *nāḍīs*, *prāṇas*, *agnis*, and *liptās*. At every daily moment, there is an increase or decrease of four breaths (*śvāsa*s) and three *pāṇīpala*s per solar division (*ayanāṅga*). This measurement applies up to the Himavat mountains from the northern part of Kailāśa. A solar division (*ayanāṅga*) consists of one hundred and eighty-two and a half days; by those days, the solar division is completed. In the right [southern] course, the increase occurs at night, while in the north, it occurs during the day.

To the south of Kailāśa, as will be explained here regarding the measurement to be stated: on the day of the southern solstice transit (*dakṣiṇāyana-saṃkrānti*), the day consists of thirty-six *ghaṭikās* and the night consists of twenty-four;
thus, during the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), the duration of night and day is to be understood by reversing [the order].

Now the movement of Rāhu through the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) is described: The months, mixed with [the sum of] the eyes (2) and the suns (12), multiplied by two (2), and mixed with one [for the] moon’s parvan (synodic month), are divided by sixty-four (64). Multiplied by seventy (70), they are the asterism [obtained] by the portion of zero and so forth (0, 1, 2, etc.). The remainder, multiplied by sixty, are the ghaṭikās; those again, multiplied by sixty, are the liptās. The quotient is the wheel (cakra); it is not the mouth (vaktra) of the eclipsing planet (taminaḥ), but rather the tail-asterism (puccha-ṛkṣa) mixed with half [of the wheel].
"Months" means months; "karaṇa-months" means [months] mixed with two and twelve;
this refers to the *karaṇas* and not to the *siddhānta*.
"Netrārka" means one hundred and twenty-two; "mixed with" means multiplied by two for the purpose of the heap of fortnights. Thus, they are doubled.

The single month mixed with the lunar festival (parvan) is for the purpose of the full-moon phase; the month mixed with both fortnights is for the purpose of the new-moon phase. This occurs within the heap of fortnights according to the rule "divided by zero, ocean, and earth" (400). This division by the circle of fortnights—namely, four hundred and sixty fortnights—is for the purpose of determining Rāhu’s fortnightly course.

The remaining fortnights, divided by that ocean [four], become multiplied by the qualities of the Sage [seven] for the purpose of calculating the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) enjoyment; by means of the division by "sky and so forth" (*khādi*),
that is, by the division of four hundred and sixty [days], the resulting asterism (*ṛkṣa*) is obtained.
Furthermore, whatever remains as the remainder, when multiplied by sixty and divided by that same divisor, the result is *ghaṭikās*.
Likewise, when multiplied by sixty and divided by that same divisor, the result is *liptās*; and when multiplied by six and divided by that same divisor, the result is *śvāsas*.
The wheel is obtained;

that which is the "mouth" (*vaktra*) here is subtracted from the wheel consisting of twenty-seven constellations by the portion obtained through division by four (*kharvva-abdhinā*). When the wheel is thus diminished, it becomes the mouth.
The mouth occurs in the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) of Aśvinī and so forth for *tamī*; *tamī* is one who possesses darkness (*tamas*), and thus [he] is *tamī*. For him, [it is] *taminaḥ*.

"Mixed with half a constellation" means mixed with thirteen and a half constellations (*ṛkṣārddha*); [the phrase] "the tail in the enjoyment of the mouth" means that there is the enjoyment of the tail (*pucchabhoga*).
(Ga. "Twenty-four" means it becomes night and day; (Gha. by twenty-four, there is an increase of the night.
In the manuscripts designated as ka, kha, and gha, the word "bhāga" does not appear in the hundreds [of verses].

[In the chapter on Aśvinī: This is the Great Chapter on the Method for Knowing the Luminaries. The months multiplied by thirty are placed in three positions and mixed; [the middle value] is mixed with mountains (7) and [the first] with fire (3). Added to each day and divided by mountain-space-arrows (507), the remainder is further reduced by the quotient obtained from dividing by ocean-tastes (64). This is the uncorrected day-count; when divided by mountain-nāgas-seasons (687), the remainder is multiplied by eyes (2) and again by taste (6); these are the nāḍīs beginning with mountains (7).

40. Now, for the purpose of calculating the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) occupied by the planets beginning with Maṅgala, the accumulated days (*ahargaṇa*) are stated: "The months" refers to the *karaṇa* months; multiplied by thirty, they become the heap of days.
Those days, together with the current month's daily increment, become [the total].
The remainder from the three places is multiplied by the celestial bodies (nine) and divided by seven hundred and seven; the quotient obtained is added to the middle quantity.
Then, the middle quantity is also diminished by the quotient obtained from dividing it by sixty-four (the oceans and tastes); this is the non-corrected day.

In some cases, for the sake of clarity, one weekday is subtracted from the daily count; thus, the true *ahargaṇa* (day-count) is obtained. Now, regarding Mars (*maṅgala*), it is said: "mixed with *śaila*, *vaka*, and *ruci*"—this refers to the *Karaṇa* system and not the *Siddhānta*. "Mixed with one hundred and sixty-seven" means mixed with *śaila*, *vaka*, and *ruci*;
thus, the true day-count is divided by *śaila*, *nāga*, and *ṛtu*.

That number of days is divided by six hundred and eighty-seven—the revolutions of Mars—and thus the revolution of Mars is known. The remainder is multiplied by sixty (the *cakras*), then divided by twenty-seven; the result is the asterism (*nakṣatra*).

It is further multiplied by sixty (the *kharasas*) and divided by the same [six hundred and eighty-seven]—mountains, oceans, and seasons—to obtain the *nāḍīs* (degrees) obtained through the motion of Mars.
"By the previously mentioned method, [one calculates] the *pāṇīpala* and so forth.

Here, there are five types of places for the experience (*bhoga*) of all the planets: the place of the zodiac sign (*rāśisthāna*), the place of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatrasthāna*), the place of the *ghaṭikā*, the place of the *pāṇīpala*, and the place of the breath (*śvāsasthāna*). These are arranged one below the other. In the places of the breaths, the breaths do not remain above; those obtained by a division of six enter into the *pāṇīpala*s. The *pāṇīpala*s do not remain when divided by sixty; those obtained by a division of sixty enter into the *ghaṭikā*s, which then enter into the zodiac sign.

In this manner, even a single *ghaṭikā* enters into the asterism and the zodiacal sign (*rāśi*). The asterisms remain for thirteen and a half [periods] within the two types of karma, while six signs remain; such is the established rule (*niyama*). Now, the purification of Mars (*maṅgalaśuddhi*) is stated: If there is a debt (*ṛṇa*) exceeding nine and a half [units] in the weekday (*āra*), it is to be subtracted when mixed with the cycle (*cakra*); if it exceeds half the cycle, that half-cycle is to be discarded. Furthermore, the remainder after discarding [the cycle] shall be in reverse order (*utkrama*).

When the asterism is multiplied by sixty and increased by the [elapsed] yogas, it is divided by eighteen hundred; the quotient obtained is added or subtracted, respectively in reverse and direct order, even in the slow-motion calculation.

Regarding the phrase "nine and a half [nakṣatras] are to be subtracted from Āra," here, when the Moon’s enjoyment of the asterism and so forth has been separated out, it occurs that for one such enjoyment on Āra,
nine asterisms and a half— meaning thirty ghaṭīs— are to be subtracted; thus, [the value] thirty is placed in the position of the ghaṭīs.
In the place of *śailanāgartya*, [the reading] *ka* has *sthāneṣa*; *kha* has *sthāne ṣaḍupari*;
and *gha* has *bhavanti*.
Ka. Trayodaśārddhana ka. gha.
Thus, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, [the purification of the world-system is for the sake of taking birth and conduct].
Regarding the statement "if the debt is greater in the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) enjoyment beginning with Aśvinī, it should be subtracted from the mixed circle":

here, in the lunar mansion enjoyment beginning with Aśvinī, the debt must necessarily be subtracted; if the debt is greater—that is, if the quantity of the debt is larger than the quantity of the enjoyment—then it should be subtracted from the mixed circle. The "circle" refers to the aggregate of twenty-seven lunar mansions; the meaning is that the debt should be subtracted from what is mixed with that circle, i.e., it should be discarded from the circle.

In this case, if the remainder after subtraction is half [of the circle] or more, then it should be discarded; even if it exceeds half, that remainder which is greater than half becomes the inverse (utkrama) of the discarded remainder. In the calculation of the slow motion (mandakārya), by means of the inverse, there is a positive value for all planets, whereas in the direct order (krama) there is a negative value. When the asterism (ṛkṣa) is multiplied by sixty, whatever results are the ghaṭikās for the purpose of the total of ghaṭikās.
When the *ṛkṣa*-piṇḍa is multiplied by sixty, the lower *ghaṭikā*-piṇḍa becomes the "head" (*mūrdhan*).
Divided by 135 for the sake of determining the zodiacal signs and quarters, the quotient obtained from dividing the *ghaṭikā* total by 135 constitutes the zodiacal sign and quarter.

Furthermore, in the case of slow-moving planets (*mandakarma*), wealth and debt should be understood respectively according to the reverse and direct order. Herein are the *pada*s for the movement through the zodiac signs: twenty-five *tattva*s in the first sign from birth, eighteen in the second, and seven (the "mountains") in the third; these are the *pada*s for the first three signs in the forward order. In the half-circle (*ardhacakra*), one should multiply the visible *rasa*-padas by the elapsed portion above and below, and divide the result by fifty-nine; the quotient is subtracted from the circle, and the resulting *tattva*s are [calculated] from the first sign of birth. In the first sign, there are twenty-five; in the second, eighteen; and in the third, "mountains" means seven. These are the *pada*s for the first triad of signs.

Then, in the enemy-circle (paracakra), there are seven in the fourth zodiac sign (rāśi), eighteen in the fifth, and twenty-five in the sixth; thus, one should multiply the "manifest juice-steps" (prakaṭarasapada) by the nadīs according to their position above or below in the half-circle. The zodiacal heap of ghaṭikās, divided by one hundred and thirty-five, results in the zodiacal movement (rāśibhoga);
that itself is the step within the six steps. Then comes the second; "movement" (bhoga) means that which is experienced; by that remaining movement, one should multiply the remaining nadīs.
The quotient obtained by dividing [the elapsed time] by the moon's [mean] motion in *nāḍīs* (multiplied by the number of lunar months) is taken from the [total] wheel;

this is multiplied by the *nāḍī*-motion and divided by one hundred and thirty-five. The resulting quotient is to be added in the first half [of the orbit], according to the position of the *pada*, as long as the planet has not yet reached the second half; thereafter, it is indeed to be subtracted in the second half.

That very portion is to be subtracted in the latter half (aparārddha), having made the elapsed [portion] into a single aggregate (ekapiṇḍa). That which has been traversed by the planets according to the sign (rāśi) is placed as a single aggregate in the former half; in the latter half, having made the untraversed portion into a single aggregate and having discarded the elapsed [portion] of both the former and latter halves, there is addition or subtraction in the nāḍīs according to the movement of the planets.

The movement of the planets is both retrograde (*utkrama*) and direct (*krama*). According to that [movement], there is addition or subtraction: by virtue of retrogression there is addition, and by virtue of progression there is subtraction from the *nāḍī*; this is the rule regarding the zodiacal sign of the *ghaṭikā*, namely, [the calculation] by means of the planet's longitude within the sign of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). In all cases of slow motion (*mandakarma*), such as that of Mars and the others, this is the procedure for the operation of the signs (*rāśikarmavidhi*). [Note: *janmacaraṇaśuddhi* refers to the purification of the birth-foot;
*cakram* is the circle. [Variant readings: *ekapiṇḍam* in manuscripts Ga and Gha.]

In this chapter, the great section on the procedure for the knowledge of astrology, the rule for the swift calculation (*śīghrakarma*) is now stated: In the swift calculation, Mars is to be subtracted from the Sun, and Jupiter as well as Saturn; likewise, Mercury and Venus [are subtracted] from the Sun. Indeed, in the swift operation, the Sun becomes the positive quantity; [the others] are to be subtracted in sequence. The remainder here is the movement (*cāra*); having multiplied it by the remaining *nāḍīs* and divided by sixty, the quotient is the step of the planet’s movement (*grahacaraṇapada*), which is to be added or subtracted in the same manner. Thus, in the swift calculation, Mars is to be subtracted from the Sun, and Jupiter as well as Saturn likewise.
Immediately thereafter,
the portion of the planets purified by the [previously calculated] heap is to be subtracted from the solar longitude,

according to the rule "Mars is to be subtracted from the Sun. When the slow [mean] motion is devoid of the solar correction, having set the planetary motion apart, then likewise Jupiter is also to be subtracted, and Saturn— the son of the Sun— is also to be subtracted, just as Mars is indicated by the word "also" (*api*).
Where? In swift motion;

likewise, in gentle [motion], when there is a gentle aspect, the Sun is to be subtracted for the sake of Mercury’s aspect, and Venus is also to be subtracted from the Sun for the sake of Venus’s aspect.
Herein lies the rule: a planet at its exaltation is to be subtracted by a planet at its depression.
Therefore, in the case of Mercury and Venus, the Sun must indeed be subtracted;
in the case of the swifter planet, wealth [the result] occurs in sequence during the process of swift calculation (*śīghrakarma*).
Here, in the operation of swift calculation, wealth arises in due order.
The word "khalu" indicates certainty:

in the sequence described, there is a debt; when half a circle has been subtracted, the remaining asterism—purified by the transit of the exalted planet—is the movement of the planets through the asterisms (*nakṣatracaraṇa*) according to their daily transit.

That very unit of planetary motion (*grahacaraṇapada*), consisting of many *ghaṭikās*, is multiplied by those *ghaṭikās* of the planetary motion-unit; the result obtained by dividing by sixty is to be added to or subtracted from the planetary motion-unit in the same manner as before—specifically, it is to be added in the first half and subtracted in the latter half. Having thus made the elapsed portion into a single aggregate, all the [planetary] movements, such as "victory" (*jina*) and so forth, are to be clearly established in their respective positions for Mars (*bhauma*), according to whether they are to be added or subtracted based on the planet's course.
O Lord of Men, the sequential calculation is to be understood as follows: thus, among all the planets, the Sun becomes purified in relation to Mercury and Venus.
Having made a single aggregate of the traversed portions of Mercury and Venus according to their movement, everything—whether to be added or subtracted—is determined.
Here, in the process of rapid motion (*śīghrakarma*), it is to be added in direct order and subtracted in reverse order.
In the first half [of the month], the *piṇḍa* is consumed; in the second half, the *piṇḍa* is unconsumed, as before.

Regarding Mars (*bhauma*), "the movements begin with the Jinas" means that the Jinas are twenty-four; those movements beginning with the Jinas belong to the fourteen *padas* which stand at the beginning of the *manu-pada*, the fourteenth *pada*. Thus, starting from Mars, all these movements beginning with the Jinas are to be established in the fourteen lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) of the manifest *manu-pada*.
O King, in this way the sequential enumeration for all the planets is to be understood.

In the case of Mercury, when its longitude is subtracted from that of Venus, it becomes the Sun; and when Mercury is subtracted from Venus, it becomes Mercury. Since both Mercury and Venus [are derived] from their longitudes, this is the purification of Mars; and the Moon as well [is purified].

According to the Tibetan tradition, the purification of the remainder *kha* is as follows in the *Vimalaprabhā* [on the *Lokadhātu*]: Now, the planet Mercury (*budha*) is described: The entire total number of days, multiplied by zero, space, and the moon (010), minus fire, sun, and mountain (312), is divided by mountain, void, and serpent (897) and further multiplied; the remainder is distinguished by the constellations (*ṛkṣa*) and so forth.

The *cakṣa* is obtained by the aforementioned portion; furthermore, the *ghaṭikās* occur in the *saumya-bhoga*. Having subtracted the *saumya*, O Good King, subtract the King from the midst of the Sun, as well as half a lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*) correctly.
The entire total of days is multiplied by zero, space, and the moon (0-0-1);
thus, the previously purified total number of days is multiplied by one hundred and then multiplied by zero, space, and the moon.

That same number of days multiplied by one hundred is diminished by fire (3), sun (12), and mountain (7)—that is, diminished by seven hundred twenty-three—and then divided by "from mountain, void, beginning, snake" (8779);

"from mountain" means from seven; "void, beginning, snake" means eight thousand seven hundred ninety-seven; thus, it is divided—that is, partitioned—by these eighty-seven hundred seventy-nine days of the maṇḍala for its own movement.

"Even the remainder [of the revolutions] multiplied by the differences of the asterisms and so forth"— meaning that even the remainder of the days of the cycle multiplied by the number of days is further multiplied by twenty-seven, which are the differences of the asterisms and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), it is implied that the remainder of the degrees of the cycle is likewise multiplied by sixty,
and similarly, the remainder of the minutes is multiplied by sixty, and the remainder of the breaths is multiplied by six.

The asterism (ṛkṣa) is obtained by dividing the stated days of the mandala; furthermore, the ghaṭikās are likewise [obtained], and the pāṇīpala breaths are obtained in this manner. These occur in the movement of Mercury and the movement of the quarters. O good King, having subtracted Mercury from the Sun, correctly discard the king and half the asterism.

Having subtracted from the swift calculation for the purpose of purification that lunar motion which was obtained by means of the circle of days and so forth, O good king, you must therefore subtract from the midday of the Sun sixteen asterisms, half an asterism, and thirty *ghaṭikās* in the solar *ghaṭikā* motion. If the debt is not cleared at that time, then one should add the circle of asterisms (*nakṣatracakra*) and clear the debt, according to the previous rule.

The remaining calculation is to be performed as for Mars, resulting in debt or credit, and the slow and fast operations. For Mercury, in the slow operation, one should take ten, seven, and three; in the fast operation, one should take sixteen and so forth. Having calculated the sum of days, its square root is divided by sixty-four and four hundred and eighty-four. The remainder is multiplied by the asterism and [divided] again by the asterism; in the slow operation, the result is in *ghaṭikās*. For Jupiter, the remaining calculation is to be performed as for Mars, resulting in debt or credit, and the slow and fast operations; this is easily understood.

Regarding the statement "in the case of Mercury, for the slow-motion calculation, the periods are ten, seven, and three": in the case of Mercury (*saumya*), during the slow-motion calculation (*mandakārya*), that is, in the work concerning the zodiacal signs (*rāśikarma*), there are ten in the first sign-quarter (*rāśipada*) of both the preceding and following [halves], seven (*giri*) in the second sign-quarter, and three (*śikhin*) in the third sign-quarter; such is the first half.

Then, in the latter half, there are three in the fourth sign-position, seven in the fifth sign-position, and ten in the sixth sign-position; thus, for the slow-motion calculation (*mandakārya*), the steps (*pada*) are ten, seven, and eleven.

For the fast-motion calculation (*śīghrakārya*), in the operation of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatrakarma*), the [steps] beginning with the kings (16) and so forth are fourteen in the fourteenth place, and these fourteen days are to be stated in what follows. This is the purification of Mercury (*budhapariśuddhi*). [The term *guṇyāṃ* is rendered as *guṇya* according to the Tibetan version.]

Regarding the statement "the asterism is to be subtracted from the Sun":
here, in the calculation of Jupiter's [mean] motion, twelve asterisms are to be subtracted; the remaining operation is to be performed as with Mars.
For the slow-motion calculation of Saturn (*haranavaśikhin*), the steps are as before: eleven degrees in the six-sign step are called *hara*, then nine, and then three for *śikhin*.
In the same way, in the latter half [of the year], it is done in reverse order.

Thus, regarding the further *śīghra-karman* (swift calculation), those *manu-padas* which were in the fourteen *pada*s of the *manu-pada* (the "clear" *manu-pada*) starting from the *dik-pada*—namely, the *pada*s for the movement (*cāra*) of the ten lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and so forth—are to be stated as they will be explained below; this is the purification (*śuddhi*) of Jupiter (*bṛhaspati*).

Now Venus is described: having multiplied the number of days by ten (khendu), as stated in "having killed [multiplied] the day by khendu"; having subtracted eighty-four (jalanidhivasu) as stated in "subtracted by the oceans and Vasus";
and having divided by two thousand two hundred and forty-seven (abrejinākṣa) as stated in "divided by abrejinākṣa."

For the purpose of purifying the fast motion (*śīghracaraṇa*) by means of the days of the circle of revolutions (*caraṇamaṇḍala*), when the remaining [days] are subtracted from the [number of] asterisms (*ṛkṣaghna*), the planetary position (*ṛkṣabhoga*) is again [calculated] by means of the *ghaṭikā* positions, just as in the case of Mars. In this manner, the position in *pāṇīpala* and so forth for Venus occurs in its fast motion; and for Venus in its slow motion (*mandakārya*), the season-asterism (*ṛtvṛkṣa*) is to be subtracted from the Sun. In the slow motion, the *pada*s are [determined] by the divisions beginning with the principles (*tattva*), which are clearly explained in the *Anupada*; likewise for Mars, they are to be added or subtracted.

The true number of elapsed days, diminished by eighty-four thousand six hundred and eight, and divided by sixty-six thousand one hundred and twenty-seven, yields the asterism of the Moon (or Saturn); eighteen asterisms are to be subtracted from it. // 48 //
"Ṛtvakṣa" means six constellations to be subtracted from the Sun; in the phrase "sūryabhoge," the locative case is to be understood everywhere as having the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*).

In the slow calculation (*mandakārye*), "arrows, pairs, and moon" refers to the *padas*; as before, these are to be placed in the position of the six signs (*ṣaḍrāśisthāne*), with "arrows" (*śara*) representing five.
The eastern group consists of Ka, Ka, and Bhaga;

Now, the time of the setting and rising of the planets is stated: Any planet whatsoever that enters the solar domain certainly sets; having left the sun, it shall rise. And its path is determined by the division of the movement of the solstices (ayanagati).

He who stands on the left path travels by the north due to the movement of the sun, while he standing on the right clearly travels by the south; moreover, there is mutual combat between the two enemies here.
Thus, there are five [parameters] for *yuga*, four for *śaśin*, and one for *pūrvārddha*; in this way, for the latter half (*aparārddha*) in the case of the swift operation (*śīghrakarma*),
there are twenty-five divisions and so forth, according to the distinctions of the principles (*tattva*) and other categories.

In the manifest *anupada* [section] concerning the fourteen lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and their movements, that which is to be given and that which is to be abandoned is as follows: just as it is for Maṅgala (Mars), so too for Śukra (Venus) the movement (*cārapada*) is both to be given and to be abandoned. This is the purification of Venus (*śukraśuddhi*). Now Saturn (*śani*) is described: "The clear day-count (*sphuṭadivasagaṇa*) diminished by four thousand eight hundred and twenty" means that the previously established clear day-count is reduced by four thousand eight hundred and twenty; this is in accordance with the *Karaṇa* system, not the *Siddhānta*. Therefore, "divided by ten thousand seven hundred and sixty-six" means divided by the number of days in a cycle (*maṇḍaladinaiḥ*), which is ten thousand seven hundred and sixty-six.
The quotient obtained by dividing the remaining degrees of the day-circle by the [degrees] of the killer of the asterism (*ṛkṣaghna*) becomes the asterism.
In this way, the motion [of the moon] in *pāṇīpala* and so forth is determined. Regarding the phrase "eighteen are to be subtracted from the moon":

eighteen asterisms are to be subtracted from the motion of Saturn; and when [the result] is greater than a debt, the zodiacal circle (*cakra*) is added and then they are to be subtracted. This prior rule is for the purpose of determining the quarter of the birth asterism within its slow-motion calculation (*mandakarma*).

The season consists of twenty-six days; in matters requiring speed, the [planets] beginning with Mercury (Rasa) are swift. Their motion is direct when proceeding through the sequential positions, and retrograde when moving in reverse order.

In the first half and the second half [of the year], the emergence of the planets occurs by virtue of the Sun's movement over thirty-seven months multiplied by four (forty-four). And for Ketu, there is both swift and retrograde motion.

Regarding the phrase "six, twenty-six, seasons": in the six positions of the *āśis*, there are twenty-two units in the first zodiac sign (*rāśi*), followed by fifteen days, and then "seasons," which are six.

The latter half [of the calculation] should be understood in the same way. Because of the statement "in the position of the manifest flavors" (*prakaṭarasapade*), in the matter of swift motion (*śīghrakārye*)—that is, in the operation concerning the swift lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*)—the "flavors and so forth" (*rasādyāḥ*) are to be added or subtracted in the fourteenth place; these, beginning with the six units, are to be stated as they will be explained in the entire collection of planetary movements. This is the purification of Saturn (*śanaiśvaraśuddhi*).
Now the characteristic of motion (*cāra*) is stated: "Motion is swift (*śīghra*) and slow (*manda*), consisting of movement through the steps in sequence.

In the case of swift action, the enjoyment (*bhoga*) of a planet that has risen from the solar disc during the fourteen *ghaṭikās* of the first half is called swift motion (*śīghracāra*). Regarding "movement through the steps in sequence," the enjoyment that occurs in the latter half is called slow motion (*mandacāra*).
Then, when the half-circle has been traversed in reverse order, the planet enters retrograde motion;
that retrograde motion is called *vakracāra* (retrograde movement).

In the first half and the second half [of the zodiac], due to the movement of the Sun, the emergence of the planets is called their "direct motion" (*nirgamacāra*), because they have abandoned retrogression (*vakra*). From sunrise, as they move in regular order (*anuloma*) until the first half [is completed], there is an increase in wealth (*dhana*); then, in the second half until the midpoint of the circle (*cakrārddha*), there is a decrease in wealth. Then, having abandoned the half-circle, by moving in reverse order (*pratiloma*), there is an increase in debt (*ṛṇa*) in the first half and a decrease in debt in the second half, until the entry into the solar asterism (*sūryanakṣatra*). When the Sun has set, the sunrise occurs again; this should be understood to follow that same sequence.

This concludes the section on the planets. According to the Tibetan [tradition]: "The divisions of the six, five, and so forth, are themselves known as the divisions. [This is] the increase.

97. Whosoever enters the solar orbit, that planet necessarily sets; because it is no longer visible due to the rays of the solar disc, it is said to have "set," yet it is not that the planet has ceased to exist in every respect. Having left the sun, it shall rise: that very same planet which had set, having left the sun by virtue of its own movement, becomes risen again because it has been abandoned by the solar rays. And its path is according to the division of the motion of the solstices (*ayana*).

Regarding that risen planet, there is a division according to the movement of its solstice (*ayanagativibhāga*). The "path" (*mārga*) refers to the division of the two solstices (*ayanavibhāga*): from the Fire-Circle (*agnivalaya*) to Kailāsa (or *Kailāśa*) on the north, up to the Himavat mountains; and from the Himavat mountains to the south, up to the Fire-Circle. This is by way of a division of one hundred and eighty-two and a half days. Thus, it is the division of the solstitial movement of the Sun. By means of that division of the Sun's movement, the path of the planets that have arisen occurs for them. That which is situated on the left path, by virtue of the Sun's course, travels by the northern route.

In this system of the left-hand path (*vāmamārga*), because Mercury, Venus, and Ketu—the "gentle" (*saumya*) planets—arise from the left side, they enter the solar disc at the time of setting with the left side, and likewise rise with the left side. Therefore, any planet situated on the left-hand path moves to the north of the malefic planets; just as one situated on the right (*savya*) moves to the south of the Sun. Here, "situated on the right" refers to those who set in the solar disc on the right-hand path—Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—who are malefic and move to the south of the gentle planets, because they arise from the right side.

Here, because Ketu is born from the left side, he is gentle (*saumya*) by way of bodily division; because Jupiter (*bṛhaspati*) is born from the right side, he is fierce (*raudra*) by way of bodily division. Likewise, it is clearly stated that there is mutual combat between enemies here:

there is mutual combat between these two—the gentle and the cruel, Mercury and Mars, Jupiter and Venus, and Saturn and Ketu—because they are enemies. If this occurs while they are situated in their own signs, the combat is certain.
Indeed, no battle occurs between two constellations; rather, there is a conjunction with one another here.

If the entry of the moon occurs in the left [quarter] and its exit from the sun occurs in the north, or if the rising of the horns occurs in the left, it may happen in some cases due to the influence of the solstice that the exit occurs in the south.
If there is a certain battle for those situated in their own domain (*svakṣetra*), then in that case there will certainly be war.

Here, the own domain of Mars is the sign of Aries and the sign of Scorpio; if Mercury's transit occurs while he is situated in that domain, then at that time there is certainly war. Likewise, if Mars is present in Mercury's domain—namely Gemini or Virgo—there is conflict.
The enjoyer becomes so by the power of his position; nevertheless, there is war.
Thus, if Venus is in Sagittarius or Pisces within the domain of Jupiter, then there is war between Venus and Jupiter.
Likewise, if it is in Taurus or Libra within the domain of Venus.
Likewise, if Ketu is in Capricorn or Aquarius—the domain of Saturn—then there is war;
similarly, if Saturn is in Cancer, which is its own domain, then there is war with Ketu because Ketu is born from it;
however, in the case of a lunar mansion (nakṣatra), there is no war with anything else.

Furthermore, in this context, the birth of the planets is considered with respect to their *nakṣatras*; thus, a battle does not occur only when they are in their own *rāśi*, but a battle also occurs for an enemy in its own *janmanakṣatra*. Specifically, Venus has a battle in its own *nakṣatra* Punarvasu, Mars in Maghā, Jupiter in Hastā, Mercury in Anurādhā, Saturn in Mūla, and Ketu in Uttarāṣāḍhā; thus, Saumya (Mercury) and Maṅgala (Mars) have battles in their respective *nakṣatras*.

Thus it is for Venus and Jupiter, as well as for Saturn and Ketu; indeed, it is certain that no battle occurs in another asterism or field except in one's own asterism, and that there is mutual conjunction in another asterism. Likewise, regarding the moon's rising horns (*śṛṅgonnati*): if the entry of the moon occurs on the left [side] of the sun, and its exit occurs to the north, then the rising of the horn is in the north.

In some cases, by the power of the solstice—during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) due to famine or drought, or by its very nature—and during the interruption of the lunar nodes (parvaccheda), Rāhu moves facing forward; that is, he swallows [the moon] face-to-face when moving to the left (vāmecāra), and from the right (apasavya) when following the movement of the sun to the right (savyabhāga). Thus, Rāhu swallows the moon in the intermediate directions (vidikṣu), having emerged from behind. From Aśvinī up to half of Citrā, night and day are equal at the center of the celestial sphere (golarekhā).

Now the entry of Rāhu is described: at the "cutting of the node" (*parvacchede*), that is, at the cutting of the full moon (*pūrṇimā*), and by the word "and" (*ca*), also at the cutting of the new moon (*amāvasyā*); the moon enters Rāhu with its face turned toward it, which constitutes a "frontal eclipse" (*sammukhagrāsa*).

Here, "frontal" means an eclipse occurring from the east; this very phenomenon is to be understood through the power of Rāhu’s orbital deviation (*valana*), as it is well-known in all other astronomical systems (*karaṇa*).
Since this is established elsewhere, no effort was made to explain it here by the Blessed Mañjuśrī.

In the left movement [of Rāhu] there is an eclipse on the right, and in the right movement there is an eclipse on the left; "by the power of the Sun's course" means on the right side. This is because, by the power of the Sun's course—that is, by the power of the Moon's movement as it has emerged from the Sun's sphere—there is an eclipse of the Moon on the right when there is a rightward deviation.
Thus, Rāhu swallows the Moon in the intermediate directions.

In the sequence thus described, by virtue of its revolution (*valana*), Rāhu devours the Moon in the intermediate directions (*vidik*); and it devours it from behind when it has emerged [from the eclipse]. Because of the revolution starting from the east, it devours it from behind during the revolution toward the west; thus, the revolution and other parameters of Rāhu are to be understood from the Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*) or from other treatises (*karaṇa*). Now, the stellar sphere (*nakṣatragola*) is described: the line of the sphere runs through the middle of the night and day, starting from the half of Aśvinī up to Citrā.

From Aśvinī to the midpoint of Citrā, and from the midpoint of Citrā to the end of Revatī, [the zodiacal signs] are Aries and so forth. At the equinoxes, beginning with Libra, the day and night are equal; the line of the celestial sphere (golarekhā) is exactly in the middle, consisting of thirty *daṇḍas* each, due to the cause of the Sun’s rising and setting. That very sphere exists through the division of the lunar mansions (*ṛkṣa*). Indeed, the mansion is situated in the position of the world, both clockwise and counter-clockwise, according to the division of the signs. In the sign of the bow-shaped season, it is situated in the southern hemisphere of the sphere from the center of the globe, having entered the circle of fire.

To the left is that Cool Mountain (Śītācala), which is like the petal of a beautiful lotus; from the boundary of the Cool Mountain at the beginning of Aries and Libra, there are five thousand yojanas [to the edge] of the Fire [Mountain]. || 53 ||
"The bear [Ursa Major] is indeed situated on the left and right in the station of the world through the divisions of the zodiac signs.

Thus, in this land of action (*karmabhūmi*), due to the power of ignorance, many kinds of theories regarding the celestial sphere (*golamata*)—such as the orbits (*kakṣā*) and other distinctions—have been stated here.
Indeed, in this sphere, it is said that the movement of the eight planets, whether swift or slow, is equal to the passage through the zodiac signs.

Just as in the threshing of grain, the ox that wanders far from the central post is a fast-moving one and completes its circumambulation in many steps, whereas the one that wanders near the post is a slow-moving one and completes its circumambulation in few steps; in this same way, the planets are also to be understood.

The worldly view is first examined by means of reasoning: here, there is no practical calculation [based on observation]; because of the influence of their respective established doctrines, there is no single consensus. Therefore, it is investigated as follows: regarding these planets in this celestial sphere (*gola*) that move faster or slower than the Sun, are they situated one above the other, or are they situated from the left side to the right side? In both cases, there is a contradiction. If they were situated below or above the Sun, then there would be no conjunction of the fast and slow-moving planets, because of their abandonment of their own orbits (*kakṣā*).

Then the proponent of the opposing doctrine says: "Beings situated below perceive the conjunction of the lower and upper planets as equal; that is, the equality of the upper planet being eclipsed by the lower planet. To this it is replied: Here, equality occurs at the time of midday, not at sunrise, nor at the time of sunset.

At the time of rising, the planets are seen by sentient beings below and above due to the influence of their distinct orbital paths (*kakṣā*); the same is not the case at the time of setting. Thus, here in this zodiacal wheel (*rāśicakra*), the Moon is in the first orbit, Mercury in the second, Venus in the third, the Sun in the fourth, Mars in the fifth, Jupiter in the sixth, Rāhu in the seventh, and Saturn in the eighth.

Here, for all the planets, there is both northward and southward motion, just as the Sun has [motion] by virtue of its transit through the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and by virtue of its transit through the six signs (*rāśi*).

And when that [sun] moves northward or southward at its conjunction with the sun, no planet goes above or below the sun in this zodiacal wheel (*rāśicakra*). Due to slow motion (*mandagati*), some planets follow behind the sun; the moon, having risen, moves ahead; and due to swift motion (*śīghragati*), Mercury and Venus—by virtue of their orbital positions—sometimes rise and move ahead, and sometimes rise and move behind.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, for the purpose of fully understanding their movement, the sphere of the zodiac signs (*rāśigola*) is described: "The asterism is situated in the fourteenth position on the right, and in the fourteenth position on the left, according to the divisions of the zodiac signs. The division of the zodiac signs consists of two and a quarter asterisms for each sign. By these divisions of the signs, there are thirteen and a half asterisms from the central meridian line of the sphere: starting from Aśvinī up to the midpoint of Citrā on the north, and again from the midpoint of Citrā up to Revatī, ending with thirteen and a half asterisms on the south.

In the six signs beginning with Sagittarius (Cāpa), which form a bow-shape from the center of the southern sphere, the half-circle of constellations—the stellar wheel—is situated to the south; it lies at the equatorial line of the sphere at its midpoint.
To the left [of that], the Snow Mountain (Himālaya) is like the petal of a beautiful lotus, positioned at the beginning of Aries and Libra.

Just as [the zodiacal signs] are situated in the six signs starting from the southern [equinox], each occupying half a circle of constellations, so too are they situated in the six signs starting from the northern meridian of the celestial sphere, according to the division of each individual sign; that is, from the beginning of Aries up to the end of Virgo, and from the beginning of Libra up to the end of Pisces. Thus it is situated from the beginning of Libra up to the end of Pisces.

Here, in the eastern half [of the sphere], there is Aries; in the northeast (Īśāna), Taurus; in the northern half, Gemini; again in the northern half, Cancer; in the northwest (Vāyavya), Leo; in the western half, Virgo; again in the west, Libra; in the southwest (Nairṛtya), Scorpio; in the southern half, Sagittarius; and in the eastern half, Pisces—such is the arrangement of the zodiac signs on the sphere. Furthermore, in the southern half is Capricorn, and in the southeast (Āgneyī), Aquarius. In this [system], when Aries rises, Libra sets; when Taurus rises, Scorpio sets; thus, in all cases, it should be understood that the setting of the seventh sign occurs simultaneously with the rising of the [preceding] sign, within one day and night.

Now, the measurement of the sphere according to the common worldly view is stated: from the fire [boundary] to the limit of the Great Snowy Mountain (Himavat), which is the moon, there are thirty thousand and five hundred yojanas.

Here, from the southern circle of fire to the northern Great Himavat boundary, the measurement of the sphere is seventy-five thousand yojanas; thus it is clearly to be explained in the fifth chapter as being from the eastern to the western circumference.

The middle [point] is the arrival at the meridian line; the sun also moves for one night in the poison [direction], and thereafter it moves to the left and right by day and night. There is a division of the asterisms in sequence through the paths until, by day and night, it abandons the "sky-snake-moon" (0°) at the end of the solstice. Indeed, the decrease and increase of the sun and moon occur within six degrees during the sixty nāḍīs of night and day.

"From the middle of the wheel, the line of the equator" means that the equinoctial line of the middle zodiac-wheel occurs at thirty-seven and a half thousand *yojanas* out of seventy-five thousand *yojanas*. The "movement upon that [line]" refers to the movement upon the central meridian line of the half-circle of the wheel;

by the word "also," it is implied that for all planets, the movement upon the central meridian line of their respective half-circles of the wheel occurs at their own equinoxes, for one night, and not at all times.

"Subsequently, it moves to the left and right" means that after the equinoctial day (*viṣuvaddin*), during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) it moves southward, and during the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) it moves northward. Regarding "left and right," this refers to the signs beginning with Libra (*tulā*) and Aries (*meṣa*). There is a daily difference in the night and day; sequentially, [the sun] abandons the paths numbering one hundred and eighty (*khāhicandra*)—that is, from the end of the northern solstice until the southern solstice, and from the end of the southern solstice until the northern solstice. *The Great Chapter on the Method for Knowing the Luminaries, in the [chapter on] Paths.*

The decrease and increase of the sun and moon occur in six parts within sixty nāḍīs; thus, in this context of six parts, there is decrease and there is increase. Within sixty nāḍīs, ten nāḍīs constitute the decrease of the night; from Capricorn until the end of Gemini, there is an increase of the day, which is the decrease of the day; and from Cancer until Sagittarius, there is an increase of the night.

Indeed, in this region of Kailāsa, the decrease and increase of the sun's shadow occur in six parts; however, in the land of Āryāvarta, the decrease and increase occur in ten parts— from the end of the northern solstice to the end of the southern solstice, and from the end of the southern solstice to the end of the northern solstice— by virtue of the rule of the shadow.

Thus, in countries such as Bhoṭa, Līca, and Cīna, the decrease and increase [of the shadow] up to the limit of the region of Sambhala should be understood by means of the shadow, according to the ninth part, the eighth part, and the seventh part.

Now, in the twelve divisions (*dvādaśakhaṇḍa*), the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*) is described with respect to the revolution of the sun above it: Because for the people on the mountain [Meru] there is indeed the equinox (*viṣuva*) when the sun is in Aries and when the sun is in Libra; therefore, in the second and eighth divisions, when the sun has entered Taurus and likewise Scorpio; in the ninth and third divisions, when the sun has entered Gemini and Sagittarius; in the fourth division, when the sun is in Cancer; and also in the fifth and eleventh, when the sun is in Capricorn. Because for the people on the mountain there is indeed the equinox when the sun is in Aries and when the sun is in Libra.
In whichever region of the earth the spring equinox occurs when the sun is in Aries and the autumn equinox occurs when the sun is in Libra,
in that very place, conversely, autumn occurs when the sun is in Aries and the spring season-equinox occurs when the sun is in Libra.

Thus, by virtue of mutual dependence, since the sign of Aquarius occurs on the seventh land-segment from the first land-segment—on Mount Meru, south of the seventh segment to the north, and north of the seventh segment to the south—it is likewise when the Sun has entered Taurus in the eighth land-segment.

In this regard, just as the equinox occurs when the sun is in Aries and the sun is in Libra within the southern terrestrial sector previously described by me, so too—this is certain—it occurs that when the sun is in Taurus and situated in the half-part of the northeast (īśāna) corner, while being located in the southwest (naiṛtya) corner, the equinox then takes place; that is, the half of spring and the half of autumn. Likewise, in the ninth terrestrial sector called *randhra*, which is the third and numbered with fire (*vahni*), when the sun is situated in the latter half of the southwest corner and the former half of the northeast corner, the equinox occurs.
When the sun is in Gemini and in Sagittarius, it is the half of spring and autumn respectively;
at the tenth and fourth [measures] from Meru, in the eastern land-portion and the western land-portion,
the equinox occurs, such that there is the half of spring and the half of autumn.

When the Sun is in Cancer, even though it is situated in the western [hemisphere], and when it has entered Capricorn, the equinox occurs in the eastern land-mass; thus there is half of spring and half of autumn. When the Sun has entered Leo or Aquarius, at twenty-two thousand [yojanas], and when it has entered Pisces or Virgo, this would be the northern solstice (vāmāyana). When the Sun is in Capricorn, in the second [land-mass] with the Sun in Aquarius, and in the third [land-mass] in Pisces, there is likewise a solstice for men.
When the Sun is in Aries in the fourth [land-mass] called Bhūta, and when the Sun is in Taurus, and when the Sun is in Gemini in the sixth [land-mass], and in the seventh. // 56 //

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, when the Sun has entered the Lion [sign] in the jar [constellation], being situated in the fifth [house] in the half of the northwest corner and in the eleventh [house] in the half of the southeast corner, there occurs the equinox (*viṣuva*), that is, the half of spring and the half of autumn.

This is because of the phrase "twelve twice" (*dvidaśarasamahāvit*). When the Sun is situated in the latter half of the southeast corner and in the latter half of the northwest corner, this is the reading of the scripture regarding the "great twice" (*mahāviti*) in the twelfth [house].
When the sun has entered Pisces and when it has entered Virgo, the two equinoxes occur; thus, the half of spring and the half of autumn come into being.
In this way, on the twelve grounds, by virtue of the twelve zodiac signs and through the division of the rising and setting of the sun, there are twelve months and six seasons.

Now, regarding the twelve northern solstices and twelve southern solstices on the twelve grounds according to the revolution of the sun through the zodiac signs, it is said: "In this [ground], there shall be the leftward solstice."
"In this" refers to the southern portion of the earth, south of Mount Meru;
why "south"?
Because it is the Lesser Jambūdvīpa, by virtue of the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma there.

Therefore, in the southern land-mass there is the northern course (*vāmāyana*) and the southern course (*uttarāyaṇa*). When the sun is in Capricorn, it is thus; when the sun is in Aquarius, it is in the second land-mass;
in Pisces, in the third land-mass; and when the sun is in Aries, it is in the fourth for men.

In the western land, the fourth, known as Bhūta, when the fifth sun is situated in Taurus, and the sun has entered Gemini, the sixth great [period] is the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) in the seventh [land],
to the north of Meru.

When the Sun is in Cancer, the northern solstice occurs in the eighth land-section (bhūmikhaṇḍa) at Harigata; when in Virgo, it occurs in the ninth section at Kanyārandhra; when in Libra, it occurs in the tenth section at Tulārka; and when in Scorpio, it occurs in the eleventh section at Rudrakhaṇḍa.

When in Sagittarius, the northern solstice for men occurs in the twelfth section at Dvādaśāra on the earth. Thus, by virtue of the Sun's movement through the zodiacal signs beginning with Cancer, the northern course (savyāyana) proceeds. When the Sun is in Cancer, the southern course (vāmāyana) occurs; when in Leo, it occurs in the eighth land-section at Harigata.

When the Sun is in Virgo, it is the ninth land-section; when the Sun is in Libra, it occurs in the tenth land-section; when the Sun is in Scorpio, O Rudra, it is in the eleventh section; and when the Sun is in Sagittarius, it would be in the twelfth section—thus the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) for human beings is conceived according to the division of the twelve zodiac signs among the worlds situated upon the twelve-spoked earth. In this manner, the southern solstice (*savyāyana*) would likewise occur.
In the sequence thus described, the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) occurs in the zodiac signs beginning with Cancer due to the movement of the sun;

in this small Jambūdvīpa region to the south of Meru, the southern solstice occurs when the sun is in Cancer. Likewise, in the second [region] to the right, it occurs when the sun is in Leo; in the third, when the sun is in Virgo; and in the fourth, when the sun is in Libra—the southern solstice occurs on the western side of Meru.

In the fifth terrestrial region, when the Sun is in Scorpio; in the sixth, in Sagittarius; in the seventh, in Capricorn; in the eighth to the north of Meru, in Aquarius; in the ninth, in Pisces; in the tenth, in Aries; in the eleventh, in Taurus; and in the twelfth, in Gemini—thus, O King, the southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*) of the world occurs for the people according to the division of the twelve zodiac signs.

Now, the measure of the Sun’s declination (*krānti*) above the terrestrial sphere is stated: Above [the equator], the number of six serpents (six) is the extent of the Sun's heat during the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*); at its end, it becomes diminished by that same amount in the southern transit (*savya*), reaching a thousand times the number of Rudras (eleven thousand).

Eighty-one thousand [yojanas] minus one hundred arrows (five) is the equatorial line at the center; from that, there are two descents of zero-zero arrows (10,000) to the north and south. This is the Great Chapter on the Method for Knowing the Luminaries. "Above, the number is six-nāgas" means that here, above the seventh terrestrial circle, the distance is eighty-six thousand yojanas. Regarding the sun's movement, at the end of the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) and at the beginning of the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), the southern course occurs in its respective segment starting with Cancer, on the day of its respective transit (*saṃkrānti*), occurring sequentially across the twelve segments.

Therefore, O Lord of Men, it becomes diminished by eleven thousand Rudra-numbers (eleven thousand one hundred and twenty-five) from that day of the transition of the southern solstice until the northern solstice; thus, the heating [of the sun] above should be known as seventy-five thousand five hundred. When eighty-one thousand minus five hundred and fifty is subtracted from the center, it becomes the equatorial line of the sphere; this is the measurement in *yojanas*.

Just as there occurs a double fall (or increase) of the sun from that meridian line at five thousand five hundred *yojanas*—that is, five thousand five hundred *yojanas*—due to the movement through the zodiacal signs (*rāśibhoga*) in their respective segments to the north and south of the line;

now, the daily transverse declination (*tiryakkrānti*) of the sun in the twelve segments, both clockwise and counter-clockwise, is described: having crossed the salt ocean, the sun travels as far as the Fire [Mountain] to the south, and to the north he travels to Kailāsa; and being situated in the north, he travels to the Snowy Mountain (*Himagiri*) in the north.
Struck by the lunar days (tithis), the arrows travel a thousand and five hundred yojanas; diminished by the moon, the five elements abandon [the earth] day by day on all sides.
Having crossed the salt ocean, the sun travels southward as far as the fire-limit (Agnimita).

Here, on this twelve-spoked earth, in each individual continent according to the zodiacal signs (rāśi), the sun, situated in the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana), having crossed the salt ocean, travels as far as the circle of the Southern Fire (Dakṣiṇāgni-valaya) and so forth, reaching the boundary of the ocean.

Then, from the boundary of the circle of fire, one proceeds to the north of Kailāsa toward the Snowy Mountain. On the northern path, while the sun is situated in the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), from the beginning of the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) until the end of the day, the "arrows" (*bāṇa*) are multiplied by the "lunar days" (*tithi*).
Here, "arrow" (*bāṇa*) means five, and "lunar day" (*tithi*) means fifteen; those arrows multiplied by those fifteen result in seventy-five.

The sun traverses that distance of seventy-five thousand *yojanas* during its movement through the quarters of the solstices—from the Himavat to the Fire and from the Fire to the Himavat—constituting the division of the directions for the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) and so forth. It traverses that division of the directions in six months according to the sequence of the northern and southern solstices.
Regarding the phrase "he abandons one and a half *akṣas* obtained by the moon day by day":
the sun abandons daily a portion of the seventy-five thousand *yojanas* of the directional division, which is the amount obtained by dividing [the total] by one hundred and eighty-two and a half.
Thus, by means of the movement through both courses, the days of the solar mandala for the wheel of zodiac signs amount to three hundred and sixty-five;
in this way, the transverse course of the sun across the twelve sectors is to be understood.
Now, according to the revolution through the twelve sectors of the sun situated in each individual zodiac sign, there is a division of the twelve months.
It is said: When the Sun is situated in a zodiacal sign (rāśi), it produces the entire collection of seasons along with months and fortnights;

and in each successive segment (khaṇḍa) on the twelve-spoked [mandala] upon the surface of the earth, a month occurs in due order. Whatever measurement occurs in whichever segment by virtue of the days, that same measurement occurs in the seventh [segment] as night. On the half-path of three hundred thousand [yojanas], there is day in front of the Sun and night behind it. || 60 ||
"Stationed in a single zodiac sign, the Sun produces the entire collection of seasons,

months, and fortnights"— here, the Sun, situated in any one sign such as Aries and so forth, produces the six seasons, twelve months, and twenty-four fortnights within the twelve divisions [of the year] by virtue of revolving through the circle of the zodiac signs.

In this regard, on every side of Meru, that which touches the Dakṣiṇāgni fire by virtue of the rotation of the zodiacal wheel reaches the direction of the seventh sector and touches the peak of Meru; according to the principle that the Himavat mountain moves upward, the entire collection of seasons and so forth must be understood for the Sun situated in each individual sign. Thus, in each and every sector, a month occurs in succession within the twelve-spoked [wheel] of movement.

Here, on the surface of the earth consisting of twelve spokes, there is a month for each individual segment; the manner in which this occurs for the sun situated in a single zodiac sign is explained as follows: here, by the designation of one zodiac sign, all zodiac signs are to be understood.

In this small Jambudvīpa, it is well known that the zodiac signs begin with Aries (Meṣa) to the south of Meru, as do the seasons beginning with Spring (Vasanta), the months beginning with Caitra, and likewise all the fortnights. Therefore, it is explained how the sun, situated in the sign of Aries, produces the entire cycle of seasons and so forth across the twelve sectors (*khaṇḍa*): here in the southern sector of Meru, the sun situated in Aries produces the season of Spring and the month of Vaiśākha; in the second sector, the eastern half of the southeast corner (*agni-koṇa*), it produces the month of Jyeṣṭha; likewise, in the sector beyond the southeast corner, it produces Āṣāḍha; in the third [sector], and similarly in the fourth, in the eastern sector of Meru and Pūrvavideha, it produces the month of Śrāvaṇa; in the fifth, the eastern half of the northeast corner (*īśārddha*), it produces Bhādrapada; in the sixth sector, the western half of the northeast corner, it produces Āśvina; in the seventh sector to the north of Meru, it produces Kārttika; in the eighth sector, the eastern half of the northwest corner (*vāyavya-koṇa*), it produces Mārgaśīrṣa; in the ninth sector, the western half of the northwest corner, it produces Puṣya; in the tenth sector to the west of Meru, it produces Māgha; in the eleventh sector, the western half of the southwest corner (*naiṛtya-koṇa*), it produces Phālguna; and in the twelfth sector, the western half of the southwest corner, it produces Caitra.
Thus, by means of two months, a season (*ṛtu*) occurs within two segments;
in each segment there are two fortnights (*pakṣa*) distinguished by the bright and dark halves of the month.
In this way, it should be understood that the six seasons, twelve months, and twenty-four fortnights revolve in the shape of a wheel across the twelve segments.

In this southern hemisphere, whichever month occurs according to the sequence of the twelve zodiac signs at the solar transits (saṃkrānti), that [month] moves by way of a clockwise rotation to the south-western corner (naiṛtya) at the next transit. From the south-western corner, it goes to the other half of the corner; from the other half of the corner, it goes to Aparagodānīya on the western side of Meru; situated in Aparagodānīya, it goes to the north-western half-corner; situated in the north-western half-corner, it goes to the other half of the corner; situated in the other half of the corner, it goes to Uttarakuru; situated in Uttarakuru, it goes to the north-eastern half-corner; situated there, it goes to the other half of the corner; situated in the other half of the south-western corner, it goes to Godānīya; situated in the other half of the corner, it goes to Pūrvavideha; situated in Pūrvavideha, it goes to the south-eastern half-corner; situated in the eastern half, it goes to the other half of the corner; and situated in the other half of the corner, it goes to the southern Jambūdvīpa. Thus, one should understand the movement through the twelve sectors according to the successive transits of the twelve months.
Whatever the measure of day becomes in a particular region by virtue of the solar day, that same measure occurs at night in the seventh [region].

Here, at the solstice of the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*), the measure of day is diminished and the measure of night is increased in the southern region; that very same measure occurs in the seventh terrestrial region of Uttarakuru by virtue of the sunrise [there], whereas here it does not occur due to the increase of night in the south. In Jambūdvīpa, by virtue of the southern sunrise and the decrease of night in the seventh [region], it occurs in the south;
thus it should be understood in this way for every individual region everywhere.
On half the path from three hundred thousand [yojanas], there is day in front of the sun and night behind it;

thus, the measure of the sphere here is six hundred thousand [yojanas]. Due to the movement of the sun, on half the path there is day for three hundred thousand [yojanas] from sunrise until sunset, and night for three hundred thousand [yojanas] from sunset until sunrise.
In this way, it should be understood for the day and night.

Now, the position of Meru within the twelve sectors is described: "O Lord of Men, the King of Mountains stands to the north of all people; sunrise occurs in the east, and at the same time as the mountain, sunset occurs in the west.

These times—the four twilights, the watches, the days, and the nights—constantly shifting, revolve around the directions of Meru, clearly manifesting upon the great sun-disk, divided by the differences of the ascendants."
"O Lord of Men, the king of mountains stands to the north of all," means that here,
for the people residing in the twelve regions (*dvādaśakhaṇḍa*), Mount Meru, the king of mountains, is situated to the north.

"East" means that where the sun rises for everyone—both those situated on Mount Meru and those residing in all the other continents—that is the eastern direction. For those situated in Jambūdvīpa, Pūrvavideha is the east; for those in Aparagodānī, Jambūdvīpa is the east; for those situated in Uttarakuru, Aparagodānī is the east; and for those situated in Pūrvavideha, Uttarakuru is the east. This is due to the rotation and rising of the sun; thus it should be understood regarding the eight continents situated at the intermediate points. In each individual continent, the sun rises every five *daṇḍas*.

Regarding the phrase "the movement of the mountain-like [sun]": in each individual section (*khaṇḍa*), the sun’s movement toward the mountain—that is, toward Meru—occurs in the north, south, and west, and it sets there.

Thus, in the twelve sections, just as there is sunrise in the east, so too should one understand that there is sunset in the west. Consequently, there are three times: dawn (*prabhāta*), midday (*madhyāhna*), and evening (*vikāla*).
There are four junctions (*sandhyā*): the midnight junction, the morning junction, the midday junction, and the evening junction.
There are eight watches (*prahara*): four during the day and four at night;
thus, day and night are always passing away.
In this way, time and the other factors, transiting through every period of day and night, revolve from one sector to another around the directions of Mount Meru—
[as stated] in the *Vimalaprabhā* regarding the "manifest sun-wheel" in the twelve-spoked wheel of days, distinguished by the divisions of the zodiacal signs (*lagna*).
Twelve ascendants, differentiated by their divisions, revolve as time and so forth;
time revolves through four-four ascendants; each individual twilight revolves through three ascendants; each individual watch (prahara) revolves through one and a half ascendants;

thus, each individual ascendant revolves through fifteen danda-measures; a half-watch revolves through half a watch; a muhurta revolves through half of half a watch; a ghaṭikā revolves through sixty pāṇīpala-measures; and each individual pāṇīpala revolves through six breaths (śvāsa).

In this way, by means of the divisions of breath and the divisions of the zodiacal signs (*lagna*), time revolves and passes for embodied beings day and night. Now, the measurement of the sun’s revolution in all directions around Meru is stated: In one *nāḍī* (twenty-four minutes), the sun traverses six thousand and five hundred *yojanas*. In sixty *nāḍīs*, it revolves through eleven million five hundred thousand *yojanas* day and night. In half the sphere (*golārddha*), it moves fifteen thousand *yojanas* per *nāḍī* day and night. And during the decrease and increase [of the day], in the sphere, it moves five hundred *yojanas* daily to the right and to the left; from that, there is a pair of breaths (*śvāsa*) and three *liptās*.

In a *nāḍī-abdhi*—that is, during the period consisting of three hundred and sixty breaths—the Sun traverses six thousand and five hundred *yojanas*. Thus, while situated in a *rāśi* within the sky, this is the speed of the revolution of the *rāśi*; it is not the speed of the Sun itself as it remains supported by the *rāśi*. Here, the wheel of *rāśis* revolves clockwise (*savyāvarta*), whereas the planets move counter-clockwise (*apasavya*) through the *rāśis*.
Just as the zodiacal wheel revolves, so too Rāhu moves, circumambulating Mount Meru while facing westward;
whereas the other planets, facing eastward, circumambulate Mount Meru while traversing the zodiacal wheel.
Thus, according to the logic of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-yukti*), Rāhu is meritorious, while the Sun and others are called malevolent, evil planets.

"Sixty lakhs of fires" means that during the period of sixty *nāḍīs*—that is, during the time consisting of twenty-two thousand six hundred breaths—one traverses three lakhs [of *yojanas*].
