"Five mountains and a thousand" refers to a distance of seventy-five thousand *yojanas* which it revolves through. "Day and night" (*ahorātra*) means that in one half of the sphere (*golārddha*), day and night consist of thirty *nāḍīs*. Here, on the day of the equinoxal transition (*viṣuvatsaṃkrānti*), on the aforementioned meridian line of the sphere, the sun flows for thirty *nāḍīs* as day and for thirty *nāḍīs* as night; this is the meaning of "the sun [traversing] equal day and night."
The basis for decrease and increase (and the decrease and increase themselves) in the sphere (*gola*) is five *nāḍīs* in both the clockwise (*savya*) and counter-clockwise (*apasavya*) directions.

Therefore, from that half-sphere, in three months in the clockwise direction there is an increase of the night by five *nāḍīs*, and in the counter-clockwise direction in three months there is an increase of the day by five *nāḍīs*.
Here, it should be understood that when there is an increase of the night there is a decrease of the day, and when there is an increase of the day there is a decrease of the night.
Therefore, even on a daily basis, no alteration has been made here at this root by means of this support.
In this chapter, regarding the "Great Overview of the Method for Knowing the Luminous [Breaths]," that pair of breaths is three *liptas*.
Here, in the left (*savya*) and right (*apasavya*), there is an increase or decrease of two breaths and three *pāṇīpala*s per day and night over the course of the three months.

This increase or decrease of two *liptās* (pāṇīpala) per day and night should be understood to occur in the region of Kailāsa and in the regions of the Āryas and so forth. Over a period of three months from the middle solstice (*viṣuva*), an increase or decrease of three *nāḍīs*—equivalent to thirty days and nights—should be understood according to the [solar] course (*ayana*).

Now, the time of rising of the twelve ascendants according to the division of the Kailāsa [Sakhaṇḍa] is stated: In the Aries ascendant, there would be 900 liptās; in Taurus, 2400; in Gemini, 1560 ghatis; and in Cancer and Leo, likewise. In Virgo, it is indeed six and a half. All this applies in reverse order starting from Libra. This same [calculation] applies to the setting of the six ascendants, as well as to the sun and the lunar mansions. (63)

"Liptā syānmeṣalagne" means that here, in the case of Aries lagna, the time from the first rising until the next lagna rises is a mass of *liptās*—that is, *pāṇīpala*s—equal to two hundred and ninety, which is the "sky-nine-hand" (*gagananavakara*) figure. Therefore, by dividing this by sixty, the time for the rising of Aries lagna is four *ghaṭikās* and fifty *pāṇīpalas*; such is the rule in the region of Kailāsa.
"Khartu-netra (260) should be for Taurus"— thus,
the time of the rising of the Taurus ascendant is a mass of 260 *pāṇīpala*s, which is four *nāḍīs* and twenty *pāṇīpala*s.
For Gemini as well— "ākāśa-kha-de" (200)— the time of rising for Gemini also is a mass of 200 *liptās*, which is three *nāḍīs* and twenty *pāṇīpala*s.
"Arrows and tastes in ghaṭikās" means that five ghaṭikās are the time of rising for Cancer (Kulīra) as the ascendant;

then, for Leo (Siṃha), "tastes" means six ghaṭikās at the time of the ascendant's rising; for Virgo (Kanyā), "six and a half" means the time of the rising of the Virgo ascendant is six ghaṭikās and thirty pāṇīpala-s, which constitutes six and a half.
All [the times] from Libra (Tulā) onwards follow this same sequence in reverse order.
Therefore, from the time-limit of the first six signs, in the other six signs beginning with Libra, [the calculation proceeds] in reverse order;
by this method, everything becomes complete without remainder—this is the rule.

Here, at the time of the rising of the ascendant, the rule for the region of Kailāsa is as follows: in Libra, six *ghāṭikās* and thirty *pāṇīpalas*; in Scorpio, six; in Sagittarius, five; in Capricorn, three *nāḍīs* and twenty *pāṇīpalas*; in Aquarius, four *nāḍīs* and twenty *pāṇīpalas*; and in Pisces, four *ghāṭikās* and fifty *pāṇīpalas*.
"By six signs, this has set, thus it is said to have risen. For indeed, because it has risen by six signs, it therefore sets.

Regarding "by the divisions of the asterisms of the sun": at the end of thirteen and a half asterisms, it sets; likewise, at the end of thirteen and a half asterisms, it rises. By the division of day and night, through six signs and thirteen and a half asterisms, the time of day occurs; through six signs and thirteen and a half asterisms, the time of night occurs. Day and night become shorter or longer according to the time of the rising of the signs, due to the movement of the sun.

Now, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the body, the number of breaths and so forth for the days of a hundred years in the central channel (*madhyamā*) is stated, beginning with "one thousand twenty-one," and so on: "One thousand twenty-one, increased by one hundred flavors (six), have emerged through the tooth-parts; those breaths in excess within the body at every daily time are numbered as 'element-mountain' (seven). Even when multiplied by thirty-six thousand, this is the well-known measure of a hundred-year lifespan. Divided by zero-fire (three), it results in *ghaṭikās*; and from the sixty-fold division, a day arises. (64)
It enters into one thousand, two tens of thousands, one thousand more, and six hundred plus six;
thus, by the tooth-portions, it has emerged from this heap by thirty-two parts.

In the body, regarding those breaths that exceed [the daily count] at the time of each daily transit (saṃkrānti) through the twelve zodiac signs (*dvādaśalagna*), the well-known measure for a hundred-year lifespan is six hundred and seventy-five thousand breaths—this number being multiplied by thirty-six thousand. Those breaths, when multiplied by the thirty-six thousand days of a hundred years, constitute the total measure of breaths for a hundred-year lifespan.

In this context, the daily breaths of three nāḍīs, numbering two thousand one hundred and sixteen, when multiplied by the number of days in a hundred years, become seventy-seven crores and six hundred and seventy thousand.

The breaths of the central channel, *avadhūtī*, are those obtained by dividing [the total] by thirty-two, numbering two crores and forty-three lakhs; the remaining seventy-five crores and thirty-three lakhs are the carriers of the five *maṇḍalas* in the *lalanā* and *rasanā*. Of these, divided equally, half flow through the *lalanā* and half through the *rasanā* from the left and right respectively until the end of the hundred-year limit. The *ghaṭikā* (unit of time) is produced by dividing [the total breaths] by zero, seasons, and fire (360).
Then, the heap of breaths divided by three hundred and sixty yields the heap of ghaṭikās; from the sixtyfold portion, the days are obtained.

Then, the quotient obtained by dividing the heap of *ghaṭikās* by sixty becomes the *dinapiṇḍa* (the sum of days) for the *madhyamā* [channel]. From the thirty-six thousand [breaths], the remainder—the *dinapiṇḍa* of three *ayutas* (30,000), eight hundred and seventy-five—is to be known as the duration of the hundred-year limit for the *lalanā* and *rasanā*. Thus it is said: Now, the measure of the hundred years of the eight planets, through their enjoyment of the wheel and a half (*sārddhacakra*) as a single aggregate, is as follows: in the Moon, when devoid of the Sun, there is a fortnight; in the Sun, a solstice (*ayana*); in Mars, nine months; in Jupiter, a night; in Venus, six years; and in the Son of the Moon (Mercury), a solstice.

O King, the years known as the lunar days (tithis) are sixty; likewise, in the year of the Sun (śauri), there are nine minus Ketu. All that, added together as a single sum, consists of eighty-four years and three and a half months. || 65 ||
[71b] Regarding "the fortnight in the moon" and so forth:

"the fortnight in the moon" means that the moon's fortnight consists of one night comprising thirty *daṇḍas*, due to its enjoyment of half the circle of the zodiac signs (*rāśicakra*). Likewise, for the sun, there is also the solstice (*ayana*); thus, the sun's solstice is half a day. As for the phrase "and devoid of the comet, O King," no such Sanskrit commentary is seen here, and likewise, it does not exist in the Tibetan translation either.
In the chapter on the Great Summary of the Method for Knowing Luminosity: [the night] occurs due to the enjoyment of half the cycle;
there are nine months, and on Mars, the night is likewise—this is the intended meaning of the calculation.
Thus, there would be six years for Jupiter.

Just as it is for the Sun, so too is the revolution (*ayana*) for Bhṛgu (Venus), and the revolution for the Moon’s son (Mercury) and Budha (Mercury) consists of fifteen years known as *tithis*. For Saura (Saturn), that is Śanaiścara, it is nine years; and for Tamina (Rāhu), it is half a day and night (*ahorātra*), arising from the enjoyment of half the circle of asterisms (*nakṣatra-cakra*).

All of this, taken as a single aggregate, amounts to eight times the years of a *yuga* (eighty-four years), thirty-two years, and three and a half months; such is the division of the *sattva* quality among living beings.

That number [of breaths] in half a day may also amount to one hundred years; this is the mantra known as Kālacakra. The vital breaths flow within beings during the states of passion (*rajas*), darkness (*tamas*), and goodness (*sattva*); through the divisions of body, speech, and mind, they reach the state of fivefold dissolution.
Therefore, O King, for gods, humans, and serpents, this number is well-established and certain in Kālacakra as occurring in half a night of the moon. (66)

That number [of breaths] in half a day is due to the enjoyment of the circle of constellations together with the [twelve] signs; through the division of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, there would also be one hundred years minus the *Kālacakra*—that is, a total of ninety-six years plus ten and a half months, less three years and three fortnights—since the eight planets are a single aggregate. Thus, the vital breaths flow within *sattva*.

In this [world], for beings, the vital breaths and the qualities of being flow within the *sattva* state for thirty-two years and a half; thereafter, they proceed to dissolution in *rajas* by that same measure, and then in *tamas* by that very same sequence. From that limit, under the influence of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, gods, humans, and animals [pass away] according to their own respective lifespan of one hundred years.
"By half a night of the moon and by three fortnights of the *kālacakra*"; by the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that through the previous three years, transmigrating beings here undergo death.

This is worldly convention based on the scriptural statement, "Man has a lifespan of a hundred [years] and a hundred faculties. However, according to ultimate reasoning, there is no fixed rule for sentient beings; their arising and cessation must be understood by Buddhists as being under the power of their own respective karma.
Thus, the statement "Man has a lifespan of a hundred [years] and a hundred faculties" is *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).

The Puruṣa, whose nature consists of the four yugas, is characterized by thirty-four lakh and twenty thousand breaths externally; internally, he likewise consists of the four yugas by that same measure of breath, at which time all the planets enter the void. This is the reasoning of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-yukti*).

Furthermore, the lifespan of sentient beings becomes shorter or longer according to the power of their virtuous or non-virtuous [karma]; there is no fixed rule that one lives for exactly one hundred years, as stated in the words of the Tathāgata.
Thus, this number is well-established and perfectly determined in the *Kālacakra*, the King of Tantras.
"Narendra" is an address for Vajrapāṇi;
"Sucandra" is not the sequential order [of the address]— thus [it is] for the Guru.

According to the Tibetan [translation], this is not present in the *Vimalaprabhā*. Now, regarding the sixty-part *ghaṭikās* of the central *avadhūtī*, the *ghaṭikās* for the movement of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) of the five planets beginning with Mars—their aggregate—is stated as "not severed" (*nocchinna*), and so forth: "In the *Kālacakra*, which is not severed, having added nine [units] for the debt of the solstices (*ayanarṇa*), the total *ghaṭikās* of the movement for the five [planets] in their swift operation (*śīghrakarma*) belong to the planets beginning with Mars."

On Mars, four and three (seven) prevail in the planetary positions according to the division of the planets; they are to be applied to the divisions of the places in the eastern and western halves, according to their respective positions in the movements of debt and credit. (67)

When the wheel of time has not been cut off—within the period of three years, three fortnights, and one day—and when the two solstices (ayanāni) numbering one thousand one hundred and twenty-five have not been interrupted, one adds nine units of debt for the [solar] year and nine debt-ghaṭīs for the nine months of gestation; thus the total aggregate of ghaṭīs becomes eleven hundred and thirty-four in number. This is for the five [planets] in the calculation of the *śīghra-karma* and the *nakṣatra-karma*. Furthermore, regarding the *caraṇa-ghaṭī* of the planets beginning with Mars: for Mars, it is four, six, two, and three; from these, for Mars, it is three hundred and sixty-four.

There is a numerical calculation: the aggregate of *ghaṭikās* is "bha" (15); in the fourteen-fold division of the forest station (*vanasthānaka*), it is derived from the enjoyment of thirteen and a half lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*);
and by means of the divisions of motion (*cāra*), such as the twenty-fourfold divisions and so forth.

The [nakṣatra] divisions are equal in the first and second halves; by virtue of the movement of the constellations, there are one hundred and eighty-two nakṣatras in the first half and one hundred and eighty-two in the second half, as they are halved again and again.
Regarding "in the movements of debt and wealth":
according to the stated sequence, they should be applied to the different positions in the movements of debt and, respectively, in the movements of wealth.

The constellation risen from the solar disc is the first position; from that division of positions, there are fourteen other positions. By means of those divisions of positions, those *ghaṭikās* are to be applied. First, the number of Jaina-Indras (twenty-four) prevails as the *ghaṭikā*; then three times "fire-eye" (thirty-six); then twice "with one" (two); then "eye-less" (zero), eighteen, fifteen, and eleven. Here, fifty-three, thirty-eight, and eighty are the durations in the state of the worlds. When that sun is purified, there is both debt and wealth, by way of reverse and direct order respectively. (68)

In the first [place], the number of Jaina lords is twenty-four, which is the portion of the first lunar mansion; outside, the "two eyes" (2) and "threefold" (3) prevail, making twenty-three, occurring in three ways from the first position to the second, third, and fourth.
In two places, it is "one eye plus one" (21); then, from the fourth position, in the fifth and sixth positions, it is twenty-one, occurring in two places.
[The sequence continues as] eighteen, fifteen, and eleven.

Then, from the sixth position, in the seventh, eighth, and ninth positions, there are respectively eighteen, fifteen (as indicated by *tithi*), and eleven (*harā*). Outside, starting from the root, the "excellent" (*vara*) is three; then from the ninth position, in the tenth position, there are three "wheels" (*cārā*); then from the root, in the latter half, in the eleventh position, there are eleven *harā*.

In the twelfth [station], there are thirty-eight; in the thirteenth, eighty; and in the fourteenth station of the abode of stability, there are fifty-three—meaning fifty together with three, thus fifty-three. This is the rule for the fourteenth station.

When the Sun has been purified in that half-circle of constellations (*nakṣatrārddhacakra*), a debt occurs in reverse order and wealth occurs in direct order; for Mars and the others, a debt in the lunar mansion's usage is to be subtracted, and wealth is to be added.
Thus, there is no end [to this].

[In this] chapter, the Great Instruction on the Method of Knowledge of Luminaries: In the calculation for the swift motion of Mercury, there arises a number of *ghaṭikās* equal to the Vedas (4), mountains (7), and moon (1), i.e., 170. In two places, there are sixteen; then fifteen (tithi), eleven (manu), and five (madana); then eleven (rudra), seven (śaila), five (indriya), and zero (kha).

From the root, four (veda) and three (dhara) are clearly established as fixed. In the twelfth [place], twenty; and twenty-eight, thirty-four, and fourteen (manu) are situated according to the divisions of the days. (69)
In the calculation of the swift motion (śīghrakārya) of Mercury, the number of *ghaṭikās* is produced as "Veda-adri-randhra-indu" (4708).

Here, the total mass of *ghaṭikās* for Mercury is one hundred and ninety-four; just as the mass of its own *ghaṭikās* for Mars is placed in the fourteenth position, so too should it be understood for Mercury.
Regarding the "swift operation" (*śīghrakarma*) and the "stellar operation" (*nakṣatrakarma*), there are sixteen in two places: sixteen in the first place and sixteen in the second place as well.
Others say the lunar days are as follows: fifteen in the third, fourteen in the fourth, thirteen in the fifth;
Rudra (eleven), Śailendra (seven), and Kha (zero) [in the sixth];
eleven in the sixth, seven in the seventh, five in the eighth, and zero in the ninth.
From the root [position] comes Vedādhara.

Then, from the ninth position, in the latter half of the root [position], four are to be placed in the tenth position, eleven in the eleventh, twenty in the twelfth, twenty-eight in the thirteenth, and thirty-four in the fourteenth.
Thus, established in their respective order, the ghaṭikās of Mercury are to be understood through the divisions of the *āra*.
This total of *ghaṭikās* is indeed four hundred and one; and for the Guru [Jupiter], it is in two places: ten, nine, eight, six, five, and one from the *mūla*.
Fire, six, apertures, Rudras, kings, and sages are the movements of all [the planets] in order.
This is the rule for the host of planets in their fast, slow, and retrograde motions as they move according to the divisions of the Sun.

The aggregate of one hundred and four *ghaṭikās*—numbered as "unbound" (*abadhya*) and "moon in the sky" (*ākāśendu*)—is divided according to the divisions of the *cāra* (movement) into fourteen places of the Guru.

From that aggregate of *ghaṭikās*, in two places there are ten each, the measure of the directions: ten in the first place and ten in the second; in the third, nine, as "nights" (*vasu*) and "seasons" (*ṛtu*);
in the fourth, eight; in the fifth, six; and "six-rayed moon" (*ṣaṭkarendu*) means six in the sixth; two in the seventh; and one in the eighth.

From the root [number] up to the second half [of the sequence], there are six, five, and four; thus, in the ninth [house] there are three, in the tenth six, in the eleventh nine, and in the twelfth eleven.
"Kings and sages" refers to sixteen in the thirteenth, and seven in the fourteenth house; these are all the movements in order.
In this way, the ghaṭikās for all the movements of all the planets are to be understood according to their respective sequence.

In the case of swift motion, the rule for the host of planets is that they move in the eastern half during the rising of the planet, and in the western half during slow motion; in retrograde motion (*vakra*), they move in the eastern half in reverse order, and by the word "and" (*ca*), in the western half in reverse order during emergence. They move according to the divisions of the Sun's subtraction from the Sun. There are sixty *ghaṭikās* in number for the Moon in the calculation of swift motion; for Venus, there are twenty-five in three places, and likewise, the hands and eyes (*2512*) should be divided into two parts.

The defects are derived from the eighth root of the lunar days; and the six, as well as the hundred diminished by one and nine, multiplied by the sky-qualities (0), constitute the number for Venus (Bhṛgu) according to the *Vimalaprabhā*: "six, moon, and ocean" (146). Therefore, the *ghaṭikās* are in three places: twenty-five in the first place, likewise twenty-five in the second and third; "twice the Victors" (24) in the fourth; likewise in the fifth; and "hand and eye" (22) in two ways, thus twenty-two in the sixth.
In the seventh [house], there are eight defects;
in the eighth, eighteen; in the ninth, fifteen; in the eighth, eight; then from the latter half of Mūla, six and also thirty (khaguṇa);
in the eleventh, six; in the twelfth, thirty; and in the thirteenth, one hundred less one.
In the fourteenth [station], it is the number of fire-mountain, which is seventy-three.
The movements of Venus in the fourteen stations of the state of stability are to be understood in sequence.
For Saturn, the number of six elements prevails.
O King, this aggregate of ghaṭīs from the beginning [of the cycle] is six, five, four, four, four, ocean [four], eye [two], pair [two], and zero;

then fortnights [two], Vedas [four], elements [five], flavors [six], Vasus [eight], and fire [three]. These should be established in sequence; thus the entire, well-determined motion of the planets occurs within the Kālacakra. ||72||
The "six elemental numbers" of Saturn (*sauri*) constitute a total of fifty-six *ghaṭikās* in the fourteenth place for Saturn;
from that [total], there are six in the first quadrant (*pada*), five in the second, five in the third, and four in the fourth—thus: *ṣaḍ-bha-tā-bha-ta-veda*.
Regarding the phrase "the eyes of the ocean" (*jalanidhinayana*): there are four [nāḍīs] in the fifth [house], two in the sixth, a pair [i.e., two] in the seventh, and zero in the eighth.
From that root, the latter half follows:

two in the ninth (two *pakṣau*, four *vedās*, and five *bhūtās*), four in the tenth, five in the eleventh, six in the twelfth (six being the *rasas*, *vasus*, and *śikhis*), eight in the thirteenth, and three nāḍīs are to be established in sequence in the fourteenth place for Saturn.

Thus, the movement of the planets is perfectly determined as a whole in the Kālacakra; that is, within the wheel of breath-days in the central channel (*madhyamā*), there are one hundred years in the Kālacakra, which constitutes the enjoyment (*bhoga*) of the rising movements and *ghaṭikās* of the planets.

Now, for the sake of the slow motion (*mandakārya*), the slow steps (*mandapada*) of the birth-constellation *ghaṭikās* are stated: "The thirty-six and a half months multiplied by the Vasus (eight) indeed become the steps in the slow motion; and the number of eyes (two), apertures (nine), and eyes (two) becomes the *ghaṭikās* for the planets beginning with Mars."
The true positions (tattvas) are eighteen for Mars; for Mercury, they are sixty-one in the western and eastern halves; and for Jupiter, they are ninety-one in the eastern and western halves. 73.
"Thirty-six," and so forth:
thirty-six half-months constitute the thirty-six months of three years; by taking one fortnight from the three fortnights, it is indeed certain (*khalu*).

"Multiplied by the eight qualities" means multiplied by the eight qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, smell, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; by these eight qualities multiplied, the *pada*s of the five planets in their slow motion (*mandakārya*) are produced.
From the eyes [2], the number of *randhra* (nine) and *akṣi* (two) is two hundred and ninety-two; this is the number of *ghaṭikās* in the zodiac signs (*rāśi*).
Therefore, in the six steps of the manifest [planets] beginning with Mars, they should be known in reverse order in the first half and the second half.
Their own [values] are eighteen and seven (*ka*).
It is not in the manuscript [at this point in the chapter].
Regarding the "Great Chapter on the Method for Knowing the Luminaries":

"The position of the son of the Earth (Avanisuta) in the latter half and the former part" means that the principles (*tattva*) are twenty-five, eighteen, and seven—where "mountains" (*adri*) signifies seven; these refer to the latter half and the former part of the son of the Earth, Maṅgala, respectively.
Thus, for Mercury, the directions, mountains, and fires: "directions" means ten, "mountains" means seven, and "fires" means three. Likewise for Jupiter (the teacher):
"eleven, nine, and fire"—these are the three for Jupiter, Bṛhaspati.

The remainder is according to the previously stated sequence, both in the first part and the subsequent part. For Venus, [the daily motion] is 141; for the Moon, it is 26; for Mars, it is 59 ghaṭīs per month; and for Mercury, it is 51. Thus, the sum of the piṇḍas for Venus and Mercury is 190. This is the monthly motion in days, minutes, and seconds for these three, which over three months constitutes their annual motion.
Thus, for Venus, [the values] are five,
four, and one— namely, "five" (*iṣu*), "four" (*adhi*), and "one" (*candra*).
In this way, for Venus, it becomes twenty-four days (*sākṣinetraṃ dinatuḥ*).
The eyes of the witness are twenty-two, the days are fifteen, and the seasons are six; this sequence has been stated previously.
Thus, the *ghaṭikās* for the movement through the zodiac signs—obtained by dividing sixty by eight times the monthly consumption of the Kālacakra—should be understood.

Now, the consumption of *ghaṭikās* equal to the number of days in three years, resulting from the three-sign consumption of the five planets beginning with Mars, is described starting with the words "in a month": "The consumption of Mars in a month is ninety *ghaṭikās*; this is worldly convention (*lokarūḍhi*). In its true nature, the *ghaṭikās* obtained by means of the portion of the mandala are [the actual value]."

A month also consists of thirty and a half days. Therefore, according to the measure of the Siddhānta, ninety *ghaṭikās*—the result of subtracting the three planets from the Sun while including the movements of Jupiter and Saturn—is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). It is not correct to state that the number for Venus is "five times the moons" (fifty-five), because that contradicts the authority of the Siddhānta. Since the Sun's movement is subtracted from Venus to yield Venus itself, the total *ghaṭikā*-count for the monthly movement of Venus is one hundred and thirty-five.
It is the same for Mercury as well.
The sum of the [mean] days (*kharasa*) and the fire-eater (*hutabhuj*) combined into a single mass becomes the mass of three hundred and sixty *ghaṭikās*.
In manuscript Gha, the portion beginning with "the principles" (*tattvāni*) and ending with "in sequence" (*krameṇeti*) is absent; this section is also missing from the Tibetan translation.

In manuscript Gha, the portion beginning with "iti" and ending with "tisraḥ" is absent; this section is also absent in the Tibetan translation. In manuscript Gha, the portion beginning with "ekādaśaḥ" and ending with "krameṇeti" is absent; this section is also absent in the Tibetan translation.
In manuscript Gha, the portion beginning with "śukrasya" and ending with "candra ekaḥ" is absent.

In the Tibetan translation, however, the portion beginning with "of the semen" and ending with "the season is six" is absent. In manuscript *gha*, the text from "is joined" in verse 86 up to "by the power of the moon's steps" is missing.
[According to the Tibetan:

In the Vimalaprabhā, regarding the five [elements] of the world-system: "By means of these three months, there are the days of the year, the debt, and the ghaṭīs; one thousand eighty ghaṭīs are the share for these three," as stated in the Siddhāntakaṭakṣa, thus it was proclaimed by Mañjuśrī. [75a]

The monthly motion of Jupiter is thirty ghaṭīs, with the number of pādas (quarters) being eleven; the motion of Saturn is thirty sphuṭa yuga-ghaṭīs (fourteen ghaṭīs). These, when unified, constitute a day;

and that same value multiplied by three is a month and a half, including the night. In the case of the other six planets, there is a daily subtraction from the days in their respective motions. || 75 ||
"Devotion to the Guru should be maintained for one month," and so forth—this verse from the Siddhānta was stated with a specific intent (*kaṭākṣārtha*) in order to eliminate worldly misconceptions.

In this regard, those who hold that the three fortnights (*tripakṣa*) are related to the rising and transit of Ketu have been declared as the fundamental view (*mūlasiddhānta*) concerning the five planets; therefore, they should not be added to the transits of Jupiter and Saturn.

Now, the transit of Ketu is described based on the transit of Rāhu: "That which has not yet been traversed by the planets during the month of the Lord of Wealth (Venus), even in the slow-motion calculation (*mandakarma*), [is equal to] seventy-three and a half ghaṭīs of transit within that very month."

The monthly revolution of Rāhu is the position of the Sun and Moon diminished by half a nāḍī; that of the Sun is three ayanāḍīs; on the day of the Moon's love (the fifth lunar day), the revolutions of the Moon are five nāḍīs. [Verse 76] "One month," etc.

Here, in the calculation of the slow motion (*manda-kārya*), regarding the remainder of thirty-six and a half months, that very month which has not yet been traversed by the planets is multiplied by eight. From that, one-sixtieth part—eight *ghaṭikās*—is to be taken; of these, seven and a half *ghaṭikās* constitute the monthly revolution of Rāhu.
"In that very place" refers to the motion of Rāhu within the measure of a solar month.

Regarding "the positions of the Sun and Moon": the Sun has three quarters consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; the Moon has five quarters consisting of the qualities (*guṇas*) of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound. These eight quarters constitute the seven and a half *ghaṭikās* of Rāhu; the remaining half-*ghaṭī* is of the nature of being devoid of darkness (*nistama*). [The time] diminished by that is reduced by half a *nāḍī*. At the commencement of the first fortnight of the Capricorn transit (*makarasaṃkrānti*), when the Sun is in Tiṣya (Punarvasu), there are three *nāḍīs* consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which constitute the enjoyment of wealth.
Thus, in the first fortnight of Cancer, there is the enjoyment of debt.

On the day of the moon’s love (the first day), in the first *pada*, when fourteen parts remain in the place of the *piṇḍa* or in the thirteenth, there are five *nāḍīs* of the Moon, consisting of five-fold qualities.

That half-*nāḍī* not yet consumed at the time of the seasonal day (*ṛtudina*) is the Moon diminished by a digit; that indeed becomes an excess for the Sun, calculated as four *yugas* in a solar month—that is the day.
The *nāḍīs* of Ketu are obtained from the monthly course of Rāhu multiplied by twelve and divided by the fortnightly course; this is from the monthly course of Rāhu at the time of each day.

[In the chapter on] the Great Exposition of the Method for the Knowledge of Astrology (Jyotirjñānavidhimahoddeśa): when half a *nāḍī* has not been traversed—that is, when it has not been traversed by Rāhu—at the time of the sixty-four days of the season (*ṛtudina*), that is the moon with diminished digits; the meaning is that the digits of the moon are lost.

That [day] would be an extra day for the Sun; having become two *nāḍīs* for the Sun, it becomes an extra day every day multiplied by the yuga, according to the rule "multiplied by the Vedas and the lunar days" (*vedaistithyāhatam*), and so forth. That very day which is the middle day of the month becomes the extra one. It should be understood that in a solar month—a month of solar transition (*saṃkrānti*)—that single extra day is precisely the middle constituent part.

Regarding the phrase "from the moon's portion multiplied by the eyes": from Rāhu’s "seasonal portion" (ṛtubhoga), which is fifteen ghaṭikās, one should divide by the "fortnightly portion" (pakṣabhoga) and then divide by four minus one-quarter; the resulting *nāḍīs* for Ketu are four at every time of day. Furthermore, having multiplied Rāhu’s monthly portion by seven and a half *liptās*, it is indeed multiplied by the qualities (three); Ketu moves together with the Sun, being ahead when one subtracts [the correction] from the Sun’s portion, and behind during its swift motion (*śīghracāra*).

In its course, it moves by degrees from the solar orbit at two and a half liptās day by day; in thirty-six good months, it traverses [the zodiac] along with the ghaṭikās multiplied by the lunar days of the world. || 78 ||
Having subtracted seven and a half *liptās*, there remain three *likās* and three breaths (*śvāsas*).
When these are multiplied by three, they become twenty-two and a half *liptās*; this is the intended meaning of the *karaṇa* according to its formal nature.

Since the daily motion of the sun is four *nāḍīs* and twenty-six *pāṇīpala*s when multiplied by three and a half, one should subtract [the former] from the solar longitude according to the intended meaning of the *karaṇa*.

This solar revolution consists of four ghaṭikās and twenty pāṇīpala-s daily; according to the Siddhānta, it is six pāṇīpala-s more. One should subtract this from the solar revolution; the remainder after subtraction becomes the *caraṇa*. Ketu moves together with the Sun: in its forward motion (*śīghracāra*), it moves in regular order (*krama*) ahead of the Sun, and in its retrograde motion (*vakracāra*), it moves in reverse order (*utkrama*) behind the Sun. In its course, it moves two liptā-s every day, either in regular or reverse order, according to the solar revolution.

He moves for thirty-six good months along with the *ghaṭikās*. [The number of days] struck by the lunar dates of the world is struck by three and multiplied by fifteen, which is forty-five. For one and a half months, there is an increase of two *nāḍīs* every day; whether in direct or retrograde motion, at the front or the back, as long as it lasts for one and a half months, its rising is visible in the mortal world.

Furthermore, when he enters the glorious Kālacakra, even if he is invisible during his annual course (*varṣabhoga*), once his degrees of rising (*udayāṃśa*) are known, his rising is known for infinite time. (79)

For one and a half months, there is an increase of two *nāḍīs* every day. At the conclusion of three years, having abandoned the movement in *liptās*, for three fortnights, the movement of two *nāḍīs* occurs daily—both in front during direct motion (*śīghra*) and behind during retrograde motion (*vaktra*).

Thus its rising lasts for one and a half months; however, for one month it is smokeless (*nidhūma*), and then for the final fortnight it is smoky (*sadhūma*), whereby it becomes manifest to living beings as a comet (*dhūmaketu*).
Through its coming and going, one month passes, and with the abandonment of smoke, it appears like a star.
Furthermore, when that [Ketu] enters the three-year period within the Śrī Kālacakra, it becomes invisible during its annual course.
Once its rising degrees are known—in this way, when the rising degrees of that Ketu are known—its rising is understood to occur at an infinite time.

Now, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the mandalas of the planets are described—the days of the three years of Kālacakra multiplied by twenty-five, diminished by the days of the solstices, and increased by nine: "The days of the year multiplied by five, further struck by five (the arrows), and diminished by the days of the solstice, become the mandalas of the planets according to the power of their own motion. For Mars, the number of days is sixty-seven; for Mercury, it is eighty-seven; for Jupiter, thirty-four; and for Venus, twenty-two. (80)
"Varṣāhaḥ," and so forth.

A *varṣāha* is one thousand eighty; that very number, when multiplied by five—that is, struck or multiplied by five, as the word "iṣu" signifies—becomes twenty-five times the value of the *khaṇḍa*. Thus, it is multiplied by twenty-five.

The solar year consists of one hundred and eighty days. [The planetary revolutions] are diminished by that [number]; due to the motion of the planets in the single path (*ekāyana*), the days of the single path are subtracted. "Holes" (*randhra*) means nine; the circles of days for the five planets, according to their respective motions, are three hundred and six, mixed with eight. When these are totaled together, they amount to sixty-two thousand, eight hundred and twenty-nine. Then, for Mars (*bhauma*), "mountains, snakes, and six" (*śailāhiṣaṭka*) refers to a total of six hundred and eighty-seven days.
In the north, for the Naga [Mars], it is eight thousand seven hundred and ninety-seven;
for Mercury, it is four thousand three hundred and thirty-two; for Jupiter, it is two thousand two hundred and forty-seven;
and for Venus, it is two thousand two hundred and forty-seven.

The number of days for the solar mandala is one hundred and sixty-six; for the son of the Sun (Saturn), it is one hundred and seventy; for Mars, it is indeed one hundred and eighty; for Mercury, it is one thousand minus that [eighty], which is nine hundred and twenty; for Venus, it is ten times that number of days minus four and eight, which is ninety-two thousand; and for the son of Mantri (Jupiter), it would be a debt of one hundred and twenty-eight thousand.

On Mars, [the correction] is nine and a half plus half a degree; on Mercury, it is one degree; on Jupiter, it is six; and on Venus, it is the square root of ten (three). One should subtract all these from the middle motion. O King, thereafter, the correction for those planets arises from their movement through the birth asterism. For a planet in its sign of debilitation, the correction occurs within its own division; for one in exaltation, it occurs within the twelve signs by virtue of its motion. || 82 ||
Six times six [is] thirty-six; with the sky [0] added, it becomes one hundred and thirty-six thousand seven hundred and sixty—the number of days for the mandala of the Sun’s son (Saturn).
As for Mars and the others, it is as previously stated, up to the two verses in the commentary beginning with "Mars is mountain and arrow" (*śailaveṅka*).

Now, for the sake of purifying the birth [horoscope] of the planets, the collection of asterisms (*nakṣatra*) is stated: The monthly consumption [of asterisms] multiplied by six months shall be divided by the months of a *Kālacakra* year; the quotient obtained is a debt. Even for the Sun and Moon, there is no half-*nāḍī* that has not been consumed.
Six times six [is] one hundred and eight;

O, this is the great instruction on the method of astrological knowledge in the chapter [on] Ketu. That which is greater than the fear of Ketu must be multiplied at every time of day by the days of the Moon; and by a sixtieth part, it becomes a nāḍī at every time of day, both for the swift motion and the retrograde rising.

In the Siddhānta, it is established that purity is attained after six months for what was consumed during a month; however, depending on the disposition of sentient beings (*sattvāśaya*), there is a dependence on specific actions.
Thus, when Ketu rises, the position of its course is multiplied by twenty-one days, resulting in a total of one hundred and twelve and a half *liptās*.
It should be understood that this very amount occurs daily from the rising of Ketu, and thus the calculation must be performed accordingly.
"Whatever half-nāḍīs are obtained in the place of the asterism's debt," says Mātṛmodaka, for the sake of maturing sentient beings.

Now, the strength of the planets' motion (cārabala) is described: Mars and Mercury are powerful when moving swiftly; Mars and Ketu are powerful when retrograde; Saturn and Venus are powerful when slow, according to the influence of their natural qualities. In other motions they are weak. When moving swiftly, they face east; when entering retrogression, they face west; when moving slowly, they face south; and upon emerging [from retrogression], they face north, according to the quality of their own movement. ||84||
"Sauma" and so forth: Saumya is Mercury; Mantrī is Jupiter; when risen during its swift motion (*śīghracāra*), it becomes powerful and effective in the first half [of the zodiac].
Mars and Ketu—Mars and Ketu—are powerful when they have completed the curved path (*vakre*) in the half-mandala, due to their retrograde movement (*utkramabhogāt*).

Mars, Saturn, and Venus are strong in the latter half [of their periods] according to the order of slowness; this is due to the influence of the qualities of their natures, or rather, due to the influence of the qualities of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*). In the remaining three movements, Mars and the others are weak.

In the swift [motion], they face the east: all planets, during the first half of their swift course, face the east; furthermore, having entered retrograde motion, they face the west (the other direction) in the second half according to the sequence of slow motion, due to the influence of the qualities of their own movement; and upon emerging, in the second half, they face north in reverse order—this statement is for the purpose of determining the strength of the earth based on the *Svarodaya*.

The positions of the sun and moon are stated: the thirty days of a month multiplied by four (the oceans) equal eighty-four; this is the position of the moon among the twelve zodiac signs. The position of the sun is four times eight (thirty-two). Within that, the decrease and increase occur respectively in reverse and direct order due to the motion of the solstices, across each half of the circle; O King, the total calculation should be understood as sixty-four.

The thirty-six days that are destroyed by the ocean, multiplied by four, become thirty; this is the "moon's" [pada], which is one hundred and twenty—the number of the sky (zero), eyes (two), and moon (one). For the purpose of increasing the digits of the moon over a period of seven days, it will be stated later:
the twelve zodiac signs, multiplied by four, become forty-eight, which is the "sun's" pada for a period of six months. That same point will be stated later;
here, the rule for these *padas* is given merely in summary.

In the midst of that, the decrease and increase occur in reverse order due to the movement of the solstices; the total count of eight and four (forty-eight) should be understood as forty-eight counts when intended for the purpose of calculation (*karaṇa*),
O friend,
since such is your [view].

In the chapter on the Great Exposition of the Method for Knowing the Luminaries, the characteristics of Rāhu’s entry into the lunar disc are now described, beginning with the words "at the junction of the lunar phases" (*parvacchede*) and so forth: "At the junction of the lunar phases, Rāhu enters the disc of the moon; the [Rāhu] disc enters the [moon] disc, and there is a total eclipse, which is purified according to the power of the moon. When half is purified, there is a partial eclipse; the duration in *nāḍīs* exists according to the power of the moon. The eclipse occurs at the time of day or night for the sun and moon, and in the dark or light fortnights, as previously stated. (86)

[In the cutting of the world-sphere, at the end of the full moon, or at the end of the new moon, the orb of the moon enters the orb of Rāhu; here, by the word "orb" (maṇḍala), sixty ghaṭikās are meant, which is the complete enjoyment of one lunar mansion (nakṣatra), and that should be understood as consisting of twelve zodiac signs (rāśi) or sixteen digits (kalā), according to the nature of the total eclipse. A total eclipse becomes pure if the movement of the moon is completely purified by the movement of Rāhu; then the total eclipse lasts for the duration of sixty nāḍikās.]
When half the orbit is pure—that is, when half of the moon's course is clear—the orb consists of sixty nāḍīs and sixteen digits (kalās) due to the movement of the moon.
Thus, by the power of the moon's movement, as long as a nāḍī remains within the orbit of Rāhu, the conjunction of the planets should be known to last for as long as one-fourth of a digit (kalā).
This [calculation] regarding the birth and other details of Rāhu in the Siddhānta is to be understood in detail for the sake of external knowledge.
In this tantra, Mañjuśrī did not reveal it due to the brevity of the cause;
rather, only that which is suitable for internal application has been stated here in summary.
Thus, all such matters as the planetary conflicts and so forth are to be understood from the Siddhānta.

In this tantra, there is a dependence on the Siddhāntas regarding the subject of astrology, such as planetary conjunctions and so forth; however, the Blessed One’s rule is that there is no intention to discuss planetary conjunctions in the context of the inner self (*adhyātma*). When an external eclipse occurs, the grasping of *śukra* (the white constituent) takes place within the inner self; the rule that the grasping of *rajas* (the red constituent) occurs from the solar eclipse does not apply everywhere. Therefore, the Blessed One’s rule is that for the sake of thoroughly understanding the external, the Siddhāntas of Brahma, Sūrya, Yama, and Romaka must be known.

Now, the entry of all the planets into the zero-position at the end of the four ages is described, beginning with "of humans" and so forth: The hundred-year lifespan of humans, when multiplied by the planetary daily motion, results in two figures; the portion obtained by dividing by ten (the directions) becomes a debt which one should subtract from the [first] figure.

One hundred thousand plus six thousand, and the number of six years, likewise occurs in the first half of the age; furthermore, by means of two signs, the fixed number of years for the four ages arises. (87)

That which is one hundred years for humans is multiplied by the annual movement of the planets according to the *Kālacakra*. Thus, by means of a planet’s movement over one and a half days, there is a movement of one hundred years; by three days, two hundred; by thirty days, two thousand; and by thirty days plus sixty, there is a movement of twenty-four thousand years. When that [period] is multiplied by one hundred years and placed in two locations, it is divided by ten. The quotient obtained by the tenfold division is to be subtracted as a debt from the upper heap (*rāśi*). What remains is one hundred and twenty-six thousand (126,000); thus, it is not [otherwise].

In the chapter on the Great Exposition of the Method for Knowing the Luminaries: when the number of years is twenty-one lakhs and six thousand, that constitutes the *yugas*. From the end of half a *yuga*, there are five steps—four steps of the Kṛta *yuga* and one step of the Tretā *yuga*. Half a *yuga* consists of the spheres of space, wind, fire, water, and earth; in due order, this is the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the lord’s left channel.
Furthermore, by means of two signs, and again by the second sign consisting of five steps...

In that regard, there are two quarters for Tretā, two quarters for Dvāpara, and one quarter for Kali, consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and space respectively. Thus, the movement of the Lord’s vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the right channel consists of five mandalas in sequence.

In this way, by means of the two zodiac signs (*rāśi*) and the years of the mandalas of both channels, the number of years for the four ages (*yuga*) is twenty thousand plus two [thousand]. Here, for each individual age—

Zero, zero, sky (0), elephants (8), hands (2), sages (7), and moon (1) is the measure of the Kṛta Yuga; for Tretā, sky (0), sky (0), zero (0), tastes (6), arms (2), and suns (12) is the well-known number of years; for Dvāpara, zero (0), sky (0), Vedas (4), tastes (6), and serpents (8) are the correct years; and for Kali, sky (0), space (0), eyes (2), qualities (3), and oceans (4) shall be the number of years. (88)
"Zero, zero, sky, snake, hand, sage, and moon"—this is the measure of years for the Kṛta Yuga, due to the enjoyment of the positions of the four mandalas.
"Sky, sky, zero, taste, and sun"—this is the well-known number of years for Tretā.
"Zero, zero, sky, Vedas, taste, and serpent"—thus, sixty-four thousand plus eight hundred thousand years correctly constitute the years of Dvāpara.
"Zero, sky, eyes, and oceans of qualities"—this is the number of years in the Kali age.

Thus, for Tretā it is three quarters, for Dvāpara two, and for Kali one quarter; consisting of three, two, and one mandalas respectively, each mandala corresponds to the duration of a year in the Kali age.

By these years, at the end of the yuga, the movement of the host of planets comes to rest in the zeroth sign, with the asterism beginning from Aśvinī, and again starting from Prabhava, as well as the month beginning with Caitra.

At that time, the day of the week, the lunar mansion, the lunar day, and the karana will likewise be unfavorable; during that period, a fierce battle between the gods and the demons shall take place upon the surface of the earth. (89)

"At the end of these years, the movement of the host of planets remains in the void of the zodiacal signs. Regarding "at the end of these years," this refers to the aforementioned end of the *yuga*, that is, the end of the four *yugas*.
The phrase beginning with "the host of planets" is easily understood.
At the end of Revatī, [the zodiacal sign] remains empty;
furthermore, the consumption of the constellations beginning with Aśvinī by the planets occurs.
It happens according to the Prabhava cycle, and likewise the Caitra month and so forth occur.
The day, the yoga, the lunar date, and likewise the karaṇa were present at that time—
namely, Sunday (Ādityavāra), the Viṣkambha yoga, the first lunar day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight, and the Vava karaṇa, and so forth— at that time.
[This] was not written for the gods, but rather an exposition is being undertaken.
Following this, it is introduced:
therein, it has come down thus—“The houses will be empty; there is no doubt.
Chapter [XV]: In the city of Vāgadāyā, which is the abode on the surface of the earth for the barbarian Dānavas, a fierce battle will take place.

Then the commencement of the Kṛtayuga will take place. Now, since the planetary positions in terms of lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth are currently situated at total zero (*sarvaśūnya*), the production of the constants (*dhruvaka*) is stated again:

"Therefore, when multiplied by the [number of] asterisms (*ṛkṣa*) and also by sixty *nāḍikās*, the motion (*bhukti*) of the planets arises from the [total] circle (*maṇḍala*); it is fixed and obtained through division."

When the month is complete, it will certainly occur again; the solar transit through the asterisms within the divisions of the days and nāḍīs becomes the count of days, with one month subtracted. || 90 ||
Thus [it is said].
This verse is not found in printed editions, nor is it found in the Tibetan translation of the root text; however, it does indeed exist in the *Vimalaprabhā* and its Tibetan translation.
The venerable Tibetan master Khedrup Je accepts this verse as part of the root text.
Therefore, this [verse] is also accepted here as being part of the root text.

The venerable Ācārya Khedrup Je, in his own commentary on the *Vimalaprabhā* titled the *Vidyāsāgara* (*Rig pa’i rgya mtsho*), page 90, has expressed his own view that this verse numbered ninety is indeed from the *Mūlakālacakra-tantra*.

They have established this: although the Tibetan translator, the venerable Locavā Śoṅ-ton, did not provide a translation for this verse during the course of his translation of the *Mūlakālacakra-tantra*, and thus its translation was not presented in his own Tibetan version, nevertheless, that omission of his work is clearly of the nature of an error.
It appears that the Sanskrit manuscript he obtained for the purpose of translation was itself of such a kind—lacking this verse and containing such a gap.
If this were omitted, the number of verses in the first chapter would be deficient.
Furthermore, the venerable Khes-ḍub-je himself, having identified this verse as the root text in Vibhūticandra’s own Sanskrit manuscript, has provided an explanation for it.
Considering all of this, this verse is also accepted here as part of the root text.

In this regard, a certain statement by the venerable Khesa, Ḍuba, and Je is presented here; namely: "It is very clear that these verses beginning with *de ni sgyu skar rnams kyis* are the root text (*mūla*). Furthermore, when examining the Indian manuscript of the tantra in the personal collection of Vibhūticandra, they are present there, and in his manuscript of the commentary as well, there are distinct marks indicating they are treated as the root text. Accordingly, they must certainly be accepted as the root text.

Since the commentary on the verses of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* by Candrakīrti is also incomplete, the fact that this [verse] does not appear within the root text of the earlier translation clearly indicates a fault arising from translating from an incorrect manuscript.
The Sanskrit equivalent for the aforementioned Tibetan portion is the verse beginning with *tasmādṛkṣaiḥ*.
It is quite evident that this is a root verse (*mūlakārikā*), because this verse exists in its original form within the handwritten manuscript of Vibhūticandra.
Even in the manuscript of the *Ṭīkā*, this verse is accepted as being the root verse (*mūlakārikā*) itself. Therefore, it is certain that this verse is indeed a root verse.

[In the chapter on] the Great Chapter on the Method of Knowledge of the Luminaries (*jyotirjñānavidhimahoddeśa*): Now, the constant values for months (*māsadhruvaka*) are stated according to the years of the *Kālacakra*: "The six groups [of consonants], together with the vowels (*sārkamātrāḥ*), multiplied by the qualities (three), are indeed the three years in the Sun; the first [group] called *svādi* (the labials), with the digits of the moon multiplied by three, are the month and a half in the Moon."

The channels beginning with Ha, together with their measures, multiplied by three, constitute the three nights of Rāhu; and the [channels] beginning with the venerable Śūnya and Anāhata, multiplied by three, constitute the three ascendants of Rāhu. || 91 ||
"The six groups [of consonants] together with the vowels (*sārkamātra*)":

the six groups—*ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and *sa*—consisting of thirty letters each, characterized as consonants (*vyañjana*), become three hundred and sixty syllables when combined with the twelve vowels, due to the distinction between short and long vowels: *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, aṃ, aḥ*. By means of these, each individual letter beginning with *ka* becomes divided into twelve varieties; thus, the thirty consonants, divided by these twelve varieties, amount to three hundred and sixty.

Furthermore, those letters beginning with *ka* are differentiated by the qualities of others (*paraguṇaiḥ*) through the substitutions of *yaṇ*; indeed, they are multiplied by the *guṇas*. The *guṇas* are: *a, e, ar, o, al, aṃ*; the *vṛddhis* are: *ā, ai, ār, au, āl, āḥ*; and the *yaṇ* substitutions are: *ha-hā, ya-yā, ra-rā, va-vā, la-lā, haṃ-hā*.
Thus, there are three years consisting of one thousand and eighty days in the solar [cycle]; these consist of the letters beginning with *ka*.

The first fifteen short vowels, known as "days," are the fifteen digits of the moon multiplied by three; together with the distinctions of short, long, and protracted [vowels], they constitute three and a half fortnights in the lunar [cycle].

In that regard, the vowels of the three fortnights (*tripakṣasvara*) are as follows: *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ; a-e-aro-al-ha-ya-vara-la; lā-vārā-yā-hā; ālū-au-ār-ai-ā; lu-ū-ṛ-ī-ā; ā~ ī ṝ oṃ ā~ aiṃ ā; au āla~; hā~ yā~ rā~ vā~ lā~*.

The channels (*nāḍīs*), numbering sixty, consist of the letters beginning with *ha* according to the division of the twelve zodiac signs (*dvādaśalagna*). By the previously mentioned method, the short vowels [correspond] from midday until midnight; the long vowels [correspond] from midnight until midday, numbering thirty.

The five [cakras] beginning with Śrī, Śūnya, and Anāhata are conjoined with the three junctions (trilagna) through the divisions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and by way of the natures of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; this is the rule regarding Rāhu and the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*). Furthermore, O King, the elements are numbered as twelve (the sun and moon); having subtracted one month and three fortnights, there remains one and a half months, which is the *Kālacakra* as determined by the best of sages.

The day of the week (*vāra*) is the [first] thrower, and the mass of jars (*ghaṭapiṇḍaka*) is twice the number of kings (two). Below that is the wheel (*cakra*), and the day of the week is divided and regulated by sixty deities.

If this verse were not a root verse (*mūlakārikā*), then the root text would be incomplete. Therefore, it is understood that the non-inclusion of this verse in the version translated by the great scholar Śoṅ-ston Lo-tsā-ba was a deficiency; he performed his work of translation based upon an incomplete manuscript. Thus it stands.
ga. gha. ṛ ṝ u ū; gha. ṝ u (not found in the manuscript).

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the number of elements, suns, and moons is again divided by three years and three fortnights; thus they become one thousand one hundred and twenty-five. "Hendupa" means "O King," referring to the three fortnights and the half-month. Having indeed set aside the half-month, and therefore having excluded that half-month, the remainder becomes one thousand and eighty.

Then, when that same [number] is divided by the seven excellent sages (7), the quotient obtained is the small *Kālacakra* consisting of one hundred and fifty-four; the remainder of the division, being two, represents within the mandala the nature of Wisdom and Means. That very [remainder] is the single revolution in the monthly constant (*māsadhruvaka*); having added thirty-two *ghaṭikā*s and the pair of aggregates, as well as one lunar day (*tithi*) and five movement-steps (*cārapada*) to the wheel, the revolution is thus divided into one hundred and fifty-six in the *Kālacakra*, meaning by sixty *ghaṭikā*s of deities.

And thirty-two nāḍīs [are added] for the deity multiplied by the eight qualities of the Sage; two piṇḍakas are to be given and subtracted, and the first lunar station (*śaśipada*) consists of five and five here.

By six, there would be three fortnights of the Moon multiplied by three, which is well-known in the solar calculation; and when divided by sixty, on the first day of the Sun, there are eleven nāḍīs along with the elapsed portion (*sabhoga*).

With thirty-two *devatīs* [or] *ghaṭikās*, the monthly constant (*māsadhruvaka*) is placed in the position of the *ghaṭikās*; with fifty-six *devatīs*, two lumps (*piṇḍa*) arise in the position of the lumps, which are to be added or subtracted, and one *devatī* remains. There are five *devatīs* for five steps; with five and one together, it becomes six.

Thus, for the Moon, three fortnights are forty-five days, which, when tripled, consist of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and this is well known in the solar calculation (*sūryabhoga*).
And there are two *dhruvaka*s for the asterisms, divided by two hundred and sixty *nāḍikās*.
On the first day of the Sun, when multiplied by four, eleven *nāḍīs*—that is, eleven *nāḍīs* beginning with four *ghaṭikās*—occur in the place of *nāḍīs*; this is the rule everywhere.
This venerable Kālacakra, together with the host of planets, is non-different from the external bodies; it is the Sun in the form of Time within the abode of the three worlds.

The cause of withdrawal and expansion, through the various divisions of wisdom and means, and by means of even and uneven families and swift or retrograde movements, is not known by those free from passion—the lineages of supreme sages, nor by the gods such as Brahmā and Rudra. (94)

This Śrī Kālacakra, together with the host of planets, according to the sequence stated in the passage beginning with "this Śrī Kālacakra together with the host of planets," is non-different from the external [world] and the bodies, being the cause of dissolution and expansion. The three worlds—desire, form, and formless—reside within that abode which is the nature of time and the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). [The phrase] "for one thousand and ten days" does not appear in the manuscript (pustaka); it is also absent in the Tibetan manuscript (bho. pustaka).

Although this is not present in the two manuscripts— and it is likewise absent in the Tibetan translation— nevertheless, the Tibetan master Khes Ḍub Jé Mahābhāga, following his own usage in his Tibetan commentary, has calculated the time in this very manner.
This is correct.

[In this] chapter, the summary of the rules for the method of the instruments of the arising of vowels (*svarodayayantravidhi*) is an address to Mañjuśrī: "O Sūryaratha! [This is taught] through the divisions of wisdom and means related to the *Laghutantra*, through the divisions of day and night, through the divisions of the moon and sun, and so forth; through the even and uneven families. 'Even' refers to the long vowel, and 'uneven' refers to the short vowel. It has not been understood by those free from passion—the supreme clans of sages, nor by the gods such as Brahmā and Rudra—due to their movements being swift, curved, and so on."

Thus, by the previously mentioned method, this Bhagavān Kālacakra—who abides in the form of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), who is all-pervasive within all things pervaded, whether stationary or moving—was not known by these [beings] beginning with Brahmā. However, just as he was known by the Bhagavān Samyaksambuddha, the Omniscient One, in both his mundane and supramundane forms of conventional and ultimate reality, so too has it been revealed to Sucandra Vajrapāṇi; and by me, O Sūryaratha, that very same Bhagavān Kālacakra has been briefly revealed through Mañjuśrī Yaśonarendra.

Thus ends the ninth great chapter on the method of the knowledge of astrology in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* in twelve thousand [verses], which follows the glorious *Mūla-tantra*. 9.

(10) The Great Chapter on the Rules for the Instrumental Method of the Arising of Vowels (*Svarodayayantravidhiniyamamahoddeśa*). Now, the arising of vowels (*svarodaya*) is explained: The first five vowels, by virtue of the first lunar day (*tithi*), produce [their effects] here at the end of their rising when conjoined with the "five joys" (*pañcananda*) and so forth, O King, provided that Mars (*bhauma*) and the other weekdays are not present there.

If indeed there is an unfavorable rising of Mars, and furthermore, it is conjoined with the asterism Kṛttikā, then for men there will be battle and disease; if it is the rising of the first vowel, there will be death.
"Ādi" (beginning with), etc.:

those vowels of which "a" is the first are the five "initial" ones—namely, *a, i, u, ṛ, lṛ*. This is because of the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term) *aiuṇ* and *ṛlṛk* as stated by Svayambhū (*Śivasūtra* 1–2). Furthermore, due to the reading *e o(ṅ)* and *[ai au]c* (*Śivasūtra* 3–4), the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) *ikāra* and *ukāra* [are included]. Here, the portions of manuscript *ka* and *kha* are missing; moreover, the commentary for manuscripts *ka* and *kha* is not available from this point of the missing portion up to the end of the first chapter (*paṭala*), and only the root text remains.

Henceforth, the citations from the commentary in manuscript Ga are presented; its variant readings are provided from manuscript Gha [80b]. Following this, the page numbers of manuscript Ga are introduced within square brackets [ ]. There is also a distinction in the presentation.

The ninth great chapter on the method of knowledge regarding astrology, within the twelve-thousand-verse commentary *Vimalaprabhā* on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja*, extracted from the glorious *Mahādibuddha*, concerning the movements of the swift wheels and so forth, which are of a conventional nature.
In this manuscript, from the word "ādityādi" up to "ādyā," the text is unclear.

At those various places where the readings are indistinct, the readings have been supplied here solely on the basis of manuscript *gha*, which was stated by Svayaṃbhu; *gha* [is] the unmanifest of Svayaṃbhu.
There is nothing further in the manuscript;

henceforth, the page numbers for manuscript *ga* are provided in brackets, whereas previously there would have been no page numbers for manuscript *ka*. This is because, since the vowels *ṛ* and *lṛ* do not differ from *i*, *u*, and so on in terms of their *guṇa* quality, the common worldly convention among beginners is: "ai u ṇ"; "[ṛ] lṛ [k]"; "e o [ṅa]".

The rule *iko yaṇ aci* is an exception (*viśeṣa*) to the principle that *aiuṇ* and *ṛlṛk* are produced from *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, and because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *ako 'ki dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101; though it is more simply stated as *ako 'ki* in the *Siddhāntakaumudī*, following the commentary on the sūtra *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*).

Those five vowels which were first explained by the Self-Arisen One (*svayambhū*) are of identical form; however, by the power of the primordial elements (*prakṛti*) such as space and so forth, they were written down by Mañjuśrī in his own grammatical treatise (*vyākaraṇa*) according to their respective order: *ai-u-ṇa*, *ṛ-ḷ-k*. These possess the natures of space, wind, fire, water, and earth respectively. Likewise, *a-e-ara-o-ala* and *ha-ya-ra-va-la-ṭa* were taught by Mañjuśrī through the application of *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and *yaṇādeśa* substitutions, based upon the reliance on the inherent natures of their respective primordial elements.

Regarding those five vowels [arising] by the power of the first lunar day (*tithi*): there are five initial lunar days—namely, the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth of the bright fortnight (*śukla*) according to the division of darkness (*tamas*). By virtue of these, specifically by the power of the first lunar day, there are the five yogas beginning with *Nanda* for the [five] vowels. For the five vowels, *Nanda* is the first lunar day, *Bhadrā* the second, *Jayā* the third, *Riktā* the fourth, and *Pūrṇā* the fifth. In this same manner, it is so for the sixth and subsequent days, as well as for the eleventh and subsequent days.

If, in this conjunction beginning with Nandā, one performs [the rite] at the end of the rising [period], and there is no weekday such as Mars and so forth—meaning, if on Nandā there is Mars, on Bhadrā Mercury, on Jayā Jupiter, on Riktā Venus, and on Pūrṇā Saturn—if on these starting from Nandā there is no weekday such as Mars and so forth, then it is a "rising" (udita); otherwise, it is an "unfavorable rising" (aniṣṭodaya). O King, when there is an unfavorable rising on a Tuesday (Bhauma), if it occurs on Nandā, then there is indeed a conjunction with Kṛttikā. Therefore, if on the lunar day (tithi) of Nandā there is battle or disease, death occurs for men—the meaning is for the first vowel, i.e., for that man or woman whose name begins with the letter 'A' (akāra).

O, those which are the five notes (*pañcasvara*) are of an identical nature, for they were prophesied by the Self-Arisen One (*svayambhu*).

[In the section on] the rules and regulations for the *svarodaya* instrument, in the chapter [on] the Great Summary: If it is the second day, Bhadrā, and the lunar mansion is Saumya (Mṛgaśirā), the king dies, provided there is the conjunction with Maghā on this day. If on the day of Jayā, the lunar mansion is Aśleṣā and Jupiter occurs, the third [person] goes to death.
If Dhaniṣṭhā falls on a new-moon day, Bhṛgu goes to his death; if Bharaṇī occurs on a full-moon day with Saturn, the fourth [planet] goes to his death. The fifth [planet] goes to his death.

Thus, on the Bhadrā tithi, if the Maghā asterism occurs, then one whose name contains the second vowel *i* dies. Likewise, on the Jayā tithi, if Bṛhaspati is in Aśleṣā, then one whose name contains the third vowel *ṛ* dies.

Similarly, on the Riktā tithi, if Śukra is in Dhaniṣṭhā, then one whose name contains the fourth vowel *u* dies; and likewise, on the Pūrṇā tithi, if Śani is in Bharaṇī, then one whose name contains the fifth vowel *ḷ* meets his death.
In this way, for the vowels that have risen in joy, there occurs a death-yoga by virtue of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) and the day of the week (vāra).

When the Sun [is the weekday], there is injury even to those who have risen in joy, and indeed affliction for the sick. When the Moon (Soma) is present, it invariably prevails over those who have risen in the Bhadra yoga; likewise in battle and in disease.
It should be known that when the Pañca yoga has arisen, it yields great fruit, being free from the death-yoga, in matters such as journeys to a country and marriage.

In illness and warfare, there is likewise an inauspicious or auspicious result. Thus, on Sunday, for those born under the *Nanda* [lagna] ascendants, a wound occurs in battle; for the sick, suffering ensues. Similarly, on Monday, this should be understood to apply to those born under the *Bhadra* ascendants. Truly, for those born under the five *Udayas*—the *Ākāra* and others—when they arise on their respective lunar days (*tithis*), there is great fruit provided it is free from the conjunctions of death (*mṛtyuyoga*). That very point must be known by one who observes omens, regarding the inauspicious or auspicious results in illness and warfare, as well as during journeys to foreign lands and at the time of marriage.

Thus, in this system, the lunar days, asterisms, weekdays, and the groups of vowels (*svaragaṇa*) arise through the divisions of the five elements (*pañcatattva*) within a month, a solstice, and a year, as well as in the sixty-year cycle (*ṣaṣṭisaṃvatsara*).

Here, the arising of the twelve limbs occurs starting from Caitra; that same division of fortnights (*pakṣabheda*) constitutes the arising of the seventy-two [elements] and so forth. In the division of months, there is the arising of the vowels (*svarāṇām*).
The letter *i* is named "Moving"; *ya-ya-ri-la-vā*; it dies.
He dies.
