O friend! Thus, among the sixty years beginning with Prabhava, the five vowels arise in their respective order for each year. Through six months, the movement of the limbs of the solstice (ayana) occurs; through twelve years, the movement of the face of Prabhava occurs. In this way, the rising and setting of the five vowels shall happen repeatedly here. In the first [year], the vowels are children by virtue of their own lunar-day qualities; in the second, they are glorious youths; in the third, they are mature; in the fourth, they are aged, in sequence; and in the fifth, on the day of the fire-ocean (14th), they have set.

99 || The rising [of the breath] occurs every six months, with twenty-four revolutions; furthermore, according to the method previously described, there is the rising of the solstices (*ayana*), and the rising of the twelve years beginning with *prabhava*. Thus, the rising of the years, including the revolutions, *prabhava*, and so forth, is to be understood. In this way, the rising of the five vowels occurs here, for they indeed set again. In this regard, regarding the division of the fortnights (*pakṣa*), *nandā* lasts for twelve days; likewise, *bhadrā* and the others [last the same]. Regarding the division of the months, *nandā* lasts for seventy-two days, and at that time, *bhadrā* and the others do as well.
In the division of the solstices (*ayana*), *nandā* is the solstice; likewise for *bhadrā* and the others.
In the division of the years, *nandā* lasts for twelve years, and likewise *bhadrā* and the others pass by.

At the beginning, first are the vowels (*svara*); "the children" (*bālāḥ*) are the consonants (*sva*). This is according to the power of the lunar days (*tithi*), and according to the power of the qualities of space, air, fire, water, and earth—as well as the qualities of sound, touch, taste, form, and smell—respectively.
Here, the letter *a* arises in Nandā, the letter *i* in Bhadrā, the letter *ṛ* in Jayā, the letter *u* in Riktā, and the letter *lṛ* in Pūrṇā.

Thus, on the second day from each respective day of their arising, the venerable Kumāras are as follows: the letter *i* in Bhadrā, the letter *i* in Jayā, the letter *ṛ* in Riktā, the letter *u* in Pūrṇā, and the letter *lṛ* in Nandā. Regarding the "mature" (*prauḍha*) and "old" (*vṛddha*) states, they become mature on the third day from their own day—corresponding to the sequence of fire and ocean days—as follows: in Jayā, the letter *a* is mature; in Riktā, the letter *i*; in Pūrṇā, the letter *ṛ*; in Nandā, the letter *u*; and in Bhadrā, the letter *l*.

On the fourth day, the vowel *a* is "increasing" (*vṛddha*) and is its own lunar day (*tithi*). [In the section on] the Great Chapter concerning the Rules for the Method of the Yantra of Svarodaya: *a* is increasing during the *riktā* tithi; *i* during the *pūrṇā*; *ṛ* during the *nandā*; *u* during the *bhadrā*; and *lṛ* during the *jayā*. On the fifth day, they become "set" (*astaṅgata*): *a* is set during the *pūrṇā*; *i* during the *nandā*; *ṛ* during the *bhadrā*; *u* during the *jayā*; and *lṛ* during the *riktā*. Thus, the fivefold distinction of the vowels, such as their rising and so forth, should be understood.

The first five vowels, when multiplied by the qualities (*guṇa*), become thirty in two ways; all of them are to be joined with the letters of the consonant groups beginning with *ka*, according to the influence of the qualities of nature (*prakṛti*). Here, the rising of the short vowels occurs during the bright fortnight through the division of the five elements, while that of the long vowels occurs during the dark fortnight, fixed by the yoga of emanation and withdrawal.
100. Indeed, those which are the first five vowels, when multiplied by the qualities—that is, multiplied by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—become fifteen.

These thirty syllables of the *pūrṇā* [group] are indeed: *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, ai, o, au, aṃ, aḥ*, and *ha, ya, ra, va, la*. These are the threefold *nandā* and others in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). Likewise, in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the *nandā* and others are: *lā, vā, rā, yā, hā*, and *ā, lā, au, ā, ra, ai, ā, ḷ, ū, ṛ, ī, ā*. Thus, for the thirty lunar days (*tithi*) of both fortnights, they are to be joined respectively with the consonantal letters beginning with *ka*, according to the influence of the qualities of *prakṛti*. All those vowels—short ones in the bright fortnight—are to be applied through the divisions of the five principles (*pañcatattva*).

In this context, whatever consonant is pronounced with a short vowel has its arising (*udaya*) in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*); for long vowels, it is in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). Thus, whatever long consonant is pronounced with a long vowel, its arising is in the dark fortnight. Regarding these consonants, one should understand the sequence of solar transits (*saṃkrānti*), due to the application of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).

The twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the *sphuṭaśara* (clear arrow) *ghaṭikās*, and the nine divisions (*navāṃśa*) of the solar ascendant (*sūryalagna*)—these are of three natures: fixed (*sthira*), mobile (*cala*), and perfectly equal (*susama*), beginning here from the ascendant of Aries (*meṣalagna*).
Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn are the movable signs here; the remaining two are fixed, and the others are dual-natured; they always rise during the times of day and night respectively.
101. There are twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) in that group; among them, with two and a quarter lunar mansions each, there are twelve solar signs (*sūryalagna*).
These are the nine degrees (*navāṃśa*), consisting of five *ghaṭikās* each, known as the "clear arrow" (*sphuṭaśara*).

Furthermore, these are of three natures: the vowels (*svarāḥ*) are movable (*cala*), beginning with Aries (*meṣa*); the consonants are fixed (*sthira*), beginning with Taurus (*vṛṣa*); and the semi-vowels are dual-natured (*sama*), beginning with Gemini (*mithuna*).

Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn are the four movable signs (*caras*); Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius are the fixed signs (*sthiras*); Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces are the dual-natured signs (*dvisvabhāvas*). Thus they are. In this context, "at the time of inquiry, with the movable signs there is a swift result; 'result' (*kārya*) refers to the task at hand."

Always arisen throughout day and night, twelve [signs] are stable through the stable [elements], and twice through the dual-natured [elements] in the middle; therein, within the duration of a day, there are thirty *muhūrtas*, and sixty *nāḍikās*.
Here, at the beginning, the rising of the twenty vowels occurs in every *muhūrta*;

the thirty syllables of the consonant groups prevail in each *ghaṭikā* according to the division of short and long [vowels]. Thus, in the center of the moon, the risings and settings are declared in the portion of the lunar days (*tithi*). || 102 ||

In that [group], there are even thirty muhūrtas; in that collection of signs, there are even thirty muhūrtas within the duration of a day consisting of eight watches (praharas). Even a single nāḍikā becomes sixty [in that context].
At the beginning, in the first muhūrta, there shall indeed be the rising of the twenty vowels here, in every muhūrta.

Regarding the phrase "in the lunar day-part, within the moon": having divided a single lunar day (*tithi*) into thirty *muhūrta* segments, the thirty vowels arise according to the sequence of creation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) on each individual lunar day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), as follows: the vowels beginning with *a* on the first (*pratipad*); those beginning with *i* on the second; those beginning with *ṛ* on the third; those beginning with *u* on the fourth; those beginning with *ṝ* on the fifth; those beginning with *ḷ* on the sixth; those beginning with *e* on the seventh; those beginning with *ai* on the eighth; those beginning with *o* on the ninth; those beginning with *au* on the tenth; those beginning with *ha* on the eleventh; those beginning with *ya* on the twelfth; those beginning with *ra* on the thirteenth; those beginning with *va* on the fourteenth; and those beginning with *la* on the full moon (*pūrṇā*). Then, in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the thirty vowels arise on the first lunar day, Nandā, according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). There, on the first day, [the vowels] beginning with *la* (*lākārādi*); on the second, those beginning with *va* (*vākārādi*); and so on for all the days.

The rising and setting [of the vowels] are indeed declared to occur within the moon, specifically in the lunar day (tithi) division; for from that moon, what vowel was uttered at the beginning of the white fortnight (śukla-pratipad) and so forth sets at the beginning of the black fortnight (kṛṣṇa-pratipad) and so forth. Zero, wind, fire, water, and earth are the family of the first five vowels. Rāhu, Agni, Indra, Ka, Soma, Bhṛgu, Guru, and the weak one (Śani) have the Sun, Rudra, and others as their presiding deities.

In each of the previously mentioned single ascendants, the number of nāḍīs must be calculated according to the duration of night and day; within that [period], whichever vowel occurs as the planet is the powerful one in the mandala, and by means of it, the calculation is to be performed. || 103 ||

"Empty" refers to wind, fire, water, earth, and the family (*kula*) of the five primary vowels; thus, according to the sequence previously stated, the family of *ā* and the other vowels begins with space (*ākāśa*).

The presiding deities are the planets beginning with Rāhu, corresponding respectively to the short and long vowels: Rāhu and Kālāgni are the [deities] of the short and long *a*; Candra and Ravi are those of *i* and *ī*; Budha and Bhauma are those of *ṛ* and *ṝ*; Śukra and Guru are those of *u* and *ū*; and Ketu and Mandāgni are those of *lṛ* and *lṝ*. [This applies also to] the *guṇa* vowels beginning with *ā*, and so forth.
[In the section on] the *lākārādi* [letters],
the *vākārādi* [letters],
and so forth, in the chapter on the rules for the method of the *svarodaya* instrument: here, the presiding deities are according to the proper system.

Thus, in each of the twelve ascendants, the *nāḍī* [the number of breaths] is to be calculated there according to the duration of night and day; at the rising of the current ascendant, there are five months (or degrees). Among those, whichever vowel has occurred is the "planet," which is powerful; by that, the mandala is to be calculated. It is to be calculated according to the distinction between odd and even ascendants, beginning with space (*śūnya*) and beginning with earth (*pṛthivī*). On the left, there is the rising of the short vowels here, and on the right, of the others. On the left is the principle (*tattva*) beginning with space, and the entire host of planets, led by Rāhu, moves [there].

In the center is the reality consisting of the elements beginning with earth; the regulation of the host of planets occurs through the son of the Sun (Saturn) and so forth. Or else, externally, the time-measure (*kālanāḍī*), equal to the houses of the planets and accompanied by vowels, should be accomplished. || 104 ||

On the left is the arising of the short vowels; here, on the left, at the odd conjunctions (*viṣamalagna*), there is the arising of the consonants of the short vowels, while on the right, at the even conjunctions (*samalagna*), there is [the arising] of the others, the long-protracted consonants.

Thus, on the left, the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Space, the five mandalas alternating [with the others], and the movement of the host of planets beginning with Rāhu—namely, Rāhu, Candra, Budha, Bhṛgu, and Ketu—are all present.

In the center, at the southern ascendant, is the reality consisting of the fivefold mandala beginning with Earth; the rule for the host of planets begins with the Son of the Sun (Saturn), namely Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, and Kālāgni.

Here, in Capricorn as the equal ascendant, there are five ghaṭikās; according to their respective order, the consonants pronounced with the long vowels—beginning with the vowel *a* and its *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* modifications—arise.

In this regard, *kā* arises in the first *ghaṭikā* in the earth mandala; *khā* in the second in the water mandala; *gā* in the third in the fire mandala; *ghā* in the fourth in the wind mandala; and *ṅā* in the fifth in the space mandala. Thus, the consonants beginning with *ka*, when uttered together with the vowels beginning with *ā*, arise in sequence within the five mandalas of Capricorn (*makara*).
Similarly, in Aquarius (*kumbha*), the consonants beginning with *ṅa*, uttered with the short vowels, should be understood to arise in reverse order within the five mandalas beginning with space.

Therein, *ṅa* arises in the first *ghaṭikā* in the space-maṇḍala; *gha* in the second; *ga* in the third; *kha* in the fourth; and *ka* in the fifth in the earth-maṇḍala. Likewise, *cā chā jā jhā trā* arise in Pisces (*mīna*); *ña jha ja cha ca* in Aries (*meṣa*); and so on in the five maṇḍalas. Similarly, *ṭā ṭhā ḍā ḍhā ṇā* arise in Taurus (*vṛṣa*); *ṇa ḍha ḍa ṭha ṭa* in Gemini (*mithuna*), in the five maṇḍalas.

Thus, *pā*, *phā*, *bā*, *bhā*, *mā* are in Cancer; *ma*, *bha*, *ba*, *pha*, *pa* are in Leo, in five mandalas. Likewise, *tā*, *thā*, *dā*, *dhā*, *nā* are in Virgo; *na*, *dha*, *da*, *tha*, *ta* are in Libra, in five mandalas. Similarly, *sā*, *yā*, *ṣā*, *śā*, *kā* are in Scorpio; *kha*, *ya*, *sa*, *dha*, *na* are in Sagittarius, in five mandalas.
At the rising of each *ghaṭikā*, the consonants are the presiding deities.
In that context, the vowel uttered along with a consonant becomes the "consonant-vowel" (*varṇasvara*), while the vowel itself becomes the "life-force-vowel" (*jīvasvara*).

That life-force-vowel is to be understood according to the divisions of the lunar quarters (*candrāṃśa*)—distinguished as short or long—and according to the divisions of the *muhūrta*s, as previously described.
The emergence of the consonant (*vyañjana*) is to be understood according to the divisions of the *ghaṭikās* of the ascendant.

In this battle, when the life-force vowel (*jīvasvara*) has set, there is death; when the phoneme vowel (*varṇasvara*) has set, there is a wound. For the sick, there is death or suffering. Nevertheless, here in the first letter of the name, there is no consonant; in that case, there is only the vowel as the life-force, so there is no fear.
O, the six (parts):
in the *Vimalaprabhā*, [it is stated that] there is the "vowel-sound" (*svara*) and the other is the "consonant-sound" (*varṇasvara*).
Thus, within the self, the arising of the consonants (*vyañjana*) is to be known through the distinction of the flow in the mandalas of the left and right nostrils.

Or, the "external time-channel" (*kālanāḍī*) refers to the channel that has arisen at that specific moment; it is equal to the external planetary houses (*bāhyagrahabhavana*), meaning the circle of the planetary houses. It should be practiced together with vowels and consonants for the sake of thoroughly discerning the auspicious and inauspicious.

Now, the results of the auspicious and inauspicious [planetary positions] are stated according to the inquiry, beginning with the words "in the inquiry," etc.: "In the inquiry, at the time of battle, death prevails when the wind [planet] arises in the void of time (*kālaśūnya*); and there shall be defeat as well as wounds when the Sun, Fire, or Mars arise."

If Jupiter is in the junction of water signs, there will be no battle; if it is in the rising of earth signs, there is death. There will be suffering, wounds, and even happiness, as well as equanimity for the querent who is ill. || 105 ||

When a question is asked at the time of battle, death prevails if [the breath] has arisen in the *kāla*, *śūnya*, or *agni* [mandalas]; and for one whose name is addressed first when [the breath] has arisen in the *kālāgni* and *śūnya* mandalas of the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*), whether he be a king or a common man, his death occurs with certainty.

Likewise, defeat occurs when the Sun has risen in the wind-mandala of Vāyu; a wound also occurs when there is the rising of the Earth and Fire mandalas; a fracture occurs when Jupiter has risen in the water-mandala; and indeed, no battle takes place in the conflict when the slow [Saturn] has risen in the Earth-mandala—such is the rule regarding questions.

Thus, when a questioner asks whether for a patient there will be death, affliction, a wound, happiness, or equanimity respectively in the empty mandala and so forth, it occurs for the patients as follows:

in battle, the destruction of the enemy certainly prevails during the rising of Rāhu in the empty [mandala], and likewise in the wind and moon [mandalas]; however, there is defeat and even wounds in battle during the rising of the gentle [Jupiter] and fire [Mars]. When Venus is in water, there is gain of wealth and even the enemy becomes submissive; thus it is in journeys and marriages. During the rising of the Earth-Ketu (Bhūmīketu), there will be many fruits on the left-hand path (vāmamārga) by means of the planets.

"In battle, there is the destruction of enemies": here, the first-mentioned result, "destruction of enemies in battle," necessarily occurs when Rāhu rises in the void-maṇḍala (*śūnya-maṇḍala*) in the left nostril.
The word *ca* (and) is for the purpose of completing the meter.
When Vāyu rises in the wind-maṇḍala, there is fortune (*bhaga*). O gentle one, when Śukra rises in the water-maṇḍala, there is also a wound; when [the Sun] rises, there is wealth, that is, gain.

Even an enemy becomes submissive when the Bhūmiketu [ascendant] rises at the time of the first utterance regarding a matter of battle; likewise, it yields great fruit in matters of journey or marriage. When a question is asked according to the Left-hand Path (vāmamārga) by means of the planets, this is the rule for the rising of the Ascendant (lagna) at the time of inquiry. [In this] chapter, the Great Section on the Rules for the Method of the Svarodaya Instrument, the inquiry concerning vowels is now stated, beginning with "by the messenger" and so forth: The vowels indeed uttered by the messenger are multiplied by ten, mixed with the zodiacal circle (rāśicakra), and further multiplied by five (bhūta). These, added to the number of nearby people, are reduced by a remainder of seven.

When the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn occupy odd-numbered houses, there is no success for men; however, when Mercury, Venus, or Jupiter occupy even-numbered houses, the accomplishment of one's purpose will occur.

The vowels spoken by the messenger, when multiplied by ten and further multiplied by the left and right mandalas, are then mixed with the twelve signs of the zodiac; these, again multiplied by five (the elements) and joined with the "near person"—that is, joined with the person standing nearby, excluding the omen itself—are [the result].

Regarding the phrase "the remainder of seven" or "the remainder of the day's enjoyment": when the Moon is situated on the first day, Fire on the third day, Arrow on the fifth day, and Aḍau (Drau) on the seventh day—if these remainders persist, there is no success for men. However, if the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn are on odd-numbered days; if the Eye (Netra) is on the second day, the Veda (Veda) on the fourth day, and Re (Rasa) on the sixth day—success in one's undertaking occurs when the Moon has reached an even position and Mercury or Venus remain as the final remainder. This is the rule for inquiries concerning vowels (*svarapraśna*).

Now, the specific distinctions of the years and so forth are stated by the verse beginning with "varṣā": The years, months, fortnights, days, nights, and moments enter into the zodiacal sign (*lagna*); the single sign, together with the host of planets, possesses the vowels and is divided into the *tattvas*. One *tattva* consists of one hundred and sixty breaths (*śvāsa*). O King, within the time-measure of a *nāḍī*, there are sixty *nāḍīs*; sixty *liptās* are its subdivisions, and six breaths constitute one *nāḍī*.

Sixty years are the rains; twelve months; twenty-four fortnights; day and night is the time of day and night; eight watches (*praharas*); and [the divisions] entered within the twelve ascendants (*lagnas*). Among these, for the sake of determining auspicious and inauspicious results, those that have entered within the ascendant and set within the ascendant possess no power other than that of the lord of the ascendant. Thus, the single ascendant, together with the host of planets, becomes possessed of its own sound and divided into principles (*tattvas*) through five types according to the previously stated method.

One *tattva* consists of six breaths (*śvāsa*), and one hundred and thirty [breaths] more than that constitute the time-measure (*kālanāḍī*) and the mandala-measure (*maṇḍalanāḍī*). These are the degrees of the nadis (*nādy-aṃśāḥ*); sixty *liptās* are the subdivisions of that, which are the *liptās*. "Subdivision" refers to the group of six breaths.
By the specific address "O King" (*narendra*), there is a distinction regarding the specific regulation of the power of the breath.

Now, within the *Vimalaprabhā*, the inauspicious and auspicious results occurring during inhalation and exhalation are described: "The inauspicious and auspicious results during inhalation and exhalation are known by those engaged in yoga and by astrologers who have purified the solar and lunar [movements] within the time-measures (*kālanāḍī*) according to the elapsed days.

He who, in this world, speaks of the inauspicious and auspicious results even when these are not known—even if he were blind—he enters the thicket strewn with elephants and lions after taking hold of his wealth."

Between exhalation (*niḥśvāsa*) and inhalation (*ucchvāsa*), there is respectively an inauspicious and auspicious result. When the breath has gone out from the navel into the nose at the time of questioning, it is inauspicious; when it has entered from the outside into the navel and the nose at the time of questioning, it is auspicious. This alone is known through the application of yoga and not by others. Furthermore, by astrologers (*daivajña-jyotiṣibhiḥ*), it is known through the "time-pulse" (*kālanāḍī*) after calculating based on the elapsed days, having subtracted the sun and moon, and having purified the left and right mandala-pulses according to whether the ascendant is odd or even.

When the aforementioned present time is not known, he who speaks of the results of the inauspicious and auspicious in this world—even if blind—enters a dense forest filled with elephants and lions after grasping that very object. This concludes the determination of the results of the auspicious and inauspicious. Now, the *lagna-yoga* (ascendant conjunctions) is stated, beginning with "when not known": when the subtle conjunction (*sūkṣma-yoga*) is not known, a *lagna-yoga* endowed with planetary strength is assigned. *Kālāgni* [is assigned] from the Sun and Mars in the seventh house from Saturn.
Death, disease, wounds, and indeed the total destruction of all wealth occur in that [ascendant]; therefore, it should clearly be avoided according to my words, and another ascendant should be given.

When the previously mentioned subtle yoga of inhalation and exhalation is not understood—that is, when the subtle yoga is not known—the planetary strength (*graha-bala*) is applied according to worldly convention through the conjunction with the ascendant (*lagna-yoga*). If Kālāgni is present in the seventh house from the rising ascendant (*udaya-lagna*), then for one seeking auspicious results, death occurs. If the Sun is there, illness occurs; if Mars is there, a wound occurs; and if Saturn (*śanaiścara*) is there, the destruction of wealth occurs.

Thus, all this that the planets produce when they are in the rising sign (*udayalagna*), the birth sign (*janmalagna*), or the seventh house—therefore, it is clear that such a configuration must be avoided; by these words of the Sage, another ascendant should be provided by the minister.

[End of chapter on] the Great Chapter concerning the Rules and Methods for the Instrument of the Arising of the Sun (*Svarodayayantra*): When Mercury is joined with Jupiter and Venus in the sign situated in the seventh house from the birth sign, there is the destruction of the enemy, self-nourishment, and victory in battle, as well as the acquisition of wealth accompanied by passion.

If all the planets are correctly situated in their signs and the left nostril (vāmanāḍī) flows in one's own body, then there is certainly the attainment of all goals on the surface of the entire earth, provided it is an auspicious weekday and lunar day. || 111 ||

In this context, if Rāhu is in the ascendant at sunrise and is also in the seventh house, then the destruction of the enemy occurs; when the Moon is there, one's own prosperity occurs; when Saumya (Mercury) is there, victory in battle occurs; when Bhṛgu (Venus) is there, there is the acquisition of wealth along with passionate union with a woman—this is certain. Furthermore, if all the lords of the ascendants are present in the twelfth houses together with benefic planets, it results in auspiciousness.

If, moreover, the left channel (vāmanāḍī) occurs within one's own body, there will certainly be the accomplishment of all aims upon the surface of the entire earth. Here, regarding the pure days (śuddhavāra) and lunar days (tithi): Sunday with the asterism Hasta; Jupiter with Puṣya; Mercury with Anurādhā; Saturn with Rohiṇī; Moon with Śravaṇa; Mars with Aśvinī; and Venus with Revatī—these are the Siddhi-yogas.

In this regard, the inauspicious ones are: Sunday with Anurādhā; Moon with Kṛttikā; Mars with Śatabhiṣaj; Mercury with Aśvinī; Jupiter with Mṛgaśīrṣa; Venus with Rohiṇī; and Saturn with Hasta—these are the Mṛtyu-yogas (death-yogas).
Excluding the burnt lunar days (dagdhatithi), all lunar days are pure with respect to all weekdays, provided one avoids those of special duration.

Here, the burnt lunar days are as follows: the twelfth day is burnt by the Sun; the eleventh day is burnt by the Moon; the tenth day is burnt by Mars; the third day by Mercury; the sixth day by Jupiter; the second day by Venus; and the seventh day by Saturn.
These lunar days (tithis) are to be avoided for auspicious undertakings; however, for inauspicious undertakings, all cruel planets, lunar days, and so forth are to be accepted.
In this regard, all astrological configurations (yogas) are commendable, with the exception of Vyatīpāta, Parigha, and Vaidhṛti.
Likewise, for gentle undertakings, three ghaṭikās of the Viṣkambha yoga are to be avoided.
One should avoid [the birth] on Pañcaśūla; one should avoid it on the six [periods], Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa, and on the nine [periods], Vyāghāta and Vajra—thus is the impurity of the *yoga*.

In this way, the purity of the day and so forth is established by worldly convention as being in a pure weekday and lunar date; however, in ultimate reality, the fruit of auspicious and inauspicious results for sentient beings arises from their previously accumulated karma—such is the rule of the Tathāgata.

Now, the power of the stars and so forth is described according to worldly convention, beginning with the phrase "having made the asterism" (*ṛkṣa*) and so on: Having divided the asterism into three parts by means of nine, nine, and nine [units], the birth asterism is first; for the sick, it is indeed death.

The malefic planets, together with the Moon, situated in odd positions within the three *nāḍīs* starting from Aśvinī, form a serpent reaching as far as Revatī. If the birth asterism of men coincides with the asterism of the evil Moon within a single *nāḍī*, there is destruction. || 112 ||

Having made the asterism into three parts—meaning these twenty-seven asterisms are divided into three parts by groups of nine, nine, and nine—it is within each of those nine [groups] that the birth asterism of the sick person or the warrior occurs first in the battle from the initial group of nine. Then, the asterism separated by one is the odd position (*viṣamapada*). If in that odd position there are malefic planets—namely the Sun, Mars, Saturn, and Rāhu—together with the Moon at the ascendant (*lagna*), then there is indeed death for the patients or for the warrior in battle.

"Victory in battle [is achieved] when they are in the same *nāḍī*"; such is the rule for the strength of the stars (*tārābala*). Now, the "Snake Wheel" (*phaṇicakra*) is described, beginning with "Aśvinī": by means of the twenty-seven lunar mansions starting from Aśvinī, the snake is likewise arranged in three *nāḍīs* as far as the *nakṣatra* Revatī. If the birth-mansion of a sick person or a warrior falls within the same *nāḍī* as a "sinful moon"—that is, a sinful planet (*pāpagraha*) and the moon (*indu*) combined as "sinful-moon"—then for that person there is destruction, meaning death. Such is the rule for the three-*nāḍī* Snake Wheel.

When the Moon has moved through three *nāḍīs* separated by one [constellation] starting from Kṛttikā, and likewise from Ārdrā and so forth—specifically when the Moon has traversed three *nāḍīs* within the interval of three constellations—he who first enters the battlefield becomes the victor; whereas when the Moon is situated in three constellations outside the *nāḍīs*, he who enters later becomes the victor. This is the third rule concerning the *phaṇicakra*.

The results of the periods (daśās) of the [planets] according to their life-span (āyurdaśā) are now stated, beginning with "six, fifteen," and so forth: The Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rahu, and Ketu consume those years—six, fifteen, eighteen, twenty-eight, twenty-one, ten, nine, twelve, and twenty-one—respectively. Furthermore, within that [period], the malefic planets cause misfortune through the letters of the Aṣṭavarga, while those planets of gentle form bestow supreme happiness. *ṣaṭ tithyaṣṭādricandrāṃ daśasanavadaśārkaikaviṃśat suvarṣān | sūryendvaṅgāro budho'rko gurubhujagaśitā bhuñjate tān krameṇa || tasminnantardaśāyāṃ punarapi ca tataścāṣṭavargākṣaraiśca | krūrā kurvanyaśānti paramasukhakarāḥ saumyarūpā grahā ye ||* 113 ||* *Note: The original verse uses the term *tithya* (fifteen), *adri* (seven), and *arka* (twelve).*

Having constructed an eight-spoked wheel here, one should then establish the one hundred and eight years of the enjoyment (*bhoga*) of the planets beginning with the Sun, starting from the eastern direction and ending with the north. Six [years] are on the eastern spoke; "the lunar date" (*tithi*), meaning fifteen, is in the southeast; eight in the south; "mountain-moon" (*adricandra*), meaning seventeen, in the southwest; ten in the west; "nine-and-ten" (*sanavadaśa*), meaning nineteen, in the northwest; "sun" (*arka*), meaning twelve, in the north; and twenty-one in the northeast.

The Sun enjoys six years; the Moon, fifteen; Mars enjoys eight years; Mercury enjoys seventeen; Saturn (Arka) enjoys ten; Jupiter (Guru-Bṛhaspati) enjoys nineteen; the Serpent (Bhujaga), that is Rāhu, enjoys twelve years; and Venus (Śita-Śukra) enjoys twenty-one years. Thus, the Sun and the others enjoy one hundred and eight years in succession according to their respective numbers.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in that sub-period" (*antardaśāyām*): it is said here that in the gross period (*sthūladaśā*), the malefics—the Sun, Mars, Saturn, and Rāhu—cause unrest, while the benefics—the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus—bring peace.

Here, moreover, within a single period of six years or more, there are again eight kinds of sub-periods (*antardaśās*). Within that sub-period, there is yet another [calculation] by means of the letters of the *aṣṭavarga*; in this context, the letters of the *vargas* are twofold: some are according to the conventional usage of the world (*lokarūḍhi-pāṭha*), and others are according to the *Svayambhū-pāṭha*.
In this regard, according to the worldly recitation (*lokapāṭha*), the *a*-group is *a, i, u, e, o*; the rule is "aiu[ṇ], ṛlag";

the *ka*-group is *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa*; likewise the *ca*-group, *ṭa*-group, *ta*-group, *pa*-group, *ya-ra-la-vāḥ*, and the *sa*-group is *śa, ṣa, sa, ha*. According to the worldly recitation, there are the rules beginning with *hayavara[ṭ]*, *laṇ*, *ña-ma-ṅa-ṇa-na-m*, *jha-bha-ñ*, *gha-ḍha-dha-ṣ*, *ja-ba-ga-ḍa-da-ś*, *kha-pha-cha-ṭha-tha-ca-ṭa-ta-v*, *ka-pa-ya*, *śa-ṣa-sa-r*, and *[hal]*—this is the rule concerning space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.
In this very context, there is no purification of the letters of the groups by means of Ākāśa and so forth, because of the recitation of the *Śaṃkaraprapañca*.
Here, however, for the Sun [represented by] *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ*, there is an eightfold enjoyment (*bhoga*) during its six-year major period (*sthūladaśā*) and its sub-period (*antardaśā*).

Thus, in the sub-period (*antardaśā*) of the Moon during its fifteenth year, the eightfold enjoyment consists of: *evaṃ hayavara* [C] *blaṇ*; in the sub-period of Mars during its eighth year, *ṅagha ga kha ka*; in the sub-period of Mercury during its seventeenth year, *ajha ja cha ca*; in the sub-period of Saturn during its tenth year, *ṇa ḍhaḍa ṭha ṭa*; in the sub-period of Jupiter during its nineteenth year, *ma bha bapha pa*; in the sub-period of Saturn and Rāhu during its twelfth year, *na dha da tha ta*; and in the sub-period of Venus during its twenty-first years, *ka śa ṣa sa ha*. Such is the eightfold enjoyment.

Thus, the eight groups (vargas), which have the nature of the sun, moon, space, wind, fire, water, earth, and the element of consciousness, consist respectively of five letters each: *e*, *o*, *ara*, *āra*, *ala*, *āla*, *ha*, and *kṣa*. Among these, the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is to be grasped as *kṣa*. In this way, within the letters of the eight groups, the sun and the other [planets] are the consumers during the five-year periods by means of the vowel of the *muhūrta* and the consonant of the mandala; according to the fivefold division, they are the consumers of the sub-periods (*antardaśā*) starting from the six-year period by means of the eighth part. This is the rule for the wheel of periods (*daśācakra*).

The individual planet is the enjoyer; in the first division, it is the lord of the period of longevity (*āyur-daśā*), and then the other seven follow in sequence—this rule regarding the periods of longevity is not found in the manuscripts *ga*, *gha*, and *bho*. *ga* and *va*.

ralaḍiti vimalaprabhāyāṃ] Now, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is explained: O King, in the month of Puṣya, when the sun has entered Capricorn (*makara*), ignorance (*avidyā*) occurs; and in Māgha, when the sun is in Aquarius (*kumbha*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) occur; and in Phālguna, when the sun is in Pisces (*mīna*), they come to be.

In the months of Caitra, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha, consciousness and name-and-form arise; when the Sun is in Taurus or Gemini, sight and the other senses occur; and when the Sun is in Cancer, touch and sensation arise during the month of Hariravi (Āṣāḍha).

O King, in Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa, even a woman [is subject to] thirst; in the month of Tulā (or Bhādrapada) and Āśvina, grasping arises; in Kārttika and Vṛścika, existence comes into being; in Dhanus (Sūrya) and Mārgaśīrṣa, birth occurs; and likewise, death occurs when the Sun is in Makara—in this sequence, O King, the twelve links [of dependent origination] arise through the distinction between the Sun and the Moon, by virtue of both modes of movement.

In the month of Puṣya or Māgha, when the conjunction occurs and the Sun has entered Capricorn, if death takes place on that day, then ignorance (avidyā) occurs; from that, O King, death occurs on the second [day], birth on the third, and so on for all [the links] beginning with existence (bhava), multiplied by their sequential progression up to the twelve links. Therefore, due to the movement in Capricorn, death may sometimes occur in the sixth month [comprising six links], such as fire, ocean, and arrows (346).

The fortnights and lunar days are designated by the day of the week according to the movement of the Sun; sometimes there is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting of sixteen parts at the junction of the month of Māgha when the Sun is in the water-pot (Aquarius).

In that case, the refinement itself is consciousness (*vijñāna*); it manifests on the second day as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and on the third day likewise. Thus, through the conjunction of creation and dissolution, the components of two months arise by the power of the Sun.

In this regard, even an inauspicious portion of ignorance may become auspicious for all undertakings through consecration and other rites; likewise, that which is inauspicious [may become so] through initiation, processions, and marriages.

Thus, by the divisions of the lunar fortnights, according to the movement of the moon, there are twelve links in both the bright and dark fortnights, arising from the sequence of the first lunar day and the conjunction of emanation and withdrawal.

The "Āyurdaśā" section follows; the page numbers for the *Gha* manuscript are indicated until the point where the text is fragmentary. From that point onward, as the *Ga* manuscript begins, its page numbers are noted within brackets. Hereafter, the root text is provided from the *Ka* manuscript alone.
[In the chapter on] the Great Summary of the Rules and Methods for the Instrument of the Arising of the Vowels (Svarodayayantra):

Regarding the passage beginning with "Puṣya," in the month of Puṣya, at the time of the departure of Puṣya and the entry into Māgha, ignorance (*avidyā*) is here the twelve-spoked wheel (*dvādaśāra*) of the zodiac, beginning with Capricorn (*makara*).

Therein, in the first spoke, on the day of Makara when the sun has moved there and the sun is in Aquarius in the month of Māgha—and by the word "and" (ca), the purification (*saṃskāra*) occurs right here at the end of Māgha on the day of entering Phālguna; likewise, at the end of Phālguna, on the day of Capricorn or Aries in Caitra and so forth, there is discernment (*vijñāna*); similarly, at the end of Caitra, on the day of Taurus in Vaiśākha and so forth, while the sun is in Aries, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); thus, at the end of Vaiśākha, on the day of Gemini in Jyeṣṭha and so forth, while the sun is in Taurus, there is the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); likewise, at the end of Jyeṣṭha, on the day of the transition into Cancer in Āṣāḍha and so forth, there is contact (*sparśa*); and thus, at the end of Āṣāḍha, on the day of the transition into Leo in Śrāvaṇa and so forth, there is sensation (*vedanā*).

Thus, at the end of Śrāvaṇa, on the day of the sun's entry into Leo (siṃha-saṃkrānti) beginning with Bhādrapada, there is *tṛṣṇā* (thirst); likewise, at the end of Bhādrapada, on the day of the sun's entry into Virgo (kanyā-saṃkrānti) beginning with Aśvinī, there is *upādāna* (grasping). Similarly, at the end of Aśvinī, on the day of the sun's entry into Libra (tulā-saṃkrānti) beginning with Kārttika, there is *bhava* (becoming); likewise, at the end of Kārttika, on the day of the sun's entry into Scorpio (vṛścika-saṃkrānti) beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, there is *jāti* (birth); and likewise, at the end of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the day of the sun's entry into Sagittarius (dhanus-saṃkrānti) beginning with Puṣya, there is *jarāmaraṇa* (old age and death). In this manner, the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*) are to be known respectively within the twelve spokes.

The division of the three suns and the division of the moon are well known everywhere; they occur by virtue of both movements, namely by virtue of the transits (*saṃkrānti*) and by virtue of the lunar days (*tithi*) of the fortnight. Thus, there are twelve factors:

when the Sun has entered Capricorn (*makara*) at the conjunction of the month of Puṣya and Māgha, on that day *avidyā* (ignorance) occurs; from that day, on the second day, which is a Wednesday (*jña-dina*), comes *jarāmaraṇa* (old age and death); on the third day, *jāti* (birth); on the fourth, *bhava* (existence); and on the fifth, *upādāna* (clinging).

Feeling occurs in the eighth [day], contact in the ninth, the six sense bases in the tenth, name-and-form in the eleventh, consciousness in the twelfth, and formations in the thirteenth—just as in the third cycle; likewise, birth occurs in the thirteenth, becoming in the fourteenth, grasping in the fifteenth cycle, and sometimes craving in the sixteenth cycle. Due to the movement of the sun, the links [of dependent origination] shift according to the zodiacal signs; thus, in the right channel, it corresponds to Capricorn by virtue of the ascendant, and there are sixteen cycles in the case of the transits.

Thus, during the conjunction of the months of Māgha and Phālguna, when the sun is situated in Aquarius (Kumbha), the purification (*saṃskāra*) occurs on that lunar day; on the second, consciousness (*vijñāna*); on the third, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); on the fourth, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); on the fifth, contact (*sparśa*); on the sixth, sensation (*vedanā*); on the seventh, craving (*tṛṣṇā*); on the eighth, grasping (*upādāna*); on the ninth, becoming (*bhava*); on the tenth, birth (*jāti*); on the eleventh, old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*); and on the twelfth, ignorance (*avidyā*). This occurs in the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*) by virtue of the ascendant (*lagna*) pertaining to Aquarius, according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).

In this regard, just as it is in the third [day], so it is in the thirteenth for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), in the fifteenth for contact (*sparśa*), and sometimes in the sixteenth for sensation (*vedanā*);

thus, the sequence of days for the sun and moon is to be understood everywhere according to the distinction between even and odd, by means of the difference in the days of the week at the transition (*saṃkrānti*) of both lunar fortnights.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the world-system: here, the "odd" (viṣama) portion—consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), sensation (*vedanā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and birth (*jāti*)—is auspicious for all peaceful rites (*saumyakārya*). The "even" (sama) portion, beginning with formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth—which consists of formative forces (*saṃskāra*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), contact (*sparśa*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), becoming (*bhava*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—is inauspicious for peaceful rites; however, this even-odd division is praised for cruel rites (*krūrakarman*).

Thus, in the bright fortnight of the month of Puṣya, on the first day (*pratipad*), there is ignorance (*avidyā*); on the second and subsequent days, there is formative activity (*saṃskāra*) according to the distinction of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). In the dark fortnight, on the first day there is ignorance, and on the second day there is aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). In this manner of withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*), the twelve links exist across the twelve lunar days. Just as the links beginning with ignorance occur in the month of Puṣya through the distinction of the bright and dark fortnights according to the sequence of emanation and withdrawal, so too in the month of Māgha, the links beginning with formative activity are to be understood through the distinction of the bright and dark fortnights according to the sequence of emanation and withdrawal. Likewise, in the bright and dark fortnights of Phālguna and the following months, there are twelve links each, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).

In this very context, just as worldly convention is to be understood as being devoid of specialized knowledge in astrology, so too is the law of dependent origination; for that reason, it was not explained in detail here. Now, the power of the *bhūmis* is stated: The Sun, Mars, Ketu, and Rāhu cause death to enemies when stationed on the right, the back, the left, or the front. Likewise, the entire host of planets in their gentle forms [bring benefit] on the battlefield.

Similarly, the Yoginīs, Viṣṭi, and the Rudras, together with the Wind, grant happiness when on the right, the back, the left, or the front. When situated in even or odd positions, these two powers bring about destruction in the form of death. || 119 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "Sūrya" and so forth:

having understood here that the ground-force (*bhūmibala*) consists of the eight directions within the zodiacal circle (*rāśicakra*), one should observe the positions of the planets and constellations on the earth in the eight directions. Wherever the Sun, Mars, Ketu, and Saturn are situated—whether all of them to the left, to the right, behind, or facing toward the enemy—they bring about death for the enemies. Those standing to the left cause death.

On the left front, the entire host of gentle planets likewise causes the destruction of enemies on the battlefield; the rule is that the host of gentle planets—namely the Moon, Mercury, Venus, and Jupiter—standing to the right or behind the enemies, brings about their destruction. Likewise, regarding what will be explained hereafter, the *yogas*, *ghaṭīs*, *gaṇīs*, *viṣṭis*, and *rudras*, together with the *pavana* (wind), grant happiness when situated to the right or behind the enemies, but become destroyers when situated on the left or in front.

When [the planets] are situated in even or odd positions, they are half-malefic for enemies; on the right and behind, they do not become half-malefic; on the left and in front, they become half-benign, yet they do not become fully benign. At that time, the two forces strike one another, and the rule is that there occurs the death of both forces.

This concludes the great chapter on the rules for the method of the *Svarodaya* instrument. Now, the force of the Yoginīs beginning with Brahmāṇī is described: Brāhmī, Raudrī, Kumārī, Khagapatigamanā (Gāruḍī), Śūkarī, Vajrahastā, Cāmuṇḍā, and Lakṣmī arise on the eighth lunar day (*tithi*), starting from the first lunar day up to the ninth.
In Śakra, Yakṣa, Agnikoṇa, Danu, Yama, Varuṇa, Māruta, and Īśabhūmi, they produce their rising; furthermore, they are divided into sixty-four varieties according to the lunar days (tithis). ||120||

Regarding the passage beginning with "Brāhmī" and so forth: here, whether in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) or the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), on the first day (*pratipad*), Brāhmī is in the east (*śakra*); on the second, Raudrī is in the southeast (*pākṣa*); on the third, Kaumārī is in the southeast (*agnikoṇa*); on the fourth, Vaiṣṇavī is in the southwest (*naiṛtya*); on the fifth, Vārāhī is in the south (*yāmya*); on the sixth, Aindrī is in the west (*vāruṇa*); on the seventh, Cāmuṇḍā is in the northwest (*vāyavya*); and on the eighth, Mahālakṣmī is in the northeast (*aiśānya*). Thus, on the eight lunar days (*vasutithi*), starting from the first day up to the ninth, [the goddesses are assigned].

Furthermore, on the ninth day, Brāhmī is in the East; on the tenth, Raudrī is in the North-East; on the eleventh, Kaumārī is in the South-East; on the twelfth, Vaiṣṇavī is in the South-West; on the thirteenth, Vārāhī is in the South; on the fourteenth, Aindrī is in the West; and on the fifteenth—the full moon and the new moon—at the half-tithi, Cāmuṇḍā is present, and at the [other] half-tithi, Mahālakṣmī is present; such is the rule. Thus they cause their rising in these eight directions; these are the Yoginīs.

Furthermore, on the lunar days (tithis) beginning with the first day of the waxing moon (pratipad), there are eight divisions in the first half and eight divisions in the second half; thus, one should know that they arise within those two sets of eight divisions upon those lunar days. Among them, the first eighth portion of each respective lunar day is the "enjoyment" (bhoga) of the presiding deity of the lunar day (tithyādhipati). Subsequently, according to the stated sequence, there are seven enjoyments for the [other] seven; this is the rule. The same should be understood for the second half of the lunar day as well; such is the rule regarding the arising of the Yoginī-cakra.

The rising of the Viṣṭis occurs here in the bright fortnight in the directions of Indra, Yama, the ocean, and the corner [of Vāyu], and again in the dark fortnight in those of Agni, the Lord [Īśāna], the wind [Vāyu], and the corner [of Īśāna] respectively.

Rudra traverses the eastern and western halves according to the day; as the sun moves further and further north, it proceeds from the western direction to the fire-colored [southeast] limit; and when the sun is in the south, it invariably proceeds toward the south.

Now the power of the *viṣṭi* is described: in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), the rising of the *viṣṭis* occurs on the fourth, eighth, eleventh, and full moon days, respectively, in the directions of Indra (East), Yama (South), Varuṇa (West), and Soma (North).

In the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the rising occurs on the third, seventh, tenth, and fourteenth days, respectively, in the directions of Agni (Southeast), Nairṛti (Southwest), Vāyu (Northwest), and Īśa (Northeast). This is the rule for the rising of the *viṣṭis*;
their application is as previously stated.

Now the power of Rudra is described: from the east, that is, from the eastern direction, Rudra proceeds as far as the west (the direction of Varuṇa) by the force of the day, which means by the force of the movement of the transits (*saṃkrānti*). When the northern sun is situated in the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), in Capricorn (*makara*) and the half of Aquarius (*kumbha*), he moves to the east; in the *Vimalaprabhā*, it says "in the half of Aquarius. In Pisces (*mīna*), he moves to the northeast (*īśāna*); in Aries (*meṣa*) and the half of Taurus (*vṛṣabha*), he moves to the north; in the half of Taurus, he moves to Gemini (*mithuna*) in the northwest (*vāyavya*).

Then, from the western [direction] to the south-eastern [direction], when the sun is situated in the southern solstice: Rudra moves to the south in Cancer; to the west in Leo; to the southwest in the latter half of Leo and in Virgo; to the south in the first half of Scorpio; and to the southeast in Sagittarius. This is the rule for the rising of Rudra. Thus, the monthly Rudra, the fortnightly Rudra, the daily Rudra, and the temporal Rudra—these six types are useless and have therefore not been mentioned by him.

Now the power of Rāhu during the half-watch is described: From the first half-watch, he enters the east; likewise, he goes to the south, then to the northeast, to the water [north], to fire [southeast], to the yakṣa [northwest], and sets in the west [northwest].
Leaving aside the illustrious Mūlarāhu, even the Wind-god (Vāyu) is victorious in hand-to-hand combat. In battle, Mūlarāhu devours the enemy force; there is no other equal to him. || 122 ||

Here, during the seven watches [of the day], at sunrise, it enters the wind [quarter] from the east, that is, from the eastern direction; after half a watch has passed, it goes to the south; again, at the end of the latter half-watch, it proceeds to the north-east (Īśa); then, at the end of the next half-watch, it goes to the west (Vāruṇī); then, at the end of the next half-watch, to the south-east (Āgneyī); then, at the end of the next half-watch, to the Yakṣa [quarter]; and finally, at the end of the next half-watch, it enters the south-west (Nairṛtī). This is the rule for the eight directions, from sunrise until sunset.
In this manner, it should be understood for the night;

setting aside Śrīmūlarāhu, this Māruta is victorious in a duel (*aṅkayuddha*), that is, in a battle between two warriors. Furthermore, in a great conflict (*saṃgrāma*), Mūlarāhu devours the enemy force; there is no other Rāhu equal to him among the various Rāhus such as those of the months, according to the rule. Now, the strength of the warrior in a duel is described: a warrior deficient in *mātrās* is slain by one who has more in a battle of even or uneven [breaths]; victory in the fight belongs to him whose name enters the heart during the exhalation (*śvāsa*).

One whose name begins with a letter of the same class as that spoken by the messenger is victorious; one whose name ends with such a letter is slain. When vowels and consonants are arranged in even or uneven positions, the prediction is indeed fruitless.

A warrior lacking the proper measure (mātrā) is slain by one who possesses it in battle, in hand-to-hand combat, in a precarious encounter, in a clash between two forces, or in a balanced or unbalanced fight; specifically, one with a name of fewer syllables is slain by one with more, a short-vowel name by a long-vowel name, and a long-vowel name by a protracted (pluta) vowel name. Furthermore, regarding the secondary cause: "In the battle, victory belongs to that one of the two names which enters the heart during the breath."

He whose name exits with the breath goes forth externally; he dies. This is another application: the one whose name is uttered first by the messenger prevails and is victorious, while the one whose name is uttered last is slain—this is the rule. According to the Āryas, the [eight] castes are: the flag, smoke, lion, dog, bull, donkey, elephant, and crow. Their colors are: dark, fair, red, and black. Likewise, they correspond to the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. Their vowels are—

The great chapter on the rules and methods for the instrument of the rising of the breath (*svarodayayantra*): the aggregate of syllables is doubled by the vowels, and the aggregate of measures (*mātrā*) is quadrupled; the remainder when divided by seven is the result.
By means of these vowels and others, through various elaborations involving even and uneven positions, there is indeed the prediction of results.

Why? Because of the absence of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*). It is a statement that produces delusion in the ignorant through all worldly conventions, being devoid of the experience of the fruits of one's own karma.

Under the pretext of the power of the planets and so forth, false compositions have been made by the sages; under the pretext of the power of the Lord, those established in the dharma of the Lord have composed the *Svarodaya*. Thus, they deceive the people with the false statement that "this was spoken by the Lord. This elaboration should be explained at length in the *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*; let it suffice here. Now, the power of the Root-Rāhu (*mūlarāhubala*) is stated, beginning with the words "Time" (*kāla*), etc.: "If Time (*kāla*) is on the left (*savya*) and Rāhu (*tamī*) is on the right (*apasavya*) on the battlefield, then in the battle of kings, even the Lord of Gods, together with Hari and Hara, is slain by men."

Therefore, at the time of battle, one must recognize the illustrious Mūla-Rāhu, the conqueror of the three worlds, as being among the crooked Rudras and Asuras when he has reached the circle of the earth; otherwise, there can be no destruction of the enemy. (124)

Having placed the constellations on the ground as arranged by the pair of sages—Indra (3), Yakṣa (2), Ocean (4), and Yāmya (7)—that entire wheel should be understood as revolving by the power of the sun's course.

In whichever constellation the time prevails, and when the shadow falls upon two [consecutive] ones, the enemy army will suddenly fall [in defeat] in battle; victory shall be in the middle of the womb. 125.

When the forces are stationed at equal degrees of aspect during the time of Rāhu, there occurs a balanced engagement; however, for those who have emerged from the degrees of aspect due to the movement of the serpent (Rāhu), there is indeed a rout of the army.

For those excluded from the degrees of aspect, victory prevails; and when both are in the "entry into the womb" (garbhavedha) configuration, thus is the illustrious Mūla-Rāhu understood in the Kālacakra according to the words of the Guru. (126)

Having established the constellations here on the ground, there are twenty-eight constellations. The constellation in which the sun resides is situated among the seven preceding constellations; three constellations each are designated as "sages" (*muni*) in the east, arranged in seven groups. Just as they are in the east, so too in the north, west, and south. As the wheel revolves clockwise, the arrangement of the constellations revolves counter-clockwise. Within one day and night, the sun completes its transit through each of the twenty-eight constellations.

In this context, due to the movement [of the nodes], when at a certain asterism *Kāla-Rāhu* is at the tail and *Tamī* (Mukha-Rāhu) prevails on the left (*savya*), or when *Kāla* is on the right (*apasavya*) and *Tamī* is at the mouth (*mukha-rāhu*), then on the battlefield of kings, the Lord of Gods (*devanātha*) together with Hari and Hara is slain by men through the casting of glances by both the mouth- and tail-Rāhus. Furthermore, in such a battle, the enemy army falls suddenly, and victory shall belong to the one in the center of the womb (*garbhamadhya*).

In this regard, if the face is in the east and the tail in the west, then the gaze is in the south and the womb in the north; when the face is in the southeast, then the tail is in the northwest, the gaze is in the southwest, and the womb is in the northeast; when the face is in the south, then the tail is in the north, the gaze is in the west, and the womb is in the east; when the face is in the southwest, then the tail is in the northeast, the gaze is in the northwest, and the womb is in the southeast; when the face is in the west, then the tail is in the east, the gaze is in the north, and the womb is in the south; when the face is in the northwest, then the tail is in the southeast, the gaze is in the northeast, and the womb is in the southwest; when the face is in the north, then the tail is in the south, the gaze is in the east, and the womb is in the west; and when the face is in the northeast, then the tail is in the southwest, the gaze is in the southeast, and the womb is in the northwest.

Thus, for those situated in the mouth of Rāhu, or situated at the time [of the eclipse], or situated at the tail, death occurs; there is an equal fall of the forces. For those who have emerged from the sector of vision—here, within the sector of vision, when twelve constellations have come into the sight of Rāhu, three parts to the right and left, four constellations belonging to Rāhu and four belonging to Kāla—the army is indeed broken there due to the movement of the serpent.

Regarding the aspect of the vision (*dṛṣṭyaṃśa*), for those situated within the womb of the twelve lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) that have abandoned [the opposing side], one-third is the region of the womb; four *nakṣatras* are on the right and four are below the right.
Here, those situated in the aspect of the vision enter the womb-region and become face-to-face; with them, there is indeed battle.
Thus, in the *Kālacakra*, it is known from the words of the venerable Mūlarāhu as they have come down through the lineage of gurus.

Because the word of the Guru is the word of the Buddha, for that reason, the illustrious Mūla-Rāhu is the "wheel" (cakra) that conquers the three worlds. The planets are the Rudras, and the "Asurī" refers to the sixty Yoginīs; he is the conqueror of them—the Rudras and Asurīs—within the midst of which he stands. He must be known as being situated upon the circle of the earth at the time of battle, and not otherwise will there be destruction.
This is the rule: Rāhu is to be known according to the sequence thus described.
Having abandoned the Yoginīs, Viṣṇu, Rudra, along with the planets, and the rising of Saṃvara—all those things—the sole conqueror of the three worlds must be seized by the Kṣatriyas;

he by whom Indra and Sūrya, who cause fear to the thirty gods, are swallowed—those two of fierce form, resembling collyrium, who wander day and night over the earth from east to west, south, and north. || 127 ||

In this matter, O Lord, at the time of battle, having abandoned all forces such as the yoginīs and others, this one Rāhu—the devourer who eclipses the moon and sun, who is terrifying to the gods, possessing a fierce form with the luster of collyrium, and who traverses the earth from east to west, south to north, and through the eight directions in a single day and night—is alone to be seized; this is the rule regarding the limb of vision.

[Chapter on] the Great Compendium of the Rules for the Method of Mechanical Devices (*yantra*) in the *Svarodaya*: Now, the mechanical devices for the purpose of destroying the fortresses of wicked enemies are described, beginning with "In battle," and so forth: If an enemy, broken in battle, should suddenly enter the middle of the fortress, [the defender], having prepared mechanical devices outside, should incessantly rain down stones, fire, and arrows;

and by means of machines that sever [with] swords and the like, and by means of enclosures (*pañjara*) upon the surface of the earth, he should crush that fortress with "horn-piercing" (*śṛṅgabhedaka*) weapons. Having thus pulverized that fortress, that wicked one shall be subdued within a few days. (128)

If, at some point, one whose enemies have been broken in battle suddenly enters the midst of a fortress, then—having constructed machines on the exterior and having secured the defense of one's own residence with those open machines through incessant showers of stones, fire-arrows, and cutting machines such as swords—one should pulverize that fort with "thunderbolt-cages" (*vajrapañjara*) and "horn-breakers" (*śṛṅgabhedaka*) situated upon the ground; thus, that wicked one is to be subdued within a few days: this is the rule.

Regarding the characteristics of the stone-mechanism (*pāṣāṇayantra*) for the fortress walls and ramparts here, it is said, beginning with "four," and so forth: Four pillars, measuring sixteen cubits [in height], with eight sections pierced at even and uneven intervals, are joined at their base by cross-beams (*bhinnārgalā*) of four and two [cubits] respectively, along with a rear support (*pṛṣṭhaka*). The measurement of the mechanism is ten cubits at its base; at the top portion, it is half of that. The shaft (*yaṣṭi*) is reduced by two [cubits]; at the summit, the sockets (*kaṇaya*) are four cubits in measure. *Note on terminology:* *Bhinnārgalā* refers to horizontal cross-beams used to secure the structure; *pṛṣṭhaka* is a rear support or back-piece; *yaṣṭi* is the vertical shaft or central axis; *kaṇaya* refers to the sockets or mortises at the top where the mechanism's parts are inserted. The dimensions provided (16, 4, 2, 10, 5, 2) suggest a specific architectural proportion for the siege engine.

There are four pillars, each measuring sixteen cubits (two times eight) in height; they are square in shape, sixteen finger-breadths in width for the superior machine, fourteen cubits in height and fourteen finger-breadths in width for the medium one, and twelve cubits in height and twelve finger-breadths in width for the inferior one. These are perforated at eight locations by means of even and uneven steps: the front and back edges are even, while the left and right edges are uneven; at those eight places they are perforated, and each hole is one-third of the width.

And these [holes] are made with four bolts on the east, four on the south, four on the north, and one on the rear lower part; thus there are five apertures in the two rear pillars and eight in the two front pillars. The measurement of the machine is ten cubits at its base and five cubits in height; the shaft is two cubits less than the pillars, while the measurement of the socket-ring is six cubits, shaped like a cow's tail on the left and right sides of the ring.

The circumference is two and a half cubits; it is fashioned according to the measurement of the Sage (Viśvakarman), with a single hole of two finger-breadths [in diameter]. A staff enters the handle when it is fixed by a pin at the back;

on the head, which is bound with fifty cords, there is a ring at the top of the circle measuring one cubit. At the end of the staff, a ring with a finger-guard enters; the circumference is one span (vitasti). || 130 ||
And so forth; there are no stones that are not perforated.
Its eight holes were equal; it was being measured by means of broken bolts.

Regarding the phrase "not reaching the support with the two southern [arms]," the *Vimalaprabhā* states: In the center of the world-system, the circle is two and a half cubits [in diameter], twenty finger-breadths on both sides, and thirty finger-breadths for the front pitchers. In the middle of the central circle, there is a hole fourteen finger-breadths in width and seven finger-breadths in depth. Into that hole for the pin, having set aside one cubit, one makes thirteen cubits in the shape of a cow's tail; the pin enters that hole and is secured by being fixed from behind with an iron nail.

At the top of the staff, at a distance of one cubit, there are two holes separated by a third part [of that length]. In those two holes, there are two rings, sixty finger-breadths in circumference and six finger-breadths in width, made of circular iron rods. Fifty ropes are tied to each ring on the top of the staff.

At the end of the staff, there is a ring twelve finger-breadths in circumference; it enters the tip of the staff by one finger-breadth. Together with the staff, it is pinned with two pegs and a tongue; at the tip of the tongue, a finger should be known as being six finger-breadths long.

The tongue, being coiled and inserted into the end of the staff-coil, becomes three cubits long when extended by the hand; the throwing distance is fixed at one and a half rope-lengths. A stone placed in its center and whirled vigorously with thorny sticks flies swiftly into the sky when released, falling suddenly upon watchtowers, gateways, and the like, pulverizing them entirely as it strikes the ground like a thunderbolt.
In this case, the throwing-net is three cubits long with a cord of one and a half [cubits].

Here, the leather net is twenty-four finger-breadths in width; it is twelve finger-breadths in the middle and shaped like a cow's tail on both the left and right sides. On both sides, there are two cords made of thread, measuring two and a half cubits and so forth.
A stone enters into the middle of that net, being fastened by strong thorny cords.

Once released, it moves swiftly through the sky; having gone there, it suddenly falls upon a watchtower, a wall, or a rampart, pulverizing them entirely and descending to the surface of the earth like the falling of a thunderbolt. Its "half-moon" [mark] on the finger is located at the base of the earth within the Brahma-line on both sides of the two [fingers]; these eight points of liberation are released from the palms of both hands by the closing of the fists.

In the case of liberation, there is indeed the touching of the ground by those situated within the mechanical womb, whether on level or uneven terrain; and by the power of the threefold movement, stones fall at will for the purpose of destroying the fortress. || 132 ||
The half-finger [measurement] of that machine, shaped like a crescent moon, is the Brahma-line situated on the surface of the earth; below the finger it becomes level.
On both sides of that line are eight points of liberation (*mokṣapradeśa*), each separated by one span (*vitasti*), where the noose is attached with two rings.
That staff was in the hole at the top of his head, which measured a hand's breadth.
One hundred and twenty finger-breadths in length.
"Three cubits with a finger-breadth [is the measure]; three cubits with a finger-breadth for the cord,
and upwards everywhere," so it is said.
In the *Varatrakaṭṭaka*, *Balavatka*,
*Adulaka*, and other such texts, this passage is unclear.
Below the finger; O sir, it destroys the tip [of the finger],
half a finger.

[In this] chapter, the great summary concerning the rules for the method of the *svarodaya* machine: [the stones] belong to stone; their release occurs from the binding of the fists of both palms at the time of liberation. The touching of the ground by the stone occurs when one enters the interior of the machine with equal steps using the right feet, or with uneven steps using the left feet—thus, due to the threefold movement according to one's own will, and due to the movement on the left, right, or middle, for the purpose of destroying fortresses; such is the rule for breaching land fortresses.

If even an elephant falls suddenly under his blows, what need be said of a mere small creature? If he were to strike down the entire enemy force stationed within the fortress towers while they remain outside, what rivalry could there be with him for archers dwelling on the surface of the earth in a siege-war? For who would enter that fortress as an enemy when it is like the mouth of Yama, where the blows of mechanical engines fall? || 133 ||
The verse beginning with "aibhaṃ yasya prahāraiḥ" is easy to understand.

Now, the characteristics of water-machines (*jalayantra*) for the purpose of capturing a fortress protected by water are described: There should be six pillars (*stambha*) and six arms (*bhuja*) on both sides, equal in measure; within the space of two cubits (*hastayugma*), there should be a single inner chamber (*garbha*) measuring twelve cubits, equal to both sides, neither more nor less. Every individual compartment (*koṣṭha*) should be covered with fruits, leather, beeswax (*siktha*), and cloth. Within the interior, one should construct a single mechanism (*ekamantra*) using the seasonal months (*ṛtu*), the eight defects (*doṣa*), and thrice-twelve (thirty-six) suns (*dinakara*). || 134 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "six," etc.: here, for the purpose of the water-mechanism (*jalayantra*), [the structure] is fourteen cubits in width from a wooden beam six finger-breadths thick; for the elephant-mechanism (*hastiyantra*) it is twenty-four finger-breadths; for the horse-mechanism (*aśvayantra*) it is twenty finger-breadths; and for the human-mechanism (*narayantra*) it is sixteen finger-breadths. With six pillars situated at intervals of twelve cubits each, the two chambers (*puṭa*) are equal—neither more nor less. Within the interior (*garbha*), each is twelve cubits. In the lower and upper chambers, with a distance of two cubits between them, or a distance of four cubits, there are six pillars such that each chamber is formed by the two sections; this is the rule.
Every individual compartment should be covered with wooden planks.

Having fashioned arms on both sides here, one should fashion them on one side of each plank; on the other side, having protected the upper and lower edges of the planks, one should insert one finger’s breadth between the planks in the middle and secure it, so that no water enters—this should be done everywhere: below, above, front, back, left, and right.

The interior cavity (*garbha*) of elephants is three cubits in height, that of horses two and a half cubits, and that of men two cubits. These cavities should be sealed at the joints of each plank with leather strips and fastenings so that water from the waves cannot enter. Within the middle of the cavity, an opening two cubits high should be made at the position of the neck to allow entry into the interior.
By means of these cavities—distinguished as inferior, middling, and superior—various types of vessels are formed.

The womb-machine (*garbhayantra*) consists of six seasons, or eight defects, or eighteen; or with three times the number of suns (*dinakara*), that is, thirty-six, or twice that, or twice that again, it becomes the womb-machine up to a thousand wombs for the purpose of crossing the great ocean; however, the "exceeding womb" (*vyatugarbha*) is not in the manuscript.
A flat stone on uneven ground.
In the commentary on the 134th verse in the Gha manuscript, the reading "garbhaḥ" is found up to the left footnotes; furthermore, the portion of the verse commentary is found thereafter.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the world-system: Two by two within the interior of the womb, even what is faltering is sealed on all sides by the arms; on the back are six streams of sections, and equal to both arms, the machine-drivers are at the front.
Bound by well-posts with moving wind-cloths, it is not moved by the wind; mounted thereon, one's own army proceeds into the ocean for the purpose of destroying the water-fortress. (135)

Here, on the exterior, within each of the four-armed [sections], in the two pairs of front and back arms, and in the left and right parts of the body—among these six, specifically within these four arms—the pillars should be fixed. These pillars emerge from the openings of the arms, measuring one-third of the arm's width, and are joined by three-cubit wooden planks pierced at both ends; thus, all the inner chambers should be mutually secured at the four corners of the interior.

"One should lead the *kītivāla* (rein-like ropes) to the remaining places of illumination. This means that, excluding the locations for the flow of the *kītivāla*—whether sealed at the top or extending from front to back on all sides—there are six *kāṇḍadhārā* (shaft-supports) on the back of every machine. Thus, there may be twelve, twenty, or up to a hundred; they are equal in both arms and at the front. The shaft-drives (*yantravāha*) for those *kāṇḍadhārā*s extend up to a thousand, according to the dimensions of the machine.

Alternatively, having ascertained that they are without a base, one should cause that water-machine to be moved by the wind using moving sails (vātapata) fastened to well-poles; while mounted upon it, one's own army proceeds into the ocean for the purpose of destroying a water-fortress or for the purpose of seizing another island—this is the principle for the subduing of the wicked, and such is the definition of a water-machine.

Now, the wind-machine for the purpose of discharging fire and oil to destroy mountain fortresses is described: On a single platform, with a moving cloth driven by the wind and bound to a flagstaff, it moves even when obstructed by men on its side or back; being pulled by a rope over the head, it is lifted by the wind and travels through the sky to the summit of the mountain fortress. From there, the discharged fire and oil burn the enemy force and the entire fortress on all sides. (136)
Regarding the passage beginning with "one," etc.:

here, upon a square wooden board or pedestal measuring four cubits, there is a pillar in the center measuring three cubits in height and twelve *aṅgulas* in circumference. At the left, right, rear, and front corners, there are iron spikes provided with rings (*kaṭaka*). One should secure the pillar at its top to those rings with ropes.
Both parts of the mechanism, from the top to the bottom, should be covered with a firm cloth.

In this corner, there are five banners, each one cubit in width. From the lower left and right corners, three ropes extend down to the rim for a distance of two cubits. Among them, one is equal in length to the height of the mountain fort when measured together; by means of that rope, when people hold it from behind and move with it over their heads, that machine, being lifted up by the wind, indeed travels through the sky for the purpose of destroying the mountain fort.

Into the opening at its top, one should insert a man together with fire and oil into that machine. By means of that man, the fire-oil released from that wind-machine burns the enemy force and all fortresses on every side; this is the certain rule for the destruction of mountain fortresses. (Note:
This portion is not present in the Tibetan translation.)
Or when [the breath] has gone out through the left, the right, the back, the front, or the corners.
Immediately after that, the phrase "the bracelet among them" does not exist for human beings;
it extends only as far as the lower-left and right corners.

The book is obtained; beyond this there is nothing [in this] chapter. This is the Great Chapter on the Rules and Procedures for the Svarodaya Instrument: The wheel is two and a half cubits in size, and there is another peg above it as a staff; at the tip of the staff is a sharp sword which revolves with lightness when the base of the instrument is rotated. (137)
The *katūrī* machine is to be understood through direct observation; it has also been clearly described in verse.

Indeed, by means of a rope-machine (*rajjukī*), one proceeds through the sky from one's own position step by step. Having measured the rope fixed for its course toward the fortress, the messenger of the enemy likewise measures it upon the ground. Thus, in the case of piercing the peak (*śṛṅgabhed*), having set fire to the enemy's peak, one should set fire to the entire circle at the base of the enemy's dwelling. || 138 ||

In this manner, the "horn-splitter" (śṛṅgabhedaka) and the wind-machine (vātayantra) have also been clearly revealed; even though there is no circular [structure] at all, a great temple constructed on the upper portion of the wheels—circular in shape of iron and wood, and covered on all sides—is moved by these fruits, whether made of buffalo hide or human skin, and travels level upon the earth as far as the ditch; then, having filled that ditch, it suddenly enters through the gate-tower into the wall of the fortress. || 139 ||

Likewise, since there is no intention [to elaborate further] even in the *Vajrapañjara*, the iron-arrow mechanism (*nārācayantra*) for piercing elephants with sugar-lumps during battle is now described: Having fixed a bow together with its string upon two pegs on a base so that it remains motionless, one should place two iron pegs at the back on well-fashioned notches (*kaṇaya*), with half-finger-widths of the circle [of the bow].

When released by the string from the fingers, a multitude of equal arrows—sharp iron shafts (*nārāca*)—go forth at the time of battle, having pierced the bodies of elephants laden with sugar-lumps. (140)

Having fashioned a lion out of iron six *aṅgulas* long, one should fix two square iron rods, each six *aṅgulas* long, above and below it on its left and right sides; these have their holes sealed with iron pins. Having secured the bow—equipped with its string—immovably at the middle joint by means of these, one should then insert two square iron pins on the opposite side of its back into the holes of the iron rods, and cause the two ends of the *kaṇaya* (bolt) to enter the holes of the pins.
Within the middle of the *kaṇaya*, there should be six, five, four, three, or two small balls (*aṅgulikā*).

Below, a single iron rod (*ekadaṇḍikā*) the size of the little finger in width and three finger-breadths in length should be inserted into the ring of the lower peg (*kīlakaṭaka*). Above, one should fix the strings (*guṇa*) at the tips of the fingers.
