There, at each joint of the fingertips, there are steel arrows (*nārāca*) with strings; thus, when released from the sharp external steel arrows equipped with many strings, they proceed at the time of battle, piercing through the bodies of elephants armored in leather and carrying balls of molasses. This is the rule for the steel-arrow machine (*nārācayantra*).

Now, the *pātālakhaḍgayantra* (the subterranean sword-machine) for the protection of the royal palace is described: "Two pillars"—two pillars are firmly fixed in the ground and wound with ropes; between the two ropes, a sword-hilt [is placed] along with twenty finger-guards (*savalya*) and many coils.
In their midst, the sword-hilt becomes fixed, yet it can be moved and locked by means of a seal-coil (*mudrāvartta*). Thus the excellent sword is concealed and immobilized at its tip. || 141 ||

In this regard, there are two square pillars, twelve *aṅgulas* in measure [in height], four *hastas* in width, and with two *hastas* buried in the ground within the pit. With two *hastas* rising from the middle of the pit, one should leave one and a half *hastas* above the location of the pit and insert iron bolts (*argalā*) into the holes of the lower left and right pillars. Having left six *aṅgulas* at the top, one should bind them with ropes for the sake of movement; between those two ropes, the handle of a sword (*asi-muṣṭi*) is inserted into the middle of the ring (*valaya*).

First, the ring is wound with many coils; in the middle of the ring, the hilt of the sword enters and is fixed in the portion belonging to the Master (Ācārya). Likewise, it is wound in reverse order between two pillars in front, and is secured at the tip of the sword by means of the seal located at the sword's point. At the tip of the seal of the sword's point, it is secured by a cord; at the tip of the sword-hilt, there is a socket (kaṇaya) measuring six finger-breadths (aṅgula) in its portion. Above that, there is a line for the hole, and on the blade (phalaka), there is an exit for the moving sword. One small, uncut moon-shaped piece should be placed in the middle portion above.
He whose foot suddenly falls upon the moon-crested [shrine] is cut by a sword; at the end of the gate in the fortress, within the palace of the lord of men, there is indeed a striking machine.
Then, one should construct an upward-opening trap for the sword using wooden planks and hollows, so that when [the victim] moves, he is struck by iron;
"Candrama" is the secret terminology, while "Madhya" refers to the elaborate array.

Here, a plank with a ring should be placed over the tip of the sword-hilt. On that plank, whoever steps will be cut; this is to be understood as the essential nature of the "sword-killer. This is the rule for the sword-machine; such is the definition of the sword-machine.

Thus, for the destruction of fortress gates during times of war, various machines are always employed in the royal palace; excluding the main gate and the path, the machine itself is the striker. This is the rule for the *pātālakhaḍga* (underground sword) machine. Now, the characteristics of the chariot (*syandana*) for Kṣatriya warfare are described: the base platform above the axle is twelve [units] in measure, and the wheel measurement is nine parts; the pillars and bolts at the corners are of unequal and equal lengths, with a measurement of one and a half units from the base.

The Great Chapter on the Rules for the Method of the Iron Instrument of the Arising of Sounds (*svarodaya*): Half of the portion is the ground for the warriors, whether uneven or level; for horses or elephants, from that [ground], on the upper half of the marked area, mirrors, garlands, banners, and so forth are arranged. || 143 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "akṣoddhvaṃ" (above the axle) and so forth: here, first of all, for the sake of the chariot, the axle must be made firm. The measurement of the wheels of the chariot for the horses is two and a half cubits; the axle is four finger-breadths more than that. By that same measurement, the pedestal is fourfold. Then, above the axle is the pedestal (*pīṭha*). In the directions and the center of the axle, the measurement of the wheel is nine parts, consisting of nine compartments. That very [pedestal] becomes the pedestal by means of twelve arms—the divisions of the sun—six of which are six finger-breadths wide extending east-west, and six extending south-north.

The axle (*akṣa*) is fourteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width; having divided it into three parts and set aside the middle part, one should bore two holes in each of the [two] ends. Having inserted the axle-end into those two holes, one should fasten it with the axle using pins. At the end of the axle, an iron pin is fixed immovably so that the wheel enters the circular rim of the base-hole; thus, the wheel becomes attached to the base. Then, at the four corners of that pedestal (*pīṭha*), there are four pillars, equal in width to the arms of the pedestal and twice as long.

And those [chariots] are pierced by crossbars on the four sides, pierced below and above. A "level chariot" (*samaratha*) is moved by level horses, while a "discrepant chariot" (*viṣamaratha*) is moved by discrepant horses—two, four, or six being level horses, and three, five, or seven being discrepant horses. Regarding the measurement from the pedestal (*pīṭha*): the upper portion is the combat area for the warriors. Leaving aside one part of the pillars' height as the measure of the pedestal, the combat area for the warriors is in the middle portion, measuring half [the height] above the pedestal. It may have either uneven or even ridges, and it exists according to the height of the horses or elephants. In width it is eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and in length it is double the pedestal; it is fastened with bolts along with the crossbars. Then, from the bottom of the pedestal portion up to the mark, it is divided into halves.

It is four finger-breadths in width; upon that ground are fashioned mirrors, garlands, banners, and so forth—the word "and so forth" (ādi) including yak-tail whisks, canopies, bells, and the like—these being the marks of the warrior’s ground. Between the two grounds, there is illumination in the four directions for the purpose of battle. The moon, rays, and fire [are represented] by one and a half, two, and three parts respectively; the circular base, pedestal, and bolts are equal in measure to one and a half parts, while the lotus, chariot, ground, and Nandi are distinguished by their respective divisions.

The common measurement of the wheel is one and a half cubits according to the proportions of horses and elephants; the lotus-type for the gods is of two kinds as ordained by the son of the gods (Viśvakarman), while the Nandi-type is for human beings.

Thus, there are two divisions each. There is one division of the base pedestal (*mūlapīṭha*) below on the fighting ground (*yodhabhūmi*); and these two divisions—the half-virāga and the sign (*cihna*)—are in the light (*prakāśa*). Regarding "the moon-rays and the fire" (*śaśikaraśikhinaḥ*), there is one division of four *aṅgula*s for the pillars and bolts (*stambhārgalā*) above the base pedestal in the position of the lintel (*dhurāsthāna*). From that, there are two divisions of four *aṅgula*s for the pillars in the fighting place (*yuddhasthāna*). Above those, there are three parts of four *aṅgula*s; above that is the ground for the signs (*cihnabhūmi*) of the banners and so forth.
The pedestal is circular with eight and a half parts; some say it is slightly more than eight.
The ten [fingers] are the Peak (ūrdhva) and the Earring (kaṇaya).
The elephants wander about the pillars.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the previously mentioned [measurements]: in the half-measure (*sārddhabhāga*), the circular ground for the lotus-chariot (*kamalaratha*) occurs; by the "divisions of Nandi" (*nandibhedaiḥ*), meaning in the division of the Nandi-chariot, the earth becomes square.

Thus, according to the stated sequence, the measurement of the wheel-base (*cakrapīṭha*) for the horse-chariot is one and a half cubits (*sārddhahasta*). From the measurement of the horse-chariot, the measurement of the elephant-chariot (*gajaratha*) is twofold. This is the rule for the wheel-base, the bolts, the insignia, and so forth. Here, for the gods, the lotus-type chariot is circular.

"Constructed by the sons of the gods": Arjuna’s canopy is of the *nandijāti* type and square; for men, the chariot is also constructed otherwise as square for the Kṣatriyas. Here, the great chariot is of three kinds: the half-square, the equal-square, and the divine one-wheeled [chariot] of the Sun; and the uneven-horsed chariot is for the destruction of the Asuras. In battle, the great chariot may be either uneven or equal; for Kṣatriyas, when broken, it faces directly in the encounter between the even and the uneven, while the equal [chariot] results in a breakage at the rear. || 145 ||

In this world, the great chariot (*mahāsyandana*) is of three kinds: the half-chariot (*ardharatha*) and the full chariot (*samaratha*). Here, one who possesses four axles and eight wheels becomes an irreversible (*avaivartī*) great warrior (*mahāratha*) in battle;
whereas with two axles—one below and one above—and four wheels, one becomes a half-charioteer (*ardharatha*).

*Therefore, "eight" refers to the wheels; "ocean" refers to the four axles (*akṣas*). Thus, "threefold" refers to the four wheels, as well as the two [axles], and likewise the axles. "Equal to half the movement of a chariot" means they are equivalent. "The divine sun-chariot has one wheel" means that with a single wheel, it becomes a divine chariot, and likewise it exists in the sun. "Odd," and so forth, is easy to understand. With one axle and two wheels, a chariot becomes equal in its configuration of front and rear; this is the rule for the characteristics of the [chariot] on land.*

Now, the characteristics of the palanquins for gods and the moving palaces for kings are described: In the case of the gods' celestial palaces (*vimāna*), the height from the top of the pillar-base to the upper part is divided by sixty-five and four (sixty-nine), and the resulting equal parts determine the structure.

On earth, for kings, according to the three types of cities, during regional processions and festivals, the great revolving palanquin (*mahābhrāmarī*) is effective at intervals of half a cubit (*hasta*) in all directions.
For others as well (*anyeṣām api*), the connection is easy to understand: "In the case of Nandibheda and Kamalaratha, the earth becomes square.
This portion of the commentary does not exist in manuscript G, yet it is present in the Tibetan translation.
Having been translated from the Sanskrit, it is presented here; the Tibetan portion is set forth below in its entirety: "Because of that, it is called 'the eight' (*aṣṭa*);
the 'water-treasury' (*udakālaya*) is the 'life-tree' (*jīva-vṛkṣa*).
Thus, it is known as threefold: the four wheels (*cakra*) and likewise two."
Similarly, the life-tree and the wooden cart are equal to and equivalent to half a cart.
As for the "supreme solar cart" known as the single wheel, it means that by means of a single wheel, it becomes the cart of the gods; in that same way, it proceeds toward the sun.

"Mi-mñam śes-pa la-sogs-pa ni go sla'o" (The "Unequal Knowledge," etc., is easy to understand). Regarding the *Svarodayayantravidhiniyamamahoddeśa* (the Great Chapter on the Rules for the Method of the Instrument of the Arising of Sound), in the passage beginning with "six," etc.:

here, there are four pillars twenty *hasta* in height and twenty *aṅgula* in width. These have four corners pierced through, which are equal: one corner of the piercing is at the division of six *hasta*, the second at the division of five *hasta*; therein, the third occurs at the division of four *hasta*, and [the fourth] at the division of three *hasta*. Excluding one *hasta* each from the bottom and the top, the corner of the piercing faces inward.

In the Mūlabhāsa [region], it is thirteen cubits above the ground; in the Dūdhārdhabhāga [region], it is seven and a half cubits above the ground. This occurs according to each respective city on the city-ground, and in the Gaṇavimāna, the ground is four *catur-rā* [units] above the ground.

Thus, on the ground of kings, according to the three types of cities, regarding the construction of palaces for travel and residence: in the first city, within the outer opening of the pillar, above the external bolt that has protruded outward, there is a *bhrāmarī* (rotating mechanism) made of wooden planks on all sides; this *bhrāmarī* is three cubits long. In the second city, the *bhrāmarī* is one cubit long. This is the conclusion concerning the characteristics of the houses for the departure of divine celestial chariots in every direction.

Now, the characteristics of the circular swing for the spring festival are described: on the top of the pillar, there are swings in all directions according to the three types of cities; from the two [sides] there are eight, then half [of that], and four, supported by arms; thus, on the three levels, as it revolves above and below, the seats of the women held by the arms are positioned internally and externally, below and above, set in motion in the eight directions. || 147 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "above the wheel" (*cakrordhvam*), here the chariot has ten wheels and a base pedestal; above that are four pillars consisting of elephant-chariots and columns. There are swings (*dolā*) composed of three types of palaces (*vimāna*). Above each set of four crossbeams (*gala*), there are two, eight, and eight; thus, in the first palace, there are twenty-two, and sixteen swings in the four directions. In the second [palace] there are eight, and in the third there are four.

In the first city, there are swings (*dolaka*) situated on the *argala* (crossbar) by means of ten arms positioned to the right and left, front and back. In the second [city], there are six [swings] by means of the six seasons, and in the third, four. Thus, the arms of the swings are the spokes (*ārā*) in the triple wheel (*tribhramī*). Each pair of arms enters a single hole in each of the two notches (*kaṇaya*); in each notch, there are four seats for women. These are arranged internally and externally, positioned below and above, and moved by the eight directions. This is the rule for the characteristics of the wheel-swing (*cakradolā*).

Now, the description of the water-mechanism for the purpose of irrigating gardens and the like is stated, beginning with "upwards" and so forth: The tube-shaped mechanism has a curved measurement from top to bottom; on all sides, at the tip of the pipe, there is the mouth of a jar (*kumbha*) which, though having a hole, acts as a conduit for drawing up water according to the measure of the channel's opening.
Even when the water is released and spills out from the opening of the jar, it flows level across the ground wherever it is led—whether to a garden or a grove. (148)

This portion does not exist in manuscript *ga*; it has been extracted here from the Tibetan translation. However, in that [manuscript], it appears as follows: "In the division (*vibhāge*), it becomes three-fourths of a *vitasti*. According to the Tibetan, "four by four" occurs twice—*bāī bāī* in manuscript *ga*.
In the celestial palace (*vimāne*).

Regarding the "Half-Knowledge" (Phyed de Śes pa): 295, 19, 25, 152. In the *Vimalaprabhā*, concerning the upper and lower, left and right, the machine (*yantra*) has the form of two tubes (*nāla*). In the center, there is a hollow middle section, four cubits in length, which serves as the primary machine (*mūlayantra*). At the tip of its tube, there is the mouth of a pitcher (*kumbha*), and its neck enters the tip of the tube. Below, in the pitcher, there is a hole the size of the opening of the tube. At the rear of the machine, at the tip of the tube, another pipe must be made to enter into the water. Then, one should seal the hole of the pitcher so that water flows through it, or seal the hole of the front tube. Thereafter, one should cause water to enter through the hole of the primary machine until the machine is completely filled with water.

Then, by means of a hole in a drop in the middle of the water, or a hole in a pitcher, or a hole in a tube, it simultaneously draws the water into the pitcher from the arrow; that very water then proceeds to a garden or a grove, being carried over level ground wherever it goes—this is the rule for the characteristics of a water-lifting machine (*jalaśekayantra*).

Now, the instruction on the rules for Mañjuśrī’s solar chariot is spoken regarding the wicked: "For the sake of subduing the wicked, and for the victory of the righteous upon the surface of the excellent earth, that which was previously taught by the Teacher of the Three Worlds in the *Ādibuddha* to Sucandra—all of that has been explained here today by me clearly within this domain. For the sake of protection in your own place, perform all of this; let not the Sun [be obscured] by hatred or greed. (149)

In this regard, for the sake of subduing the wicked, that which was previously taught by the Teacher of the Three Worlds, Śākyasiṃha, to Sucandra—the emanation-body of Vajrapāṇi—concerning the characteristics of all the *svarodaya* instruments, from within that [teaching], specifically from the midst of that chapter on the *svarodaya* instruments, something has been clearly taught here in this land called Sambhala. O Sūryaratha, I, Mañjuśrī Yaśonarendra, have [taught] this today for the purpose of its protection in your own place. "Do not let all this be taken by hatred or greed; it is not for the sun"—such is the rule for Sūryaratha, and likewise, there is also a rule of the Blessed One regarding the others' thorough understandings of Kālacakra.

Thus ends the tenth great chapter, the "Rules for the Method of the Instrument of the Arising of the Vowels," in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* in twelve thousand verses, which follows the *Śrīmūlatantra*. (11) First, the uprooting of the Mleccha religion and the establishment of the Buddha’s religion; now, the uprooting of the Mleccha religion and the establishment of the Buddha’s religion by the Great Cakravartin is easily understood, as it has been stated in the commentary. The first chapter, named "The World System" (*lokadhātu*), begins: In the middle of the ocean of wine and milk, upon the earth-disk of the Sage, stands the land of karma; and at a distance of one hundred thousand *yojanas*, the Lord of Men revolves through the solar sectors in succession.
— *ga*. "The Great Chapter on the Rule for the Method of the Instrument of the Arising of the Vowels.
Beyond this point, there is no commentary (*ṭīkā*); in manuscript *ka*, only the root text (*mūla*) exists. Therefore, only the root text is presented here.
From this point forward, the page number references from the Tibetan translation of the root text are presented in the margins.
In the square, the folio numbering of the manuscript has been provided from the *ka* manuscript. [In the] *paṭala*:

"The uprooting of the Mleccha religion and the establishment of the Buddha-dharma, and so forth, is one section; twenty-five thousand [verses], together with eighty-four thousand *yojanas*. Kailāsa is in its center, surrounded on all sides by the excellent Snowy Mountain (*Himagiri*). (150)

On the earth, there is a portion of Kailāśa together with the Snow Mountain (Himagiri); its three parts are surrounded on all sides by one petal each, adorned with the regions of the sun’s domains (dvīpas).

In the left half is the place called Sambhala, the abode of the best of sages, inhabited by ten million villages; indeed, the domain is composed of ten million villages, and the maṇḍala consists of a hundred thousand villages. || 151 ||

Divided by the categories of one, two, three, and four; and by five, six, seven, and eight; and further distinguished by the divisions of the world and so forth—the Wheel-turner (Cakrī), the Lord of Men (Narendra), the Wandering One (Bhramati), he who is to be sought by the wise, the Wheel-turner (Cakrī), the Half-Wheel-turner (Ardhī), the Fragmentary One (Khaṇḍī), the Regional King (Viṣayanarapati), and the one with the Seal in Hand (Mudrahasta)—these others exist externally as divisions of Time, just as they do for the Lord of the World. 152.

In this world, there are seven oceans, mountains, and days; likewise, the Sāttvika incarnations from divine wombs are the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, along with Narahari (Narasimha), Vāmana, Yāmadagni (Paraśurāma), Rāma, and Kṛṣṇa—these eight cause fear to the race of Danu.

Then come the thirty-two Rājasa incarnations from the source of beings at the end of the Viṣṭara (the Dvāpara age); finally, the enemy of Danu, the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), appears for a lifespan of one hundred years.
Ādra, Anogha, Varāhī, Danu, Bhujaga—these five others are of the nature of darkness (tāmasa); that eighth one is Mleccha, Śvetavastrī, and Madhumatimathanī; he is Andhaka.
The manifestation of the seventh is clearly in the region of Makha, in Vāgādā and other places, where there dwells a powerful, merciless world of Asura-nature in the form of a Mleccha.

O King, where camels, horses, and cows are slaughtered, and food for men consists of blood and raw meat, or something cooked and pure, or beef with the juice of pressed [substances], or rice mixed with vegetables seasoned with ghee and pungent spices, all cooked together in a single fire along with fresh fruits; and where the drink for men is the eggs of birds—that is the abode of the Asuras. (155)

The Bindu, Śakti, Añjaneya, Garuḍa, the celestial river, Nārada, Kāmadhenu, Durgā, and among the learned, Vidyā, Akṣara, Paramakalā, and the divine languages—through these moving forms, the all-pervading Jñānakāya of the Jina descends; he proclaims the entirety of the Vedas, logic, and other scriptures, pertaining to the past, the present, and the future. || 156 ||
[This portion] is not in manuscript *ka*, but has been supplied from the Tibetan translation and the available reading.

25. O King, in a few days you, the illustrious one, will go to your own place in the renowned city called Sambhala, which is surrounded by mountains and measures four hundred fifty *yojanas* on each side; having installed Sureśa as the preeminent lord, [you shall depart]. In the Śrīśākyavaṃśa [of this world-system], there have been seven manifest kings, and the eighth is the illustrious Yaśas. (157)
This very Śrī Mañjuvajra, saluted by the best of gods, as Kalkī of the Vajra lineage, having bestowed the Vajra-abhiseka, shall reduce all the families of sages to a single Kalkin;

mounted upon the Perfect Vehicle (Samyagyāna), the bringer of fear to the clan of Danus, with the glorious Yaśas holding a spear in his hand, he shall manifest the great Kālacakra for the sake of the liberation of sentient beings. || 158 ||
In the midst of that, at the end of the age, there will appear from the lineage of Kalkī a lord of gods, honored by the best of deities, the fierce Kalkī;

he will be peaceful in form and a bestower of happiness to the virtuous. Likewise, as the destroyer of the Mleccha tribes, he will be a wheel-wielder mounted on a horse with mountain-like proportions, possessing the splendor of the sun, with a spear in his hand, and he shall slay all his enemies.

In the midst of the Kalkī lineage, when the age has been multiplied by four and sons and grandsons have passed away, at that time, indeed, the practice of the Mleccha religion shall prevail in the land of Makha;

and as long as the wicked Mleccha king and the fierce Kalkī, who is saluted by the best of gods, exist, during that time a terrible battle between those two shall take place upon the surface of the earth.

He who shall slay the Mlecchas in battle with his fourfold armies across the entire surface of the earth; who, at the end of the age on Mount Kailāsa in the city fashioned by the gods, shall present Rudra, Skanda, the Lord of Gaṇas, and Hari as his allies to the approaching Cakravartin; and who, together with Kalki, shall provide mountain-like horses, lordly elephants, golden chariots, kings, and soldiers with weapons in their hands. || 161 ||

Accompanied by an army consisting of mountains, horses, and elephants multiplied by their qualities [sixty], by ten million foot soldiers, by those called Vedas [four] numbering one hundred thousand, by six hundred thousand chariots, by sixty akṣauhiṇīs, and by ninety-six families of kings with bound crests— Kalkī, joined by Hari and Hara, shall effect the destruction of the Mlecchas.

In this chapter, [it is taught] that the eradication of the Mleccha religion and the establishment of the Buddha-dharma are primary; the host of Mlecchas must be slain by excellent fierce warriors, by lordly elephants, by mountain-horses, and by Saindhava steeds in battle on even and uneven ground, as kings shall slay other kings.
Aśvatthāman, the son of Mahācandra, Hanūmān, and Raudrakalkī, with his sharp weapons, shall slay the lord of the Mleccha chiefs, the ruler of all the Danavas, who possesses a cruel mind. (163)

Having slain the Mlecchas in battle, Kalkī—the sole leader of all armies—accompanied by Hari and Hara, shall go to Mount Kailāsa; and when that Cakrī is established in the city built by the gods, at that time the entire body of water on earth will be filled with righteousness, desire, and wealth, and the trees, bent with steady fruit, will yield forest-grown crops.

When the host of Mlecchas, along with their followers, has been exterminated at the end of the Manu-era after five hundred years, Kalkī will attain perfection in a city fashioned by the gods upon the high slopes of Mount Kailāsa.

Brahmā and Sureśa shall become the two sons of the Teacher of the Thirty-three Gods during the Yuga-dharma; Brahmā shall rule over the single western region, while Sureśa shall become the sovereign of the eastern land.

Having completely eradicated the Mleccha dharma from the three worlds by means of the [teachings of] the Guru, and having established the Brāhmaṇas, he proceeds to the state of bliss for eight hundred years.
Furthermore, O Lord of Men, within that very [realm] there arises a division of castes; among those sons, some become lords of Asuras, some kings, some sages, and others become commoners.

For the sake of destroying the Mlecchas, the Lord of the Gods proceeds accompanied by twelve Indras; and in every region, the Cakrin proceeds after having struck down the Mleccha-dharma, [establishing] the state of bliss for his two sons. Brahmā and the Lord of the Gods follow behind the Guru here, and likewise [in front]; in the lineage of Brahmā and others, on the surface of various lands, there arise many divisions.

In the age of Brahmā and others, the lifespan of men is eighteen hundred human years; half of that belongs to Kāśyapa on this excellent earth, and half of that again—diminished by sixty—belongs to Nārasiṃha. Likewise, at the time of each daily (yuga) cycle, beginning with Vāmana and ending with Kalki, the lifespan of a person prevails at the count of one hundred years.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "Thus, in all the regions (*khaṇḍas*) as well, the duration of the age (*yugasamaya*) is the onset of the Mleccha dharma. One hundred and one years is the duration of that Mleccha dharma, and after that comes its destruction.
Therefore, twenty thousand minus one hundred is the duration of the Buddha-dharma; the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages proceed upon the earth by this power. (169)

The origin of the world-system, the simultaneous movement of the planets, the appearance of the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), the destruction of the Dharma by the Mlecchas, and the granting of the path to Kalkin at the stage of supreme bliss—all this has been told by me to you, Sucandra, exactly as it is, according to the three times. For the benefit of all people and for the sake of liberation, what more do you ask me? (170)
Thus ends the first chapter, on the arrangement of the world-system, in the glorious Mahākālacakra extracted from the glorious Ādibuddha. || 1 ||
(1) The Great Chapter on the Determination of the Four Noble Truths Concerning the Arising of Body, Speech, and Mind. Homage to Śākyamuni!

Homage to that Protector who performs this conception for the sake of maturing great beings; who, though liberated from the bonds of existence, enters existence for the sake of the path of living beings; and whose virtuous garland of various Jātaka tales is seen for the benefit of sentient beings—homage to that Buddha of great power, the Savior. Having prostrated to Vajrasattva, the glorious Lion of the Śākyas...
The commentary on the Adhyātmapaṭala is being written by Puṇḍarīka, having been exhorted by Mañjuśrī and authorized by the Sugata.

By me, the glorious Lokanātha, whose nature is compassion for the world, here—in the glorious great jeweled pavilion at the end of the eastern gate of the mandala house of the glorious Mahākālacakra—sitting upon a jeweled lion throne and having been requested by Sūryaratha, the Lord Mañjuśrī, the emanation-body (nirmāṇakāya) known as King Yaśas, spoke with his first verse regarding the request made by Sucandra to the Blessed Śākyamuni for the sake of teaching the chapter on the Inner [Science]: namely—
"O Father of the Victors, I did not know the measurement of the universe as it was taught by you; furthermore, I desire to hear how the entire threefold world could exist within the body.

Having heard the words of Sucandra, the Sugata, granting his approval, spoke out of supreme compassion for the sake of the liberation of sentient beings concerning the measurement of the universe within the body.

In this chapter on the inner self (*adhyātmapaṭala*), I shall expand upon the narrative concerning the summary of the requester and the teacher, as taught in the *Laghutantra* by Mañjuśrī, the compiler, beginning with the words "is not known" (*na jñātam*). Here, within the body, the universal measurement (*viśvamāna*) is not known. "O Father of the Victors" (*jinajanaka*) refers to Vajrasattva Śākyamuni; the Father of the Victors is the progenitor of the undefiled aggregates (*skandhas*), and this is his address: "O Father of the Victors! You have taught the universal measurement externally, but that is not known within the body. Therefore, I desire to hear once more: how and in what manner does the entirety of the three worlds exist within the body?"

Therefore, having heard the request consisting of Sucandra’s words, the Sugata, having bestowed his approval upon Sucandra, speaks with excellence for the sake of the liberation of sentient beings; out of supreme compassion, he establishes the universal measure within the body, and by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), he teaches all other tantras as well within the body for the purpose of the instruction in the second chapter. This is the summary of the requester and the teacher.
To the glorious Kālacakra:
"Existence" (*bhava*).
Thus,
[this] instruction is by way of a cause.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, he states the verse concerning the teaching, beginning with "Earth," and so forth: "Earth, water, fire, and wind; the thunderbolt, the rainbow of the gods, and the winds; the wheel of the zodiac signs, the moon and sun, Rāhu, Meru, the serpents, humans, and gods; the retrograde planets together with the stars; the transits, months, fortnights, days, nights, and lunar dates—all this within the body is to be known by the yogi through the divisions of the voids (*śūnya*) and the threefold movement according to their respective colors.
In this body, the entire aggregate beginning with earth is to be known through their respective phonemes (*varṇas*).

Thus, earth is to be known by the dental phonemes, water by the labials, fire by the retroflexes, and wind by the palatals; furthermore, earth, water, fire, and wind are [represented by] the thunderbolt and lightning through the retroflexes.
The rainbow is by the letters *su-ra-dha-nu*, Indra’s bow by *i-n-dra-dha-nu*;

the winds are by the ten palatal (*tālavya*) letters; the zodiac wheel (*rāśicakra*) by all the letters beginning with *a* and *ka*; the Moon by the nasal bindu; the Sun by the visarga; Rāhu by the vowelless consonant; Meru by the first letter of its name; the abode of the serpents (*phaṇin*) by the syllable *oṃ*; the abode of humans, the mortal world (*martyaloka*), by the letter *ā*; and the abode of the gods, heaven (*svarga*), by the syllable *hūṃ*.

The planets, Maṅgala and the rest, are crooked [due to their movement] by means of the previously mentioned seed-syllables of the right and left [channels]; the transits (*saṃkrānti*) are likewise through the divisions of the twelve groups; the months are also thus; the fortnights (*pakṣa*) are through the divisions of half the six groups; and the days, nights, and lunar dates (*tithi*) are through the previously mentioned [syllables] beginning with *ka* together with the vowels. All this within the body is to be known by the yogin.

The threefold movement of the yogin through the divisions of emptiness according to the previously stated sequence is also threefold for the threefold Vajrasattva—whose nature consists of the desire, form, and formless realms—because he abides as the self of all through great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

And that [is to be known] "by the divisions of emptiness," meaning by the divisions of the four drops of *bodhicitta*. Thus ends the rule on the summary of the collection of the universe within the body. Now, for the sake of explaining the causal complex for the arising of the human body, he states the third verse beginning with "In the body" (*dehe*), etc.: "In this body, the entire multitude of elements (*dhātu*) indeed arises from food and drink of the six tastes; and the six tastes arise from the primary elements (*bhūta*); and the multitude of primary elements is manifestly and invariably established in the element of space (*khadhātu*)."

In the void, knowledge becomes blended, becoming of equal taste (*samarasa*), imperishable, and eternal; thus, one should know that the peace abiding in such a state pervades the threefold existence within one's own body. In this body, there is a collection of elements (*dhātuvṛnda*); namely, the collection of elements consisting of hair, skin, blood, flesh, bone, marrow, and so forth. Indeed, this entire collection of elements arises from food and drink of the six tastes—salt, sweet, pungent, bitter, astringent, and sour; by the power of these foods and drinks, the collection of elements comes to be.

"From the elements, the six tastes": from earth, water, fire, wind, and space, the six tastes arise; "the collection of elements in the space-element": the collection of earth, water, fire, wind, and taste exists within the space-element, which is the previously mentioned nature of the atom in emptiness. "Knowledge is mixed in emptiness": here, by means of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader, that consciousness of all sentient beings which exists within one's own body according to conventional truth—precisely that becomes the unchanging and eternal, with the perceiving mind mixed and of one flavor with the appearance of the perceived mind, through the power of meditation upon the empty image of emptiness.
Here, "Śā" is said to be without obscuration (*nirāvaraṇa*).

Thus, the peaceful great bliss (*mahāsukha*) abiding in suchness, which pertains to the threefold existence, is to be understood within one's own body. [In the] chapter on the arising of body, speech, and mind, this is the Great Summary (*mahoddeśa*) determining the Four Noble Truths. Regarding the "Yogin," here in the internal chapter, a concise commentary on this verse shall be spoken; it must be explained in detail in the forthcoming Knowledge Chapter (*jñānapaṭala*), in the *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*. This concludes the rule regarding the collection of causes and conditions for the arising of the body.

He describes the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) and so forth, starting with the words "the seed" (*bīja*): "The earth holds the seed; thereafter, water makes it sprout as it resides within the womb; fire brings about consciousness; the wind swallows the essence of the fluids and causes its growth;

and space provides the room for that growth. O King, in this way, through time, the [five] divine elements bring about the various stages, from the moment of birth until the period of childhood and beyond.
In this context, that which has fallen from the union of the two organs, being discharged and red, into the secret lotus—that is called the seed (*bīja*).
"The earth bears that seed" means that which is the earth-element (*pṛthvī-dhātu*) within the secret lotus.

"Situated in the lotus" means situated in the secret lotus. Therefore, water causes it to sprout from the secret lotus, and subsequently fire brings about its awakening; for this seed, once sprouted by water, fire effects its full development.
It swallows the "taste of tastes," meaning it consumes the six flavors (ṣaḍrasa) that have been eaten and drunk by the mother; this fiery energy (tejas) swallows the essence of the taste,
while the wind (māruta) brings about the growth of this seed, and from that growth, space (kha)— that is, the void— provides room.
"O King" is the address;
thus, in due time, accomplishment occurs in this very manner and by this sequence, namely, the accomplishment of the Fish and the other [emanations], which is the manifestation of the womb.

The divine [factors] produce the states; thus, the ten divine states beginning with smoke (dhūma) produce the ten states beginning with the embryo, child, and youth. At the time of birth and in childhood and so forth, it is "time" (kāla); this is the rule for conception.
He describes the function of the seed upon its own elements, starting with the words "of the seed," etc.: its growth...

Earth makes the seed firm and clearly dense; water alone provides fluidity; fire brings about ripening; the excellent tenfold wind causes further growth; and space indeed grants room from time to time. Thus, through various and manifold states, the powers of body, speech, and mind expand—this is truly creation.

In this case, that which is the earth-element of the seed—the semen and blood—having consumed the six flavors residing in the secret lotus, clearly brings about heaviness and density; water likewise produces fluidity for the sake of the body's formation; fire performs the digestion of the consumed flavors; the preeminent tenfold wind, beginning with prāṇa, effects their increase for the sake of this seed’s body; and space indeed provides the room for that growth. Thus, from time, creation proceeds according to the previously described method.

"Constantly sounding through various and manifold states"—this refers to the statement regarding the function of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the elements (*dhātu*), wherein the powers (*śakti*) of body, speech, and mind—smoke and the other signs—emanate as the attributes (*dharmin*) of body, speech, and mind.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the ten states of the internal mind-holding Viṣṇu are described starting with the words "In the secret [lotus]" (*guhya*): "When the seed of enlightenment (*bodhibīja*), even though fallen into the midst of the blood in the secret lotus, becomes endowed with life, it becomes the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, the Dwarf, Rāma, and Rāma."

Kṛṣṇa becomes the Buddha, the Lord of Men; and there are these ten stages: three in the womb, one at the time of birth, two in childhood, another in youth, one vast stage in adulthood, and likewise one perfect [stage]. (6)
Even in old age, there is but one peace; for those born from a womb, death is the final end.
In the Matsya [age], he has the form of a fish for some days; in the Kaurma, the state of a tortoise; in the Vārāhya, he has the abode of a boar; and in the Nārasiṃha, his birth occurs. ||7||

In this case, when the seed of enlightenment—that is, the semen—falls into the center of the red [lotus] within the secret lotus, being endowed with life and accompanied by the *ālayavijñāna*, then it possesses the characteristics of the ten stages (*daśāvasthā*). Among those, while in the womb, there are three stages: those of the fish, the tortoise, and Rāhu. Likewise, at the time of birth, there is one stage: that of Narasiṃha (the Man-Lion). Furthermore, during childhood, there are two: from the eruption of the teeth until the falling out of the teeth is the stage of Vāmana, and from the falling out of the teeth until their regrowth is the stage of Paraśurāma.

"In childhood and youth there are others"—thus, from the falling of the teeth until the age of sixteen is the first *vipulā*, the stage of *rāmā*; likewise, another *vipulā* is the stage of *kṛṣṇā* from the sixteenth year until the appearance of grey hair; the stage of *buddhā* is from the appearance of grey hair until the day of death; on the day of death, because of becoming one with all beings (*sarvabhūtaikalolībhūtatvāt*), the stage of *kalkī* occurs in the body;
even in old age, there is the state of being solely peaceful (*ekaśāntā*) and final dissolution (*nidhanatā*); such is the rule of the ten stages for those born from a womb.

Regarding the internal state of Viṣṇu, the activity of the ten stages of the Mind-Vajradhara is described starting with "Matsya" (the Fish) and so forth: here, in the state of the Fish (*mātsya*), the Bodhicitta-Vajra becomes the form of a fish for as many days as there are days in the season (*ṛtudina*); then, in the state of the Tortoise (*kūrma*), the state of the tortoise occurs for another period of seasonal days, as indicated by the word "and" (*ca*); in the state of Vārāhī, for the Bodhicitta-Viṣṇu, the twelve sense-bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) arise, which is the abode of the Sun, lasting until the third seasonal day; likewise, from seven months until the day of birth, the state of Narasiṃha (the Man-Lion) occurs, because of the tearing open of the womb with both hands.
In Vāmana [the child] is in a state of infancy; in Dvāpara [the teeth] of two kings emerge; in Rāmya [they] fall out again; in Rāmya [again], even though it is manifest, she causes deceit in action;
in Bauddha she brings peace; in Kālki she observes vows and enters into restraint; and in Śukra, marrow, bone, and the channels arise from the *rajas*, as do skin, blood, and flesh. ||8||

[In this] chapter: The Great Summary on the Determination of the Four Noble Truths Concerning the Arising of Body, Speech, and Mind. The red seed, having entered the essence of nectar, sprouts within the womb during the first month. Subsequently, ten extremely subtle channels arise from the friendly sprout of the seed at the navel;
another eight times eight [channels] extend upwards toward the hands, feet, and mouth. When the second month is complete, there is some indication of the hands, feet, and mouth here.

In the state of Vāmana, the previously mentioned state of childhood occurs; in the state of Rāma, thirty-two teeth emerge; and in the state of Paraśurāma, they clearly fall out. He, that very Viṣṇu of the *bodhicitta*, would cause illusion (*māyā*) to be enacted in the state of activity; in the Buddhist state, he brings peace to sentient beings, and in the Kalkin state, he undergoes vows, observances, and even death.
In the state of Kalki, one undergoes death according to the previously mentioned procedure; this is the "ten incarnations" (daśāvatāra).

Regarding the statement here that the Purāṇas concerning the Fish incarnation and others were composed by wicked Brahmin sages for the purpose of deceiving the ignorant and are the cause for attaining hell—this must be explained in detail in the forthcoming *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*.

The transformations of the semen and the menstrual blood residing in the mother’s womb, from conception until birth, are described by the words beginning with "semen" (*śukra*). In this body, six sheaths (*koṣa*) arise for the newborn: from semen, marrow arises; bones arise; and sinews and ligaments arise. From the menstrual blood (*rajas*), skin and blood arise; and flesh arises, because from that single blood there is the germination of the seed of blood.

In this womb, for one month the seed-blood grows, permeated by the essence of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). After that, from the sprout of the seed, and from above that month, ten kinds of channels (*nāḍī*)—which serve as the support for the winds such as *prāṇa* and so forth—arise in the center of the heart for the bodhicitta that has become a sprout. These are extremely subtle, with a measure like a hair. In the navel, in the region of the navel, there are sixty-four channels carrying the staffs (days) of eight times eight. Although not explicitly stated, because of the transition through the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*), there are twelve channels that serve as the support for those sixty-four; they are likewise extremely subtle. All those aforementioned navel-channels, moving upward to perform the functions of the hands, feet, and mouth, proceed to the locations of the hands, feet, and mouth; it is by the power of their proceeding therefrom [that the body is formed].

When the second month is complete, there is the formation of the face, hands, and feet; here, after some days have passed from the previous fish-stage, in this tortoise-stage, five swellings arise at the locations of the face, hands, and feet—the two hands, the two feet, and the neck—and the head becomes fully formed at the end of the third month. In the fourth month, subtle channels (nāḍikā) appear in the hands, feet, face, and the region of the neck.

The tortoise state (*kūrmāvasthā*) occurs when the hands, feet, and neck have formed with a symmetrical head; furthermore, other subtle channels (*sūkṣmanāḍyaḥ*) appear in the hands, feet, face, and the region of the throat, as well as the extremely subtle *sahaja-sambhoga* channels at the six joints of the hands and feet and at the mouth and throat, once the fourth month is completed.

In the fifth month, in the Vārāhī bhāva, relying upon the flesh and the bones, there are three hundred and sixty bones and an equal number of joints—[the phrase] "by the fire of the harsh [wind]" (kharasahutabhuj) [refers to this]. And in the sixth month, by the word "and" (ca), in the Vārāhī bhāva, there arises flesh and blood; sensation arises, and one experiences pleasure and pain. By the power of higher knowledge (abhijñā), one recollects former existences (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti); through one's own mind, one practices detachment, censures the suffering of existence, and praises the path of the Buddha.

The eyebrows, the hair of the head, and the body hairs also arise in the best of sages; from one month onwards, the channels (nāḍikās) remain with a remainder. Day by day, at the time of birth, the vital points (marmas), bones, marrow, tongue, urine, and feces are formed in the eighth [month], known as the "aperture" (randhra), when there is terrible suffering for the one oppressed by the womb during the moment of delivery.

Then, in the state of Vārāhī, when the seventh month has been completed, the hair, the pores of the skin, the eyes and so forth, as well as all the sense bases (*āyatana*), become fully formed. From this point on, after the months of gestation, at every daily interval, there are two hundred channels (*nāḍī*)— numbered by "zero-zero-eyes"— which arise each day.

Then there are three hundred and sixty vital points (*marmāṇi*) and bones; within them is the marrow. The tongue arises for the production of the gustatory faculty (*jihvendriya*); previously, the eyes and so forth were solid. Then, at the time of the production of the tongue, urine and excrement arise here during the eighth month.

In the ninth month, known as the *randhra* (the void), when the period of the *vārāhī* house has been completed—whether in the tenth, eleventh, or twelfth month—at the conclusion of the *vārāhī* state, there occurs terrible suffering at the time of birth for the one born from the womb who is oppressed by the birth canal in the *nārasiṃha* state; such is the rule regarding the emergence of the fetus.

Regarding the Four Noble Truths, he speaks of the truth of suffering for those in cyclic existence, beginning with "in the womb," and so forth: "In the womb, there is the suffering of being in the womb; at the time of birth, and even in infancy, there is suffering; in childhood and youth, there is the great suffering of afflictions struck down by wealth and power; in old age, there is the suffering of death; and once again, one takes up suffering from the six realms of existence, which is terrifying from the very beginning. This entire world is afflicted and deluded by illusion. (12)

In this world, for transmigrating beings, first of all, while remaining in the womb, there is suffering like that of being boiled in a cauldron (*kumbhīpāka*); at the time of birth, it is like being crushed by a mallet or a machine; even in infancy, it is like a pig eating excrement; in childhood and youth, there is the suffering of separation from fortune and the suffering of being struck down by wealth and power;

in the absence of those, even in old age, there is the suffering of decay and death; and again, at the end of death, there is the terrifying realm of Raurava and other hells within the six states of existence.

From the very beginning, terrible suffering arises in the realms of hungry ghosts and animals due to the power of evil; through the abandonment of the ten wholesome [actions], one thus grasps suffering from suffering. In this entire world, this world is deluded by illusion (*māyā*). Deluded here in *saṃsāra* by illusion—which consists of the notions of "I" and "mine"—one grasps suffering in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. [This concludes] the Great Summary (*Mahoddeśa*) on the Determination of the Four Noble Truths regarding the arising of body, speech, and mind.

He speaks of the Truth of the Path, beginning with "In saṃsāra" and so forth: "In saṃsāra, human birth may occur somewhere; at some time, there may arise an inclination toward the Dharma. From that, through the power of merit, devotion to the Buddha arises, and one enters the Primordial Vehicle (Ādiyāna). From that, in some cases, the entire mind becomes engaged in the practice of meditation within the glorious Vajrayāna. Through that meditation, Buddhahood is desired. Alas! Entry into the state of supreme bliss is exceedingly difficult! (kaṣṭam) ||13||

[89b] Here, within this saṃsāra consisting of the six realms of existence, human birth may occur somewhere; from that, a mind directed toward the Dharma sometimes arises in humans regarding the teachings of non-Buddhist outsiders such as generosity and so forth.

Consequently, through the power of merit, an affection for the Buddha sometimes arises; and even more than that, through the power of merit, an inclination toward the first vehicle—the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—arises, as well as an inclination toward generosity and other virtues.

Therefore, there is engagement in the glorious Vajrayāna. "Vajra" means that which is indivisible, indestructible, and great; that itself is the vehicle (*yāna*), consisting of both the Mantra system and the Pāramitā system, characterized by cause and fruit, and unified as one. Engagement in that is engagement in the Vajrayāna. Consequently, in some instances, the entire mind is directed toward meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This cultivation consists of objectless compassion based upon objective emptiness, occurring through the power of merit and gnosis. In that cultivation, Buddhahood is attained as the desired goal.
Thus, entry into the state of supreme bliss is exceedingly difficult—indeed, far, far beyond reach—for worldly beings who long for the pleasures of cyclic existence.

With the words beginning with "in the womb," he explains the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*): "In the womb, the perfectly pure body; at the time of birth, the state of teeth [and] the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); and when the teeth fall out, O King, the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) of the Victor arises."

Therefore, the nirmāṇakāya, which is manifest and fixed until the limit of death for humans, becomes fourfold within the womb and outside [the womb] again, due to the distinction between primordial wisdom (jñāna) and consciousness (vijñāna). || 14 ||

In this world, first of all, the pure body and so forth are perceived within the body of one born from a womb according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*); subsequently, that very [purity] of the Buddha, the Blessed One—the utterly pure body and so forth—is to be understood by yogins through the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
Here, as long as he remains in the mother’s womb, the embodied one possesses a perfectly pure body endowed with the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).
Then, beginning from the time of birth until the eruption of the teeth, it is the *dharmakāya*.
From the eruption of the teeth until their falling out, it is the *saṃbhogakāya* of the Jina, the Vajra of Bodhicitta.
"O King" is an address.
Therefore, the Nirmāṇakāya is manifested from the falling of the teeth; it is certain that for humans born from a womb, death is the sleep of the moon.

This collection of bodies exists fourfold, both within the womb and externally: again, this is due to the division of *jñāna* (primordial wisdom) within the womb and the division of the six *vijñānas* (consciousnesses) externally, according to the distinction between *jñāna* and *vijñāna*.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*: "The internal consciousness, as well as the moon and sun situated in the lotuses, is the Pure Body (*śuddhakāya*) within the womb. That which arises from the elements and aggregates is the tenfold *Dharmakāya* of the Victor."

Therefore, the enjoyment body (sambhogakāya) arises by the power of qualities when the sense objects such as sound are produced; therefore, when hair and so forth are produced, the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) is present here at the time of birth. || 15 ||
In this womb, first of all, consciousness is the *ālayavijñāna*, which is existence (*sat*), bliss, and gnosis (*jñāna*).
The moon and sun are the semen and the menses; these three, having entered the lotus—that is, having entered the mother’s womb—become one for the formation of the embryo.

That [embryo] is called the Pure Body (*śuddhakāya*) of the Blessed One within the womb, because it arises from the state of the singular bliss of the dissolution-consciousness (*layavijñāna*) of the mother and father.
The tenfold arising of the elements and aggregates is the *dharmakāya* of the Victor, the Vajra of Bodhicitta.

Therefore, when the internal sense faculties such as the ear and so forth, and their objects such as sound and so forth, have arisen, the *saṃbhogakāya* comes into being by virtue of the qualities and the [passage of] days.
From that, once hair and so forth have arisen, the production of body hair, feces, and urine begins at first.

The emergence from the womb at the time of birth is called the *nirmāṇakāya* while in the embryo; that which occurs upon birth as the arising of breath is the *śuddhakāya*, free from qualities. Therefore, the arising of teeth, even when speech is still indistinct, is likewise the *dharmakāya*.
From that, O King, the falling out of the teeth produces the *saṃbhogakāya* of the Victor; and until the limit of death, there exists for the Lord of Victors the external *nirmāṇakāya*.

Then, when the four bodies have arisen externally, that which is the first emergence of the breath occurring in the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) is the *saṃśuddhakāya* (completely pure body) with respect to the *vāgvajra* (speech-vajra); that very [body] remains as the *śuddhakāya* (pure body) through the flow of the central channel for as long as it lasts until the group of fifty-six and a quarter breaths.

Thereafter, by the power of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that which is the emergence of teeth and the indistinct speech is characterized by *saṃjñā* (perception); that is the *dharmakāya* with respect to the *vāgvajra*.
Therefore, for the twice-born, the falling of the teeth occurs at dawn, until the Sambhogakāya [is present] up to the age of eight years due to the clarity of speech.
From the falling of the teeth until death, the Nirmāṇakāya exists externally.
Here, within the womb, there is a fourfold division of the body according to the differentiation of the bodies.

Externally, through the divisions of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is a fourfold division of the body, as well as gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) within the body. Both internally and externally, these are accompanied by the body and the vital breath. Here, the division of the body pertains to semen (*śukra*), while the division of speech pertains to blood (*rakta*);
thus, through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader, the fourfold division of the body occurs by way of the division of the mind (*citta*).

The fourfold division of the body occurs through the fourfold division of cognition characterized by the waking state and so forth, as well as through the fourfold nature consisting of bliss and so forth; this is the rule for the arising of the external Sahaja-kāya and others within the body.

He describes the arising of body, speech, mind, and gnosis with the verse beginning "In the womb" (*garbhe*): "In the womb, first there is here the glorious Body-Vajra; at birth, it takes the form of Speech; the Mind arises at the eruption of the teeth; and again, upon the emergence from falling [from the mother's lap], there is Gnosis-Vajra."

Knowledge mixed with consciousness, joined with the sun and moon, and all that consists of the knowledge-vajra and so forth, having ascended into the womb, gradually arises powerfully through the body-vajra and the rest. (17)

In this chapter, the Great Summary on the Determination of the Four Noble Truths Concerning the Arising of Body, Speech, and Mind: Here, within the mother’s womb, *jñāna* is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), the *ālayavijñāna* mixed with consciousness; accompanied by the sun and moon, and joined with *rajas* and semen, it becomes all things beginning with the *jñānavajra* and innate bliss.
Once established in the womb, it gradually arises powerfully through the *kāyavajra* and the rest.
Here, first, the glorious *kāyavajra* exists in the womb until the time of birth; the meaning is that it is the completion of the limbs of the body.
Then, upon giving birth, the vajra of speech arises, followed by the movement of the vital breath and the emergence of the vital breath;
thereafter, the mind arises.
This occurs when the thirty-two teeth have appeared, as it is the grasper of designations.
The word *vai* means "certainly" or "decisively.

Furthermore, after the falling out of the primary teeth and the emergence of the thirty-two [permanent] teeth, it should be understood that for women, up until the age of twelve, and for men, up until the age of sixteen, there occurs the state characterized by the emission of semen known as the *jñānavajra*, which is characterized by innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). This is the explanation of the perfection of body, speech, mind, and gnosis.

He explains the relationship between the support and the supported with the verse beginning "pṛthvī" and so forth: Fire has earth as its womb; earth and wind have space as their womb; and water indeed has wind and earth as its womb, being itself devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) yet possessing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Water is the support of earth, fire is the support of water, wind is the support of fire, and space, O King, arises as the support of wind; thus indeed does the support become the supported. (18)
In this context, fire (hutāśa) becomes the embryo of the earth, yet it does not belong to that family (tatkulī), because it lacks the inherent nature of the qualities of earth.
Within the womb of space—that is, in the midst of the void—the earth and wind do not originate from that family, due to the absence of the qualities of space.
Likewise, water becomes the embryo of both wind and earth.

That very [element] remains within the womb of the wind in accordance with its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); wherever the wind migrates, it goes along with it. That which is situated within the earth is seen as having a liquid nature when the earth is being excavated. Furthermore, in this context, space (*ākāśa*) is the support (*ādhāra*) for all [elements] such as earth, while the elements such as earth are the supported (*ādheya*).
In this context, the support and the supported occur respectively:
just as for the earth-element (bhūmi), water is the support—the external water-circle being the support of the earth-circle—so too it is within the body.
Furthermore, fire, which is the fire-circle, is the support of water; that is, it is the support of the water-circle.

"Anila" refers to the sphere of wind. For the fire-sphere (pāvaka), which is the fire-maṇḍala, the support is the wind, which is the wind-maṇḍala; for the wind-maṇḍala, emptiness (śūnya) is the support, which is space (ākāśa).
In this way, emptiness becomes the support for all elements (bhūta), beginning with earth.

He explains the aggregate as the substratum and that which is supported, beginning with the word "skandha" (aggregate): The substratum of the aggregates is indeed the material element within the beautiful body; the channels belong to the collection of elements; the tenfold vital wind belongs to the channels; and consciousness belongs to the vital wind.

That mind is of a dual nature due to the influence of the qualities (*guṇas*), being both with intrinsic nature and without intrinsic nature. And the Lord who supports those two is the unstruck (*anāhata*) sound, saluted by the three worlds, who is all-pervading. (19)
In this body, the support for the five aggregates is indeed the elemental, which is the collection of the elements such as earth and so forth.
For what reason?
Because here, due to the absence of the primary nature (prakṛti) of earth and the other elements, there is no causal condition such as ignorance and the rest.
In the absence of conditions such as ignorance (*avidyā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), there is an absence of the aggregates (*skandha*) such as form (*rūpa*).
Since form consists of the four elements and the Great Being (*mahāpuruṣapuṅgala*) consists of the six constituents (*ṣaḍdhātu*), the aggregate of form is indeed the support for the [other] elements.

Within the excellent body, there are seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*) that serve as the support for the collection of elements; and the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) is the support even for those channels, because it is the cause of their formation.
And that [consciousness] is to be explained as tenfold, as will be described.
Volition (*cetanā*) is the support of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*);

that volition is itself the mind (*citta*) which possesses a dual nature. By virtue of the qualities (*guṇas*), specifically by the power of *sattva* and *rajas*, it becomes "with-nature" (*sasvabhāva*), characterized by the states of waking and dreaming; by the power of the quality of *tamas*, it becomes "without-nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*), characterized by deep sleep and devoid of the senses.

And the master, the support, and the sustainer of those two—the one possessing intrinsic nature and the one lacking intrinsic nature—is the transmigrating being who wanders through states of pleasure and pain.
Yet he who is devoid of pleasure and pain, saluted by the three worlds, is the Unstruck (*anāhata*), omnipresent, the end-maker of pleasure and pain, and the ultimate ground.

The arising of odor occurs in the earth; likewise, taste in fire, the element of form in water, touch in wind, and sound in the tranquil ether; and in the ether of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), there is the arising of sound.

Indeed, the progenitor of the Jinas perceives sound as empty; the wind [perceives] the dharmadhātu; fire [perceives] smell; water [perceives] form and taste; and the earth [perceives] touch alone. 20.

He explains the relationship of producer and produced among the elements with the words "smell" (*gandha*) and so forth: here, whether externally or internally, the production of smell occurs primarily in the element of earth (*dharaṇī*); however, the production of taste and the other qualities occurs only secondarily. The word "api" (also) indicates possibility: in the fire-element (*śikhin*), which is the element of fire, the production of the sixfold taste occurs due to the cause of digestion by fire; from that [fire], the production of form occurs in water. Here, the sprouting and so forth of seeds and the like—possessing various colors and various shapes—occur primarily from water; secondarily, however, there is also the production of taste and the other qualities.
In this way, the arising of touch occurs in the wind and the wind-element;
in the peaceful element of gnosis, the arising of sound occurs as "rava.
In the sky, within the fivefold essence-element—the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and the element of bodhicitta—there occurs the arising of the state of bliss during the period of impurity.

Now, the relationship between the grasped and the grasper is explained: here, the accomplishment of the effect occurs through union with another family (*parakula*), because there is a contradiction in action within one's own self through union with one's own family (*svakula*);
therefore, union with another family is the cause for the arising of the body.

"Empty of that" means that the auditory faculty, which arises from the element of emptiness, perceives sound, which indeed arises from the element of gnosis—this is certain, as it is said, "O Progenitor of the Victors. The mental faculty, which arises from the element of gnosis, perceives the object of the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), which arises from the space element.
Furthermore, by virtue of the inseparability of the produced and the producer, the olfactory faculty, having become wind, perceives the object of smell, which has become the earth element.
Furthermore, fire grasps the visual faculty produced from the fire element and the object of form produced from the water element; it also grasps the object of taste produced from the fire element.
Water grasps the gustatory faculty produced from the water element and the object of touch produced from the earth element.

Earth grasps the tactile faculty produced from the earth element and the object of touch produced from the wind element. Such is the fixed rule regarding the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped among objects and their corresponding faculties.

He states the establishment of the aggregates, such as form and so forth, within each individual element according to worldly convention, beginning with the words "established" (*siddham*): Form is established in the earth, and in water, the abode of the three worlds; the notion of "established" is indeed in fire, and sensation (*vedanā*) arises in wind;

the formation (*saṃskāra*) is established there, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is established in the vajra of space mixed with gnosis (*jñāna*). Thus, all the elements, aggregates, and so forth, come to be in this body through the union of passion (*rajas*) with the bodhicitta and the rest. (21)

Here, the identity of the elements and the aggregates is stated as established; in this world, form is established primarily in the element of earth, while perception and the others are established only secondarily.
This applies to the abode of the three worlds, the domain of the three realms, but it does not apply to the dharma of nirvāṇa.

By the use of the word "and" (ca), the designation "water" is established here. Since the moon is the nature of sound (*svara*) and semen is of the nature of water, the designation "water" is established because of its watery nature; this is the certainty regarding "water. Furthermore, regarding "feeling" (*vedanā*) in fire: here, the sun is the nature of fire and is *rajas*, while *Kālī* is the sun’s *rajas*; thus, feeling has the nature of *Kālī*.
Therefore, sensation (*vedanā*) is established primarily in fire, while the remaining [aggregates] arise secondarily;

in wind, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is established. Thus, in this context, wind is the mover of body, speech, and mind, and the generator of formations; by that, formations, whose nature is wind, are established.
Likewise, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is mixed with knowledge (*jñāna*), being accompanied by knowledge.
Respectively, in the sky-vajra, consciousness is established in space, characterized by auditory consciousness and the rest;
in the vajra, the element of gnosis, gnosis is established at the end of the emission of the bodhicitta, consisting of the moment of bliss.
Here, "kāra" refers to the Great Being (*mahāpuruṣapuṃgala*), who consists of the six elements.
Why [is it said] "all, such as the elements and aggregates"? He says:

because of the union with passion (*rajas*), which is the bodhicitta and so forth. Here, in this body, whatever exists—such as the elements and aggregates—that all arises from the conjunction with the states of the moments of bliss of the *ālayavijñāna* and the white seminal essence (*śukra*).

Regarding how the ears and other sense-faculties, as perceivers, possess the nature of grasping objects such as sound, he says "the ear," and so forth: "The ear has the nature of the Vajra, O Lord of Men; the mind has the nature of space; the nose has the nature of earth; and likewise the tongue has the nature of fire."

In the abode of the three worlds, the eye has the nature of water and the body has the nature of air; likewise, all [faculties] such as the ear come into being through the power of the qualities (guṇa) by means of the union of primordial wisdom (jñāna) and consciousness (vijñāna). // 22 //

In this context, regarding the properties of the body, the ear is characterized by emptiness as the subject; through its grasping of the object of sound, it has the nature of a vajra and the nature of sound.
Here, the subject-property (*grāhaka-dharma*) is said to be a division of the body, while the object-property (*grāhya-dharma*) is a division of existence (*bhāva*).
Therefore, O King—this is an address—the nature of the produced and the producer is to be understood by means of the nature of the object.

The mind (*citta*) and the intellect (*manas*) have the nature of space (*ākāśa*) and the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, because they grasp the objects of the *dharmadhātu*. The nose has the nature of earth and the nature of odor, because it grasps odor. Likewise, the tongue has the nature of fire, just as previously stated in the *Vimalaprabhā* regarding the internal [chapter], because it grasps taste, which has the nature of fire.
The eye has the nature of water, because it perceives forms produced by water within the abode of the three worlds; nor is it in nirvāṇa,
and the body is its own nature, while the body-faculty is produced from wind, because it perceives the object of touch.

In the sequence thus stated, everything beginning with the ear arises through the power of the qualities (*guṇa*); that is, by the power of sound, the *dharmadhātu*, smell, taste, form, and touch, there arise the ear, mind, nose, tongue, eye, and body—these six sense-faculties (*indriyadhātu*) are to be understood through their connection with gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). By means of the six elements (*dhātu*), he speaks of the six mental fluctuations, such as stinginess and so forth, beginning with "stinginess": Stinginess (*mātsarya*) occurs in the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*), and in the excellent body and in space (*ākāśa*), the diamond-like mind of hatred (*dveṣavajra*) [arises]; indeed, the mind of envy (*īrṣyācitta*) is manifest in wind, and likewise, the mind of passion (*rāgacitta*) in fire.
In water, the glorious Vajra-mind [arose] by the power of its natural quality; on earth, the Moha-vajra-mind arose; and in wind, fire, water, and earth, all the others came into being. // 23 //

In this body, the mind’s envy [is said to be] in the element of gnosis; here the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative, meaning that by virtue of the element of gnosis, there is a mind of envy in sentient beings.
"The diamond of hatred in space" means that by virtue of the space element, there is a mind of hatred in sentient beings.
Likewise, by virtue of the wind element there is a mind of jealousy, by virtue of the fire element a mind of passion; this very point was revealed by the Sage.

In the same way, the mind of pride arises from the power of the water element; the mind of delusion arises from the power of the earth element. Nature (*prakṛti*) consists of the qualities and intrinsic natures of the elements such as gnosis (*jñāna*); by the power of those intrinsic natures, stinginess and other afflictions arise in the minds of transmigrating beings.
Regarding the sense organs [arising] from the power of the elements, he says "speech," and so forth:

here, the vocal organ arises from the wind element, the hand organ from the fire element, the foot organ from the water element, and the anal organ from the earth element. Since it was not explicitly mentioned, the secret organ arises from the space element.

At the end of sixteen years, the divine faculty arises within the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*); thus, from the six action-faculties and the six elements, the winds beginning with *apāna* are described by the verse beginning with "in *apāna*" and so forth: In the element of gnosis, *apāna* is threefold; *prāṇa-vāyu* is in the void (*śūnya*); *samāna* is in the center of the wind; furthermore, *udāna* is in fire (*śikhin*); *vyāna* is in water (*ambhas*);
and *nāga*, *kūrma*, *kṛkara*, *devadatta*, and *dhanañjaya* arise respectively in earth (*bhūmi*), wind and fire (*vāyuvahni*), and water and earth (*payasi mahaḥ*). // 24 //

In this body, the apāna wind arises from the element of gnosis (jñānadhātu); here too, the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative, and it is threefold due to its extraction of feces, urine, and semen. And the prāṇa wind arises in the void (śūnya), from the element of space (ākāśadhātu); by the word "and" (ca), that too is threefold due to its flow through the left, right, and central channels.
Between the winds, the samāna wind arises from the nature of the element of air (vāyudhātu).
Furthermore, in the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) of Śikhin, there is Udāna; in water, the water element, there is Vyāna;
and on earth, the earth element, there is Nāga, which is *ran bsin* (svabhāva).

*Saṃbhavanti*, Chapter One: The Great Summary on the Determination of the Four Noble Truths Concerning the Arising of Body, Speech, and Mind. Immediately following this, there are four [winds] beginning with Kūrma: from the wind element comes Kūrma; from the fire element comes Kṛkara; from the water element comes Devadatta; and from the earth element comes Dhanañjaya.

Up to the end of the sixteenth year, there is the wind of *ānanda* (joy) belonging to the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), and the wind of *sahajānanda* (innate joy) belonging to the gnosis element (*jñānadhātu*). According to the [five] elements, the wheels (*cakras*) and so forth are described as being at the joints of the hands and other parts of the body, beginning with the *uṣṇīṣa*: The *uṣṇīṣa* occurs in the space element for gods and humans; the secret place in the gnosis element; the heart-lotus in the wind element; and in the manifest fire element, the throat-wheel (*kaṇṭhacakra*) clearly shines. In the water element, the lotus between the eyebrows has sixty-four petals (*vasu-vasu-dalaka*); and on earth, the navel-wheel (*nābhicakra*) has sixty-four petals. There are six joints in the hands and feet: two each in earth, water, fire, and wind. (25)
In this context, from the element of space (ākāśa), there arises either a turban or a lotus-wheel;
the number of petals shall be stated later.
Furthermore, for gods and humans, it becomes the secret [element] of the wisdom-element (jñānadhātu), meaning the secret lotus.
The heart-lotus arises from the wind element;
the throat-chakra clearly blazes forth from the fire element; "hi" indicates certainty; and the lotus between the eyebrows arises from the water element.
The *vasu-vasu* [sixty-four] petalled navel-cakra (*padma*) exists in the earth element;
the singular number is used for the plural "six joints.
In the feet and hands, there are three in the left foot due to the division of the qualities of the earth element: *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
The word *mahī* is a synonym for the earth (*bhū*) with a short vowel.

There are three [cakras] in the right foot due to the division of the three qualities of the water element; there are three in the left hand due to the division of the three qualities of fire; and there are three in the right hand due to the division of the three qualities of wind—thus, the number three applies to the Maruts. These twelve cakras are to be explained in what follows; this is the rule regarding the eighteen cakras.

Now, he describes the arising of the fingers by virtue of the elements, beginning with the words "earth" (*bhūmi*) and so forth: "In the five elements, starting with earth, by the power of the threefold qualities, there arose the fingers and thumbs of the feet and hands; all ten [fingers] multiplied by three, consisting of joints, are to be grasped as ending in the nails. Furthermore, in the differentiation of the principles (*tattva*), whatever else exists on the beautiful body ending with the body hair, that likewise arises from the element. (26)

Here, in both the left and right hands, the fingers beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger consist of three joints each, having as their nature the five elements and the three qualities. Thus, by the power of the earth element, there is the thumb; by the power of the three qualities of the earth element, there are the three joints of the thumb. Likewise, by the nature of the water element, there is the index finger; similarly, by the nature of the fire element, there is the middle finger; likewise, by the nature of the air element, there is the ring finger; and by the nature of the space element, there is the little finger.
Just as it is with the left hand, so it is with the right; thus it should be understood for the two feet.
Therefore, in both hands and both feet, the thirty joints—ten multiplied by three—are to be taken in their entirety, including the nails.
The ten teeth are described as follows: if, in this case, the first two teeth of the child appear above, then the right one has the nature of earth and the left one has the nature of water;
if they appear below, then the right one has the nature of fire and the left one has the nature of wind. Clearly, [this is] the lotus.
