In the Vimalaprabhā, the left [channel] within the internal body has the nature of wind (vam).

Likewise, again, the upper [channels] have the nature of fire and wind; the lower [channels] have the nature of earth and water; again, the lower [channels] have the nature of wind and fire; and again, the upper [channels] have the nature of earth and water.
In this way, by means of the nature of the four elements in direct and reverse order, as well as above and below, the thirty-two teeth are to be understood.
When the teeth are curved, that is the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
Thus, the body hair and head hair are to be known according to the differentiation of the elements.

Whatever else exists on the beautiful body, ending with the hair, all that should be understood as the five elements (*pañcadhātu*); the transformations of the elements (*dhātuvikāra*) consist of the distinctions of the body, numbering three and a half million varieties.

The transformation of the elements occurs by the power of the *rajas* (blood) and *śukra* (semen); "the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) is of many kinds in the body," so it was said by the Blessed One.

The Great Summary on the Truth of Origination and so forth. Now, the collection of the support and the supported is described with the words beginning "In the secret," and so on: "In the secret place, the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), and the navel, [the bodies] are the natureless nature of the Sahaja-jina; in the heart-cakra, O King, there is indeed the Dharmakāya of the Jina, and in the Sambhogacakra.

In the drop (*bindu*), the Nirmāṇakāya arises by the power of qualities through the sequence of the presiding deities. In the heart-cakra, the throat-cakra, and the head, there are the lotuses purified as Dharma, Sambhoga, and Śuddha [Kāyas]. (27)

In this body, there are six cakras that serve as the supports, and four bodies that are supported by them. Among these, within the three secret lotuses, the Sahajakāya is divided according to its own-nature and lack of own-nature.

Therefore, in the secret lotus, the crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) lotus, and the navel lotus, the Viśuddhakāya is the presiding deity; it is devoid of own-nature, its nature is non-conceptual, and it is like a reflected image.
In the heart is the Dharmakāya, and in the throat lotus is the Sambhogakāya as the presiding deity, distinguished by their respective bodies.
"In the *bindu*" means in the lotus of the head, the *śuddhacakra*; the *nirmāṇakāya* is the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*).

By way of the division of bodies, at the navel in the *nirmāṇacakra*, the *nirmāṇakāya* is the presiding deity; such is the rule regarding the division of bodies. "By virtue of qualities" refers to the qualities of the wheels (*cakras*): the qualities of space and gnosis belong to the supports of the *sahajakāya*; the quality of wind belongs to the support of the *dharmakāya*; the quality of fire belongs to the support of the *sambhogakāya*; and the quality of water belongs to the support of the *nirmāṇakāya*. This is the relationship between the support and that which is supported.

According to the stated sequence, there is the lotus of the heart-cakra, the throat-cakra, and the head, known as the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Śuddha [Kāyas]. Likewise, at the navel, throat, secret place, head, heart, and the center of the uṣṇīṣa, there are the threefold Vajras of Body, Speech, and Mind belonging respectively to the Mother and the Father. These are the six families—the Wheel, Jewel, Sky-lotus, Water-born, and Excellent Sword—joined with the Vajra. These [families] correspond to the three channels above and below, which follow the three paths through the divisions of Moon, Sun, and Fire. (28)

In this chapter, the "Great Summary on the Truth of Origination and so forth," the six families (*ṣaṭkula*) are described according to the divisions of the support of the body, beginning with the words "in the navel" (*nābhau*) and so on: here, in this body, by virtue of the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*), there are six families in the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) respectively—the three families of the mother and the three families of the husband, the father.

In the navel, in the earth-wheel (*pṛthivīcakra*), there is the Wheel family (*cakrakula*); in the throat, in the fire-wheel, there is the Lotus-Jewel family (*padmaratnakula*); in the secret place, in the wisdom-lotus (*jñānakamala*), there is the Sword family (*katikākula*). These correspond respectively to the body, speech, and mind of the mother.
Thus, on the head, in the water-lotus, there is the Lotus family; in the heart, in the wind-lotus, there is the Sword family.
Likewise, in the center of the uṣṇīṣa, in the space-element lotus, there is the Vajra family.
And the body, speech, and mind of the Lord are, respectively, the families of the female and male reproductive fluids (rajas and śukra).
Regarding the transformations produced from the elements such as earth and so forth, according to their respective order.

He states those very [channels] through the division of the channels of the winds, beginning with the words "those" (*tāni*) and so forth: here, due to the division of the three channels of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, there arise the characteristics designated as the "three channels. The feces-channel (*viḍnāḍī*) is the Wheel family (*cakrakula*) in the *apāna*; the sun-channel (*sūryanāḍī*) is the Jewel family (*ratnakula*) in the *prāṇa*; and the semen-channel (*śukranāḍī*) is the Knife family (*kartikākula*) in the *apāna*. Thus, these are the three families of the Mother—the body, speech, and mind. Likewise, the moon-channel (*candranāḍī*) is the Lotus family (*kamalakula*) in the *prāṇa*; the urine-channel (*mūtranāḍī*) is the Sword family (*khaḍgakula*) in the *apāna*; and in the center of the *prāṇa*, the Rāhu-channel (*rāhunāḍī*) is the Vajra family (*vajrakula*). These are the body, speech, and mind of the Father. This is the rule of the six families.

The colors of the elements for the entry into the nature within the body are described by the words "in the body" and so forth: "The entry into the nature in the body is like space, of equal taste; and the body within the nature should be known by those engaged in yoga through the divisions of the colors of the elements according to the power of their natural qualities. Yellow, black, and red are the colors, while white occurs in earth, wind, fire, and water; and blue and green occur in the element of gnosis and in space, according to the specific divisions of the body and its nature. (29) Here, in this body, there arises a mutual distinction between the elements as the grasped and the grasper.

In that regard, the element which is the grasper becomes designated as "body" (*kāya*) by the power of the totality (*sāmagrī*); that which is the grasped becomes designated as "entity" (*bhāva*) by the power of the totality.
Therefore, there is a mutual identity and a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) between the grasped and the grasper; thus, the entity enters into the body.

Like space, the entity is of equal flavor within the body, and it should be known by those engaged in yoga through the distinctions of the colors and so forth of the elements, according to the power of their natural qualities.
In this context, the elements (dhātus) such as earth and the rest constitute the nature of the body-faculty (kāyendriya) and so forth, as well as the four objects (viṣayas) beginning with odor.

Here, by way of bodily division, there is the body-faculty, the object of odor, and the anus-faculty; speech is yellow in color by virtue of its nature as the earth-body, and black in color by virtue of its nature as wind.

Likewise, the olfactory faculty, touch, the vocal faculty, and the excretion of feces are of the nature of wind (*vāyu-prakṛti*); they are black in color due to the division of the body, and yellow due to the division of their state (*bhāva*). The visual faculty, taste, the manual faculty, and movement are of the nature of fire (*tejas-prakṛti*); they become red in color by virtue of the body, and white by virtue of their state, being of the nature of water (*udaka-prakṛti*).

In this way, the tongue faculty, color-form (*varṇarūpa*), the foot faculty, grasping, and the [four] elements—earth, water, fire, and air—become white in color through the differentiation of the body; they become red in color by virtue of the presence of the nature of fire.
One should understand that color is determined by whether there is a predominance of earth, wind, fire, or water.

Thus, the ear faculty (*śrotrendriya*), the object-field of the element of heat (*gharmadhātu*), the male organ (*bhagendriya*), and the emission of semen (*śukracyavana*)—these have the nature of space (*ākāśaprakṛti*); by way of bodily division they are green in color, but in the *Vimalaprabhā*, by way of the division of the nature of internal gnosis (*jñānaprakṛtibhāva*), they are blue.

Likewise, the mind faculty (*manendriya*), sound (*śabda*), the divine organ (*divyendriya*), and the flow of urine (*mūtrasrāva*)—these have the nature of the gnosis-element (*jñānadhātuprakṛti*); by way of temporal division they are blue in color, while by way of the division of existence (*bhāvabheda*) they are green, having the nature of space.
Therefore, in the space of gnosis (*jñānākāśa*), there arises blue and green through the various distinctions of bodily states; this is the rule for the colors of the natural states of the body.

Regarding the embrace of wisdom and method (*prajñopāyāliṅgana*) by means of the elements such as bone, flesh, and so forth, he says "wisdom" and so on: Wisdom and method are bone and flesh; water is blood, and fire is indeed urine; wind is feces, and the void is semen. In the excellent body, the glorious *rajas* is mind itself. From the ear, sound and the others [arise], and from the power of their respective Buddha-families, speech, form, and so forth [arise]. Thus, the goddesses together with the Buddhas—the objects and the subjects—are to be understood within the mandala. (30)

In this body, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the bone-element (*asthidhātu*), and method (*upāya*) is the flesh-element (*māṃsadhātu*). Their mutual conjunction is like that of earth and formative forces (*saṃskāra*); because it is taught that "that which is solid is the earth-element," [it follows that] wisdom and method are bone and flesh. Likewise, wisdom and method are the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) together with the water-element, consisting of saliva and blood.
Similarly, fire is heat, and urine is perception (*saṃjñā*); these two arise from wisdom and method.
Now, one might ask: "The semen-element is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); why then is it called 'urine'?

Here, in this body, that which is perception is the knowledge of great bliss (*mahāsukha-jñāna*) that arises from the emission of urine in a newborn infant; this persists until the limit of sixteen years due to the nature of the emission of semen.
Therefore, because of the distinction that urine is the property of perception while semen is the property of knowledge, urine is the aggregate of perception.
Thus, wind is *vit*, the element of wisdom and method, and the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
"Empty" is the element of dust (*rajodhātu*), and "semen" is the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*); these are wisdom and method.
In the body of excellent beauty, Śrī is the object of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and *ra* is indeed the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
In this way, sound and the others are distinct from the ear.

Sound is wisdom (*prajñā*), the ear is the means (*upāya*); smell is wisdom, the nose is the means; form is wisdom, the eye is the means; taste is wisdom, the tongue is the means; touch is wisdom, the body is the means; the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is wisdom, the mind is the means; the excretion of feces is wisdom, the anus is the means; movement is wisdom, the feet are the means; grasping is wisdom, the hands are the means; speech is wisdom, the organ of speech is the means; the act of urination is wisdom, the female organ (*bhaga*) is the means; or the male organ (*liṅga*) and the emission of semen are wisdom, while the *śaṅkhinī* organ is the means.
25.3. According to the power of one's own Jina family, the nature of speech and so forth, as well as the organs of action and so forth [are established].

Thus, in the order described, the goddesses beginning with Earth, together with the Buddhas such as Vairocana, who are the objects and subjects, are to be explained in the mandala to be described; this is the rule for the mutual embrace of Wisdom and Means (*prajñopāya*). Now, the function of the moon, the sun, semen (*śuka*), and menses (*rajas*) is stated in the verse beginning with "the channels" (*nāḍī*): Having established six thousand channels within the womb, multiplied by the qualities of the sun (twelve), the moon (*śaśadhara*) abandons its increase when a year is complete, and the sun (*arka*) causes its increase.
In twelve years, the Sun abandons the increase of the elements within its own body;
it produces the severance of the channels (nāḍīccheda) day by day, according to the sequence of the number of pairs. [31]
In this body, from the first month of gestation onwards, two hundred channels (nāḍīs) arise each day.
Within a month, by means of thirty days, the number reaches six thousand. By the end of twelve months, through three hundred and sixty days, the number reaches seventy-two thousand.
The six thousand channels multiplied by the sun (twelve) means they are multiplied by twelve, having increased within the womb.
By virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), [this applies] even externally until the end of twelve months.

Having omitted one month from his conception (*garbhādhāna*), when the year is complete, the Moon (*śaśadhara*) abandons its increase; by virtue of the word "and," this means for thirteen months. And the Sun (*arka*) effects the increase. Then, once the measurement of the number of the lunar and seminal channels (*nāḍī*) and the elements (*dhātu*) has been determined, the Moon causes the increase of the elements and the appearance of the menses (*rajas*) for up to twelve years.
By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it also produces semen and increases the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
The Sun abandons the increase of the bodily constituents in its own body after twelve years; this is the increase of the Sun, lasting until the onset of menstruation (*rajas*) in women.
For men, it lasts until the limit of sixteen years, which is the period until the production of semen.
The letter *ca* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*).

Thus, the severing of the channels (*nāḍī*) also occurs when giving birth, proceeding day by day in the sequence of even numbers; this shall be explained in detail as it is to be stated later. This is the rule for the increase of the elements in the channels.

Now, the principles (*tattva*) beginning with space are described, starting with the words "the glorious elements" (*śrī bhūtāni*), etc.: "The ten glorious elements and sense-faculties arise; the five organs of action, and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are also declared; along with the mind (*manas*) possessing qualities, the intellect (*buddhi*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the divine [principles]."

These principles exist within the body, which is the abode of the three worlds; this is the experience of the All-pervading Lord, who consists of the five aggregates, who has entered the threefold states of existence, and who is acquired through his own karma.

In this body of the child, there are the five elements, the five sense organs such as hearing and so forth, and the five [elements] beginning with space; thus, these ten are together in one place. Likewise, the five organs of action and the five subtle elements (tanmātras)—namely, the subtle element of sound and so forth—are said to be present.
Furthermore, the mind is endowed with qualities; that is, the mind is accompanied by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

In this way, intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and even the divine primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—these are the twenty-four principles (*tattva*). This experience belongs to the All-pervading Lord within the body, which is the abode of the three worlds, as well as externally.

Of what kind is he? By worldly convention, he consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), is situated within the threefold existence (*trividhabhava*), and his experience is acquired through his own karma.
Nature (*prakṛti*), consisting of twenty-four principles, possesses the quality of being the object of perception for the *puruṣa*, who possesses the quality of the perceiver.
Furthermore, there exists another nature, which is luminous and devoid of the quality of being an object of perception; such is the determination of the relationship between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.

Now, the characteristics of earth and the other elements within the body are stated, beginning with "earth" and so forth: earth is solidity, water is fluidity, fire is heat, air is lightness, space is the cavity, the skin is firm bone, the mountain Meru is the best [of the limbs], and here rain is nectar.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*: the vajra, sound, wind, feces, and the ghaṭikās; a pair of inhalations and exhalations; with pairs, there is one transition; by two times nine hundred, the divisions of the apertures of the luminaries. ||33||
In this body, earth is solidity, water is fluidity,
and fire is heat;
wind is lightness, by which it performs contraction and expansion.
The cavity is the void; the solid bone is the spinal column (*pṛṣṭhāsthidaṇḍa*), extending from the waist to the shoulders, which is Meru, the supreme mountain of the immortals.

The rain that exists externally is here, in this body, nectar—the flow of the *stukā* [fluid] from both the tongue and the *lambikā*. The thunderbolt is sound; the roar of the intestines is within the heart.
The wind [is represented by] the rainbow of Indra.

That which is a *ghaṭikā* externally, consisting of sixty *pāṇīpala*s, is in the body a pair of inhalations and exhalations—a pair of outgoing and incoming breaths—known as the *prāṇa* wind; this is the *ghaṭikā*.
By these pairs, numbering two times nine hundred—that is, eighteen hundred—there occurs one *saṃkrānti*.
Externally, the transition occurs every three months and three days; internally, there are five channels that carry the five maṇḍalas.
In astrology, the planets beginning with the Sun constitute the ten divisions of the apertures.

In this context, the anus is the Moon, the urinary opening is the Sun, the seminal opening is Kālāgni, the mouth-opening is Rāhu, the right eye-opening is Maṅgala, the left eye-opening is Budha, the right nostril-opening is Bṛhaspati, the left nostril-opening is Śukra, the right ear-opening is Manda, and the left ear-opening is Ketu.

Furthermore, the differentiation of the six sense organs for these [planets] beginning with Maṅgala will be explained in the fifth chapter as it is to be stated; such is the rule regarding Earth and the other elements.

Now, the constellations and so forth are described, beginning with the words "The constellation": The constellation is the row of teeth; the daily ghaṭikās arise from the divisions of the joints. The channels, rivers, machines, clouds, and the digits of the other moon are the dual-natured elements.

Body hair, lice, semen, along with the host of worms, are the fourfold source of beings. The joints of the big toe beginning with Nanda, the lotus of the head, and the secret lotus are the Śakti. (34)
Including Abhijit, there are twenty-eight constellations (*nakṣatras*) according to the division of the seven-spoked wheel.
There are four staff-constellations at the four corners of the spokes; thus, there are thirty-two.

Due to the distinction of the forward and reverse movement of the teeth, fourteen constellations are situated in the upper wheel and fourteen in the lower wheel. The rows of teeth exist above and below; due to the division of the half-wheels, the row of teeth constitutes the constellations.

In this context, since there are divisions of the junctions (*sandhibheda*) within the *ghaṭikās* of the day, the number of breaths (*śvāsa*) per day becomes sixty *ghaṭikās*. Those *ghaṭikās* amount to three hundred and sixty days of the year; and since those are three hundred and sixty junctions, they constitute the "divisions of the junctions" (*sandhibheda*).

"Channels are rivers": in this world-system, externally there are seventy-two thousand rivers flowing to the ocean; internally, there are seventy-two thousand channels that carry the vital essence (*rasa*).
"Clouds of intestines": *antra* is an indeclinable word [here]; "intestines are clouds" because of the flowing of the vital essence, which has the characteristic of thundering.

The constituents (*dhātu*) of the other lunar digit (*apara-śaśikalā*) possess a dual nature. Here, the digit is twofold: one is by way of the transformation of the constituents such as body hair (*loma*), and the other is by way of the property of the emission of semen (*śukra*). Furthermore, those among these two that exist through the transformation of the constituents such as body hair are themselves twofold, according to their further division.
[In the] *Paṭala* [entitled] "The Great Summary on the Truth of Origination and so forth," it says: "The digit of the moon.

Here, the first lunar day (*pratipad*) corresponds to the fine body hair and the second to the coarse body hair; likewise, the third and fourth correspond to the skin; the fifth and sixth to the blood; likewise, the seventh and eighth to the flesh; similarly, the ninth and tenth to the channels (*nāḍī*); likewise, the eleventh and twelfth to the bones; similarly, the thirteenth and fourteenth to the marrow; and likewise, the fifteenth and sixteenth digits to the semen. This is the rule: the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) possess a dual nature.

Now, the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) is described by the passage beginning with "hair" (*loma*), and so forth: In this world-system, the source of beings is fourfold. Here, the earth-source is external stationary beings, while internally it is hair; the wind-source is external egg-born beings, while internally it is lice; the water-source is external worms and the like born from moisture, while within the body there are also worms and the like; the external womb-born beings arise from semen, while internally it is semen itself. Since it was not explicitly mentioned [as a separate category], the space-element consists of spontaneously born beings in the form of fluids externally, while internally they are subtle living beings in the form of eggs; thus, the source of beings is fourfold.
"Beginning with Nandā, [the sequence is] on the thumb-joint," etc. Here, in the external [correspondence], the five lunar days beginning with the first (pratipadā) are called Nandā and so forth.

And these, according to the division of the bright and dark fortnights, become the joints of the fingers of the left hand—beginning with the little finger and the thumb—by way of three joints each, through the division of the elements starting with space (*ākāśa*).

The joints of the fingers of the right hand are fifteen, according to the divisions of earth and the other elements, and by the division of the joints of the thumb and the other fingers; likewise, the joints of the toes of the feet are to be known according to the divisions of the lunar days of the second month. Thus, through the division of each season, there are six cycles in a year by means of the six seasons; this is the rule for the joints of the thumb beginning with Nanda. Furthermore, the lotus [of the heart] reaches the head and the navel, and because it is not a power (*śakti*), it becomes the innate body (*sahajatanu*) according to the previously mentioned method; this is the rule for the power (*śakti*).

Now, heaven and the other realms are described by the passage beginning with "the Egg of Brahmā" (*brahmāṇḍam*): The Egg of Brahmā is the heavenly world; the hands and feet are the mortal and nether worlds; the oceans, islands, and mountains are the elements—liquid, soft, and hard—which possess the three natures.
O King, the salt ocean is their urine; the ring of fire is their blood and skin; and all the Siddhas are their hair, established through manifold divisions within the abode of the three worlds.
In this body, from the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) down to the throat-center (*kaṇṭhacakra*), the heavenly world (*svargaloka*) exists;
the hands and arms are the mortal world (*martyaloka*);
and the feet are the netherworld (*pātālaloka*).
The oceans and the islands are "ocean-islands";
likewise, the seven mountains correspond respectively to the seven liquid elements (dravadhātu) in the body,
which are the seven seas.

Among them, the salt ocean is urine; the wine ocean is sweat; the water ocean is phlegm (*stuka*); the milk ocean is the milk of women and the phlegm-element (*śleṣmadhātu*) of men; the curd ocean is the brain matter of the head; the ghee ocean is fat (*vasā*); and the honey ocean is semen.
[These are distinguished] by the divisions of the joints of the thumb of an elder and so forth.
[Sanskrit: *citta*; Tibetan: *dus* (season)]
kha. Chapter on the Skeleton: In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the internal [anatomy], there are likewise the continents (*dvīpa*).

Jambūdvīpa has twelve spokes; in the twelve segments of the hands and feet, there is flesh (*māṃsa*), which is Raudra; Kālaja is Krauñca; Kinnaraja is Bukka; Kuśa is Meda (fat); Sitābha is Mūtra (urine); and Candra is the channels (*nāḍī*)—these are the soft elements (*mṛdudhātu*).
The "mountains" are the vajra-mountains, which are the toenails;

Śītādri is the bones of the hands; Droṇa is the bones of the forearms; Maṇikara is the bones of the upper arms; Niṣadha is the bones of the feet; Mandarādri is the bones of the shanks; and Nīlābha is the bones of the thighs—these are the seven mountains, the solid elements.
The eighth is Meru; the rule is that the skeletal remains of the body extend from the waist up to the shoulders.
The elements (dhātus) possess three natures: liquid, soft, and hard.
Regarding the phrase "the circle of fire and the circle of wind": the circle of fire is blood, and the circle of wind is the skins.
"O King" is the address.
"All the Keśas are perfected" means they are perfected through manifold divisions within the abode of the three worlds.

Here, in this external world-system, they are perfected in three ways: those who move in the sky (khecaras), those who move on the earth (bhūcaras), and those who dwell in the subterranean realm (pātālavāsins).

Among them, those who move in the sky have hair on their heads; those who move on earth are produced from the armpits; and those who dwell in the subterranean realm (pātāla) are produced from the vulva and the penis. Since body hair has not been specifically mentioned, it is characterized by three and a half crores; such is the rule regarding heaven and the other realms. Now, the three fires are described starting with the word "heart": In the lotuses of the heart, throat, and navel, the lightning-fire (pavi), the sun-fire (ravi), and the fire-arrow (viśikhi) manifest in sequence within a bow-shaped, circular, daily-offering, and ocean-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

Above them is the supreme Fire, whose pure rays quiver, the embodiment of knowledge at the end of darkness; in which neither the sun, nor lightning, nor the lord of stars (the moon), nor the planets, nor the stars and so forth are found.

In this body, there is a triad of fires: the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Gārhapatya, and the Āhavanīya.

Corresponding respectively, the Paviragni (lightning-fire) shines in the heart-lotus, which is shaped like a bow; the Sūryāgni (sun-fire), the Gārhapatya, in the circular throat-lotus; and the Kravyādāgni (flesh-eating fire), the Āhavanīya, in the square sacrificial pit at the navel.
This is the rule for the daily oblation in the four-cornered pit.
Above them is the supreme fire, which has pure, shimmering rays and is the embodiment of gnosis (*jñānamūrti*); it is unbroken at the end of darkness within the secret lotus and the forehead lotus.

In that place where neither the sun, nor lightning, nor the lord of the moon, nor the planets, nor the stars and so forth exist, there is first the fire of the flesh-eater (*kravyādāgni*), and fourth is the true fire, the embodiment of gnosis; such is the rule regarding the three fires.

Now, the days of the week (*vāra*), the *ghaṭikās*, and so forth are described, beginning with the words "the days": The days of the week are on the petals of the heart-lotus; the *ghaṭikās* are manifest in the navel-lotus; and the sixty [units] are in the center of the earth. O King, the day (*ahaḥ*) is indeed in the *manu* [lotus], and the asterism (*ṛkṣa*) is also in the wheel of enjoyment (*sambhogacakra*). Again, the navel-lotus is for the asterisms, while the *ghaṭikās* are to be known by the yogis in the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*); the *pāṇīpalas* are in the joints of the hands, feet, and so forth throughout the entire manifest body.
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in classical Indian scripts typically mark the end of a section or verse. [End of Section]

Here, externally, there are seven days; the eighth is the *kulikā* period of enjoyment (*bhukti*). Within the body, these eight occur upon the eight petals of the heart-lotus: the Sun on the eastern petal, the Moon in the southeast, Mars in the south, Mercury in the southwest, Jupiter in the west, Venus in the northwest, Saturn in the north, and Ketu in the northeast during the enjoyment of the *kulikā*; and Rāhu in the other half of that enjoyment. Thus, the manifest *ghaṭikās* in the navel-lotus are sixty.

There are four petals that are empty *ghaṭikā*-petals; the remaining sixty petals are those that carry the sixty *maṇḍalas*, and these sixty petals correspond to the sixty *ghaṭikās*. Thus, for each day (*vāra*), the number is sixty.
In the sixteen-petaled [lotus] at the center of the brows, two petals are carriers of emptiness.
In the fourteen petals are the fourteen words of the Moon, beginning with "in the elements and non-elements" (*bhūtābhūteṣu*).
There, on the first petal is *bhūtā*, which is a word consisting of five *ghaṭikās*; likewise on the second and third.
On the fourth petal is *vedā*, which consists of four *ghaṭikās*.
On the fifth is the word *śikhini*, which consists of three *nāḍīs*.
The word *kara*—consisting of two *ghaṭikās*—is on the sixth petal. The word *śaśinaḥ*—consisting of one *ghaṭikā*—is the seventh [word] on the seventh petal.

Thus, in reverse order: on the eighth is a word consisting of one *ghaṭikā*; on the ninth, one consisting of two *ghaṭikās*; on the tenth, one consisting of three *ghaṭikās*; on the eleventh, one consisting of four *ghaṭikās*; on the twelfth, one consisting of five *ghaṭikās*; and it should be understood that the same applies to the thirteenth and fourteenth as well.
The lunar positions (*candrapada*) are equal in number to the [six] seasons (*manu*).
"O King" is an address.
In the wheel of enjoyment (*sambhogacakra*), that is, the throat wheel (*kaṇṭhacakra*), four petals among the thirty-two petals are empty.

On the other twenty-eight petals, there are the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) together with Abhijit; these are arranged counter-clockwise on the seven previous spokes, starting from the middle of the central spoke and ending at Revatī.

Aśvinī is on the second, Bharaṇī on the third, Kṛttikā on the fourth; thereafter, the staff-mansion (*daṇḍanakṣatra*) is on the seventh spoke, which is designated as the *nāḍī* of the seven-petaled [group].

Then, on the seven northern spokes, moving counter-clockwise: Rohiṇī is on the first spoke, Mṛgaśiras on the second, Ārdrā on the third, Punarvasu on the fourth, Puṣya on the fifth, Aśleṣā on the sixth, and Maghā on the seventh; in this manner, the others are also to be understood.
Furthermore, it should be known that there are sixty *ghaṭikās* for each of the constellations at the positions of the nave.

The *nāḍīs* are sixty *pāṇīpala*s; thirty-six hundred [of these] are in every joint of the limbs, such as the hands and feet, as will be explained in detail later. This is the rule for the days and so forth. Now, the movement of the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) through the wheels (*cakras*) starting from the navel is described with the words beginning "at the navel" (verse 20): Just as here in the external world the sun revolves through the twelve zodiac signs according to the divisions of the annual transits (*saṃkrānti*), so too within the self the vital energy revolves through the twelve zodiac signs every day according to the divisions of the twelve transits.
The supreme digit, the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*), revolves within the lotus of the navel whose petals are the sun, moving sequentially through the petals of the twelve zodiac signs.
A transit (*saṃkrānti*) consists of eighteen hundred [breaths] of the pair of vital airs (*prāṇa*).
Here, in the external world, one transit of the sun occurs in eighteen hundred *daṇḍas*; likewise, there is no such thing as a "petal" (*dala*) here.
The word "dalāni" does not appear in the manuscript. Regarding the "filled and unfilled" (bhṛtābhṛteṣu); in manuscript kha, there is the term "ekaghaṭikā.
(Three thousand).
With eighteen hundred breaths, the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*) undergoes a transition (*saṃkrānti*) into a single petal;
and that occurs, O King, at the Cancer (*karkaṭa*) ascendant.
Here, externally, Cancer is the birth sign (*janmarāśi*) of the Sun.

In this way, among all birth stories (*jātaka*), the zodiac sign in which one's birth occurs should be understood as being designated "Cancer" (*karkaṭa*), according to the principle that "the Cancer sign serves as the locus for the birth of living beings. The address "O King" (*narendra*) is used when the Cancer ascendant is present.
That [sign] in which the sun, situated externally, revolves day and night from the time of its rising should be understood by means of the division of the seven [zodiacal] sticks (*śalākā*).
The measure of the ascendant (*lagnamāna*) is to be known.

Just as externally the Sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*) is to be understood as deficient or excessive by means of days, so too internally it is to be understood as deficient or excessive by means of breaths (*śvāsa*). Thus, according to the divisions of the Sun’s hours (*daṇḍabheda*), there is a regulation of the breaths within the body. Regarding the equinox of the life-force (*prāṇa*) in terms of debt and wealth: from Cancer onwards, by virtue of the Sun’s quarters (*pāda*), there is debt; from Capricorn onwards, there is wealth.

According to the method taught in the *Jyotiṣa*, the day of the equinox (*viṣuva*) or the day of a transitory movement (*saṃkrānti*) consists of fifty-six and a quarter *daṇḍas* externally; internally, it consists of breaths according to the distinction of each zodiacal sign (*lagna*) transitory movement, thus constituting the revolution of the twelve transitory movements.

Now, the flow of the five mandalas within each lotus petal is described, beginning with the words "each one" (*ekaika*), etc.: In each individual lotus petal, Earth flows in the west and Water in the north; Fire flows in the right and the east, and Space flows in the middle of the petal.

The transition (*saṃkrānti*) flows through five divisions; the equinox (*viṣuva*) consists of sixty minus one breaths. Thus, the divisions of the transitions occur at every moment of the day according to the divisions of the ascendants (*lagna*).

In this context, externally, during each transit (*saṃkrānti*) of the sun, there is the experience of five mandalas. The experience of five mandalas occurs in thirty days; the experience of one mandala occurs in six days, which is three hundred and sixty *daṇḍas*. Likewise, internally, the experience of five mandalas occurs in eighteen hundred breaths (*śvāsa*), and the experience of one mandala occurs in three hundred and sixty breaths; such is the rule. Here, in each petal of the transit, there are five locations: the western, northern, southern, eastern, and central parts of the petal.

There, on each individual lotus petal, the earth mandala flows; on the northern petal, the water mandala flows; on the southern petal, the fire mandala flows; and again, on the eastern petal, the wind mandala flows.
And in the center of the petal, the space mandala flows.
On each [petal], the life-force (*prāṇaśakti*) consists of three hundred and sixty breaths; thus, each transition (*saṃkrānti*) occurs in five distinct ways.

In these mandalas, within the three hundred and sixty breaths, the equinox (*viṣuva*) flows by taking eleven and one-quarter breaths at the junctions of the rising of the zodiac signs (*lagnodayābhisandhi*). This amounts to sixty minus one breath, meaning it flows for fifty-six and one-quarter breaths less three and three-quarters breaths. Thus, the divisions of the transits (*saṃkrānti*) occur internally through the divisions of the twelve zodiac signs; such is the rule regarding the transits.

30. Now, the presiding deities of the five mandalas are described, beginning with "void" (śūnya) and so forth: The five principles, beginning with the void, flow constantly in the north; on the right [side], earth and the others [flow]. Rāhu and Agni, Moon and Sun, Buddha and the son of Earth (Mars), the minister of the Daityas (Venus) and Jupiter, Ketu and Saturn—these are the ten lords in the elements starting from space (ākāśa). These are the presiding deities of the fields within the mandalas for six months. O Lord of Men, the Moon is the lord in the north, and the Sun is the lord in the south.

In this [chapter], the Great Summary on the Truth of Origination and so forth (179): here, externally, in the odd lunar mansions (*viṣamalagna*) such as Aries and so forth, there is the enjoyment of the mandalas of space and so forth; in the even lunar mansions (*samanagna*) such as Taurus and so forth, there is the enjoyment of the mandalas of earth and so forth. Likewise, internally, the five principles beginning with space—namely, space, wind, fire, water, and the earth mandala—flow necessarily in the left nostril during the northern course.
The spheres of earth, water, fire, air, and space flow through the right nostril.

In these ten mandalas, alternating left (apasavya) and right (savya), respectively: in the left [mandala] is the mandala of space, with Rāhu as its presiding deity during the time of flow; in the right, the fire of time (kālāgni); in the left, the mandala of wind, with the Moon; in the right, the Sun; in the left, the mandala of fire, with Mercury; in the right, Mars; in the left, the mandala of water, with Venus; in the right, Jupiter; in the left, the mandala of earth, with Ketu; and in the right, Saturn. Thus, there are ten presiding lords over the mandalas of space and the other elements who act as the possessors of the fields.

Thus, for six months the Moon is the lord [of the left channel] in the zodiac signs of Aries, Gemini, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius, and Aquarius; in the left channel (vāmanāḍī), the Moon is the lord of the semen-element (śukradhātu) in the north. In the south, in the signs of Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Capricorn, and Pisces, the Sun is the lord of the blood-element (rajodhātu), O King—this is the address—and this is the rule regarding the lords of the mandalas.

Now, the winds beginning with Prāṇa are described by the words "of that" and so forth: Above that, in the region of the heart, resides a wheel of channels (nāḍicakra) within an eight-petaled lotus. Therein is the collection of winds beginning with Prāṇa; the Sun, Moon, and Fire are located on the left, the right, and in the middle respectively.

Indeed, in the left channel flows the white Moon; in the right flows the red Sun; and in the middle flows the one whose form is the Fire of Time (Kālāgni). During the equinox (viṣuva), sixty breaths are diminished. || 41 ||

5. Here, at the navel-cakra, there is a four-petaled [lotus] within the womb; surrounding that is an eight-petaled one; surrounding that is a twelve-petaled one; and surrounding that is a sixty-four-petaled one.
By the word "petals" (dala), the channels (nāḍīs) characterized by the movement of breath are intended.

Above that navel-cakra, at a distance of twelve and a half finger-breadths upward, situated in the region of the heart, is the channel-wheel (nāḍīcakra), which has eight spokes and consists of eight channels.
Within those [lotuses], the group of winds beginning with *prāṇa* resides in the eight-petaled lotus; there, the flames of the Moon, Sun, and Fire blaze forth, and Rāhu is present.

On the left, the lunar channel (*candranāḍī*) flows as the Moon, white in color; on the right, the solar channel flows, red in color. In the midst of the eight petals, the channel in the form of the fire of time (*kālāgni*), the channel of Rāhu, flows. At the equinox (*viṣuva*), at the junction of the rising of the ascendant, there are fifty-six breaths plus one-quarter (*sapāda-ṣaṭpañcāśat-śvāsāni*).
In this eight-petaled heart-lotus, the channels of the transition of the watches (prahara) are to be known;
these channels, which carry the five mandalas, exist within the nostrils.

The movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) occurs through each individual channel by means of one hundred and twenty-seven inhalations and exhalations, which correspond to seven and a half danda-measures.

Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya—these ten kinds of winds are situated within the wheel of the channels (nāḍī-cakra) according to their various functions; they extend from the heart-lotus and the navel-wheel up to the iḍā and ending at the śaṅkhinī. || 42 ||

Maṇḍa [is located] in the eight-petaled [lotus]; in the *alambuṣā* channel on the western petal; Devadatta in the northern petal in the *iḍā* channel; Dhanañjaya in the northeastern petal in the *kuhā* channel; and Prāṇa is in the *suṣumnā*. In the *śaṅkhinī*, which has the number of directions [ten], the *bodhicitta* flows; its presiding deity is Apāna. Thus, in this wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*), the ten types of winds are situated according to their functional divisions. However, while all these [winds], beginning with Prāṇa, pervade the seventy-two thousand channels, they are specifically born in eight locations.

The rule regarding the cakras is as follows: from the *saṃ* (or *śaṃ*) at the end up to the *iḍā* and so forth, the entire lotus of one’s own heart and the navel-cakra are the birthplaces of the *samāna* and the other winds.

Now, the functions of the *prāṇa* and the others are described, beginning with the word "prāṇa": The *prāṇa*, moving along the paths of the sun and the moon, performs the function of inhaling and exhaling all food and drink. The *apāna* leads [them] downwards; the *samāna* leads everything into a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) within the body. The *udāna* vibrates in the body and performs singing and dancing with the mouth, hands, and feet. The *vyāna* causes disease and likewise causes the breaking of limbs through the influence of the qualities of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*).

In this body, the *prāṇa* imparts vitality (*bala*) to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), while moving along the paths of the sun and the moon. The path of the sun is either the *piṅgalā* or the *rasanā*; the path of the moon is either the *iḍā* or the *lalanā*. Regarding the phrase "moving along its path," the traditional teaching (*āgama*) states that all food and drink—whatever essence has been eaten and whatever water and so forth have been drunk—is led downward entirely by the *apāna* wind.

The wind named *samāna* leads everything to a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) and uniform taste (*tulyarasa*) throughout the body; the meaning is that it renders the seven constituent elements (*dhātu*) of equal flavor.
The wind named *udāna* vibrates within the body and performs singing and dancing with the mouth, hands, and feet.

In this body, that very *udāna* produces singing and so forth with the mouth, such as laughter and conversation, performs dancing with the hands and feet, and also [performs] walking and other movements.

Vyāna causes disease according to the power of its inherent qualities; likewise, by the power of its watery nature, it causes the breaking of the limbs just as it causes disease. The Naga wind causes belching through the expansion of the hands and feet; contracting like a tortoise, that Kṛkara wind causes anger and total agitation; Devadatta causes yawning;
and O King, the single Dhananjaya wind does not abandon the body when it has reached the five elements. Thus, all these winds do not abandon their inherent qualities.

The *nāga* wind indeed causes belching; the *kūrma* wind, contracting the limbs and hands and feet, causes that [movement]; the *kṛkara* wind produces all anger and agitation; the *devadatta* wind causes yawning; and when the body has reached the state of the five elements (*pañcatva*), O Lord of Men—the address—this single wind, *dhanañjaya*, does not abandon the body. Thus, there is but one wind, *dhanañjaya*.

In this sequence thus described, all the winds, beginning with *prāṇa*, do not abandon the qualities inherent in their respective *prakṛtis*; that is, they do not abandon the qualities of the *prakṛtis* such as space (*ākāśa*). This is the rule for the functions of *prāṇa* and the others, in the chapter on the Great Summary of the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*) and so forth. Now, the designations of the channels (*nāḍī*) are stated according to the terminology of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), beginning with the word "piṅgā": "Piṅgā, Sūkṣmā, and Iḍā and the others, situated in the three paths; Rohiṇī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, the sixth Jayā, and Agā; then Vasu in the ninth, Alambuṣā, and Śrīkuhā."

O Lord of Men, that which is the tenth digit, the Śaṅkhinī, flows with the *bodhicitta* at the end of bliss; this is the glorious wheel of channels (*nāḍicakra*), consisting of many various types of channel-junctions.
Piṅgalā, Sūkṣmā, and Iḍā—these three are the primary channels.

"Those who have entered the three paths" refers to the *iḍā*, which has entered the path of the moon; the *piṅgalā*, which has entered the path of the sun; and the *suṣumnā*, which has entered the path of Rāhu—this is Rohiṇī as the fourth. Hastijihvā is the fifth; Pūṣā is the sixth; Jayā is the seventh; Vasu is the eighth; Alambuṣā is the ninth; and Kuhā is the tenth, numbering the directions. As for Śaṅkhinī, she is the tenth; she is Śaṅkhinī because she flows with the bodhicitta at the end of bliss.
This is the glorious wheel of channels (*nāḍicakra*), which becomes manifold through its many various divisions of junctions.
In this body, there are three hundred and sixty types of joints; through these joint-divisions, there arise three hundred and sixty divisions of the network of channels (*nāḍī-cakra*).

In this manner, the various forms of the vital winds, such as *prāṇa* and the rest, are also to be understood. This is the rule regarding the network of channels: in Indra, Agni, Yama, Daitya (Nairṛta), Varuṇa, Pavana (Vāyu), Yakṣa, Rudra, and in the center—in these locations, the Śakti revolves day and night, assuming their respective forms.

Above that, in the throat-cakra, the wheel of the constellations is situated together with the hosts of planets; in the Brahma-egg, at the illustrious forehead, [the moon] is surrounded by vowels and is indeed dripping a white drop. (46)

Now, the presiding deities such as Indra and others within that very wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) are described, beginning with the word "Indra": here, on the petal of Indra, the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*) assumes the nature of Indra for the duration of one watch (*prahara*); on the petal of Agni, the nature of Agni; on the petal of Yama, the nature of Yama; on the petal of Nairṛti, the nature of Nairṛti; on the petal of Varuṇa, the nature of Varuṇa; on the petal of Vāyu, the nature of Vāyu; on the petal of Dhanada, the nature of Dhanada; and on the petal of Īśa, the nature of Rudra.
Thus, the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*) revolves while partaking in their respective natures within these eight petals; this is the rule regarding the natures of Indra and the others.

Now, the throat-chakra (*kaṇṭhacakra*) is described: here, at the end of twelve and a half finger-breadths above the heart-lotus, in the throat-chakra, resides the wheel of the planets along with the host of stars—the wheel of the four *daṇḍa*-nakṣatras and the twenty-eight principal nakṣatras; by these, it consists of thirty-two petals.

Excluding the fourteen *daṇḍa*-constellations, the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the twenty-eight petals [of the heart] during a day and night is determined by dividing sixty *daṇḍas* by the number of petals; thus, there is a circulation through each individual petal.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa*, at the forehead (*lalāṭa*), a white drop surrounded by vowels flows upward from that [heart];

at the end of twelve and a half finger-breadths above that throat-lotus, in the sixteen-petaled forehead-lotus, two petals are excluded, and the movement of the *prāṇa* during a day and night occurs within the fourteen remaining petals; the exclusion of each individual petal occurs by dividing sixty *daṇḍas* by fourteen.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it should be understood that the drops (*bindu*) and emissions (*visarga*) are located in the pericarp (*kaṇikā*), which is called the "moon-step.

Furthermore, in the navel wheel (*nābhicakra*) there are sixty-four channels (*nāḍī*) known by names such as Bhīmā and so forth; in the heart, eight [channels] known by names such as Iḍā and so forth; in the throat, [sixteen channels] known by the names of the Aśvinīs and so forth, and by the names of the four junctions (*sandhyā*); in the channel of the forehead, [sixteen channels] known by the names of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and so forth; and in the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*), [sixteen channels] known by the names of the four principles (*tattva*) according to the division of the four junctions. Thus, within these petals of the lotuses of the throat and the forehead, an eight-petaled wheel (*cakra*) is to be understood as being included.

Thus, at the navel, heart, throat, and forehead, there is an eight-spoked wheel whose nature consists of earth, water, fire, and air; at the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), a four-petaled wheel whose nature is emptiness (*śūnya*); at the navel, a four-petaled wheel whose nature is gnosis (*jñāna*); and at the secret place, a thirty-two-petaled wheel. On the sixteen outer petals are the channels of the vowels; on the ten inner petals are the channels of the aggregates and elements; and within those, on the inner petals, are the six channels of emptiness. Thus, the number of channels in the six wheels to be described hereafter—one hundred and fifty-six—is to be stated. This is the rule for the six wheels.

At the base, earth and water flow in the left; fire flows in the right; wind flows at the crown; and space flows in the middle. Between these two nostrils, the equinox (viṣuva) flows according to the sequence of the apertures.

Piercing through these, the Power (Śakti) proceeds to the supreme state—the end of the twelve, the end of the digits (kalā), the field, and so forth—extending from the hands and feet to the tips of the thumbs within the hollow of the lotus-palms.

Now, the flow of the five maṇḍalas through the two nostrils is described by the verse beginning with "mūle" (at the root), and so forth: here, in the left and right nostrils, at the root—that is, in the lower part—the earth maṇḍala flows in the right [nostril], while water flows in the left nostril. This is because of the indicator that "Meru stands to the north of all," facing the central line between the two nostrils. The fire maṇḍala flows in the right [nostril], and the right [portion] is the outer part of the nostril opening, situated to the north of both [the left and right].

The wind-maṇḍala flows at the crown [of the head]. Between both nostrils—in the space between the two nostrils, amidst the earth, water, fire, and wind-maṇḍalas—the space-maṇḍala (vyomamaṇḍala) flows. When the movement is fixed on the left, the flow of the maṇḍalas is in the left; when the movement is fixed on the right, it is in the right.
Furthermore, when [the breath] flows simultaneously through both nostrils, the life-force (prāṇaśakti) flows as the equinox (viṣuva), the maṇḍala of knowledge (jñānamaṇḍala).

These pierce the navel, heart, throat, forehead, cranial aperture (uṣṇīṣa), and the circles of the nostrils; piercing through the divisions of the staff, the heap, the striking, the lunar mansions, the lunar days, and the circles of the twilights, the power—the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti)—proceeds to the supreme state, the supportless limit of twelve, which is the end of twelve finger-breadths, the end of the digits, and the end of the sixteen digits.

In this context, the wind of the earth-mandala flows twelve finger-breadths from the nostrils and then returns; the wind of the water-mandala flows thirteen finger-breadths and then returns; the wind of the fire-mandala flows fourteen finger-breadths and then returns; the wind of the air-mandala flows fifteen finger-breadths and then returns; the wind of the space-mandala flows sixteen finger-breadths and then returns; and the wind of the gnosis-mandala, having entered between the ends of the earth-mandala, flows twelve finger-breadths through both nostrils, and having entered the middle at the end of space, it flows sixteen finger-breadths.

In this context, when there is an increase externally, then there is a decrease internally; when there is a decrease externally at sixteen [mātrās] and so forth by the power of the channels of the vital air (vāyu), then they increase by four finger-breadths at the navel—this is the rule for the flow of the power of prāṇa.

Now, the fields (*kṣetra*) and so forth are described by the passage beginning with "the field" (*kṣetra*): here in this body, there are two fields at the two joints of the arms; two secondary fields (*upakṣetra*) at the two joints of the thighs; two *chandoha*s at the two joints of the forearms; two secondary *chandoha*s (*upacchandoha*) at the two joints of the knees; two meeting places (*melāpaka*) at the two joints of the hands; two secondary meeting places (*upamelāpaka*) at the two joints of the feet; two cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) on the palms of the two hands; two secondary cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*) on the soles of the two feet; four great cremation grounds on the fingers of the two hands; and four secondary cremation grounds on the toes of the two feet—this is the rule for the fields and so forth.

Thus ends the second major section, beginning with the Truth of Origination, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja*, which follows the *Śrīmūla-tantra*.

The Great Chapter on the Origin of the Families of Channels: The Battle between the Cakravartin and the Mlecchas according to the *Kālacakra Kulatantra*. Now, the battle between the Cakravartin and the Mlecchas within one's own body is described, beginning with the words "The Cakrī" (*cakrī*): The Cakrī is in the vajra [of the body]; the lords of the best of gods (the Buddhas) are the twelve links [of dependent origination] obstructed [within it]. Kalkī is indeed perfect gnosis (*samyagjñāna*). The elephants, horses, and chariots are the servants (*kiṅkara*) who are the noble means (*pramāṇa*).

Each possesses the name Rudra. Hanumān prevails; he is the listener (*śrāvaka*) regarding the sin of living beings. But the wicked lord of the Mlecchas—who possesses a mind that performs even what is unwholesome—is the giver of suffering.

Here, within one's own human body, he who was described as the "Outer Wheel-Holder" (*bāhyacakrī*) in the first chapter is the "Vajra-Holder" (*vajrī*) in the body, meaning the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*).
Those twelve lords of the best of gods, beginning with Īśvara, are the twelve links [of dependent origination] that have been restrained.
Therefore, he is the "Kalkī" because of that perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) within his own body.

Those external elephants, horses, chariots, servants, and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are within the body. He who is Rudra externally is known as the knowledge of individuality (*pratyekajñāna*) within the body; he who is Hanumān externally is the knowledge of the disciples (*śrāvakajñāna*) in one’s own body. Thus, in one’s own body, there arises the Great Wheel-turner (*mahācakrī*) together with his retinue, as well as Kalkī.
Likewise, he who is the wicked Mleccha lord externally is the sinful mind in the body;
he who is Kṛnmati externally, the giver of suffering and the path of unwholesomeness, is likewise in the body.

Aśvatthāman is ignorance; the entire army of Danu is the fourfold faction of Māra. Its destruction in battle is the end of the fear of worldly existence, and his glorious victory is the path to liberation.

On Mount Kailāsa, there is the gift of Dharma which removes the fear of worldly existence, and the earth is filled with wealth. He who stands behind and before the teacher of gods and men is the son of Brahmā and the Lord of Asuras.

Mañjuśrī is the Lord of the World, the conqueror of the three realms; Śrī-raja is the *bodhicitta*. On its back are the lineages of Brahmā and the others, and upon the various great earths are the many pure Buddhas.

Thus, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said that a battle with the barbarians (*mleccha*) certainly occurs within the bodies of embodied beings. Indeed, the illusory form exists internally, while externally, in the realm of ritual (*makha*), there is no battle with barbarians—there is only the battle within the body.

That which is the external Aśvatthāman is, within the body, the activity of ignorance (*avidyā*). That which is the external army of Danu—consisting of elephants, horses, and infantry—is, within the body, the fourfold destruction of the faction of Māra in battle. That which is among the external Mlecchas is, in one's own body, the destruction of the fear of existence (*bhava*).
The glorious victory is the attainment of the path to liberation (*mokṣamārga*) within one's own body, which corresponds to the external [victory] of the Great Wheel-turner Kalkin.
That gift of Dharma which belongs to the Great Wheel-Bearer (Mahācakrin) externally on Kailāśa is, within one's own body, the remover of the fear of cyclic existence (bhava).

That earth which is externally filled with material wealth is, within the body, the purified aggregate of the elements (dhātu-samūha). As for the two sons of the Wheel-Bearer who existed externally as Brahmā and Īśvara, [internally] he who teaches the Dharma is at the back in the single segment (ekakhaṇḍa), while he who seeks the destruction of the Mleccha-dharma is in front in the foremost segment (agrakhaṇḍa).

Ārya Mañjuśrī, the Lord of the World, the conqueror of the three realms, is the *rajas* (passion) within one’s own body, which bestows bliss; this refers to the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhānacitta*) and the mind of application (*prasthānacitta*).

Furthermore, those various lineages beginning with Brahmā in the rear section are the many pure Buddhas within one’s own body, whose nature consists of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). Indeed, the battle between the barbarians and the senses occurs inevitably within the bodies of embodied beings.

The illusory form (*māyārūpa*) in the external sphere of ritual action is indeed not a battle with barbarians (*mleccha*), but rather a [spiritual] battle; the details of this will be explained in the fifth chapter, in the section on the attainment of the knowledge of the Supreme Syllable (*paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*).

Now, the division of the *Trika* into three sides and three years—the distinctions of the Tantras such as the *Samāja* and others—is described starting from the verse beginning with "the year of time" (*kālābda*): In the year of time numbered by fire (three), multiplied by the total number of days in a year, there are the six families (*ṣaṭkula*) from the numerical value of the solstices (*ayanāṅka*). From the division of thirty-six months, and from the flavors multiplied by the qualities (six times six), there are the families of the Yoginīs.

O Lord of Men, when the divisions [of time] are cut away, the deities are obtained and their fixed nature is revealed; in the cutting of the wings of Kālacakra, there is the designation by means of the male and female deities.

In this context, regarding the intermediate *nāḍī*-year—the year numbered as fire (three)—when multiplied by the number of days in three years and divided by the three hundred and sixty days of a year, the resulting total is one thousand and eighty days. That very [period] of three years constitutes the "Three Families" (*trikula*)—body, speech, and mind—which, according to the division of the years, have the nature of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Then, from that total of days, by dividing according to the distinction of the solstices (*ayana*) with a divisor of one hundred and eighty, six families are obtained.
Furthermore, by dividing that same total of days according to the distinction of months with a divisor of thirty, thirty-six families are obtained.

"Multiplied by the qualities of taste" means multiplied by six; thus, there are thirty-six families of yoginīs. Likewise, this applies to the methods (upāyas) of the yoginīs. Therefore, from the total of one thousand and eighty days, by dividing according to the days of the week, the revealed and fixed deities who are the maṇḍala-deities of Kālacakra are obtained.

The remainder of one hundred and fifty-four is the pair of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya-yugala*). Thus, one hundred and fifty-six is the *Kālacakra*. The remainder of seven parts is the circle of deities and goddesses at the station of Kulikā, which is the defining characteristic of Kulikā. Furthermore, from that [total] of one thousand and eighty mentioned in the previous chapter on the cutting of the fortnights (*pakṣaccheda*) regarding the battle between the Cakravartin and the Mlecchas, there is an enumeration by means of the deities and goddesses obtained through division by fifteen. This is the Great Chapter on the Origin of the Families of Channels (*nāḍīkulotpatti*) within the *Kālacakra-kulatantra*.

The characteristic of the seventy-two deities and goddesses together with the couple who are the lords of Kālacakra is the rule of the Yoginītantras according to the three-year division. According to worldly convention, the three families, the six families, and the thirty-six families constitute the Yoginītantras; such is the rule of the Yoginītantras. The *Māyājāla* consists of three types based on the limbs of the days (360), correctly [divided] by the apertures (9) and the Vedas (4); it becomes [the *Bhūta-tantra*] by the elements (5) and the oceans of elements (71), and the *Śrī-samāja* by the divisions of the seasons (6). That which is called *Tattva* is reduced by six (24); furthermore, the other [is divided] by half the division of those two.
Furthermore, the mixed [type] has two varieties: one with three, ten, nine, ten, and the void (zero), along with the principles (tattvas). || 52 ||

Now, the Kriyāyoga and Yogatantras are explained according to a division of three times six types, beginning with the words "The Māyājāla," and so forth. Here, the forty-five days of the middle three fortnights, multiplied by twelve, become five hundred and forty in number as the constituent parts of those days, due to the division of the twelve zodiacal signs for each day.

Therefore, subtracted from that fifty-fourth part of the day, the *Māyājāla* becomes threefold: the first consists of forty-nine deity pairs (*yugma*) by means of one *randhra* (nine) and *veda* (four); the second consists of forty-five deity pairs by means of *bhūta* (five) and *arṇava* (four);
and the other consists of forty-three deity pairs by means of *śikhin* (three) and *jalanidhi* (four).

Therefore, when the components of the day are subtracted by the three [groups], there are one hundred and thirty-seven; when doubled for the male and female deities, there are two hundred and seventy-four. This is the rule of the *Māyājāla*. The detailed exposition of this shall be stated in the fifth chapter; such is the rule of the *Māyājālakriyāyogatantra*. Now, the sixfold division of the *Samāja* is described: "From that remainder resulting from the subtraction, the seasonal division of the venerable *Samāja* [is derived]."
That which is called "Reality" (*tattva*) consists of twenty-five; therefore, from that "limb of days," it becomes [the number] twenty-five by subtracting the pairs of deities.
Furthermore, twenty-five minus six is nineteen; thus, it is by subtracting nineteen deities.
Moreover, there is a division into halves within those two [groups] consisting of twenty-five and nineteen.
Twenty-five, half [of that] is twelve and a half; nineteen, half [of that] is nine and a half; from this, half enters into twelve and a half.
Therein, one assembly consists of nine, while the other consists of thirteen.
Furthermore, another mixed assembly becomes twofold.
"Tridaśa" means thirteen.
"Navadiśā" means nineteen. With these thirty-two pairs of deities—namely, the tridaśas and the navadiśās—the *Samāja* comes to be.
With nine apertures (*randhra*) together with the six principles (*tattva*), and along with twenty-five, the second *Samāja* consists of thirty-four pairs of deities (*devatā-yugma*).
Thus, the *Samāja* is divided into six varieties.

In these six great tantras (*tantrarāja*), the number of deities is doubled by means of one hundred and thirty-two pairs of deities and their consorts, resulting in a total of two hundred and sixty-four deities and goddesses.
Thus, in the nine great tantra kings, such as the *Samāja* and the *Māyājāla*, there are five hundred and forty deities and goddesses together with the pair of presiding lords.

The distinction among these tantras, according to the differentiation of the completion of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), moon, and sun within the womb, is to be explained in the fifth chapter by way of the distinction of their seats; such is the rule for the Yoga Tantras.

In this context, for one born in the womb, there is a ninefold *samāja* through the perfection of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*); likewise, a thirteenfold one through the perfection of the aggregates, elements, and the wheels of the innate (*sahaja*), enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*), and emanation (*nirmāṇa*); likewise, a nineteenfold one through the perfection of the aggregates, elements, wheels, and objects; likewise, a twenty-fivefold one through the perfection of the aggregates, elements, wheels, objects, and the six [faculties] beginning with the eyes;
and likewise, a thirty-two-fold one through the perfection of the aggregates, elements, wheels, objects, sense organs, action organs, and the secret and crown lotuses.

Likewise, the *Samāja* consists of thirty-four elements, comprising the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), the six wheels (*cakra*), objects (*viṣaya*), sense organs (*indriya*), action organs (*karmendriya*), and divine organs (*divyendriya*), along with the attainments of bliss (*ānanda*).
From conception until the age of sixteen, there is a sixfold generation for children; this rule of the *Samāja* is to be explained in detail in the fifth chapter.

Thus, in the *Māyājāla*, the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*) consist of nine, the eight elements beginning with hair (*loma*), the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*), together with the four wheels (*cakra*), and together with the elements of wind, bile, phlegm, and their combination (*sannipāta*), as well as the six action-faculties (*karmendriya*). This constitutes the *Māyājāla* consisting of forty-three [components].

Together with the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*) and the secret lotus (*guhyakamala*), it consists of forty-five components; and together with passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), and pride (*māna*), it consists of forty-nine components. This is the rule for the *Māyājāla*, which is to be explained in detail in the fifth chapter; this is the rule for the origin of the *Yoginīyogatantra*.
Now, the outer and inner mudrās are explained: here, in every case, the effect is to be sealed by the cause, and the cause is to be sealed by the effect.
Because it possesses the nature of *rajas*, the sun is the cause that is wisdom (*prajñā*); because it possesses the nature of *śukra*, the moon is the effect that is skillful means (*upāya*).

From a relative perspective, because it possesses the nature of *śukra*, the moon is the cause that is wisdom; because it possesses the nature of *rajas*, the sun is the effect that is skillful means.

Thus, in all cases, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the cause of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and means (*upāya*) is compassion (*karuṇā*), which is the fruit. Regarding the lunar portion, those six days indeed obtained by the division of the weekday within the total number of days are the six mudrās of the Vajrin; these are the mudrās of body, speech, and mind for the subsequent number of days. In the *Yogatantro*, the Yoginī is manifest and fixed as the three-fold *prajñā*-body; she is the power (*śakti*). The ten wrathful deities arise in sequence, as do the five Buddhas and goddesses. (53)

In this context, from those forty-five days that constitute the lunar portion, six days and six mudrās of the Vajrī are obtained by means of the division by the [lunar] day-count: the discus, earring, necklace, bracelet, girdle, and the ash-sacred thread. These are the external mudrās of Kālacakra; they are the remaining days.
The remainder, numbering three, are the body, speech, and mind mudrās of the Vajrī within; thus, nine mudrās are to be understood as both external and internal.

In the *Prajñākāya* and *Prajñātantra*, and in the *Upāyakāya* and *Upāyatantra*, the three attachments—consisting of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and characterized by body, speech, and mind—are revealed as the rule for the *mudrās* in the *Yoginīyogatantra*.

[106a] In this chapter, the "Great Chapter on the Origin of the Families of Channels" (*nāḍīkulotpatti-mahoddeśa*) concerning the battle between the Cakravartin and the Mlecchas and the *Kālacakra*-family tantra, the number of the deities and goddesses of *Kālacakra* is now stated, beginning with the word "powers" (*śakti*): here, the host of deities has the nature of the manifold channels of the six wheels.
"The ten powers and wrathful ones arise in sequence" means that there are ten powers and ten perfections (*pāramitā*);
the ten wrathful ones, beginning with Uṣṇīṣa, likewise constitute ten groups of ten.
"The five Buddhas and goddesses" means the five Buddhas, beginning with Akṣobhya, and the five goddesses, beginning with Vajradhātvīśvarī; these likewise constitute five groups of five.

Furthermore, O King, the group of six beginning with form and the group of six beginning with the eye, as well as the host of deities, the twelve [senses], the yoginīs, and the eight [groups] of nāgas and caṇḍas—all this in the world is doubled.

This is the glorious Kālacakra consisting of one hundred and four; half of that exists in the three realms. And that which is the sixty ghaṭikās of the sun's portion that emerge daily within the month— 54.
"Form and so forth, the six beginning with the eye":

the six such as Rūpavajrā, the six such as Kṣitigarbha, and likewise each group of six; furthermore, the "twelvefold host of deities" refers to the twelve beginning with Indra; "the eight Yoginīs, Nāgas, and Caṇḍas" refers to the eight beginning with Cakrī, the eight beginning with Ananta, and the eight beginning with Śvānāsyā—all these groups of deities are to be described individually by their distinct names in the *Sādhanāpaṭala*.
Regarding "the worlds," all this, both externally and internally, is again doubled by means of the division into Wisdom (*prajñā*) and Means (*upāya*).
This Śrī Kālacakra consists of one hundred and four [deities], and half of that consists of fifty-two deities.

Thus, by the division of sun and moon, that very same Kālacakra should be understood as consisting of one hundred and fifty-six deities through their unity; this is the rule for the host of deities residing in the pericarp of the lotus.

Now, the goddesses on the petals of the lotus, beginning with Carcikā, are described: from the breath-wheel, by dividing the solar portion into thirty-two parts, two *ghaṭikās* are obtained each day; over the course of thirty days in a month, these become sixty *nāḍīs*, which take the form of Kulikā.

All those Yoginīs, mixed with the [planetary] conjunctions and doubled, reside in the abode of the three worlds within the solar portion; that host of Yoginīs, when multiplied by two and condensed into a single mantra-piṇḍa, becomes the totality of the days of the sun tripled along with their designations. In the case of the Moon, there is a division of fortnights (pakṣa), while in the Sun, there is a complete division of groups (varga). || 55 ||
And those Yoginīs, when mixed with the *lagna* (ascendant) and mixed with the four *sandhyā*-kulikas of the *lagna*, become sixty-four.
When doubled by way of the division of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), they become one hundred and twenty-eight in number.
Furthermore, within the solar portion, the day is divided into three hundred and sixty days, which constitute the host of deities characterized by the lunar dates (*tithi*) beginning with Caitra.

That same [group], when doubled by adding the twelve, such as Lāsyā and the rest, becomes a host of seventy-two deities. "All condensed into a single mass" means that these goddesses, together with their namesakes—the seventy-two deities—and along with the six mudrās, amount to one thousand and eighty, being three times the number of solar days (i.e., the days of three years). Thus, the intention is that in the Yoginītantra, the deities and goddesses should be understood as having the nature of the aggregate of days in three years.

Thus, there is the division of the solar year in the Moon (Śaśadhara); the entire division of the fortnights consists of five hundred and forty deities in nine groups within the Māyājāla and Samāja [Tantras].
[This is] the section on the aggregates in the Vimalaprabhā; thus, therein in the Ādibuddha, there are [five hundred and forty] deities and goddesses corresponding to the sun and the lords of men.
The internal wisdom and means indeed become night and day when they are equally divided at midnight and midday;

he by whom this is known within his own body through the divisions of the transitions of the months during the times of day and night, is the glorious Mañjuvajra, the destroyer of the fear of existence, a Buddha in this very life. || 56 ||

Thus, when unified with the hosts of solar and lunar deities, one becomes Ādibuddha. When he has manifested, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred [deities], which is the number of his own rays. Among those male and female deities, wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) are respectively night and day. Wisdom is the nocturnal portion, and means is the diurnal portion. The equal division occurs from midday to midnight, and from midnight to midday, consisting of thirteen and a half constellations, or eight hundred and ten *daṇḍas*, or *ghaṭikās*; such is the division of night. Likewise is the division of day.
The illustrious Lord has stated in the *Ādibuddha* that within the circle of the Kṣatriyas, the host of deities consists of the number of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and channels (*nāḍī*).

Just as externally there is the enjoyment of the lunar mansion-hours by all the planets, so too internally, within body, speech, mind, and gnosis, there is the [enjoyment] of the phenomena of the six sense faculties;
he who knows this in his own body—

Thus, by the sequence described, the yogi who has realized within his own body the Ādibuddha—which consists of wisdom and means—through the divisions of day and night, of the junctions (*saṃdhyā*) and watches (*prahara*), and through the twelve divisions of the monthly transits (*saṃkrānti*), becomes the glorious Mañjuvajra, the destroyer of the fear of cyclic existence; he is a Buddha in this very life. This is the rule for the arising of the deities of the Root Tantra from the Abridged Tantra.

From that [total], by a thirtyfold part, the deities are fixed as three times that number in the Kālacakra; likewise, there is the external set of six mudrās, and the channels of the wheels are similarly fixed. In the uṣṇīṣa they are twice [that]; in the heart, eight; on the head, sixteen (the number of kings); in the throat, thirty-two (the number of teeth); and in the navel, sixty-four (eight times eight). In the center of the secret place, they are established as double the number of kings (thirty-two). || 57 ||

Now, the arising of the *laghutantro* from this *paramādibuddha* is described by the verse beginning with "thirty," and so forth: here, from the *paramādibuddha* consisting of sixteen hundred and twenty [verses], the deities are obtained as fifty-four by means of a thirtyfold division.
Furthermore, when multiplied by the qualities of body, speech, and mind—thus tripled—they become one hundred and sixty-two.

Among these, the number of deities in the mandala (*māṇḍaleya*) is one hundred and fifty-four; this includes the lord of the mandala (*maṇḍaleśa*) as a pair of wisdom and method, along with the six external mudrās.

The *Kālacakra* has emerged from the *Paramādibuddha* by way of a tenfold division according to the distinction of the channels beginning with *iḍā* and ending with *śaṃkhinī*; this is the outer *neyārtha* (interpretable meaning), such is the rule of the *Laghukālacakra*. Now, the channels of *Kālacakra* are described starting with "the channels of the wheels are likewise," and so forth: here in this body, there are three channels of the three families (*trikula*) which sustain the drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, and mind, located at the navel, the secret place, and the jewel. Likewise, there are six channels of the six families (*ṣaṭkula*), namely *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtī*, which carry feces, urine, and semen.

Likewise, there are thirty-six family channels (*kulanāḍī*): the six channels of the six wheels beginning with the *uṣṇīṣa*; two that perceive sound, two that perceive touch, two that perceive taste, two that perceive form, and two that perceive smell—these ten channels;
the twelve channels of the transitions (*saṃkrānti*) in the other mandalas within the center of the navel wheel; and the eight channels of the watches (*prahara*).
