Regarding *rohaṇa* (ascent): twenty-eight days at the throat; fourteen days at the forehead as previously mentioned; thirty days at the secret place (*guhya*)—that is, ten days plus twenty; then four days at the throat and two days at the forehead. For life, there is another three nights. Here, in the cutting of the vowels (*svaraccheda*), a lunar day (*tithi*) consisting of fifty-six *daṇḍas* is to be taken. Thus, there are forty-five lunar days characterized by the vowels (*svaradharmiṇyaḥ*) and three characterized by the voids (*śūnyadharmiṇyaḥ*). In the same way, there are two days even in the dharma of the consonants (*vyañjanadharme*).

During these [days], for eight days it ascends within the heart-lotus; thereafter, there is a gathering of the ten winds at the pericarp (*kaṇikā*). This continues until the time of the day and night of the loss of the cycle of inhalation and exhalation, when life becomes a single night.

Then, by the power of karma, the consciousness (*vijñāna*) transmigrates elsewhere. Such is the rule for living beings with a lifespan of a hundred years when death occurs through the central channel (*madhyamā*); this is the rule for the severance of the channels (*nāḍī*).

Now, regarding the remaining channels (*nāḍikā*) that carry the ten winds until death at the limit of six days in the *nirmāṇacakra* and the other centers, it is said starting with the words "at the navel" (*nābhau*), etc.: "At the navel, the throat, the forehead, and in the lotus of one's own heart, the channels remain with their residue; the sun, the moon, and the fire abide in the lotus of one's own heart, likewise for one and a half channels."

At the joint of the hand and the foot, for six days, the subtle [wind] flows through all [the channels], abandoning the heart-lotus day by day. Here, in the navel-cakra, the channel flowing through the external mandala remains through the movement of the breath as the twelve zodiacal channels—consisting of the void-mandala and the earth-mandala—for six days, following the abandonment of the decay of the channels after three years and the ascent of the consonants during the three fortnights of the Rohiṇī [period]; this is called the Sun (arka).

Thus, in the throat, there are three channels carrying for six muhūrtas called "Rasa" (Taste), which carry for half a prahara of the Moon; [three] called "Agni" (Fire) carry for one prahara in the heart-lotus; and likewise, in the lotus of one's own heart, there is one channel and a half, which carries with a remainder.

Regarding "at the joints of the hand and the foot": within the three hundred and sixty channels (*nāḍī*) of the *karmacakra* and *kriyācakra*, at the joints there are "the Yugas multiplied by the lunar days," which means sixty channels; these are the carriers of the ten winds. Thus, for each of the twelve joints, there are five channels each that carry the ten winds. As for the remainder, the Kāla, Mṛtyu, Vāyu, Mahātamas, and Dharma [channels] in the *kriyācakra* at the sixty joints are such that each single channel carries the ten winds, while five channels each carry the great winds of Kāla and Mṛtyu.

In this manner, for up to six days, and then for another six days, having brought about the exhaustion of the channels of the sense objects, finally on the day of death, the subtle *madhyamā* or *avadhūtī* flows everywhere, leaving behind the channels that carry the moon, the sun, feces, and urine; the great darkness, the *kāla-vāyu*, flows until the end of death, as long as the wheel of breath persists—this is the rule. And "they abandon the day" refers to the heart-lotus.

Thus has the Blessed One taught the rule for death through the cutting off of breaths—the channel for the ascent of the sun and moon, the channels remaining in the wheels of the activities of consonants and actions, and the time of death—[in this] Great Chapter on the Signs of Death from Illness and the Cutting of the Channels.

Now, the increase of time through the exhaustion of the movements of the moon and sun is described by the verse beginning with "by thirty-six," etc.: "By thirty-six thousand [days], the time-pulse (*kālanāḍī*) ascends within the total number of days known as *dhru* (one hundred). Whichever [pulse] is filled by the respective movements of the sun and moon during the day and night; the solar day occurs in the solar movement, and there is also a debt in the lunar movement, which is half of that. In the division of the lunar day (*nakṣatrāha*), the movement of the sun and moon is zero in the month of death. In this context, when the number of days in one hundred years is calculated, there are thirty-six thousand days; *dhru* is the designation for a year. By those thirty-six thousand days of the *dhru* period, the time-pulse—death—ascends; it increases within the pulses, and the death-wind enters into seventy-two thousand [pulses]. The five-maṇḍala wind gradually recedes, having established its sixth part therein. Which time-pulse does the death-wind ascend? Whichever is filled by the respective movements of the sun and moon during the day and night of their power: by the movement of the constellations, the sun's power [is exhausted]; by the movements of the lunar dates (*tithi*), the moon's power [is exhausted]. The "solar day" (*sūryāha*) consists of twelve days in the solar movement; however, in the lunar movement, there is a debt of six days, which is half of that.

In this context, because the sun does not traverse one zodiac sign in thirty days per month, nor does the moon traverse sixty *daṇḍas*, the movement of the sun and moon through the divisions of the lunar days (*nakṣatrāha*) results in a "void month" (*śūnyamāsa*) for the sake of death. That void month occurs at the end of thirty-two months; it consists of sixty-four *nāḍīs*. Within those sixty-four *nāḍīs*, the void-wind (*śūnyavāyu*) sprouts within the navel-lotus among the seventy-two thousand channels. Specifically, two channels sprout every day; such is the general rule regarding the piercing of the channels (*nāḍī*).

Now, the ascent by means of the division of breaths day by day is described starting with the words "the vital breaths" (*prāṇā*) and so forth: "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) which have authority over the body—sixty minus a quarter of a Veda (56¼)—manifest during the equinox (*viṣuva*). Through all the divisions of the transits (*saṃkrānti*), they strike two channels (*nāḍī*) at every moment of each day. Again and again, within the course of a year, due to the movement of the feet of the Sun and Moon, [they strike] a number equal to zero, eyes, and mountains (720). Thus, time passes for gods and men through hundreds of years according to their respective measures of lifespan. (Verse 71) In this context, among the twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths, those that flow through the circle of knowledge (*jñānamaṇḍala*) are said to have authority over the breaths in the body. During the manifest equinox, in the middle of both junctions (*lagna*), sixty minus a quarter of a Veda—that is, fifty-six and a quarter (56¼)—all of them, becoming one hundred seventy-five pulses (*puṭa*) through the twelve divisions of the transits, "strike two channels" at every moment of each day; such is the reading of the scripture. The form *ghnantī* (they strike) is used here. They strike these two channels among the seventy-two thousand channels on the left and right; the destruction of the movement of the winds of the five circles occurs. The remaining forty-five breaths remain. Again and again, within the course of a year, as two channels are struck every day, within the year by the days of the year—three hundred and sixty days—from the movement of the feet of the Sun and Moon, that is, from the movement of the right and left circles, the number is "zero, eyes, and mountains," meaning seven hundred and twenty (720).

Thus, time passes for gods and humans in thirty-six thousand years and one hundred days; or, according to their own respective measures previously mentioned, it consists of seventy-two thousand nāḍīs that carry the five maṇḍalas and constitute the movement of the moon and sun. This is the rule for the cutting of the nāḍīs by means of the days of the subtle body, the elements, the deities, and so forth.

Now, the nature of the *kālanāḍī* (the time-channel) is described, beginning with the words "If bitten," and so forth: "If men are ever bitten, afflicted by disease, or struck [by a weapon] during the *kālanāḍī*, then Time enters suddenly and swiftly through that very support into the six root-chakras. Having blocked the channels in the chakras and having severed the entire movement of the sun and moon, O Lord of Men, it seizes the life of living beings which resides in the subtle center. (72) In this body, when the *madhyamā* flows during the time of the *kālanāḍī*, if men are ever bitten, afflicted by disease, or struck, then Time—namely the wind of great darkness (*mahātamas*)—enters suddenly and swiftly into the six root-chakras. Having entered, it blocks the one hundred and fifty-six channels within the six chakras; having severed the movement of the sun and moon in the left and right channels entirely, it seizes the life—the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*)—which resides in the subtle center, supported by the *avadhūtī* channel. Thus, O Lord of Men, it takes away the life of living beings. This is the rule regarding the *kālanāḍī*.

Now, the movements of the moon (*candracaraṇa*) on the Wheel of Dharma are described starting from "In the heart-lotus" and so forth: "In the heart-lotus and the illustrious forehead, the lunar quarter (*śaśipada*) moves, known as the elements (5), directions (10), and days (7). In the *saṃbhoga* [wheel], in the navel-chakra, there are nineteen [quarters] together with the pair of Rudras (2) called the Victors (5). Known as the principles (*tattva*), he abandons them after seven nights; furthermore, this moon, having completed the full [course] in the drop (*bindu*), enters the heart in due order during the bright fortnight while ascending. (Verse 73) Here, by the division of the moon's quarters through its fourteen-fold movement—whether even or odd—there is an increase or decrease among the lunar days (*tithi*). On the seventh day, among the seven lunar days, that increase or decrease, which is multiplied by the five objects of the senses (5), ceases according to the divisions of the infant (*bāla*), the youth (*kumāra*), and so forth. When the one hundred and twenty quarters are complete, the portions of one hundred and twenty are stated here: when one remaining quarter out of the fourteen parts is seen, then of the sixty-nāḍī portions of the digit (*kalā*) of that day, five nāḍī-portions become added to the wealth of the digit, whether it be black or white; or they become subtracted in the place of debt. On the second day, the five portions of the second [digit] are to be known as doubled by the first [digit] through the division of the youth (*kumāra*).

Thus, on the third day, there are five parts for the third [tithi], ten for the second, and fifteen for the first through the division of *vāyu* (wind); thus, by the division of *bāla* (childhood), there are five parts for the fourth, ten for the third, and fifteen for the second, while for the first there are nineteen through the division of *yuvan* (youth). Thus, on the fifth day, there are five parts for the fifth, ten for the fourth, fifteen for the third, nineteen for the second, and twenty-two for the first through the division of *vṛddha* (old age). Thus, on the sixth day, there are five parts for the sixth, ten for the fifth, fifteen for the fourth, nineteen for the third, twenty-two for the second, and twenty-four for the first through the division of *ativṛddha* (extreme old age).

Thus, on the seventh day, there are twenty-five parts: five from the seventh [tithi], ten from the sixth, fifteen from the fifth, nineteen from the fourth, twenty-two from the third, and twenty-four from the second; and from the first, twenty-five parts—whether as wealth or as debt—occur according to the division of the matured state and the influence of the *caraṇas*.
In this manner, the measurement for all [days] is to be known through the sequence beginning with the "infant" (*bāla*) and so forth.

Thus, having taken the degrees of the seven lunar days (*tithis*), the Moon traverses the one hundred and twenty petals of the heart-lotus and other centers; thereafter, it again moves upward through its own stations (*padam*), meaning through the lunar stations. Specifically, there are eight degrees in the eight petals of the heart, sixteen degrees in the sixteen petals, thirty-two degrees in the thirty-two petals of the *sambhoga*, and sixty-four degrees in the sixty-four petals of the navel-lotus.

Thus, after consuming one hundred and twenty parts, the waning or waxing of the lunar digit ceases. In the heart-lotus and the forehead, [the moon] abandons that which is called the elements (5), the directions (10), and the days (7); in the throat, that which is called the enjoyments (6); in the navel, that which is called the Rudras (11) together with nine and ten (29), and that which is called the Jinas (24).
This moon, as it ascends upward, abandons these over seven nights.

Twenty-five parts of the first digit (kalā) become fully matured; on the eighth day, that [digit] becomes the presiding deity of the navel. Then, on the full moon day, it makes [the digits] complete in the navel, heart, throat, and forehead, having filled the drop (bindu) in the location of the drop according to its nature. Thereafter, ascending again from the navel, there are sixty-four parts in the sixty-four petals, eight parts in the heart, thirty-two parts in the throat, and sixteen parts in the forehead. Thus, in fourteen days, the completion of the stages (padāni) occurs.
Having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* in that [navel], one enters the heart during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*)—the fortnight of wealth—and proceeds further in sequence;

likewise, during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa*), one returns from the lotus of the feet up to the navel-lotus. Indeed, in the heart and the head, there are the eight-spoked and sixteen-spoked [lotuses] known as the black and white lotuses;

at the throat is the thirty-two-spoked [lotus], and another double that (sixty-four-spoked) at the navel, which is red and yellow. The eighth [day] occurs at the navel and the throat, while the full moon (*pūrṇā*) is at the head and the heart, being white and black respectively.

The first thirty vowels, joined with *ha*, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, and *la*, become sixty when differentiated by the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the auspicious visarga; these are twenty-one hundred in number. These are the filaments at the tips of which the groups of consonants beginning with *ka* are distributed across the petals of the excellent lotus by means of the forms of the *bindu* and *visarga*. By virtue of the movement of the watches (praharas), the Sun rises and sets.

Furthermore, in the case of Kṛṣṇa, similarly on the side of debt (*ṛṇapakṣa*), by means of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*)—either in the forward order as before or in reverse order—the [debt] reaches fullness upon the petals of the wind, earth, water, fire, and lotus, until it resides in the heart of the words of Kṛṣṇa; such is the rule for the words (*padaniyama*).

Here, regarding the lotuses: there is an eight-spoked [lotus] for Kṛṣṇa in the heart, a sixteen-spoked white one in the head, a thirty-two-spoked red one in the throat, and another double that, a sixty-four-spoked yellow one, in the navel; such is the rule for the lotus petals (*padmadalaniyama*).

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the locations of the four joints (*parva*) are now described, beginning with the words "the two eighths," and so forth: Here, within the heart-lotus and other centers—which possess the natures of the elements wind, fire, water, and earth—the Moon moves through the filaments and the tips of the stamens by means of the distinctions of the vowels.
There are thirty initial vowels which, when divided by the *bindus* and the glorious *visargas*, become sixty.

Here, as previously stated, there are five short vowels, five in the form of *guṇas*, and five short vowels resulting from the *yaṇādeśa* substitutions; these fifteen, when divided by the *bindus*, become thirty.

The fifteen consonants beginning with *ha*—namely *ha*, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *kṣa*, *ma*, *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *na*, and *pa*—each become thirty when divided by the visarga (*visargavibhinna*). Thus they become sixty.
As it is said: "They are the kings of the ages (*yuga*), the Vasus, and the teeth [sixty], located on the tips of the filaments.

Here, in the heart-lotus, the Moon, having made the new moon (*amā*), moves through the vowels consisting of thirty parts via fifteen lunar days (*tithi*) by means of the division of the first and second halves of each day.

Here, in the lotus of the heart, on the tip of the filaments: on the first lunar day (pratipad), in the first half [of the petal] is *a*, and in the second half is *aṃ*; on the second lunar day, in the first half is *i*, and in the second half is *ī*. Thus, there are four pairs in the heart, excluding the pericarp (*kaṇikā*).

Then, on the third [day], the first and second halves of *ṛ* and *ṝ* move upon the tips of the filaments of the throat-lotus (*kaṇṭhakamala*). Likewise, on the fourth [day], *u* and *ū*; on the fifth, *ḷ* and *ḹ*; on the sixth, *a* and *aṃ*; and on the seventh, *e* and *eṃ*. On the eighth, *ara* moves on the tip of a filament in the first half, and *araṃ* on the pericarp (*kaṇikā*) in the second half. On the ninth, *o* and *oṃ*; and on the tenth, *ala* and *alaṃ*—thus it moves upon the tips of the filaments of the throat-lotus.

Then, on the forehead-lotus, at the tips of the filaments: on the eleventh day, *ha haṃ* in the first and second halves; on the twelfth day, *ya yaṃ* in the first and second halves; on the thirteenth day, *ra raṃ*; on the fourteenth day, *va vaṃ*; and on the full moon day, *la* at the tip of the filament in the first half, and *laṃ* in the pericarp in the second half.

In the head, the full moon moves through the wind, fire, water, and the pericarp of the lotus according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*); thereafter, during the dark fortnight, it moves through the earth and the pericarps of the lotuses according to the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) as long vowels with the visarga. For example: on the first day of the dark fortnight, *lāḥ* in the first half and *lā* in the second half.

Thus, on the second [petal] is *vāḥ* or *vā*; on the third, *rāḥ* or *rā*; on the fourth, *yāḥ* or *yā*; on the fifth, *hāḥ* or *hā*; on the sixth, *ālaḥ* or *āla*; on the seventh, *auḥ* or *au*; on the eighth, *āraḥ*; in the pericarp (*kaṇikā*), *āra*; on the ninth, *aiḥ* or *ai*; on the tenth, *āḥ* or *ā*; on the eleventh, *lū*; on the twelfth, *ūḥ* or *ū*; on the thirteenth, *ṛḥ* or *ṛ*; on the fourteenth, *īḥ* or *i*; and on the fifteenth, *āḥ* or *ā*.
Here, in the pericarp, there are two voids (*śūnyaka*); in these two pericarps, there are neither vowels nor visargas.

Furthermore, at the end of the new moon (amāvāsya) within the heart-lotus, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad), there is a white [digit] on the tip of the filaments of the heart-lotus and a black one; this is the rule for the eighth day of the bright fortnight (śuklāṣṭamī). On the eighth day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇāṣṭamī), [the digits reside] on the tip of the filaments and in the pericarp (kaṇikā) of the throat-lotus. In the navel-lotus, [they reside] on the tip of the filaments and in the pericarp. The full digit resides in the heart, and the end of the full digit is in the head. Thus, "in the heart" refers to the time of entry into the first lunar day at the conclusion of the new moon; this is the rule.

Now, the enjoyments of the solar signs (*sūryavyañjana*) are described beginning with the word *bindu*: here, the consonant groups starting with *ka* are divided by the four *bindus* and *visargas*, resulting in one hundred and twenty syllables. That very [number] rises and wanes upon the petals of the excellent lotus—one hundred and twenty in total—by way of the movement of the watches (*prahara*), through the distinction between withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). Here, "the movement of the watches" refers to the four junctions (*sandhyā*); it is "by way of their movement," that is, by way of the movement of the watches.

Here, within the heart-lotus, up to the end of the new moon (*amāvāsya*), during the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) and so forth, four petals among the sixty-four are empty. On those [petals], on the first day, there are *ssāḥ ssā* and *yāḥ yā* in the four petals; thus, the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*) of the first day are presided over by the Sun (*arka*) starting with *ssā*.
Likewise, on the second day, there are *ṣṣāḥ ṣṣā* and *śśāḥ śśā*;
likewise, on the third day, there are *kkāḥ kkā* and *ttāḥ ttā*. [In these cases] there are no vowels or visargas (*na svaravisargau*).

The Great Chapter on the Signs of Untimely Death and the Severing of the Pulse: On the fourth [day], *thāḥ thā*, *ddāḥ ddā*; on the fifth, *dhdhāḥ dhdhā*, *nnāḥ nnā*; on the sixth, *ppāḥ ppā*, *phphāḥ phphā*; on the seventh, *bbāḥ bbā*, *bbhāḥ bbhā*; on the eighth, *mmāḥ mmā*, *ṭṭāḥ ṭṭā*; on the ninth, *ṭhṭhāḥ ṭhṭhā*, *ḍḍāḥ ḍḍā*; on the tenth, *ḍhḍhāḥ ḍhḍhā*, *ṇṇāḥ ṇṇā*; on the eleventh, *ccāḥ ccā*, *chchāḥ chchā*; on the twelfth, *jjāḥ jjā*, *jjhāḥ jjhā*; on the thirteenth, *ññāḥ ññā*, *kkāḥ kkā*; on the fourteenth, *khkhāḥ khkhā*, *ggāḥ ggā*; on the full moon of the bright fortnight, *ghghāḥ ghghā*, *ṅṅāḥ ṅṅā*.
Having enjoyed the syllables of the *sa*-group on the petals of the navel-lotus, the sun returns;
thus, by its own movement, the moon enters the head.

Then the moon comes to the lotus released by the sun, and the sun goes to the lotuses enjoyed by the moon. In the dark fortnight, the sun proceeds according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), and the moon according to the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*).

In all these cases, the rule is that when the Moon moves by way of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), then the Sun moves by way of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); and when the Sun moves by way of emanation, then the Moon moves by way of withdrawal. Now, regarding the petals of the lotus of the forehead and so forth, the Sun moves through the letters of the *ṅa*-group and other groups in reverse order (*utkrama*). On the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapratipad*), he moves through *ṅa ṅaṃ* and *gha ghaṃ* on the four petals of the forehead. On the second day, he moves through *ga gaṃ* and *kha khaṃ*; on the third day, through *ka kaṃ* and *ña ñaṃ*; and on the fourth day, through *jha jhaṃ* and *ja jaṃ*.

Then, on the petals of the throat-lotus: on the fifth [tithi], *cha chaṃ* and *ca caṃ*; on the sixth, *ṇa ṇaṃ* and *ḍha ḍhaṃ*; on the seventh, *ḍa ḍaṃ* and *ṭha ṭhaṃ*; on the eighth, *ṭa ṭaṃ* and *ma maṃ*; on the ninth, *bha bhaṃ* and *ba baṃ*; on the tenth, *pha phaṃ* and *pa paṃ*; on the eleventh, *na naṃ* and *dha dhaṃ*; on the twelfth, *da daṃ* and *tha thaṃ*; on the thirteenth, *ta taṃ* and *ka kaṃ*—these are on the petals of the heart-lotus. On the fourteenth, *śa śaṃ* and *ṣa ṣaṃ*.
Then, on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), *ya ya~* and *sa saṃ* are on the pericarp and the tips of the filaments.

The heart is the unstruck (*anāhata*) within the *amānta*, the void-bindu (*binduśūnya*), the six-syllabled as the five-syllabled, and the great void (*mahāśūnya*); such is the rule for the moon and sun.

Now, the debt and credit of the moon and sun are described, beginning with the words "the moon": "In a fortnight, the moon incurs a debt through its own movements called 'days'; furthermore, by another two months, one more day increases through the conjunction of the year."
When a year is complete, there shall be six days; likewise it increases further until the limit of death. Thus, O King, this debt of the sun increases twofold year after year. (76)

In this context, regarding the constant value of the lunar day (*tithi-dhruvaka*), because of the rule "it is to be added, subtracted, and [again] added" every day, a *kalā* consisting of sixty *ghaṭikās* is added to the place of the weekday; however, due to its being a debt, the *ghaṭikās* are diminished from the place of the *ghaṭikās*. Therefore, by a rough calculation, one *ghaṭikā* less per day is the *kalā*; by a precise calculation, it is fifty-six and a quarter *pāṇīpala*s.

Why? Because a debt occurs in the *ahargaṇa* when divided by sixty-four. Thus, the meaning is that there is a daily loss of one *kalā*, which amounts to fifty-six and a quarter *pāṇīpala*s per day over a period of sixty-four days.

For the sun, it is two days; thus, in a fortnight, the moon also incurs a debt through its own movement, consisting of the stage called "days" and the stage called "fifteen ghaṭīs. Regarding the lunar date (*tithi*), the sequence of the four parts is as follows in the Tibetan tradition: "In the dark fortnight, by the order of the sun's increase, and by the order of the moon's decrease."
In the *Vimalaprabhā*,
by the word "and" (*ca*) it is meant that [the day] is further diminished by fifty-six and a quarter *pāṇīpala*s;
thus, through the daily decrease over two months, another day becomes a debt at sixty-four days, and it increases again through the connection with the year.

When a full year has passed, there shall be six days [of debt], lessened according to the previously mentioned rule; likewise, another [period] increases up to the limit of death—the limit of death being one hundred years. From that limit of death, a total of five hundred and sixty-two and a half days of debt increase;

thus, O King, this double debt of the Sun increases from the hundred-year limit of death. Up to the limit of death, an aggregate of eleven hundred and twenty-five days increases; such is the rule regarding debt up to the limit of death.

Now, the number of years is stated according to the divisions of breath and so forth, beginning with "six breaths": Six breaths constitute one *liptā*; sixty *pāṇīpala*s make one *nāḍī*, and sixty *nāḍīs* form a day. A month consists of thirty days; six months make a solstice (*ayana*), and two solstices are well known as one year. The lifespan of men, extending to a hundred years, is determined by the force of the temporal *nāḍīs* within the cycles of the four ages (*yugas*). || 77 ||
In this body of human beings, six inhalations and exhalations constitute one *liptā*, and that is called a *pāṇīpala*. Sixty such *pāṇīpalas* make one *ghaṭikā*, which consists of one *daṇḍa*.
Sixty such *nāḍīs* (ghaṭikās) form a day and night (*ahorātra*). Thirty such days, multiplied by three [months], constitute one month.
By those six months beginning with Capricorn, one solstice (*ayana*) occurs; that same solstice doubled is known as one year.

Therefore, the lifespan of men is one hundred years. In the paths of debt (*ṛṇagati*), time has passed; in the paths of the dark *nāḍīs*, death has passed. By the power of its *nāḍīs*, according to the principle of the number of *avadhūtīs*, such is the rule for the *nāḍīs* of time.

Now, the state of being "lazy" (kuśīda) regarding Īśvara and others is described with the verse beginning "In the three worlds," and so forth: "In the three worlds, there is no yogi among gods, serpents, or humans who is capable of filling [the void]; the Moon and Sun move within their own bodies for many days.

The Sun moves through all the constellations by his own movements, while the Moon, by its own courses, swallows the world along with the earth, year by year, in due order; thus the Wheel of Time is the true hero. (78)
In this triple world, among gods, serpents, and humans, there is no yogi who is capable of filling the moon and sun within his own body.
For what reason?

Because, by its own movement, the moon does not traverse the count of three hundred and sixty days until the end of the year; and the sun does not traverse all twenty-seven constellations within the body in the course of a year, according to the previously mentioned method. Therefore, year after year, it devours the world and the body through its debt.

The Kālacakra Hero is the cause of the arising and destruction of transmigrating beings; therefore, that Kālacakra Hero must be accomplished. Having filled the moon and sun—the wind and the passion (*rajas*)—and having filled the inhalation and exhalation (*prāṇāpāna*) with the Bodhicitta, this is the rule for the yogin according to the Blessed Buddha. [In this regard, in manuscript *ka*, there is a further insertion: "In this body of humans, by means of six inhalations and exhalations, one *ekaliptā* occurs. This is the Great Chapter on the Signs of Death through *ariṣṭa*, the Severing of the Channels.

Now, the characteristics of the transformation of the elements, such as urine and so forth, are described by the verse beginning with "If one channel is severed" (*chinnā yadyekanāḍī*): O Lord of Men, if one channel is severed due to the influence of the *ariṣṭa*, the urine becomes watery (sour); it abandons its own measure for five nights.

At the time of the dissolution of the bodily aggregate, the supreme energy (*parakalā*) abandons sound in the ear, taste in the mouth, the star-like light in the center of the eyes, and smell in the nose of men; and in the hands, feet, and body, it gradually abandons the state of warmth. (79)

In this body, if one channel—either the left or the right—is severed and becomes devoid of the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), O Lord of Men, this is the sign that within the limit of six months there will be the state of urine being acidic (*amlatva*).

The supreme power, the vital force (*prāṇaśakti*), abandons the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) over a period of six days in successive order: on each day, at the time of the dissolution of the body, she abandons the object of sound from the ears—using the locative case for the ablative sense according to the reading in the *Āgama*; she indeed abandons taste from the mouth, that is, the tongue, up to the fifth day; the stars [the object of sight] from the middle of the eyes up to the fourth day; smell from the nose up to the third day; and the state of warmth and the state of touch within the hands, feet, and body of men up to the second day; finally, on the last day, she abandons the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the emission of semen, and the wheel of breath (*śvāsacakra*).
The signs of death within the next six days are now described: on that very day, death itself occurs. || 80 ||
With his arms held over his head, he is seen with his nose hanging down; though his two palms are rubbed with the dye of lac, they do not take on any color at all.

The sun appears black in color, and the full moon appears yellow. O King, when death has entered this body, the urine and the body become cold; one's own nose-tip is seen hanging down in the shape of an elephant's trunk; with the arms placed upon the head, one sees that very form [of the deity], but it is not seen as subtle. Likewise, even when rubbed with lac-dye, no redness appears on the palms of both hands or on the skin of the palms; the sun is seen black in color, and the full moon—the moon of the fifteenth day—is seen completely yellow for a period of six days. Then, on whichever day the urine and the body become cold, death occurs on that very day.
"O Lord of Men"—this is the address.

Furthermore, another sign of death within six days is stated: "Amṛta"; "Bho" [is] *skur ba nid* (sourness). According to the Tibetan, the reading *amlatva* (sourness) in place of *ambutva* (water-ness) is correctly understood and observed; thus there is this additional reading.

That former [sign] is described in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "The entire host of planets is seen above the breast, enveloped in the inner stage (*adhyātma-kakṣā*), accompanied by sparks; with neck stiffened and limbs rigid, even the whirling of the body is a sign of the eighth death. (81)

In this world, for one seized by untimely death (ariṣṭamaraṇa), there appears a black line like a cord of time beneath the tongue; likewise, in the eyes, there appears an extremely fine line above the *brahmarekhā* measuring the thickness of a hair, which pierces the black and red circles; and the breath flickers through the paths of the moon and the sun, while both cheeks throb.

Likewise, when the armpits are affected—that is, when the two channels (nāḍīs) extending above the breasts are affected—one sees the entire host of planets, yet it appears as if accompanied by sparks. His neck, along with his limbs, hands, and feet, becomes stiff and motionless; even a spinning sensation occurs in the body. These are said to be the eight signs of death.

Furthermore, whatever else is seen to be abnormal in the body or externally, such as the appearance of a shadow-person (chāyāpuruṣa), all that should be understood by the yogi as a sign of death. Having known this, he should perform acts such as giving charity.

If one lives by the power of merit, that is excellent; yet if one goes to death, even then one experiences the fruit of what was given. Therefore, the rule of the Blessed One is that gifts should be given by followers of the Sugata who desire happiness, for both sides.

Thus ends the fifth great chapter on the signs of death and the cessation of the channels, and the fourth great chapter on the definition of moments and the rule of the Kālacakra, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakratantrarāja* following the *Śrīmūlatantra*.

Now, the agent characterized by creation and destruction is described according to worldly convention, beginning with the words "He who creates birth" (utpattim): "He who effects birth at the time of procreation, in the forms of childhood and youth—that very one is the Destroyer; and he again performs that same act in the world as Kālacakrin, not the Sun.

That Blessed One swallows the gods, such as the Moon and Sun, along with all beings during the portion of night; then, for the sake of creation, he gradually releases them once more during the time of day, even though they are infinite. (82)

In this saṃsāra, that moment of death (*cyutikṣaṇa*) which causes the birth of sentient beings—possessing the nature of the *ālayavijñāna* and joined with semen and blood—is within the womb; from that, it brings about the period of gestation in the womb and produces the forms of infancy, childhood, and so forth. That very moment of death is the creator and sustainer of the body; it is he who, as Kālacakra, again acts in the world, in heaven, among mortals, and in the netherworld (*pātāla*). It does not mean the sun; the sun is the *rajas* and the moon is the semen. The meaning is that without the *ālayavijñāna*, and without Kālacakra, neither [the sun nor the moon] can act.
Why does he not do so here?
It is said that this is a well-known statement: "Rajas and Śukra have the nature of the Sun and Moon," and "here, everywhere, the world consists of Fire, Sun, and Soma."

The *Vimalaprabhā* commentary does not exist in this manuscript. [From the] *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja*, [the section on] *ariṣṭa* (signs of death), *bālakaumārī* (childhood and youth), *cyutikaraṇa* (the process of emission/death), and *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) [in the relevant] chapter: the *Mahoddeśa* on the rules of *Kālacakra* regarding the characteristics of moments:
"In the mother's womb, the moon is the semen (*śukra*) and the sun is the menses (*rajas*)."

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is meant that [the central channel] swallows those things produced from feces and urine together with the elements of earth, water, fire, air, and space—namely, *rajas* (the menstrual flow), which resides in the seat of semen (*śukra*) for the sake of producing body, speech, and mind; *candra* (the moon) is semen (*śukra*), *īśvara*; *rajas* is *sūrya* (the sun), *sadāśiva*; *majjā* (marrow) is *rudra*; *mūtra* (urine) is *viṣṇu*; and *brahmā* is *viṭ* (feces).
Thus, it swallows the deities beginning with Candra and Āditya during the portion of the night at the time of emanation (*utpatti*).

Furthermore, when the body has been swallowed by various states, they indeed release the infinite [deities] transformed [into those states] during the daytime at the time of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); this is the meaning of "he abandons."

For the sake of emanation—that is, for the cause of the subsequent production—he emits [the elements], gradually abandoning the elements beginning with earth, sequentially at the supports of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown; this is the rule regarding the agent of conventional reality.

Now, the instruments of action and so forth are described according to worldly convention, beginning with "sound and so forth": The sixfold group beginning with sound constitutes the six actions, while the sixfold group of sense organs constitutes the instruments; the years, months, fortnights, days, nights, lunar days, and the moon and sun are the agent.

There may be another here who is the agent of their withdrawal, but he is not the agent of creation; he is the one who pervades space, the Space-Vajrin, devoid of sense objects, without qualities, and without intrinsic nature.

When this body has been produced, there arises the sixfold object-group consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, smell, and the dharma-sphere; the sixfold instrument-group of the sense-faculties consisting of ear, body, eye, tongue, nose, and mind;

the twelve months and years according to the divisions of the zodiac signs and the divisions of the lunar digits; the twenty-four fortnights; day and night as a single *ahorātra*; the fifteen lunar days (*tithis*); and the moon and sun—all these constitute the instruments.
The agent, characterized by the *ālayavijñāna*, is the moment of the emission of semen, which, according to worldly convention, is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).

If there were another agent here who were the performer of the destruction of these [elements], such as the moment of death and so forth—since the creator of emanation is not the agent—then [that other] would be the pervasive one, the space-faced one, devoid of objects, without qualities, without intrinsic nature, the innate body, partless, possessing the [five] aggregates, all-pervading, and "ra.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no creator of emanation and destruction characterized by nirvāṇa; thus is the rule regarding the exhaustion of the agent.

Now, the origination and so forth are described with the words beginning with "scent" (gandha): "Scent, color, taste, and touch—earth, water, fire, and air—these eight indeed possess form; they are the objects of the aggregate, unified and principal in their entirety.

This entire triple world undergoes emanation and dissolution through the power of Time. Sound is indeed the formless void, O Lord of Men, as are the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and the mind. (84)

In this saṃsāra, arising occurs from a collection, not from a single factor. Here, "collection" refers to smell, color, taste, and touch, as well as earth, water, fire, and air—these eight are the material [elements]. When these objects are combined, they constitute a single primary whole;
among these eight material elements, one quality becomes primary, while the remaining ones become secondary, as previously stated.
Sound is indeed empty and formless, O Lord of Men; the dharmadhātu and the mind—these four are here [included among] the material.
Here, by the word "empty," the semen-element (*śukradhātu*) is meant.
This entire triple world undergoes emanation and dissolution through the power of time, which means through the power of the moment of death (*cyūtikṣaṇa*). Thus is the rule regarding origination.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is not found in the manuscript that "the all-pervading one" is mentioned here; now, the bondage of *saṃsāra* is described starting with the words "it binds the self," etc. [Adhyātma]: The self binds itself by means of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) through the qualities residing in *prakṛti*, just as a silkworm [binds itself] with its own [cocoon]. Furthermore, the self indeed liberates itself from conceptual construction by means of the mind.

Therefore, O King, one's own karma—consisting of the qualities inherent in nature—produces suffering and happiness; these are characterized by the mental constructs of existence and non-existence within the mind of saṃsāra. By means of those conceptualizations belonging to the qualities of nature, one binds oneself, just as a silkworm binds itself with the threads produced from its own body.

Furthermore, by means of the mind itself, one releases the self from conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*); thus, that self, being freed from the conceptualizations of the qualities inherent in *prakṛti*, becomes free from conceptualization. Therefore, with a mind free from conceptualization, one releases the self from the suffering of *saṃsāra*. Hence, O King, it is one's own action—governed by the qualities of *prakṛti*—that produces pleasure and pain. Who is the agent? What does he do? One who is devoid of *prakṛti* and devoid of the eighteen constituents (*dhātu*) does nothing; this is the meaning. Thus, the ignorant world is deluded by the false imagination of a personal agent; such is the rule regarding the bondage of karma.

Now, the eightfold primordial nature (*prakṛti*), beginning with earth and so forth, is described by the words "earth" and so on: earth, water, fire, wind, space, as well as mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness; gross, subtle, and supreme, it is comprised of the three qualities (*guṇa*) through the divisions of phonemes, points (*bindu*), and so forth. The primordial nature is attained as the gross within the gross sense organs; as the subtle within the subtle mind; and as the embodiment of gnosis within gnosis. This primordial nature is unchanging, having become the living being (*jīva*), yet not [merely] an element (*bhūta*). [127b] 86.

In this body, there is initially an eightfold *prakṛti*, consisting of earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*). For the mind of transmigratory existence, these are further threefold: gross (*sthūlā*), subtle (*sūkṣmā*), and supreme (*parā*). These are "gone to the qualities" (*guṇagatā*), meaning they reside within the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. The "gross" (*sthūlā*) is that which resides in the gross and subtle senses through the distinctions of phonemes, points, and so forth; it possesses the characteristics of the waking state (*jāgrat-avasthādharmiṇī*), because it grasps the objects of the waking state. This pertains to the gross mind (*sthūlacitta*), which apprehends the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of insentient matter.

The subtle state of mind has the dream state as its substrate (*adhamaṇī*), because it perceives illusory objects through the mental sense-faculties; thus it is subtle and supreme (*parā*). The deep sleep state has the state beyond all senses as its substrate, characterized by the cessation of all sense-faculties; it is supreme because of the abandonment of all objective phenomena (*bhāva*). Regarding the statement "he does not see," it is characterized by such descriptions as "having become one. Thus, *prakṛti* possesses the threefold nature of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep according to the divisions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Alternatively, it is characterized as gross (*sthūla*) and so forth; the subtle is characterized by the twilight (*sandhyā*), and the supreme is characterized by the great night (*mahāniśā*).

By the word "and" (*ca*), there is a fourth nature, the embodiment of gnosis (*jñānamūrti*). It is the embodiment of gnosis because it is the cause of the arising and cessation of sentient beings, being the essence of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*) at the time of the emission of the seminal essence (*śukra*) of the mind of gnosis, which is the fourth mind. Furthermore, that nature is unchanging (*avikṛti*), the living being (*jīvabhūtā*), the great vital breath (*mahāprāṇabhūtā*), and has the nature of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātusvabhāva*);
thus, it is "not an element" (*na bhūtā*), meaning it does not consist of the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, or the seminal essence.
In this way, there is a fourfold regulation of the nature according to the divisions of the mundane mind, such as the waking state and so forth.

[In the chapter on the non-arising and non-ceasing of sentient beings, the Great Exposition on the Momentary Characteristic of Kālacakra: Now, the designations of the phenomena of the fourth state (*turya*) and so forth are explained, beginning with the word "first" (*ādyā*): The first are the five voids; [then] nature (*prakṛti*), which is non-modification (*avikṛti*); the glorious *kalā*, *bindu*, and *nāda*; time (*kāla*), mind (*citta*), and intellect (*buddhi*); likewise, nature (*prakṛti*) again; and other vowels beginning with wind (*māruta*); the gross syllables of the consonant groups (*varga*); ten multiplied by three; and sixteen others which are modifications (*vikāra*). In their midst, Vajra is neither nature nor modification; he is all-pervasive and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). ||87||
In this saṃsāra, there is the designation of the perceived and the perceiver which conveys meaning; and that [designation] exists by way of the relationship between the signified and the signifier.

Herein, the first five voids (*śūnya*) belong to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*): the first five voids are Anāhata and the others. In the center of Anāhata is the void of the letter *a*; in the east, the void of *i*; in the south, the void of *ṛ*; in the north, the void of *u*; and in the west, the void of *l*. Thus, the first five voids are the primordial nature, which is non-modification (*avikṛti*). [The subsequent principles are: Śrī, Kalā, Bindu, Nāda, Kāla, Citta, and Buddhi.

*Kalā* is the sun; *bindu* is the moon; *nāda* is Rāhu; *kāla* is the fire of time (*kālāgni*); and *citta* is the intellect (*buddhi*). Thus, *prakṛti* also possesses the nature of the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
The other vowels are the winds and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), space and the rest are included. [These are: *a, i, ṛ, u, lṛ*; *a, e, ar, o, al*; and *ha, ya, ra, va, la*.
Thus, "long" (dīrgha) is the nature of sleep;
the gross syllables of the classes (*varga*), numbering three hundred and sixty together with the twelve *mātrās*, are the nature of the waking state;
and the other sixteen are the gross modifications (*vikāra*).

By taking fifteen vowels for each individual letter together with a consonant, there are sixteen modifications (*vikāra*). Thus, in every case, the five elements, the five sense organs, and the five objects are the modifications; these, together with the mind (*manas*), constitute sixteen. Among these [sixteen], beginning with earth, *vastu* is neither the primal nature (*prakṛti*) nor a modification (*vikṛti*); it is all-pervading and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Since it is free from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of cyclic existence and possesses the nature of consciousness (*cittadharmin*), therefore that consciousness exists which is "consciousness that is non-consciousness" (*Acintyaprabhāsa, Prastāvanā 1*).
There exists no other mind of nirvāṇa apart from the mind of saṃsāra; this was spoken by the Blessed One using the designation "Vajrī. This is the rule regarding the fourfold nature.

Now, the enjoyment of the fruits of their own karma by sentient beings is described by the words beginning with "In saṃsāra": "In saṃsāra, there is happiness and suffering belonging to the qualities of nature (*prakṛti*), as well as that born of karma; it may be gross, subtle, or tranquil (and supreme)—this karma of humans is threefold."
"I am the agent, and Vikarman is another Paśupati who is the agent"—this is action; "I am not the agent, nor is the other, for he is known to be devoid of material nature"—that is not action. (88)

In this saṃsāra, for a sentient being, whether it be happiness, suffering, or both happiness and suffering—whether it pertains to the qualities of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) or to the previously mentioned qualities—the meaning is that it is self-made. It is born from karma, produced by one's own performed actions; "born from karma" means that one experiences what has arisen from such action. That very [experience] here is threefold—gross, subtle, and supreme—by virtue of body, speech, and mind.
Action is threefold: *vikarma* (mis-action), *karma* (action), and *akarma* (inaction).
Among these, that in which the thought "I am the doer" arises is designated as *vikarma*. [The others are] Paśupati, Anya, Ga, Ai, Ṛ, U, La, and Bho.
Regarding the five faculties of action (*pañca karmendriyāṇi*) in the *Vimalaprabhā*:
"Or, there is no agent; whatever mind arises, that is designated as 'action'."

I am not the agent, nor is another; [the self] is devoid of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and devoid of the collection of aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. Whatever mind arises is designated as "action" (*karman*).
Thus, that which is known to be free from the grasping of self, other, or agent—that action is not performed by an agent, nor does it have an agent as its cause.

The arising of action occurs through the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*): just as rice is produced from a rice seed, so too is the production of the fruit of virtuous action from virtuous action; just as *kodrava* grain is produced from a *kodrava* seed, so too is the production of non-virtuous fruit from non-virtuous action.

Regarding what will be stated in the verse beginning with "Neither from itself nor from another" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.2), namely the determination of the fruits of action, it is now explained that action bears fruit even without an agent, starting with the words "Therefore": "Therefore, no agent here bestows or takes away the happiness and suffering of living beings in saṃsāra; rather, it is their prior karma—performed in its threefold manner—that arises and yields the fruit."

This is the intellect of the deluded; it burns [them], while He, the agent of creation and dissolution, takes away [the merit]. They do not perceive the aperture within the body, wherein immeasurable auspiciousness is being carried off by their own senses. 89.

In this saṃsāra, no creator bestows or takes away the happiness and suffering of living beings, because one's own previously committed karma arises as the yielder of fruit—whatever has been performed in its threefold manner. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no creator who gives or takes; such is the notion of the deluded that "He bestows, He takes, He is the creator of emanation and withdrawal."
Why?

Because they do not perceive the openings in their own bodies while immeasurable merit is being carried away by their own eyes—that is, by their own sense organs—which are engaged with external objects and, in the case of the internal self, are without refuge (*anāśraya*) and devoid of happiness; such is the rule for the experience of the fruits of one's own karma.

Now, the state of mutual conjunction of the agent of desire and the others is described, beginning with "desire" (icchā): Desire is power; action is that which is in one's own mind; the third is the power of knowledge of the world; it effects the entry into the illumination of existence (*bhāvāloka*) and the perception of objects through the process of making them of equal flavor (*samarasakaraṇa*).

The fourth is the abandonment; she is bowed to by the three worlds, non-dual, and indeed, in their midst, the Vajrin sequentially swallows nothing at all, nor does he ever release anything, O Lord of Men. (90)

In this world, the power of the will (*icchā-śakti*) of sentient beings brings light to phenomena; its meaning is that it causes the mind to engage in activity and initiates action toward objects. The power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) effects the realization of the object by bringing about the state of aesthetic resonance (*samarasa*) with the phenomenon; its meaning is the ascertainment of the object, which is the ascertainment of knowledge. Furthermore, the fourth power—the non-dual one saluted by the three worlds—gradually effects the relinquishment of the previous knowledge. These are the four powers of the mind; among these four, [the fourth] does not swallow anything.

One whose self is a pure mind does not at all release light, entry, the act of equalizing flavors, the attainment of objects, or the abandonment of knowledge; such is the restraint of desire and so forth.
1. ka. *hṛtam* 2–3. ka. kha. *vināśaphalam*.
4. ka. kha. *dahate*; ga. *dadate*; bho. *dadate* 5. ka. kha. *dahati* 6. ka. *grahatirmanasaḥ*

In the chapter on the Great Summary of the Rules of Kālacakra Concerning the Characteristics of Moments: Now, the giver of suffering and happiness is described, beginning with the words "the self," and so forth: "O King, the self is not the agent; it has no power there as the giver of suffering and happiness. O Lord of Men, neither bondage nor liberation exists apart from the power of the mind (*cittaśakti*).

Just as space enters into the middle of a jar yet the water does not [enter] when it is being carried away, so too the Space-Vajra (*khavajrī*), pervading the void, remains within the body, devoid of sense objects. (91)

O King, in this saṃsāra, the self (*ātman*) is not the agent; it has no power therein as the bestower of suffering and happiness. There is no one at all within the abode of the three worlds who is the bestower of suffering and happiness, apart from the power of consciousness (*cittaśakti*). The powers of consciousness here are characterized as waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turyā*). Among these, the bestower is the state of the fourth, which possesses the nature of arising and ceasing. Apart from that power of consciousness, there is no other self, agent, or bestower of happiness and suffering.
For sentient beings, there is no other bondage or liberation apart from the emission of semen; this means that apart from the mind of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, the mind of nirvāṇa—which transcends saṃsāra and abides within every body—is neither bound nor liberated by anything whatsoever.

Just as space enters into the middle of a jar even when water is being carried away, so too is the mind that pervades space called "Space-Vajra" (Khavajra), purified by the liberations such as emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*). Being devoid of objects means it is without qualities (*nirguṇa*), meaning it is free from the constituents of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and free from the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turīya*). Likewise, being without intrinsic nature within the body means that it possesses neither existence (*bhāva*)—which is white—or non-existence (*abhāva*)—which is cessation (*uccheda*); he who has neither of these is the "Vajrin," meaning the pure mind. This is the regulation concerning the mind of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

Now the doctrine of karma is explained with the words "thus," and so forth: Thus, he who maintains the existence of karma is this Blessed One, the sole Teacher; he is not a creator, yet he is the omniscient Ādibuddha, bowed to by the three worlds, the Kālacakrin—not a [mundane] Cakrin, nor Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Rudra—at the base of whose lotus feet I have gone for refuge. I salute that Kālacakra, the progenitor of the best of Jinas, who is devoid of [material] qualities and free from conceptual construction. (92)

By this sequence of statements, one who asserts the existence of karma becomes a proponent of non-existence and a proponent of selflessness; that Blessed One, whose nature is a pure mind, is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither; he is the sole teacher in the three realms, not a creator, the omniscient primordial Buddha, possessing omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of the aspects of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*); he is saluted by the three worlds, the Kālacakra-holder, whose nature consists of all phenomena in the form of untainted bliss.
He is not Cakrin nor Viṣṇu;
why?

Because even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra have sought refuge at the base of his lotus feet. I bow to that Kālacakra—namely, I, Mañjuśrī, the progenitor of the best of Victors, who is devoid of qualities, free from conceptual construction, and possesses the characteristics previously described; such is the rule for the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyatāvādin*).

Now, he describes birth at the end of death according to the state of being (*bhāva*), beginning with the words "In the peaceful" (*śānte*) and so forth: "In the peaceful state, O Lord of Men, immortality occurs; in the *tāmasa* state, hellishness; in the *rājasa* state, animality; and in the mixed state on this excellent surface of the earth, humanity.

(1–2) O Vimalaprabhā, there are three kinds of existence (*bhūtatva*)—in *rajas*, in *tamas*, and the *sāttvika*—which are mutually mixed. Whatever state one remembers with the mind at the time of death, there the living being comes into existence. (93)
[The Internal: Here, in this saṃsāra, the existence of the qualities of sentient beings arises through the power of their own karma; he speaks of their arising from that state.

In this regard, at the time of death, by the power of virtuous karma, there occurs a peaceful state consisting of the qualities of a sentient being. When that state has arisen, at the end of death, immortality is attained—O King, this is an address to Sucandra.]
Through the power of the inauspicious, a fierce state arises which is of the nature of the quality of darkness (tamas); when that state of darkness exists, one attains the condition of a hell-being.

Through the power of a middling inauspiciousness, a passionate state (rājasa) arises; when that passionate state exists, one attains the condition of an animal. At the end of death, on this excellent earth, there is the human state, which is mixed; when [karma] is conjoined with both auspicious and inauspicious, the human state occurs.
The earthly realm (*bhūtalama*) is of three kinds—consisting of *rajas*, *tamas*, and *sattva*—which are mutually mixed.
Here, when *sattva* predominates, the *pretas* are superior; when *rajas* predominates, they are middling; and when *tamas* predominates, they are inferior.

As for the *asuras*, however, they are included within the category of the gods. Likewise, among humans, those in whom *sattva* predominates are happy; those in whom *rajas* predominates are miserable; and those in whom *tamas* predominates are always miserable. This applies everywhere, even in [realms] such as heaven.

The ripening of the infinite fruits of karma occurs for sentient beings according to the power of their own karma. Therefore, whatever state a being remembers with the mind at the time of death, birth occurs therein; such is the rule for the arising of existence.

Now, the divisions of gods and so forth are described, beginning with the words "divinity" and so on: divinity has eight divisions in the abode of the excellent gods; humanhood is likewise one; animals are indeed of four types; and in the hellish realm, the state of being a hell-being is likewise one.

Bound by the snares of karma, a living being wanders through these states, moving according to its latent impressions; unless liberated, it does not attain liberation—the state of supreme bliss—even after many hundreds of thousands of births.

In this abode of the best of gods, heaven, divinity arises through eight modes: by means of the cultivation of the totality of earth, the totality of water, the totality of fire, the totality of air, the totality of space, the totality of the moon, the totality of the sun, and the totality of Rāhu—through the power of merit such as generosity and the abandonment of the ten unwholesome actions. Divinity thus arises in eight modes. Human existence is one, yet consists of six elements (*dhātu*). Animals are of four types, like the four oceans; they are of four kinds.

Consisting of the six elements, the state of being a hell-being is likewise one [state] within the hell-realm, produced from the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the six elements and equal to a dream. The state of being an *asura* is included within the gods; the state of being a *preta* is included within the hells due to the experience of suffering.

Within these fourteen places—consisting of eight, four, and one births—the sentient being, whose nature is the *ālayavijñāna*, wanders through the six realms like one moving in a liquid, bound by the nooses of karma. As long as one is not released from the nooses of karma, one does not attain liberation, the state of supreme bliss, even after many hundreds of thousands of births. This is the rule for the distinctions among gods and the other [beings], according to the disposition of sentient beings.

Now, the cause of bondage is stated by the verse beginning with "by the aggregates," etc.: "By the aggregates, elements, and sense-faculties; by the five organs of action together with the subtle elements (tanmātras), the defects of karma, the qualities (guṇas), and the mind; and by intellect, ego, and the rest—[these constitute] the terrible [bondage], [which is] unrighteousness. (Note: *ka. kha.* and *ka. kha.* in the source text appear to be scribal markers for commentary sections.)

Bound by these two types of factors—sentient beings bound to the phenomena of the *ālayavijñāna*—the living being indeed wanders through the course of the fluids in a subtle state. Once that state is abandoned, it proceeds to the imperishable supreme state, where one who was born does not come into existence again. (95)
In this saṃsāra of the six realms of existence, by what means does the living being— whose nature consists of the vital breaths, the substrate consciousness, and mental phenomena— wander while bound?

Bound by the six elements which have become the trunk [of the tree], by the sense organs, by the fears of the three kinds of existence, by the six objects and their subtle counterparts (*tanmātra*), by the five organs of action, along with the defects of action—both auspicious and inauspicious—and together with the qualities, the mind, intellect, ego, and so forth (the word "and so forth" including the vital energy, the root-nature, and primordial matter), the individual soul (*jīva*) indeed wanders in the course of worldly experience in a subtle state; furthermore, through the bliss of non-falling away, this bondage exists in both subtle and gross forms, characterized by the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turyā*).

When this state is abandoned, one proceeds to the imperishable supreme state, having reached which one is no longer born again as a transmigrating being; such is the rule regarding the ignorance of worldly tendencies (*saṃsāra-vāsanā-avidyā*). Now, its opposite, knowledge (*vidyā*), is described by the words "the Veda with its limbs" and so forth: The Veda with its limbs, together with the *Smṛtis*, the *Mata-s*, logic (*tarka*), and established tenets (*siddhānta-yukta*), as well as other scriptures composed in the world by poets such as Vyāsa, Vaiśvānara, and others—this is not [itself] knowledge.

"Vidyā," O Lord of Men, is said by the sages here in this world to be both the inner science (adhyātmavidyā) and the Imperishable (akṣara); it is that wherein the entire three worlds exist and wherein they are again dissolved. 96.

In this world, within the conventional usage of people, that which is knowledge regarding the reality of the ultimate truth is "ignorance" (avidyā) in the primary sense; it is the Veda together with its six limbs—the limbs being Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Chandas, Nirukti, and Jyotiṣa—and the meaning is "together with these.
Furthermore, it is accompanied by the Smṛtis and the Mīmāṃsās; the Smṛtis are those of Manu and others, and it is conjoined with them.

"Reasoning" (*tarka*) refers to the treatises on worldly objects and the sciences of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "Tenets" (*siddhānta*) are those that accomplish worldly attainments, such as the dharmas of conceptual meditations on the *maṇḍala*, the *cakra*, and so forth; the epithet "endowed with these" is used [to describe the scripture]. Furthermore, there are other scriptures composed by poets in the world, such as Vyāsa, Vaiśvānara, and others. By "Vyāsa's poetry," the *Bhārata* is meant; by "Vaiśvānara's poetry," the dharma of meditation (*bhāvanā-dharma*); by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), Vālmīki’s poetry, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, Mārkaṇḍeya’s poetry, the Purāṇic dharmas, and others are included. Knowledge is not something created by these poets.

Then, he asks: "What is knowledge? He says: Knowledge is non-conceptual inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), emptiness endowed with all aspects; furthermore, the syllable (*akṣara*) is also knowledge, which is without objective support (*anālambinī*) and has the nature of bliss free from all substrates (*anāśraya*).

Thus, knowledge consists of cause and fruit, being a single fusion of cause and fruit, like the radiance of fire being a single fusion with burning—so it has been declared here in this world by the sages of the past and present who abide in the Wheel of Dharma.

What is its nature? He says: "In which the entire threefold world [is contained]. Because from that moment of bliss the entire threefold world comes into being at the time of origination, and it dissolves back into it again at the time of death;

that very moment in which the aggregate of phenomena dissolves at the moment of flux is called the imperishable bliss of non-outflow (*anāsrava-sukha*), from which Buddhas arise for the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and in which there is indeed the Great Parinirvāṇa, O King—this is the rule regarding Vidyā.

Now, the power of the practice of former yoga is described by the verse beginning with "The lord of yogis," and so forth: "The lord of yogis who has not attained yoga may, at some point, meet death while his mind is still wavering. Endowed with glory, he is born in the human world into a lineage of eminent sages, united with yoga. O [Saguṇa], through that former practice, he again attains the vast yoga of primordial wisdom (*jñānayoga*). Once knowledge is obtained, he proceeds to the imperishable supreme state, where he is no longer subject to birth. (97) *Vimalaprabhā*, Adhyātma section. *Bho. Yon Tan Dan bCas* (Saguṇa).

If a yogin in this mortal world, while practicing the yoga of knowledge, should meet death before attaining perfection due to a distracted mind, that illustrious one will be reborn in the human world within a preeminent lineage of sages—the family of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. "Yoga" refers to the pure reality and pure mind in which emptiness and compassion are indivisible; one who is joined with that is "yoga-yukta. However, he is not yet perfected in yoga. By means of that previous practice, he recovers [the path], for he has attained the vast yoga of gnosis—meaning it is not limited but possesses all aspects; such is the sense.

When knowledge is fully attained, one proceeds to the imperishable supreme state (*akṣayaparamapada*). The analysis of the compound is: "that supreme state which has no decay" is the imperishable supreme state. To explain what that is, he says: "where there is no further birth, no further arising"—that is the state of all Buddhas, the supreme state. Now, the time for the arising of knowledge for the Buddhists, the Asuras, and the Mlecchas is stated with the words beginning with "knowledge": for the Jinas, at the time of the sun’s day; for the Asuras, at midnight, the end of night, and midday; and for the Vasus (Brahmins), at the time of the moon’s night, during its waning.

In the discernment of perfect knowledge, he is the master of both refined (Sanskrit) and vernacular (Prakrit) speech; likewise, within the abode of the three worlds, he is the source of both peaceful and fierce action, whether human or natural. 98.
Indeed, in this context, there are three types of yogic practice: the Buddhist (*bauddha*), the demonic (*āsura*), and the materialistic (*bhautika*).

Among these, the Buddhist yoga consists of emptiness and compassion; the demonic yoga is characterized by conceptual construction; and the materialistic yoga is of two kinds: eternalist (*śāśvatika*) and nihilist (*uccheda-rūpa*).
Thus, one who delights in the practice of those respective yogas is known as a practitioner of that particular type of yoga.

Among these, the arising of knowledge for Buddhist yogins occurs during the daytime; for demonic (āsura) yogins, it occurs during the night; and for elemental (bhautika) yogins, the arising of knowledge occurs at a time devoid of the four junctions (saṃdhyā). This is the division of time regarding the arising of knowledge for the Victors: at the time of the sun’s day, at midnight, at the end of the night, and at midday for the demons;
and for the elemental ones, since no specific time is mentioned, it occurs at a time devoid of the junctions, at the departure of the moon and night.

At this time, at midnight or during the morning twilight, the empowerment of the knowledge of speech occurs for the Buddhists; for the Asuras, it occurs at midday twilight or at sunset twilight. For the Bhūtas, the empowerment of eternal knowledge occurs during the fourth watch of the day, while the empowerment of nihilistic knowledge occurs during the night portion—these respectively for the Buddhists and the Asuras. Right knowledge arises for the Buddhists, whereas a distorted [knowledge], which is contrary to their doctrine, arises for the Asuras.

How is it known that *samyagjñāna* (perfect knowledge) is like daylight, seeing all things, while *vibhaṅgajñāna* (limited knowledge) is like nightlight, perceiving only some aspects of the birth and death of sentient beings? To this, he says: "By means of the teaching of the Dharma. Here, within *samyagjñāna*, both refined (*saṃskṛta*) and vernacular (*prākṛta*) speech arise;

for those born of *samyagjñāna*, their speech consists of refined language, which embodies all sounds. For those born of *vibhaṅgajñāna*, the speech of the teachers becomes vernacular, according to the specific regional language of each particular location.

The knowledge of the Buddhists is that which teaches peaceful activities and has compassion for all sentient beings as its essence; the knowledge of the Asuras is that which teaches fierce activities for the purpose of eating the flesh of those who harm animals.
(ka. kha. *ātmaviṣaya*;
Bho. *Yul gCig Gi sKad gCig Gi Khyad Par Gyis* [by way of a difference in language within a single place and a single time]).
In the abode of the three worlds, he teaches the *pauruṣa* (human) karma and the knowledge of the Buddhists; on earth, he teaches the *prākṛta* (natural) karma and the knowledge of the Asuras;
and on earth, he teaches the mixed karma of the Bhūtas—such is the rule for the teaching of knowledge.

Now, the time of the meal for the Buddhists and Asuras is stated, beginning with "from midday": from midday until midnight, during the periods of day and night, is the time of their meal; their food is beef, and their drink is the semen of the *maṇḍa*, which provides many kinds of flavors.

Red and white garments, like the movements of the sun and the moon; dwelling in heaven and the netherworld; righteousness and non-violence, yet violence through the power of strict observances; and the vajra-throne of the Daityas. ||99||
In this context, from midday until midnight is the period of day;
from midnight until midday is the period of night.

Within that time of day and night, the period of eating for each respective [group] is the latter half of their own specific time. This is the rule: for ascetics, not for householders, among these two—the Buddhists and the Mlecchas—respectively.
Furthermore, regarding the food and drink of the Buddhists and the Asuras, they are as follows respectively:
the food of the Buddhists is more excellent, while that of the Mlecchas is accompanied by beef;
their drinks are respectively sweet, providing many kinds of flavors for the Buddhists, and the drinking of semen from the eggs of chickens and other such creatures for the Mlecchas.
The clothing is according to their respective numbers: red garments for the Buddhists, and white for the *mleccha* ascetics; for householders there is no fixed rule.

Likewise, at the end of life, their abodes are according to their respective numbers, like the movements of the sun and the moon: the movement of the sun is upward, and the movement of the moon is downward. Like their movements, the residence in heaven is the solar course for the Buddhists, while the residence in the netherworld (*pātāla*) is the lunar course for the asuras. As the Blessed One said in the *Sekoddeśa* of the Root Tantra: "At death, the nectar of the moon goes downward for all embodied beings."
Above are the sun, the dust, Rāhu, and consciousness, according to their characteristic states.
Likewise, the dharma is according to their respective numbers:

the dharma of the Buddhists is non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), while that of the Mlecchas is violence (*hiṃsā*). By the word "and" (*ca*), it is meant that for living beings, during the time of meditation and the time of praising the chosen deity, due to the power of strict observances, the *vajrāsana* is recommended for the Buddhists and the *daityāsana* is recommended for the Mlecchas. By the word "and," another [posture] is common to both; thus, there is neither a rule nor a prohibition regarding it.

In this regard, regarding the Daityas on the surface of the earth: the left knee is extended; the right foot is above the left knee; the extension of the right knee is above the left foot; and by the word "ca" (and), the right foot is below. The right foot is above, and by the word "ca," even on the sole of the foot, [the body] is seated upon the hips at the back—this is to be stated as in the forthcoming description of the *vajrāsana* and other postures. This is the rule for the ritual actions (*kriyā*) of the Buddhist Asuras. For the spirits (*bhūtas*), mixed rites prevail; their speech is mixed *paiśācika*; and while their dharma is non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), there is indeed violence due to the faults of killing living beings arising from the heavy observances of their gurus.
O Lord of Men, there occurs engagement in activities such as sacrifice, or sometimes withdrawal; and food and drink are mixed, for the path is mixed due to the movement of the Sun and Moon elsewhere.
Furthermore, regarding the elements (*bhūta*), the previously mentioned mixed activity has not been clearly explained here in this verse.

It is as follows: the activity of the elements is mixed, and their speech is the mixed Paiśācika; the Dharma is non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), whereas violence (*hiṃsā*) is indeed a heavy fault arising from the destruction of life and so forth due to a lack of restraint.

"Engagement for the sake of yoga" (meaning for the sake of sacrifice and so forth)—by the word "and so forth," engagement in violence for the sake of battle is included—whereas cessation for the sake of the fruit becomes non-violence, O Lord of Men, or sometimes there is cessation [of even that].

Because of the movement of the Sun and Moon, food to be chewed and food to be drunk are mixed; thus, in the "mixed path" hereafter, every [action] of living beings is to be understood as occurring on the mixed path. This is the rule for the activity of living beings.

Now, desiring to explain the path, he says "Jyotiḥ" and so forth: Light (*jyotis*) is the sun’s path; the northern course (*ayana*) is the day, and the southern is half a year. The moon is light; night is its dark course. This [light] exists in the path of smoke (*dhūmamārga*):

in the celestial realm (*svarga*), it belongs to the gods; in the world of the serpents (*nāgaloka*), it belongs to the asuras; in the mortal world, O King, it is mixed for the sake of ghosts, animals, and humans. || 101 ||
In this context, indeed, there are three paths: the path of light (*jyotirmārga*), the path of smoke (*dhūmamārga*), and the mixed path (*vimiśramārga*).

Among these, "Acirā" refers to light—the sun, the bright fortnight, the northern course, and the characteristic increase of the day—lasting half a year externally; internally, it consists of the six zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn, designated as "rising and setting."

The path of smoke (*dhūmamārga*), light, the moon, and night constitute this dark course (*asitamayana*) in the south. On the southern path of smoke, beginning with Cancer (*karkaṭa*), there is the six-month southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*); that in which the night increases is the southern course. The rule extends from sunset until sunrise. Here, the path of light (*arciḥ*) is for the gods to travel to heaven, while the dark course—the path of smoke—is for the asuras to go to the world of the nāgas.

The rule of the path is thus revealed: the mixed nature of day and night phenomena for the purpose of going to the mortal world and for the birth of *pretas*, animals, and humans, arises through the inherent nature of the qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* produced by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of previous births. Now, the grasping of the latencies of sentient beings—those devoted to the activities of Śrāvakas, Buddhists, Asuras, and spirits—is described by the words "whichever among them," and so forth: "Whichever [group] he has entered, being devoted to its vows and observances, bound by the snares of karma—he becomes, O Lord of Men, of that very nature within that [group], through the influence of that [group]."

O King, as long as there is the state of mind under the influence of the threefold existence, so long will there be the experience of pleasure and pain; thus, one wanders here in the terrible cycle of saṃsāra—among gods, mortals, and below. 102.

In this saṃsāra, by the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma, one who is devoted to the activities of gods, asuras, or spirits enters into whichever [category] they may be; being intent on vows and observances, they are bound by the fetters of karma. They are bound by the ritual actions (*kriyā*) of that particular dharma, and within that, they exist according to their own respective natures. "O Lord of Men" is the address; "in that family" refers to the family of gods, asuras, or spirits.
"By the grasping of that" means by the grasping of its state;

by that [grasping], one is born into the families of gods, asuras, or spirits, through the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, according to the previously mentioned method—that is, as long as the state of the mind exists due to the power of the threefold existence.
