In this context, for the mind within *saṃsāra*, due to the power of the threefold existence—that is, by the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the existences of desire, form, and formlessness—there is worldly sensation consisting of pleasure and pain. To that extent, O King, there is the wandering of the mind characterized by suffering throughout *saṃsāra* among the heavens and the mortal world; and furthermore, there is the wandering of the *ālayavijñāna* through the six realms below, such as the gods, humans, and hells. This is the rule regarding the grasping of latent impressions.

Therefore, he who has transcended the threefold latent impressions (*vāsanā*) stands at the far shore of cyclic existence, established in the state where all that is to be done has been accomplished. He is the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*), whose lotus feet have been worshipped by gods, asuras, nāgas, and others; he is Kālacakra. This is the rule for the removal of latent impressions.

Now, just as the production of consonants and vowels occurred in the womb, so too the characteristics of death are described with the words beginning "the classes starting with *ka*," etc.: "The classes starting with *ka*, together with their measures (*mātrā*), multiplied by the qualities (*guṇa*), and the thirty consonants along with the vowels of the three fortnights—death ascends through these by the power of the three types of movement."

The movements of the five planets, the course of the sun and moon, and the positions of Rāhu and Ketu, as well as thirty-two years and fortnights multiplied by three, divided by the moon, the sun, and fire (three). || 103 ||

Here, at the time of conception, the female element (*rajas*) consists of the thirty consonants and the male element (*śukra*) consists of the thirty vowels; their union is presided over by the *ālayavijñāna*.

In this production of the embryo, during the first fortnight, the thirty consonants beginning with *ka* are presided over by short vowels, while in the other fortnight they are presided over by long vowels; thus, these two groups of consonants become manifest at death.

In this way, there is the entry of the semen (*śukra*) into the space element (*ākāśadhātu*); during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), there is the entry of the menstrual flow (*rajas*) into the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), and during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), likewise, whether the menstrual flow has arisen or not, there is the entry of the earth and space elements into the seminal element. Thus, in the first fortnight of the second month, the consonants presided over by the vowel *i* enter the wind element (*vāyudhātu*) in the menstrual flow, while in the latter fortnight, those presided over by the vowel *ū* enter the water element (*udakadhātu*).

In the first fortnight of the third month, those presided over by the vowel *ṛ* are for the entry into the fire element (*tejodhātu*); in the second fortnight, those presided over by *ṛ* are likewise for the entry into the fire element. In the first fortnight of the fourth month, those presided over by the vowel *u* are for the entry into the water element (*udakadhātu*); in the second fortnight, those presided over by *ī* are for the entry into the wind element (*vāyudhātu*).

In the first fortnight of the fifth month, those presided over by the vowel *lṛ* are for the entry into the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*); in the second fortnight, those presided over by the long vowel *ā* are for the entry into the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).

Through the distinction between creation and dissolution, there is the entry of ether and the rest, as well as earth and the rest, into one another within the semen and the menstrual blood; for the purpose of providing a substratum for the sense organs and the organs of action, the vowels *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and *hādi* (short and long) enter into the consonants.

In the first half of the sixth month: *a*; in the second half of the first half: *ha*; in the first half of the second half: *āla*; in the second half of the second half: *lā*. For the seventh month: likewise, *e*, *ya*, *o*, *vā*. For the eighth month: *ara*, *ra*, *ār*, *rā*. For the ninth month: *o*, *vā*, *ai*, *yā*. For the tenth month: *ala*, *ra*, *la*, *ā*, *hā*, *lā*. Thus, through the thirty consonants over ten months, there is the completion of the aggregates (*skandhas*), elements (*dhātus*), sense-bases (*āyatanas*), and so forth; this occurs from the time after the months of gestation, following the union of semen and blood, as the radiation of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases proceeds according to the sequence of emanation and withdrawal.
Thus, in the eleventh month, they are presided over by the *bindu*, and in the twelfth month, they become presided over by the *visarga*.

Therefore, this is the determination of the production of the lunar element (*candradhātu*), the seminal element (*śukradhātu*), the channels (*nāḍī*), the marrow (*majjā*), and the bones (*asthi*). The Sun (*arka*) increases the *rajas* of the Wisdom (*prajñā*) for twelve years, and that of the Means (*upāya*) for sixteen years. [Then follows] the Great Chapter on the Rule of the Kālacakra regarding the Characteristics of Moments, from the Vimalaprabhā, concerning the internal maturation of the elements.

The maturation of the *rajas* element occurs through wisdom (*prajñā*), and the maturation of the *śukra* element occurs through means (*upāya*). Thereafter, for another twelve years of wisdom and sixteen years of means, there is the maturation of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).
From this limit, the sattva portion becomes middling.

For another eighteen years of wisdom, there is the maturation of the water element (*toyadhātu*); and for means, as before, for sixteen years plus one month and twenty-two and a half days, there is the maturation of the water element.

As before, there is the fire-maturation of wisdom (*prajñā*), and likewise, as before, the air-element maturation (*vāyudhātupāka*) and the space-element maturation (*ākāśadhātupāka*). At ninety-six years and ten and a half months, the maturation of all the elements occurs through the divisions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Thereafter, time (*kāla*) sprouts within the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) by means of the measure of years, fortnights, days, and the thirty consonants; specifically, by a count of one thousand one hundred and fifty-five days.

One ascends through the classes beginning with *ka*, which have been previously mentioned as being multiplied by their qualities (*guṇa*) to become one thousand eighty days; likewise, one ascends through the vowels of the three fortnights—short, long, and protracted—and the forty-five consonants, according to the threefold movement, that is, by way of the left, right, and middle paths. These are the movements of the five planets, Mars and the rest, numbering one thousand one hundred thirty-four, as previously stated. Thus, death occurs when these movements cease.

The portion for the Sun and Moon consists of thirty-six months; that for Mars consists of twenty-four months; that for Mercury consists of eleven months; the portion for Rāhu and Ketu consists of seven and a half months; and the portion for the rising of Ketu consists of two *ghaṭikās* per day.
These portions, measured in *ghaṭikās*, correspond to a total number of three years, three fortnights, and thirty consonant-days (365 days). Death ascends through these very [portions].

Thus, there are also thirty-two years and fortnights, multiplied by the qualities (*guṇas*), distinguished by the Moon, Sun, and Fire, and distinguished by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Furthermore, at ninety-six years, there are another ten and a half months and fortnights.

The fortnights for the three [planets] are thirty; the qualities of the moon are thirty-six; and the time, fire, and two sides (sixteen) are the fortnights for the sun. When these are subtracted from one hundred years, the remaining fortnights of the sun and moon follow even and odd courses.
The days and nights amount to sixty-three; all the groups, minus their lords, and the morae, according to the movement of the sun and moon, result in death starting from the consonants. || 104 ||

Among the fortnights of the hundred-year period consisting of the left and right channels, there are seventy-two fortnights for three years; likewise, the qualities of the Moon are three fortnights, and those of the Fire of Time are two fortnights. Thus, seventy-seven fortnights are subtracted from the century—the heap of fortnights in a hundred years numbering twenty-four hundred; the remaining fortnights on the right and left of the Sun and the Moon number two thousand three hundred and twenty-three (2323), according to the count of "eyes of the world" and "eyes of fire."

Thus, death devours all the days and nights devoid of their lords—thirty-six thousand such units within a hundred years; or [units] devoid of three years, three fortnights, consonants, months, and days, which death devours on the left and the right.

Death swallows the groups (*varga*) and measures (*mātrā*) of the sun and moon according to the movement of the [breath], as well as the consonants and so forth. Starting from the *ariṣṭa* [signs], it devours them during the intermediate time;

indeed, it devours those half-cakra channels, excluding the lunar steps and devoid of the weekday channels, along with the divisions of wisdom and method, by means of the times of day and night. And death devours them.

Thus, one should recite the groups [of consonants] with their respective measures, accompanied by the sets of vowels; likewise, the consonants themselves should be repeated according to the number of days, whether in the deficient, the middling, or the desired [period], when the moon and sun have died out, and when the consonant is the presiding deity. (105)
In the Tibetan manuscript, prior to the word "of wisdom" (*prajñāyāḥ*), there is the phrase "as before" (*pūrvavat*);
thereafter, Ka has *dhārā*, Ga has *vārā*, and Bo has *rkam pa* (*pada*).
[In the manuscript, the word "apakṣā" does not appear in this chapter. This is the Great Chapter on the Rules of the Kālacakra regarding the Characteristics of Moments (*kṣaṇa*).

Thus, the channels of the wheel (*cakranāḍī*) are indeed one and a half wheels; the number of the eighteen zodiac signs (*rāśi*), multiplied by one hundred and twenty-five, results in the number of *ghaṭikās* being two thousand four hundred and thirty.

The lunar steps (*śaśipada*) consist of one hundred divisions, including those with and without sequence, such as the Vedas and so forth; those devoid of them are the seven "lunar-step-free" channels (*vāranāḍī*). Devoid even of these, they total three thousand two hundred and twenty-three in number. Death observes them through the various distinctions of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), and through the divisions of withdrawal and emanation, during the times of day and night.

In this way, the groups [of consonants], together with their measures and accompanied by the collection of vowels, are repeated as many times as there are consonants. In the case of a "low" (hīna) death due to the lunar affliction (*ariṣṭa*), or a "middle" (madhyama) death due to the solar affliction, it is said: "in the consonant and its presiding deity. Thus, in the case of a low death from the lunar affliction, a middle death from the solar affliction, or a death from the consonant and its presiding deity—a middle death—the previously stated rule applies: when the thirty-two red [units] have passed during the movement of the moon and sun, this is the cutting of the channels (*nāḍikā*). Furthermore, after thirty-six nights, one abandons the aggregates, elements, sense faculties, and so forth, along with the vajra.
Having abandoned the lunar and solar channels, the vital breath enters the Śaṅkhinī for one day, until there is a cessation of the elements of earth, water, fire, air, and space. 106.

Then, for thirty-three days—counting the thirty-two days [previously mentioned] plus the day when it is red—the moon and sun move together; that is, while moving to the left, they proceed through the channels (*nāḍī*) in the rightward direction. This is the common [sign] regarding the fatal portents of the moon and sun. Furthermore, at the time of death, after another three hundred and three nights—that is, thirty-three days—they abandon the defiled aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense faculties (*indriya*), and so forth, along with body, speech, and mind.

Then, having abandoned the channel of the moon and sun—the tongue of the woman—he enters the conch-like *avadhūtī*. As long as there is no severance of the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), on this day of death, the vital breath having entered the central channel and being overcome by the wind of time, he abandons the earth element at the navel, which possesses the nature of five qualities; thereafter, the severance of the earth element occurs.

In the heart, one abandons the water element, which has the nature of four qualities, and thus there is the cessation of the water element; in the throat, one abandons the fire element, which has the nature of three qualities, and thus there is the cessation of the fire element; in the forehead, one abandons the wind element, which has the nature of two qualities, and thus there is the cessation of the wind element;
at the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), one abandons the space element, which has the nature of one quality, and thus there is the cessation of the space element.
The abandonment of the vital element (prāṇadhātu) occurs above and below the navel: one abandons the apāna, which has the nature of the bindu, and thereby the state of waking is destroyed;
at the secret place, one abandons the vāgbindu, and thereby the state of dreaming is severed.
In the jewel, he abandons the mind-drop (*cittabindu*); from that, the severance of the state of deep sleep occurs.
Likewise, above [in the throat], he abandons the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) along with the drops of the passion-element (*rajo-dhātu*); from that, indeed, the severance of body, speech, and mind occurs.
At the time of transition, he abandons the sixth element, the gnosis-element (*jñāna-dhātu*).
The semen is emitted from all parts of the body downward, and the menstrual blood (rajas) is emitted upward; thus occurs the severance of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*).
Such is the rule for the time of death for those born from a womb.

This concludes the fifth great chapter, "The Rule of Kālacakra Concerning the Characteristics of Moments as the Cause of Arising and Cessation in Worldly Convention," in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakratantrarāja* following the *Śrīmūlatantra*. ||5||
The phrase "kramoktam" does not exist in the manuscript;
[it should be] "dharmamayānam."

In the *Vimalaprabhā* commentary on the *Mūlatantra*, this is the Great Chapter on Alchemy and the Science of Child-Rearing (*Rasāyanādibālatantra*). [Regarding] the inner [science]: At the outset, for the sake of attaining accomplishment (*siddhi*), the mantra-practitioner must protect the body, which is the embodiment of all the Victors. In the absence of the body, there is no accomplishment, nor is the supreme bliss attained in this life.

Therefore, for the sake of the body, one should daily practice the yoga of the channels (*nāḍīyoga*). When the body is perfected, other accomplishments within the abode of the three worlds come under one's command. (107)

In this very saṃsāra, the prāṇa and apāna of sentient beings exit the body by way of the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra) and enter it by way of the process of emanation (sṛṣṭi). Just so, the Blessed One stated in the *Sekoddeśa* within the *Mūlatantra*: "In the lotus of the navel, the heart, the throat, the forehead, and the crown of the head—earth, water, fire, wind, and space flow out by way of withdrawal;
entering, she enters the earth by way of emanation."
Likewise, the apāna power, flowing through the body, speech, and mind at the navel and the secret lotus, emerges and enters; it is of the nature of withdrawal and emanation.

For this reason, at the outset, the body of all the Victors—the body consisting of the five aggregates and so forth—must be protected by the practitioner for the sake of accomplishment. In the absence of the body, there is no accomplishment, nor is the supreme bliss, the untainted bliss, attained in this life. Therefore, for the sake of the body, "for the sake of the body" means for the sake of the *bodhicitta*; for the sake of protecting it, one should daily practice the yoga of the channels (*nāḍī*). Through the union of *lalanā* and *rasanā*, one should practice the yoga of the channels in the *madhyamā*, [controlling] the *prāṇa* wind; and the *apāna* [wind] in the *śaṅkhinī*, which is the yoga of the channels of feces and urine.
At the time of day and night, in the twelfth *lagna*, one should meditate here upon the union of the channels (*nāḍī-yoga*).

By means of this meditation, the perfection of the body is attained; when the body is perfected, other mundane perfections come under its service. This is the rule for the accomplishment of mundane perfections. Now, the path for the accomplishment of supramundane perfections is described, beginning with the word "void" (*śūnya*): "In the void, one should meditate on the path of smoke and so forth, up to the limit of the universe, within the wheels of channels (*nāḍī-cakra*) by the power of the guru’s instructions; from that, one makes both the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds stable."
Thereafter, like a planet eclipsing the moon, the yogi effects the cessation of the bodhicitta; therefore, whatever is desired here in this life is obtained within a few days. 108.

Here, in the void, by means of the path beginning with smoke and so forth, according to the constraint of the Guru and the sequence to be described, the yogi should meditate upon the universe of Viśvasoma; he should stabilize the mind—which is the entire universe in all its forms—up to that limit within the circles of the channels (*nāḍīcakra*). From that point, the yogi also makes the *prāṇa* and the *apāna* wind steady within the navel circle (*nābhicakra*).
"Subsequently, O Moon, [he] effects the cessation," means like a planet, like Rāhu;
O Noble One, the yogi effects the cessation of the *bodhicitta*. This is from the "Great Chapter on Alchemy and the Tantra of Childlike Conduct."

Yoga is the mutual union of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths; one who possesses this is a *yogī*. Because he brings about the cessation of the moment of emission of the *bodhicitta*, making it the immutable (*akṣara*) state consisting of the outflow (*niṣyanda*) and so forth, whatever is desired—whether that desired outflow, its maturation (*vipāka*), its human effort (*puruṣakāra*), or its purity (*vaimalya*), or even that which is inexpressible—is attained within a few days in this very life.

"Several days" refers to the three years and three fortnights of the *Kālacakra*; by these, the "attainment of Mahāmudrā" is reached through these aggregates purified by the liberations such as emptiness (*śūnya*)—this is the rule for the path of the means of attaining Mahāmudrā. Now, the deception of untimely death is described starting with the words "Mārttaṇḍa" and so forth: "The cessation of the Sun and Moon, their entry into the central Fire during their even and uneven courses, and the [cessation] of both Prāṇa and Apāna on the first day—[this is] the deception of the time of death."

Having filled [the body] with the vital breath (prāṇa) along with the hands and feet, up to the joints of the fingers and the tips of the nails, the Buddhas and their goddesses, holding lotuses in their fearless hands, are to be meditated upon by the yogi within the six cakras. || 109 ||

In this context, when the yogi perceives the signs of untimely death, then there is the cessation of the sun and moon—the cessation of the right and left channels during their even and uneven movements. During the processes of withdrawal and emanation, one must effect the entry into the central fire, which is Rāhu and the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), within the middle channel.
When both prāṇa and apāna have entered the flow of the middle channel for the first time on that day, that constitutes the "deception" of untimely death for yogis.

Having filled [the body] with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) that flows through the five maṇḍalas, together with the yoga of the central channel (*madhyamā*), and having filled the fingers, toes, joints, and nails with the hands and feet, the Buddhas and their Consorts—with lotus hands in the gesture of fearlessness—should be meditated upon by the yogi in the six wheels beginning with the *uṣṇīṣa*, according to the sequence to be described; this is the rule for deceiving untimely death. Now, the pacification of wind-diseases and so forth is explained, beginning with the words "by the downward breath" (*apāna*): "In the case of all wind-diseases in the excellent body, the contraction of the downward breath (*apāna*) is desired; in the case of phlegm (*kapha*), there should be breath control (*prāṇāyāma*); and furthermore, in the case of the disorder of bile (*pitta*), there should be the releasing of both."

The complete suppression [of the breath] from above and below brings about happiness; in cases of fever caused by the derangement of the humors (sannipāta), the prāṇa-vāyu located above the navel removes all diseases, while that situated at the root of the navel does the same for others.

In this body, there are eighty previously mentioned channels that cause the disorder of wind (*vāta*); for the sake of balancing their constituent elements (*dhātu*), the contraction of the downward breath (*apāna*) is desired and brings happiness to practitioners of mantra when all wind-related diseases, such as colic and the like, afflict the fair-bodied woman.
Likewise, on the forehead and the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), there are twenty channels that cause the disorder of phlegm (*śleṣman*);
for the sake of balancing their constituent elements, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is desired.

"In phlegm" means that when a phlegmatic disease has arisen, the practitioner of yoga (yogin) should perform the retention of the breath (prāṇanirodha); furthermore, "and the releasing of those two in the case of the bile-humor (pitta-doṣa)" means that when a bile-humor disease has arisen, having released those two— the prāṇa and apāna— outwardly, one should take in the external air with a hissing sound (śītkāra) according to the method to be described, place the tongue against the uvula (lambikā), and perform the drinking of nectar (amṛtapāna), such as [the practice of] *stūka* and so forth, in all cases of bile-disease.
It is not in the book.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it says: "In the throat and the heart, there are forty channels (*nāḍī*) that cause the disorder of bile (*pitta*).
This yoga should be performed for the purpose of bringing equilibrium to their constituent elements (*dhātu*)."
The simultaneous restraint of the upward and downward [breaths] brings about relief in cases of fever caused by the derangement of the three humors (*sannipāta*).

Here, in the secret place, there are ten channels that cause the *sannipāta*; for the purpose of restoring equilibrium to the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), the restraint of both the upward-moving *prāṇa* and the downward-moving *apāna* breaths is desired, and this is likewise desired in the case of fever.
For what reason?

Since the *prāṇa* wind does not flow above the navel, therefore the *apāna* flows at the root of the navel as the remover of all diseases; and below the navel, another [wind] flows as the remover of all diseases—this is the rule for the pacification of diseases such as those of the wind (*vāta*).

Now, teaching the remedy for the pacification of abdominal diseases, he says with the words beginning "by contracting" (*ākuñcya*): "By contracting the *apāna* wind and the *prāṇa* itself which has gone upon the three paths, [one should hold them] upward until the fire becomes powerful, pervading the entire body."
When taken for a month, it destroys splenic enlargement, diseases located in the abdomen, upward breathlessness, cough, the three types of poison, eye diseases, and so forth. (111)

When waking and other states occur here in the belly, then one should contract the apāna wind located in the three paths—namely, the paths of feces, urine, and semen—and likewise contract the prāṇa itself as it moves upward through the paths of the moon, sun, and fire. Through their friction, the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni) becomes powerful and pervades the entire body.

This Agnijārī destroys diseases such as splenic disorders and dropsy through its use for one month; it also cures upward breath (ūrdhva-śvāsa), cough, and all three types of poison—stationary, mobile, and artificial—as well as eye diseases and headaches. This is the rule for the pacification of abdominal diseases.

When the left channel does not suddenly flow due to the forceful compression of the breast on both the left and right sides, and the right armpit [channel] likewise ceases, a yogi disciplined in yoga removes the ill omen that brings death within half a month. Furthermore, by placing the feet in the vajra posture with the hands held like lotuses, one destroys back pain.

Now, the method for binding the channels (*nāḍībandha*) in order to deceive death (*ariṣṭa*) is described, beginning with the words "from the armpit" (*kakṣāt*) and so forth: here, when a yogi is able to cause the breath (*prāṇa*) to enter the central channel (*madhyamā*) for a full day and night, then he causes the movement of the breath to shift from the left to the right in the event of a left-side omen of death, and shifts it to the left in the event of a right-side omen, for half a month or up to one full month.
By this aforementioned means, the breast on the left or right side is also forcefully pressed from the armpit due to the restraint of the breath.

When the right breast is pressed, the left channel does not flow; when the left armpit is pressed, the right channel does not flow. Thus, even by [this method], a yogi who is disciplined in yoga removes the ill omen (*ariṣṭa*) that brings death within half a month. "Yoga" is the unification of inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*), which is retention (*kumbhaka*); one who is joined with that is "disciplined in yoga. "He removes" means he takes away; this is the rule for deceiving untimely death. Not too high; Ga. reads *nāstyūrdhvam*.
O, above the navel (*nābhyūrdhva*), the upward-moving breath (*prāṇa*) should be drawn up and contracted.

[In this] chapter, the method for destroying back pain is now explained: "The feet are in the *vajrāsana* position. This means that the left foot is placed upon the right thigh and the right foot upon the left thigh; those two feet, bound by the *vajra-bandha* with the arms positioned behind the back—the right foot held by the left hand and the left foot by the right—those two feet, like lotus-hands, bring about the destruction of back pain.

By pressing the feet upward and the head downward, one removes all phlegm-related diseases from the body; by restraining the breath, one destroys urinary disorders (mūtrakṛcchra) within a few days through urination.

At dawn, having rubbed the rows of teeth with the two ring fingers while the mouth is free of water, there should be collyrium for the eyes, which removes eye ailments, or else splashing them with water. || 113 ||

By restraining the breath (*prāṇarodha*), *ūdhava* removes all phlegm diseases from the body, including the feet and head; thus, through the practice of mantra for a few days, it destroys everything entirely. At dawn, when the mouth is free of water and the teeth have not been washed, one should rub the rows of teeth with *pragharṣaṇa*; this becomes an ointment for the eyes that removes eye ailments.

At dawn, striking the eyes with water removes their pain. Holding a lotus bud in the hand while sleeping destroys the colic of indigestion. When boils (gaṇḍas) arise, fomentation with salt and ghee indeed destroys their growth. An application of the milk of the *arka* plant may sometimes [cure] tooth-worms; likewise, the smoke of *vyāghrī* seeds held by means of a tube and the like destroys worms and other such pests. || 114 ||
When one is asleep, that which is held in the left nostril at the navel is called *dhṛtakarakamalā*; when combined with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), it destroys the pain of indigestion.

Regarding "the emergence of swellings" (*gaṇḍānāmudbhava*): at the time of the appearance of swellings, pustules, and the like, applying salt and ghee wrapped in cloth and applying heat destroys their growth. Furthermore, the rule regarding "the application of milk" is for the emergence of swellings and so forth; if at any time a tooth becomes painful due to a worm (*koṭa*), then the smoke of *vyāghrī* seeds applied via a tube or similar device destroys the worm.
"Vyāghrī" and "Kaṇṭhakārī" constitute the rule for the pacification of common diseases.

Now, the remedial procedure for the pacification of the disease of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) is stated, beginning with the word "varṣa": "In half a year, it removes white leprosy from the beautiful bodies of practitioners; what else could it not do? When wisdom is well-established through the constant restraint of the vital winds (*prāṇavāyu*), even a seventy-year-old person with grey hair becomes [rejuvenated] upon the completion of two years. Beyond that, the perfection of the *mudrā* occurs within a few days due to the application of the mind toward the path. (115)

This is Mahāyoga, which is accomplished through the preliminary signs such as smoke and so forth by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); it is the moment of imperishable bliss. Having caused the *bodhicitta* to flow [down] through union with a consort (*mudrā*), that very *bodhicitta*, having flowed down through the yoga of the consort, reaches the mouth due to the cessation of the birth-places of *prāṇa* and *apāna*. Within half a year, it removes white leprosy from the excellent bodies of practitioners; what else could it be?

If it does not remove leprosy, then the yogi should employ a sixteen-year-old consort (*mudrā*), consuming meat and drinking liquor daily. Within six months, his *bodhicitta*—having slipped during sexual union (*yonimanthana*)—is retained through the yoga of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), and this removes the disease of leprosy; there is no doubt in this regarding the word of the Tathāgata. Not only does it remove leprosy, but it also removes the seventy-year-old aging accompanied by graying hair, provided that the *bodhicitta* slips during union with the consort when two years have been completed.

By this very yoga, for the yogi, within a few days—specifically after the three years and three fortnights of the Kālacakra—the perfection of the mudrā occurs, following the destruction of old age; this is due to the application of the path-consciousness. This is the rule for the pacification of leprosy. The sound which exists in the region of the heart of excellent men is heard through the openings of the ears; from there it indeed goes upward to the *muṣṭi* (the crown of the head), having been made into a single element and abandoned as equal flavor (*samarasa*).

O Lord, whatever sound exists in the world of living beings, whether produced by strength or otherwise, that the yogin hears from afar; O All-pervading One, this higher knowledge of distant hearing is indeed to be cultivated by the yogin. (116)

Having assumed the cross-legged posture (paryaṅkabandha), with an open face, one should touch the opposing teeth; the external wind, drawn in and equal to the essence of nectar, enters the navel-cakra.
Restrained within the body of the beautiful woman, it removes heat, hunger, and thirst, as well as poison; or else, the white drop on the forehead, surrounded by a circle of light, releases nectar.

When the two nostrils are closed by the mouth, the entire external air is drawn in with force by the *prāṇa*; the *apāna* wind, struck [by it] like lightning-fire, reaches the navel at the proper time through yoga and attains a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) in the midst of the moon, sun, and fire. It removes hunger and thirst from the excellent body and bestows immortality.

Up to this point, the commentary on six verses is not found in the Tibetan translation; furthermore, the Vimalaprabhā commentary upon them is not found in either the Sanskrit manuscripts or the Tibetan translations.

Nevertheless, regarding this matter, neither Ācārya Khedrup Jé nor his predecessors—such as Butön, Mipham Rinpoche, and other masters—raised any doubt in their respective commentaries; therefore, they maintained a silence on the subject.
I consider the reason for this to be the non-availability of such Sanskrit manuscripts in Tibet where these six verses might be located.
Regarding this matter, even among those Sanskrit manuscripts that have been obtained, there is a twofold situation: in some cases all six verses are found, while in others they are not.

Just as the six verses are seen to be extant in the manuscript that served as the basis for the present edition, other two or three manuscripts of the same kind exist in the collection of ancient manuscripts preserved by Dr. Lokesh Chandra.

However, these verses are not found in the ancient manuscript written by Vibhūticandra and preserved at the Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute in Patna, Bihar; there may be other such manuscripts as well.
Under these circumstances, it is likely that the Tibetan scholars did not produce a Tibetan translation precisely because the text was unavailable.
[Chapter]
The Great Chapter on Alchemy and the Science of Child-Rearing:

Having observed one’s own reflection in the sunlight with a steady gaze while facing away from the sun, and then looking toward the sky, the smoke-colored *samarasa-puruṣa* (the person of equal flavor) is seen through six months of yogic practice; he reveals hidden treasures and the openings in the earth. Likewise, having entered the shadow of a tree, the garland of drops (*bindumālā*) is meditated upon within the expanse of the sky.

That power which proceeds from the center of the navel to the supreme station—the end of the digits (kalā) and the end of the twelve—is firmly restrained at the navel; measured by that [distance], it rises in the form of a staff, moving with a soft and graceful gait from one wheel to another within the central channel, until, by means of forceful practice, it touches the aperture of the crown of the head like a needle fixed there.

At that time, by means of supreme persistence, one should force the two downward-voiding winds (*apāna*) upward along the path; having pierced the *uṣṇīṣa*, they proceed to the city [of the crown] once the pair of winds is restrained.

Thus, through the awakening of the vajra within the body and the mind, he attains the state of a sky-walker (*khecara*); possessing the nature of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), she becomes the Mother of the Universe (*viśvamātā*) for yogins. 121.

Now the rule for breath control (prāṇāyāma) is stated: One should perform breath control in the heart and likewise in the head until heat arises; for beyond that, one enters into a swoon. If unrestrained or by force, having pierced the crown-lock (uṣṇīṣa), it departs to the supreme city, leaving behind the aggregates and elements. Having perished through the union with the mudrā, it does not indeed bestow the fruit of bliss upon men in this very birth. || 122 ||

In this body, the practitioner of mantra should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the retention of breath (kumbhaka) at the heart and likewise at the head. As long as there is pain from the fire, so long is the heart burned and pain occurs in the head; the rule is that one should not perform it beyond that point. If one does so, then above that, O fair-limbed one, the vital breath (prāṇa) falls into a swoon within the navel-lotus.

For if one goes forth by force, uncontrolled, having broken through the *uṣṇīṣa*, death indeed occurs as one leaves behind the aggregates (*skandhas*) and elements (*dhātus*); therefore, breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) that has perished through union with a consort does not grant the fruit of happiness to men in this very life—such is the rule for breath-control.

The consort is taught for the sake of meditation, at the time of day and night, neither for the sake of destroying passion nor for the sake of satiating the speech-vajra; indeed, it is said that for practitioners, it does not produce intoxication. Thus [it is stated].

Therefore, this point requires further investigation: why, despite the presence of six verses in the Sanskrit manuscripts, their commentary is not found there? Regarding this matter, various hypotheses may arise;
all these facts should be examined in the introduction, so we shall desist here.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated that all food is for the sake of comfort at every daily occasion, and not because of indigestion; nor is it mentioned in the *Śrīcaryāsiddhi* that even a single morsel should be used for the purpose of "nailing" the mind, nor at night. (123)

Now, the rule for the enjoyment of the consort (*mudrā*), food, and conduct for yogins is stated. Regarding the *mudrā*: here, the Blessed One has taught the *mudrā* as the "yoga-mudrā" for the purpose of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), not for the sake of the exhaustion of passion. During the time of day and night, one engages in play with a woman; likewise, there is a slight drinking of wine for the purpose of refreshing the mouth, not like from a flask or similar vessel, for intoxication does not grant liberation to the lords of yogins. Likewise, the taking of food here consists of all types of food for the sake of pleasure; whatever taking of food there is, all of that serves for a small amount of pleasure.
Therefore, it should not be performed at the time of every day due to the cause of indigestion; this is the rule regarding food.

For the sake of the attainment of the *śrīcaryā* (glorious conduct) and *yogacaryā* (yoga conduct)—that is, for the sake of *siddhi*—one wanders through cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*), secondary cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*), and so forth at night, but not for the sake of sport; such is the meaning.

The commentary on the verse beginning with "The mudrā is taught for the purpose of meditation" (mudroktā bhāvanārtham), which concerns the discipline of yogic practice (yogacaryāniyamaḥ), was not found by me in the Sanskrit manuscripts; however, it was obtained in the Tibetan translation.
Therefore, having retranslated it from the Tibetan version back into Sanskrit, I have presented it here in the box above.

The Tibetan translation exists thus in the *Tanjurasaṃgraha*: "Now, by means of the phrase 'the mudrās known as... and so forth, the certainty regarding the mudrās, tastes, food, and movement of yogins is taught.
Here, the mudrās spoken of by the Blessed One are the yoga-mudrās taught for the purpose of meditation;
they are for the purpose of exhausting the karmic obscurations. It is not that he spoke of sporting with women day and night."
The drinking of wine is merely for the purpose of slight refreshment;
it is not for the sake of intoxication, such as from a full flask and so forth,
for the sense faculty of experience will not grant liberation to the lords of yoga.
Regarding eating moderately:
here, all food is for the sake of happiness; whatever one eats, all of it becomes extremely light and pleasant.
Therefore, knowing that one must not become a cause for regret at each individual mealtime is the rule for eating.
The glorious conduct is indeed the conduct of yoga; it is known as the cause of *siddhi* (accomplishment).
Because it is the cause of *siddhi*, wandering at night through charnel grounds, *pīṭhas*, *upapīṭhas*, and so forth, is not for the sake of play. This is the meaning;
it is the definitive rule of yogic conduct.

The commentary on this verse is not found in the Sanskrit manuscripts, yet it is found in the Tibetan translation; regarding the reason for this, the venerable Ācārya Khedrup Jé stated that in the pure Indian Sanskrit manuscripts of the commentary, only the following is found: "Now, the rules for the yogins’ mudrās, tastes, food, and conduct are being explained—this is easy to understand. Even that portion was not seen by me in the Sanskrit manuscripts. Here, the opinion of the venerable Khedrup Jé must be recorded.

He said: Now, the medicine for the *avadhūta* yogin is described in this chapter on the great instructions concerning alchemy (*rasāyana*) and the science of pediatrics (*bālatantra*). A small amount of Akṣobhya slightly warmed alleviates mouth diseases and toothache. At dawn, the nasal administration (*nasya*) of Akṣobhya removes pain in the head; likewise, water as a nasal administration does the same. When introduced into the ear or the eye, it removes both types of pain. Warm or cold urine, along with the nasal administration of Akṣobhya mixed with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), bestows well-being even when one is bitten by a venomous creature. (124)

In this regard, when a disease of the mouth occurs for a yogin, if Akṣobhya is made slightly warm and held in the mouth, it becomes a pacifier of mouth diseases as well as toothache— the word "and" (ca) implying it also removes dental caries. When there is a disease in the head, then at dawn, Akṣobhya used as a nasal drop (nasya) becomes a remover of pain in the head.
"Likewise, for yogins, there is the application of urine as a nasal drop (*nasya*).

When ear disease occurs, warm urine is applied; when eye disease occurs, cold urine is applied. Thus, respectively, it removes both types of pain. "Urine is both warm and cold" means that for one afflicted by spirits (*bhūtārta*)—that is, one seized by ghosts, *pretas*, and so forth—the application of *akṣobhya* urine combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) bestows happiness even when bitten. It bestows happiness even when bitten by a snake. This is the rule for the pacification of diseases of the mouth and other ailments.

Feces, urine, semen, and blood, together with the king’s [excrement] (the *tala*), when consumed, bestow longevity; when used as an ointment with meditation, it removes grey hair and wrinkles born of passion.
The "five lamps" (*pañcapradīpa*), when eaten mixed with fly-vomit and menstrual blood, removes all diseases; when taken for a year, it combined with semen likewise dispels illness. || 125 ||

Now, the *pañcāmṛtayoga* for the purpose of increasing longevity is explained with the words beginning "viḍ" and so forth. Here, according to the statement, "As it is externally, so it is in the body," one unifies the five substances externally with the five substances internally; this is the *pañcāmṛtayoga*. Consequently, it is accepted by the Tibetan master Śrī Paṅ lo and others that the consumption of the *pañcāmṛta* shall grant longevity to yogins. This portion of the commentary found in the Tibetan translation does not exist in the original Sanskrit, but was rather interpolated into the Tibetan translation by some Tibetan scholar.

Regarding this matter, that which was stated by the venerable Khedubje is cited here: "In all the authentic Tibetan translations of this [text], it says: 'Now, regarding the statements concerning the yogis' mudrās, enjoyments, food, and movements, beginning with the words "as for the mudrā," this is easy to understand. Although there are no other words from the commentary [to support this], the fact that it appears here [in the current version] is clearly an interpolation inserted by some unlearned Tibetan; thus say the learned scholars such as Dpal Lo and Chos rje Bu."
Some say that when Paṭṭipāda was preaching,
he placed a mark on the side of his ear;
[this is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā-ṭīkā*].

In the *Vimalaprabhā* [on the internal and external]: Regarding the term "excrement" (*viṭ*), externally it is Vairocana, Vali; by virtue of Vali, it is called sulphur (*gandhaka*). Internally, it is excrement itself. These two are in equal parts. Externally, urine is King Viṣṇu, the juice of the *bhiṅgarāja*; internally, it is urine itself. Externally, blood is mica (*abhraka*); internally, it is the female flower (*strīpuṣpa*). These are in equal parts. Externally, semen is mercury (*pārada*); internally, it is semen itself. These two are in equal parts. Externally, human flesh is the three myrobalans (*triphalā*); internally, it is marrow (*majjā*). These two are also in equal parts. Thus, one part of excrement, three-quarters of a part of flesh, half a part of blood, and one-quarter of a part of semen—having combined these, one should saturate them with urine seven times.

Having dried it repeatedly in the sun, if one consumes one *karṣa* daily with ghee and honey for a period of six months—provided there is avoidance of vegetables, acidic substances, oil, and salt—it becomes a giver of longevity; this is the rule regarding the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).

Now, the nasal administration of flowers (*puṣpanasya*) is described starting with the words "together with meditation" (*sadhyānam*), etc.: here, meditation (*dhyāna*) is the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the central channel (*madhyamā*); "together with meditation" means accompanied by that meditation.

"Flower" refers to female menses (*strīrajas*). Externally, "keśarājikā" is *bhṛṅgarāja*; its juice, when combined with female menses and used as a nasal drop (*puṣpanasya*) accompanied by meditation, removes gray hair, ailments born of passion, and the signs of old age within six months—this is the rule for the nasal treatment (*nasya*). Now, the "five lamps" (*pañcapradīpa*) is described: the meat of cow, horse, elephant, donkey, and man, mixed with the vomit of flies and honey, when consumed, becomes the "five lamps" that removes all diseases. Furthermore, "makṣikācchardi" is *mādhavī* (climbing asparagus); together with it, it removes all diseases—this is the rule.

The previously mentioned female flower, mixed with semen—whether external or internal—removes old age when consumed for a year; this is the aforementioned rule regarding diet. Now, the pacification of wind and the other humors is described: alkaline water is a destroyer of wind (*vāta*); that which is sweet is the enemy of bile (*pitta*); astringent is the destroyer of phlegm (*śleṣman*); and likewise, all bitter substances, whether medicinal herbs or their juices, as well as pungent ones, [are destroyers of phlegm].

Goat's milk, when combined with the three pungents (trikaṭuka), destroys phlegm; buffalo's milk is the enemy of bile; camel's milk is a destroyer of wind; and cow's milk and ghee indeed remove all three types of disease. (126)

Alkaline water is a subduer of wind (*vāta*) and becomes sweet; astringent substances are enemies of bile (*pitta*); everything bitter, when combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), is a subduer of phlegm (*śleṣman*). Whether it be a medicinal herb or a juice, consumed or drunk, [these qualities apply]. Goat’s milk, when combined with the three pungents, is a subduer of phlegm; buffalo milk is an enemy of bile; cow’s milk, when combined with sugar, is a subduer of wind; and camel’s milk, when combined with rock salt (*saindhava*), removes the three types of disease respectively. When combined with rock salt and the other [substances], it is a subduer of wind, bile, and phlegm.
Cow’s ghee alone pacifies the three kinds of diseases for those free from fever; this is the rule in the chapter on the Great Exposition of Rasāyana and Pediatrics.

Now, for the purpose of pacifying diseases of the mouth and so forth, the decoctions, oils, and other remedies are described starting with the word *jātī*: "Warm water boiled with *jātī* pacifies diseases of the mouth and likewise toothache; oil cooked with bladder-plant (*vastu*) water and the salts of *trikaṭu* destroys ear disease."

Clarified butter boiled with milk and red ahi-rakta always destroys diseases of the nose; likewise, karkoṭī and lāṅgaladrī, applied as a paste along with donkey urine, remove scrofula (gaṇḍamālā). // 127 //

5. Here, water eight times the quantity of all the medicinal substances, water eight times the quantity of *jātī* leaves, and water from a decoction of *jātī* reduced to one-fourth, slightly warmed, serves as a remedy for diseases of the mouth and for toothache. Likewise, sesame oil, *vastu* water, and goat’s urine—cooked together with these in equal parts until only the oil remains—and into which are added *trikaṭu* and salts in a quarter-part of the total, when applied after the cooking process is complete, its entry into the ear results in the destruction of ear disease.

Thus, at the conclusion of the decoction, one should prepare a medicated ghee (*ghṛta*) with eight times the amount of clarified butter, cow’s milk, and curd; then, adding *ahi* (Tagara), *nāgakeśara*, and red *kuṅkuma* in a quarter-part of the total, an application of this ghee as a nasal drop (*nasya*) results in the certain destruction of diseases of the nose.

*Karkoṭī*, *vandhyākarkoṭī*, *lāṅgalī*, *indrī* (Indravāruṇī), and *tiktā* (Kākamācī)—these, when smeared with donkey urine (*sahakharā*), remove *gaṇḍamālā* by means of an external plaster (*pralepa*). This is the rule in brief; it should be understood in detail from the medical treatises (*vaidyaśāstra*).

Now, the pacification of the "thorn of the vajra" (*vajrakaṇṭhaka*) is described, beginning with the words "one should make the hands," and so forth: One should let the two hands hang down while standing with feet level on a lotus; one should restrain the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) until the body no longer falls to the ground and the fever is released.

By repeatedly practicing this in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one shall destroy those thorns that cause the fear of death. Indeed, Viśvamātā—resembling the stainless moon—is visualized within the heart-lotus at the summit of the moon.
In this regard, when an affliction of a malignant disease occurs, first there is fever, pain arises in the joints of the hands and feet, and the head aches;
having recognized these symptoms, one should take recourse in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

In this regard, the procedure is as follows: having entered a windowless room, the one afflicted by fever should let both arms hang down to the level of the thighs with the feet placed evenly together. He should perform *kumbhaka* (breath retention), which is the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), until the collapse of the body onto the ground occurs due to the fever. This is the rule: he should repeatedly perform *prāṇāyāma* as long as there is no collapse on the ground. Furthermore, this should be practiced until the fever is released; once the fever has been released, he should not continue—this is the rule.
Again and again, one established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) shall indeed destroy the thorns that cause the fear of death.

Within the heart-lotus, the Mother of the Universe (*Viśvamātā*), stainless and resembling the moon, is to be meditated upon; by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), she has two arms and one face, holds a lotus and a boon-granting gesture, sits in the vajra-lotus posture (*vajrapadmāsana*) upon a lunar disc—this is the rule. Thus ends the pacification of sins and diseases.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the medicine for the pacification of sinful diseases is now stated: Having ground them with cold water, the Sun [mantra] destroys the thorns of fever in afflicted men. Mixed with *akṣobhya* [butter], it removes terrifying [symptoms]; or, at the end of the fever, one should perform protection on the head, throat, heart, navel, private parts, and so forth, using the skull and the mantra preceded by *oṃ*, as well as the names of Water, Fire, and Wind preceded by *vajra*. // 129 //

In this case, when the signs of a "sinful disease" (*pāparoga*) appear—such as fever and pain in the joints of the hands and feet—one should grind *masūrī* seeds with cold water and give them to those afflicted by fever; this destroys the thorns [of the disease]. Likewise, at the end of the fever, on the third day when the thorns are about to arise, one should drink the skull of a person who died of a sinful disease; if such a skull is unavailable, one may use whatever is obtained. A man's skull mixed with Akṣobhya should be drunk by a man, and a woman's skull by a woman.

If it is not obtained, one drinks whatever is available; this removes the terrifying thorns [of disease]. "Dhā" means that the skull-cup (*kapāla*) is used as it is obtained at the end of the fever; this is the rule.
Here, there is a mantra for the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the lentils (*masūra*) and so forth, and that mantra is preceded by the syllable *oṃ*; thus, the mantra begins with *oṃ*.

The *oṃkāra* of water, fire, and wind comes first: "water" refers to the second letter of the *pa*-group, the water element, which is *pha*; "fire" refers to the letter *ra* below; and above them is the letter *e*. The unity of these—water, fire, and wind—is *phreṃ*; the *anusvāra* is space (*ākāśa*) because it is all-pervasive.

The name of the thorns begins with *vajra*. One should perform protection (*rakṣā*) by means of that very [name], just as one does for *masūrī* and other ailments when consecrated seven times. In the same way, one should perform protection over the head, throat, heart, navel, and secret place; by the word "etc.," the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) is included. The rule is that one should perform protection at these six locations during the three junctions of the day.
Here is the mantra: *oṃ phreṃ viśvamātā vajrakaṇṭakān nāśaya nāśaya mama śāntiṃ kuru kuru svāhā*; for the sake of protecting others: *devadattasya śāntiṃ kuru kuru svāhā*. This is the rule.
This is the injunction of the Blessed One: "The Blessed Mother, the Universal Mother, should be recollected in all calamities for the protection of oneself and others.

Having empowered *masūrikā* seven times with this mantra, one should grind it with cold water and give it to drink. For one afflicted by fever, one should grind *akṣobhya* with a skull and give it. For one possessed by spirits, one should grind *akṣobhya* together with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) and give it. This is the injunction for the pacification of sinful diseases.

Now, the rule for the pacification of the sun’s heat is set forth with the words beginning "tulya": One should boil an equal amount of *dhātrī* (myrobalan), grain, and likewise the powder of *tintiḍī* leaves in water purified by the moon and sun—that is, in water free from impurities—until reduced to one-fourth.

This decoction, mixed with sugar, when drunk for three days starting from the following day, removes the burning sensation caused by the sun's rays during the summer, even that which has reached the seven bodily constituents and threatens death. (130)

In this context, when there is the heat of the sun’s rays on the road during the summer, then "equal to *dhātrī*" means equal to the powder of *āmalaka* fruit; "*dhānya*" refers to *kustumburu*, and "the other is equal to that"; likewise, the powder of *tintirī* leaves and the powder of *bandhulī* leaves are equal. Having thus made all [ingredients] in equal parts, one should boil them in water "frequented by the moon and sun"—that is, touched by the rays of the moon and sun—indeed "free from impurity," meaning devoid of moss and other such stains; one should boil the three substances until one-quarter remains—that is, until the decoction is reduced to one-fourth its original volume—having added eight times the amount of water to the substances.

In this case, there is no measurement by *tulā* (weight); rather, the rule is that in all instances regarding decoctions (*kvātha*), the measurement is by *āḍhaka*. Having taken one part from that decoction, one should drink it mixed with an equal amount of sugar on the following day. Following this sequence for three nights at dawn during the summer removes the burning sensation from the sun's rays and [the poison] that has entered the seven constituents (*dhātu*)—including the hair and skin—as indicated by the word "and" (*ca*). This is the rule.

Now, another elixir is described beginning with the words "heme'rkam" and so forth: One should cause mercury (*rasa*) to be processed (*vāhayet*) with gold, copper, iron, magnetite (*kāntaloha*), or mica (*paṭalaja*), using half a seed-measure (*bījārddha*) of lac (*makṣika*). Once it has become free of impurities, one should cause it to be processed with six *palas* [of the aforementioned substances] and then break it into pills (*golaka*). Having indeed roasted it with a fierce fire, the essence (*agra*) should be taken; it should be boiled again in a vessel with a paste of *śrī* (vermilion) until it reaches half its original measure.

In this body, whoever seeks an external elixir (*bāhyarasāyana*) should perform this intermediate elixir (*madhyarasāyana*) in the absence of the perfected elixir (*siddharasa*). Its procedure is stated as follows: "In gold" means in purified gold; "arkam" means copper; "kānta" means magnetite iron; "paṭalaja" means common iron; and "ayas" means steel. Of each of these, having made equal parts, one portion—equal to the gold—of *mākṣika* powder should be blown with a bellows into an open crucible using a strong blast until the gold remains; that alone is the seed (*bīja*). With half of that seed, [using] two *palas* of gold and four *palas* of mercury from which impurities have been removed, and having performed seven purifications (*pātana*), one should cause six *palas* of paste (*piṣṭa*) to be prepared.

Then, having split the *gotraka* (mineral ore) from which the butter has been removed using a sharp-pointed, intense fire, one should strain it through a cloth and take the clear whey (*mastu*), discarding the dregs.

That same whey should then be boiled again with gold-dust in a magnet stone vessel until it reaches half its original volume. Having removed it, eight *pala* of impure sugar should be added there as before. Indeed, that is to be consumed at all times, free from food, for as long as the year lasts.

Within six months, one attains a divine body; even one overcome by wrinkles and grey hair attains immortality through this. Therefore, that very [substance] should be consumed at every daily occasion, provided it is free from flour. 132.

Then, having extracted eight *pala* of impure sugar-candy, one should add to it black pepper powder—one sixty-fourth part of the sugar-candy—varying from nine down to seven parts according to the digestive capacity of those who are not kings and so forth. This very substance is to be eaten at all times, free from food for as long as six months; by this, one attains a divine body and reaches immortality, transcending wrinkles and grey hair.
In this context, the consumption of betel is prescribed; however, excluding the paste of betel, that food is to be eaten at all times.

That very *mastu* (whey) is to be eaten according to that rule, but it should be devoid of gold-dust (*hemapiṣṭa*); nevertheless, as long as the flour-paste (*piṣṭikā*) remains, it should be taken together with it.
Thereafter, "at all times without her" refers to the rule for elixirs (*rasāyana*).

Now, he speaks of gold and more for the enjoyment of food and so forth, beginning with the words "the previously mentioned," etc.: The previously mentioned king of seeds (*bījarāja*), even if equal [in weight], having been digested in mercury, one should grind it with half its measure of alkaline salts and acids, along with many various *viḍa* salts, until it attains oneness with bile, acids, sulfur, and the rest; likewise, one should grind vermilion and mica equal to the mercury. By anointing a silver leaf with that, it attains the state of gold, even if it is only half-cooked.

In this context, the previously mentioned king of seeds (*bījarāja*), though equal [in weight], has been processed (*cārita*) with mercury for half a measure; having ground it with alkaline and sour substances and many various *viḍa* salts to be described later until it attains unity, one should then grind it with bile-acid substances such as sulfur and so forth, as well as cinnabar and realgar—these three substances being equal in weight to the mercury—for the purpose of making the mercury penetrable (*rasakrāmaṇa*). One should grind it together with the mercury using bile-acid substances.

Cow-bile, fish-bile, or sour fruit such as *bījapūraka* and others as available; sulphur (*gandhaka*), vermilion (*darada*), realgar (*śilā*), orpiment (*tālaka*), *śaśaka*, *kākṣī*, *kāśīṣa*, blue vitriol (*tutthaka*), and *hemagirikā*. Of these, starting with sulphur, there are two secondary minerals (*uparasa*) and one primary mineral (*mahārasa*). With three parts equal to the mercury, by smearing [the leaf] with this, a silver leaf placed beneath a furnace for three days attains the state of gold when cooked by the furnace fire—this is the rule for gold using "half-gold" (*addhika-hema*).

Now the preparation of the *puṣpa* (flower-essence) is described, beginning with the words "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*) and so forth: The sharp [metal] born from space (iron), and that produced from salt, alkaline salt, and barley-ash, should be increased in sequence and heated in twice the amount of copper (*arka*) to achieve a state of equal flavor; thus one should burn until only the copper remains. Again, it becomes purified by means of alkali and becomes soft when poured over cow-dung and the like. When applied in a third part to silver (*tāra*), even if it has been removed, once filled again, it attains the state of pure *puṣpa*. || 134 ||

Here, by the word "flower" (*puṣpa*), the substance in the form of a *ḍramma* coin is meant; it is [the metal] struck with mercury (*tāra*) and filled with it. This is its purification of the leaf (*dalaśuddhi*):
the mercury born from space is the essence of *abhra* (mica).
"Alam" refers to talaka, lavaṇa, and saindhava; yavakṣāra and sarjarasa; and "tīkṣṇādyaṃ krameṇa vṛddham" means increased in sequence by one, two, three, four, five, and six parts respectively.

Then, having combined everything, one should first blow it in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) using double the amount of copper (*arka*) to achieve a uniform fusion; thereafter, one should burn it in an open crucible (*prakaṭamūṣā*) until only a small residue remains.

Furthermore, it becomes purified by means of alkali, specifically borax-alkali (*ṭaṅgaṇakṣāra*); likewise, it becomes soft when sprinkled with cow-dung and other substances—where "cow-dung" (*gomaya*) refers to cow's urine, and "and others" (*āditaḥ*) refers to the root of *arka*, the root of *vajrīkanaka*, the root of *eraṇḍa*, and the root of *kṣīrakañcukī*. Having nourished [the metal] in this way, one should perform the soaking (*sandhāna*) for up to seven days. Then, one should give it a sprinkling of buttermilk (*takra*) until it becomes soft.
When that very [metal] is applied to silver (*tāra*) in a proportion of one-third—whether subtracted or added—it attains the state of pure flower-like quality (*śuddhapuṣpatva*).
This is the rule regarding the flower-pieces (*puṣpadala*).

In this chapter on the Great Instruction on Alchemy and Pediatrics, the *kakṣapuṭa* (perfume compendium) consisting of incense, perfumes, and so forth, for the purpose of worshipping the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, is now described beginning with the word *elā*. *Elā*, camphor (*karpūra*), *mālā*, *vala*, *ghanaphalinī*, *vāyasa*, and *adrija*—these purified substances should be cast here into the *kakṣapuṭa* consisting of twenty-five compartments, according to the procedure taught in the *Gandhasāstra*.

In the first square is *elā* (cardamom); in the second, *karpūra* (camphor); in the third, *mālā* which is *spṛkkā* flower; in the fourth, *vala* which is *sihlaka* powder; in the fifth, *ghana* which is *mustaka*; in the sixth, *phalinī* which is *priyaṅgu* flower; in the seventh, *vāyasa* which is black *aguru*; in the eighth, *adrija* which is *śaileyaka*; in the ninth, *karkolaka*; in the tenth, *siṃhamūtra* (lion's urine); in the eleventh, *utpala* which is *kuṣṭha*; in the twelfth, *phala* which is *jātiphala*; in the thirteenth, *mṛgajā* which is *kastūrikā* (musk); in the fourteenth, *rakta* which is *kuṅkuma* (saffron); in the fifteenth, *daitya* which is *murā*; in the sixteenth, *pūti* which is *putrakeśa*; in the seventeenth, *nāga* which is *nāgakeśara* flower; in the eighteenth, *śīta* which is *candana* (sandalwood); in the nineteenth, *raṇa* which is *uśīraka*; in the twentieth, *patra* which is *tamālapatra*; in the twenty-first, *pala* which is *māṃsī*; in the twenty-second, *jala* which is *vālaka*; in the twenty-third, *latā*, by which *latā* means *kastūrikā*; in the twenty-fourth, *ambara* which is *bheruṇḍaviṣṭha*; in the twenty-fifth, *cakra* which is *piṇḍīnagara* flower. These are the substances.

The rule for producing a beautiful fragrance is as follows: using these five substances as desired, extracted from a *kakṣapuṭa* (perfume box), one should apply them. With "mṛgaśaśibhiḥ" (deer and moon), meaning with camphor and musk along with incense, one should sprinkle [the powder]; or one should scent it with fragrant flowers. With "āsavādyaiḥ" (liquors, etc.), meaning with all the intoxicants to be described hereafter, together with camphor, musk, and nutmeg, one should infuse it; such is the rule for the application of substances.

Now, the proportions of the substances contained within the *kakṣapuṭa* are stated, beginning with "eyes" (*netra*) and so forth: Eyes (2), moon (1), fire (3), oceans (4), and arrows (5); virtues (3), oceans (4), and arrows (5); hands (2), moon (1), and eyes (2); moon (1), fire (3), oceans (4), and moon (1) and time (6); yugas (4), arrows (5), eyes (2), and oceans (4); eyes (2), moon (1), and worlds (3)—these are the numbers of parts for the substances beginning with cardamom (*elā*), arranged in sequence across five sets of five compartments. The fragrance arises from the substances located within the city of the *kakṣapuṭa*, using pure parts numbering according to the days (i.e., thirty).

In this context, for the substance falling in the first square, there are two parts, "netra" (eye); in the second, "indu" (moon), which is one part; in the third, "agni" (fire), which is three; in the fourth, "abdhi" (ocean), which is four; in the fifth, "bāṇa" (arrow), which is five; in the sixth, "guṇa" (quality), which is three; in the seventh, "jaladhi" (sea), which is four; in the eighth, "śara" (arrow), which is five; in the ninth, "hasta" (hand), which is two; in the tenth, "indu" (moon), which is one; in the eleventh, "iṣu" (arrow), which is five; in the twelfth, "netra" (eye), which is two; in the thirteenth, "candra" (moon), which is one; in the fourteenth, "agni" (fire), which is three; in the fifteenth, "abdhi" (ocean), which is four; in the sixteenth, "indu" (moon), which is one; in the seventeenth, "kāla" (time), which is three; in the eighteenth, "yuga" (age), which is four; in the nineteenth, "śara" (arrow), which is five; in the twentieth, "nayana" (eye), which is two; in the twenty-first, "abdhi" (ocean), which is four; in the twenty-second, "iṣu" (arrow), which is five; in the twenty-third, "netra" (eye), which is two; in the twenty-fourth, "indu" (moon), which is one; and in the twenty-fifth, "loka" (world), which is three.

In the sequence thus described, the proportions of cardamom (*elā*) and the other ingredients are arranged in order within five-by-five squares. By means of those five substances located in the *kakṣapuṭapura*—where "city" (*pura*) refers to a square (*koṣṭhaka*) consisting of fifteen parts according to the pure substance portions called "days" (fifteen)—there arises a fragrance. The rule for the portions of the substances is that they are unified as one, two, three, four, and five respectively. In the *kakṣapuṭa* of the fragrance, [the substances] such as *jātī* and cardamom creepers should be applied in sequence to the leaf-vessel-city (*dalakalaśapura*). Furthermore, lac, *sarja*, milk, and white [sandalwood] are also to be used as incense in incense-preparations.

One should prepare a paste from pieces of camphor mixed with the juices of flowers, using four parts [of the former] and one part of nakha; this should be ground with fragrant water. One should then prepare an incense-stick (dhūpavarti) sweetened with honey. || 137 ||

Now, the incense-powder (*kakṣapuṭa*) is described, beginning with the words "jātī" and so forth: here, among the substances for the incense-powder previously mentioned, having removed five substances starting with *jātī*, another five should be substituted in their place in due order.

Therein, "jātī" refers first to *jātīphala* (nutmeg); second is *elā* (cardamom); third is "latā," which is musk (*kastūrikā*); fourth is "dala," which is *tamālapatra* (cinnamon leaf); and fifth is "kalaśa," which is *kakkola*.

These should be deposited in their respective compartments in the following order: lac in the nutmeg compartment (*jātīphala-koṣṭha*); resin (*sarjarasa*) in the cardamom compartment (*elā-koṣṭha*); "suffering" (*duḥkha*), meaning *śrīvāsa* (benzoin), in the cinnamon-bark compartment (*latā-koṣṭha*); "town" (*pura*), meaning *guggulu* (bdellium), in the leaf-compartment (*dala-koṣṭha*); and "white" (*sita*), meaning *kunduruka*, in the *kakkola* compartment. This is the rule for preparing incense for incense-offerings using these five substances in the aforementioned proportions.
Wherever there is sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*), honey should be added along with it; and wherever there are parts of camphor, it should be combined with the sugar-candy and the "nails" (*nakha*).

Thus, with eighteen parts, the six-component incense (*ṣaḍaṅga-dhūpa*) is formed; when combined with pieces of camphor, *madhuka*, and musk, it becomes ten components. This is the rule for the substances in the *dhūpakakṣapuṭa*. Now, the method for the incense-wick (*dhūpavarti*) is stated, beginning with "that [substance] ground," and so forth. Here, one should grind the substances mentioned in the *dhūpakakṣapuṭa*—excluding *madhuka*—with scented water mixed with a little sugar-candy, and from that, one should make an incense-wick in the shape of an iron arrow (*nārāca*). This is the rule for burning incense upon garments and the like for the sake of the images of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

One should cast [the ingredients] into lion’s urine at the navel and other locations, in the city of the moon and the sky, for the purpose of bathing: *granthi*, tiger-pearl (*vyāghra*), and *hareṇu* (even when crushed), as well as three parts of conch-shell bark, coriander, *mūrvā*, *śatāhvā*, and *damanaka*; likewise, for the previously mentioned unguent that has not yet been applied, one should add lotus-root and *granthiparṇa* to the oil.

Now, the powder for bathing (*snānakakṣapuṭa*) is described starting with the words "In the navel, etc. Here, among the substances included in the previous powder (*kakṣapuṭa*), four substances beginning with the navel are extracted; in their respective squares within the bathing powder, other substances are to be added according to the sequence. Among them, one should place *granthiparṇa* in the square of the navel; in the square of lion’s urine, *vyāghranakha*; in the city of the moon (*śaśipura*), *hareṇu*; and in the city of the sky (*gaganapura*), "the slain," which is *kacoraka*.

Furthermore, just as in the preparation of incense, one part of *saṅkha* and three parts of *nakha* are used, so too should three parts of bark be given; in the application for bathing, among the bathing substances,
when divided into eighteen parts, the bath is performed with six substances—
this is the rule for the substances in the bathing *kakṣapuṭa*.

Now the powder for body massage (*udvartana-kakṣapuṭa*) is described: here, as in the case of the bath-powder (*snāna-kakṣapuṭa*), three parts of the five substances are to be given from among the five substances, just like the bark.

"Grain" (*dhānya*) means coriander (*kastūmburu*); "mūrvī" means *maruvaka*; "śatāhvā" means *śatapuṣpā*; "dama" means *damanaka*. These three parts of the five [substances] are sweet. Thus, the body massage consists of eighteen parts;
this is the rule for the substances of the body massage.

Now, for the purpose of preparing processed oil (*pakataila*), the *tailakakṣapuṭa* is described, beginning with "here, first" (*iha pūrva*) and so forth: here, when the group of substances for the previously mentioned *gandhakakṣapuṭa* has not been completed, one should add "aquatic" (*jalaja*), which means *nakha* (onion), and "slender like the aquatic," which means *tvak* (cinnamon bark), as well as *granthiparṇa*; having added three parts of these two, together with the five substances of the *gandhakakṣapuṭa*, one should cook the oil with these seven substances in eighteen parts according to the sequence to be described. This is the rule for the substances of the *tailakakṣapuṭa*, and it results in various fragrant oils (*nānāgandhataila*).

In this way, one should prepare various well-composed mixtures of perfumes, incenses, and so forth, through three hundred different varieties—such as powders, pills (*granthi*), and likewise those for the body, the drink, the dwelling, and the mouth; as well as *tvagvola*, *granthiśaṅkha*, and those prepared by the *phaladalapuṭapāka* method, and those beginning with the *haṃsa* [method]—using substances that are purified, cooked in fruit-cases, scented, and pierced. // 139 //
"In powder" means in the context of powdered substances; "and likewise in a knot" means that *granthiparṇaka* is to be added among the five substances as in the case of *nakha*.

There, it is to be used when the substance has been processed for use in mouth-perfumes (*pānavāsa*). For mouth-perfumes, there is a set of four substances—*tvak*, *vola*, *granthi*, and *śaṅkha*—of which three parts are to be used. It is to be added at the beginning during the ripening of the fruit, during *dalapuṭapāka*, during *haṃsapāka*, and during the *dolāpāka* (swinging-pot distillation) which is about to be described.

Having spoken thus, one who desires fragrance and the like should, according to the stated sequence, prepare thirty well-composed varieties of applications beginning with perfume—namely, various applications of incense and so forth, as well as those for bathing, rubbing the body, and the like. With what kind of substances? With pure ones, or those ripened in fruit-pouches, perfumed, and pierced; such is the rule for the collection of substances. Now, the preparation of incense is described, beginning with "one-eighth part" and so forth: at the start, there is a decoction [of herbs] in eight parts according to the number of petals; twice that amount is the potent incense; thereafter, there should be an equal measure of jaggery (guḍa), which increases due to its application during the summer heat.

One should burn one-quarter part of conch-shell incense, along with Madhuka and sugar equal in measure to the substance; likewise, a ball the size of a conch-shell made of light Malaya sandalwood combined with moon-fragrance (Karpūra). // 140 //
In this formulation of perfumes (*gandhayoga*), there are three types of ingredients—inferior, middling, and superior.
Among them, the inferior ones are: *mustaka*, *śailēya*, *uśīraka*, *vālaka*, *kapittha*, *vilva*, *murā*, and *māṃsī*. These are the inferior ingredients.
By virtue of these ingredients—that is, according to the nature of the ingredients—the initial decoction, mixed with jaggery and the powder of *harītakī*, becomes incense (*dhūpa*).

First, one should fumigate for one day with that eighth part of the leaf; then, having allowed the flowers to soak for two days, on the third day one should mix in the middle leaf. Then, doubling that, it is called "intense incense" (*ugradhūpa*).
That is to say, by doubling the preceding and following [parts], there is intense incense:
lac, resin, *śrīvāsa*, *ra* [meaning] *guggulu*, and *kunduruka*. With these five primary ingredients, sweetened with jaggery, it becomes intense incense.
Twice the amount of the decoction (*kaṣāya*) should be given, and one-fourth the amount of the leaf (*dala*).
Here, "leaf-group" refers to the *madhyama-dala*, the flower-group, sandalwood, and aloe-wood; the "fruit-group," the nail-group (*nakha*), the bark-group, and the resin-group (*niryāsa*).

In this manner, one should fumigate it with intense incense for two days; then, on alternate days for two days, one should perform the perfuming with flowers. Afterwards, during the summer, one should burn an amount of jaggery (*guḍa*) equal to the quantity of the substances together with the incense.

Thereafter, it increases due to the onset of summer; in the rainy season, the substance is doubled, and in winter, it should be given tripled. Then, when the molasses has been burnt, one should burn "conch" (śaṅkha)—that is, a nail-measure—with the molasses as a quarter-portion for two days according to the previous procedure.
After that, one should burn madhuka, sugar, and jaggery in quantities equal to the substance, together with the ball-incense (piṇḍadhūpa);
at the beginning and end of the incense-offering, one should burn them alone.

In this manner, one should also burn three morsels of jaggery (*guḍa*) every day and allow it to rest; every day, one should burn incense consisting of one-eighth part of the substance. Otherwise, by [insufficient burning] it remains uncooked, and by [excessive burning] it becomes smoky; the rule is that if it is uncooked, it becomes sour—this is called *piṇḍa*, meaning "lump-incense. As stated in the *Kakṣapuṭa*, it should be mixed with camphor and devoid of pungent substances; using the five substances sweetened with honey and sugar, one makes the lump-incense. That very [incense] should be of the measure of a conch-shell; thus, one should burn it using a quarter-part of the substance.

In that regard, one should burn *putrakeśa* (nutmeg), *jātīphala* (cloves), *karpūra* (camphor), and *nābhi* (musk); furthermore, having added the excellent *dala* (leaf) mentioned in the *Kakṣapuṭa*, along with *malaya* (sandalwood), *laghu* (agallochum), *cala* (sihnaka resin), and *candra* (camphor)—these three substances combined—just like the ingredients for the *piṇḍadhūpa*. It should be burned together with honey and *śakairā* (sugar).
Here, *guḍa* refers to pill-sugar (*vaṭikā-guḍa*) and not the first type of substance; this is the rule.

One should spread the fragrance of the cooked [substance] with fine flowers for as many days as desired; thereafter, one should perform the *vedha* (infusion) using a hundredth part of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), camphor (*śaśin*), and honey, along with fermented liquors (*sāsavaiḥ*).
