One should boil *śikhambu*, goat’s urine, and the juice of flowers in equal proportions until the end of the flowering [process], for one month. When cooked in grain, it becomes like the meat of a deer; this is the *nābhividdha* liquor. // 141 //

Then, having recognized that the fragrance has matured—if, by smelling the fragrance of this [substance] after it has been rubbed, the palm of the hand becomes red, then it is fully matured; otherwise, it is not yet matured. Therefore, one should not burn the cold incense until maturity is reached.

Once this matured fragrance has been treated with fragrant flowers such as *campaka* and others for several days—whether for half a fortnight or a full fortnight—until the defects of the incense are abandoned, it then becomes fit for use.

Afterwards, one should perform the perfuming (*vedha*) by a hundredth part (*śatāṃśa*) of the following: *satāṃsa* [corrected to *śatāṃśa*] refers to the fruit known as *jātīphala* (nutmeg), *kakkola*, or alternatively, *elā* in place of *kakkola*; *latā* is musk (*kastūrikā*); *śaśī* is camphor (*karpūra*); and *mada* is musk. Having made these into equal parts, one should cause the perfuming of the fragrance by a hundredth part. This perfuming should be administered by a hundredth part together with the intoxicating liquors (*āsava*) to be mentioned later. "Eightfold for all" is the rule for perfuming.

Now, for the purpose of delighting with fragrances, the *āsava* is described starting with the word *śigru*. Here, the detailed procedure regarding the cooking of *āsava* and so forth, as taught in the treatises on perfumes (*gandhaśāstra*), should be understood from those very texts;

it is stated here only in brief. "Śigru-water" means the juice of *śigru*; "flower-juice" means honey. One should boil these together with an equal measure [of other ingredients] over fire until the end of the "flower-born," that is, until honey is reached. Then, having extracted it and placed it in a coconut shell or similar vessel, it becomes cooked after one month in the midst of a heap of grain.

Regarding the phrase "the liquor is pierced like a deer": at the conclusion of the heating by fire, *nābhi* refers to musk (*kastūrī*); although not explicitly mentioned, camphor (*karpūra*) is also included. Together with these, one should apply a hundredth-part (*śatāṃśa*) piercing using the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and thereafter store it in grain.
Then, one should perform the previously described piercing of the fragrance with that [mixture]; this is the rule.

In all treatises on perfumes (*gandhaśāstra*), there are three types of incense-burners (*dhūpayantra*) for the preparation of incense: the flat one, the one shaped like a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), and the one shaped like a shallow bowl (*sarāva*). The inferior type has a hole two finger-widths wide and six finger-widths high, intended for potent incense (*ugradhūpa*). The medium type is eight finger-widths high, intended for incense made from *nakhaguḍapiṇḍa*. The superior type is ten finger-widths high, intended for cold incense (*śītadhūpa*). To use this burner: place a shallow pan (*kharpara*) filled with sand upon a hearth; set the burner on top of the heated sand. Place a lump of fragrant paste (*gandhakalka*) smeared over the burner, rising half a finger-width in height. If the paste is thin, place a coconut shell over it. Having determined the appropriate length of the incense stick—either one or half a cubit—one should burn the incense.

Then, having removed the skull-cup and placed a cloth upon the wooden board, one should set it face down so that the smoke does not escape; furthermore, during the time of cooking, one should wrap the space between the skull-cup and the apparatus with a damp cloth— this is the rule for the preparation of incense (*dhūpapāka*).

Having extracted the inner grain from a citron (*bījapūraka*) when its fruit has ripened, and having removed the rind, one should place a paste of fragrance (*gandhakalka*) inside. Having wrapped the exterior with bark fibers, one should coat it with clay to a thickness of one finger-breadth. Afterwards, one should cook it using the *puṭapāka* method with a fire of dried cow-dung cakes until the coating becomes the color of fire; beyond that point, the fragrance would be destroyed. Then, having removed it from the fire and once it has cooled, one should pierce the fragrance at the navel and other points according to the previously mentioned procedure. This is the rule for the ripening of the fruit.
In the *dalapuṭapāka* (leaf-pot baking) method as well, one should form a packet using *ketakī* leaves and place the medicinal paste (*gandhakalka*) inside;
the rest is like the *phalapāka*.

In the *haṃsapāka*, a golden or silver vessel should have its interior smeared with the medicinal paste to a height of one finger-breadth. Floating in a copper cauldron half-filled with fragrant water, undergoing boiling while floating like a swan (*haṃsa*), it is called *haṃsapāka*; the processes such as *vedha* are as before—this is the rule for *haṃsapāka*, according to the statement "and in the *haṃsapāka*."

Regarding dolāpāka and so forth, it is said: among the nine types of substances mentioned in the science of perfumes (gandhaśāstra), there are eight methods of processing for the purification of the inferior petals—namely, washing, sweating, rubbing, roasting, impregnation, fumigation, perfuming, and binding.

In that regard, for the inferior types of petals such as *mustaka* and others belonging to the flower group, one should perform washing with *kāñjika*, steaming by means of *dolāpāka*, rubbing with scented water, roasting of the crushed [petals] with molasses-water and the like, infusion (*bhāvanā*) with the urine of children, goats, and so forth, fumigation with the fire of decoctions (*kaṣāya*), perfuming (*vāsana*) with flowers such as *ketakī*, and piercing (*vedhana*) with substances such as the navel [of a conch]; however, one should exclude roasting (*bharjana*).

Thus, in the group of bark (*tvaggaṇa*), the middle leaf-group (*madhyamadalānām*), the root-group (*mūlaguṇa*), the wood-group (*kāṣṭhagaṇa*), the leaf-group (*patragaṇa*), and the life-force group (*jīvagaṇa*), there is the roasting (*bharjanam*) of the nail and the steaming (*puṭapākaḥ*) of the *putrakeśa*;
the remainder is like the flower-group (*puṣpagaṇavat*).
In the fruit-group (*phalagaṇa*), the exudate-group (*niryāsagaṇa*), and the liquid substance-group (*dravadravyagaṇa*), no action whatsoever is to be performed.

Having ground these aforementioned substances into a powder, one should place the powder upon a cloth at the mouth of the vessel. Having filled the vessel halfway with scented water and placed the powder on top, one should steam it with steam-sudation until the powder becomes moistened. Then, having removed it, one should perform anointing and other such treatments.

In this way, for *putrakeśa* as well, there is the process of swinging (*dolāveṣṭa*). For *nakha*, at the place where sweating occurs, there is boiling with cow dung or clay, roasting, and sprinkling with decoction water; the remainder is as before—this is the fivefold rule for cooking. The rest should be understood from the *Gandhaśāstra* by one who desires fragrance. Now, the secret [instruction] regarding perfumes and so forth is stated, beginning with "the secret": The secret among perfumes is *pūti*; in incense preparations, it is the volatile part of the tongue and nails. Likewise, the secret is *turuṣka*, *guru*, and *śaśin*, which are cold; and in the preparation of scents, it is the flower.

In the process of extraction (*vedha*), camphor, nutmeg, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and liquor are used; likewise, in the application for bathing, one should properly employ *guhya*, cinnamon bark (*tvak*), *granthiparṇa*, and *vanacarā* as an ointment (*udvartana*) along with *granthi*.
Here, at the time of preparing the cool incense (*śītadhūpa*) from perfumes and other ingredients, one should add *pūti* to the fragrances;
"the flickering of the tongue and nails" is the secret instruction.
In this process of incense-purification (*dhūpapāka*), one should offer incense for the purification of the scents of the elements.

Having prepared the incense mixture, regarding the application of incense: having purified the fragrant resin (*gandharasa*), *nakha*, and *sihnaka* with molasses, one should let it sit for one or two days, or until the acidity is lost. Then, one should offer the ball (*piṇḍa*) and so forth; this is the rule.

Now, if by the "rough cooking" (*kharapāka*) the scent has been scorched, one should let the scent be touched by the rays of the moon at night. In the absence of that, one should place it on a riverbank until the defect of burning has subsided.

The causes for the destruction of fragrances are stated here: the mixing of pure and impure substances is a cause of destruction; likewise, oil, a moist place, chaff, alkaline substances, contact with excrement or urine, contact with mice, wind, and an excessively hot place [are causes]. Similarly, coldness is a cause; thus, sandalwood, turuṣka, gurusāśina, and guhya [should be used]. At the conclusion of the cooking process, incense such as *śītādi* should be applied once the hair of the *putra* has fallen out; this is the rule. In matters of perfuming, flowers and *guhya* [substances] should be used until the defects of the incense have subsided.

Regarding "piercing" (*vedha*): in the context of piercing, there are camphor, musk, the three fruits (*triphalā*), and *madasure*—which is musk-liquor—as far as the secret [ingredients] that serve to pacify the defects of the flower's infusion; this is the rule for the application of perfumes.

Regarding the application of bathing substances (*snāna-yoga*), the word "properly" (*samyak*) implies that in the context of bathing, these secret ingredients must necessarily be given among the collection of bathing materials. Among them, cinnamon (*tvak*) and *granthiparṇa* are to be provided together with *vanacara* (wild hair/fiber), which means together with *putrakeśa*; the rule is that these three parts are to be given within fifteen parts.

In the yoga of rubbing the body with unguents, *granthiparṇa* should be used; in bathing, it should be applied according to the prescribed proportions. Thus, the procedure for the *gandhakakṣapuṭa* is described. Now, the fragrance called *nābhibhartṛ* is explained by the verse beginning with "pure lotus" (*śuddhābja*) and so forth: Pure lotus (*śuddhābja*)—meaning devoid of other substances and free from *madhuka*—is ground with fragrant water and cooked with incenses consisting of the powders of *kaṣāya*, *ugra*, and *madhuka*. One should increase the dose (*grāsa*) gradually: two doses mixed with sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*), and then [portions] of *malaya* (sandalwood), *capala* (camphor), iron, and camphor. At the beginning and end of each dose, one should burn *madhuka* and sugar, starting from the initial incense.

In this context, when one wishes to prepare *gandharāja* with a single substance, then "pure lotus" refers to the fingernail; that [nail] is generally of four types: elephant-ear, horse-hoof, lotus-petal, and jujube-leaf (*varada*).
Among these, for the preparation of perfumes (*gandhayoga*), the elephant-ear and horse-hoof should be used; for incense preparations (*dhūpayoga*), the jujube-leaf and lotus-petal should be used.

In this context, the *varuṇa* (or *badara*) leaf is best; in its absence, lotus leaves and the like should be taken. It is "pure" when boiled according to the procedure prescribed in the *Gandhaśāstra*, sprinkled with water decocted from molasses and medicinal extracts (*kaṣāya*), powdered, smeared with *triphalā* and other substances, and perfumed—thus it is pure.
That very [leaf], when devoid of other substances, is called *madhuka*; it is "without *āsava*" when free from that.

Regarding the instruction "ground with fragrant water" (*gandhatoyena piṣṭam*): here, for the purpose of fragrant water (*gandhodaka*), one should take clear water and place one *karṣa* each of cardamom (*elā*), cinnamon bark (*tvak*), spikenard (*māṃsī*), vetiver (*vālaka*), and sandalwood (*candana*) tied in a small cloth bag into eight *āḍhakas* of water.
Then, one should boil it down until one-quarter remains, at which point it becomes fragrant water;
with that, one should grind the other fragrant substances—this is the rule.

"Ripened by incenses": that same [substance] with pure nails, ground and ripened by the procedure for cooking incense, with incenses consisting of the powders of *kaṣāya*, *ugra*, and *madhuka*, increased gradually by one mouthful (*grāsa*) at a time; together with honey and sugar, one mouthful of the decoction on the first day—at the beginning and end of each mouthful, one should also burn *madhuka* and white sugar—according to the rule "starting from the initial incense."

First, a morsel of honey and sugar should be given; in the middle, of the decoction-incense; and again at the end, one should burn honey and sugar. On the second day, one should perform the "flower-vow" (*puṣpavāsa*). In this manner, alternating [the days], one should burn two morsels of fierce incense over two days. Then, three morsels of *nakha* over three days; thereafter, two morsels mixed with sugar for *malaya* over two days; and one for *capala*.
For iron and camphor as well, at the beginning and end of the digestion, honey and sugar are used as before;
thus, having been cooked with incense at intervals for twenty-four days, it becomes processed.

Having performed the ritual of perfuming (*vāsa*) with beautiful flowers for several days, it should be mixed with scented water and placed in a clay pot that does not leak, its mouth firmly sealed and wrapped in cloth and beeswax. Then, having placed it in a wide vessel filled with sand on the surface of the earth, it becomes cooked through the application of six months; submerged in water, it becomes fragrant and possesses the power to support the navel [of the world].

Then, having stayed for ten days with excellent flowers, one should boil fragrant water every day according to the previous procedure until the pacification of the defects of the site occurs; one must not add cold water.

It becomes sour with cold water; having mixed that fragrance with fragrant water, one should place it in a leak-proof earthen pot whose exterior is wrapped in silk cloth and whose mouth is firmly sealed. This [pot] is then placed inside another large vessel—either in a *jātikā* or on the ground—and in the absence of such a vessel, having poured it into that [earthen] vessel, one should fill it with sand on top until the vessel is filled up to its neck.

In that regard, when the vessel has been filled with *vālī* (or *lū*) fruits, ordinary water heated by the sun should be added; one should place that very vessel in the heat of the sun for as long as six months.

Thus, through this six-month application, it becomes cooked, and the fragrance residing in the water becomes the "Lord of Scents" (*gandharāja*), which supports the navel [of the body]. This is the rule for the King of Scents.

Now, for the sake of flower-oil and scented oil, the purification of sesame seeds is described, beginning with the words "having performed," etc.: having performed the purification of the sesame seeds with boiled leaf-water and with incense, ointments, and so forth, one should subsequently infuse them with jasmine and other flowers for several days, or until the desired result is achieved.

O King, having extracted the oil from the press, one should skillfully place it in a glass vessel; for this unrefined flower-oil becomes intoxicating when used for bathing or anointing the body. (145) Here, having gathered fresh, fully ripened sesame seeds, one should rub them with "leaf-water"—the leaves being those of the mango (*āmra*), as well as the leaves of the five trees, namely the *jambū*, *kapittha*, *mātuluṅga*, and *vilva*. Having rubbed the seeds with that boiled leaf-water, the removal of the husks constitutes the first purification.

Then, having placed a cloth over the net-mesh and covered it with sesame seeds in a vessel, one should fumigate it; this is the second purification. Regarding purification by means of ointments and so forth: an ointment made from the three fruits (*triphalā*) ground with scented water should be applied. From the beginning, one should dry it with the rays of the sun.

Having thus performed the purification of the sesame seeds, one should afterwards perfume them for several days, a fortnight, or ten days—continuously—with *jāti* and other flowers, until the crushed seeds exude the fragrance of the perfumed flowers. Then, the desired perfuming is accomplished.

Then, having extracted the oil by means of a *koluhuyanta* press, the king—so addressed—should carefully place that oil in a glass vessel; for this flower-oil, being unrefined (*apakva*), is intoxicating when used for bathing or anointing.
Now, if one wishes to prepare refined oil (*pakataila*), then one should boil that same oil with an equal amount of fragrant water until the oil releases its froth.
Then, at the time of introducing [the essence], one should grind fragrant substances with eight parts of scented water and apply them; afterwards, one should introduce it until it becomes cool.
Then, having performed the *vedha* (infusion) with musk and other ingredients, one should place it in a glass vessel.

That very substance, mixed with a quarter part of honey-wine (*madāsava*), heated for seven days in a lacquer vessel by the rays of the sun, becomes musk-essence oil (*kastūrikā-taila*). This is the great instruction on the *rasāyana* and other practices for children.

That which is cooked in a bamboo tube becomes "cooked by the sun" (*sūryapāka*); likewise, ointments and other substances cooked in a bamboo tube become divine ointments. Having pierced [the vessel] at the navel and other locations, one should thus prepare the various applications of perfumes and so forth as described in the treatises on perfumery.

Here, the rule for the preparation of perfumes has been stated briefly by the Blessed One. Now, for the sake of the delivery of pregnant women, the thirty-four-fold yantra in its entirety is described, beginning with the words "bhūbhṛt" (mountain-bearer) and so forth: The mountain-bearer (7), the sun (12), the moon (1), the manvantara (14), the eye (2), Madana (3), the Vasus (8), the Rudras (11), the kings (16), the fires (3), the directions (10), the elements (5), the apertures (9), the six (6), the lunar days (15), and the oceans (4) are to be placed in the squares.
Having written the total number [34] in four numbered squares, one should draw the entire Śrīcakra on a measuring board and show it to pregnant women at the time of delivery. || 146 ||

In this context, when there is an obstruction of the fetus for pregnant women at the time of delivery due to the fault of an external *dūtī*, one should then draw this yantra on the back of a measure-vessel; "measure" (*māna*) here refers to an *āḍhaka*.

Having made sixteen squares on its back, one should place the following numbers: seven in the first square (the mountains), twelve in the second (the sun), one in the third (Indra), fourteen in the fourth (Manu), two in the fifth (the eyes), thirteen in the sixth (Madana), eight in the seventh (the Vasus), eleven in the eighth (Rudra), sixteen in the ninth (the kings), three in the tenth (the fires), ten in the eleventh (the directions), five in the twelfth (the elements), nine in the thirteenth (the apertures), six in the fourteenth (the hexad), fifteen in the fifteenth (the lunar days), and four in the sixteenth (the oceans); these are to be established in the sixteenth moving square.

The total number of these figures situated within the four squares, when added together as one sum, is "the ocean and the fire" (34). Having written this entire *yantra* everywhere on the surface of the measuring board at the time of delivery, one should show it to the mother of the child; such is the rule for the release of the fetus.

Now, the *tantra* concerning the infant from birth onwards is stated, beginning with "the Yoginīs": the Yoginīs who are the sixty-four [deities], and those Mothers well-known upon the manifest earth, known as the "Womb" (*garbha*) and the "Days" (*vāsara*), numbering three, nine, ten, eleven, and another five.

Those known as the Month-Names and the Year-Names seize the child upon the entire surface of the earth; they cause colic in the womb and likewise inflict pain during the time of birth in the vaginal passage. (147)

On this surface of the earth, those sixty-four Yoginīs who are manifest are well known as the eight groups of eight Mothers (*mātṛkāḥ*). Among them, twenty-seven are called *garbhāḥ* (the womb-born), being nine times three; ten are called *vāsarāḥ* (the days); eleven are called *māsāḥ* (the months); and fifteen others—consisting of three *pañca*s (fives)—are called *vatsarāḥ* (the years). These sixty-three seize the child on the entire surface of the earth; they cause colic in the womb and likewise inflict pain at the time of birth in the vagina.

Here, among those known as *garbhākhya*, starting from the fifteenth day of conception (*ādhāna*) for fifteen days, they cause *garbhaśūla* (pain in the womb); thereafter, until the ninth month, there are nine; at the time of birth, one; and two that drain the saltiness from the breasts—such is the rule for the *garbhākhya*. For those who have been born, there is the science of pediatrics (*bālatantra*), according to the division of days, months, and years. [From the Adhyātma-tantra: Five cruel youths are established at the joints of the lunar nodes (*parvasandhi*) by virtue of their natural qualities.

O King, those fools indeed seize [the victim] when he has fallen into fear of his guests, and they do not release him at all; for their pacification, various rites such as fire-oblations (homa) and so forth are effective within this maṇḍala. || 148 ||

Regarding the statement, "For children who have been born, there is the *bālatantra* according to the division of days, months, and years," here "child-tantra" refers to the medical treatment for children afflicted by the Mothers (*mātṛ*). In that regard, one should offer the oblation (*bali*) to be described later to those known as the "Days. Starting from the birth day of those who have been born, until the tenth day, on their respective days, one should perform [the rites] for each of the eleven months for the children who cause affliction, up until the eleventh month.

Then, for fifteen years up to the age of fifteen, there is an absence of childhood beyond that; the rule is that in the sixteenth year, [childhood ends] due to the emission of semen (*śukracyavana*). Now, the five cruel ones are described, beginning with the word "cruel": here, in the realm of experience (*bhukti*), at the junctions of the five lunar days (*tithi*) starting from Nandā, the Kaumāras are stationed according to the qualities of the primordial elements (*prakṛti-guṇa*) such as space and so forth. At the junction of the lunar festivals (*parva-sandhi*), they seize the child who has fallen into danger on their own lunar day; by their general power, they do not release the child at all.
"O King"—this is the address used for their pacification in this various maṇḍala; the fire-oblation and other rites to be described hereafter constitute the rule for cruel rites.

Now, the medicinal treatment for pregnant women afflicted by those known as "wombs" (garbha) is stated, beginning with *kuṣṭha*: having ground *kuṣṭha*, *uśīra*, *kaseru*, *tagara*, *kuvalaya*, and the filaments (*kesara*) of the lotus with cold water, it should be administered even when consecrated with mantras and empowered by vajras against womb-afflictions.

In the case of the arrest of fetal development (*garbhastambha*), one should grind the eight feathers of a peacock from a noble lineage and apply them; furthermore, milk, clarified butter, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and curd with jaggery should be given to the women for a period of days. || 149 ||

In this regard, when pregnant women experience uterine pain (*garbha-śūla*), the remedy is as follows: *kuṣṭha*, *uśīra*, *kaseru*, the root of *tagara*, the bulb of the blue lotus (*utpala-kanda*), and the filaments of the lotus (*padma-kesara*). Having ground these substances with water that has stood overnight and cooled, one should empower them with the mantra: "Oṃ āḥ hūṃ, remove, remove the uterine pain of [Name], svāhā!"—this is the mantra called "by the thunderbolts" (*kuliśaiḥ*). The rule is that, having empowered them with this, they should be administered for cases of uterine pain.

Likewise, for the stabilization of the embryo (*garbhastambha*), one should take the eight hairs of a mongoose and the tail-feathers of a peacock (*śikhin*); having ground these with cold water and consecrated them as before, one should administer them.

Then, one should bathe the woman at the foot of a milk-tree (*kṣīravṛkṣa*) using seven *mallika* flowers filled with cow’s milk. One should offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) of milk-rice. This is the rule regarding those [rites] called "the stabilization of the embryo."

Now, the ritual for the *vāsarinīs* (day-demons) is described starting with the word "milk" (*dugdha*) and so forth: here, within ten days, for the sake of pacifying a child who has been seized, milk, clarified butter, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), curd with jaggery, *polikā* cakes, and *modaka* sweets, as well as perfume, flowers, and a lamp, are offered as a *bali* to the *vāsarinīs*. Bathing and incense are to be performed as will be described; this is the rule for the three-night *bali* offering to the *vāsarinīs*.

Now, the ritual for those born in the months is described, beginning with the word "pakve" (cooked): one should perform the five-night rite with cooked food of five varieties, curd and jaggery, *polikā* cakes and *modaka* sweets, as well as perfume, flowers, lamps, and bathing with leaves; furthermore, for the sake of nourishing children born in these months, the entire offering (*bali*) is said to include cow-tusk, ram-horn, deer-claw, hair, and snake-skin incense. || 150 ||

In this context, after ten days, for one month, and thereafter up until eleven months, one should offer a *bali* to the Mothers for the sake of pacifying those born during that month. The "five distinct items" consist of cooked food prepared with ghee—namely *pūrikā* (fried cakes) and *ghṛtapūra* (ghee-filled pastries)—along with *saumālī*, *sevāla*, and *vaṭaka*. Furthermore, there is boiled rice accompanied by curd and molasses, as well as *polikā* and *modaka* sweets.
For the "fragrance," one uses sandalwood; for the "scented flowers," [various blossoms]; and for the "lamp," either sesame oil or ghee.

Regarding "bathing with leaves" as well: one should bathe the child with slightly boiled water made warm with the leaves of the five milk-exuding trees (*pañcakṣīravṛkṣa*), such as the *aśvattha* and others, for a period of five nights; one should perform this entirely until the end of the bathing, and at the conclusion of the bath, one should offer incense to the child consisting of cow-tusk, ram-horn, human nail, deer-hair, human hair, and snake-skin.

Having combined these, one should offer incense with intense charcoal; in the offering to the deity (*devatābali*), the previously mentioned perfumes, incense, and so forth should be given in the four directions and in the center of the village—this rule for children born within a month has been stated for the sake of nourishment. Now, the offering for those one year old is described by the verse beginning with "five foods" (*pañcānna*): five foods, five edibles, the flesh of aquatic creatures, perfume, flowers, a lamp, liquor, the aforementioned incense, and likewise the ritual bathing (*snāpana*) in the directional offering (*digbali*) according to the division of the directions.

O King, for the sake of nourishing children born in the year who have manifested upon the earth, the worship of the Yoginīs certainly becomes necessary after five or three years from conception. (151)

In this context, "year" refers to two months after ten months have passed; therefore, for the sake of pacifying those born in the year who are fifteen years of age and honored by kings, one should offer the annual *bali* consisting of "five foods. Having colored these with turmeric and other substances into white, yellow, red, black, and green, these five foods—known as the five edibles—are the aforementioned cooked foods: the aquatic creature, fish, meat, and flesh, along with the previously mentioned perfumes and so forth.

Having placed all the previously mentioned substances, such as liquor, incense, and so forth, into a bamboo basket, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (*nirmañchana*) three times with an offering of food and lamps in each direction.
Thus, for ten days, offerings should be given in the ten cardinal directions— from Indra to Īśāna, including below and above— at the crossroads in the center of the village.
It is proclaimed on earth for the sake of the nourishment of children born in the year that "O King" is the address;
such is the rule for the worship of those who have completed one year.

Thus, from the womb up to fifteen years—three times five years—the worship of the sixty-three Yoginīs must be performed regularly; otherwise, there will be no pacification and so forth for children. This is the rule for the worship of the Yoginīs.

Now, the symptoms of the defects of those seized by the Mothers are described, beginning with "aṅga" and so forth: There is emaciation of the limbs, pain in the eyes, and the mouth, hands, and feet turn yellow; there is excessive discharge of a yellow color, fever, vomiting, dryness, and fainting.

O King, having recognized these signs, one should perform the rite within the maṇḍala and the fire-oblation (homa). If [the rite] is not performed, the Mothers born of the elements will not release them, due to the power of their innate qualities. || 152 ||

In this case, when a child is seized by the Mothers (*mātṛ*), then there occurs a wasting away of his limbs, pain in the eyes, and the face, hands, and feet become pale; the urine becomes yellowish, fever arises, vomiting occurs, and emaciation as well as fainting ensue—having recognized these signs of the Mothers' affliction in those children, [one should act].

By the use of the word "api" (also), it is indicated that for those seized by cruel planets, rituals such as fire-offerings (*homa*) should be performed within the mandala; otherwise, the aforementioned Mothers born of the elements (*bhūtajā mātaraḥ*), acting under the influence of their natural qualities, will not release them when the *bali* offering has not been given. This concludes the description of the medical treatment.
Now, the signs of death for one seized by the sixty-fourth *kulikā* are stated, beginning with the words "white" (*śveta*) and so forth:
"O Lord of Men, he whose entire body becomes white, who has extremely minute pustules, and whose neck and limbs are crooked, from his mouth, private parts, and anus blood flows."

One should not perform worship toward that [image], for there is indeed a loss of dignity for practitioners who are deluded; death will surely come upon him, and he cannot be protected by gods, humans, or serpents. 153.
In this context, the sixty-fourth *kulikā* abides as the pervasive form at every juncture of all the *yoginīs*, specifically at the junctures of the days, months, and years of the womb.
By her, the body of the child she has grasped becomes entirely white;
and the eruptions (*sphoṭakāḥ*) are extremely subtle, the size of mustard seeds or *rājikā* grains.
The neck becomes crooked; blood flows from the limbs,
or from the mouth, or from the private parts, or from the anus.
Having observed such characteristics, one should not perform worship toward that object. If one does so, then due to the greed of deluded practitioners, a state of insignificance arises.
Why?
Since death certainly exists for him, he cannot be protected by gods, humans, or serpents; such is the rule regarding the signs of death.

This concludes the great section on the elixirs and the science of pediatrics in this chapter. Now, those who have been worshipped in the mandala and who bring about happiness are described, beginning with "the nāgas":
The nāgas, yakṣas, and grahas, as well as those born of the race of Danu, the rākṣasas, piśācas, śākinīs, and the wicked nāgas who delight in human blood and take the form of ḍākinīs.

The Kumbhāṇḍas, the Kṣetrapālas, the Gaṇapatis, the Kṣetra-vetālas, the Siddhas, along with the Apasmāras and the lords of birds—when worshipped in the mandala, they shall become bestowers of supreme happiness. || 154 ||
In this world, for those afflicted by *nāgas* and other spirits, the worship of the *nāgas* and others within the mandala to be described hereafter brings about happiness.
Their many characteristics, as taught in the *Bhūtatantra*, are to be understood through the binding of mudrās; however, how many of these will be mentioned right here in what follows?

Now, for the sake of the fierce worship, the mandala and the location of the mandala are described, beginning with "of the fierce ones" (*krūrāṇām*), etc.: "O Lord of Men, for the purpose of worshipping the fierce ones, the mandala is located outside the village, at a place of trees, in a cremation ground, in the abode of the best of gods, or at the confluence of rivers."

In the measurement of the deities, [the mandala] may be one cubit, two, four, three, ten, nine, or eight; in the center, there is an eight-spoked wheel, which by virtue of its qualities occupies half the portion of the mandala. || 155 ||
In this context, for the purpose of worshipping the fierce deities (*krūra*), the mandala is located outside the village.

It may be at a site with a single tree, in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), in a temple of the supreme gods—that is, a deserted shrine—or at the confluence of rivers; it should measure one cubit, two, or four.
Here, according to one's wealth, the preceptor (*ācārya*) should construct the mandala starting from one cubit, or two, or four, up to as much as a thousand cubits.
Regarding the phrase "by the thirty-three and nine kings": here, the measurement for the nine deities is a mandala of one cubit; for thirteen, it is two cubits;

and "by the king" refers to sixteen, which is four cubits. Starting from these, one should construct [the mandalas] according to one's wealth, up to the limit of one thousand cubits for sixteen hundred and twenty [deities].
Here, in the center of all mandalas, there is either an eight-spoked wheel or a lotus, measuring half the portion of the mandala.

The door shall indeed be one-eighth of the wheel, and the altar (vedī) and the garlands (hārāḥ) shall be half of that; the walls (prākārāḥ) shall be half the size of the altar, and the archway (toraṇa) shall be three times the measurement of the door.

One should make the circular pit (kuṇḍa) consist of a white lotus divided into three parts and filled with white colors; [one should also place] the respective insignia (svacihna) of the deities in their own family directions using the five auspicious colors (pañcaraṅga). ||156||

The door is one-eighth of the circumference of the mandala circle. The door, the altar (vedikā), and the ground for the hanging garlands (hārabhūmi) consist of five lines for the walls; the altar is half [the height] of that, and the jeweled band (ratnapaṭṭikā) is likewise. The turret (niryūha), the wing (pakṣaka), and the cheek (kapola) are according to the measurement of the door. The archway (toraṇa) is three times the size of the door—this is the rule for the characteristics of the mandala. Now, the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) for pacification (śāntika) is described, beginning with "circular" and so forth: here, among the fire-pits to be described, the circular pit is to be taken for pacification; that very same [shape], being divided into three parts, has a diameter of two vitastis and a depth of one vitasti.

"Śi (Si) is composed of semen and impurity"—thus, within the womb [of the mandala], there is a lotus by means of white *rajas* (dust/powder); upon the pedestal (*vedikā*) is a row of lotuses, and outside, below, are the petals of the lotus.
In this way, it is filled with white colors.

Then, one should cause the symbols of the deities to be made with five colors upon the petals of the pericarp of the white lotus, situated in their respective directions according to their family (*kula*) and according to the five Tathāgatas.

The vajra is in the center; according to the family, the sword is in the east, the red jewel in the south, and the white hundred-petalled lotus in the north; in the west is the mark of the wheel. In the southeast is indeed the knife resting upon a lotus petal; in the corner of the Daityas (the southwest) there should be the hook; in the northwest, O King, is the vajra-noose; and on the Rudra petal (the northeast) is the trident. (157)

Regarding "the vajra in the center": as it will be stated here in the passage, "or the vajra in all rites," there is a blue vajra upon the pericarp of the lotus, which is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). On the eastern petal is a black sword, which is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); this occurs according to the [respective] family. On the right is a red jewel, which is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*).
On the left, on the northern petal, is a white hundred-petaled lotus, which is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).
In the west, the yellow wheel-mark is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

On the southeastern petal, the black knife situated on the lotus petal is wind; in the southwestern corner of the Daityas, the red hook is fire; in the northwest is the yellow vajra-noose, which is earth;
on the northern petal of Rudra, the white trident is the water element; and in the center is the vajra, the space element together with consciousness.
At the eastern gate, there is a sword resembling a dark cloud; at the south, a vajra-staff; at the western quarter, the glorious mace prevails; and at the north, the mallet is certainly present.

Having understood this according to one's intention, perform this manifold Kālacakra ritual for as long as necessary—for the sake of sons of barren women, for men struck down by planetary afflictions, and for the purpose of pacification and nourishment. 158.
And at the eastern gate is Khaḍga, black, the Wrathful One who is the Vajra of Envy;
at the southern gate is Vajradaṇḍa, red, the Wrathful One who is the Vajra of Passion;
and at the western gate, in the direction of Varuṇa, is [Śrī]Gadā, yellow, the Wrathful One who is the Vajra of Delusion.
At the northern gate is the white Mudgara, the wrathful Mānavajra;
in the center is the Vajra, the blue wrathful king Dveṣavajra.
From "having known" up to "this is for the sake of nourishment" is easy to understand.

Now, the procedure for bathing those afflicted by planetary influences is described, beginning with the word "kumbha" [jar]: One should perform the bathing with eight jars containing gems, whose mouths are shaped like lotus petals, along with seven uncooked *malla* fruits, water, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and so forth; as well as a sprinkling (*nirmuñcana*) with mustard seeds and other substances.
Having performed a diverse worship with perfumes, incenses, lamps, various fruit juices, white flowers, and cloths, one should then again offer oblations (*homa*) of pacifying materials. || 159 ||
—ga. [The row of lotuses on the pedestal].

In this chapter, the "Great Instruction on Alchemy and the Tantra of Child Protection," there are eight vases at the cardinal directions of the mandala, endowed with the characteristics to be described, containing gems—that is, accompanied by the five precious gems—and joined with the medicinal herbs and other substances to be described.
Regarding the term "petals" (dala), these are the sprouts of milk-producing trees with lotus-like openings; "by them" refers to these.

Likewise, "with seven *mallas*" means with seven unbaked earthen bowls (*sarāva*) accompanied by waters such as the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*); that is, with these seven bowls filled respectively with water, milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugarcane juice, and scented water, one should perform the ritual bath.
Then, [one should do so] with eight jars, including the two jars of *jaya* and *vijaya*, as indicated by the word "also" (*api*).

One should perform the ritual cleansing (*nirmārjana*) with mustard seeds and so forth—first with five lumps of cow dung, then with flaming tufts of grass, mustard seeds and the like, and also with balls of cooked rice and so on.
Then, having performed worship with perfumes and other offerings, and having performed the consecration of the mandala, one should cause [the disciple] to enter the mandala.

There, having bestowed the empowerment, and having performed the water empowerment and so forth using the water from the mandala vase, one should then offer the oblation for pacification (*śāntihavya*).

Milk, grain, sesame and so forth, [clarified] butter, and fuel-sticks of five kinds of milky trees—[one should perform] the removal of evil, the invocation, the sipping of water, as well as the worship and adoration.
O King, one should perform this at all times for the sake of pacification of those afflicted by the Mothers and the thirty-six Yoginīs upon this excellent earth; for this is indeed their worship.
The passage beginning with "milk" (*dugdha*) and so forth is easy to understand.

Furthermore, whatever has not been mentioned [here], all that should be performed by the Master according to the procedure taught in the Chapter on Consecration (*Abhiṣeka-paṭala*); this is the rule everywhere.

Thus ends the sixth great section, the Mahoddeśa on Alchemy and Pediatrics (*Rasāyanādibālatantra*), in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja*, which follows the *Śrī-mūla-tantra*. 6.

The Great Chapter on the Investigation of the Logic of One’s Own and Others’ Views: Selflessness, the ripening of karma, the three worlds, the four truths, and the six destinies; the arising of the twelvefold dependent origination, the Vedas, and the truths; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; the five aggregates, the three bodies, and the innate—likewise, non-inert emptiness: that in which these are proclaimed is the teaching of the Vajrī, revealed with certainty. (161)
Having prostrated before Kālacakra, the Lord of the World and Great Bliss,
I shall set forth somewhat of my own view regarding both our own and other philosophical systems.
ka. bhaṇḍa;
ka. kha. mūla0;
- ka. kha. [this occurs] in the *Vimalaprabhā* commentary on the *Dvādaśasāhasrikā*.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, [the section on] the inner [science], that which was spoken by Mañjuśrī from the *Paramādibuddha*—which accords with the views of both oneself and others—is now expanded upon through a commentary, beginning with the words "Nairātmyā" and so forth.

Here, when examined according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), the established tenets of all philosophical systems are identical for the sake of worldly accomplishment; as it is said: "For by whatever state of being the minds of men are joined, they become absorbed in that very thing, just like a multiform gem."
The intention regarding the nature of things as being "empirical" today is the same; likewise, the analysis of the elements (dhātu), the sense-faculties (indriya), and so forth is identical.

The agent, the instrument, and so on are also the same. There is no difference between the Buddhist and the non-Buddhist [outsider] regarding the principle of emptiness; that distinction lies in [the Buddhist doctrine of] selflessness (nairātmya) and the like.
Here, selflessness is twofold: the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
The ripening of karma is threefold: physical, vocal, and mental.
The three realms of existence are the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

"Destination of the seasons" refers to the six destinies—the destinies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, asuras, and gods; it is the direct manifestation of the twelve-linked dependent origination for those in the six destinies.
"Truth of the Vedas" refers to the four noble truths, characterized by suffering, origin, path, and cessation.
"Twice-ninety" refers to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), which will be explained in what follows.
The "five aggregates" refers to form and so forth.
The "three bodies" refers to the dharma-body and so forth, with the innate body (*sahajakāya*) as the fourth.
Likewise, non-inert emptiness, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, is like a reflected image (*pratisenopama*).

"In which" refers to the three vehicles (*yānatraya*); that which the Teacher proclaims therein—this teaching on selflessness and so forth—is the definitive teaching of the Vajrī. It is by the power of the Buddha's vision, according to the disposition of sentient beings; such is the rule of the Tathāgata’s doctrine. Now, the doctrine of Brahmā and Viṣṇu is stated, beginning with "In which": "In which the Veda is self-born, and [the body] born from a womb arises from the mouth, hands, feet, and so forth, and there is no dharma other than the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*)—that is the teaching of Brahmā."

The self is the agent, as are karma, time, primordial nature, the qualities, emptiness, and even that which has lost its properties; Viṣṇu’s teaching here is that the cause of the fruit is the agent, and it is a doctrine that reveals necessity. 162.

In this system, the Veda is self-existent (*svayambhū*), uncreated, and like space; and regarding the "wombs" (*yoni*) of the various classes, it is said that the mouth of Brahmā is the womb of the Brāhmaṇas, the two arms are the womb of the Kṣatriyas, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) the two thighs are the womb of the Vaiśyas, and the two feet are the womb of the Śūdras. Furthermore, the teaching that "there is no other dharma superior to the Aśvamedha"—meaning that among the means for attaining heaven, there is no other dharma such as giving (*dāna*) superior to the Aśvamedha sacrifice—this is the doctrine of Brahmā. Such is the rule of the Brahmā-system.

In this [chapter], within the *Gītā-dharma* belonging to the system of Viṣṇu, there is the great summary concerning the investigation of the logic of one’s own and others’ philosophical systems (*svapara-darśana-nyāya-vicāra*), as follows: "The agent exists; the self (*ātman*) exists; auspicious and inauspicious karma exists; time exists; the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consisting of earth and so forth exists; the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* exist; emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—the state of the destruction of phenomena—exists. This is established from the passage beginning with, "They say that he who has become one does not see," and so on. The agent is the cause, the bestower of the fruit of what has been performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious. This revealed teaching of necessity is here [attributed] to Viṣṇu in the *Kālacakra*; such is the rule of the Vaiṣṇava system.

Now the doctrine of Īśvara is stated, beginning with "the six paths" and so forth: The six paths, the five principles (*pañcatattva*), the supreme state (*parapada*), the entire lower state (*aparapada*), the body of mantra (*mantradeha*), the essence of knowledge (*vidyātman*), the state of Śiva (*sacchivatva*), the conjunction through the movement toward the three states, the state of renunciation (*tyāgabhāva*), the piercing of the *bindu*, the state of Śiva residing in the body of all things, and the piercing of the twelve knots—all this indeed originates from that wherein the teaching of Śiva is fixed. || 163 ||

In this context, why is the sixfold path (*ṣaṇmārga*) and so forth mentioned alongside the previously stated view of Viṣṇu? Because of the statement from the *Adhyātma*: "The one form is the three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. Furthermore: "The agent is the Self; the action is time; the qualities of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*), emptiness, the destruction of phenomena, and nirvāṇa are the ultimate state (*kāṣṭhāvasthā*)."
The rule is that together with these, the six paths and so forth are to be understood.
Here, in this body, the six paths are those that operate within the six sense objects.

"The five principles" refers to the collection of elements beginning with space; "the supreme state" refers to the sixth element, the element of consciousness; "entirety" means that which has become unified within all the elements; and by the word "and," there is further the mantra-body, which is the reality of mantra consisting of the vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*).

"Vidyā" refers to the reality (*tattva*) of Ānanda and the rest; "Ātman" refers to the eternal reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*); and "Sacchivatva" refers to the all-pervading reality of Śiva (*śivatattva*). For that which is devoid of form, there is a threefold movement of the stages (*pada-gati*): *piṇḍasthā*, *padasthā*, and *rūpasthā*. These belong to the nature of the conceptualizations of body, speech, and mind. The "joining" (*yojana*) refers to the conjunction of these three types of movement of the stages.
Regarding these six paths and so forth, "joining" (*melāpaka*) means their union at the time of arising; "the state of abandonment" at the time of death means their disintegration.

"Breaking the drop is Śiva-hood": here, the breaking of the semen-drop (*śukra-bindu*), characterized by the state of the bliss of emission, is itself Śiva-hood. "Pervading all things" means it extends through the moving and the unmoving.

"The breaking of the twelve knots": here, the twelve zodiac signs inherent in living beings are called "knots"; the divisions of those twelve signs are the year, solstice, season, age-cycle (*yuga*), season (*ṛtu*), month, fortnight, day, hour (*ghaṭikā*), *pāṇīpala*, and breath (*śvāsa*).
All this indeed prevails within that established doctrine (*siddhānta*); that teaching is the teaching of Śiva.

Thus ends the rule of the Śivamata. Here, within these collected discourses on the dharma of the Gītā concerning the Vaiṣṇavas, that which is accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and Naiyāyikas is the assertion that "the Creator exists"—meaning there exists an eternal, partless atom who is the fashioner of all the world. It is not their intention that the creator of all is Brahmā or Viṣṇu; for this very reason, when refuting those two schools later on, it was only the agency of the partless atom that was critiqued, and Viṣṇu’s status as a creator was not challenged in that context.

The Great Chapter on the Investigation of the Logic of One's Own and Others' Views: "There is no Lord, nor even the ripening of karma; rather, the multitude of elements (*bhūtavṛnda*) experiences the objects of the qualities (*guṇa*). In the absence of that [Lord], the fruit is not manifest"—this is to be understood as the teaching of the Teacher of the Immortals (*amaraguru*).

"The Creator fashioned the entire universe, including all moving and non-moving beings, for the sake of the enjoyment of the *Tāyi*s (Jainas). Heaven arises from his satisfaction"—this is indeed the teaching of *Rahmaṇa* (the Muslim God). (164)
Now the Lokāyata doctrine is stated, beginning with "it does not exist" and so forth: Here, for embodied beings, there is no Lord; there is no agent, and thus no ripening of karma either.

Regarding "the qualities and objects": the qualities (*guṇas*) are *sattva* and the others; the objects (*viṣayas*) are smell and the rest. "The collection of elements" refers to earth and the other [elements]; it experiences these. Since that collection of elements ceases at the end of death, there is no fruit of karma.

Just as the power of intoxication arises from the combination of *harītakī*, molasses, and other ingredients, so too is the power of the elements produced by their conjunction. It should be understood that the teaching of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, is clear on this point: "In the absence of that [power], there is no body for the next world. This is the established tenet of the Lokāyata school.

Now, the doctrine of the Mleccha Tāyi (Jina) is stated, beginning with the word "kartā" (the creator): "In this world, everything—whether moving (*cara*), meaning mobile, or unmoving (*acara*), meaning stationary—was created by the Creator (*kartā*) Brahmā (*Rahmāna*).
[The term] 'Tāyi (Jina)' refers to the Mlecchas who wear white garments (*Śvetavāsins*), for the sake of their livelihood."
Heaven results from the propitiation of that *Rahmaṇa*, while hell indeed comes to men from his displeasure;
that aforementioned practice is the rule of the *Tāyi* (Jaina) doctrine.

[154a] Now, the doctrine of the *Kṣapaṇakas* is stated, beginning with "the three times," etc.: there are the three times, the six substances, the nine categories as prescribed, the six classes of living beings, the five other bodies, the vows, the restraints (*samiti*), the states of existence (*gati*), and the divisions of knowledge and conduct.

The soul is indeed the size of the body; through celibacy over immeasurable births, liberation is attained. That in which the measure of liberation is declared above is the teaching of the Jinas. 165.
In this system of the Kṣapaṇakas, the doctrine of *syādvāda*, the conventional usage of permanence and impermanence is established through substance (*dravya*) and modification (*paryāya*).

Among these, "the three times" refers to the past, the future, and the present; and "the six substances" are the soul (*jīva*), matter (*pudgala*), time (*kāla*), space (*ākāśa*), merit (*puṇya* or *dharma*), and demerit (*pāpa* or *adharma*).

Among these, the living being (*jīva*), time (*kāla*), and that which is established by the nine categories—namely, the living being (*jīva*), the non-living (*ajīva*), influx (*āsrava*), restraint (*saṃvara*), and shedding (*nirjarā*)—are eternal like space (*ākāśa*); [the remaining categories are] bondage (*bandha*), liberation (*mokṣa*), and movement (*gati*). The six classes of living beings (*ṣaṭkāya*) are as follows: the class of earth-beings (*pṛthvīkāya*), the class of water-beings (*apkāya*), the class of fire-beings (*tejaḥkāya*), the class of air-beings (*vāyukāya*), the class of plant-beings (*vanaspatikāya*), and the class of mobile-beings (*trasakāya*).

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the internal [chapter], it is said that there are six types of bodies for living beings (*jīva*): the five other bodies and the *āhārika-kāya* (assimilative body), *jyotiḥ-kāya* (luminous body), *naissargika-kāya* (natural body), *upapāduka-kāya* (spontaneously born body), and *carama-kāya* (final body). These are the distinctions of the vows, restraints, states of existence, knowledge, and conduct of living beings. According to the Kṣapaṇakas, there are five vows: first, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*); second, truthfulness (*satya*); third, taking only what is given (*dattādāna*); fourth, celibacy (*brahmacarya*); and fifth, renunciation of all possessions (*sarvaparigraha-parityāga*).

The five restraints (*samiti*) are: restraint in movement (*īryā-samiti*), restraint in speech (*bhāṣā-samiti*), restraint in seeking alms (*eṣaṇā-samiti*), restraint in taking up and setting down objects (*ādāna-nikṣepaṇa-samiti*), and restraint in the disposal of waste (*utsarga-samiti*).
The five types of destinies (*gati-bheda*) are: hell-beings, animals, humans, gods, and liberation (*mokṣa-gati*).

The five types of knowledge (*jñāna-bheda*) are: sensory cognition (*mati*), scriptural knowledge (*śruta*), clairvoyance (*avadhi*), telepathy (*manaḥ-paryeṣaṇa*), and perfect knowledge (*kevalya-jñāna*).

There are thirteen divisions of conduct: the five divisions of vows, the five divisions of carefulness (*samiti*), and the three protections—protection of body, protection of speech, and protection of mind.
This path to liberation has been proclaimed by the Arhats;
the soul (*jīva*) is of the same dimension as the body.

In that doctrine where liberation does not exist for one whose life is eternal across immeasurable births, the measure of liberation is indeed described as being thirty-five hundred thousand *yojanas* in extent and shaped like an umbrella throughout the three worlds; such is the teaching of the Jinas—this is the rule of the Kṣapaṇakas. Now, the refutation of the views of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthikas*) through logical analysis is stated, beginning with "The Veda," etc.: This Veda is not self-existent within the abode of the three worlds; the word "Veda" denotes a meaning. In the past, Brahmā revealed the meaning by means of the word "Veda" through his four mouths.

If the meaning of a word were also non-different from the word itself, then why does the word "fire" not burn the mouth when it is uttered? Therefore, there certainly exists a teacher even regarding an unknown object, as well as regarding a future or a past matter.
When examined here through reasoning, the Veda is not self-existent;
why?
It is said: because the word "Veda" denotes an object.
In this context, it is established that since any word denoting an object is produced through the effort of the throat, palate, and so forth, it is therefore not self-existent (*svayambhū*).

Now, if it is argued that this is not the Vedic word, but rather that the Veda is something else—an eternal entity consisting of all word-meanings merged together within the cavity of the ear, and that this [articulation] is its manifestor—that too is established.

Therefore, he says: If the eternal Veda were here established as being merged (*kalolībhūta*) within the meaning of every word, then when the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) is uttered, there ought to be a clamor within the cavity of the ear; yet this is not the case. Therefore, this proposition—that there is another eternal sound which is all-pervasive and non-different from its object—is futile.
If there were identity between word and meaning, then why does the word "fire" (*agni*), when uttered, not burn one's own mouth?
Thus, it is established that the Veda is not eternal, nor is it identical with its meaning.

Furthermore, it is heard here that when there is an absence of the Vedas— when the Vedic dharma has been destroyed by the Mlecchas— then Brahmā reveals the meaning through his four mouths by means of the ancient Vedic words, such as the recitation beginning with "Indra was the sacrificial animal.
Therefore, it is established in the *Mahoddeśa* on the investigation of the logic of one's own and others' systems that the meaning is one thing and the Veda is another.
Therefore, there exists a teacher who is Brahmā; he is established as a teacher because he knows that which is unknown, the future, and the past.
[The Veda] was established through recitation, through oral transmission.

The Veda is not uncreated like space; it is created here, uttered from the mouth, and due to the difference in vocal organs, it is established by reasoning as being localized. It is recited from the mouths of the twice-born; others claim it is all-pervading.
Since this Veda—which is not accessible to all—is read and written by those of the Śūdra and other castes, it is therefore not an authoritative source for men who are wise and learned. ||167||

Therefore, the Veda is not equal to space; it is produced here, uttered from the mouth, and is restricted by the distinction of its places of articulation. By logic, it is localized, being recited from the mouths of the twice-born; whereas others recite it, and since people of the Śūdra and other castes also read and write it, this Veda is not all-pervading. Consequently, the Veda is not an authoritative means of knowledge for men who are wise and learned. Thus, it is established that the Veda is a product; this is the rule of Mañjuśrī, which should be understood in brief, while it may be known in detail from the treatises on logic (*pramāṇa-śāstra*).

Now, the previously mentioned corruption of the wombs (*yonidūṣaṇa*) of the Brāhmaṇas and others is described: here, it is said that the mouth of Brahmā is the womb of the Brāhmaṇas because they were produced from it;
likewise, the two arms are the womb of the Kṣatriyas;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the two thighs are the womb of the Vaiśyas, and the two feet are the womb of the Śūdras—thus are the four castes.

Of these four, the last caste is the fifth, that of the Caṇḍālas; their origin is not known by the Brāhmaṇas even to this day. Furthermore, is it true that here the Brāhmaṇas were born from the mouth of Brahmā?
Therefore, I ask: are those born from that [same womb] also Brāhmaṇīs? If they were, then they would be sisters, because they have arisen from a single womb.
In this way, would there also be marriage with a sister for Kṣatriyas and the others?
How so?
If that were the case, then the practice of the barbarian dharma would arise;
when the barbarian dharma arises, there is the destruction of the caste system, and from the destruction of the caste system comes hell—this is the logical conclusion.
Furthermore, another point is considered: if there is here a single creator of all beings, then how is it that there are four castes?
Just as a father has four sons whose caste is not distinct from one another, so it is with the castes (*varṇas*).
Now, if there were a distinction among them based on the division of Brahmā’s mouth and other parts [of his body], how could that very [distinction] not be logically untenable?

Just as there is no distinction among the fruits of the *udumbara* tree produced from their roots, middles, or tips, so too no distinction is seen among living beings, even by way of differences in color such as white, red, yellow, or black. Likewise, no distinction is seen through differences in elements (*dhātu*), faculties (*indriya*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), or the acquisition of knowledge (*vidyā-gama*) and so forth. Since this is the case, it is established that birth is not fixed (*anitya*). Thus, the fruit of sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) has been refuted by Śuka. For example: "Having cut down the sacrificial post, having killed the animal, and having made a mire of blood..."

"If it is understood in this way, by whom is heaven reached, and by whom is hell reached? [Adhyātma]. Thus, the statement of Śuka is well-known. Therefore, the Veda is not self-existent (*svayambhū*); nor is it the source of a person's mouth and other [limbs]; nor is there any dharma other than the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). When all such prattle is examined, it is found to be meaningless. Thus, the doctrine of the Brahmans and the doctrine of the Vaiṣṇavas, along with that of the Lord (*Īśvara*), are to be refuted.

Now, the refutation of the doctrine of Īśvara is stated, beginning with "asti" and so forth: "If there exists an Īśvara who is the creator of all, and he alone—and no other—is the enjoyer of the fruits of the world's actions; or if there is no Īśvara who is the performer of actions, and if he were not the creator of everything in every respect; or if another creator, being impelled by him, were the one [to act]—then this dependence of the creator upon another would be total. Therefore, the Īśvara is not the creator who bestows the fruits of good and evil upon living beings, apart from their own karma. [168]
If there exists here an Īśvara who is the creator of all, then how is it that he is not the experiencer of karma, nor anyone else?
For one person eats a cake, while another dies of thirst.
And it is not the case that he who acts is the agent and that which is acted upon is the object; nor is the enjoyer of the fruit of that performed action the agent of the action.
Furthermore, an agent is not established without an action, just as one is called a potter because he makes a pot.
Thus, the principle is that he who performs an action is the agent;
it is said [in response]: "Nor is the Lord the agent of action, for He is an independent instigator.
If, in this case, He is not the agent of action, then the claim that He is the "omnipresent creator of all" is meaningless.
In this world, if an agent performs an action while being impelled [by another], then that agent is dependent on another.

For one who is dependent on another, how could the instigator not exercise restraint when a contrary action has been committed? Without independence, independence is indeed pervaded by God; thus, for those who maintain the existence of an agent, the absence of the fruit of action would be established, but such is not the case. Therefore, there is no agent whatsoever—neither God nor anyone else—who bestows the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious deeds upon living beings apart from their own karma. Thus, the experience of the fruits of one's own actions is established even without [an external] agent.

Now, the dependence of an independent agent upon other factors is stated, beginning with the word "earth": If, at the outset, the oceans of earth, water, fire, and air do not exist here in space for the agent, then in the absence of material substance, the omniscient creator cannot produce the universe devoid of objects. O Lord of Men, everything arises from conjunction alone; the form of action does not come about by the mere will of this agent who is devoid of objects, for he is neither perceptible nor imperceptible. Thus, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such an agent.

In this regard, if atoms of earth and so forth do not exist here in space (kha) at the beginning for the Creator, then, in the absence of material substance, He—being devoid of objects and partless—cannot create the universe. How then can He be the creator of all? Since there is no means of valid cognition, whether direct perception or indirect inference, to establish this object-less Creator, it follows by logic that the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings arises solely from the conjunction of substances, and not through the will of the Creator in the form of an action; such is the refutation of the Creator’s will.

[In this] chapter, the great summary concerning the investigation of the logic of one's own and others' philosophical systems; now, dependent origination is explained, beginning with "from conjunction," and so forth: From the moonstone, water arises due to conjunction; in a mirror, the reflection of an object appears; sourness arises from the cause of a sour thing, as does its opposite from that which possesses sweetness; a sprout arises from pure seed; iron becomes a needle through magnetism; and even the spinning [of a wheel] occurs not by will. Of these things, no such power was created by anyone within the abode of the three worlds. (170)

In this world, the production of all things arises from conjunction (*saṃyoga*); having obtained this, that is produced through conjunction. For example, from the conjunction with moonlight, water arises from the moonstone (*candrakānti*); by the word "and" (*ca*), fire arises from the sunstone (*sūryakānti*);
and due to the conjunction with an object in a mirror, the reflection of that object arises.
Just as the tongue of one person becomes numb due to the contact of another eating sour food— arising from that sour cause—
and just as an echo arises from the contact of sound within a well or similar place,
so too does the sprout arise from the pure seed.
It would stand [due to] the conjunction of earth, water, and so forth;

"from the magnet" means from a magnetic stone (*kāntapāṣāṇa*), whereby the whirling of an iron rod occurs. Because it is "due to conjunction," no such thing among these objects occurs by will; rather, this is the inherent power (*śakti*) of things.
The production [of the world] by someone is established through the cognition that it was not created by anyone else within the abode of the three worlds.
He says: "In this world, an effect does not arise without a cause; therefore, a cause exists. From this, it follows that God and so forth are established.
To this he replies: "In this case, regarding the effect that arises from a cause, is that effect pre-existent (*satkārya*) or non-existent (*asat*)?"

The effect does not exist within the cause; for instance, clay and other such materials do not constitute the causes of an already existing jar, because it already exists. Nor is the effect non-existent, because it is not non-existent, like a tortoise’s hair. Likewise, threads, the shuttle, the loom, and so forth do not constitute the causes of a cloth.
An effect that is of both natures does not exist, because of mutual contradiction:
that which is existent cannot be non-existent, and that which is non-existent cannot be existent, due to this contradiction.
Therefore, it is established that the effect is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent in the cause. He says this:
here, by the negation of the cause, there is also the negation of the effect; from the negation of both, the non-existence of everything is established.
He says this: here, the non-existence of everything is not [absolute], because it is relative to another.

In this case, the causality that belongs to a cause is conceived only in relation to an effect, and the effect is likewise conceived only in relation to a cause. Thus, because both are mutually dependent, it follows that both would be causes.

Since both would be causes, there would be an absence of an effect; in the absence of an effect, there would be an absence of a cause, because a cause is dependent upon an effect. Consequently, due to this lack of necessity, it follows that there is no causality at all.

Thus, it is established that all [proposed] causes, such as Īśvara and the rest, are non-definitive and lack causal status. He states: "The establishment of a cause is not relative; for that which is a cause is indeed a cause, and that which is an effect is indeed an effect—this is established, O Venerable One. This refers to their non-definitive nature (*aniyatatva*).
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the internal [practice], it says: "Here, the claim that 'success comes from your will, but not from mine' is indeed a state of partiality.
If success were achieved through will, then it would also be achieved through my will.
That which is non-existent for you would be non-existent for me as well, because it is devoid of logical justification."

He said: "According to our authoritative scripture (āptāgama), this is our established tenet (samaya). It is not permissible to say that a tenet is 'unestablished' simply because it is a tenet; for so it has been stated by those learned in the treatises."

He said: "Sometimes a logical argument (*yukti*) is stated here: 'Because nothing can arise from every [possible] material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), and because a capable [cause] produces only that which it is capable of producing, the pre-existence of the effect (*satkārya-siddhi*) is established. He replied: "In this case, your reason (*hetu*) is futile."
How so?
If your thesis possesses the characteristics of a proof, then it will prove my thesis as well;
if your thesis possesses the characteristics of a refutation, then it will refute my thesis as well—just as fire burns both, and not only one.
In this context, for those who maintain that sound is eternal, the proposition is: "Sound is eternal"; what is the reason?
"Because it is formless";
what is the example?
Like space; just as space is eternal because it is formless, so too is sound. Therefore, he says that sound is established as eternal.
[The opponent replies: This is not a valid proposition (*pratijñā*), for the other party will also say: "Sound is impermanent; what is the reason?"
What is the example for "because of being produced"?

It is like a jar; just as a jar is produced from clay, a staff, a wheel, a string, and the exertion of a person's hand, so too sound is generated through effort by means of the throat, palate, and other organs. Therefore, it is established that sound is impermanent.
Therefore, the establishment of an effect does not occur through the mere designation of a reason;
rather, that which speaks according to reality would be the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not the designation of a reason—
thus, the reason is futile.
Furthermore: for those who hold the thesis (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) does not become a prover because it contradicts the proposition (*pratijñā*).

At the time when the proposition exists, the reason does not exist; at the time when the reason exists, the proposition does not exist. Therefore, to what would that reason belong, since it cannot coexist with the proposition due to their non-simultaneous nature?
At the time when there is the syllable *pra*, at that time there is neither the syllable *ati* nor the syllable *ajña*;

likewise for the syllables *pa*, *ra*, and *a*. Just as it is not possible to perform the function of a son by means of a son who is unborn or dead—this being the case with every single letter—so too it is with the cause.
Therefore, because the cause is perceived, the effect does not exist [independently], since it is established through non-causality;
for "non-causality" (*ahetutaḥ*) and "cause" (*hetu*) or "reason" (*kāraṇa*) are not different in meaning.

Thus, the effect is not in the cause, nor does the effect arise without a cause. Consequently, it is established that the effect does not exist from itself, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause; this constitutes the refutation of the agent and the eternal cause.

Now, the refutation of the self (ātman) is stated, beginning with "If": If the self were all-pervading, how could it experience the suffering of separation from loved ones? And if this [self] were eternal, why does it fall into such a state when struck by the arrows of Love?

And if it were active, how does it fall into this stupor at the time of sleep? Thus, indeed, it would have to be all-pervading and omnipresent; yet previously this self was not active. Therefore, the self [as conceived by you] does not exist.

In this [chapter], the Great Exposition on the Investigation of the Logic of One’s Own and Others’ Views: If the self were all-pervading, how could it experience the suffering of separation from loved ones?
Here, that self which is all-pervading is one; for such a one, there is no suffering of separation from loved ones.
Thus, through the suffering of a single sentient being, there would be suffering for all sentient beings, because the self is all-pervading.

If, on the other hand, the self were manifold, then that which is manifold would lack omnipresence. Furthermore, if this [self] were eternal, then when it is struck by the arrows of Love, what state could it possibly undergo? For that which is eternal here has no change of state, because it is devoid of modification. Therefore, how can one struck by the arrows of Love undergo these ten states of passion? Consequently, the self must be non-eternal, due to its association with modification.

"If it was active, how does it fall into this state of stupor at the time of sleep?"—if, during the waking state, it were active (as indicated by the word "and" [ca] meaning it is also eternal), then how could it fall into stupor—that is, become devoid of activity—at the time of sleep?

Thus, when investigated with absolute rigor, it follows that [the soul] would be either omnipresent, or else it would not be all-pervading, nor the master, nor eternal, nor active; and thus it is established that it is not the Self.

Now the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is proclaimed: "There is no self, yet there is arising; there is the fruit of the unwholesome and the wholesome, though it is devoid of an agent. There is no goer, yet there is the journey toward liberation. There is bondage in its entirety, yet there is no one who is bound. There is both existence and non-existence, and there is a state of being that is momentary and devoid of intrinsic nature. This is my word of truth; this word of truth is not subverted by the words of gods or serpents, even when they employ all their powers."
In this context, from the cessation of dependently originated phenomena there is arising, and from arising there is cessation.
Thus, for phenomena characterized by cessation, there is no self (*ātman*), because of the absence of anything belonging to a self (*ātmīya*);
yet for phenomena characterized by arising, there is occurrence, due to the taking up of rebirth.

It will be stated later that the establishment of these [entities] is through examples such as Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*); it must be explained that there is both an inauspicious and an auspicious fruit.

For things whose nature is to arise, there is an auspicious or inauspicious fruit; for things whose nature is to cease, there is no fruit because they are devoid of an agent—the meaning being "without an agent."

Because of such statements as, "There is no goer; there is a collection of phenomena subject to cessation, yet there is a going toward liberation, and for others there is another form of that," it follows that the entirety—the whole—is bondage, and there is no one bound. Here, there is bondage for those things characterized by arising, but there is no one bound among the phenomena characterized by cessation. Furthermore, both existence and non-existence exist; there is an existence that is momentary, devoid [of permanence], and lacking intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

In this context, there exists for the Buddhas a reality that is a fusion of existence and non-existence, devoid of intrinsic nature, free from the conceptualization of substantiality, comparable to a reflected image, devoid of momentariness, and free from arising and ceasing; for the sake of turning the Wheel of Dharma, this is my word, liberated from all grasping, which cannot be refuted by the words of the gods, the serpents, or by means of logical collections.

In this context, just as a wrestler seized by a demon cannot kill a wrestler who is free from that demon, so too those seized by the demon of conceptual construction cannot kill one who is free from the demon of conceptual construction; thus, the proof of selflessness and so forth is stated here in brief. The rule is that the detailed exposition is to be understood from the extensive scriptures.

Now, the refutation of the views of the Vaibhāṣikas, Sautrāntikas, and Yogācāras is stated, beginning with "He who [speaks of] reality," and so forth: He who asserts that the reality called the *pudgala* resides within the body because of its intrinsic nature is ruined; for he is a proponent of conventional truth who, not knowing the ultimate truth, considers it non-existent.

O [you who follow] the teachings of cessation (*nirodhadharmāṇām*), the Vijñānavādin who considers all the three worlds to be consciousness alone is ruined, even though he is not ruined; he is one who propounds the non-duality of compassion and emptiness. // 173 //
