In this context, there is this adherence to a position by these non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) and Buddhists alike; through that adherence to their own position, there also occurs an adherence to the opposing position, whether by way of its similarity (*sadharmya*) or its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Regarding those of immature intellect, here the Vaibhāṣika who asserts that the reality called the *pudgala* is subtle because it has that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [is refuted by the statement] "that is destroyed.

Here, if there exists a *pudgala* that is a constituent of rebirth (*upapattyaṅgika*) and resides within the *pudgala*, then its intrinsic nature must be stated: is it of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna-svabhāva*) or of the nature of non-knowledge (*ajñāna-svabhāva*)?
If it has the nature of cognition, then it is impermanent; for here, when the cognition of a jar has ceased, the cognition of a cloth arises, and therefore it is impermanent.
Alternatively, if it has the nature of cognition, then for one who lacks cognition there would be an absence of pleasure and pain;
therefore, when examined from the perspective of its own nature, that Vaibhāṣika is ruined.

"In this regard, there is a person who carries the burden; I do not say he is a knower (*jñānin*), nor do I say he is not a knower"— this statement of the Blessed One is to be explained in detail in the *Jñānapaṭala*,
and thus it is a figurative expression (*arthavāda*) from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).

Regarding the statement, "For one who does not know the ultimate truth considers that which is non-existent," how is it that the proponent of the apprehension of objects such as blue and so forth is lost here according to conventional reality? One who does not know the ultimate truth considers the *jñānakāya* (body of gnosis) to be non-existent, like the son of a barren woman. Thus it is said: "Space and the two types of cessation—these three unconditioned phenomena are eternal."
All conditioned phenomena are momentary, empty of self, and devoid of an agent.
The cognition born of the senses, being devoid of mental aspects (nirākāra), perceives the collection of atoms directly;
this is considered the Vaibhāṣika doctrine, the majesty of the ocean of the Kāśmīra school.
Thus,
those objects of the senses which produce the knowledge of their own forms are visible; however, space and cessation are like the son of a barren woman and are similar to space.

“Formations (saṃskāras) are not insentient, nor do they persist through the three times; form that is non-existent and non-obstructive—thus the Sautrāntikas understand. Therefore, non-obstructive form is the knower of the three times.

If [Buddhahood] were like the extinction of a lamp, then, in the absence of non-obstructive form (*apratigha-rūpa*), one would not be omniscient; without the four bodies (*kāya*), Buddhahood would not exist through a merely localized body (*prādeśika-kāya*).

Here, without the non-obstructive body, the Buddha’s display of all modes of miraculous power (*sarvākāra-ṛddhi*) would not occur, his utterance of all sounds would not take place, knowledge of the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*) would not function, and everything such as the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) would be fruitless—such is the fault in the position of the Sautrāntikas.

Now, the fault regarding the proponents of Yoga (Yogācāras) is stated: "The proponent of consciousness (Vijñānavādin), considering the entire threefold world to be consciousness alone, says: 'There is no such thing as a composite whole, nor do atoms exist;
the appearance is without objective support, resembling the experience of a dream.'"
Because it is devoid of the grasped and the grasper, consciousness is proclaimed by those who have reached the further shore of the ocean of the Yogācāra doctrine to be ultimately real.

[In this] chapter, the Great Summary on the Investigation of the Logic of One’s Own and Others’ Views: Therefore, through the investigation of consciousness by means of its nature as being neither one nor many, the proponents of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*) are destroyed due to their separation [from reality].

Here, if the triple world is mere consciousness and there exists no external object-form other than cognition, then how does an external form appear as an apprehended nature to the eye-consciousness which is the apprehender? He says: "By the power of the latencies of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*)."

He asked: "Is there no removal of this ignorance for consciousness? Is ignorance not characterized by the three realms (*traidhātuka*)? If ignorance were not characterized by the three realms, then it would be characterized as transcending *saṃsāra*; yet this is not the case for this Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Therefore, this ignorance is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of *saṃsāra*, and *saṃsāra* is also characterized by the three worlds (*tribhuvana*). The three worlds are the three realms, and the three realms are merely consciousness (*vijñānamātra*)."

Thus, ignorance is mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*), and mere consciousness is its very nature (*tadātmakatva*). Because it is of that nature, there is no removal of ignorance, since consciousness consists solely of ignorance.

Now, if the triple world (*traidhātuka*) were not merely consciousness, then there would be a loss of one's thesis; therefore, the state of being "merely the triple world" is unestablished. Now, the fault regarding momentary destruction and arising is stated: Here, this destruction and arising of phenomena that occurs from a single moment—does that occur without stability (*sthiti*)? If destruction and arising occurred without stability, then it would also apply to a rabbit’s horn.

Now, if there is duration from arising, destruction from duration, and arising from destruction, then in this way, duration, destruction, and arising do not possess oneness; they must have distinct characteristics. For at the time when there is duration, there is neither arising nor destruction; at the time when there is destruction, there is neither arising nor duration; and at the time when there is arising, there is neither duration nor destruction! "Time" here means a moment (*kṣaṇa*). If these were to exist at one and the same time, there would be an identity of birth, old age, and death. Furthermore:

In this context, regarding the destruction and arising of a phenomenon within a single moment: does that arising of a subsequent phenomenon occur from a preceding phenomenon that has ceased, or from one that has not ceased? If the arising occurs from a ceased phenomenon, then it would be like the arising of a subsequent lamp from a lamp that has already ceased. If, however, the arising occurs from one that has not ceased, then it would be like the arising of a lamp from a lamp that has not ceased; thus, there would be an arising from that very same thing. In this way, through arising from arising, there would be a series of consciousnesses like a garland of lamps.

Therefore, it cannot be said that another [consciousness] arises from the cessation of a prior consciousness, nor can it arise from one that has not ceased; for since they are mutually exclusive, there is no identity between them, even when mixed.
Consequently, the Mādhyamika says: "That consciousness is also not accepted by the wise as ultimately real, because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, like a lotus in the sky."
“The Madhyamikas know reality to be neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither; it is free from the four extremes.
Thus, he is one who has not lost the position that [others] have lost.

Who is he? He is the proponent of the non-duality of compassion and emptiness, for whom it is the established rule of the Buddhist tenets that here compassion is without objective support and free from conceptual construction, while emptiness is endowed with the excellence of all aspects and exists throughout the three times for the sake of fully knowing the three times.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, [the section on] the internal [tantra], the refutation of the experience of past karma and the accumulation of present karma is now stated, beginning with the words "The living being" (*jantuḥ*), etc.: "If a living being experiences past karmas performed here in this life in another birth, then there would be no destruction of karma for humans through one birth after another; there would be no exit from cyclic existence due to immeasurable existences, and there would certainly be no entry into liberation. This indeed is the doctrine of the Tāyins, which is devoid of other births. (174) In this regard, for those whose view is that a living being experiences karmas performed previously in this birth, or karmas performed here in this life in another birth—if it were so, then there would be no destruction of karma for humans through one birth after another, because of the continued experience of the fruits of karma.

Thus, there would be no exit from saṃsāra through immeasurable births, nor would there ever be entry into liberation; this indeed is the prevailing doctrine of the Tāyins (Jainas). However, the doctrine of the Mlecchas among the Tāyins is that one is liberated from another birth;
[they hold] that by the decree of Rahmaṇa, a human who has died experiences either happiness or suffering in heaven or hell with this very human form.
Therefore, the rule is that [the self] is devoid of other births.

Now, the refutation of the Cārvāka doctrine is stated, beginning with "by the elements" (bhūtaiḥ): "By the elements—just as the power of intoxication arises from various substances—why indeed would the witnessing consciousness not arise in trees through the conjunction of earth, water, fire, air, and space?"

These beings possess no power of their own; rather, it is the power of the combination of elements. This statement of the Cārvākas does not yield the fruit of happiness for men who have lost their way. (175) If it were established here that the sentient mind of humans arises from the previously mentioned elements—earth and so forth—united together, just as the power of intoxication arises from the combination of *harītakī*, molasses, and *dhātaka* flowers, then why would trees, which are likewise composed of earth and the other elements united together, not also possess a sentient mind? [This follows] from the combination of elements.

Now, if it is argued that these stationary beings lack the power of sentience (*jantuśakti*), then the power of the conjunction of elements (*bhūtasaṃyogaśakti*) would be utterly false. Therefore, this statement of the Cārvākas does not yield the fruit of happiness for men who have lost their way; such is the rule for the refutation of the Lokāyata doctrine. Now, the refutation of the Kṣapaṇaka doctrine is stated, beginning with "the soul" (*jīva*): If the soul (*jīva*) is of the same size as the body, then upon the cutting off of hands and feet, why does it not diminish? Is it eternal, or because of the influence of the body does it become minute? And how could it attain bulkiness?

Released from karma, he departs from saṃsāra for the state of bliss situated at the summit of the world; and though the three worlds are composed of atoms, they are eternally constant and not subject to time. [This concludes] the Great Chapter on the Investigation of the Logic of One's Own and Others' Views. Here, in the doctrine of the Kṣapaṇakas, it is established that the soul (*jīva*) is eternal and that its size is equal to the body. If this is so, then when a limb such as a hand or foot is severed from the body, does the soul perish? [No,] because there is no absence of the soul even when a part of the physical form has been cut off.

If the body were eternal, it would have to be minute due to its power of manifestation, because of the assumption of a subtle body; yet, because of the assumption of a gross body, how does it attain grossness? In this regard, it is established that whatever is eternal is unchanging, and whatever is changing is non-eternal. To this, he says: "By way of substance and mode, it is both eternal and non-eternal"—this is the doctrine of *syādvāda*. He explains: just as gold is eternal and non-eternal by way of the substance and the earring, so too the soul-substance is eternal by way of substance and non-eternal by way of modification; such is the *syādvāda*.
"In some places the soul is powerful; in some places the karmas are powerful.
For both the soul and the karma, there are enmities bound from the past.
Thus he explains the meaning of this verse, beginning with "in some places."
Regarding the matter of liberation, the soul (*jīva*) is powerful through the power of the knowledge of absolute isolation (*kaivalya-jñāna*);

however, in certain respects within the cycle of the four states of existence (*caturgati-saṃsāra*), karma is powerful through the power of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Thus, it is established that there is a mutual enmity between the soul and karma bound since beginningless time.

Therefore, the final doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that [the soul] consists of the nature of arising and passing away of substance (*dravya*) while endowed with its own qualities (*svaguṇa*), and not otherwise.

He said: "Is there identity or difference between substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*)? If here there is identity, then there is no distinction between substance and mode; if, however, there is difference, then the mode would exist without the substance, yet this is not observed—just as a cloth does not exist without its threads.
Thus, for genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*) as well, there is the fault of their conjunction being either eternal or non-eternal."
There is no unity between the eternal and the non-eternal due to their mutual contradiction, just as there is none between the dissimilar and the similar;

therefore, it is established that the substance consisting of the soul, its birth, and so forth, is non-eternal. Likewise, liberated from karma through the cycle of existence, one goes to the state of bliss which abides at the summit of the world.

In this Siddhānta of the Kṣapaṇakas, there is only one triple-world (*tribhuvana*); a second does not exist. Therefore, this triple-world is without beginning or end, devoid of arising and passing away, entirely composed of diamond (*vajramaya*), and shall never undergo destruction.

For if this world were to perish, then, due to the absence of any other triple-world, where would all living beings reside? For that reason, it is eternal. The soul (*jīva*) is also eternal; being liberated from karma through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), it proceeds to liberation (*mokṣa*), the state of bliss measuring four million five hundred thousand *yojanas*, which is devoid of matter (*pudgala*). Thus it is established.

He said: "In this world, the three realms are produced from atoms (*aṇu*), and not without atoms; and by the word 'and' (*ca*), liberation (*mokṣa*) is also included. Therefore, how can it be eternal? For even that which is constructed of atoms and is itself permanent does not become eternal—always, at all times—but will go to destruction under the power of the time of dissolution (*saṃhāra-kāla*). Because of its destruction, the destruction of the established doctrines (*siddhānta*) will also follow; this is proven by the principle of logic. Furthermore:"

Here, among the previously mentioned six classes of living beings (*ṣaḍjīvakāya*) and their dispositions (*leśyā*), there is the life-force (*jīva*) of plants (*vanaspati*). Does that [life-force] experience pleasure or pain under the influence of karma as a single entity within each individual plant-body, or as many? To this he says: In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the inner science (*adhyātma*): A single life-force (*jīva*) grasps a single person (*pudgala*), by whose power the designation "living" (*jīvitasaṃjñā*) is established for plants such as grain and so forth. If the life-force did not exist, then how could the term "tree" (*pādapa*) be established? Furthermore, it is established that non-living wood does not drink water and produce flowers and the like according to the seasons.

He said: "If, in this world, there were a single soul (*jīva*) in each individual person, then when a stalk of sugarcane is cut into many pieces, that eternal soul would have entered one of those pieces by the power of karma, contracting [to fit].

What [parts] would have been abandoned by it? Yet, when examined through reasoning, this is not tenable; for why is it that when those pieces are planted back in the earth, sprouts and so forth are seen to emerge from every single piece?"
Therefore, it is established that the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of trees is their capacity for sprouts and so forth; this concludes the refutation of the Kṣapaṇaka doctrine.

The extensive and manifold tenets of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), which must be rejected by means of many treatises on valid cognition (*pramāṇaśāstra*) and by the Madhyamaka, [are here concluded].

"That which is equal to the word of the Perfect Buddha, whether by way of convention (*saṃvṛti*) or ultimate reality (*vivṛti*), is not to be criticized"—this is the rule of the Blessed One, the *Ādibuddha* of the *Kālacakra*.

As it is said: "For the sake of primordial knowledge, the *Kālacakra* reveals the great teaching according to the mental dispositions of men, whether they be soft or hard, through the power of their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Since the mind indeed becomes colored by objective attachments like a crystal due to proximity, therefore no phenomenon whatsoever—whether belonging to one's own or another's lineage—should be criticized by a yogi. (177)

—One's own power is thus established. This concludes the great summary on the investigation of the logic of viewing oneself and others. Dharma is that which benefits sentient beings; adharma is that which causes harm even when devoid of an object. Violence, though sanctioned by the authority of the Vedas, does not yield the fruit of happiness but always yields suffering. True friendship is that which brings supreme bliss even from the words of a fool and is affectionate toward all beings. Therefore, O King, with your mind, cultivate the single contemplation of the welfare of sentient beings as being devoid of intrinsic nature. (178)

In the heavenly realm I am Indra; on earth I am the preceptor of the thirty gods; in Pātāla I am the King of Serpents, bowed to by the race of *phaṇis*; I am the all-pervading and supreme one. I am knowledge; I am the Buddha, the Lord of Sages; I am the imperishable, supreme, and all-powerful *vajrayoga* of yogins; I am the Veda, the sacred syllable *oṃ*. O King, come to me for refuge with your whole being! (179)

Thus concludes the rule for taking refuge. Now follows the homage to Sūryaratha: "You are my mother, you are my father, you are the teacher in this world, and you are my kinsman; you are my good friend, you are my lord, you are the creator, the benefactor, and the remover of sins. You are the state of all prosperity, you are the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya), you are the abode of excellent qualities, and you alone are free from all defects. You are the wish-fulfilling gem for the poor and the helpless; O Lord of Jinas, I have come to you for refuge. (180)
Thus ends the second chapter, the Determination of the Inner Self, in the glorious Mahākālacakra extracted from the glorious Ādibuddha. ||2||
Thus, Sūryaratha, having praised the Blessed Mañjuśrī with a salutation to the Guru and having placed his two feet upon his head, sat down again on his own seat.

Thus ends the seventh great chapter, "The Investigation of the Logic of One's Own and Others' Views," in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Śrī-mūla-tantra*. 7.
This commentary on the Adhyātmapaṭala is completed. ||2||

The Sanskrit translation of the above-mentioned Tibetan passage: "In the treatises on valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or in the Madhyamaka treatises, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are to be refuted by means of the extensive methods of refutation therein set forth;

however, those other than the non-Buddhists who, having accepted either the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) or the ultimate (*paramārtha*), establish their own position in accordance with the words of the Buddha, are not to be refuted at all.
— *Śrīmahākālacakratantrarāja*, Chapter Ka.
Ka. Second Chapter.

In the *Vimalaprabhā* commentary on the glorious Tantra, in the first chapter, the world that has become a fit vessel [for the teaching] was clearly indicated; the distinctions regarding the origin, the configuration, and the measurements of the wheel [of the universe] have been explained.
Her own body, which is peerless and equal to those [distinctions], is clear in its perception of the reality of the objects of experience.
